Because SPI-1 expression is a cooperative trait in which a minority of invasive SPI-1ON cells benefits the wider bacterial population, inflammatory infection models readily select for permanently avirulent "cheater" mutants defective in SPI-1 function. However, while frequently observed during acute infection, isolates from persistent human NTS infection rarely exhibit obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function mutations, raising the question of whether SPI-1 contributes to bacterial fitness beyond induction of acute intestinal inflammation and tissue persistence. Here, we addressed this question using a metabolically attenuated yet epithelial-invasive auxotrophic Salmonella serovar Typhimurium (STm) vaccine strain (STmAux) that persistently colonizes the murine intestine without causing overt inflammatory pathology or tissue infection while retaining SPI-1-dependent host interaction and immunogenicity. Following within-host evolution for up to five years, STmAux populations did not accumulate classical hilD or other obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function cheater mutants. Instead, parallel evolution repeatedly targeted the BarA/SirA two-component regulatory system, closely mirroring previous observations in persistent human NTS infections. Functional analyses demonstrated that evolved barA and sirA alleles tune rather than abolish SPI-1 function by sharply reducing the proportion of SPI-1ON cells while preserving their individual epithelial invasion competence. Reconstructed in a prototrophic strain background, early evolved isolates retained full intestinal and systemic virulence in vivo despite exhibiting strongly reduced SPI-1ON frequencies in vitro. Remarkably, identical sirA mutant alleles also emerged in a hilD-deficient strain background, indicating that selection for these adaptive variants is not contingent on canonical HilD-dependent SPI-1 activation. During prolonged evolution, additional mutations accumulated that were associated with loss of systemic virulence despite preservation of epithelial invasiveness, suggesting subsequent adaptation affecting host-interaction pathways beyond SPI-1-mediated virulence. Together, these findings identify regulatory tuning of the BarA/SirA control network as a conserved evolutionary trajectory during prolonged NTS persistence. Rather than favoring classical cheater-driven loss of virulence functions, long-term adaptation preserves substantial SPI-1-dependent host interaction while reducing the proportion of phenotypically virulent SPI-1ON cells.

papers.title: Sensory context gates oxytocin effects on auditory processing in macaques
papers.abstract: Oxytocin shapes social perception, yet its neural effects vary substantially across experiments and clinical trials yield inconsistent results. A key unresolved question is whether oxytocin modulates early sensory processing in primates as a function of sensory context. Using high-resolution pharmacological fMRI in two awake rhesus macaques, we compared systemic oxytocin with saline during unimodal auditory and audiovisual tasks. During unimodal auditory stimulation, oxytocin attenuated sound-evoked responses throughout auditory core, belt and associative regions for both vocal and non-vocal sounds, while distributed sound-category information remained decodable. In contrast, when the same vocalizations were presented within an audiovisual task, this attenuation disappeared and responses increased in a restricted set of auditory core and belt regions. Oxytocin also reorganized resting-state coupling among auditory, visual and prefrontal systems and changed how evoked responses covaried across runs. Together, these findings suggest that oxytocin modulates sensory response magnitude and inter-regional coordination in a context-dependent manner rather than uniformly enhancing social signals.

papers.title: Moderately acid-tolerant Nitrospira strains obtained by single-colony isolation on plates
papers.abstract: Nitrospira are difficult to cultivate, and pure cultures are mainly obtained by dilution-to-extinction combined with other methods, a process that usually takes years to over a decade. Here, we isolated three Nitrospira strains from activated sludge and sediment within one year using conventional single-colony isolation. Pure cultures of two strains could grow and reform single colonies within 25-60 days on all three types of plates prepared with agar, agarose, and gellan gum. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed them within lineage I and indicated that they represent potential novel species, with the provisional names Nitrospira monocolonialis for strain Z02 and Nitrospira limosa for strains Z47 and Z70. All three strains were moderately acid-tolerant, with a minimum tolerable pH of 5.0; strain Z02 showed the highest acid tolerance, retaining 74% of its activity at pH 5.5. Strain Z02 was also highly adaptable to oxygen concentrations of 1-21%, retaining 78% and 85% of its maximum growth rate at 1% and 21% O2, respectively. Compared with the representative lineage I strain Nitrospira defluvii, all three strains contain superoxide dismutase encoding genes and some unique genes. Comparative transcriptomic analysis suggested that strain Z02 upregulated genes involved in stress responses, cell envelope modification, and putative type IVa pilus systems under acidic condition. Overall, this study provides the first demonstration that Nitrospira can grow on plates prepared with common gelling agents and form single colonies within a short period, and that Nitrospira can also tolerate moderately acid conditions.

papers.title: Single-nucleus analysis reveals renal STAT1/CEBPB signaling as a modifiable relay of proinflammatory FGF23 effects in diabetic kidney disease
papers.abstract: Background Circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) rises dramatically in chronic kidney disease, particularly in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). At high concentrations, and with declining Klotho, FGF23 has been linked to renal inflammation. The cell types and transcriptional programs mediating these off-target actions remain undefined. We asked whether the diseased kidney responds to FGF23 differently from the healthy kidney, and whether any disease-specific response could be targeted. Methods Male and female DBA/2J mice received streptozotocin or vehicle to induce DKD. On day 56, mice received a single dose intravenous injection of FGF23 (0.3 g) or vehicle, with tissue collected 1 h later for single-nucleus RNA sequencing, differential expression and regulon (inferred transcription factor activity) analysis. Candidate pathways were tested in precision-cut kidney slices using the CEBPB inhibitor ST-101. Results Streptozotocin-treated male mice developed early DKD with a 6-fold increase in urinary albumin/creatinine ratio and 50% higher blood urea nitrogen with preserved glomerular filtration rate. All major renal cell types were annotated. Canonical FGF23 signaling was intact in disease, with segment-specific target induction conserved in both conditions (e.g. Cyp24a1 in PT-S1 and DCT1). Superimposed on this were disease-restricted responses, including Wsb1 in DCT1 and Pdk4 in PT-S2, PST, DCT1 and DCT2. Regulon analysis revealed DKD-specific induction of CEBPB regulon activity by FGF23 across all analyzed tubular segments, and of STAT1 in several segments. Pre-treatment with a CEBPB inhibitor suppressed CEBPB activity, downstream NF-KB and pro-inflammatory gene sets, and immune-like cell abundance in diseased slices. Conclusion In the diabetic kidney, FGF23 engages a STAT1-CEBPB-NF-{kappa}B axis absent from healthy kidney and extending beyond its canonical Klotho-dependent target segments, identifying CEBPB as a potential treatment target for FGF23's pathological inflammatory actions.

papers.title: Alpha-beta oscillatory dynamics underlying auditory inhibitory control in children
papers.abstract: Response inhibition, the ability to withhold an unwanted response, is a fundamental component of cognitive control. While evoked responses in inhibitory tasks have been widely studied, induced oscillatory dynamics, particularly in the auditory modality and in children, remain largely unexplored. Here, we used magnetoencephalography (MEG) to examine induced alpha (8-12 Hz) and beta (13-20 Hz) oscillations during passive listening and an auditory Go/Nogo task in 67 children (6-14 years) and 16 adults (20-30 years). During passive listening, both groups showed an early alpha power increase in right fronto-temporo-parietal regions, followed by an alpha decrease in temporal regions. Under inhibitory demands, adults displayed a late alpha and beta power increase within a left fronto-temporo-occipital network, whereas children exhibited an early-onset, prolonged beta power decrease in somatomotor and temporo-parietal regions. Our findings indicate that children and adults engage spectrally, temporally, and spatially different neural dynamics during inhibitory control: in children, oscillatory modulation emerges earlier and is dominated by a beta decrease in sensorimotor regions, whereas adults recruit synchronized late alpha-beta dynamics in executive networks, possibly reflecting more efficient and evaluative inhibitory processing.

papers.title: Quantifying electro-osmotic flow in mutant MspA nanopores
papers.abstract: Nanopores have emerged as a powerful tool for single-molecule sensing and sequencing. In a typical nanopore experiment, a charged analyte such as DNA is driven through the pore by an electrophoretic force generated by the applied electric field. This can be problematic, however, when analytes such as proteins carry mixed charges. An alternative driving force can be from electro-osmotic flow (EOF), the water flow that arises from an asymmetric migration of cations and anions through the nanopore. However, despite much recent interest, there is no straightforward experimental method to quantify EOF in nanopores. Here, we trap a dipolar peptide in an MspA nanopore, where studying its escape rate versus voltage allows us to extract the work done by the EOF in various MspA mutants and wildtype MspA compared to a M2-MspA reference. For the 30 amino acid model peptide, this yields values of ~5.6-16.7 kBT for the work done by the EOF at 80 mV. Finite-element simulations confirm the trends observed in the experiments. Charged mutations close to the nanopore's constriction site are found to produce the highest EOF. Our novel method provides a quantitative metric of the EOF in nanopores, opening up its study and broad use in future nanopore sequencing and sensing applications.

papers.title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
papers.abstract: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.

papers.title: INSULIN MODULATES FOOD VALENCE THROUGH ASTROCYTES
papers.abstract: Brain cells involved in assigning affective value (i.e.: valence) to stimuli modulating brain states are not yet fully identified. Since astrocytes modulate brain states, and insulin regulates feeding behavior and exerts its central actions in part through astrocytes, we analyzed the role of the insulin receptor in astrocytes in assigning valence to food. We used the modulatory actions of food on anxiety and fear, as proxies of the affective influence of food on mood. Mice lacking insulin receptors (IR) in GFAP astrocytes (GFAP-IR KO mice) showed increased anxiety and fear in response to food, while control littermates showed the opposite behavior. Since orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) are involved in fear conditioning, and are inhibited by feeding, we determined whether they are involved in mood alterations observed in fear-conditioned fed GFAP-IR KO mice. We observed increased c-fos expression in orexin neurons of these animals, indicating that the lack of IR in astrocytes modifies the response of these neurons to food. Moreover, chemogenetic stimulation of LH astrocytes in fed GFAP-IR KO mice was sufficient to significantly attenuate their fear responses. These findings suggest that astrocytic insulin receptors modulate the responses of hypothalamic orexin neurons to food. We speculate that cellular mechanisms underlying eating disorders may involve insulin modulation of food valence through astrocytes.

papers.title: Evidence of silent nociceptor activation during the formalin test in rats
papers.abstract: Background: Abnormal ongoing activity in C-mechano-insensitive (C-Mi) nociceptors is seen in patients with chronic pain. These 'silent' nociceptors are often under-reported in preclinical pain models - precisely because they aren't mechanically sensitive. The formalin test is widely used as a preclinical model of persistent sensitisation characterised by two behavioural phases, where phase 2 is considered to reflect central sensitisation and the role of peripheral afferent drive in its maintenance is disputed. Increased activity in C-mechanosensitive (C-M) nociceptors has been reported during both phases, but the behaviour of C-Mi nociceptors has not been assessed. Methods: Multi-contact microneurography was conducted from the saphenous nerve of male and female rats. An activity dependent slowing protocol was used to segregate C-fibres, and responses to mechanical stimuli were assessed. Formalin- (2.5%) or saline-evoked activity was then assessed during the two test phases. Results: 168 A- and C-fibres were identified with latency tracking, and classified using activity dependent slowing into C-M and C-Mi nociceptors. ADS-classified C-Mi nociceptors were active in both phase 1 and phase 2 (33.3% and 31.0%, n=18 and n=16, respectively). We find no evidence that formalin mechanically sensitises C-Mi nociceptors or alters the ADS profiles of C-fibres. There was no sex specific difference in C-fibre classes or the effect of formalin. Conclusions: These results indicate the presence of ongoing activity in a substantial population of C-Mi nociceptors in a commonly used persistent pain assay that may play a role in the sensitisation that is seen in phase 2 of the behavioural response.

papers.title: High spatiotemporal resolution in vivo imaging reveals preferential PACAP38 action on dural vasculature and a functional therapeutic readout
papers.abstract: PACAP38-induced cephalic vasodilation is used to assess functional PACAP pathway inhibition in humans, but the vascular populations underlying this response are not fully resolved. Defining these compartments in a preclinical model could help connect clinical pharmacodynamic responses with the underlying vascular mechanisms and support further development of PACAP-targeted therapies. Using chronic cranial windows and head-mounted microscopy, we tracked meningeal vascular responses in freely moving mice. Nitroglycerin, levcromakalim, and PACAP38 each produced net vasodilation, yet the underlying responses were markedly heterogeneous and distributed differently across the vascular populations. Notably, PACAP38 evoked greater early vasodilation in dural than pial vessels, and anti-PACAP pretreatment attenuated PACAP38-induced vasodilation. These findings show that net vasodilation can conceal vessel-level response patterns and identify preferential early dural vasodilation as a spatially defined, pharmacologically modifiable feature of the systemic PACAP38 response. This phenotype provides a translational platform for mechanistic interrogation and evaluation of functional pathway inhibition by migraine-targeted therapies.

papers.title: A ribosome-dependent small-ORF switch controls flagellar gene expression and virulence
papers.abstract: RNA structures are active regulators of bacterial translation. Here, we identified a naturally occurring translation-enhancing small open reading frame (tesORF) that controls the expression of the flagellar operon fliFGHIJK in Salmonella enterica and other motile Enterobacterales. Nucleotide-resolution ribosome profiling revealed this previously unannotated 54-nucleotide ORF immediately upstream of fliF. Genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical analyses support a model in which tesORF translation counteracts an inhibitory RNA structure, exposing the fliF ribosome-binding site and promoting translation initiation independently of the encoded peptide sequence. Disruption of tesORF translation reduced expression of the downstream operon and impaired motility and virulence-associated phenotypes in Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Together, our findings reveal how translation of a conserved small ORF regulates an entire flagellar operon through RNA structural remodelling, with consequences expending to the wider flagellar regulon, linking RNA structural dynamics to bacterial motility and virulence.

papers.title: Phase-specific stimulation of prefrontal beta oscillations modulates distinct cognitive processes
papers.abstract: Oscillatory phase has been proposed to organize neural information processing, but whether endogenous phase can be leveraged to causally shape human cognition remains unclear. Here, we tested whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) delivered at specific phases of endogenous beta oscillations over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates working memory and response inhibition. Participants received EEG phase-controlled, closed-loop rTMS delivered at either the peak or trough of their endogenous beta rhythm, using each participant's dominant beta frequency (20-30 Hz). A conventional 20-Hz rTMS delivered independently of the beta phase served as an active control. Compared to this control and each other, peak-targeted rTMS improved response inhibition, whereas trough-targeted rTMS improved working memory. Both phase-specific behavioral effects were accompanied by corresponding increases in event-related potentials, which were not observed after conventional stimulation. Across participants, behavioral improvements correlated with stimulation-induced electrophysiological changes. Finally, phase-specific rTMS induced distinct DLPFC network expansions that complemented the behavioral effects: peak stimulation enhanced posterior centro-parietal connectivity for inhibitory control, while trough stimulation expanded anterior prefrontal networks for working memory. These findings provide first evidence that opposite phases of endogenous prefrontal beta oscillations coordinate distinct cognitive and neural processes. This establishes prefrontal beta phase as a causal dimension for shaping executive function and as a target for prefrontal rTMS to modulate cognition and non-invasively probe phase-dependent brain function.

papers.title: Structural signatures of salinity adaptation in Microviricetes capsids
papers.abstract: Phages, like their bacterial hosts, have evolved to proliferate across the full range of environments on Earth, but the specific amino acid residues that underlie their environmental adaptations remain elusive. Here, we developed a computational framework that uses structure-based multiple sequence alignments, a random forest classifier, and a phylogeny-aware regression model to find amino acid residues linked to specific environments. Applying this framework to public metagenomic data, we analyzed 1,110 Microviricetes major capsid proteins (MCPs) from the lake and ocean biomes, and found that ocean virus capsids were highly enriched in negatively charged residues on internal and external surfaces. This adaptation likely helps maintain solubility at high salt concentrations and stabilizes ssDNA-capsid interactions by sequestering positively charged ions inside the capsid. At intersubunit interfaces, ocean capsids showed enrichment of cation-{pi} and {pi}-{pi} interactions, which are more resistant to solvation than salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Amino acid residues in lake capsids were more often substituted by biochemically dissimilar amino acids in ocean capsids than the reverse. Together, these results show that microvirus capsids adapt to high-salt environments through changes in surface charge and substitutions affecting intersubunit interactions. Further, we describe a general approach for studying the adaptation and stability of any protein family under complementary environmental or phenotypic conditions.

papers.title: Deciphering the Dynamics of Leukemogenic Transformation from Clonal Hematopoiesis in Congenital Neutropenia
papers.abstract: Inherited neutropenia syndromes, severe congenital neutropenia (CN) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), confer a high cumulative risk of MDS and AML. It is not yet clear which somatic mutations, in which combination, allele frequency and sequence identify patients at high risk. We analyzed clonal hematopoiesis (CH) in the largest representative cohort of inherited neutropenia patients to date - 658 samples from 309 patients - using error-corrected panel sequencing with longitudinal sampling. This was complemented in selected cases by single-cell DNA sequencing and genotyping of single-cell derived colonies. CH was detected in early childhood, affecting 37.7% of CN and 60% of SDS patients. The somatic mutation burden remained essentially unchanged over decades. In CN, CSF3R mutations were dominant across genetic subtypes, while additional mutations were rare and included ASXL1, TET2, and DNMT3A. ASXL1 mutations most frequently co-occurred with CSF3R mutations. Co-occurring CSF3R and TP53 mutations were only found in SRP54-CN and CLPB-CN patients. In SDS, TP53 was the most frequently mutated gene, followed by low-prevalence somatic mutations in DNMT3A, IDH1, PTPN11, and RUNX1. In CN-MDS/AML, RUNX1 and SETBP1 mutations emerged shortly before progression to MDS/AML, and membrane-proximal CSF3R mutations only at the leukemic stage. In SDS, biallelic TP53-mutant clones expanded prior to transformation, and a variant allele frequency (VAF) of dominant TP53 clone above 0.074 discriminated between patients who progressed and those who did not. Peripheral blood reflected bone marrow genotype for most key drivers. Leukemic transformation in inherited neutropenia is therefore not stochastic, but rather follows a defined mutational sequence, initiated in childhood.

papers.title: Rise and Fall of a Superbug: Analyzing the epidemic success of a distinct clone of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST117/CT71 in Germany, 2017 - 2024.
papers.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections, yet outbreak analysis remains challenging, particularly for prevalent lineages. One of the most striking examples is the Sequence Type (ST) 117/Complex Type (CT) 71/vanB lineage, whose rapid expansion across Germany coincided with a sharp rise in VRE prevalence observed around 2019. Defining reliable genomic thresholds remains particularly difficult, as current core-genome Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) cutoffs are based largely on expert consensus or limited case series. Here, we evaluate the discriminatory performance of cgMLST and split k-mer analysis (SKA) for resolving relatedness within ST117/CT71 and investigate whether low core-genome diversity represents a lineage-specific trait or a population-wide property of E. faecium. While cgMLST captures the overall population structure of ST117/CT71, SKA provided higher resolution, distinguishing isolates identical by cgMLST. Analysis of 2,505 genomes showed that ST117/CT71 does not exhibit reduced allelic variability compared with other hospital-adapted lineages, suggesting that limited core-genome diversity is a broader population characteristic. Complementary transposon analyses further identified two temporally distinct ST117/CT71 sublineages carrying different Tn1549-like structures. To assess allelic variation within confirmed transmission events, we analyzed 138 outbreak clusters from 96 hospitals. Outbreak-associated isolates showed sharply compressed allelic differences (median = 1), with 90% of pairwise comparisons falling within [≤]9 alleles. Thus, the commonly applied [≤]20-allele threshold risks overestimating genomic relatedness and grouping unrelated isolates. Based on these data, we propose lowering the cgMLST alert threshold to [≤]9 alleles for initial cluster detection of local outbreaks, followed by confirmatory high-resolution analyses such as SKA.

papers.title: Non-coding RNA controls long-range enhancer-promoter interactions
papers.abstract: Transcription regulation depends on interactions between enhancers and gene promoters, which often occur over large genomic distances. The molecular drivers of long-range enhancer-promoter interactions remain poorly understood. Enhancers themselves are known to be transcribed into non-coding RNAs, but the function of these transcripts is unclear. Here, we use acute genetic and chemical perturbations of transcription elongation and termination to study the role of non-coding RNA in enhancer-promoter interactions. By integrating high-resolution 3D genome mapping, transcriptomics, proteomics, biochemistry and live-cell super-resolution imaging in these perturbation contexts, we demonstrate that a strong increase in RNA molecules at enhancers disrupts their long-range interactions with gene promoters, whereas decreased RNA levels lead to stabilization of these interactions. Using separation-of-function perturbations, we show that this regulatory function of RNA is independent from the process of transcription and the proteins recruited to initiate transcription. Functionally, we show that RNA-mediated disruption of enhancer-promoter interactions is associated with reduced transcription of target genes, indicating a regulatory feedback mechanism. Together, our results uncover an additional regulatory principle of enhancer-promoter interactions mediated by non-coding RNA.

papers.title: Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
papers.abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

papers.title: Preclinical Development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a Human-Derived Swarming Strain, as a Live Biotherapeutic Product for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) remains an area of major unmet need, and the undefined composition and manufacturing burden of fecal microbiota transplantation have motivated a shift toward single-strain Live Biotherapeutic Products (LBPs). Swarming bacteria are enriched in the stressed gut and limit mucosal damage, but no human-derived swarming strain has been developed as an LBP. We therefore report the complete preclinical development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a swarming strain isolated from human feces. Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) covered a three-tier cell bank, 30 L fed-batch fermentation and a colon-targeted enteric-coated capsule, enabling consistent pilot-scale production. No treatment-related findings emerged in safety pharmacology (Sprague-Dawley rats) or in single-dose and Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)-compliant 1-week repeat-dose toxicity studies (Sprague-Dawley rats and Beagle dogs). LS57 was identified as E. ludwigii by 16S rRNA and whole-genome sequencing and produced metabolites with reported anti-inflammatory activity in culture. In Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, LS57 reduced weight loss, preserved colon length, lowered colonic pro-inflammatory cytokines and remodeled the gut microbiota. It also attenuated Trinitrobenzene Sulfonic Acid (TNBS)-induced colitis and enhanced the effect of ciclosporin A. In vitro, LS57 was non-hemolytic, non-cytotoxic, and acid-labile, formed no biofilm, and its resistance to aminopenicillins, cephamycins and imipenem was not transferable by conjugation. In vivo, LS57 colonized the inflamed colon without translocation in wild-type and interleukin-10-deficient mice, and experimental bacteremia was treatable with gentamicin or levofloxacin. LS57 combines efficacy across two mechanistically distinct colitis models with a safety package that addresses the principal regulatory concerns for LBPs, and a scalable manufacturing process, compatible with current good manufacturing practice, in which enteric coating overcomes the strain's poor gastric survival. These data support clinical development of LS57 in IBD.

papers.title: PHYLOGENETIC SUPPORT FOR THE EVOLUTION OF APOSEMATISM BEFORE GREGARIOUSNESS IN CONIFER SAWFLIES
papers.abstract: The evolutionary origin of aposematism remains a long-standing puzzle: how can a conspicuous mutant persist and spread within a cryptic prey population? Two competing hypotheses have been proposed. The group-first hypothesis suggests that aposematism evolved secondarily in already aggregating, chemically defended cryptic ancestors, whereas the aposematism-first hypothesis suggests that aposematism arose in solitary ancestors, with gregariousness evolving subsequently. Currently, these two evolutionary pathways have only been studied in caterpillars of Lepidopteran species, but we lack wider taxonimical evidence especially from systems with cryptic but chemically defended species. We evaluated these hypotheses using phylogenetic reconstructions in chemically defended conifer sawflies (Hymenoptera: Diprionidae), a group whose larvae vary in both colouration and aggregation behaviour. Almost half the species examined (20/45) had aposematic and gregarious larvae. Aposematism and gregariousness were positively evolutionarily correlated (r = 0.29). Aposematic and gregarious species tended to evolve from aposematic, solitary ancestors, while species with cryptic and gregarious larvae (14/45) tended to evolve from aposematic and gregarious ancestors, a pattern consistent with the aposematism-first hypothesis.

papers.title: CellVocal Attributes Transcriptional Dynamics to Spatial Signalling
papers.abstract: Understanding how local signalling shapes cell-state transitions requires linking spatial context to transcriptional dynamics. Here we present CellVocal, a framework that integrates spatial RNA velocity with cell-cell communication to decompose cell-state transitions into intrinsic and communication-associated components and further attribute their contributions to signalling modules and neighbouring sender cells. CellVocal recovered complex trajectories and communication perturbations in simulations and reconstructed coherent dynamics and spatially restricted ligand-receptor programmes across the mouse brain, gut and lung. Further analyses linked inferred NCAM1-NCAM1 signalling to lower cell-cycle-associated RNA velocity during embryonic neurogenesis. In melanoma, inferred local MIF-CD74+CD44 signalling corresponded to a predicted decline in the melanocytic programme. Analysis of acute liver failure identified hepatocyte-derived ANGPTL4-SDC1 signalling in association with acetaminophen-related communication enrichment and predicted matrix-remodelling RNA dynamics. By converting static ligand-receptor maps into velocity-constrained networks of signalling influence, CellVocal provides a general strategy for generating spatially resolved hypotheses about how intercellular communication contributes to predicted transcriptional changes.

papers.title: Filament mechanics and turnover organize dynamic load bearing structures in a cellular-scale model of the actomyosin cortex
papers.abstract: The actomyosin cortex controls cell shape and movement by generating and transmitting contractile forces. Its actin filament (AF) network adopts diverse spatial organizations, while spatially biased contractility drives cortical flow that transports components and reorganizes the network. However, how turnover and spatial redistribution organize and maintain tension-bearing structures in a dynamic steady state, and how localized contractility reorganizes them through flow, remain unclear. We developed a cellular-scale discrete model of the actomyosin cortex representing AFs, cross-linkers, and myosin minifilaments. Local surface stress was reconstructed from discrete-element internal forces based on continuum mechanics. We related cortical tension to component abundance, tensile deformation, AF orientation, turnover, and network connectivity, and compared different AF disassembly, relocation, and myosin-localization mechanisms. Simulations produced a heterogeneous, network-like distribution of local cortical tension. Tensile energy per element correlated more strongly with local tension than component abundance, with the strongest correlation for AFs. Highly stretched AFs preferentially occurred in high-tension regions and aligned with the first-principal-tension orientation, indicating anisotropic load-bearing pathways. Despite continuous component replacement and reorganization of local tension patterns, global AF-network connectivity and cell-scale cortical tension were maintained. The characteristic time of tension-pattern reorganization was closest to the persistence time of myosin, suggesting an association between myosin dynamics and rapid force redistribution. AF relocation to low-density regions replenished spatial gaps, whereas bending-dependent disassembly limited the accumulation of strongly deformed AFs. Direct myosin localization and AF accumulation produced comparable equatorward cortical flows but differed in the spatial organization of the tension-bearing network. Collectively, these results demonstrate that cellular-scale cortical tension is organized not only by component abundance but also by filament-scale mechanical loading, AF orientation, and network connectivity.

papers.title: A Complete Three-Dimensional Spiral Ganglion Neuron Map in a Human Adult using a Deep Learning Pipeline
papers.abstract: The quantity and distribution of spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) greatly influence speech and hearing ability. Historically, approaches to quantify SGNs from archival human temporal bones (TBs) have utilized only every 10th section to estimate the total SGN count. The current study evaluates a novel deep-learning pipeline for SGN quantification to produce the first complete three-dimensional SGN map of the human cochlea using every tissue section. The reconstruction is based on one adult human cochlea in which all 421 consecutive, 20 um thick, celloidin-embedded sections were H&E stained, mounted and digitized. SGN nuclei were manually labeled in training sections which were subsequently used to create UNet++ models for SGN detection. These models were then applied to all other sections and compared to manual counts by three experienced histopathologists. After quantification, serial sections were aligned and SGNs were assigned percent distances along Rosenthal's canal and characteristic frequencies using a modified Greenwood formula. Models to automatically identify SGN nuclei from digitized tissue sections performed with great accuracy: SGNs were counted in 191 sections with 97% accuracy compared to manual counts. When tissue sections were systematically omitted, counting only every 10th section was determined sufficient to ensure a median inferred total count accuracy of 98%. We present a new, flexible machine learning pipeline for identifying SGNs in digitized human TBs. Further, we show the first full 3D visualization of all 27,880 SGNs in an adult human cochlea, with associated tonotopic maps and basal-to-apical SGN distributions.

papers.title: Distinct input-output relationships between basal forebrain subnuclei underlie heterogeneous cholinergic modulation of the mouse cortex
papers.abstract: The basal forebrain (BF) supports many behavioral functions via its brain-wide projections, which can be recruited independently and task specifically. However, the anatomical underpinnings for this functional heterogeneity are poorly understood. Here, we compared two mouse BF subnuclei, the horizontal diagonal band (HDB) and the substantial innominata (SI), in terms of their anatomical connectivity and functional recruitment. Using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we show that they target largely segregated forebrain regions, but their input comes from a partially overlapping subset of regions. However, many neurons within each region project to just one of the subnuclei, suggesting they can be recruited independently. To test this, we combined optogenetics and widefield Ca2+ imaging and showed that stimulating prefrontal cortical projections to the HDB or SI results in distinct large-scale patterns of cortical activity via a cholinergic mechanism. Our results provide an anatomical basis for the flexible, area-specific cholinergic modulation of brain function.

papers.title: Detection of Maximal Exact Matches in Terabases of Genome Assemblies in Compressed Space and Sublinear Time
papers.abstract: Detection of long exact matches between a pair of genomes has historically been a fundamental operation in genomics. Similarly, detection of long exact matches between all pairs of haplotypes in a large panel of genotyping array data or whole-genome sequencing variant calls is a fundamental operation in population genetics. Thanks to various recent pangenome efforts, for the first time, large panels of high-quality genome assemblies are being constructed. Therefore, we propose the intersection of these two approaches: detection of long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in panels of hundreds to thousands of high-quality assemblies. Since these datasets would contain trillions of basepairs, practically detecting all exact matches requires algorithms operating in at most linear time and compressed space. Previous methods such as Mumemto achieve this, but running them on terabase-sized pangenomes still took very large space and long time. Here, we describe more efficient algorithms for outputting all long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in compressed space and sublinear time given a compressed index of the panel. Given the construction of an O(r) space compressed index--a one-time cost that can be done in compressed space and close to linear time with previous work--we describe three algorithms taking O(r) words of memory: (1) computing all supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) in O(r) time, (2) computing all supermaximal exact matches and their occurrences in O(r + occ) time, and (3) computing all maximal exact matches (MEMs) in O(r + occ) time, where r is the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform of the panel of assemblies and occ is the number of occurrences or matches outputted. Our algorithms use 7.5 times less memory than state-of-the-art competitors on a dataset of human centromere assemblies from 625 haplotypes. They are also 20 times faster if index construction time is counted, and 2,500 times faster if index construction is excluded. Finally, we perform an analysis of all-vs-all MEMs in all well-assembled centromeres of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 dataset that reveals multiple novel insights into structural variation in centromeres. For example, we find that the active -satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) array of Chromosome 2 is flanked by a ~200 kbp inversion on one side and a ~200-300 kbp pseudopalindromic sequence on the other. We also detect large segmental duplications in the centromere of every chromosome except Chromosome Y. These segmental duplications range in size from hundreds of kbp to multiple Mbp and occur both in and out of the active -satellite HOR arrays. Our computational results make pairwise MEM analyses possible in pangenomes, while our biological results show they are likely to be useful. Our algorithms are implemented as TeraMEM in the TeraTools suite available at https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools.

papers.title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
papers.abstract: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.

papers.title: Development of a core genome Multilocus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) and Life Identification Number (LIN) code schema for the Burkholderia cepacia complex
papers.abstract: Background The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) currently comprises over 20 closely related species; however, understanding Bcc population biology is complicated due to the continual advances in taxonomy and diversity driven by extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Whilst there are conventional typing schemes for the Bcc, including Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), there remains a gap for fine-scale resolution typing of the species complex. Here, we present a 1,925 loci core genome MLST (cgMLST) and 14-digit Life Identification Number (LIN) barcoding scheme for the Bcc, that is embedded in the PubMLST database (https://PubMLST.org/organisms/burkholderia-cepacia-complex). Methods A dataset of 142 complete Bcc genomes spanning 19 species were downloaded from NCBI to develop the draft cgMLST scheme (Dataset 1). Two pangenome tools (PIRATE and PEPPAN) were then combined to give a consensus core gene list from Dataset 1. The 'core genes' from these outputs were then screened against the PubMLST loci, using a sequence tag scan, to identify their presence and curate new alleles. The core genes were then validated using a larger Bcc dataset (n = 934 genomes; 22 species) on PubMLST, which had been filtered for high-quality ([≤]200 contigs and 100% ribosomal MLST confidence). This refined the core gene list, ensuring a robust and reliable scheme using a threshold of 99% to classify the gene as 'core'. The population structure of the Bcc was subsequently analysed using the validation dataset to identify genetic clusters using ReporTree. Combined with statistical analysis, 14 allelic mismatch thresholds were identified for the LIN codes. Results The Bcc cgMLST scheme consists of 1,925 loci, which have been designated an arbitrary 'BCC' identifier. The cgMLST scheme and 14-threshold LIN code has been implemented in PubMLST and are publicly available for use. The Bcc genomes in the PubMLST database have been assigned cgSTs and LIN codes. Use cases of the LIN codes were validated using three previously published datasets, which spanned both outbreak investigation and phylogenomic lineage structures. Conclusions This stable, hierarchical LIN code nomenclature enhanced the ability to cluster isolates at multiple levels of resolution with examples overlayed on published datasets provided. The LIN code system is also backwards compatible with previous MLST and clonal complex (CC) nomenclature. Overall, the updated typing scheme will facilitate improve global public health through surveillance of the Bcc epidemiology including source tracing and outbreak investigation

papers.title: Regulatory architecture and evolution of the triphasic life cycle in the red alga Bostrychia moritziana
papers.abstract: The triphasic life cycle of florideophyte red algae represents the most complex life cycle among photosynthetic eukaryotes, yet its developmental and evolutionary origins remain unresolved. Here, we generated a comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of Bostrychia moritziana, a model red alga with a highly elaborate triphasic life history. We show that cellular specification across generations, reproductive structures and unicellular reproductive cell types in Bostrychia is associated with discrete regulatory modules that frequently cluster within the genome. We reveal that development of the cystocarp, the reproductive structure that houses the additional diploid phase characteristic of the triphasic life cycle, involves extensive and coordinated post-fertilisation reprogramming of the zygote-derived carposporophyte and surrounding maternal tissue. Evolutionary transcriptomics support a scenario in which triphasy evolved through successive elaboration of ancestral developmental programs, with lineage-specific genes and expanded transcription factor families progressively integrated into its regulatory architecture. Together, our findings provide a molecular framework for understanding the origin and evolution of the triphasic life cycle, offering broader insights into how increasingly complex multicellular life cycles emerged across eukaryotes.

papers.title: Structural and functional characterization of polyclonal antibody responses reveals shared and distinct antigenic features of RSV and hMPV fusion proteins
papers.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), members of the Pneumoviridae family, circulate widely and are leading causes of hospitalization for acute respiratory infections in infants and older adults. The viral fusion (F) protein in its prefusion (preF) conformation is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet how naturally elicited circulating polyclonal antibodies are distributed across its antigenic landscape remains poorly understood. Here, we combined serological profiling, site-specific antibody competition assays and electron microscopy-based polyclonal epitope mapping (EMPEM) to characterize preF-directed immunity to RSV and hMPV in healthy adults. All donors exhibited detectable preF-binding antibodies that positively correlated with virus neutralization and broadly recognized multiple antigenic sites, consistent with immunodominance patterns predicted by a surface-centric computational model. Despite this overall similarity, the distribution of responses across individual antigenic sites differed between RSV and hMPV. EMPEM analyses revealed consistent targeting of the highly neutralization-sensitive preF apex (site O) in both viruses, alongside less abundant responses against equatorial and upper-middle epitopes (sites II, III, IV and V). We additionally observed antibody-bound destabilized preF, supporting a model in which antibody binding promotes transient opening of the preF trimer and may interfere with the conformational rearrangements required for membrane fusion. Together, these findings highlight apex-directed antibodies as a prominent feature of naturally acquired pneumovirus immunity in adults and reveal both shared and distinct patterns of antigenic recognition that may inform next-generation vaccine design and antibody-based prophylactics.

papers.title: Geometric determinants of time series learning and attractor stability in closed-loop circuits
papers.abstract: Skilled volitional behaviours arise from recurrent circuits, which can sustain structured neural activity in the absence of external drive, through internal feedback. But how such autonomous activity is learned and stability maintained in distributed motor circuits is poorly understood. To investigate the relationship between neural representations and learning we compared a cortex-like recurrent neural network (RNN) and a cortico-cerebellar-like circuit with a feed-forward layer (RNN+FFL), both in a closed-loop configuration. RNN+FFL circuits learned periodic target signals that parameter-matched RNNs could not, due to a failure to form attractor states. Decomposing population activity by frequency, rather than variance, separated the task-relevant and task-irrelevant subspaces. Quantifying their geometric arrangement revealed that the feed-forward layer improved learning and stabilised attractor states by increasing the angles within and between these subspaces. Our results show that task-specific representational geometry is a better predictor of periodic time series learning in recurrent circuits than classical global measures such as dimensionality.

papers.title: Body weight modifies the efficacy of lifespan-extending interventions in ad libitum-fed mice
papers.abstract: Geroprotective interventions are often assessed by extension of lifespan in ad libitum-fed mice. Increased lifespan could therefore reflect rescue of adverse phenotypes of unhealthy controls. We analysed body weight and survival for 33,780 mice in the Interventions Testing Program (ITP) to test whether treatment effects varied with body weight. In males, each added standard deviation of attained adult weight made treatment 6% more favourable (HR 0.94), more apparent for interventions that lowered body weight (HR 0.90). Median lifespan increase rose from 6.2% in mice in the lightest quartile to 20.2% in the heaviest pre-dosing weight quartile among those experiments, mainly because control survival declined more steeply with weight than that of the intervention group. The effect of body weight was consistent across 13 of 14 compounds and reflected weight attained during adulthood rather than in early life. Weight-dependence of intervention effects was weak in ITP females, possibly because median survival of controls exceeded that of every sampled non-ITP female control group. Amelioration of weight-associated risk is therefore implicated as a major contributor to lifespan increases relative to heavy, short-lived controls. The geroprotective effects of these interventions may thus be less apparent in metabolically healthier mice or humans.

papers.title: Differential effects of AMPA receptor inhibition on seizure-like events in murine and human brain slices
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a frequent neurological condition with a worldwide prevalence of 0.5-1%. Current therapies are limited by adverse effects as well as drug resistance. This highlights the need for novel, target-specific antiseizure medications with improved efficacy and fewer side effects. AMPA (-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptors represent a therapeutic target as demonstrated by perampanel, an AMPA receptor antagonist used clinically as antiseizure medication. AMPA receptors typically mediate fast excitatory neurotransmission. Their properties are modulated by auxiliary proteins that can alter receptor activation, deactivation and desensitization, including converting them into slow AMPA receptors. In this study, we tested different AMPA receptor inhibitors, including perampanel, for their ability to suppress seizure-like events (SLE). SLE were recorded with extracellular electrodes in cortical brain slices from healthy mice and from epilepsy patients who underwent resective surgery. SLE were induced with 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) or a combination of 4-AP and high-potassium. We found that seizure-like events in murine tissue appeared more frequently, with higher amplitude and spike frequency, but were briefer than in human tissue. GYKI53655, NBQX and perampanel were equally effective in inhibiting SLE in murine und human brain slices. In contrast, the antagonist LY3130481, specific for the AMPA receptor auxiliary protein {gamma}-8, showed only weak efficacy in murine tissue, but blocked of SLE in human tissue almost completely. The species-specific differences we found for LY3130481 highlight the benefit of using human tissue in preclinical research and underline that auxiliary subunits remain a promising therapeutic target for the development of new antiseizure medications.

papers.title: The Confessions of a Protein Language Model: Steering, Activations, and What Predicted Confidence Cannot Certify
papers.abstract: Protein generate-and-screen pipelines use interventions and readouts to select candidates, but rarely test whether these track their intended targets. We audit published repetition steering, ESMFold confidence, and an activation readout. Steering preserves confidence at its operating point, but a fitted cliff follows at alpha_50 = 1.240x (sweep's own control: 64.0%). Direction matters at moderate matched-norm push, but not at saturation. Unsteered generator activations predict the confidence gate (ROC-AUC 0.786 +/- 0.004), supporting cost-aware, model-specific triage. We also replicate established length sensitivity, through which shortening can manufacture false nulls. Yet on composition- and length-matched design--scramble pairs, no balanced-accuracy interval excludes chance for experimental stability. Predicting the gate does not establish foldability. We should test what a readout measures before using it to select. Code and data: https://github.com/paninishah/plm-steering-audit

papers.title: Basic-peptide depletion and precursor masking in bottom-up proteomics
papers.abstract: Biomarker proteomics studies report protein identities at the canonical precursor level, yet the underlying mass-spectrometry evidence consists of peptides whose physicochemical properties may diverge from the annotated protein. We reanalyzed peptide-level evidence from public datasets with a proteoform-aware pipeline that maps detected peptides to canonical sequences under a five-level confidence taxonomy, computes sequence-derived physicochemical features for precursors, peptides, and detected regions, and tests class-composition bias against digestion-matched backgrounds. Across ten public studies spanning five result-file formats and 70,020 peptide-evidence rows, detected peptides are depleted in the basic isoelectric-point class relative to their own proteins' theoretical tryptic peptides (fixed-effect odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.44-0.46; leave-one-study-out envelope 0.44-0.49). The depletion is absent among fully tryptic peptides (OR 1.06) and concentrates in missed-cleavage peptides (OR 0.62-0.57), is invariant to detected-abundance stratification, and retains its direction under three independent pI-calculator models. Case studies reveal both directions of precursor-centric masking. Two orthogonal validations ground the framework: a digestion-free synthetic-peptide analysis (basic-class odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.76 under standard DDA) and a paired top-down benchmark, in which detected regions recover top-down sequence space (90% of spans overlapped) but do not delimit proteoform boundaries (8% containment). Pipeline, data, and code are public.

papers.title: HCMV glycoprotein B, but not the pentameric complex, is a key target of antibody-mediated phagocytosis
papers.abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a leading infectious cause of birth defects globally with devastating fetal health outcomes, and there is currently no HCMV vaccine available. Glycoprotein B (gB) and the pentameric complex (PC) are immunodominant HCMV envelope proteins and candidates of interest in vaccine development due to their ability to elicit strong anti-HCMV neutralization responses. Recent evidence implicates non-neutralizing antibody functions in protection from vertical HCMV transmission, but the involvement of gB and PC in these responses remains incompletely understood. We evaluated immune responses against HCMV elicited by a gB protein subunit vaccine with and without PC in a preclinical rabbit study. Despite improved neutralization and inhibition of cell-associated viral spread, the inclusion of PC did not enhance antibody-mediated phagocytosis or Fc{gamma}R activation against HCMV virions or infected cells compared to gB alone. We additionally found a reduction in phagocytosis function by an HCMV hyperimmune globulin when blocked against gB, but not PC, suggesting that gB is a target of phagocytosis-mediating antibodies while PC is not. Given that antibody-mediated phagocytosis but not neutralization has been associated with protection from vertical HCMV transmission, these findings support the continued assessment of gB, but not PC, as a vaccine antigen for the prevention of vertical transmission via non-neutralizing antibodies to reduce the congenital HCMV burden worldwide.

papers.title: Investigating the causal and consequential role of the nuclear encoded mitochondrial genome in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but which mitochondrial pathways are involved, and whether their involvement is a cause or a consequence of disease remains unclear. We investigated whether nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene (NEMG) pathways are enriched for ALS genetic risk, which are dysregulated in ALS tissue, whether pathway activity defines patient subgroups that differ in survival, and whether co-expression between the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes is altered. We tested MitoCarta3.0 pathways for enrichment of ALS genetic risk using MAGMA and the largest European ALS GWAS to date (27,205 cases and 110,881 controls), using hierarchical testing across pathway tiers, and annotated the direction of gene-level effects using published TWAS and SMR results. In >1,500 bulk RNA-seq samples from post-mortem motor cortex and spinal cord (KCL Brain Bank, NYGC ALS Consortium) and iPSC-derived motor neurones (Answer ALS), we performed cell type adjusted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA)-based clustering with exploratory survival analysis, and nuclear-mitochondrial co-expression analysis. Of seven broad mitochondrial categories, only the mitochondrial central dogma was enriched for ALS risk after correction (Padj = 0.044). Hierarchical testing within this pathway localised the signal to translation (Padj = 0.008) and the mitoribosome (Padj = 0.014). Genetically predicted expression pointed in opposite directions for different mitoribosomal genes (lower MRPS33 and higher MRPL28 expression with increased risk), and did not agree in direction with differential expression in ALS tissue more often than expected by chance. A nominal enrichment in ROS and glutathione metabolism was largely attributable to SOD1. In tissue, mitochondrial genes were broadly more highly expressed in ALS motor cortex in both cohorts, largely as a global shift across mitochondrial genes. OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome were enriched beyond this shift in ALS Consortium motor cortex (both PFDR = 0.027), as were OXPHOS subunits in iPSC-derived motor neurones (PFDR = 2.4 x 10-), whereas spinal cord showed no genome-wide enrichment. GSVA based clusters were associated with diagnosis in motor cortex, and nominally with survival in lumbar spinal cord (adjusted HR 0.69, Punadj = 0.013), where cluster structure was weakest. No individual pathway was associated with survival after correction in adjusted models. In all four post-mortem tissues, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes were more negatively co-expressed with mtDNA-encoded genes in ALS than in controls, most strongly in lumbar spinal cord, whereas iPSC-derived motor neurones showed the opposite pattern. In conclusion, inherited ALS risk shows a modest enrichment centred on mitochondrial translation, with gene specific rather than uniform directions of effect. The same pathway, alongside OXPHOS, is more highly expressed in end-stage ALS motor cortex, which may reflect a response to disease, residual differences in cell composition, or both. At the gene level, genetically predicted and observed expression changes did not agree in direction, so whether inherited risk and these tissue changes are linked remains unresolved.

papers.title: Selective activation of estrogen receptors modulates electrical activity and insulin secretion in human EndoC-βH1 cells
papers.abstract: Estrogen receptors (ERs), ER and ER{beta} have important roles in the physiology of the endocrine pancreas in animal models, but the effects of ER activation on insulin-secreting human cells are still poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of ER and ER{beta} as modulators of electrical activity and insulin secretion in the insulin-secreting human cell line EndoC-{beta}H1. Immunocytochemical analysis revealed a widespread cellular distribution of ER, while ER{beta} was predominantly localized outside the nucleus. We observed that both estradiol (E2) and the ER{beta} agonist diarylpropionitrile (DPN) led to a decrease in insulin secretion in the absence of stimulatory glucose concentrations, without affecting insulin content. Patch-clamp experiments revealed that a 48-hour treatment with either the ER agonist PPT or DPN resulted in depolarization of the resting membrane potential, increased action potential firing frequency, and altered the action potential waveform in EndoC-{beta}H1 cells. PPT increased voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel currents, while DPN reduced K+ and Na+ currents. These results suggest that activation of ER and ER{beta} modulates beta-cell electrical activity through distinct pathways involving ion channels. The effects of E2, PPT, and DPN were not caused by altered expression levels of ion channel genes after 48 hours of treatment. This suggests that these receptors act extranuclearly without affecting gene expression. Together, our findings demonstrate that selective activation of ER and ER{beta} modulates beta-cell excitability through distinct electrophysiological mechanisms and that E2 and DPN reduce basal insulin secretion in human EndoC-{beta}H1 cells. These results support ER and ER{beta} as potential targets for modulating human pancreatic beta-cell function.

papers.title: A Glutamate-Neuropeptide Circuit Converts Transient Mate Contact into a Persistent Local Search State in Caenorhabditis elegans Males
papers.abstract: Transient sensory encounters can trigger behavioral states that persist long after the initiating stimulus has disappeared, yet how neural circuits initiate and sustain these states remains poorly understood. Here, we show that brief contact with a suitable mate induces a persistent local search state in male Caenorhabditis elegans, characterized by increased reversals and spatially restricted exploration that continues after mate removal. Transient optogenetic activation of male-specific ray type B (RnB) sensory neurons recapitulates this state, with its magnitude and persistence increasing with stimulation strength. Glutamatergic signaling promotes neuronal responses within the interconnected RnB sensory network and contributes to prolonged activity in downstream LUA interneurons. In contrast, loss of the LUA-derived neuropeptide NLP-13 or its receptor DMSR-2 preserves initial stimulus-evoked neuronal responses but reduces prolonged LUA calcium activity and behavioral persistence. LUA-specific restoration of NLP-13 rescues persistent local search, identifying these interneurons as a functionally important source of the neuropeptide. Together, our findings reveal complementary contributions of glutamatergic and neuropeptidergic signaling to the generation and persistence of behavioral states, illustrating how distinct signaling mechanisms cooperate to transform transient social encounters into prolonged circuit activity and persistent behavior.

papers.title: A Xenopus laevis Model for Systemic Fungal Infections
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis possesses both innate and adaptive immune systems, and we previously demonstrated its utility as an infection model for human bacterial pathogens. In this study, we investigated the utility of X. laevis as a model for fungal infections. The human-pathogenic fungi Candida albicans and Aspergillus fumigatus exhibited greater lethality in X. laevis than the nonpathogenic fungi Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. In frogs infected with C. albicans, viable fungal cells were detected in the blood and multiple organs early after infection, and gross white lesions and fungal hyphae were observed in the kidneys. C. albicans infection also increased renal expression of the proinflammatory cytokine gene s tnf and il1b, as well as the tissue injury-associated gene clu. Treatment with the antifungal agents amphotericin B and micafungin significantly improved the survival of C. albicans-infected frogs. Furthermore, a homozygous deletion mutant of UME6, a gene associated with C. albicans virulence, exhibited reduced lethality compared with the wild-type strain. These findings establish X. laevis as a vertebrate model of systemic fungal infection that enables the evaluation of fungal virulence, host responses, and the therapeutic efficacy of antifungal agents.

papers.title: Preferential recruitment of PML isoform II by incoming HPV16 genome transport vesicles facilitates early stage of infection
papers.abstract: The interplay between promyelocytic leukemia nuclear bodies (PML NBs) and viral infections is complex and multifaceted, with viruses often engaging in a delicate balance of exploitation and evasion of host immune responses. It is well-established that incoming human papillomavirus (HPV) virions associate with PML NBs; however, the mechanism by which HPV targets PML NBs to facilitate early transcription and replication remains elusive. We have shown that HPV genomes are delivered to the nucleus inside membrane-bound vesicles during mitosis and that PML proteins are recruited to HPV-harboring nuclear vesicles prior to egress. Herein, we demonstrate that the PML isoform II (PMLII), but not other PML isoforms, is selectively attracted to incoming HPV still residing in transport vesicles. Using individual PML NB isoform and HPV16 minor protein, L2, over-expression experiments in HeLa cells, we conclude that PML II binds to the lipids of the HPV harbouring membrane-bound vesicles rather than L2. This is in line with previous observations that PML II is the only isoform binding to lipid droplets in the nucleus. We observed that the association of PML NBs with the HPV16 viral genome was transient and lost over time. We also found that nuclear Phospholipase C {beta}4 and {gamma}1 colocalize with PML II-L1 complexes in infected cells. Our data support a model in which PML II contributes to the establishment of early HPV16 infection by organizing host lipid regulatory factors at incoming viral transport vesicles.

papers.title: Aperiodic Exponent as an EEG Marker of Interoceptive Attention during Gastric Fullness
papers.abstract: Gastric interoceptive attention to internal, bodily signals such as hunger, satiety, and fullness are important for regulating feeding behaviors. However, abnormal processing or sensitivity to these can lead to disorders that result in overly restrictive or excessive consumption, highlighting the need for better understanding of the cortical processing of these cues. Specifically, understanding cortical representations of self-perceived gastric fullness have yet to be studied in humans. In this work, we demonstrate that consistently across individuals, the broadband power spectral density of EEG signals, as quantified by the aperiodic exponent, flattens after individuals drink water until fullness. Simultaneous measures of the stomach and heart demonstrate increased vagal drive to peripheral organs. We further find that changes in cortical aperiodic exponent patterns are associated with changes in the frequency of gastric oscillations. Overall, this suggests that the EEG aperiodic exponent may be a useful noninvasive biomarker for assessing gastric interoceptive attention.

papers.title: DE-Rigor-Agent: An Agentic Workflow for Assumption-Aware Differential Expression Analysis of Bulk RNA-seq Data
papers.abstract: Differential expression (DE) methods for bulk RNA-seq differ in their statistical assumptions, input data requirements, and supported study designs. Large language model (LLM) agents can automate DE analysis, but they may default to popular methods without checking whether these methods are appropriate for the data. We introduce DE-Rigor-Agent, an assumption-aware agent that organizes DE analysis into three stages: input standardization, method filtering, and method execution. Before executing any DE method, the agent uses expert-curated criteria and dataset-specific diagnostics to evaluate six commonly used methods, documents the reasons for retaining or excluding each method, and executes all retained methods. We evaluated DE-Rigor-Agent on 140 simulated datasets spanning 14 challenging scenarios involving small sample sizes, zero inflation, expression outliers, pre-normalized inputs, and confounded batch effects. Benchmarks showed that method-dataset incompatibilities could lead to inflated false discovery rates (FDRs) or reduced statistical power. Two general-purpose LLM agent baselines, including one explicitly prompted to consider statistical assumptions, selected DESeq2 or edgeR for nearly all datasets. In contrast, DE-Rigor-Agent's filtering decisions closely matched the incompatibilities introduced in the simulations and remained consistent across random seeds, with little additional computational cost. These results demonstrate that DE-Rigor-Agent provides an automated approach to assessing method suitability, making DE analysis more rigorous and transparent.

papers.title: Differential properties of gp120 from HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B
papers.abstract: HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B differ substantially in their gp120 sequence. To determine whether these differences contribute to subtype-specific complications, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), rats were injected with gp120 from subtype A or B. Pulmonary artery (PA) remodeling was assessed after four weeks using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and the Vessel Morphometry Analysis tool by Autona (autona.org). Subtype A gp120 potently increased PA wall thickness and right ventricular hypertrophy. The CD4-binding region of subtype A lacks a stretch of 16 amino acids (V1 N-glycosylation site), and experiments showed stronger binding of subtype B to CD4. Subtype B gp120 contains an RGKV sequence, which resembles the RGKR sequence of the rabies virus glycoprotein G that binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR). Subtype A gp120 possesses a KDKK sequence instead. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that both sites are surface-exposed. Although nAChR is expressed in PA cells and could potentially drive the pronounced effects of subtype A, MD simulations estimated that subtype B gp120 binds more strongly to nAChR. We also noted a single amino acid difference immediately preceding the REKR furin cleavage sequence: glutamate in subtype A versus glutamine in subtype B gp120. Simulations predicted that subtype A gp120 interacts more effectively with furin, and enzyme assays demonstrated that subtype A promotes a positive feedback loop more strongly than subtype B. Thus, HIV-1 gp120 subtype A is more potent in promoting PAH, and the mechanism may involve enhancing furin activity to elevate gp120 levels.

papers.title: Maternal E-Cigarette Exposure Exacerbates Neonatal Ischemic Brain Injury Through the miR-30c-5p-Neurod1 Axis
papers.abstract: Background: Neonatal ischemic stroke is an important cause of mortality and long-term neurological morbidity in infants. Maternal smoking and e-cigarette exposure are recognized risk factors for adverse neonatal outcomes, but the mechanisms underlying increased susceptibility to ischemic brain injury remain unclear. This study investigated whether dysregulation of the miR-30c-5p-Neurod1 axis contributes to this susceptibility. Methods: Pregnant rats were exposed to e-cigarette aerosols from embryonic day 4 to 20. Studies were conducted in male offspring on postnatal day 10. Baseline molecular changes were assessed using microRNA sequencing, quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, Western blotting, RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and luciferase reporter assays. Ischemic injury was evaluated following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). Flow cytometry and molecular analyses were performed to characterize associated cellular changes. The effects of in vivo miR-30c-5p mimic administration, Neurod1 knockdown, and miR-30c-5p inhibition were also investigated. Results: Maternal e-cigarette exposure increased tMCAO-induced infarct size and was associated with increased apoptosis and senescence-associated changes, together with reduced expression of markers of neurogenesis and synaptic development. Under baseline conditions, microRNA profiling and molecular analyses revealed increased miR-30c-5p expression and decreased Neurod1 mRNA and protein levels in the neonatal brain. RISC and luciferase reporter assays supported an interaction between miR-30c-5p and Neurod1 mRNA. In vivo administration of a miR-30c-5p mimic reduced Neurod1 expression and increased infarct size, whereas Neurod1 knockdown independently exacerbated ischemic injury and associated cellular changes. Conversely, inhibition of miR-30c-5p restored Neurod1 expression, reduced infarct size, and ameliorated associated pathological changes. Conclusions: Maternal e-cigarette exposure is associated with baseline dysregulation of the miR-30c-5p-Neurod1 axis and increased susceptibility to neonatal ischemic brain injury in male rats. These findings suggest that this regulatory axis may contribute to the effects of prenatal e-cigarette exposure on the developing brain and may increase susceptibility to neonatal ischemic stroke.

papers.title: 28S-rsRNA facilitates PASMC proliferation through PKM2 β-hydroxybutyrylation
papers.abstract: Ribosomal RNA-derived small RNAs (rsRNAs) are nucleic acid fragments originating from rRNA, the functions and roles of which in diseases remain incompletely understood. We identified 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20, an rsRNA whose expression is upregulated in hypoxic pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) and in lung tissues of pulmonary hypertension (PH) models. In hypoxic cells, 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20 promotes PASMC proliferation, and its knockdown mitigates SuHx-induced pulmonary hypertension and vascular remodeling. Mechanistically, 28S rsRNA-CTC_L20 modulates {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) production by maintaining the stability of ketogenic enzyme mRNAs through its "CTGNNGG" motif. Elevated levels of BHB enhance the {beta}-hydroxybutyrylation modification at K166 of pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), increasing its activity and driving glycolysis to sustain proliferation. These results link ketone body metabolism to glycolysis in hypoxic cells and define an rsRNA-BHB-PKM2 {beta}-hydroxybutyrylation axis in PH.
