We developed a computational method combining optimal transport, RNA velocity and comparative program analysis across 34,533 monocytes and macrophages from seven human cohorts. Optimal transport quantified all 15 pairwise relationships among six macrophage states, and target-association gradients supported source- and destination-program comparisons across 11 relationships. Expression contrasts were calculated within libraries and source subtypes. Robustness was assessed through resampling, cohort omission and held-out-gene analyses. Paired RNA and protein measurements provided complementary molecular evidence, and patient-label permutation tests evaluated exploratory clinical associations in 18 patients. We also applied the method to an independent human liver dataset. Scavenging and inflammatory macrophages formed the closest transcriptional pair in the full atlas and every cohort-omission analysis. Scavenging macrophages retained selected source features alongside inflammatory programming, whereas fibrotic association coincided with attenuation of the broader scavenging signature. This signature showed a lower change along fibrotic than inflammatory association in all 19 matched libraries. Protein measurements corroborated selected changes and revealed coexisting scavenging and activation features within individual cells. Symptomatic patients had a higher fraction of monocytes with strong inflammatory association than asymptomatic patients (median difference, 13.0 percentage points; unadjusted one-sided permutation $p = 0.0017$). Analysis of 8,536 liver mononuclear phagocytes further resolved contrasting source-marker responses along scar-associated macrophage association. These findings connect macrophage heterogeneity to selective identity remodeling across disease-associated states. Integrating population relationships with RNA, protein and clinical measurements provides a strategy for prioritizing candidate pathogenic routes and their associated molecular programs for functional investigation.

papers.title: Real-time AI integration for MR to detect artifacts and guide pulse sequence adaptations
papers.abstract: This work presents a first-of-its-kind artificial intelligence (AI-)integrated MR pulse sequence that detects out-of-voxel (OOV) artifacts in real-time (within-TR) and responds prospectively by updating the crusher gradient scheme. Per Excitation Real-time Execution & Guided Responses with Integrated Neural-network Evaluation (PEREGRINE), allows for deployment of deep learning models and pulse sequence updates. In this study, PEREGRINE operated a time-domain (TD) and frequency-domain (FD) convolutional autoencoder that detect OOV artifacts. Scans without (AI-off) and with (AI-on) updates were collected from the medial prefrontal cortex of healthy volunteers using a MEGA-edited MRS experiment. The degree of OOV contamination (OOV Score) was quantified per transient based upon the prevalence of OOV signals in the TD and FD data. OOV Scores above a user-defined threshold triggered an update of the crusher gradient scheme, iterating through 48 permutations (6 axis transpositions x 8 polarity flips). Within each 2-second TR, PEREGRINE successfully provided single-transient OOV Scores and updated gradients accordingly. No difference was observed between the OOV Scores from the full ('Full' condition) AI-on and AI-off sessions due to the AI-on scan cycling over better and worse gradient permutations relative to the AI-off scan. However, the AI-on scan had significantly lower OOV Scores than the AI-off scan when selecting the transients where PEREGRINE persisted ('Dwell' condition) on a given gradient permutation. Ultimately, Fit Quality Number (FQN) from linear combination modeling improved significantly for the AI-on compared to the AI-off scan. PEREGRINE enabled an adaptive and AI-integrated sequence allowing for real-time evaluation and response to OOV artifacts, identifying gradient modifications that produced less OOV contamination.

papers.title: ER-associated control of axonal vesicle trafficking during neuronal development
papers.abstract: Axonal vesicle trafficking is essential for presynaptic assembly, yet the intracellular structures that spatially and temporally regulate vesicle transport during neuronal development remain unclear. Here we identify previously uncharacterized membrane contact sites (MCSs) between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and both synaptic vesicle precursors (SVPs) and dense-core vesicles (DCVs). Using live confocal and cryo-electron microscopy, we reveal that vesicle transport undergoes a transient developmental slowdown in the axons of rat hippocampal neurons, associated with increased tripartite ER-vesicle-microtubule interfaces. Using proximity biotinylation, we identify the ER protein PRG1 as a developmentally regulated factor that modulates vesicle retention at these sites by interacting with KIF5A. Notably, a disease-associated PRG1 mutant fails to regulate vesicle trafficking. Finally, we demonstrate that PRG1 modulation of vesicle trafficking serves as a developmental checkpoint by delaying synapse formation and preventing network hyperactivity. Together, our findings establish ER-vesicle contact sites as a previously unrecognized layer of control of axonal trafficking and link intracellular organization to the timing of synapse assembly.

papers.title: Track Display Jockey (trackDJ): a user-friendly R package for visualization of epigenomic data
papers.abstract: Background Visualization of epigenomic data such as coverage tracks, peak calls, and chromatin interactions is a critical task in genomic data analysis. Although genome browsers such as the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) and the UCSC Genome Browser permit user-friendly exploration of genomic tracks, they are not optimized for fully programmatic and reproducible generation of publication-quality figures. In contrast, existing programmatic tools lack a user-friendly interface and require extensive configuration. Results We present trackDJ (Track Display Jockey), an R package for visualization of epigenomic data. trackDJ prioritizes usability by favoring convention over configuration; it provides high-level plotting functions with sensible defaults, aiming to allow users with minimal programming experience to generate clear, publication-quality figures with relatively little coding. Within a unified plotting framework, users can stack and align multiple data types, including coverage tracks, peak annotations, chromatin loops, and gene annotations. trackDJ allows users to select plotted genomic regions by coordinates or by gene name, enabling rapid visualization without knowledge of precise locus boundaries. Conclusions trackDJ complements existing epigenomics toolkits by providing a user-friendly, reproducible alternative to interactive genome browsers for epigenomic visualization. By enabling scripted generation of clean, customizable genomic illustrations, trackDJ readily integrates into R-based analysis workflows to streamline the creation of publication-quality figures.

papers.title: TXNDC15 modulated quality control at the endoplasmic reticulum shapes ciliogenesis
papers.abstract: At the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), membrane protein quality control is tightly regulated to ensure excess subunits are recognized and degraded to protect cellular homeostasis. Using genome wide CRISPR screens, we identified a factor of unknown function, thioredoxin domain containing protein 15 (TXNDC15), and showed that it regulates membrane protein stability by tuning the activity of the E3-ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6. TXNDC15 modulates MARCHF6 in two opposing ways: first, it enhances the binding, ubiquitination, and degradation of membrane protein subunits with soluble cytosolic domains; and second, it prevents the inappropriate recruitment and ubiquitination of subunits with globular lumenal domains. Patient mutations to TXNDC15 that cause the ciliopathy Meckel-Gruber syndrome, disrupted its binding to MARCHF6, allowing degradation of critical ciliary proteins as they transit through the ER leading to defects in ciliogenesis. The regulatory function of TXNDC15 therefore exemplifies how protein quality control maintains the integrity of the proteome to prevent disease.

papers.title: Chemotaxis and motility of Achromatium oxaliferum in response to oxygen, sulfide, and nitrate
papers.abstract: Bacteria of the genus Achromatium are known for their large cell sizes and intracellular calcium carbonate deposits. Achromatium cells inhabit freshwater, brackish, and marine sediments where they accumulate to high abundances at the oxic-anoxic interface. These bacteria alter their vertical position in the sediment along with daily fluctuations in oxygen concentrations. Yet, the mechanism behind their migration in the sediment remains unknown. In this study, we used chemotaxis assays and time-lapse microphotography to analyze the motility and chemotactic behavior of Achromatium oxaliferum. Microscopic observations revealed that rolling and gliding were the main forms of locomotion exhibited by Achromatium. In absence of any stimulant, the movement appeared to be mostly random and changes in direction frequently occurred. Chemotaxis assays showed a negative response of Achromatium to oxygen, sulfide, and nitrate, as evidenced by the change from undirected to directed locomotion against the respective chemical gradient. For periods of more than 1 hour, Achromatium cells moved continuously towards regions of low concentration. We further show that the genetic repertoire of Achromatium corresponds to our observations. Based on lab experiments and bioinformatic analyses we propose that Achromatium motility is propelled by type IV pili guided by a plethora of chemo- and photoreceptors. We further suggest that Achromatium uses negative chemo- and phototaxis to confine their distribution in aquatic sediments between opposing oxygen and sulfide gradients. This allows Achromatium to dynamically adjust its position in redox gradients, and thus is likely to have a major contribution to its success in the global colonization of diverse aquatic sediments.

papers.title: Prefrontal 5-GABA-A receptors: putative role in perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is a dynamic process involving the acquisition and integration of sensory information necessary for adaptive decision making. Resolving the neural basis of perceptual learning may have relevance for our understanding of schizophrenia and other neurodevelopmental disorders that implicate impaired perceptual acuity. We developed a novel touchscreen task that utilizes orientation discrimination and variable attentional load to elucidate the perceptual and attentional components of visual perceptual learning (VPL) in male and female rats. Based on previous evidence we hypothesised that individual variation in VPL may depend in part on inhibitory neurotransmission mediated by {gamma}-amino butyric acid (GABA). Segregating subjects based on 'poor' and 'good' learning after task pretraining revealed dose-dependent improvements in VPL in poor learners following the administration of an 5 subunit specific GABA-A (GABRA5) positive allosteric modulator (Alogabat) and a GABA-B agonist (R-baclofen) early in learning. Poor VPL performance was associated with significantly reduced GABRA5 mRNA expression in dorsal regions of the prefrontal cortex (PFC), notably the prelimbic cortex. Decreased GABRA5 expression in this region was co-localized to somatostatin- and parvalbumin-expressing interneurons. These findings reveal a potential link between GABRA5 expression in selective PFC populations of inhibitory interneurons and the speed and acuity of VPL.

papers.title: GraphHDBSCAN*: Graph-based Hierarchical Clustering on High-dimensional Spaces with Applications to Single-cell RNA Sequencing Data
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is widely used to resolve cellular heterogeneity across thousands to millions of cells. A major challenge is identifying biologically meaningful cell populations while preserving their hierarchical organization, because broad cell types often split into more specialized subtypes. However, state-of-the-art approaches mostly focus on flat partitions and ignore the hierarchical nature of single-cell data. Here we introduce GraphHDBSCAN*, a graph-based extension of HDBSCAN* with an effectively hyperparameter-free hierarchical clustering stage that operates on a graph representation of the data, enabling robust recovery of both hierarchical and non-hierarchical (flat) relationships in very high-dimensional, noisy datasets. We evaluate GraphHDBSCAN* across multiple scRNA-seq datasets and show that it recovers biologically meaningful hierarchies that agree more closely with curated biological references than alternative hierarchical clustering methods, while revealing fine-grained structure, including monocyte subpopulations. In addition, the method yields high-quality flat partitions that outperform widely used community-detection methods.

papers.title: Integrating Long-Read Structural Variant Analysis with single-nucleus RNA-seq to Elucidate Gene Expression Effects in Disease
papers.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

papers.title: Defining the Antigenic Topology and Prospective Binding Breadth of Vaccination-induced SARS-CoV-2 Neutralizing Antibodies
papers.abstract: Antibodies that neutralize SARS-CoV-2 primarily target the viral spike glycoprotein, yet the breadth of these responses is continually challenged by viral evolution. While extensive structural studies have defined epitopes across the spike protein, how antibodies elicited by the initial mRNA vaccination campaigns perform against subsequently emerging variants remains an important question.Here, we structurally and functionally characterize a panel of early plasmablast-derived human monoclonal antibodies isolated following primary mRNA vaccination, targeting both the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the N-terminal domain (NTD) of spike. Using cryo-electron microscopy, variant-binding analyses, and viral-fusion inhibition assays, we observe that antibodies directed against immunodominant regions of the RBD and NTD are highly potent but more frequently impacted by variant-associated mutations. In contrast, antibodies engaging a conserved hydrophobic pocket within the NTD exhibit broader reactivity and neutralize through distinct molecular mechanisms. Together, these findings extend prior structural studies of spike-directed antibodies by prospectively assessing the breadth of vaccine-elicited antibodies against later variants and identifying structural features associated with differential escape sensitivity. These results contribute to a growing understanding of how early vaccine-induced antibody repertoires relate to subsequent viral evolution.

papers.title: Astrocytes mediate a positive feedback loop for oxytocin
papers.abstract: Social interactions are critical for well-being and survival. Oxytocin neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus help regulate social behaviors in many species, and respond to social stimuli to promote pro-social interactions. Here, we show that chronic social isolation reduced production of oxytocin peptide, and led to a delay in the onset of huddling behavior upon resocialization in male mice. Exogenous oxytocin treatment prevented both the behavioral and molecular effects of social deprivation. Using conditional knockouts, we found that oxytocin-induced oxytocin expression was mediated by local hypothalamic astrocytes. Oxytocin signaling in astrocytes upregulated the expression of a retinoic acid-synthesizing enzyme Aldh1a1, and retinoic acid increased oxytocin expression. These findings reveal a mechanism in which astrocytes can sense and control neuropeptide levels to influence social behaviors.

papers.title: BIG-TB: A benchmark for evaluating prediction and interpretability of sequence-based machine learning using Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes
papers.abstract: Foundation models aim to learn useful representations of biological sequences, but are hindered by a lack of benchmarks to jointly evaluate predictive performance and variant attribution on diverse tasks. To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally measured antibiotic resistance phenotypes, combined with a curated list of WHO-catalogue of resistance-associated variants, and provide these data in an ML-ready format. BIG-TB defines two tasks: (1) predictive performance of antibiotic resistance phenotypes, and (2) attribution of predictions to known resistance-conferring variants. Using our tasks, we evaluate DNA- and protein-based foundation models, showing that DNA-based foundation models do not yet outperform simple machine learning baselines (mean test AUC = 0.888 vs. 0.865 for best CNN variant vs. best Evo2 variant across drugs). In a lineage-informed evaluation across DNA and protein modalities, predictive signal for well-characterized drugs was largely preserved (mean AUC 0.846-0.963). Across both evaluation settings, models with the highest predictive performance did not necessarily achieve the strongest recovery of resistance variants, underscoring the value of evaluating both predictive accuracy and biological interpretability. Overall, BIG-TB provides a reusable resource for developing sequence representations that are both accurate and mechanistically meaningful.

papers.title: Floral traits predict nectar rewards across diverse plant communities
papers.abstract: Floral nectar is a key energy resource for many animals, yet direct measurement of nectar rewards is time consuming and difficult to apply across taxonomically diverse plant communities. We tested whether certain floral traits can predict nectar rewards across a broad taxonomic and morphological range of flowering plants. We analysed relationships between floral traits and nectar rewards in 156 species from 42 families. Corolla tube length, corolla base width and corolla shape were recorded alongside nectar volume, sugar concentration and total sugar content, and linear mixed-effects models were used to quantify floral trait nectar relationships in tubular and non tubular flowers. Predictive performance was evaluated using observation- and species-level cross-validation, and phylogenetic signal in nectar volume was assessed using Blomberg's K and Pagel's {lambda}. Nectar volume increased strongly with floral dimensions in both tubular and non-tubular flowers, while sugar content was closely associated with nectar volume, with an approximately proportional relationship on the log scale. These relationships support the use of floral traits to predict sugar content, with predictive performance retained for species not included in model fitting (species-level cross-validation R^2 = 0.43 for tubular and 0.51 for non-tubular flowers). Nectar volume also showed weak but significant phylogenetic signal. Overall, our findings demonstrate that simple floral traits can provide useful predictors of potential nectar rewards across a taxonomically and morphologically diverse range of flowering plants. Such an approach opens the way for future studies to combine trait-based predictions with information on floral abundance, flowering phenology to investigate how nectar resources vary across landscapes in space and time, with potential applications in pollination ecology and the study of nectar feeding insects. Keywords: corolla morphology, floral traits, nectar sugar content, nectar volume, trait based prediction.

papers.title: Connecting spatial regions to clinical phenotypes by transferring knowledge from bulk gene expression data
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) technology has enabled a new level of knowledge about tumors. Many critical tumor properties, such as invasiveness and growth, depend on both specific transcriptomic changes in tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment. However, computational methods to study clinical phenotypes of spatial regions, such as hazard and drug response, have not yet been developed. Since clinical phenotypes are measured at the patient level and not at the level of spatial regions, such a method would require transferring knowledge from the patient level domain to the spot level domain. To overcome this challenge, we developed SpacePhenotyper. Our approach uses algebraic spectral techniques to transfer the predictive relationship between gene expression and clinical phenotypes from bulk gene expression data to SRT data. Our approach captures a gene expression pattern that is predictive of the phenotype of interest in the form of a vector, the Eigen-Patient, which is then used to quantify the phenotype in spatial spots. After extensively validating SpacePhenotyper on simulated and real data, we utilize it to study how the spatial heterogeneity of breast cancer tumors influences residual cancer burden after treatment. By assigning relative quantities of clinical phenotypes to spatial locations, SpacePhenotyper has proven a powerful tool for the identification and interpretation of transcriptional changes over spatial regions and of spatially-regulated patterns of cellular states.

papers.title: CBKMR: A Copula-based Bayesian Kernel Machine Regression Framework for Optimal Marker Detection in Omics Data
papers.abstract: High-throughput bulk and single-cell omics technologies enable comprehensive molecular profiling, yet identifying compact, biologically interpretable marker sets that distinguish cell types, conditions, or disease states remains challenging. Standard pipelines rely on univariate differential expression tests, which ignore gene--gene dependencies and nonlinear effects, while multivariate machine-learning (ML) methods often lack principled feature selection} and {uncertainty quantification. The Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) framework offers an appealing alternative because it (a) captures nonlinear gene--outcome relationships and higher-order interactions, and (b) enables {automatic relevance determination (ARD)} through sparsity-inducing priors. However, we show that the traditional latent Gaussian process (GP) formulation of BKMR is inadequate for discrete outcomes (e.g., cell-type labels), leading to biased inference and unstable variable selection. We propose a copula-based Bayesian kernel machine regression (CBKMR) model that uses outcome-appropriate discrete marginals while a Gaussian copula captures kernel-induced dependence across observations. To ensure scalability to modern single-cell datasets, we further introduce a nearest-neighbor GP-based variant, NNCBKMR, which reduces computational complexity from O(N3) to nearly linear in N. Simulation studies show that CBKMR more accurately captures nonlinear effects and yields stronger marker-selection performance than BKMR and top ensemble ML methods (e.g., random forests, XGBoost). Applications to multiple scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that CBKMR identifies concise marker panels that align closely with expert-annotated gene signatures while providing{posterior uncertainty} for principled decision-making.

papers.title: Modulating inter-mitochondrial contacts to increase membrane potential for mitigating blue light damage
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) is essential for mitochondrial functions, yet current methods for modulating MMP lack precise spatial and temporal control. Here, we developed an optogenetic mitochondrial tethering system, termed OptoMitoTether, that enables reversible control of inter-mitochondrial proximity with high spatiotemporal precision. Blue light activation induced CRY2PHR oligomerization between adjacent mitochondrial outer membranes, reduced mitochondrial nearest-neighbor distances, and promoted inter-mitochondrial tethering. OptoMitoTether activation was associated with elevated MMP and was associated with lower reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preserved ATP production during prolonged blue light stress. Moreover, OptoMitoTether expression preserved mitochondrial bioenergetic function in human retinal cells and extended lifespan in C. elegans during chronic blue light exposure. These findings establish OptoMitoTether as a tool for manipulating mitochondrial proximity and reveal a link between inter-mitochondrial tethering and mitochondrial bioenergetic state during blue light stress.

papers.title: FTO does not function as an m6A eraser in AML: a reassessment using direct RNA nanopore sequencing
papers.abstract: A central concept in epitranscriptomics is that the RNA demethylase FTO acts as a site-selective eraser of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) in specific mRNAs. This is most well-established in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where demethylation of MYC is thought to promote leukemogenesis. Using nanopore direct RNA sequencing to quantify m6A transcriptome-wide, we find that m6A stoichiometry, including at MYC-specific sites, remains unaffected by FTO knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition in AML. Conversely, levels of N6-2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) are markedly increased in snRNAs, indicating that m6Am, not m6A, is the major substrate of FTO in AML. We extend these results outside the AML context in FTO knockout brain and HEK293T cells, detecting no selective increases in mRNA m6A but widespread increases in snRNA m6Am levels following FTO depletion. These findings suggest that FTO has minimal ability to erase m6A in mRNA. Instead, the reported biological effects of FTO are likely mediated by demethylation of m6Am.

papers.title: Differential expression and novel activity of FaCCR1 regulate medium-chain ester content and strawberry fruit aroma
papers.abstract: Fruit flavor and aroma are influenced by the sugars-to-acid ratio and most importantly by the specific profile and abundance of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). While over 550 VOCs have been identified in strawberry fruit, fewer than 20 are believed to be key for aroma, being esters the major components. A major and stable quantitative trait locus (QTL) explaining a large percentage (40%) of phenotypic variation for several medium-chain esters (MCE) was mapped at about 19 Mb in chromosome 6A using both a biparental population and genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Using a combination of genetic mapping, global transcriptomic studies of bulked contrasting lines, and in vivo and in silico functional analyses, we identified the cinnamoyl Co-A reductase FaCCR1(6A) and the organic cation/carnitine transporter FaOCT4(6A) as underlying genes. Subcellular localization experiments indicated that FaCCR1(6A) and FaOCT4(6A) localize at the cytosol and tonoplast membrane respectively. Transient overexpression of FaCCR1(6A) and FaOCT4(6A) in fruits resulted in a significant increase in MCE content. Despite the well-described function of CCRs in the biosynthesis of monolignols, in vitro enzymatic assays and molecular docking revealed that FaCCR1(6A) also presents high affinity for MCE precursors, indicating a previously unidentified function of this protein in volatile biosynthesis. Based in our findings, we have developed a predictive KASP assay in FaOCT4(6A) for selecting superior cultivars with enhanced fruit aroma.

papers.title: A neural geometry for forelimb proprioception in the cervical spinal cord
papers.abstract: Precise, real-time somatosensory feedback is essential for coordinated movement, yet how the nervous system constructs a kinematic representation of the limb from this feedback is unclear. Here, using single-unit electrophysiology in the cervical spinal cords of awake and anesthetized mice, we show that spinal neurons generate a precise, ordered, low-dimensional representation of forelimb kinematic state from muscle and tendon afferent input. This representation arises from two molecularly distinct, developmentally defined classes of dorsal horn neurons. One class encodes limb speed, position and direction; the other fires phasically, with precise, radially periodic firing fields that tile kinematic space. Transient perturbation of muscle and tendon afferents in mice reaching to spatial targets causes endpoint errors predicted by deficits in the neural code. These findings show that spinal networks, one synapse removed from the periphery, are sufficient to construct a precise representation of forelimb movement.

papers.title: The nucleus spatially partitions mechanoprotection and mechanosensing
papers.abstract: Mechanical forces shape cell behavior, but how the nucleus integrates its roles as genome protector and mechanosensor remains unresolved. Here, we dissect the spatiotemporal control of transcriptional response to forces during epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). By combining genome-wide approaches, in vivo nuclear micromanipulation, and quantitative live imaging, we uncover two key properties of nuclear mechanosensing. First, mechanically induced changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription are spatially patterned within the nucleus: genes closest to deformations appear protected, revealing a local shielding mechanism associated with chromatin closure. Second, relocating a gene between chromatin environments is sufficient to alter its mechanosensitivity, challenging the concept of inherently force-sensitive genes. These findings demonstrate unexpected spatial partition of nuclear response to forces.

papers.title: Aberrant splicing prediction during human organ development
papers.abstract: Developmental disorders constitute a major class of genetic diseases, yet tools to identify splicing-disruptive variants during development are lacking. To address this need we extended the AbSplice framework to incorporate splicing dynamics across developmental stages. Moreover, we introduced several improvements including a continuous representation of splice site usage and integration of the rich set of predictions from the sequence-based model Pangolin. These advances improve the performance of the original model at predicting aberrant splicing events and help outperform purely sequence-based models including AlphaGenome, enabling predictions across embryonic, childhood, and adult tissues. Genome-wide scores for all single-nucleotide variants and a web interface to score indels are available to facilitate the exploration of the predictions. Our genome-wide predictions reveal a class of variants with splicing-disruptive effects confined to early development, particularly abundant in the brain (>18,000 variants). These variants are enriched in loss-of-function intolerant genes and neurodevelopmental disorder genes. Within the rare-disease cohort Solve-RD, high-impact brain-specific predictions are significantly enriched in individuals affected by neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) in NDD-linked genes. Furthermore, the predicted developmental timing of the splicing disruption correlates with the clinical age of onset. Analysis of genomes of individuals with a suspected Mendelian disorder from Genomics England identified 26 unique variants in disease-linked genes, with stronger predicted effects during development than in adulthood, including a candidate new diagnosis in the gene FGFR1. Altogether, these results improve the accuracy of splice-disruptive variant prediction and provide tissue and developmental context to aid interpretation in rare disease diagnostics.

papers.title: Individual differences in fear memory expression engage distinct functional brain networks
papers.abstract: Fearful stimuli elicit a mix of active (e.g., evasion) and passive (e.g., freezing) behaviors in a wide range of species, including zebrafish (Danio rerio). Yet, how individuals vary in these responses, and how such differences are encoded in the brain, remains unclear. Here, we developed a contextual fear conditioning paradigm in which adult zebrafish learned to associate a specific tank with an aversive pheromone, conspecific alarm substance (CAS). Behavior during memory expression comprised of a mix of active and passive responses that clustered into four behavioral clusters: non-reactive, evaders, evading freezers, and freezers with the two high-freezing groups most clearly reflecting fear memory formation. We tested memory in four strains (AB, TU, TL, and WIK), and both sexes, finding that they shaped fear memory responses: males were more likely to increase evasion during CAS exposure, whereas TU fish were more likely non-reactive during recall. Whole-brain activity mapping during memory expression revealed that freezing engaged widespread neural activity that was particularly strong in the cerebellum, reticular formation, and parts of the telencephalon associated with olfactory processing. Evasion recruited visual threat detection regions and suppressed foraging and navigation circuits. Functional network analysis revealed that fish that froze, but had low levels of evasion (i.e., freezers) during memory expression had strong pallial-cerebellar connections and heightened interconnectivity between visual (pretectal) and thalamic like (preglomerular) nuclei. Animals that mixed freezing with evasive behaviors (i.e., evading freezers) had higher subpallial connectivity with autonomic and stress-regulatory regions like the hypothalamus and preoptic areas. Together, these findings demonstrate that distinct behavioral types during fear memory recall are supported by divergent brain-wide networks.

papers.title: Aevol-9: A simulation platform to decipher the evolution of genome architecture
papers.abstract: Aevol is a forward-in-time simulator of genome architecture. It simulates a population of individuals, each with an explicit genome whose sequence and architecture can be modified by various mutational operators, including substitutions, indels, and large-scale chromosomal rearrangements. This enables performing in silico experiments to decipher the effects of evolutionary conditions (e.g. population size, selection strength, mutation rates, and biases) on genome organization.

papers.title: Neural drift during rest drives walking direction and memory consolidation in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Heading is represented in head direction systems across species, including Drosophila. However, how navigation decisions are made and how goal memories are maintained, particularly during rest, is little understood. Here, using a navigation learning assay for flies walking in virtual reality, we describe neural dynamics for direction selection and memory. Activity of a subset of neurons in the fan-shaped body, a navigation and memory-related structure, continually drifts when the animal is at rest, centered 180 degrees opposite to the walking direction. Optogenetic activation during rest biases subsequent walking direction. Learning shifts rest activity, revealing a memory of goal direction. Downstream neurons correct the 180 degree shift, reactivating walking directions during rest; the connectome reveals a compact circuit consistent with reactivation, validated by computational modeling. Thus, rest activity drives behavior, reactivates walking directions, and is shaped by memory, suggesting shared principles for memory consolidation in navigation circuits across species.

papers.title: A reformulation of the t-test in single-cell transcriptomics dramatically reduces false positives
papers.abstract: The default differential expression tests in single-cell analysis software provide fast and simple approaches that help practitioners annotate cell populations identified through clustering algorithms. Here, we use theoretical arguments and empirical studies to show that these tests suffer from inflated false positive rates that affect the resulting annotations. We introduce LN's t-test, which tests a novel, asymptotically unbiased log-fold change estimator and avoids these false positives, without compromising speed.

papers.title: Aperiodic activity in the prefrontal cortex compensates for age-related decline in hippocampal theta and gamma oscillations during navigation
papers.abstract: A critical gap remains in our understanding of age-related periodic and aperiodic electrophysiological changes across the human brain and their association with memory function. Using direct intracranial recordings from 69 epilepsy patients aged 19-61 performing a virtual navigation task, we separated oscillatory power from the aperiodic component. Hippocampal theta and gamma power decreased with age and correlated with impaired spatial memory. Age-related hippocampal spectral changes were replicated in an independent resting-state dataset. Aperiodic spectral slopes flattened in the prefrontal cortex but steepened in the hippocampus with age, suggesting region-specific changes in excitation-inhibition balance. Individuals with flatter dorsolateral prefrontal spectral slopes performed well despite reduced hippocampal theta and gamma power, suggesting a compensatory mechanism. This shift from hippocampal memory processes to prefrontal upregulation provides insight into cognitive resilience in aging and suggests potential targets for promoting healthy memory aging.

papers.title: An interactive web application for exploring human plasma and fibroblast metabolomics data from patients with inborn errors of metabolism
papers.abstract: Metabolomic profiling is instrumental in understanding the systemic and cellular impact of inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs), monogenic disorders caused by pathogenic genomic variants in genes involved in metabolism. This study encompasses metabolomics analysis of plasma from 474 individuals and fibroblasts from 67 subjects, incorporating healthy controls, patients with 65 different monogenic diseases, and numerous undiagnosed cases. We introduce a web application designed for the in-depth exploration of this extensive metabolomics database. The application offers a user-friendly interface for data review, download, and detailed analysis of metabolic deviations linked to IEMs at the level of individual patients or groups of patients with the same diagnosis. It also provides interactive tools for investigating metabolic relationships and offers comparative analyses of plasma and fibroblast profiles. This tool emphasizes the metabolic interplay within and across biological matrices, enriching our understanding of metabolic regulation in health and disease. As a resource, the application provides broad utility in research, offering novel insights into metabolic pathways and their alterations in various disorders.

papers.title: Onsager's relations and Ecology
papers.abstract: There are two complementary approaches to thermodynamics, one is an empirical, phenomenological representation of macroscopic states and the second is a model-based, statistical-mechanical representation of microscopic states. If only a few energy transformation steps are involved, macroscopic quantities such as energy and entropy can be estimated without ambiguity, and often the associated microscopic states are well characterised. Both approaches have been used to develop and guide many key early ecological ideas. However, most ecosystems are characterized by uncountably many transformations that operate on a wide range of space and time scales. This renders the bounds of such systems ambiguous making both the macroscopic and microscopic approaches a challenge. As such, the implementation of both approaches remain areas ripe for further investigation. In particular, the Onsager reciprocal relations permit simplification of expectations that are yet to be fully understood in an ecological context. This review explores the far-reaching ramifications of these thermodynamic relations in an ecological context.

papers.title: Epigenetic Mechanisms Inhibit Smad7 and Contribute to Fibrosis in Crohn's Disease
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: TGF-beta1 is a central regulator of profibrotic gene expression, extracellular matrix deposition, and the development of intestinal fibrosis in patients with fibrostenotic Crohns disease (CD). Unlike the increased expression of Smad7 in mucosal and lamina propria monocytes, where it impairs Treg function, mesenchymal cells from patients with fibrostenotic CD do not exhibit elevated Smad7 expression and instead display sustained TGF-beta1 signaling. We therefore sought to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the unexpected silencing of Smad7 in fibrostenotic CD. Methods: Subepithelial myofibroblasts (SEMFs) and muscularis smooth muscle cells were isolated from paired normal and affected ileal tissues obtained from the same patients with each Montreal phenotype of CD, as well as from non-CD controls. Gene expression, RNA-binding affinity, transcriptional activity, promoter methylation, protein levels, and the mechanisms that regulate Smad7 expression were evaluated in ex vivo tissues and primary cultured cells. MicroRNA-21 (miR-21) localization was assessed by RNAscope. miR-21-mediated suppression of Smad7 was investigated using antagomiR-21. Smad7 silencing through promoter hypermethylation was confirmed using 5-Azacytidine treatment and DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) knockdown. Smad7 lysine acetylation and Smurf1/2-mediated ubiquitination were examined using selective inhibitors and proximity ligation assays. Results: In SEMFs from patients with fibrostenotic CD, aberrant silencing of Smad7 resulted from DNMT1-dependent promoter hypermethylation and pSmad3-driven, miR-21-mediated degradation of Smad7 mRNA. In addition, Smurf1/2 promoted ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of acetylated Smad7 protein. Inhibition of miR-21 with antagomiR-21 restored Smad7 expression and reduced TGF-beta 1-dependent profibrotic gene expression. Likewise, demethylation with 5-Azacytidine or knockdown of DNMT1 induced Smad7 promoter hypomethylation and restored Smad7 expression. Furthermore, modulation of the balance between p300 acetyltransferase and histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) stabilized Smad7 protein by protecting it from degradation. Conclusions: A distinctive pattern of epigenetic silencing and post-translational regulation of Smad7 was identified in patients with fibrostenotic CD. These mechanisms collectively promote unrestrained TGF-beta1 signaling by suppressing Smad7 expression and stability in SEMFs, thereby contributing to the development of intestinal fibrosis.

papers.title: Donor-associated variation outweighs PMOS status in patient-derived iPSC transcriptomes: a genotyped, BMI-adjusted study of 14 lines
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patients have been little used to model polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, formerly polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS), and differences between unrelated donors can masquerade as disease effects. Earlier comparisons of three or four donors per group reported hundreds to thousands of differentially expressed genes. We asked whether a disease signature is detectable in a larger, genotyped panel, balanced for BMI category and BMI-adjusted, of full-phenotype patients. Methods: We studied 14 clonal, transgene-free iPSC lines reprogrammed by CRISPR activation from endometrial stromal fibroblasts of seven women with PMOS meeting all three Rotterdam criteria, and seven controls frequency-matched for BMI category (<25 or >30 kg/m2). Bulk RNA-seq (16,489 expressed genes) was related to diagnosis, hormones, metabolic traits, age, and X-inactive specific transcript (XIST) status using gene-wise models, exact enumeration of all 3,432 group splits, and permutation-calibrated gene-set tests. Donors were genotyped within a cohort of 140 women and scored with an imputation-based genome-wide PMOS polygenic risk score (PRS). PMOS risk-locus genes were examined against a 202-line iPSC proteome. Results: PMOS donors had higher anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), testosterone, and free androgen index than controls. No gene was differentially expressed between PMOS and control lines (false discovery rate < 0.1), and the number of nominally associated genes was no greater than for random 7-versus-7 splits of the lines (p = 0.75). This was unchanged with an alternative read quantification and with count-based models. With seven donors per group, the design could detect 1.8-fold differences per gene, compared with roughly 3- to 6-fold for the three- or four-donor designs used previously. Neither diagnosis nor any hormonal or metabolic trait explained more expression variance than chance, and neither PMOS GWAS-locus genes nor Hallmark pathways were enriched. Two control lines showed near-complete loss of XIST, potentially indicative of X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion, and a third was borderline. Endocrine PMOS-locus genes (e.g., FSHR, AMH) were not expressed, whereas DNA-repair and growth genes were. Across 129 genotyped women, the PRS was higher in PMOS (odds ratio 1.81 per SD; AUC 0.65), but PMOS and control iPSC donors overlapped fully in polygenic risk. Conclusions: In this panel of 14 undifferentiated iPSC lines from women with the full PMOS phenotype, no robust PMOS-associated transcriptomic differences were detected. Expression variation was dominated by line-to-line differences, consistent with donor background as their main source, although with one clone per donor a contribution of clonal variation cannot be excluded. Reduced XIST expression in some control lines is potentially indicative of, but does not establish, X-chromosome inactivation erosion. Disease-associated differences in differentiated, hormone-responsive cells cannot be excluded, and differences reported in smaller panels may partly reflect inter-donor variability. Future studies should use adequately sized panels, control for XIST erosion, select donors by polygenic risk, and examine hormone-responsive derivatives. Keywords: polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome; polycystic ovary syndrome; induced pluripotent stem cells; transcriptome; polygenic risk; XIST erosion; disease modelling; experimental design

papers.title: Pharmaco-genetic evidence of presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction coupled to detrimental DPR secretion in Drosophila Models of C9orf72-linked ALS/FTD.
papers.abstract: Hexanucleotide repeat expansions in C9orf72, the most common genetic cause of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), drive neurodegeneration through both loss of gene function and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms, including transcription of repeat RNA and repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation into dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs). Both disease mechanisms have been linked to disruption of the autophagy-lysosome pathway (ALP), though how this contributes to disease progression remains unclear. By expressing toxic C9orf72 repeats in Drosophila melanogaster, we observed presymptomatic lysosome impairment, coupled with largely preserved autophagosome formation. Pharmacological treatment with valproic acid (VPA) partially prevented neurodegenerative and locomotor phenotypes in expressing animals in presence of Mitf, which is required for lysosomal biogenesis. Genetic inhibition of residual lysosomal degradation enhanced neurotoxicity, whereas downregulation of autophagy and secretory autophagy genes suppressed toxicity, uncovering a previously unrecognized contribution of secretion to disease. Consistent with this, in vitro experiments indicated that disabling lysosome function, but not autophagy induction, leads to an increase in neuronal release of autophagy-associated proteins and DPRs, which can be found be uptaken by nearby neurons and glia in vivo. We propose that repeat-driven presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction, prevented by pharmacologic treatment, promotes secretory autophagy, which, in turn facilitates extracellular release and intercellular propagation of neurotoxic DPRs.

papers.title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
papers.abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG's 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.

papers.title: Why don't transcription factors exploit inter-nucleotide correlations in binding motifs? Evolution of information encoding strategies on DNA
papers.abstract: Transcription factors have been shown to predominantly rely on independent contributions from each position of their target sequence motifs, even though sequence motifs can encode information through correlations among nucleotide positions. As a result, the position-weight matrix, a simple modeling approach that assumes independence among positions, has long since become the dominant model of TF-DNA binding. Why evolution would favor this comparatively simple strategy, known as single locus information (SI), over a correlation-based one remains unaddressed. Here, we use analytical derivations, numerical approaches and evolutionary simulations to show that SI is intrinsically more robust to mutation than correlated (multi-locus) encodings and is therefore indirectly favored under selection for functional transcriptional regulatory networks. At the same time, we show that SI smooths the affinity landscape, ensuring the evolvability of regulatory interactions. We find the same marked bias toward SI in the genetic code, suggesting that the preference for SI is not specific to transcriptional regulation, but may be a general property of biological codes that must reliably store information on DNA in the face of mutational noise.

papers.title: Evolutionary games on networks with negative edge-based environmental feedback
papers.abstract: Environmental feedback can fundamentally alter the game payoff structure underlying the evolution of cooperation. How feedback-evolving games interact with population structure under non-weak selection remains incompletely understood. We study an evolutionary game on networks in which each edge has a binary environmental state that determines the payoff matrix used by the two connected individuals. By assumption, cooperation tends to improve the local environment, which in turn favors defection, thereby creating negative feedback between strategies coupled with the environmental condition. We analyze the model under strong selection using a mean-field approximation, a pair approximation that tracks both strategy pairs and edge environments, and agent-based simulations. In well-mixed populations, the feedback can generate bistability between full cooperation and full defection, as well as sustained oscillations arising through a Hopf bifurcation. Sparse networks (i.e., with low nodes' degrees) can eliminate bistability, suppress oscillations, and produce stable intermediate levels of cooperation. The pair approximation captures these effects and generally agrees more closely with simulations on sparse networks than the mean-field approximation. Our results show that edge-based environmental feedback and network structure, such as density of edges, interact to determine whether the fraction of cooperators stabilizes or oscillates over time.

papers.title: Parallel transcriptome profiling of soybean cyst nematodes (SCN) during a three-way interaction among SCN, soybean aphids, and soybean
papers.abstract: The soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Heterodera glycines (Ichinoe) (Rhabditida: Heteroderidae) is arguably the greatest yield-limiting factor for soybean (Glycine max [L.] Merr.) production in the United States. Previous research found that the impact of SCN infestation on yield is exacerbated during concurrent infestations with soybean aphids (SBA), Aphis glycines (Matsurmura) (Hemiptera: Aphididae). Although recent research has characterized the host root transcriptomic response during these infestations little is known about the corresponding in planta gene expression dynamics of either pest. This study examines the transcriptomic expression of SCN in soybean cultivars' roots under single or combined SBA infestations at two different time points: 5 and 30 days post-infestation (DPI). The SCN transcriptomics for SCN-susceptible (S) PI 518671 (Williams 82) cultivar reacted equivalently to both SCN and SCN + SBA treatments. However, transcriptomics in SCN-resistant (R) MN1806CN (H. glycines HG type 0/race 3 resistant) demonstrated an elevated significant expression pattern under the SCN + SBA combined treatment. During the early infestation period (i.e., sampled at 5 DPI), both S and R cultivars reacted similarly, irrespective of treatment conditions. The functional enrichment analysis of 1829 differentially expressed genes/transcripts showed that during the early co-infestation period (5 DPI), SCN genes were significant and mapped towards resistance breakage, whereas in the late stage (30 DPI), the gene flux oriented towards nematode dormancy. Together, these results suggest that SCN activity is amplified when combined with SBA, offering foundational data for molecular breeding to produce SCN resistant soybean cultivars.

papers.title: DaliScope: Distilling Biological Insights from Deep Structural Alignments
papers.abstract: Structural similarity searches reveal protein relationships that sequence alignments miss, but treating DALI results as isolated match lists misses deeper connections. We present DaliScope, an interactive Python framework that treats complete DALI target sets as structured populations for systematic analysis of protein structural neighbourhoods. DaliScope combines structural community detection with sequence profiling, Pfam annotation, residue mapping, and 3D visualization, enabling target sets to be subdivided and examined at the residue level. We demonstrate two applications. In a multidomain protein with sparse domain annotation, structural analysis uncovered previously unannotated domains. A structurally anchored HxD...H signature occurred in 697 of 1,093 Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains and in 15 domains lacking Pfam annotation; relaxing the central residue constraint recovered 96% of Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains among the DALI targets. In a second application, a DALI search with transitive closure returned >12,000 hits. Applying an 80% coverage criterion to a conserved structural core reduced this set to 6,708 domain instances, resolved into 23 structural communities. (80% was chosen instead of the default 50% because the GOLD domain has a compact core with short loops.) Many communities were strongly enriched for individual Pfam families while providing structural context for 1,097 targets lacking Pfam assignments. Three-dimensional superimposition revealed structural continuity among related {beta}-sandwich architectures through progressive changes in sheet geometry and auxiliary elements. Together, these examples show how a single DALI query provides a structural anchor for organizing large neighbourhoods, extending interpretation beyond sequence-based annotations, and deriving structurally anchored sequence signatures from defined populations.

papers.title: Whole-Brain MRSI Metabolic Connectomics Reveals Network Disruptions and Altered Gradient Coherence in Psychosis Risk
papers.abstract: Brain network alterations preceding first-episode psychosis often escape connectomic approaches based on conventional neuroimaging, such as diffusion or functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Whole-brain magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) offers a potentially more sensitive alternative: by mapping neurometabolites across the brain, it enables the construction of metabolic connectomes that may capture very early and subtle disruptions of brain network properties. We combined whole-brain proton MRSI, diffusion MRI, and resting-state functional MRI in a sample of 29 individuals meeting DSM-5 criteria for Attenuated Psychosis Syndrome (APS) or Schizotypal Personality Disorder (SCZT), pooled into a single High Risk for Psychosis (HR) group, and 30 healthy controls (HC) to construct metabolic, structural, and functional connectomes. Network-based statistics identified a significant metabolic connectivity subnetwork with higher connectivity in HR than in HC, whereas no corresponding structural or functional connectivity differences were detected. Nodes of this subnetwork had modestly higher structural strength but were not consistently enriched among structural hubs, and no significant regional abnormalities in individual metabolite concentrations were detected. Eigenmode analysis of metabolic connectivity revealed a low-dimensional organization spanning a posterior unimodal-to-transmodal axis and a transmodal-to-limbic axis. Path analysis revealed higher bilateral energy in HR, indicating reduced coherence along a metabolic gradient that parallels the neurodevelopmental sensorimotor-to-association axis. These findings identify whole-brain metabolic network organization derived from MRSI as a systems-level phenotype of psychosis risk and raise the possibility that it captures altered development of large-scale cortical organization.

papers.title: Dynamical Fingerprints of Rare-Event Transitions from Transition Corridors
papers.abstract: Rare transitions are central in science, yet their mechanisms are obscured by the high dimensionality of complex dynamics, a challenge particularly pronounced in biomolecules where rare conformational transitions underlie functional processes. A transition-conditioned dynamical fingerprint is introduced for a rare \(A \mathbin{\text{--}} B\) event, in which the transition-relevant subset is targeted rather than a global decomposition and the problem is treated dynamically. Within a selected transition corridor, barrier-crossing motion is extracted and microscopic players are ranked through a corridor-conditioned informativeness measure, after which the highest-ranked players are subjected to intervention tests of their transition leverage using the REST2 scaling scheme, metadynamics, and targeted mutation. Across three benchmark proteins, targeting these players facilitates basin-to-basin transitions while maintaining high fidelity to the prescribed transition corridor, providing handles for mechanistic analysis, enhanced sampling, control, and design.

papers.title: Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
papers.abstract: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.

papers.title: HMGB1/CXCL12 heterocomplex activates CXCR4 to suppress the ability of Muller glia to become proliferating progenitor-like cells in the chick retina
papers.abstract: We investigated how High Mobility Group Box 1 (HMGB1) signaling regulates glial reactivity and Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) formation in the chick retina. HMGB1 released from stressed cells is known to form a heterocomplex with C-X-C chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12) to activate C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4). HMGB1 is broadly expressed in retinal neurons and glia and is rapidly exported from the nuclei of stressed inner retinal neurons after damage, a process blocked by inflachromene. Stressed or damaged amacrine cells also exported different transcription factors out nuclei. CXCL12 is expressed by amacrine, horizontal, and bipolar cells, whereas CXCR4 is expressed by Muller glia and is rapidly upregulated following damage. CXCR4 agonist or recombinant HMGB1/CXCL12 treatment selectively stimulates mTOR and Jak/Stat signaling in Muller glia in undamaged retinas. Inhibition of CXCR4 signaling, HMGB1 nuclear export, or HMGB1/CXCL12 complex formation potently stimulated MGPC proliferation without affecting neuronal death or microglial activation. In retinas treated with insulin and FGF2, to induce MGPC proliferation independent of injury, HMGB1 remains confined to nuclei, CXCR4 is downregulated, and inhibition of HMGB1 or CXCR4 has no effect. We further demonstrate that microglia are required to maintain CXCR4 expression in Muller glia, and blockade of HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling does not restore MGPC proliferation in microglia-depleted retinas. Together, these findings identify HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling as an injury-induced pathway that limits Muller glia reprogramming and MGPC formation in damaged retinas.

papers.title: A coral-linked adaptive radiation in butterflyfishes
papers.abstract: Coral reefs harbour a disproportionate share of marine biodiversity, yet whether reef fish diversity reflects steady accumulation or rapid, ecologically driven diversification remains unclear. Butterflyfishes and bannerfishes (Chaetodontidae) include more than half of all coral-feeding fish species, making them a natural test of adaptive radiation on coral reefs. Here we present a time-calibrated phylogeny of 120 of the 138 species, built from 1,009 ultraconserved elements. The species-rich butterflyfishes (Chaetodontinae) are a recent radiation that originated in the Late Miocene (7.78 million years ago; 95% highest posterior density 7.13 to 8.49 million years ago), with much of their extant species diversity arising within the past 2 million years. The crown diversification rate of butterflyfishes is the highest among 29 comparator reef-fish lineages. Ancestral state reconstructions indicate that the ancestor of Chaetodontinae was a facultative corallivore, that a unique jaw joint arose before obligate corallivory, and that obligate corallivory then evolved repeatedly from facultative ancestors, alongside derived tooth morphologies. Together, these results suggest that Late Miocene coral reef turnover and the diversification of branching corals generated an ecological opportunity that functional innovations allowed butterflyfishes to exploit, extending the adaptive radiation framework to open marine seascapes beyond the island and lake systems where it has most often been applied.

papers.title: Sensory and Motor Building Blocks of an Extra Robotic Digit Representation
papers.abstract: Supernumerary limbs provide a unique opportunity to ask how the brain represents an entirely novel effector within an existing sensorimotor system. Here, we investigated how primary motor cortex (M1) represents a robotic extra digit (the Third Thumb; Dani Clode Design), and how this representation changes with experience. Using fMRI, we compared participants following short-term exposure with participants who had undergone longitudinal Third Thumb training. The device was controlled by the toes but operated alongside the biological fingers, while its sensory consequences were experienced on the hand. Following prolonged experience, greater activity was elicited in the M1 hand area both during Third Thumb control, and in response to its sensory consequences alone. Multivariate analyses showed that the Third Thumb representation became more distinct from its biological toe controller. Pattern component modelling further showed that the representation could be explained by a combination of its constituent motor and sensory patterns, but their relative contributions changed substantially with experience, from toe-dominated following short-term exposure to sensory-dominated following longitudinal training. These findings suggest that M1 can represent a novel effector through flexible recombination of existing sensorimotor representations, with experience altering how these pre-existing resources contribute to the emerging representation.

papers.title: Object features survive motion at saccadic speed but lose their link to specific objects
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements sweep objects across the retina at high speed, and this motion is routinely omitted from conscious perception. Whether object identity survives such motion is unclear. In two preregistered experiments (N = 20 and N = 19), we asked how object motion at saccadic speeds, while the eyes fixate, affects object continuity in the object-reviewing paradigm (Kahneman et al., 1992; Sasi et al., 2023). Two Gabor patches each carried a digit, then disappeared and reappeared in place, reappeared displaced, or travelled continuously to their new locations; the intervening interval lasted 300 ms or was matched to the mean or peak speed of a saccade. A target digit then appeared in one patch, and participants identified it. At the long duration, we replicated the Object-Specific Preview Benefit (OSPB): responses were faster when the target had been previewed in that same object than in the other one. At saccadic durations, the OSPB disappeared, and adding a distinguishing surface feature in Experiment 2 did not restore it. The general preview benefit, faster responses to any previewed digit than to a new one, persisted at every duration. Object features therefore survive motion at saccadic speed, but their link to a particular object does not.

papers.title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease.
papers.abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10-based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ-brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer's disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (delta ROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

papers.title: A complete adult Drosophila melanogaster brain tracheolar network
papers.abstract: The tracheal system of the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, is a complex network of epithelial tubules that supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide throughout the organism, with gases entering and exiting through spiracles along the body. While tracheal development and patterning in the embryonic and larval stages have been extensively studied, particularly in the body, much less is known about tracheal and tracheolar organization within the adult brain. To address this gap, we manually traced every tracheole in the brain of a female adult Drosophila using the Full Adult Fly Brain (FAFB) open-access electron microscopy dataset. We reconstructed 117 tracheoles that branch within the parenchyma, terminating in 1,376 endings without forming an interconnected network. Joint analysis of these skeleton reconstructions with volumetric mesh segmentations from the FlyWire connectome revealed that tracheole volume fraction is heterogeneous across neuropils and largely symmetric in overall tracheation between left and right hemispheres. We observe that synapses are not preferentially positioned near tracheoles, and are instead slightly depleted from a region approximately 15 um around tracheoles, relative to other points along the same neurons. We also quantify the relative proximity of neurotransmitter-specific synapses and cables to tracheoles across neuropils. This detailed anatomical description of the tracheolar network establishes a reference for future studies examining how neuronal patterning, activity, and metabolic demand couple with tracheole development and function.

papers.title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
papers.abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.

papers.title: PhyMorphS: A Physics-Guided Framework for Mesh-Based Morphological Synthesis of White Matter Microstructures
papers.abstract: Numerical phantoms provide controlled 3D representations of brain tissue microstructure for developing and evaluating biophysical models of diffusion-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI). Existing phantom synthesizers employ different geometric primitives and optimization strategies to generate densely packed substrates with diverse axonal morphologies. However, direct deformation of axonal surfaces under mechanical constraints remains less explored. We propose PhyMorphS, a mesh-based framework in which axonal morphology emerges through physics-guided growth and interactions with the local microstructural environment, without constraining cross-sections to predefined symmetric shapes. In PhyMorphS, axons, myelin sheaths, and cell bodies are represented by triangle meshes, while a mass-spring system and collision-resolution scheme guide iterative axonal growth under mechanical and packing constraints. This enables irregular, asymmetric, and non-convex cross-sections, longitudinal diameter variation, and user-defined morphological alterations such as axonal beading and myelin layer decompaction. We evaluate PhyMorphS against large-scale X-ray nano-holotomography segmentations of real 3D axons from four white matter regions with distinct fiber organizations. The synthesized axons reproduce key region-specific morphological characteristics and achieve high packing densities, while the parallelized implementation scales approximately linearly with axon count in the generation voxel. By reproducing the geometric variability observed in real WM tissue, PhyMorphS provides controlled substrates for investigating how realistic morphology influences simulated dMRI signals, testing the geometric assumptions of biophysical microstructure models, and generating diverse paired microstructure-signal datasets for training machine-learning models.

papers.title: The Where and When of Tracking Sound Sources Head-based auditory motion tracking integrates velocity and spatial error within a common delayed frame
papers.abstract: Auditory objects in everyday environments remain seldomly at the same position but move about in the environment and keeping track of their motion is an essential task for the auditory system to maintain a correct representation of auditory space/scene. Following such a moving sound source in two-dimensional space requires the nervous system to guide head movements using delayed and uncertain sensory information. How the auditory system integrates such information for combined horizontal and vertical movements is still debated. 116 117 We recorded head movements from 14 participants tracking a physically moving loudspeaker along unpredictable two-dimensional trajectories. Participants followed source motion with substantial delays and retained measurable spatial discrepancies. To explain these behaviours, we developed a hybrid model combining source velocity with the spatial discrepancy between source and head at the matched, delayed time points. The model predicts head velocity on previously unseen trajectories more accurately than formulations relying on either signal alone. Importantly, using preceding rather than current head orientation improved prediction, highlighting the importance of temporal correspondence between sensory and motor states. These findings suggest that head-based auditory motion tracking depends on complementary motion and spatial information represented within a common delayed reference frame.

papers.title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
