papers.abstract: Bladder outlet obstruction leads to pathological remodeling and emergence of lower urinary tract symptoms. Although relief of obstruction is associated with symptomatic improvement, it is not universally successful, reflecting persistent alterations in the bladder. Reliable surrogate biomarkers of obstruction are lacking, particularly early in the disease course before irreversible damage to the bladder may have occurred. In this study, re-analysis of publicly available transcriptomic datasets from diverse rodent models of obstruction identified tissue transcripts including Cthrc1, Grem1, Ltbp2, Acta1 and Msn that were induced in response to injury. Candidate markers were validated experimentally in an independent model of neurogenic obstruction demonstrating time-dependent changes, and a subset (GREM1, LTBP2, ACTA1, MSN) was increased in bladder tissue from pediatric patients with neurogenic bladder. Several candidates including CTHRC1, ACTA1 and MSN were also differentially abundant in independent proteomic datasets from a rat model of partial bladder outlet obstruction. Candidate markers were also attenuated in datasets from rats with either surgical removal of obstruction or treatment with anticholinergic medication or inosine. Integrated analysis of tissue transcriptomics data and tissue and urine proteomics data from a model of neurogenic obstruction revealed modest but statistically significant concordance between markers observed in tissue and urine. These findings identify tissue and urine biomarkers of both non-neurogenic and neurogenic obstruction that may reflect early changes in obstructive uropathy that could be monitored in a non-invasive manner.

papers.title: MitoScope: a comprehensive mitochondrial genome analysis workflow for long-read sequencing data
papers.abstract: The mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), rich in repeats and prone to nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), is implicated in cancer, metabolic syndromes, and neurodegeneration, yet short-read sequencing yields incomplete catalogs, mapping artifacts, and false heteroplasmies. We introduce MitoScope, a scalable end-to-end long-read mitochondrial analysis workflow that integrates mtDNA-read selection, heteroplasmic variant detection, assembly, copy number estimation, read-level haplotyping, and NUMT profiling. Applied to benchmarking data from the Somatic Mosaicism Across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, we reveal high sensitivity and precision compared to existing methods and successfully uncover known mitochondrial biology relevant for variant interpretation, aging, and human disease.

papers.title: Geometric Kinematics of Human Eyes
papers.abstract: In previous studies by the author on binocular vision with the asymmetric eye (AE), which models a healthy human eye with misaligned optical components, the results were primarily presented in the Rodrigues' vector (RV) framework and supported by simulations and 3D visualizations in GeoGebra's dynamic geometry environment. In this paper, the novel geometric kinematics of the human eye, that is, the eye with misaligned optics, and simplified assumptions about the eye rotations (the eye's translational movements are disregarded), are developed within the framework of rigid-body rotations. The originality of the analysis lies in a precise geometric decomposition of a full rotation of the eye's posture into a torsion-free rotation (the geodesic part) and a torsional rotation (the non-geodesic extension of the geodesic part). This decomposition is extended to the corresponding decomposition of the angular velocity. A novel derivation of the eye's angular velocity from the RV formulation of the eye kinematics is proposed.

papers.title: Intraguild predation and life-history variation in a natural nematode predator-prey system
papers.abstract: Predator-prey interactions are key drivers of behavioural and life-history evolution, as reciprocal selection can shape adaptations in both predators and prey. Yet, understanding how such interactions evolve in nature remains challenging because the ecological context in which they occur is often difficult to experimentally access. The nematode Pristionchus pacificus is a well-established model for studying predatory behaviour, but most experimental work has examined its predatory interactions with Caenorhabditis elegans, a species that P. pacificus is unlikely to encounter frequently in nature. Here, we investigate predation in a natural ecological context by focusing on nematode communities associated with beetles, the native necromenic habitat of P. pacificus. We identify Oscheius myriophilus as a species that co-occurs with P. pacificus in this niche and represents a natural prey species. Using established predatory assays, we show that P. pacificus actively attacks, kills, and consumes O. myriophilus. Strikingly, predation rates are significantly lower than those observed for C. elegans, consistent with the possibility that prolonged ecological association has favoured adaptations that reduce predation susceptibility. Supporting this interpretation, we identify distinct life-history traits in O. myriophilus, including a mixed reproductive strategy involving early oviposition followed by internal hatching of later progeny and matricide. Later developmental stages are more resistant to predatory attack, suggesting that retaining embryos within the maternal body may provide a protected environment in which offspring can develop while remaining buffered from predation. Together, our findings establish P. pacificus and O. myriophilus as a tractable system for investigating predator-prey interactions in a natural ecological context and provide a foundation for dissecting how predatory behaviour and prey life-history strategies evolve in response to one another.

papers.title: Damaged motile cilia undergo phagolysosomal clearance during regeneration
papers.abstract: The remodelling and regeneration of motile cilia are widespread yet poorly understood cellular responses to stress. Whether components from damaged cilia are reutilised during regeneration remains unclear. Here, we apply acute, non-lethal stress to the multiciliated eukaryote Tetrahymena thermophila to investigate the fate of damaged motile cilia during regeneration. We find that damaged axonemes accumulate intracellularly as coiled structures, termed c-rings, which are sequestered within phagosome-associated membrane compartments and subsequently associate with acidic compartments for clearance. Imaging, quantitative proteomics and genetic perturbations reveal a phagolysosomal route for processing damaged axonemes, accompanied by recruitment of autophagy-associated machinery. Remarkably, ciliary regeneration proceeds without detectable c-ring accumulation, even when new protein synthesis is inhibited, indicating that reutilisation of internalised axonemal material is not essential for ciliogenesis. Our findings uncover an unexpected mechanism for clearing damaged motile cilia and reveal how ciliary degradation and regeneration can operate as distinct cellular processes.

papers.title: Functional genomics reveals mediators of beta cell survival in ER stress and type 2 diabetes risk
papers.abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in pancreatic beta cells contributes to impaired function and type 2 diabetes (T2D). In this study we performed genome-wide perturbation screens and genomic profiling in beta cells to identify novel mediators of ER stress responses and diabetes risk. We defined gene regulatory networks in beta cells and identified specific beta cell networks enriched for T2D risk variants with altered expression in ER stress. We performed a loss-of-function CRISPR screen for survival under ER stress in EndoC-bH1 cells, which identified 167 pro-survival and 47 pro-death genes involved in processes related to insulin secretion, mitochondrial transport and protein ubiquitination. Beta cell survival genes collectively had limited genomic change in stress yet showed significant, independent enrichment for T2D risk variants, including novel T2D candidate gene DTNB which we validated protects against beta cell death during stress. Overall, our results revealed mediators of ER stress responses in beta cells and identified novel therapeutic targets to preserve beta cells in diabetes pathogenesis.

papers.title: CCIDeconv: Hierarchical model for deconvolution of subcellular cell-cell interactions in single-cell data
papers.abstract: Cell-cell interaction (CCI) underlies several fundamental biological processes, including development, homeostasis and disease progression. Subcellular spatial transcriptomics (sST) provides an opportunity to examine whether CCI-associated signals show compartment-specific patterns within cells. Assessing CCI at subcellular level can help us gain insights into the distinct pathway activation and signalling patterns. We developed a novel approach that deconvolutes CCI into subcellular CCI (sCCI) information from non-spatial single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA- seq) based CCI using a modified CellChat-derived communication score. By estimating communication scores separately for cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments, we identified compartment-associated sCCI. We then deconvolved whole-cell communication scores into subcellular compartments using a hierarchical classification and regression framework, which we call CCIDeconv. To ensure biological fidelity, we integrated protein localization data from the Human Protein Atlas in our deconvolution model. Across nine publicly available human sST datasets, leave-one- dataset-out validation achieved a median composite score of 0.75, with mean R2 values of 0.87 and 0.80 for cytoplasmic- and nuclear-associated scores, respectively. Performance without spatial features approached that of spatial models as the number of training datasets increased, supporting application to non-spatial scRNA-seq data. This highlighted the potential for prediction of sCCI from scRNA-seq, given a sufficiently large number of training datasets. Overall, our method can attribute whole-cell CCI to its subcellular compartments, allowing researchers to dissect sCCI patterns and gain insights into the underlying biology of healthy and disease tissues. Keywords Cell-Cell Communication, Single Cell RNA-seq, Predictive Modeling, Bioinformatics, Transcriptomics, Machine Learning

papers.title: Molecular Modulation of the SAM-I Riboswitch Drives Global Dynamical Shifts
papers.abstract: A surge in antimicrobial resistance in recent years has made protein-targeting antibiotics less effective against key pathogens. It is possible to expand the range of therapeutic targets by using RNA-based therapies, but it remains necessary to improve the molecular-level understanding of interactions between RNA and known and potential binders. The SAM-I riboswitch, which controls the transcriptional termination of gene expression involved in sulfur metabolism in most bacteria, is an excellent ligand target. Thus, understanding its behavior with and without ligand complexes would be helpful for drug design. Here, we studied the interactions between the SAM-I riboswitch and its natural ligand, SAM, which controls riboswitch function, and compared those to its interactions with the similar small molecule SAH, which does not control riboswitch function, and to its interactions with a potential binder JS4, identified via virtual screening. From our simulations, we deepen understanding of small molecule interactions with the SAM-I riboswitch on both a local and a distal level. The results reveal how differently ligands (SAM, SAH and JS4) can bind to and potentially induce conformational changes in the riboswitch. Our findings offer valuable insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying riboswitch RNA-ligand interactions for the design of more effective RNA-targeting therapeutics.

papers.title: DNA-MGC+: A versatile codec for reliable and resource-efficient data storage on synthetic DNA
papers.abstract: The biochemical processes underlying DNA data storage, including synthesis, amplification, and sequencing, are inherently noisy, leading to insertion, deletion, and substitution errors as well as sequence dropouts that challenge reliable data retrieval. Here we introduce DNA-MGC+, a DNA storage codec designed for reliable and resource-efficient retrieval under diverse operating conditions. We evaluate DNA-MGC+ across various in silico and in vitro settings. In comparison with selected representative codecs, the results show that DNA-MGC+ consistently improves key performance metrics under explicit reliability constraints, including required sequencing depth, read cost, decoding time, storage density, and error-correction capability. In silico experiments show that DNA-MGC+ supports reliable decoding at error rates up to 24% for a 15-KB file, while separate scalability experiments demonstrate reliable decoding of files up to 200 MB at a 5% error rate. In vitro experiments involving a 24-KB file and electrochemical synthesis show that different DNA-MGC+ configurations achieve minimum sequencing depths below 3x and read costs below 3.5 nts/bit under both Illumina and Nanopore sequencing.

papers.title: A FUL-SHP-AP2 module regulates fruit development in petunia
papers.abstract: Fruit development is a key angiosperm innovation for seed dispersal, yet it remains unclear whether a conserved gene regulatory network operates during early fruit development. We investigated Petunia x hybrida homologs of FRUITFULL (FUL), SHATTERPROOF (SHP), and APETALA 2 (AP2), transcription factors repeatedly linked to fruit development/ripening. As a model species close to tomato, but producing dry dehiscent fruits like Arabidopsis, petunia is ideal for investigating conserved regulatory mechanisms in early fruit patterning. We used reverse genetics to dissect the roles of the petunia FUL, SHP and AP2 homologs in pericarp development. We found that the three petunia FUL-like genes redundantly regulate endocarp formation, likely via auxin/brassinosteroid signalling and cell-wall modification. Interestingly, FBP6 (SHP-like) has an opposite effect on endocarp cell morphology, suggesting antagonistic interactions. Mutants in the AP2-like ROB genes show the most severe pericarp patterning defects, with failure of dehiscence in rob1/2/3 mutants. ROB factors repress FUL-like activity and, along with FBP6, oppositely regulate auxin/brassinosteroid signalling genes. Our findings uncover a conserved module of antagonistically acting transcription factors (AP2, FUL, SHP co-orthologs) that regulates early pericarp patterning via hormonal signalling, providing a framework for comparative fruit development studies across angiosperms.

papers.title: Localization of candidate clock neurons in Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba)
papers.abstract: Organisms are exposed to predictable daily and seasonal environmental oscillations. Biological clocks enable organisms to anticipate these changes and coordinate physiology and behaviour accordingly. While circadian mechanisms are well studied in terrestrial model organisms, little is known about the neuronal organisation of biological clocks in non-model species, especially those inhabiting marine environments. Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is central to the functioning of the Southern Ocean ecosystem and relies on precise timing to cope with the extreme, high-latitude fluctuations in photoperiod, food availability, and sea-ice cover in its habitat. Despite evidence for circadian and seasonal rhythms in krill behaviour and physiology, the neuronal architecture underlying these timing processes has remained unresolved. In this study, we use in situ hybridisation and antibody staining to characterise the circadian clock in the krill brain. Immunostaining with an antibody against crustacean {beta}-pigment-dispersing hormone ({beta}-PDH) reveals distinct clusters of PDH-positive neurons in the eyestalks and dorsal central brain, along with an extensive PDH-positive fibre network. We further localise transcripts of the core clock genes cryptochrome-2 (cry2) and period (per) in cell clusters in the eyestalks, which also include the PDH-positive neurons. More specifically, PDH-positive neurons are a subgroup of the cry2- and per-positive cells. Together, these findings provide the first description of the neuronal architecture of the circadian clock in Antarctic krill and establish essential groundwork for future studies on biological timing and environmental adaptation.

papers.title: CRISPR screens of noncanonical coding sequences and integrative multiomics uncover novel retrovirus-derived proteins
papers.abstract: Ribosome profiling has revealed thousands of noncanonical translation events across mammalian genomes, yet functional characterization has overwhelmingly focused on proliferative fitness in cancer cell lines. Here, we present a comprehensive survey of noncanonical translation in the mouse immune system and its functional consequences in macrophages. By performing a meta-analysis of Ribo-seq across 20 public mouse leukocyte and 5 human leukocyte datasets we define a compendium of 22,572 mouse and 18,701 human noncanonical coding sequences (nCDSs), including upstream ORFs (uORFs), downstream ORFs, and ORFs on noncoding RNAs and pseudogenes (ncORFs). Cross species conservation and proteogenomic integration with reanalyzed mass spectrometry data prioritizes a high-confidence subset. To move beyond cataloging, we carried out two orthogonal CRISPR screens in immortalized bone marrow-derived macrophages: a fitness screen identifying nCDSs required for macrophage viability, and a TLR1/TLR2-NF{kappa}B reporter screen uncovering nCDSs that modulate innate immune signaling. These screens suggested dozens of nCDSs for functional follow up including a family of endogenous retroviral envelope-derived proteins translated in adult mouse myeloid cells. Updated single-cell RNA-seq annotations and an interactive UCSC Genome Browser session integrating Ribo-seq, proteomics, and CRISPR screen data are provided as community resources. Together, these findings expand the functional landscape of noncanonical translation in immunity and nominate endogenous retroviral proteins as previously unrecognized regulators of murine macrophage biology.

papers.title: Harvest probabilities of European ducks: the very first estimation based on reward rings
papers.abstract: Ringing-recoveries are an overarching element of population dynamic studies that allow estimating mortality causes and hence improve wildlife management. However, possible drawbacks of recovered rings reside in the fact that reporting probability is rarely known, but consistently lower than 100%. Thus, estimating harvest probabilities (mortality probability due to harvesting) of exploited species without knowledge of ring reporting probability by people exploiting these animals is not straightforward. We here provide the first ever reward-ring study carried out to evaluate European reporting probabilities, hence European harvest probabilities, in three species of ducks (Mallard Anas platyrhynchos, Eurasian Teal A. crecca and Common Pochard Aythya ferina). The 70 Euros reward on some rings was considered to yield a total return of the rings, allowing by comparison to evaluate the reporting probability of standard rings. After the initial year of ringing, annual reporting probability was very similar among the three species, at 0.70-0.76, suggesting two-thirds of the found rings are sent back to the ringing centre. This allowed computation of the annual harvest probability, which was up to 0.25 during the first months after ringing in fall but decreased to 0.04-0.09 during later years. Compared to North American results, the present estimates suggest birds are subjected to a heavy hunting mortality during the first months after ringing, but this pressure declines in later years, likely owing to counter selection of vulnerable/exposed individuals and/or learning by the birds.

papers.title: kache-hash: A dynamic, concurrent, and cache-efficient hash table for streaming k-mer operations
papers.abstract: Many computational genomic analyses spend much of their time inserting and looking up k-mers in large hash tables. These operations stream through sequences, and consecutive k-mers share k - 1 characters. General hash tables ignore this locality. Each k-mer costs them a memory access, and in concurrent builds, a synchronization. We present kache-hash, an exact, dynamic, concurrent, and resizable hash table that places k-mers by their minimizers. A run of consecutive k-mers with the same minimizer then shares its buckets, which it fetches and locks only once. Building on Iceberg hashing, kache-hash handles skewed minimizers with secondary buckets. A compact spill filter lets lookups stop early, yet stay exact. The table stores sets or maps, and doubles in place in parallel. Under a cache-residency assumption, we show that a run that stays in its primary bucket brings in at most that bucket's cache lines, however long the run is. We compare kache-hash with six general-purpose and k-mer-specific tables on five genomic datasets. At 56 threads, it builds k-mer sets 3.5--7.0x faster than the fastest baseline, and answers queries 1.5--5.4x faster. On the human genome, its positive and mixed queries fetch 3.1--3.2x fewer cache lines per k-mer than those of the fastest baseline. In PanGenie, kache-hash speeds up end-to-end genotyping 1.96x with identical outputs. In K2Rmini, it speeds up read filtering 10.7--19.4x over a fixed control version of the release, also making the filter exact. kache-hash is implemented in C++20 and is available at https://github.com/jamshed/kache-hash.

papers.title: Skiver: Reference-free quality control of metagenomic sequencing datasets using (k,v)-mer sketches
papers.abstract: Quality control is essential in numerous Bioinformatics pipelines, yet existing approaches often depend on inefficient mapping to reference genomes or potentially uncalibrated quality scores. We present skiver, a reference-free, alignment-free quality control tool that uses (k, v)-mer sketches. By deriving consensus from sketched (k, v)-mers, skiver estimates survival and hazard rates that capture the positional distribution of errors. Across simulated and real datasets from multiple sequencing platforms, skiver accurately estimates overall error rates, error-type proportions, and quality-score calibration. An iterative outlier-filtering strategy enables robust performance on complex datasets with multiple strains, alleles, and repetitive regions.

papers.title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

papers.title: Thalassolituus haligoni sp. nov., BB40, a model species for non-cyanobacterial diazotrophs within Oceanospirillales isolated from a Fjord-like Inlet in Kjipuktuk
papers.abstract: Marine non-cyanobacterial diazotrophs (NCDs) are recognized as globally distributed, however, few representatives have been isolated in pure cultures. As a result, understanding the physiology, growth rate, substrate preference and dinitrogen (N2) fixation capabilities proves difficult. Thalassolituus haligoni. sp. nov., BB40 was isolated from a fjord-like inlet within Kjipuktuk (Halifax), Nova Scotia. The fully sequenced genome displayed all necessary genes required for N2 fixation, and various carbon uptake pathways. The gram-negative flagellated rod shape bacterium displayed significantly higher growth rates in medium amended with nitrate (NO3-) or ammonia (NH3), compared to dissolved N2, as the sole nitrogen source. Biological N2 fixation rates were detectable across all conditions, measuring a range from 9.34 x 10-6 to 1.4 x 10-1 fmol N cell-1 day-1. Growth of the isolate was successful between 4 oC up to 35 oC, with a Topt of 20 oC for N2, and between 27 - 30 oC for fixed nitrogen (NO3- and NH3). The closest relatives to T. haligoni, were found to be the uncultured Arc-gamma-03 (99% average nucleotide identity (ANI)) and Oceanobacter antarcticus (97% ANI). T. haligoni also displays versatile capabilities for growth on various carbon, and nitrogen sources, and antibiotics. Collectively this study provides an in-depth physiological assessment of an Oceanospirillales diazotrophic species which we presently have limited knowledge of.

papers.title: Sex differences in astrocytic reactivity and its association with cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older adults
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Astrocyte reactivity may contribute to increased Alzheimers disease (AD) risk in women. Although plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels have been reported to be higher in women than in men, few studies have examined sex-specific associations with other plasma AD biomarkers and cognition. METHODS: Participants were enrolled in the Memory Education and Research Initiative, a longitudinal community-based cohort, and underwent evaluation including blood biomarker sampling. The Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) was included as a replication cohort. RESULTS: Females had higher plasma GFAP levels than males in MERI (N{equiv}584), a finding that was replicated in ADNI. In MERI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with lower A{beta}42/40 and higher p-Tau231 and NfL levels. Higher baseline GFAP was also associated with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and episodic memory; however, GFAP x sex x time interactions were not significant. In ADNI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with higher p-Tau217 and NfL levels and with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and selected executive and semantic measures, without consistent evidence of sex-specific longitudinal effects. DISCUSSION: Plasma GFAP levels were consistently higher in females across two independent cohorts. GFAP was associated with AD-related blood biomarkers and longitudinal cognitive decline, but sex did not consistently modify these associations. These findings support a role for astrocytic reactivity in early AD-related processes while underscoring the need for further replication of sex-specific effects.

papers.title: An integrated virtual reality platform for naturalistic neuroimaging with magnetoencephalography
papers.abstract: Studying the brain in motion promises deep insights into the neural circuits that support complex, real-world behaviour. In humans, wearable optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) enable magnetoencephalography (MEG) with millisecond temporal resolution and millimetre spatial precision during movement. Integrating this technology with virtual reality (VR) could enable fully naturalistic experimental paradigms, but magnetic interference from existing head-mounted displays (HMDs) prevents reliable whole-brain MEG recordings. Here, we present and validate a VR system that integrates with wearable, OPM-based MEG. At its core is a purpose-designed HMD with minimal ferromagnetic material, resulting in magnetic flux density two orders of magnitude lower than consumer-grade alternatives at comparable resolution and weight. Using phantom measurements and established perceptual and cognitive benchmark tasks across participants, we demonstrate robust stimulus-induced neuronal activity at both sensor and source level. Crucially, these sources span a broad set of brain regions, including visual, motor and prefrontal cortices. There remain significant noise peaks which will challenge certain experimental designs however, the system is straightforward to produce, readily extendable, and enables whole-brain MEG during immersive, naturalistic behaviours.

papers.title: Stimulated human cortical waves: spatiotemporal dynamics across development
papers.abstract: Traveling waves of neural activity are fundamental to cortical function, yet their spatiotemporal dynamics and structural constraints remain less understood in human brain. Conventional analyses focus on network topology and spatial geometry of neural signals, with limited emphasis on wave dynamics at high spatiotemporal resolutions. Here, we applied a manifold-based optical flow algorithm to an open-access intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) dataset from the single-pulse stimulation cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) paradigm, enabling direct construction of high-temporal-resolution cortical neural activity velocity fields. Spatiotemporal mode decomposition revealed a hierarchical organization: large-scale plane waves (mediating global propagation) dominate, complemented by local patterns for local computation. Dominant plane wave directions correlate with underlying white matter fibre tract orientations, indicating anatomical guidance of cortical dynamics. Velocity field singular points (sources, sinks, spirals and saddles) are non-randomly distributed, associating with default mode network (DMN) hubs. We further identified a nonlinear relationship between cortical wave speed and age, with developmental phases paralleling white matter maturation and aging. Our findings link cortical wave dynamics to anatomy, functional networks, and neurodevelopment, establishing wave speed as a potential yet important biomarker for brain function and health.

papers.title: Massage Engages Spinal Oxytocin Circuits to Reduce Pain and Enhance Well-Being
papers.abstract: Context determines how the nervous system interprets sensory information to guide adaptive behavior. Nowhere is this more consequential than in the somatosensory system where the same touch can signal threat from a predator or safety from a caregiver, injury during attack or comfort during healing. Oxytocin, a neuropeptide released across a broad range of social interactions, is well positioned to convey social context to somatosensory circuits, but at what stage of processing does this convergence occur and through what mechanism? Here we show that affiliative touch triggers oxytocin release at the earliest stage of sensory processing, the spinal cord, shaping both pain relief and touch reward through a single, state-dependent circuit that is conserved from mice to humans. In humans, massage drives endogenous oxytocin release, enhanced pain relief and well-being. Modeling this in mice shows that social touch activates hypothalamic oxytocin neurons that project to the spinal cord, where oxytocin signaling is both necessary and sufficient for pain suppression and touch reward. Moreover, spinal calcium imaging and slice electrophysiology demonstrate that oxytocin acts on both excitatory and inhibitory spinal neurons to differentially modulate the relative activity of spinal ascending systems that convey both pain and social touch to the brain. We find that this circuit architecture is conserved in humans, as oxytocin receptors are similarly expressed on spinal excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Massage-induced oxytocin release in humans correlates with slowed somatosensory processing within the spinal cord in response to aversive stimuli and reduced negative affect. Thus, spinal oxytocin circuits provide an evolutionarily conserved mechanism through which affiliative touch reduces pain and enhances well-being, linking the earliest stage of sensory processing to the social bonds on which survival depends.

papers.title: Sequestration-based Protein Neural Networks Tolerate the Effects of Shared Translational Resources
papers.abstract: Biochemical neural networks offer a promising framework for implementing advanced computation in living cells, yet how competition for shared cellular resources shapes their behavior remains poorly characterized. In this work, we develop a resource-aware mathematical framework to analyze how competition for ribosomes affects protein neural networks implemented via molecular sequestration in bacterial systems. Focusing on classification tasks, we show that when all mRNA species share identical ribosome-binding affinities, competition induces a uniform rescaling of the network's effective weights, reducing the output magnitude while preserving the geometry of the decision boundary. When these affinities differ, competition introduces curvature in the decision boundary, transforming a linear classifier into a nonlinear one through resource coupling. This curvature is constrained to a well-defined region of the input space whose extent is determined by the degree of variability in the binding affinities, making the effect both predictable and, potentially, exploitable for design. Next, we numerically extend our analysis from a single perceptron to multi-layer architectures with two hidden-layer nodes and show that, for both closed and non-convex decision boundaries, resource competition preserves the boundary geometry in the homogeneous-affinity case, while in the heterogeneous case, curvature distortions from hidden-layer nodes propagate and compose at the output within a bounded uncertainty region. Finally, we incorporate growth-mediated feedback into the framework and show that the structural form of the activation function and decision boundary is preserved. Overall, our results provide a quantitative basis for understanding how translational resource competition shapes the behavior of protein-level molecular classifiers.

papers.title: Memory traces bias new learning for hippocampal generalization
papers.abstract: Generalizing prior experience to guide behavior in novel situations is a fundamental cognitive function, yet how this occurs remains poorly understood. Here we combined longitudinal imaging in mice with modeling and circuit perturbation to examine generalization in hippocampal CA1 across environments with shared task structure. Prior training accelerated behavioral adaptation and preserved cross-environment representations. We identified putative memory traces associated with generalization. At the cellular level, spatially informative residual activity reflecting generalizable information biased which neurons formed place fields (PFs) and where via behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP). At the population level, BTSP was associated with rapid alignment of novel-environment network dynamics to familiar neural subspaces. Chemogenetic suppression of local CA1 during training reduced residual activity, BTSP induction, place cell recruitment and generalization. In sum, the influence of memory traces on new PF formation may allow past experience to guide new learning to form representations based on generalizable features.

papers.title: Quantitative profiling of whole-brain projectomes at single-axon resolution using deep learning and high-resolution light sheet microscopy
papers.abstract: Revealing how individual axons contribute to a brain-wide projectome is indispensable for understanding brain function and behavior, yet remains technically challenging, with contemporary models failing to generalize. We introduce MAPL3, an end-to-end pipeline that integrates self-supervised learning with an innovative deep architecture to segment axons and reconstruct brain-wide projections in tera-voxel-scale light-sheet fluorescence microscopy. Its SPECTRE network integrates local axonal features with broader information shared across neighboring 3D patches. MAPL3 generalizes across out-of-distribution datasets with different tracers, microscopes, resolutions, and protocols, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. It also provides model uncertainty estimates and improves segmentation precision on unseen data. MAPL3 tractography module reconstructs long-range projections and quantifies passing vs. terminating streamlines. We showcase its ability to map the projectome of the orbitofrontal cortex, reconstructing streamlines that innervate established projection regions, which were missed by current pipelines. MAPL3 enables subject- and population-level quantitative profiling of whole-brain projectomes in tera-voxel-scale light sheet microscopy.

papers.title: The staphylococcal type VII secretion system delays inflammatory cell death during macrophage infection
papers.abstract: The human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a facultatively intracellular bacterium that can replicate and survive within macrophages. While macrophage-mediated immune modulation is pivotal in S. aureus pathogenesis, bacterial manipulation of macrophage pathways remains poorly understood. The specialised type VII secretion system (T7SSb) is an important virulence-associated factor during staphylococcal infection, although, unlike its mycobacterial counterparts, its role in controlling staphylococcal-macrophage interactions remains unclear. Employing high-resolution time-lapse imaging, we demonstrated an induction of pore-induced cellular traps (PITs) during S. aureus infection of macrophages in vitro, with a higher number of PITs forming in macrophages infected with S. aureus lacking EssC ({Delta}essC), a central T7SS transporter. Interestingly, {Delta}essC-infected macrophages displayed increased bacterial escape compared to wild type (WT)-infected cells, implicating a role for T7SS in delaying macrophage cell death. Changes in cell death were accompanied by a reduction in efferocytosis of {Delta}essC-infected cells in vitro. Investigation of cell death signalling markers in WT and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages demonstrated that the T7SS delayed induction of key cell death pathways, necroptosis and pyroptosis, and a dual RNAseq analysis of WT- and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages indicated a T7SS-dependent modulation of bacterial oxidative stress and selected host chemokines. We also demonstrated that T7SS effectors, EsxA and EsxC individually delayed macrophage cell death. Interestingly, {Delta}esxC mutants demonstrated accelerated calcium fluxes, indicating that the T7SS-mediated suppression of cellular calcium signalling may cause the delay in cell death. Furthermore, in a murine skin infection model, we showed that effector and transporter mutants have distinct S. aureus infection outcomes. Our findings suggest for the first time a key role for T7SSb proteins in controlling macrophage cell death, which impacts staphylococcal survival within the host during infection.

papers.title: The stabilized gaze signalling hypothesis and the evolution of human eye appearance
papers.abstract: Human eyes are commonly described as having a 'white sclera': they typically combine scleral exposure with depigmentation, making eye direction readily visible. However, variation in scleral pigmentation among other primates has challenged claims of human uniqueness and renewed debate about its role in gaze communication. Here we develop the stabilized gaze-signalling hypothesis (SGSH), which makes four predictions: (1) depigmented, exposed sclera supports more robust eye-gaze direction discrimination than pigmented sclera across variable viewing conditions by preserving joint visibility of the iris and eye outline; (2) coordination benefits increase when viewing conditions vary or monitoring more group members increases attentional demands, relative to sustained close-range dyadic interaction; (3) humans show greater receiver sensitivity to eye-gaze cues than other primates across development; and (4) heritable morphological variation was available for selection, with signalling benefits potentially exceeding costs of revealing information. Existing evidence supports perceptual benefits under some conditions; the other predictions require further testing. We also consider selective pressures, alternative origins, and complementary functions. The SGSH provides a revised framework for testing whether social benefits from maintaining readable eye direction during group activities could explain the spread and maintenance of depigmentation of exposed sclera in humans.

papers.title: Promoter-responsiveness to distal regulatory elements is mediated by the promoter-proximal region
papers.abstract: Gene promoters induce transcription in response to distal enhancers located in large gene regulatory domains. How this long-range regulation specifically activates the target promoter while bypassing other promoters located in the same regulatory domain remains unclear. Here, we find that the promoter-proximal region is critical for cell-type specific promoter responsiveness. Using high-throughput genome-engineering in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC), we systematically replace the endogenous Sox9 promoter with different libraries of core and extended (i.e. full) promoters and assess their response to long-range regulatory elements in mESCs and neural progenitor cells. We find that only a subset of full promoters is activated by distal neuronal enhancers and that the promoter-proximal region is necessary for this promoter responsiveness. Core promoters alone are insufficient to respond to distal enhancers but modulate the transcriptional output of responsive promoters. Our results suggest that within multipartite regulatory domains, the promoter-proximal region fulfills a facilitator-like function that filters and transmits signal from distal enhancers, ultimately conferring promoter responsiveness to long-range regulatory elements.

papers.title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

papers.title: Illuminating the Role of A-to-I Editing in Cancer using EndoVIA 2.0
papers.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is an essential post-transcriptional modification catalyzed by adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR) enzymes, and emerging evidence suggests its dysregulation can contribute to cancer. However, technical barriers have hindered spatial analysis of editing activity in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues - an abundant but challenging sample type. Here, we introduce EndoVIA 2.0, an optimized immunostaining assay that enables quantification and spatial mapping of edited RNAs in FFPE tissues. Using human Endonuclease V (hEndoV) as a molecular affinity reagent, we developed a calcium-dependent staining workflow compatible with crosslinked tissues. EndoVIA 2.0 was validated in cell lines having altered ADAR1 expression, fresh frozen (FF) tissues, gastric organoids, and FFPE tissue sections. Using quantitative imaging combined with machine-learning segmentation and spatial analysis, EndoVIA 2.0 successfully detected A-to-I editing changes in ADAR1 knockout (KO) and overexpression models, revealing differential editing patterns across tissues. In gastric organoids and FFPE tissues, the assay also spatially resolved editing heterogeneity and distinguished ADAR1-deficient from ADAR1-sufficient cells. Application to long-archived lung and breast cancer FFPE tissues suggest EndoVIA 2.0's broad utility and potential for capturing disease-associated changes in A-to-I editing. Finally, staining across the gastric neoplastic cascade revealed stage-dependent increases in A-to-I editing and changes in subcellular localization, further supporting the possibility that ADAR plays a critical role in the early development of gastric cancer. EndoVIA 2.0 enables robust, spatial detection of A-to-I editing in FFPE tissues - circumventing the limitations of RNA extraction and unlocking access to archived clinical specimens. This platform lays the foundation for mapping RNA editing dynamics in cancer progression and may support future biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Getting a head start: Craniofacial heterochrony in marsupials involves dynamic changes to cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying neural crest migration
papers.abstract: The neural crest is a vertebrate innovation central to craniofacial development and evolution. While the gene regulatory networks guiding neural crest development are well characterized, the mechanisms generating species-specific craniofacial diversity remain poorly understood. Marsupials provide a unique model for studying neural crest plasticity, having evolved accelerated patterns of craniofacial development. This adaptation arises because marsupials are born altricial after a short gestation yet require well-developed mouthparts to attach to a teat and continue development in the pouch. However, how marsupials achieve this heterochronic shift in neural crest development is largely unknown. Here we investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their distinct heterochrony across three marsupial species, with mouse and chicken as comparators. We reveal that marsupials produce dense pre-migratory aggregates of neural crest cells at the borders of a still-flat, pre-neurulation embryo, which emigrate as cohesive, E-cadherin-positive, vimentin-negative epithelial-like sheets, potentially facilitating rapid establishment of the facial prominences. Re-analysis of published marsupial single-cell data further suggests that the mesenchymal transcriptional programme is deployed after delamination and migration. These cellular behaviours have not been described in other amniotes, instead resembling patterns in anamniotes which similarly exhibit accelerated craniofacial development to support early feeding. Marsupials thus appear to have evolved a similar mechanism of neural crest migration to facilitate their developmental heterochrony. These findings suggest that vertebrate neural crest migration may be shaped by life history as well as phylogeny, providing new perspectives on neural crest plasticity and the developmental mechanisms driving craniofacial diversity.

papers.title: Comparative phylogenomics reveals multilevel genomic differentiation between annual and perennial Hordeum species
papers.abstract: Annual plants complete their life cycle with a single reproductive episode, whereas perennials must balance reproduction with the maintenance of tissues that sustain future growth. Despite the fundamental importance of this distinction, the genomic differences associated with these contrasting life histories remain poorly understood. Here, we utilize independent occurrences of annuality in the grass genus Hordeum to identify recurrent differences between annual and perennial species. Combining transcriptomes from 82 accessions with recently published reference genomes, we compared protein-coding sequence evolution, gene copy number, gene expression and co-expression while accounting for evolutionary non-independence. We found widespread genomic differentiation, with several consistent patterns. Genes involved in cell division and genome maintenance showed evidence of stronger evolutionary constraint in perennials, while gene families associated with developmental regulation and senescence were more frequently retained in higher copy numbers in perennials. Differences in gene expression and coordination were particularly pronounced during reproduction, when perennials showed higher expression of genes involved in cell division, cytoskeletal organisation, cell-wall formation and resource transport, together with extensive reorganisation of gene co-expression relationships. Across these complementary analyses, processes involved in cellular proliferation, developmental regulation and tissue maintenance repeatedly distinguished the two life histories. Our findings suggest that annual-perennial differentiation extends beyond individual flowering regulators to broader genomic differences associated with a more complex coordination of processes balancing growth and senescence in perennials. By identifying these recurrent patterns across evolutionary lineages, this study provides a comparative framework for understanding the genomic differentiation underlying contrasting plant life histories.

papers.title: Protein sequence evolution underlies interspecies incompatibility of a cell fate determinant
papers.abstract: Novel and rapidly evolving genes can integrate into conserved gene networks and play critical roles in development. Understanding how sequence variation in the orthologs of such genes influences functional interactions with the molecular products of older, more conserved genes requires investigation at the level of protein function. Here, we ask this question using the oskar gene as a case study. oskar is essential for primordial germ cell specification and embryonic patterning in fruit flies. Previous work showed functional incompatibility between oskar orthologs from the congeneric fruit fly species Drosophila melanogaster and Drosophila virilis. However, the region(s) of Oskar in which protein-coding sequence evolution led to this incompatibility, and the molecular mechanisms underlying it, remained unknown. To address these questions, we generated chimeric versions of oskar comprising different combinations of Oskar protein domains from each species, expressed these chimeric oskar sequences in D. melanogaster, and quantified their ability to assemble functional germ line and abdominal patterning determinants (germ plasm). We found that a specific portion of D. virilis Oskar, namely the OSK domain, was primarily responsible for the cross-species incompatibility of Oskar. In the absence of endogenous D. melanogaster Oskar, chimeras containing the D. virilis OSK domain could not localize posterior germ plasm well enough to generate primordial germ cells, but were sufficient to specify the anteroposterior axis. We also found that the D. virilis OSK domain had dominant-negative effects on D. melanogaster Oskar's ability to localize germ plasm mRNAs, resulting in severe axial patterning defects. Both in vivo and in silico analyses support the hypothesis that evolved changes in the ability of the OSK domain to interact with conserved germ plasm mRNAs played a significant role in the evolution of interspecies incompatibility of Oskar. Under this hypothesis, an essential germ line determinant evolved to be incompatible across species of the same genus in less than 50 million years, while retaining functional within-species molecular interactions. Thus, by investigating in vivo protein function, we link genomic and molecular evolution with phenotypic variation and fitness at higher scales.

papers.title: Phylogenetic detection of protein sites associated with continuous traits
papers.abstract: Comparative genomic data can be used to look for substitutions in coding sequences that are associated with the variation of a particular phenotypic trait. A few statistical methods have been proposed to do so for phenotypes represented by discrete values. For continuous traits, no such statistical approach has been proposed, and researchers have resorted to sensible but uncharacterized criteria. Here, we investigate a phylogenetic model for coding sequences where amino acid preferences at a site are given by a continuous function of a quantitative trait. This function is inferred from the amino acids and the trait values in extant species and requires inferred point estimates of ancestral values of the trait at internal nodes. For detecting sites whose evolution is associated with this trait, we use a significance test against the hypothesis that amino acid preference does not depend on the trait. This procedure is compared to simpler strategies on simulated alignments. It displays an increased recall for low false positive rates, which is of special importance for performing whole-genome scans. This comes however at a much higher computational cost, and we suggest using a simple test to filter promising candidate sites. We then revisit a dataset of alignments for 62 species of mammals, using longevity as a phenotypic trait. We apply our method to three protein families that have previously been proposed to display sites associated with variation in lifespan in mammals. Using a graphical representation extracted from the detailed phylogenetic analysis of candidate sites, we suggest that the evidence for this in the sequence data alone is weak. The proposed method has been added to our Pelican software. It is available at https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/phoogle/pelican and can now be used with both discrete and continuous phenotypes to search for sites associated with phenotypic variation, on data sets with thousands of alignments.

papers.title: mRNABench: A curated benchmark for mature mRNA property and function prediction
papers.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is central to gene expression, and its half-life, localization, and translation efficiency drive phenotypic diversity in eukaryotic cells. While supervised learning has been used to study the mRNA regulatory code, self-supervised foundation models support a wider range of transfer learning tasks. However, the dearth of standardized benchmarks limits efforts to pinpoint the strengths of various models. Here, we present mRNABench, a benchmarking suite for mature mRNA biology, focused on human transcripts, that evaluates the representational quality of mature mRNA embeddings from self-supervised nucleotide foundation models. We curate 13 datasets and 81 prediction tasks that broadly capture salient properties of mature mRNA, and assess the performance of 29 families of nucleotide foundation models for a total of 750k experiments. Using these experiments, we study parameter scaling, correlations between sequence compressibility and performance, data-splitting strategies, and the effects of self-supervised training objective on mRNA property prediction. mRNABench can be found at: https://github.com/morrislab/mRNABench.

papers.title: Multiplexed Targeted iprm-PASEF Assays for MALDI Mass Spectrometry Imaging of Lipids, NAD+ 2 , and Related Metabolites in CD38 Knockout Mice
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) maps the molecular landscape of tissues; however, confident in situ identification and accurate quantification of analytes by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)-MSI remain challenging. We present a new targeted imaging methodology, imaging parallel reaction monitoring parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (iprm-PASEF), which utilizes trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) and MALDI for assessment of metabolites and lipids on the fragment ion level in tissue. We investigated liver tissues from wild-type and CD38 knockout (CD38-/-) mice, as CD38 contributes to age-related nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) decline and direct detection of NAD+ within tissue remains challenging. The iprm-PASEF workflow enabled confident differentiation of lipid isomers, resolving phosphatidylinositols at m/z 857.52 and confirming the presence of PI 36:4(16:0/20:4) and absence of PI 36:4(14:0/22:4) at the fragment ion level. We confirmed a more than 2-fold increase in NAD+ in CD38-/- liver tissues of male and female animals (n = 3 per genotype and sex) and decreased adenosine diphosphate ribose (ADPR) through relative quantification of characteristic fragment ions, confirming alteration of NAD metabolism in these animals. This approach provided confident and specific MS2-based identification and relative quantification of fragment ions in MSI experiments, with consistent fold changes across multiple characteristic fragment ions and biological replicates.

papers.title: Mitochondrial heterogeneity disrupts osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption by impairing respiratory complex I
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy, the co-existence of different mitochondrial genomes within a cell, is linked to aging and disease. Patients with heteroplasmy due to mitochondrial mutations experience multiple organ complications, particularly poor bone health and bone structure defects. However, the mechanisms involved are generally unknown, due largely to the difficulty of manipulating mtDNA in vivo. To overcome this, we leveraged a heteroplasmic mouse model and discovered that mitochondrial heteroplasmy affects a fundamental developmental process. Specifically, the differentiation of osteoclasts, which resorb bone tissue and maintain bone homeostasis. Mechanistically, there was a reduced localization of specifically respiratory complex I subunits in mitochondria in heteroplasmic mice, disrupting ATP production and osteoclast differentiation. In addition, autophagic flux is exhausted, and the autophagy inducer spermidine restores mitochondrial health and rescues osteoclast activity, both in mice and in cells from patients with primary mitochondrial disease. Together, we identify the mechanisms by which mitochondrial heteroplasmy impacts osteoclastogenesis and discover spermidine as a modulator of this process, which presents a potential treatment for human heteroplasmic conditions such as mitochondrial diseases, which are largely untreatable.

papers.title: A chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of the impressed tortoise, Manouria impressa
papers.abstract: Background. The impressed tortoise, Manouria impressa (Gunther, 1882), is an Endangered, largely fungivorous tortoise of the montane forests of Southeast Asia and one of the two living species of the basal testudinid genus Manouria. It is one of the least-studied tortoises, and no chromosome-level genome was available for the genus. Findings. From 68.5 Gb of PacBio HiFi reads (28x), 9.8 Gb of Hi-C read pairs and RNA-seq of heart and lung from a single female, we assembled a 2.42 Gb primary assembly with a contig N50 of 86.9 Mb and a scaffold N50 of 138.6 Mb. Hi-C scaffolding followed by quantitative curation -- every scaffold join scored against the within-contig contact-decay expectation -- placed 94.5 % of the sequence in 26 chromosomes, matching the testudinid karyotype (2n = 52); the remaining 335 scaffolds are unplaced. Consensus accuracy is QV 67.9 (Merqury), k-mer completeness 95.1 %, and 99.3 % of vertebrate BUSCO genes are complete. Two phased haplotype assemblies (scaffold N50 87.8 and 91.6 Mb; QV 69.1 and 68.5; 99.2 % combined k-mer completeness) and the 18.1-kb mitochondrial genome were assembled from the same data. Repeats mask 48.6 % of the genome (LINEs 11.5 %, LTR retrotransposons 10.0 %, DNA transposons 7.6 %, SINEs 2.6 %, unclassified families 15.4 %); 24,875 protein-coding genes were predicted from RNA-seq and OrthoDB protein evidence (97.6 % complete vertebrate BUSCOs), 89.0 % of them functionally annotated. Conclusions. This haplotype-resolved reference, with its curation evidence and scripts, provides the first chromosome-level genomic resource for Manouria and a foundation for conservation genomics and for studies of the dietary specialisation of this fungivorous tortoise.

papers.title: YAP1-2α-TAZ heterodimerization promotes BRD4-associated LLPS-like assembly at candidate super-enhancers and cancer cell malignancy
papers.abstract: YAP1 is a transcriptional coactivator expressed as multiple splice isoforms, but how individual isoforms specify malignant cell states remains unclear. Here, we identify YAP1-2 as an isoform that drives a distinct transcriptional state in cancer cells. The YAP1-2-TAZ heterodimer, together with TEAD, forms BRD4-associated nuclear assemblies with LLPS-like properties. These assemblies are enriched at candidate super-enhancer-associated regions and promote transcription. Disrupting YAP1-2-TAZ heterodimerization, TEAD binding, or BRD4 interaction impairs assembly formation and associated phenotypes. Exon-6 exclusion promotes YAP1-2-associated nuclear puncta, invasion, and therapeutic resistance in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), and enhances intraperitoneal tumor progression in gastric cancer xenografts. Gastric cancer cells selected through peritoneal dissemination exhibit increased YAP1-2, nuclear YAP1 puncta, and therapeutic resistance. In HGSOC specimens, YAP1-2 abundance, YAP1-BRD4 proximity, and nuclear YAP1 puncta are associated with advanced stages. Thus, YAP1-2 drives a BRD4-associated condensate-like transcriptional state linked to malignant progression across multiple cancer contexts.

papers.title: Use of Antibody Structural Information in Disease Prediction Models Reveals Antigen Specific B Cell Receptor Sequences in Bulk Repertoire Data
papers.abstract: Convergent antibodies are highly similar antibodies elicited in multiple individuals in response to the same antigen. Convergent antibodies provide insight into shared immunological responses and show great promise as diagnostic biomarkers. They have typically been identified using methods that consider the amino acid sequence of the third complementarity-determining region (CDR3) of immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH). In this study, we extend this definition of convergent antibodies to use structural information about the three IgH CDR regions (CDR1-3) and antibody isotype. We measure the performance of both definitions of convergence by their ability to predict disease status from bulk IgH sequencing data for two different disease cohorts: HIV infection and food allergen sensitization. We show that using predicted structural information outperforms prior approaches for the prediction of food sensitization status and performs on par for HIV infection status. Additionally, the use of structural information and antibody isotype enables better model interpretation and more immunological insights. The structurally convergent antibody groups driving HIV prediction accuracy are from known HIV-binding antibodies expressing the appropriate isotype. Thus, the incorporation of structural information can enable the identification of antigen specific antibody groups from bulk IgH sequencing data.

papers.title: Mapping the journey of a neuro-invasive virus in zebrafish larvae: contrasted viral spread and type I interferon responses in periphery and central nervous system
papers.abstract: Organ-to-organ dissemination of viruses is a critical feature of host-virus interactions. Neuroinvasive viruses can enter the central nervous systems (CNS), which often results in death or permanent neurological impairment. The complex mechanisms underpinning this spread are poorly understood, as they depend on a variety of parameters, including initial site of entry, route of access to the CNS, and immune responses. To better understand these phenomena, we analyzed the spatial dynamics of Sindbis virus (SINV) dissemination in the transparent zebrafish larva. Using fluorescent reporter viruses, we observed that SINV readily invaded the CNS after inoculation at various peripheral sites. Both sensory and motor neurons were gateways to the CNS, with 2 to 3 occurrences of CNS entry par larva. While peripheral infection was transient, CNS infection was persistent and more variable. Within the CNS, viral dissemination resulted both from long-distance axonal transport and short distance shedding. Type I interferon (IFN) response was systemic in the periphery, and local in the CNS; nevertheless, it played a key role in controlling the infection in both compartments, as shown by IFN receptor knockdown or with IFN triple mutants. We built a mathematical model of the infection based on our quantitative imaging, providing additional insight. The rate of new virion production was estimated around 1 to 2 infective virions per productively infected cell per hour. The model also found that IFN did not only prevent new infections but accelerated the death of infected cells, and had a stronger effect in periphery than CNS. This study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the mechanisms at play in pathogen- and host response- mediated neurological damage during viral encephalitis.

papers.title: Rapid generation of marsupial induced pluripotent stem cells suitable for use in next-generation conservation
papers.abstract: Marsupials account for a disproportionate share of recent and impending mammalian extinctions, that has prompted investment in the development of "next generation" conservation biotechnologies. These include the generation of genetically selected/modified individuals for improved population fitness. Given the inherent limitations of working with threatened species, a flexible vehicle to develop these technologies is through the generation and editing of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). However, it is deemed necessary to derive transgene-free iPSCs for conservation target species, which can be highly time consuming and expensive. This study describes the generation of iPSCs from the marsupial fat-tailed dunnart (diPSCs) that serves as a model species for next generation conservation initiatives. These diPSCs exhibit features of totipotency when cells are maintained with exogenous reprogramming factors for long periods, until differentiation potential is required. Neonatal dunnart fibroblasts were reprogrammed using doxycycline-inducible Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, Lin28 and Myc, and the resulting iPSC lines were characterised at the transcriptomic, epigenetic and functional level (trilineage differentiation, embryoid body formation and mouse blastocyst injection assays). Dunnart iPSCs exhibited robust transcriptional and epigenetic activation of core pluripotency factors (POU5F1, POU5F3, SALL4) as well as factors associated with the naive and primed states of eutherian pluripotency (TBX3, KLF2, TFCP2L1, SOX11, DNMT3A). Dunnart iPSCs readily differentiated in trilineage and embryoid body formation assays, where they expressed markers of all three germ lineages. When injected into 8-cell mouse blastocysts, dunnart iPSCs integrated into both the inner cell mass and trophoblast, reflecting a capacity to contribute to embryonic and extra embryonic lineages during early development. Further, we show that diPSCs can maintain their potential in the presence of exogenous pluripotency factors, until required for differentiation. This robust iPSC generation and maintenance approach is a valuable avenue for the rapid application of next-generation conservation technologies in threatened species.

papers.title: IL4Ra Controls The Medullary Dwell Time Of Mature Thymocytes By Scheduling Their Release From The Thymus
papers.abstract: Following their generation, newly produced single positive (SP) thymocytes must remain in the thymus to undergo post-selection maturation, a process supported by the thymic medulla. This ensures that SP thymocytes are equipped with functional competence prior to S1PR1-mediated thymic emigration. Despite this importance, the intrathymic mechanisms that control the balance between retention and release of SP thymocytes is unclear. Here, we describe a cell autonomous requirement for IL4Ra-signalling in SP thymocytes, that determines the duration of their medullary occupancy. We show that the period of this occupancy is prolonged in the absence of IL4R expression by SP thymocytes, which occurs as a result of impaired interactions with medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTEC). Importantly, extending the duration of medullary occupancy enhances the maturational status and functional capabilities of SP thymocytes, including improved TNF and IL2 production. Collectively, we show that IL4Ra regulates the medullary occupancy of mature thymocytes, which in turn determines the functional properties of thymic output.

papers.title: Network inference at single-cell resolution reveals morphoregulatory divergence and multilayered buffering in limb evolution
papers.abstract: How changes in conserved developmental genetic programs contribute to morphological evolution remains poorly understood, particularly in non-conventional model species. Here, we combine single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility profiling with cross-species label transfer and gene regulatory network inference to compare mouse and pig limb development. Our analyses identify broadly conserved cellular organization but discrete divergence in HOX-, FGF- and SHH-regulated programs. FGFR inhibition in mouse limb buds phenocopies the distal expansion of pig GREM1 expression, while altered SHH responses and anterior-posterior polarity converge on the PTCH1 regulatory landscape. Its functional dissection reveals degeneration of a limb regulatory module in artiodactyls, conservation of an additional distal enhancer, and extensive redundancy among cis-regulatory inputs. Allele-specific analyses further show that reduced Ptch1 dosage is buffered by transcriptional compensation. Together, these findings reveal how cis-regulatory and pathway-level robustness can accommodate distributed regulatory change while preserving developmental function, providing a mechanistic framework for the evolution of artiodactyl limb morphology.

papers.title: Embryonic integrin signaling establishes a program of differential cell elongation in a growing proprioceptive organ
papers.abstract: The ChO is a proprioceptive sensory organ that undergoes extensive morphological remodeling during larval growth. A key feature of this process is the dramatic elongation of cap cells, while adjacent ligament cells remain short. How these contrasting growth behaviors are established and coordinated is largely unknown. Using targeted RNAi screens of extracellular matrix (ECM) components, ECM receptors, and their intracellular effectors, we identified distinct molecular mechanisms controlling ChO architecture. We found that basement membrane components, including collagens and laminins, are required to maintain the characteristic straight morphology of cap cells, whereas Thrombospondin and Tiggrin contribute to the stability of cellular attachments. Unexpectedly, we discovered that Thrombospondin and an PS2{beta}PS integrin signaling module, comprising Talin and the ILK-PINCH-Parvin complex, regulate the relative lengths of cap and ligament cells. Cell-type-specific knockdown demonstrated that this pathway acts within ligament cells to restrict their elongation. Disruption of integrin signaling causes ligament cells to elongate dramatically at the expense of cap cell extension, effectively reversing their normal growth behaviors. Importantly, this function is distinct from the role of integrin-associated proteins in maintaining cellular attachments. Temporal manipulation of integrin expression revealed that the short morphology of ligament cells is established during a critical developmental time window during embryogenesis, before the organ becomes functional. Restoring integrin expression after hatching fails to rescue the phenotype, indicating that embryonic integrin signaling establishes a persistent developmental state. Together, these findings reveal that ligament cell elongation is actively restricted by an embryonically established integrin-dependent mechanism, providing the structural basis for subsequent cap cell elongation and organ maturation.

papers.title: Developmentally-regulated splice remodeling shapes functional CACNA1C channel diversity during human neurodevelopment
papers.abstract: CACNA1C encodes the pore-forming subunit of the CaV1.2 L-type voltage-gated calcium channel, a major regulator of neuronal calcium signaling and one of the strongest genetic risk loci for bipolar disorder and other psychiatric disorders. Although extensive alternative splicing of CACNA1C has been described in the adult human brain, how alternative splicing of CACNA1C is regulated during early human neurodevelopment remains largely unknown. Here, we used long-read RNA sequencing to characterize full-length CACNA1C transcripts during differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells, from healthy controls and patients with bipolar disorder homozygous for either the A or G allele at rs1006737, into cortical glutamatergic neurons. We identified 60 putative isoforms, including ten annotated transcripts and 23 previously reported in adult human brain. We also demonstrate that CACNA1C undergoes developmentally-regulated remodeling of isoform composition during neuronal differentiation. This remodeling was characterized by an exon-switching program involving mutually exclusive exon pairs and alternative splice site usage, including prominent developmental transitions between exon pairs 8/8a, 21/22, and 31/32. Neither rs1006737 genotype, diagnosis, sex nor age significantly affected splicing profiles. The developmental splice trajectories were recapitulated in dorsal forebrain organoids, showing that CACNA1C splice remodeling is conserved across independent human neural differentiation models. Electrophysiological characterization of the two most abundant neuronal isoforms found that exon 31/32 switching alters channel inactivation properties. Together, our findings demonstrate that developmentally-regulated alternative splicing of CACNA1C transcripts contributes to the functional diversity of CaV1.2 channels expressed during human neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Targeted Deletions Uncover Previously Uncharacterised C1-fixing Cluster Genes as Essential for Autotrophy in Clostridium autoethanogenum
papers.abstract: Recycling carbon oxides from industrial off-gases and gasified organic waste using gas fermentation offers a sustainable route for biomanufacturing of fuels and chemicals. Acetogens are attractive biocatalysts here and fix CO and CO2 via the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP). However, the incomplete functional annotation of the associated C1-fixing gene cluster limits rational engineering of acetogen cell factories. Here, we investigated five highly conserved but previously uncharacterised C1-fixing cluster genes to quantify their contributions to the growth of the model-acetogen Clostridium autoethanogenum using targeted CRISPR/Cas9-mediated single-gene deletions, physiological characterisation, comparative computational structural analyses, CRISPRi, and functional genomics. Importantly, we identified acsV, lpdA, cooC, and cooC2 as essential for autotrophy but not heterotrophy, whereas deletion of gcvH reduced autotrophic growth and shifted carbon flux from acetate towards 2,3-butanediol. Amino acid supplementation experiments and computational analyses indicate that lpdA and gcvH do not primarily function in glycine or serine biosynthesis but instead fulfil specialised roles in WLP-associated C1 and redox metabolism. Furthermore, genetic and physiological analyses showed that the two CooC-family ATPases, CooC and CooC2, have non-redundant roles in growth, with only cooC2 deletion impairing heterotrophy. Acetate supplementation tests revealed that {Delta}acsV cells retained metabolic activity despite abolished autotrophy, and computational analyses suggest a likely role for acsV in ATP-dependent corrinoid activation. Surprisingly, CRISPRi-mediated repression of acsV was translationally buffered, resulting in altered carbon partitioning without impairing autotrophy. Together, our findings provide insights into the physiological importance of the C1-fixing cluster genes in acetogens and support their metabolic engineering as gas-fermenting cell factories.

papers.title: Intracellular bio-synthesizing Gold Nanoparticles using bacterial systems and their applications in photothermal therapy (A green approach)
papers.abstract: Background: Conventional cancer therapies are heavily constrained by systemic toxicity, off-target side effects, and poor deep-tissue penetration due to the highly heterogeneous tumor microenvironment (TME). Although gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) possess exceptional localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) properties ideal for photothermal therapy (PTT), their clinical translation is bottlenecked by inconsistent passive accumulation and chemical toxicity arising from conventional synthetic surfactants. Objective: This study developed a sustainable, biocompatible bio-hybrid platform utilizing the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) as an autonomous, tumor-homing living carrier integrated with AuNPs synthesized via an eco-friendly intracellular green chemistry approach. Methods: EcN cultures were prepared in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium and subsequently exposed to a 1 mM chloroauric acid (HAuCl4) metallic precursor. A facile, room-temperature green synthesis protocol was established by utilizing ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) as a non-toxic co-reductant to drive a seed-mediated crystallization onto intra-bacterial metallic seeds. The bio-hybrid system (EcN::AuNPs) was characterized via visual inspection, UV-Vis spectroscopy, and in vitro PTT assays under continuous-wave near-infrared (NIR) laser irradiation. Results: Visual confirmation showed an irreversible color shift from pale yellow to a deep dark-brownish hue, serving as a direct diagnostic indicator of successful Au3+ to Au0 reduction. UV-Vis spectroscopic analysis revealed a distinct, broadened surface plasmon resonance (SPR) band centered at 560nm, indicating the formation of stabilized, isotropic gold nanostructures (30-60nm) subjected to near-field electromagnetic coupling within the complex intracellular compartments (periplasm and cytoplasm). Biocompatibility assays demonstrated a significant collapse in cell viability from 10^8CFU/mL down to 10^3CFU/mL, driven by a combination of trivalent gold heavy-metal toxicity, mechanical disruption of the peptidoglycan wall from spatial confinement, and severe metabolic/oxidative stress.
