We demonstrate that Ok-k-mer k-mer length ensembles remain stable (i.e. lengths and weights change only moderately) under genome subsampling within a taxonomy but vary across datasets. Ok-k-mer can annotate all subtrees of a phylogeny, which reveals distinct patterns of ensembles reflecting potential differences in genome evolution. Ok-k-mer provides a framework for moving beyond a "one-k-fits-all" k-mer analysis, improving genomic distance estimation in the era of massive-scale genomics.

papers.title: Impaired Fermentation in the Absence of Gut Microbiota Promotes Inulin-Induced Intestinal Inflammation
papers.abstract: Background and aims: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are characterized by altered gut microbiota composition and impaired dietary fiber fermentation, which can complicate symptom management. Although inulin is a well-established prebiotic fiber, it can exacerbate gut inflammation under certain conditions. We hypothesized that impaired microbial fermentation leaves intact inulin in the gut to activate epithelial immune receptors and promote inflammation, whereas effective fermentation reduces this pro-inflammatory signaling. Methods: We used germ-free (GF) and conventional (CONV) interleukin-10 knockout (Il10-/-) and wild-type (WT) C57BL/6J mice to assess the role of microbial fermentation and host genetic susceptibility in IBD. GF Il10-/- mice were colonized with fecal microbiota from ulcerative colitis (UC) patients or healthy individuals with fiber intolerance (FI). Mice were fed inulin or structurally distinct, physicochemically matched fiber analogs. Colonic inflammatory and barrier-related gene expression and protein levels were assessed by qPCR and ELISA. Results: In GF Il10-/- mice, inulin, but not cellulose, induced weight loss, diarrhea, and rectal prolapse. Increased colonic toll-like receptor expression (TLR2, TLR4) as well as elevated serum amyloid A (SAA) and lipocalin-2 levels indicated immune activation by unfermented inulin in GF mice. Colonization with dysbiotic microbiota attenuated these effects. {beta}-fructan fibers including fructooligosaccharides and chicory-derived inulin elicited marked inflammatory responses, whereas agave-derived inulin did not, highlighting the influence of fiber composition in inflammation associated with IBD. Conclusions: Effective microbial fermentation is essential for host tolerance to fermentable fibers. These findings underscore the need of personalized nutrition when recommending fiber supplementation in immune-compromised individuals or those with gut dysbiosis.

papers.title: Mapping the reactive cysteine landscape of the NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 protein
papers.abstract: NOD-like receptor pyring-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) is a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that drives assembly of an oligomeric inflammasome complex to stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine production and pyroptotic cell death. Extensive research has shown that NLRP3 activation is dependent on intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Despite this, the precise targets of ROS in this process remain undefined. In this study, a combination of chemoproteomics, in vitro biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations were used to characterize reactive Cys and how they may impact NLRP3 conformation and activity status. Affinity-captured NLRP3 was subjected to reverse-thiol trapping to reveal a pool of reactive Cys residues that were identified in subsequent chemoproteomic analyses. C150, C196, and C884 were consistently detected with both in vitro and in cellulo experiments. Several NLRP3 mutants were generated; C150A and C196A (NACHT domain) as well as C933A and C941A (LRR domain) reduced IL-1b output in a reconstituted inflammasome assay. Molecular simulation of Cys sulfenylation in the LRR suggests structural alterations that reposition the trLRR loop to destabilize the inactive NLRP3 structure. Structural modelling provided insights for how Cys oxidation of the LRR may impact on NLRP3 structure. Collectively, the results establish a mechanistic understanding for how ROS may promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

papers.title: Dual-reporter assay for selective small molecule inhibition of expanded toxic huntingtin
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in exon 1 of the human huntingtin gene (HTT). The resultant pathogenic allele (mHTT) produces a mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) containing an expanded polyglutamine tract. Because mHtt drives neurodegeneration while wildtype huntingtin (Htt) remains critical for regulation of gene transcription and cell survival, an ideal therapeutic would specifically downregulate mHtt expression while preserving Htt. Small molecules are attractive candidates for HD given their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and amenability to oral dosing, but there remains no high-throughput platform that reports both efficacy and allele selectivity. Here, we present a bacterial assay in which exon 1 of HTT and mHTT, each fused to spectrally distinct fluorescent proteins, are co-expressed in the same cell, allowing simultaneous quantification of their expression in the presence of small molecules. This high-throughput assay isolates the effect of small molecules on huntingtin expression without confounding factors present in mammalian cells, such as endogenous Htt or human RNA-binding proteins. To validate this assay, we evaluated two previously reported CAG repeat binding compounds and used circular dichroism spectroscopy and cell-free protein synthesis to investigate their underlying mechanisms. Furamidine exhibited reproducible, sequence-dependent effects, altering the structural stability of HTT RNA and selectively decreasing the wildtype Htt expression (a selectivity profile opposite to what is therapeutically required). In contrast, myricetin did not affect HTT RNA stability and its decreased signal in the dual-expression assay was due to fluorophore artifacts. This highlights the importance of complementary workflows in distinguishing genuine modulators from reporter-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings establish the dual-expression assay as a screening platform for CAG repeat-targeting small molecules and demonstrate the importance of determining which allele reported compounds preferentially affect.

papers.title: Core MCC of Arabidopsis thaliana: structural dissection provides new insights into Mad2, BubR1 and CDC20
papers.abstract: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) is a mechanism executed mainly by the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) to monitor the anchoring of mitotic spindle microtubules to ensure correct chromosome segregation. Although knowledge of protein-protein interactions in the plant cell cycle has progressed in recent years, information on the SAC mechanism in this context remains scarce. Here, we used bigBac, chemical crosslinking, mass spectrometry and structural analysis to identify protein-protein interactions (PPIs) among AtCDC20, AtBubR1 (BMF2) and AtMad2, which are components of the core MCC26 in A. thaliana. Fifty-three nonredundant crosslinks were identified, with multiple binding sites in different domains and subdomains of these proteins, such as the {beta}-propeller (AtCDC20), tetratricopeptide domain, and KEN boxes, including a new KET box (AtBubR1) and Horma domain (AtMad2). We also identified a hierarchy of interactions between these three proteins, with the potential to regulate signalling through the SAC molecular mechanism. Interactions that characterize the Mad2 tetramer, with the coupling of two dimers, were also identified. No PPIs were identified for AtBub1 (BMF1) or AtBub3:1, revealing a significant difference in MCC formation compared with that in other eukaryotes. Our findings provide a structural basis for core MCC formation in A. thaliana and offer new insights into the proteins CDC20, BubR1 and Mad2 in the context of the SAC.

papers.title: Dietary fibre combinations modulate gut microbiome composition and metabolic responses in zebrafish, with lasting effects on intestinal barrier gene expression
papers.abstract: Food sources provide a complex mixture of dietary fibres, not a single type. Consuming a diverse range of these dietary fibre-containing foods is associated with health benefits. However, how the effects of combining dietary fibres translate across different biological levels remains poorly characterised. This study uses an integrated microbiome-metabolome analytical approach that combines 16S rRNA gene sequencing with metabolomic profiling of the intestine, brain and liver. Specifically, we examined the combined effects of apple pectin (AP) and cellulose (C) within the same diet, compared with their isolated effects, in adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Notably, the combined apple pectin and cellulose diet (APC) produced a microbiome composition that could not be predicted by simply adding the changes observed with each dietary fibre individually, indicating a significant non-additive interaction between the two dietary components, specifically a less-than-additive response in gut microbiome composition. The resulting community composition under the combined diet also more closely resembled that induced by apple pectin. We found that predicted microbial functional capabilities did not translate directly into quantified intestinal and brain short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations, nor did intestinal SCFA levels directly mirror those observed in the brain. Moreover, we used targeted qPCR gene expression analysis to assess responses to a subsequent saponin challenge after dietary fibre cessation, revealing a potentially protective effect on the intestinal barrier. Collectively, we show that dietary fibres within the same diet interact to shape the gut microbiome and do not act in isolation, leading to non-linear health ramifications for the host that may persist even after active consumption ends.

papers.title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
papers.abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.

papers.title: Genomes of Solenogastres Shed Light on Ancestral Molluscan Biomineralization Genes
papers.abstract: Aplacophora (Solenogastres + Caudofoveata) is a group of worm-like molluscs that lack a shell and instead are covered with aragonitic spines and scales called sclerites. Sclerites are also found along the girdle in chitons (Polyplacophora) and are a synapomorphy for Aculifera (Aplacophora + Polyplacophora), which is the sister taxon of all other shell-bearing molluscs (Conchifera). However, whether the same genetic mechanism underlies the process of biomineralization in aculiferans and conchiferans is unknown. To investigate evolution of genes involved in biomineralization across Mollusca, we re-sequenced the genomes of two species of Solenogastres, Epimenia babai and Neomenia megatrapezata, producing near-chromosome-level assemblies through PacBio HiFi and Hi-C scaffolding. Using a combination of orthology inference and similarity searches against a known SMP database we identified 1,244 putative SMP orthogroups across Mollusca, 292 of which were present in at least one solenogaster genome. SMPs undergoing significant expansion/contraction at key nodes were further investigated. Of these, 15 were found in at least one solenogaster genome and included families containing chitin-binding, von Willebrand factor A, and C-type lectin domains. Across Mollusca, Solenogastres showed the highest number of significant losses in all gene families, including the SMPs investigated. Targeted searches for structural, silk-like proteins in Aculifera show further reductions in Solenogastres (16-17) compared to caudofoveates (29) and chitons (46-80). Altogether, our results support a conserved but reduced biomineralization toolkit underlying sclerite formation in Solenogastres and identify candidate genes for further proteomic and functional study.

papers.title: Positive relationships between interspecific association strength and elevational range overlap highlight the role of facilitation in community assembly
papers.abstract: The interplay of abiotic conditions and biotic interactions determines individual species' ranges, and by extension therefore, community assembly. To date, studies have focused predominantly on abiotic filtering (e.g., temperature) and agonistic interactions (e.g., competition) as potential drivers of community assembly; the role of facilitation in setting geographical range limits and structuring communities remains unclear. We tested how participation in compositionally distinct modules of facilitative networks of interactions in mixed-species bird flocks (MSFs) influenced interspecific elevational range overlaps across a 2000m elevational gradient in the hyperdiverse Eastern Himalaya. Species that participated in MSFs had higher average elevational range overlap compared with MSF non-participants. Positive correlations between pairwise association strength in MSFs and elevational range overlap were found for all MSF modules. We highlight the potential role of facilitation in determining species co-occurrence patterns and assembling communities across large spatial gradients.

papers.title: Dynamic regulation of single-cell contractile heterogeneity in the human trabecular meshwork
papers.abstract: Altered trabecular meshwork (TM) mechanics contribute to increased aqueous humor outflow resistance and elevated intraocular pressure in glaucoma, yet how contractility is regulated across individual TM cells remains poorly understood. Using a high-throughput single-cell contractility assay, we quantified time-resolved contractile behavior in primary human TM cells under defined extracellular matrix (ECM) compositions, substrate stiffnesses, and pharmacologic perturbations, and related functional mechanical behavior to intracellular protein abundance. Single-cell analyses revealed that TM contractility is not a uniform population property but a context-dependent contractile state shaped by both extracellular and intracellular regulation. ECM composition established distinct contractile programs, with collagen IV promoting rapid convergence toward a highly contractile state, collagen I supporting a slower but similar response, and fibronectin maintaining a persistently heterogeneous low-contractility state. In contrast, the intracellular perturbation dexamethasone (DEX) did not uniformly increase contractility but selectively prolonged contractile activity within the most mechanically active cells, thereby sustaining highly contractile states. This response was progressively constrained as ECM stiffness increased and was absent on pathologically stiff substrates, demonstrating that extracellular mechanical context conditions glucocorticoid responsiveness. Conversely, ROCK inhibition overrode both basal and DEX-induced contractile programs, collapsing the heterogeneous population into a uniformly low-contractility state. Finally, intracellular protein abundance poorly predicted functional mechanical behavior, with weak pooled associations reflecting divergent donor-specific relationships rather than consistent molecular-mechanical coupling. Together, these findings show that TM contractility emerges from integrating intrinsic cellular state and the extracellular mechanical environment rather than from either alone. More broadly, they identify single-cell contractile state as a functional dimension of TM cell identity that cannot be inferred from static molecular marker abundance or population-averaged mechanical measurements.

papers.title: Slowed aquatic invasion coincides with intensified research and prevention in Minnesota, USA
papers.abstract: Prevention is often the most cost-effective expenditure of limited environmental management resources. While demonstrating that harms occur without prevention is relatively straightforward, showing harms have lessened due to prevention--proving its effectiveness--is not, in part because it requires counterfactual data (i.e., quantification of harms that did not occur and then attributing these to prevention). Here, we attempt to measure aquatic invasive species (AIS) prevention effectiveness in Minnesota, USA, where AIS, their management, and research have increased since the 1980s. We showed the rate of new aquatic invasions slowed alongside intensified prevention investment starting around 2015. Further, mechanistic simulations grounded in real boater movement and boat inspection effectiveness data suggested prevention may have reduced new invasions of two high-priority AIS by 20-53% over a ten-year span. We argue our evidence strongly supports long-term statewide prevention, monitoring, and research.

papers.title: ERV-derived dsRNAs induce stress granules that drive neural crest fate to initiate melanoma
papers.abstract: Melanoma arises when melanocytes are oncogenically reprogrammed into neural crest-like cells, but what initiates this switch is unknown. Here we show that endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-derived double stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) induce stress granules (SGs) that drive this fate change. In zebrafish, melanoma progresses through a stage-specific ERV switch: zferv marks precursor cells before crestin activates in tumor cells. Both elements generate dsRNA that triggers eif2ak2-dependent SGs within precursor lesions and through transformation. SGs are tumorigenic as G3BP1 overexpression accelerates melanoma onset, whereas mosaic, melanocyte-specific g3bp1/2 knockout delays it. Small molecule-mediated inhibition of G3BP1/2 eliminates precursor lesions and reduces tumor burden. Similarly, blocking dsRNA sensing prevents SG formation and lowers melanoma incidence. Human nevi and melanomas show analogous, stage-specific ERV programs and SG assembly. In human melanoma cells, SGs sequester and translationally repress SOX10-regulating mRNAs, including the tumor suppressor KMT2D. Mosaic knockout of kmt2d in vivo enhances SOX10-driven neural crest reactivation. Thus, an ERV-SG axis establishes an oncogenic translatome that enables melanoma fate, with diagnostic and therapeutic potential.

papers.title: Neonatal personality is associated with sex-specific developmental trajectories in a wild mammal
papers.abstract: Animal personality, defined as consistent among-individual differences in behaviour, is an important source of phenotypic variation, but its developmental origins and associations with subsequent development remain poorly understood. We measured neonatal personalities, early-life growth, and yearling male antler length in wild fallow deer (Dama dama). Using eight years of data, we estimated repeatability and among-individual correlations among neonatal personalities and growth and applied structural equation modelling to examine associations with yearling male morphology. Heart rate and behavioural reaction measures showed repeatable among-individual variation, demonstrating that stable differences were detectable shortly after birth. Behavioural reaction was negatively correlated with growth in males but not in females. Heart rate was not associated with growth in either sex. In males, the effects of neonatal behavioural reactivity persisted beyond early life: more behaviourally reactive neonates had shorter antlers as yearlings, indirectly through reduced early-life growth. These findings show that stable among-individual differences emerge during the neonatal period and are associated with sex-specific developmental trajectories.

papers.title: Contrasting within-donor gene covariation identifies disease-associated cells and genes in case-control single-cell studies
papers.abstract: In case-control single-cell studies, disease often affects only a subset of cells of a given type within each patient. Comparing all cells from patients with all cells from control donors therefore dilutes disease signals, while donor variation and recorded or unrecorded batch effects can be confounded with disease status. We present IDC (Identification of Disease-associated Cells), which uses this cellular heterogeneity as signal. A mixture of affected and unaffected cells creates coordinated variation among disease-associated genes within each patient, whereas shifts shared by all cells of a donor leave this within-donor covariance unchanged. IDC therefore contrasts within-donor gene-gene covariance between patients and controls to learn disease-associated expression programs without batch labels, then applies positive-unlabeled learning to score each cell's disease-like state and estimate each donor's disease burden. IDC also computes, in closed form, gene contribution scores and leave-gene-out cell scores that exclude each tested gene, enabling within-donor differential expression testing and cross-donor meta-analysis without retraining. In simulations, IDC identified affected cells and estimated donor burden more accurately than deep generative and label-refinement methods, remained robust to strong unrecorded batch effects, and detected differentially expressed genes more sensitively than case-control pseudobulk methods while controlling false discoveries. In human pancreatic islets and prefrontal cortex, disease burden in held-out donors separated type 2 diabetes (T2D) from non-diabetic donors in beta cells, and late-stage Alzheimer's disease (AD) from non-AD donors in astrocytes and inhibitory neurons, while placing prediabetic and early-AD donors at intermediate levels. Genes with the highest IDC contribution scores were more strongly enriched for the KEGG T2D and AD pathways than case-control pseudobulk rankings, and within-donor testing revealed coordinated metabolic, cell-adhesion and synaptic changes along the inferred disease axis.

papers.title: PyTorch Frustratometer: An Ultra-fast, Parallelized Tool for Proteome-Scale Local Energetic Frustration Analysis
papers.abstract: Most natural protein sequences fold into well-defined three-dimensional structural ensembles, satisfying interactions that have been shaped over evolutionary timescales. The principle of minimal frustration states that most native interactions are energetically more favorable than alternative non-native ones, resulting in a funnel-shaped folding energy landscape. The FrustratometeR tool measures how the energetics of a residue or contact compares to decoys with different amino acid identities or configurations. Contacts are classified as minimally frustrated when these are more stable than random alternatives, highly frustrated when less stable, or neutral when energetically indistinguishable from them. Clusters of highly frustrated interactions are often evolutionarily conserved and are typically associated with functional regions. Therefore, identifying and quantifying local frustration can provide insights into both protein stability and function. Here we present a PyTorch reimplementation of FrustratometeR that accelerates conventional frustration calculations by 70-13,000x on a single GPU, depending on chosen frustration mode and protein size, with substantially larger gains for exhaustive mutational scanning, enabling proteome-scale local frustration analysis. We benchmark against the original algorithm on the CATH v4.4 S40 dataset and show near-identical results across all three frustration modes and mutational scanning. Source code is freely available at https://github.com/ParraLab-ESBG/pytorch-frustratometer.

papers.title: Analysis of haemolysis-based injury in immortalised proximal tubule epithelial cells is impaired by haemoglobin interference with bioluminescence assays.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious complication which is common amongst cardiac and aortic/vascular surgery patients. Although the cause of AKI following cardiac surgery is multifactorial, haemolysis is an increasingly recognised contributing factor caused by the use of cardiopulmonary bypass machines. Haemolysis, the lysis of red blood cells, releases free haemoglobin (fHb) into the bloodstream which is known to cause kidney injury. Currently, the mechanisms of haemolysis-induced kidney injury are not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the injury response to fHb in a human-derived conditionally immortalised proximal tubule epithelial cell line (ciPTECs). Results showed that fHb interference reduces bioluminescence signal output which is considerably mitigated by removing fHb solutions and haemolysed plasma prior to the beginning of the assay. Interestingly, we found that the effect of fHb on ciPTECs was different with haemolysed plasma compared to fHb solutions, potentially due to factors other than fHb within the plasma. In contrast to expectations, haemolysed plasma induced only a marginal increase in NF-B activity and had minimal effect on mitochondrial function. Together, these findings suggest that caution should be applied when using bioluminescent assays with fHb, both in solution and haemolysed plasma, and that fHb may not inflict severe injury on ciPTECs.

papers.title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
papers.abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

papers.title: Quantitative trait loci mapping identifies genetic loci modifying MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
papers.abstract: Increasing evidence has shown the role of genetic background on the penetrance of monogenic diabetes. A missense mutation of the pancreatic {beta}-cell-enriched transcription factor MafA co-segregates with diabetes (MafA-MODY) and non-syndromic insulinomatosis. We recently investigated the effects of genetic background on MafAS64F-driven dysglycemia in genetically diverse mice harboring this mutation. Here we leveraged the effects of genetic background on phenotypic penetrance to map quantitative trait loci (QTL) potentially modifying glycemia in response to this variant. We investigated MafaS64F/+ mice from an F2 intercross of the C57BL/6J and SJL/J genetic backgrounds through oral glucose tolerance testing at 4, 5, 6, and 8 weeks of age to evaluate glucose tolerance and glycemic trajectory. All F2 mice were genetically monitored for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) between the C57BL/6J and SJL/J backgrounds, allowing us to identify modifying loci on 6 chromosomes (2, 126 Mbp; 3, 59 Mbp and 103 Mbp; 7, 47 Mbp; 11 45 Mbp; 13, 4 Mbp; and 16, 85-97 Mbp), containing 172 candidate genes. For example, known MODY genes Abcc8 (Sur1) and Kcnj11 (Kir6.2) are within the QTL region on chromosome 7 and contain polymorphisms between backgrounds that may impart combinatorial effects on the phenotypic penetrance of MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia

papers.title: Assembly of host-specific bacterial and fungal communities from soil by diverse subaerial green algae
papers.abstract: Green algae recruit microbes from their environment to the phycosphere, a region closely surrounding algal cells which is analogous to the rhizosphere of land plants. Recent work showed that subaerial green algae can recruit and assemble their phycosphere microbiota from soil-derived bacteria. However, how widespread this ability is among diverse green algae, whether host identity shapes community composition, and whether soil-borne fungi can be recruited to the phycosphere remained unclear. Here, we show that subaerial green algae spanning Chlorophyta and Streptophyta assemble distinct phycosphere communities from soil-derived bacteria and fungi, with host identity as the primary driver of phycosphere composition, both in natural soil and in a liquid mesocosm. In soil, bacterial communities were strongly reshaped by algal hosts, whereas the fungal communities responded more weakly and less consistently. In liquid system, bacterial community composition was correlated with host phylogeny. Phycosphere communities included taxa known to associate with land plants in the rhizosphere, supporting the finding that some microbial taxa associate with a wide range of photosynthetic hosts. Our findings demonstrate that the green algae capacity to assemble distinct phycosphere communities possibly predates the divergence of Chlorophyta and Streptophyta. The stronger effect of host identity on bacterial than fungal community mirrors patterns observed in land plant microbiota, suggesting that principles of host-microbe interactions are conserved across evolutionarily distant photosynthetic hosts.

papers.title: Polyphosphate metabolism genes are associated with hydroxyapatite biomineralization capacity in a novel hydrogenotrophic methanogen Methanobacterium AMB_03
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea play crucial roles in sedimentary phosphorus cycling, but their capacity for phosphate biomineralization remains poorly understood. Here we demonstrate that Methanobacterium AMB_03, isolated from a serpentinizing environment, mediates extracellular precipitation of carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite (HAp) under phosphate-enriched conditions. Comparative genomic analysis of AMB_03 versus non-mineralizing strains (Methanobacterium oryzae, Methanoculleus bourgensis MAB1) shows that AMB_03 encodes polyphosphate kinase 1 (ppk1), enabling polyphosphate synthesis from ATP. In contrast, M. oryzae and MAB1 completely lack ppk1, preventing polyphosphate accumulation. Phylogenomic analysis of 320 Methanobacteriota genomes further shows that complete polyP cycling capacity is present in only ~25% of representatives, placing AMB_03 among a minority of methanogens with this capability. Experimental cultivation across phosphate gradients (0-6 mM) showed HAp early-onset precipitation was preferential at [≥]3 mM. Precipitation was eventually observed at all phosphate concentrations (except P0) by 49 weeks and was associated with extracellular polymeric substance production and localized pH increases of up to 8.08. Raman spectroscopy confirmed carbonate-substituted HAp, with characteristic peaks at 960.5 cm-1 (PO43-) and 1070-1072 cm-1 (CO32-). These findings identify a strong genomic association between polyphosphate metabolism genes and biomineralization capacity, suggesting that methanogens with complete polyP cycling systems may create localized phosphate-rich environments that promote authigenic mineral formation in sedimentary systems.

papers.title: HERACLES for fast and accurate likelihood-based reconstruction of massive lineages
papers.abstract: CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but rely on distances that may not faithfully represent the editing process, introducing biases whose magnitude and direction are unknown. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms: incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction.

papers.title: Generative design of de novo AAV vectors with unique serological profiles
papers.abstract: More than 5000 monogenic diseases are potentially curable by replacing a single defective gene with one that functions normally. Currently, the only clinically approved vector able to effectively deliver a therapeutic gene to a target tissue is Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs). However, despite decades of work, only a handful of gene replacement therapies have been approved, and many patients remain ineligible for even those. A major barrier to broad adoption of AAV therapies is pre-existing immunity to AAVs, mediated by neutralizing antibodies (nAbs). It is potentially possible to change exposed capsid surfaces in AAV capsids to avoid nAb recognition. However, traditional techniques such as rational design and directed evolution only allow modest changes. AAV function becomes compromised long before full nAb avoidance is achieved. Recent advances in protein design by generative modelling provide a new way to overcome this problem by learning AAV design constraints from natural sequences. We built a variational autoencoder that could learn these sequence constraints and generate functional AAV capsid proteins de novo. More than 255 designs were synthesized and tested in vitro in two design sets, with one set dedicated to exploring uncertain regions of the sequence space. Between the two campaigns, seven designs transduced human cells with >50% efficiency, of which four avoided nAb neutralization (NT50 < 1:50) in all human sera that were reactive to AAV. In one of these designs, sequence identity to the nearest natural AAV sequence was 18% divergent. Given the radical sequence diversity and its unique serological profile, this new capsid design would represent the first ever AAV serotype designed de novo.

papers.title: Structural and functional examination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae TfpC reveals a dynamic two-domain architecture required for type IV pilus function
papers.abstract: The Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) Type IV pilus (T4p) is a critical apparatus for colonization and virulence. This molecular machine resides at the host-pathogen interface and mediates adherence to host cells, twitching motility, natural transformation, and resistance to oxidative agents. Previously, we identified a DUF4124 family, T4p component, TfpC. TfpC is required for full T4p elaboration, and deleting the tfpC gene reduced natural transformation competence and resulted in an under-piliated colony morphology. Our earlier models suggested TfpC is composed of an N-terminal transmembrane helix and a proline-rich disordered region followed by a C-terminal coiled-coil. Here, we used targeted structural and genetic approaches to define TfpC's molecular structure. Our new data show that TfpC's N-terminal domain forms a novel, dynamic three-stranded {beta}-sheet structure. These data indicate that the flexible disordered region acts as a linker between the N- and C-terminal domains. Functionally, we illustrate TfpC requires an acidic face within the C-terminal coiled-coil domain to mediate pilus biogenesis and function. This study characterizes a unique protein fold and family and defines the contributions of TfpC's domains to its function.

papers.title: HomoeoGWAS enables experiment-wide homoeolog-group interaction mapping in allopolyploid crops
papers.abstract: Allopolyploid crops carry homoeologous gene copies from divergent subgenomes, an evolutionarily defined set of candidate interactions that association studies do not test directly. HomoeoGWAS uses these copies to define the unit of interaction testing, the homoeolog group, and analyses all eligible groups as one family with experiment-wide error calibration, combining three complementary genotype encodings per edge with a structure-aware parametric bootstrap. Family-wise error was controlled in 80-group tests in wheat, cotton and rapeseed under several null models and in full-family tests of all four crops under a structure-aligned global null (379-17,404 groups). The omnibus outperformed a SNP-by-SNP scan when interaction spanned several genotype dimensions. HomoeoGWAS detected homoeolog-group interactions for heading date in wheat, flowering time in rapeseed and fibre length in cotton; five groups at four loci retained support after regional conditioning. Rapeseed homoeolog coupling showed a weak but reproducible association with homoeologous-exchange frequency. Genome-wide interaction analyses took minutes.

papers.title: Enhanced hypoxic ventilatory response is accompanied by a decrease in carotid body mitochondrial oxygen affinity in heart failure
papers.abstract: Carotid bodies (CBs), the main peripheral oxygen sensors, play a significant role in sympathetic overdrive in heart failure (HF), resulting in worse clinical outcomes. Whilst CBs are an attractive therapeutic target, the development of CB focused therapies has been limited as the oxygen sensing mechanism is not fully understood. It has been hypothesised that the oxygen sensor is part of mitochondrial complex IV, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) signalling plays a crucial role in the oxygen sensing cascade. However, changes to CB mitochondrial function have never been determined in HF. Hence, we aimed to address this gap by characterising CB mitochondrial function and ROS production using a rapid pacing ovine model of HF. The hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) and autonomic function were assessed pre- and post HF induction. Tissue homogenates were prepared from whole CBs from control and HF and utilised to measure kinetics of mitochondrial oxygen affinity, respiration and H2O2 production rates by high-resolution respirometry. In HF, HVR and sympathetic drive were increased, while complex IV oxygen affinity was decreased. Despite an increase in abundance of mitochondrial complexes, no changes in mitochondrial respiration or H2O2 production were observed. However, aconitase activity and lipid peroxidation level were increased in HF. Overall, these results suggest that the CB mitochondrial function is altered in HF, and decreased CB mitochondrial oxygen affinity may suggest a higher complex IV oxygen sensitivity. Higher oxygen sensitivity accompanied by an increased oxidative stress may be key drivers of CB overactivity and therefore autonomic imbalance in HF.

papers.title: Multi-Enzyme Data-Independent Acquisition Mass Spectrometry for Proteoform-Aware Single-shot Proteomics
papers.abstract: Biological regulation does not operate at the level of the protein but across ensembles of protein variants shaped by alternative splicing, post-translational modification and endogenous proteolytic processing. Yet most conventional bottom-up discovery proteomics workflows remain optimized for a canonical protein census, leaving much of the sequence-level variation invisible. Multi-enzyme digestion has been recognized as an effective strategy to expand sequence coverage and proteoform sensitivity, but existing implementations rely on resource-heavy per-enzyme liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis, dedicated measurements for spectral library construction, and semi-manual reconciliation across multiple software tools, restricting the use to specialized laboratories and limited sample cohorts. Here we introduce mE-DIA, a multi-enzyme, proteoform-resolved data independent acquisition (DIA)-MS workflow that multiplexes complementary protease digested samples into a single DIA injection and processes them through a library-free pipeline within a single analysis engine, without supplemental data dependent acquisition (DDA)-MS measurements. The mE-DIA Pipeline graphical user interface orchestrates the analysis, and a dedicated proteoform inference algorithm and the interactive mE-DIA Peptide Mapper viewer make the sequence-level evidence explorable. Comparing the workflow to prevailing DDA-library-based multi-enzyme DIA on the same raw data and within shared search space showed increased identified protein groups by 30 % and protein groups quantified at [≤] 20 % CV by 47 %. A three-enzyme multiplex of the human pathogen Streptococcus pyogenes resolved 990 protein-backbone variants among 309 canonical protein entries, 1.8-fold more than the most productive single-enzyme analysis, including an H69 C-terminal proteoform of the ribosomal protein uS19 that the trypsin-only workflow did not resolve. By consolidating multi-enzyme acquisition, analysis and proteoform interpretation into one accessible toolset, mE-DIA brings sub-gene-resolved evidence within reach of routine single-shot discovery DIA proteomics.

papers.title: Engineering Nanobody Conformational Switches
papers.abstract: Conformational signaling is widely used in biology, but remains difficult to engineer into proteins. Here, we explore ligand-induced folding of nanobodies as a general strategy to generate conformational receptors for a broad range of target ligands. More specifically, we have generated partially unfolded nanobody variants that fold exclusively upon binding to their target ligand. To do so, we have introduced destabilizing mutations in the framework region, carefully tuning their stability while preserving molecular recognition. Given the high conservation of the framework across different nanobodies, this approach is broadly applicable to many other target ligands, which has enabled us to engineer conformational switches for three different important biomarkers and drugs: the pregnancy hormone chorionic gonadotropin, the cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha, and the chemotherapy and immunosuppressant drug methotrexate. Another useful property of conformational signaling is that it can directly gate signal transduction, which we have leveraged to build an optical sensor for the quantitative detection of the pregnancy hormone in urine. Finally, conformational signaling introduces new mechanisms for the allosteric modulation of binding, which we have explored to control the affinity and dynamic range of the sensor. Our work thus establishes a rational strategy for engineering conformational signaling receptors with customizable properties and generalizable for many different target ligands.

papers.title: Thienothiazolocarboxamides: rapidly cidal agents causing catastrophic thiol collapse in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
papers.abstract: Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

papers.title: Positive cooperativity enhances coupling of a second G protein to a GPCR dimer
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell surface integral membrane proteins that transduce environmental, hormonal and neurotransmitter molecular signals into intracellular responses. Here we studied a class D1 fungal receptor, Ste2, an obligate dimer that couples two G proteins per dimer and show that coupling of the second G protein has an 18-fold higher affinity than coupling of the first. The molecular mechanism uncovered suggests that coupling of the first G protein to one protomer stabilizes the adjacent protomer in an active conformation with a pre-formed G protein coupling site, thus increasing the affinity for coupling of the second G protein. Protomer-based stabilization of an adjacent protomer in a unique conformational state within a dimer may represent a general mechanism by which oligomerization alters GPCR pharmacology.

papers.title: Visual capture of the head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
papers.abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a common inherited monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability (ASD/ID), conditions frequently associated with altered sensory processing and multisensory integration. However, the circuit mechanisms underlying these alterations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the integration of visual and self-motion information in the head-direction (HD) system in a rat model of FXS (Fmr1-/y rats). Using high-density silicon probes, we recorded neuronal activity in the postsubiculum (PoSub), a cortical hub of the HD system, while adult Fmr1-/y and wild-type (WT) rats experienced repeated rotations of a visual landmark. In WT rats, the HD signal only partially followed landmark rotations, consistent with weighted integration of visual and self-motion information, and visual landmark control progressively weakened across repeated cue conflicts. In contrast, the HD signal in Fmr1-/y rats closely followed landmark rotations and failed to show experience-dependent recalibration. This enhanced visual capture was accompanied by reduced angular head velocity tuning in PoSub neurons, indicating weakened representation of self-motion information. Together, these findings reveal an altered balance between visual and self-motion inputs to the HD system in a rat model of FXS and identify a possible circuit-level mechanism through which sensory integration of vision and self-motion may be disrupted in ASD/ID.

papers.title: Photomechanical engineering of immunogenic whole-cell vaccines by laser-induced vapor nanobubbles for bladder cancer prophylaxis
papers.abstract: Whole-cell cancer vaccines can provide broad tumor-antigen repertoires, but their efficacy depends on manufacturing methods that inactivate tumor cells while preserving immunogenic danger signals. Here we show that laser-induced vapor nanobubbles (VNB) generated from dextran-coated iron oxide nanoparticles provide a drug-free photomechanical route to engineer immunogenic whole-cell vaccines against bladder cancer. Using MB49 murine urothelial carcinoma cells, we established VNB conditions that induced rapid tumor-cell killing together with calreticulin exposure and extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release. Rapid cell killing and calreticulin exposure were also reproduced in the molecularly distinct UPPL1541 bladder cancer model, supporting the generalizability of the early photomechanical response across bladder cancer cell lines. Vaccination with VNB-killed MB49 cells reduced tumor incidence and growth after subcutaneous challenge and enhanced splenocyte-mediated antitumor activity against MB49 cells. In an orthotopic bladder cancer model, vaccination prevented MRI-detectable tumor formation and was associated with marked early bladder enrichment of CD8 T cells and inflammatory monocytes. A single administration of the VNB-generated vaccine preparation showed no evident local or systemic toxicity during seven days of follow-up. These findings provide proof of concept for an externally triggered, drug-free manufacturing approach in which short laser irradiation induces rapid photomechanical killing of tumor cells on demand, generating immunogenic whole-tumor-cell vaccine preparations for further evaluation in therapeutic, post-resection and tumor-derived settings.

papers.title: The mouse midbrain periaqueductal gray is organized into target-specific output populations
papers.abstract: How brains select between behaviours and coordinate their execution is a central question in neuroscience. The vertebrate periaqueductal gray (PAG) controls a remarkable range of instinctive behaviours, from escape and freezing to hunting, vocalization, and micturition. Its columnar organization, the classical framework for mapping these functions, cannot explain how one region controls so many, often mutually exclusive, behaviours. To determine how PAG output is organized, we generated a whole-brain, column- and cell-type-specific synaptic projection atlas of the mouse PAG, showing distinct dorsal and ventral outputs and dense within-PAG connectivity. Retrograde tracing from four motor-related target regions identified segregated PAG populations, biased towards, but not confined to, individual columns. Channelrhodopsin-2-assisted circuit mapping showed that one such population, projecting to the cuneiform nucleus, provides substantial local collaterals, positioned to shape ongoing PAG activity. These findings uncover a modular output architecture that extends the columnar framework, offering a circuit logic for how one brain region produces diverse behaviours.

papers.title: Ogg1 regulates context-dependent glial states in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Oxidative DNA damage is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), but whether Ogg1, a key enzyme in oxidative DNA repair, contributes to disease pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show that Ogg1 exerts opposing effects under physiological and disease conditions. Ogg1 deficiency impaired memory and induced glial transcriptional alterations under physiological conditions, whereas in APP/PS1 mice it improved memory, reduced amyloid burden and attenuated AD-associated glial remodeling. These effects occurred without changes in global 8-oxo-dG levels and were accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility and gene expression, supporting a non-canonical role for Ogg1 in transcriptional regulation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics revealed strong transcriptional responses to Ogg1 deficiency across all major glial cell types and showed that Ogg1-dependent glial transcriptional programs are strongly conserved in human AD. These findings identify Ogg1 as a context-dependent regulator of glial cell states and reveal an unexpected role in AD-associated glial remodeling.

papers.title: A Continuum Fibre Network Model for the Anisotropic and Compressible Mechanics of Human Skin
papers.abstract: We present a Continuum Fibre Network (CFN) formulation for modelling anisotropy, strain stiffening and volume change in fibrous soft tissues. The model combines a three-dimensional fibre orientation distribution, a bilinear tensile fibre law and a separate phenomenological volumetric potential. We calibrated the model using published uniaxial tensile and volume-change data for excised human skin from separate studies. Changes in cross-sectional area affected the tensile stress estimates for models that predicted volume change. Simulations of indentation, shear and biaxial tension illustrate predictions of the calibrated formulation under additional loading conditions. The CFN formulation included a weak isotropic neo-Hookean ground matrix with a prescribed shear modulus of 0.1 MPa.

papers.title: DIALECT: DNA-Programmable Synthetic Cells Communicate with Mammalian Cells through Synthetic Receptors
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells can regulate mammalian signalling through the controlled release of diffusible protein ligands, but coupling programmable synthetic-cell senders to orthogonal, engineered mammalian receptors remains challenging. Here we present DIALECT (DNA-Instructed Assembly of Ligands for Engineered Cellular Transduction), a platform in which proteinosome-based synthetic cells translate sequence-defined DNA inputs into coiled-coil signalling ligand outputs for engineered mammalian receptors. DNA-ligand conjugates are localized within semipermeable proteinosomes through DNA hybridization and released by toehold-mediated DNA strand displacement (TMSD). The released ligands diffuse to neighbouring mammalian cells and activate cognate CC-GEMS receptors, inducing JAK/STAT3 signalling and reporter activation, with a higher response in cognate than non-cognate receiver cells under activation conditions. We further implement distributed Boolean AND logic using two independently programmed proteinosome populations that respond to distinct DNA inputs and release complementary ligand components. Simultaneous addition of both inputs produces substantially higher reporter activity than the respective single-input conditions, consistent with extracellular assembly of an active receptor agonist. DIALECT thus establishes a modular interface linking DNA-based molecular computation in synthetic cells to orthogonal signalling pathways in mammalian cells, providing a foundation for hybrid artificial-biological communication networks.

papers.title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.

papers.title: Cisplatin-triggered sensory dysfunction in NER-defective C. elegans involves GABAergic and cholinergic signaling
papers.abstract: Cisplatin (CisPt) is a widely used anticancer drug that causes neurotoxicity as a dose-limiting adverse effect. DNA damage contributes to CisPt-induced neurotoxicity, yet the molecular mechanisms involved remain unclear. Here, we aim to identify pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to DNA damage-driven development of sensory neuronal dysfunction using the 3R-compliant model organism Caenorhabditis elegans. To this end, we employed the nucleotide excision repair (NER)-deficient ercc-1 mutant, which shows enhanced CisPt-induced sensory dysfunction as monitored by the chemotaxis assay, to elucidate drug-induced alterations in neurotransmission and transcriptome. We found that CisPt reduces gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels in the nematode and that GABA supplementation rescues ercc-1 mutants from CisPt-evoked sensory neurotoxicity, pointing to a neuroprotective function of GABA in the context of our study. Moreover, CisPt impairs the morphological integrity of GABAergic neurons particularly in ercc-1 mutants, which again is rescued by GABA substitution. Conversely, the cholinergic agonist carbachol impairs sensory function and exacerbates the neurotoxic effects of CisPt in ercc-1 mutants, indicating detrimental effects resulting from cholinergic excitation. Transcriptome analysis revealed that CisPt treatment stimulates a broard transcriptional response, including pathways involved in the regulation of neuronal communication, including acetylcholine-mediated neurotransmission, with pronounced effects occurring in the absence of ERCC-1. Based on these finding we suggest impaired GABAergic signaling and the loss of neuronal integrity GABAergic neurons as well as excessive cholinergic excitation as key mechanisms linking CisPt-induced DNA damage in NER defective nematodes to sensory dysfunction. Hence, targeting the balance between GABAergic inhibition and cholinergic excitation is suggested to counteract sensory neurotoxicity triggered by CisPt.

papers.title: Bayesian Modeling of Context-Specific Goal-Directed and Habitual Control in Sequential Decision Making
papers.abstract: It is an open question how context-specific habits develop alongside goal-directed planning. We examined action sequence repetition, contingency change, and context switching using a three-step optimization task with interleaved planning and habit contexts. During an initial acquisition phase, optimal sequences varied in the planning context but remained constant in the habit context. When contingencies changed, the original habit sequence became suboptimal and another became optimal. Action sequence repetition improved response speed and optimal-choice performance in the habit context relative to the planning context. Following the contingency change, both advantages initially reversed. Optimal-choice performance in the habit context subsequently recovered but did not significantly exceed that in the planning context, while responses remained slower in the habit context. Context switches reduced optimal-choice performance in both directions, with additional slowing when switching from habit to planning. The Bayesian contextual control model captured choice patterns through learned action sequence priors, goal-directed evaluation, and context inference. Allowing a context-stability bias to vary across participants did not improve model performance. These findings suggest that sequence repetition facilitates performance under stable contingencies while impairing adaptation to change.

papers.title: Genome assembly and characterization of two Brazilian soybean cultivars contrasting for stink bug resistance
papers.abstract: Brazil's tropical soybean germplasm still has few genomic resources: only one assembly of a Brazilian cultivar is available at NCBI. Here we describe chromosome-level de novo assemblies of two contrasting cultivars: IAC-100, described as resistant to phytophagous stink bugs, and CD-215, susceptible. We sequenced high molecular weight DNA using 10x Genomics linked reads, assembled the reads with Supernova, anchored the assembly to the Williams 82 reference with RaGOO and corrected structural errors with REAPR. The assemblies span 1.057 and 1.061 Gb, with scaffold N50 values of 53.6 and 54.2 Mb (48.0 and 47.7 Mb excluding gaps), and recover more than 97% of conserved plant genes assessed by BUSCO. Homology-based projection of the reference protein-coding genes generated 46,774 and 46,620 gene models. Comparing the proteomes of the two cultivars, we identified 2,002 divergent isoforms in 1,427 loci, classified by sequence divergence, length variation, combined divergence and non-conserved homology. These data expand the genomic resources for tropical soybean germplasm, still underrepresented in public databases, and for studies of insect resistance.

papers.title: Rapid environmental DNA detection with isothermal amplification methods: a comparison with the real-time quantitative PCR in the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita).
papers.abstract: Species detection relying on environmental DNA (eDNA) traditionally relies on Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). This amplification technique takes in general a minimum of one hour and requires in most cases access to specialized laboratories and equipment. Isothermal amplification techniques, originating from clinical research, are emerging as rapid and field-deployable alternative methods. Yet, whether their sensitivity, specificity, and cost/time-efficiency are comparable to the traditional real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) remains to be assessed. In this work, we compare the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with qPCR to detect the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita) from aquatic filtrations. This objective was achieved in three steps. First, we developed LAMP and RPA primers specific to the target species based on its mitochondrial genome. Second, we amplified DNA extracts from E. calamita and from tissues of closely related species using real-time fluorescence detection with LAMP, RPA, and qPCR commercially available protocols to evaluate and compare the sensitivity and specificity of the three methods. Finally, we validated all protocols on eDNA extracts recovered from water samples from ponds surveyed by field scientists. We show that RPA had a sensitivity equivalent to that of the qPCR, while LAMP sensitivity was ten times lower. All our assays amplified the species DNA in eDNA samples where the species was observed by field scientists. Through this work, we thus propose a robust methodology for implementing isothermal amplification assays for eDNA applications and show that RPA is a good alternative to qPCR for detecting conservation-priority species (i.e. protected or invasive species) when time and lab facilities are constrained.

papers.title: Nanomechanical phenotyping uncovers a non-canonical smooth muscle-like hypercontractility program in lung squamous cell carcinoma myofibroblasts
papers.abstract: Myofibroblast-like cancer-associated fibroblasts (myCAFs) drive the stiff, tumor-promoting microenvironment, yet their mechanical phenotype in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains undefined. myCAFs from major NSCLC subtypes (lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC)) were examined combining atomic force microscopy and traction force microscopy with molecular and signaling analyses. LUAD-myCAFs displayed canonical myofibroblast features, including elevated stiffness, traction forces, ROCK-MYPT1 signaling, and -SMA-rich stress fibers. Unexpectedly, LUSC-myCAFs amplified these nanomechanical features despite reduced ROCK-MYPT1 signaling and comparable -SMA levels. Instead, they exhibited a smooth muscle cell (SMC)-like contractile program characterized by enhanced SM-MHC(MYH11) expression colocalized with -SMA, ERK1/2-RLC hyperactivation, and DNA methylation reprogramming including SMC-contractility regulators. LUSC-myCAF hypercontractility was linked with reduced proliferative capacity and smaller intratumoral vessel lumens, consistent with the low CAF density and enhanced hypoxia patterns reported in LUSC. SMC markers were enriched and associated with adverse outcomes selectively in LUSC, highlighting the relevance of SMC-like myCAFs in LUSC progression. These findings unveil subtype-specific myCAF programs in NSCLC, and identify -SMA/SM-MHC(MYH11) myCAFs as key determinants of tumor mechanics, providing a rationale for the survival benefits of antihypertensive drugs targeting SMC hypercontractility. Moreover, they demonstrate that nanomechanical phenotyping can uncover translationally relevant myCAF phenotypes invisible to molecular profiling.

papers.title: Thermosensory pathway makes a U-turn to respond to heat
papers.abstract: Plant organs exhibit a unimodal growth response to temperature, yet the mechanistic links connecting growth-promoting and growth-inhibiting thermal ranges remain unresolved. In Arabidopsis seedlings, warm temperatures promote hypocotyl elongation by relieving phytochrome B (phyB) inhibition, thereby activating the transcription factors PIF4 and PIF7 to drive auxin synthesis. Here, we demonstrate that temperatures beyond the growth optimum actively suppress growth by downregulating auxin levels, auxin signalling, and PIF4 abundance specifically within the cotyledons, the primary site of auxin production. Strikingly, whereas warm temperatures induce the shrinking of phyB nuclear bodies, heat stress causes phyB to assemble into enlarged condensates, a behaviour faithfully recapitulated in mammalian cells, demonstrating an intrinsic biophysical mechanism. Together, our findings indicate that heat-induced growth inhibition is not merely passive stress damage, but an active molecular reversal of the promotive pathway of thermomorphogenesis.

papers.title: Junction-level imaging and modeling of transient leaks in epithelia predicts a dynamic tight junction strand network
papers.abstract: Epithelial tight junctions restrict paracellular permeability, but how small solutes leak through the barrier is not fully understood, because permeability is usually measured globally. Here, we combined fast zinc-based barrier imaging (ZnUMBA) with computational modelling of the dynamic tight junction strand network to study transient leaks at single bicellular junctions in MDCK II cells. Leaks were short-lived, with a median duration of 17 s in wild-type cells, and occurred in all cell lines studied, including ZO-1 knockout, ZO-2 knockout, and ZO-1-overexpressing cells. In ZO-2 knockout and ZO-1-overexpressing cells, leaks lasted longer without changes in their frequency or transepithelial electrical resistance (TER). ZO-1 knockout increased the junctional ZnUMBA signal and reduced TER and the number of detected leaks. Simulations showed that stochastic breaking and sealing of tight junction strands is sufficient to explain the observed leak frequencies and durations, and that a single pair of strand break formation and sealing rates reproduces both junction-level leaks and global permeability. Whereas leak frequency mainly reflects the ratio of these rates, leak duration provides independent information on strand sealing that global measurements cannot resolve. Modulating myosin II activity had little effect on leaks, whereas actin depolymerization compromised the barrier. Together, these results link junction-level leaks of ions and small solutes to tight junction strand dynamics.

papers.title: Genomic signatures of local adaptation in marram grass highlight the importance of provenance in dune restoration
papers.abstract: Coastal sand dunes provide critical natural flood defences and key habitats for a range of threatened species. These systems are formed when shifting sands are stabilised by specialised coastal grasses. In Europe, marram grass (Calamagrostis arenaria) is the main dune building species. However, despite its ecological importance and its widespread use in dune restoration, little is known about the genomic innovations that facilitated the colonisation of the coast, the extent of local adaptation in current populations, or the genetic consequences of restoration practices. Using a chromosome-scale reference genome we generate here, we show that C. arenaria has significant expansions in several gene families relevant to coastal adaptation, including those associated with salinity, drought, and nutrient limitation. Using ddRAD-Seq data for over 200 individuals from 10 European populations, we identified strong genetic differentiation between northern and southern populations which corresponds to recognised subspecies. Within the northern european populations, the genetic structure is largely driven by isolation-by-distance. Although, we detected evidence of non-local planting in a restored Swedish dune system, where introduced plants were genetically distinct from the native population and both groups exhibited reduced genetic diversity. Genome-wide scans for local adaptation within the northern European marram grass individuals identified outlying genomic regions that were enriched for genes with functions associated with nutrient deficiency, drought, pathogen defence, and other environmental stressors characteristic of coastal dunes, potentially indicating local adaptation. Outlying regions also include genes associated with lignin biosynthesis and culm mechanical strength, potentially reflecting selection on the structural properties required to withstand different burial and wind exposure regimes. Overall, these findings show widespread local adaptation in C. arenaria, and support the use of local provenance in dune restoration and conservation.

papers.title: Uniformly re-analysed public omics data and graded meta-analyses of exercise responses in humans and rodents
papers.abstract: Hundreds of omics studies have profiled molecular responses to exercise, but they differ in species, tissue, protocol, sampling time and analysis pipeline, so their results are hard to combine. This dataset places the public evidence on a common scale. We screened GEO, PRIDE and Metabolomics Workbench for exercise studies in humans, mice and rats, defined exercise-control contrasts from sample-level metadata and uniformly re-analysed 1,037 contrasts from 448 independent study clusters, covering 20 tissue classes and seven molecular data types. For every contrast, the dataset provides moderated standardized effect sizes for each gene, protein, miRNA or metabolite and, for expression data, pathways. For 88 analysis units defined by tissue, exercise paradigm and molecular layer, it provides random-effects meta-analyses of every feature measured in at least three independent studies, with heterogeneity statistics, evidence classes assigned by pre-specified criteria and replication tests in two held-out training atlases. Curation records, code and a static query website are included. The data support look-up of molecules, new meta-analyses and planning and benchmarking of exercise studies.

papers.title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Testing and training geometrical knowledge in baboons through a conceptual categorization task
papers.abstract: Sensitivity to geometric regularity has been proposed as a signature of human cognitive singularity. Baboons can detect an intruder shape among quadrilaterals but, unlike humans, show no advantage for regular shapes such as squares and rectangles, suggesting they are not sensitive to geometric regularity. Here we asked whether, with symbolic training, baboons may show an enhanced attention to geometric features and their compositions. Using a symbolic match-to-sample task with frequent introduction of new generalization stimuli, we trained baboons and human controls to categorize stimuli as representing a given concept (A) or not (not-A) across two non-geometric domains (image category and line color) and three geometric domains (line perpendicularity, parallelism, and length equality). Baboons learned to perform above chance with all categories and generalize them to novel positive and negative exemplars (except for length equality). These findings provide evidence that baboons can extract geometric properties and associate them to arbitrary symbols. Crucially, this explicit geometry training did not result in the emergence of human-like performance in the quadrilateral intruder task: overall performance improved uniformly across shapes, but the geometric regularity effect failed to emerge. Thus, in baboons, recognizing individual geometric properties is insufficient to trigger the compositional perception of shapes that characterizes human cognition.

papers.title: S. pombe Mto1:Mto2 stabilizes γ-tubulin positions within the γ-TuRC
papers.abstract: Microtubules are present in all eukaryotes and are nucleated by multiprotein {gamma}-tubulin ring complexes ({gamma}-TuRCs), ring-shaped structures that contain several copies of the {gamma}-tubulin small complex ({gamma}-TuSC). {gamma}-TuRCs nucleate microtubules via a template-based mechanism in which the positions of {gamma}-tubulins in the {gamma}-TuSCs match the position of {gamma}-tubulin dimers in the microtubule lattice. Although {gamma}-TuSC proteins are highly conserved, other components of the {gamma}-TuRC can vary in different organisms, as can their relative importance. Here, we characterize two different simplified {gamma}-TuRCs from fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, using recombinant purified proteins and negative stain electron microscopy. We show that a nucleation-incompetent {gamma}-TuRC that contains only {gamma}-TuSC proteins plus the microprotein Mzt1 ({gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1) can form rings as efficiently as a large, nucleation-competent complex (MGM) that additionally contains the proteins Mto1 and Mto2. We find that the position of {gamma}-tubulins in {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 are less well defined than in MGM. Comparative modelling using our electron microscopy and crosslinking mass spectrometry data, together with structures of {gamma}-TuRCs from other organisms, suggests that Mto1 and Mto2 form a multimeric outer mantle surrounding the {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 {gamma}-TuRC. This mantle may stabilize positions of {gamma}-tubulins within MGM, explaining the microtubule-nucleating ability of MGM and highlighting the diversity of non-{gamma}-TuSC proteins in modulating {gamma}-TuRC structure and function.

papers.title: HIF1A-AS2 Regulates Hypoxia-Driven HIF Isoform Switching in Human Endothelial Cells
papers.abstract: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are central regulators of cellular adaptation to low oxygen, with a well-documented transition from HIF-1 to HIF-2 signaling during prolonged hypoxia. Here, we investigate the role of a natural antisense transcript of HIF1A, HIF1A-AS2, in modulating this transition in human endothelial cells (ECs). Genome-wide expression profiling revealed a strong hypoxia-induced upregulation of HIF1A-AS2 that coincided with a marked reduction in HIF1A mRNA levels, whereas EPAS1 remained stable. Interestingly, this negative correlation was consistent across multiple EC types and supported by silencing experiments which demonstrated that both HIF-1 and HIF-2 contribute to HIF1A-AS2 induction. Knockdown of HIF1A-AS2 partially restored HIF1A expression and increased HIF-1 protein and functional activity, as evidenced by elevated VEGFA and GLUT1 expression. Genomic analysis identified HIF-1 and HIF-2 binding motifs upstream of HIF1A-AS2, supporting the dual regulation. Furthermore, cancer tissue analysis revealed frequent downregulation of HIF1A-AS2, correlating with elevated HIF1A and EPAS1 levels. These findings suggest that HIF1A-AS2 acts as a hypoxia-responsive regulator that limits HIF-1 signaling and facilitates the HIF isoform switch, and suggests implications for endothelial adaptation, angiogenic signaling, and vascular remodeling under chronic hypoxia.
