Here, we engineered a panel of forty representative K13 variants by computing their relative deviations from wild-type K13 across ten physicochemical and structural descriptors, yielding a compact feature set which captures mutation-induced perturbations in folding, stability, and solvent exposure. These can be further utilized to train and validate AI classifier to predict resistance.

papers.title: Cell cycling throttles epithelial--mesenchymal transition
papers.abstract: Cell cycle phase is an understudied source of variation in gene expression. EMT is a case in point: this cell state transition that drives metastasis has been studied widely across tissue, stimulus, and microenvironmental conditions, yet cell cycle effects are routinely regressed out of single-cell EMT analyses. Here, we compare EMT between G1 and cycling (S/G2/M) cell states in two independent scRNA-seq datasets of TGF-{beta}-stimulated MCF10A mammary epithelial cells (varying dose and timepoint). G1 cells consistently show higher expression of EMT genes and upregulated RNA velocities than cycling cells, with the strongest upregulation in G1 EMT intermediate states. Consistent with the go-or-grow hypothesis, EMT and cell cycle programs inversely correlate; moreover, this anticorrelation extends to RNA velocity and strengthens with TGF-{beta} dose. We identify a 77-gene G1-specific EMT signature enriched for actin cytoskeletal and extracellular matrix genes that would otherwise be lost by regressing out cell cycle effects. This gene set prompts the hypothesis that, unconstrained by the cytoskeletal demands of mitosis, G1 cells have greater capacity to execute EMT. Further, we developed an EMT gene regulatory model coupled with a cell cycle module, and found through simulation that the model recapitulated this inverse EMT--cell cycle relationship. Using this model, we predict that cycle-selective chemotherapy enriches for the G1 intermediate state, which has high metastatic potential. Cell cycle phase thus ought not be regressed out of EMT states, given its influence on EMT.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
papers.abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.

papers.title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
papers.abstract: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, ablation study, and parameter analysis.

papers.title: scPolyA enables efficient, interactive and agent-guided alternative polyadenylation analysis in single-cell and spatial transcriptomes
papers.abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) changes which regulatory sequences an RNA retains, creating a layer of cellular variation that gene-level expression profiles cannot resolve. Here we present scPolyA, a unified, AI-enabled framework that transforms conventional single-cell and spatial 3'-end transcriptomes into quantitative maps of RNA-end choice. scPolyA connects de novo poly(A)-site discovery to cell- and spot-resolved measurements of terminal-site usage, 3' untranslated region length and intronic polyadenylation, enabling differential APA analysis across cell states and tissue regions. Its integrated deep-learning module, DeepCPS, improves recognition of sparsely supported poly(A) sites and predicts cleavage positions at nucleotide resolution. An integrated graphical workspace brings parameter exploration, efficient rerunning and genome browsing together, while an APA-specialised AI agent translates natural-language research questions into executed analyses, verified outputs and evidence-guided interpretation. Across diverse single-cell protocols and spatial platforms, scPolyA achieves higher reference-atlas agreement than most evaluated de novo methods, while single-cell benchmarks demonstrate competitive runtime and memory use. Applied to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, scPolyA reveals recurrent 3' untranslated region shortening in tumour keratinocytes across all ten patients and corresponding patterns in tumour-enriched regions, with tissue-level contrasts shaped by cellular composition. scPolyA extends conventional transcriptomics from gene abundance to RNA-end regulation, linking transcript choices to cellular states and tissue organisation.

papers.title: RabbitCD-HIT: Distributed High-Sensitivity Greedy Incremental Clustering for Billion-Scale Protein Sequences in Hours
papers.abstract: We present RabbitCD-HIT, a scalable distributed high-sensitivity greedy incremental clustering tool for ultra-large protein sequence datasets. It fully exploits cluster resources to enable efficient billion-scale clustering. RabbitCD-HIT clustered the March 10, 2026 NCBI nr snapshot (1.02 billion sequences; 487 GB FASTA) at 90\% identity within 5 hours on 64 nodes; the resulting representatives and cluster assignments are released as a public database resource. On a 256-core server, RabbitCD-HIT achieved a 2.1$\times$--6.6$\times$ speedup over CD-HIT with identical results under matched settings. Our approach addresses performance bottlenecks of traditional greedy incremental algorithms and provides an effective solution for large-scale protein sequence clustering.

papers.title: Interventional breath analysis reveals oral microbial conversion of 1,2-Propanediol into Propanal and 1-Propanol
papers.abstract: Background: Orally exhaled breath contains volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that may reflect local microbial metabolism as well as systemic processes. Consequently, the breath sampling route can influence VOC profiles and complicate biomarker interpretation. Previous studies have shown that 1-propanol is substantially enriched in orally compared with nasally exhaled breath. Objective: To determine whether a controlled oral challenge with 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PD) induces sampling route-dependent changes in breath 1-propanol concentrations. Methods: Ten healthy volunteers received 0.1 mL 1,2-PD diluted in approximately 50 mL water. The solution was used as an oral rinse for approximately 30 s and then expectorated. Matched oral and nasal end-tidal breath samples were collected before administration, immediately afterwards, and at 15-min intervals. Propanal, 1-propanol, acetol, acetone, and isoprene were analysed using gas chromatograph-ion mobility spectrometer (GC-IMS). Results: Oral 1,2-PD exposure produced a rapid and transient increase in exhaled propanal and 1-propanol signals, with the largest responses immediately after administration and at the second post-intervention measurement. In contrast, nasal signals remained comparatively stable. Acetone and isoprene showed no consistent intervention-related changes, regardless of the sampling route. No reproducible increase in acetol was detected, although interpretation was limited by analytical interference. Conclusion: A controlled oral 1,2-PD challenge elicited a route-specific propanal and 1-propanol response, consistent with local microbial metabolism of 1,2-PD within the oral cavity. Both fucose and 1,2-PD have been previously reported in human saliva, including elevated concentrations in selected disease-associated contexts. Bacteria can degrade salivary mucin glycans, releasing sugars including fucose. Together, these observations motivate investigation of a proposed pathway linking mucin-derived fucose to 1,2-PD and subsequent propanal and 1-propanol formation in the human oral cavity.

papers.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the pigtail macaque lung
papers.abstract: Background: The lungs undergo substantial physiological and immunological changes during respiratory illness to meet the host's increased metabolic and oxygen demands. These responses require coordination among epithelial, endothelial, stromal, and immune cells throughout the respiratory zone, interstitium, and vasculature. Nonhuman primates (NHPs) are a valuable model for studying pulmonary biology as they have similar anatomic, physiologic, and immunologic correspondence to humans. Despite the widespread use of NHPs in pulmonary research, the cellular diversity and molecular characteristics of the pigtail macaque lung remain incompletely defined. Methods: Parenchymal lung tissue from five adult female pigtail macaques (Macaca nemestrina) was dissociated into single cells and profiled using 10x Genomics 3' single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq). Next, ambient RNA was removed and quality control analyses performed. Samples were then integrated using scVI and scANVI. Cell types were labeled after unsupervised clustering and subclustering, followed by manual annotation using canonical marker genes. We compared lineages and cell types with the Level 4 Human Lung Cell Atlas (HLCA) using scArches reference mapping and with the Rhesus Immune Reference Atlas (RIRA) using Seurat label transfer. Results: The atlas includes 61,323 cells representing 37 cell types in epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, lymphoid, and myeloid populations. Annotated populations included both major and rare lung cell types, including alveolar type I and II cells, club and multiciliated cells, aerocyte capillary, and lymphatic endothelial cells, pre-terminal bronchiole secretory cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and several innate-like lymphocyte populations (gamma delta T cells, MAIT-like cells, innate-like CD8+ T cells, and group 3 innate lymphoid cells). There was strong concordance at HLCA annotation level 4, including AT1 and AT2 cells (96% and 93%), B cells (94 to 97%), CD4+ T cells (99 to 100%), classical and non-classical monocytes (84% and 85%), alveolar macrophages (80%), and mast cells (96%). Immune populations mapped to the RIRA with similar fidelity (alveolar macrophages and B cells, 99%). Conclusions: While studies of pandemic respiratory infections, vaccines, and therapeutics rely on NHP disease models, this atlas provides a unique reference for epithelial, endothelial, stromal, and immune cell states in the pigtail macaque lung. We found that single-cell populations from the pigtail macaque lung are highly similar to those in the human lung at the lineage level. This reference will enable studies of pathogenesis and vaccine and drug efficacy in a highly translational model of the human lung.

papers.title: Disentanglement of persistent and dynamic neural substrates of working memory
papers.abstract: Competing theories of working memory have alternatively emphasized the importance of persistent and dynamic substrates of this cognitive function. Here, we directly tested these theories by computationally isolating the contributions of persistent and dynamic activity to working memory. We analyzed neuronal population activity recordings in macaques doing match/non-match working memory tasks. We first extracted signatures of persistent and dynamic activity through cue-specific temporal means, temporal principal components, and correlations of activity patterns across task epochs. We then generated synthetic data constrained by these signatures, and decoded cue stimuli from these data, separately from persistent and non-persistent neurons. We found that high decoding performance arose from a nuanced interplay of persistent and dynamic activity. Specifically, we could decode stimuli at empirical or above-chance levels across all tasks only from persistent neurons, but only after constraining correlations of activity patterns across epochs. In this way, we showed distinct roles for persistent and dynamic neuronal activity that help to unify two competing theories of working memory. More broadly, we also advanced computational controlled experiments as a principled framework for adjudicating between competing models of neuronal population activity.

papers.title: Distinct mechanical signatures of dairy and plant-based cheeses
papers.abstract: Plant-based cheeses account for about 1% of U.S. retail cheese sales and often fail to match the texture and flavor of dairy cheese. Here we compare three commercial dairy and plant-based pairs, cheddar, feta, and mozzarella, with texture profile analysis (n = 60), tension, compression, and shear tests (n = 219), constitutive artificial neural networks, and a consumer panel (n = 306). Plant mozzarella is at least five times stiffer than dairy mozzarella at small strain, yet softer and less cohesive under 50% compression. Plant feta matches the initial stiffness of dairy feta but shows a peak in its shear response. Plant cheddar differs in both stiffness and shear response. Model discovery selects first-invariant models for all six cheeses, but no model term separates the two groups. Consumers rate 68--78% of attributes "just about right" for dairy cheeses and 29--38% for plant-based cheeses. These single-product comparisons define product-specific targets for plant-based cheese design.

papers.title: Homology-aware average nucleotide identity estimation at scale with TurboANI
papers.abstract: Here we introduce TurboANI, a fast homology-aware average nucleotide identity (ANI) estimation algorithm that implements the seed-chain-quasi-alignment scheme using SIMD seeding, compact indexing, lightweight chaining, and cache-friendly bitset sliding minwise hashing, achieving up to ~40,000-fold speedup over the alignment-based ANI algorithm with near-perfect agreement. TurboANI is also >40-fold faster than the state-of-the-art FastANI and ten-fold faster than skani while maintaining better accuracy. In the sensitive mode, it has a ten-fold higher true-ANI recovery rate than skani.

papers.title: Evaluation effects can rival reported concordance gains in cross-cancer survival prediction
papers.abstract: Studies of cross-cancer learning for survival prediction from tumour omics have reported concordance gains of 0.020 and 0.045, but how such gains compare with evaluation effects remains unclear. We examined these effects across 13 TCGA cancers (5,761 patients, 1,526 disease-specific deaths), using five repeats of five-fold cross-validation and paired bootstrap intervals. When model selection did not use test data, our borrowing model gained 0.009 (95% interval 0.001 to 0.016) over its target-fitted reference when cancers received equal weight (post hoc). Random-effects pooling gave a gain of 0.002 (-0.002 to 0.006), with most weight assigned to cancers where the model made little use of the pretrained score. Choosing the fusion weight on test splits raised the apparent equal-weight gain to 0.017. We reimplemented a published method, VAECox, which showed no pretraining gain over random initialisation at the last or validation-selected training step. Choosing each network's best test step, as the published code does, raised concordance by 0.03 to 0.05 across the 13-cancer and ten-cancer overall-survival settings, but barely changed the difference between networks. In a constructed post hoc experiment, choosing the best test step only for the pretrained network changed the equal-weight mean difference from -0.004 to +0.045 (+0.035 to +0.054). Across seven multi-omics comparisons, estimates from single five-fold runs differed from their cancer's five-run mean by at least 0.02 in 11% to 42% of runs. Concordance was about 0.02 lower at held-out tissue source sites. Interpreting a reported gain therefore requires each model's selection rule, variation across repeated partitions, the weighting of cancers and the evaluation population.

papers.title: Synthetic chromatin engineering for STAT1 reactivation toward restoring cisplatin sensitivity in breast cancer
papers.abstract: Chemoresistant cancers acquire transcriptomic and epigenetic alterations through changes in transcription factor activity and chromatin accessibility. Integrative in silico analyses identified STAT1 as a recurrently suppressed transcription factor in cisplatin-resistant breast cancer. Using cisplatin-resistant triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) MDA-MB-231 cells, we further confirmed reduced STAT1 expression and activity, accompanied by defective nuclear translocation, indicating that suppression of STAT1 signaling contributes to cisplatin resistance in breast cancer. To restore STAT1 activity, we sought to promote its nuclear localization and transcriptional activation through chromatin engineering. Based on the identification of PHF6 as a direct STAT1-binding protein through in silico and in vitro analyses, we engineered Dual Reader 3 (DR3), a PHF6-derived synthetic chromatin regulator designed to enhance both STAT1 interaction and chromatin engagement through histone H2B ubiquitination. DR3 induced STAT1-associated transcriptional programs, including inflammatory and tumor-suppressive miRNAs. Mechanistically, DR3 physically promoted STAT1 nuclear translocation, activated STAT1 through a non-canonical S727-dependent mechanism independent of Tyr701 phosphorylation, and enhanced chromatin accessibility at STAT1-responsive regulatory regions through histone H2B ubiquitination. CUT&RUN analysis further revealed coordinated transcriptional and epigenetic remodeling associated with DR3-mediated STAT1 activation, including upregulation of HIPK2, which enhanced cellular sensitivity to cisplatin by strengthening the intrinsic DNA damage response. Finally, we investigated whether STAT1 reactivation could alleviate acquired cisplatin resistance. In vivo delivery of DR3 restored cisplatin sensitivity in resistant breast tumors. By coupling STAT1 nuclear translocation with chromatin remodeling, DR3 reactivated STAT1-dependent transcriptional programs and restored cisplatin sensitivity in breast cancer. Together, this study establishes transcription factor reactivation through synthetic chromatin engineering as a potential therapeutic strategy for overcoming chemoresistance in solid tumors.

papers.title: Palindrome Presence, Location, and Structural Context Are Predictive of RNA Self-Association
papers.abstract: RNA self-association is a key elementary event behind many cellular processes from ribosome assembly, to regulation of gene expression, to assembly of biomolecular condensates. While RNAs self-interact in many ways, one direct and unambiguous sequence-encoded pattern for RNA self-recognition is a palindrome, or palindromic motif. In isolation palindromic motifs tend to fold back on themselves, favoring stable stem-loop secondary structures. However, palindromes have been implicated in some cases of RNA self-recognition, segregation and phase separation, raising the question of which palindromes in a given RNA are actually available for intermolecular engagement. Toward answering this question, we define three classes of palindromic regions based on local secondary-structure context, and degree of availability for interactions via their nucleobases, sorting into three classes. We then apply this framework across known structures of RNA chains and find that the majority of palindromic regions are bound up in secondary structures. We then designed a minimal set of short stem-loop RNA sequences to evaluate the self-interaction stability of each defined palindrome class using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Overall, this work provides a residue-level, structure-aware framework that connects RNA sequence, secondary-structure context, and intermolecular self-association for two interacting RNA chains.

papers.title: Host control and regulation of human anellovirus persistence
papers.abstract: Anelloviruses are the most abundant and diverse eukaryotic viruses known to infect humans and can persist throughout our lifetimes. Despite their ubiquity, the host factors governing their physiologic distribution and abundance remain poorly understood. Here, we construct a viral pangenome of 2,023 strains to quantify anellovirus DNA in >1.1 million participants spanning three genetic biobanks. Genome-wide association studies identify 121 loci linked to viral persistence, predominantly via immune regulation by NF-kB signaling. Further, we associate variable anellovirus detection with conditions characterized by immune dysfunction, including lymphoid malignancies. By screening 3.2 petabases of human single-cell sequencing data, we identify myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow as a prominent site of anellovirus transcription in vivo. Finally, Perturb-seq of anellovirus proteins reveals that anellovirus ORF2, particularly from Alphatorquevirus, attenuates TNF-a-induced NF-kB signaling, connecting host genetic variation, cellular context, and viral immunomodulation to characterize the persistence of the eukaryotic human virome's most abundant component.

papers.title: The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), genome reveals genomic and epigenomic signatures of shark evolution and demographic history
papers.abstract: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) represent one of the oldest extant vertebrate lineages, persisting for over 450 million years, yet genomic resources remain limited for many species despite widespread conservation concern. The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), the sole surviving member of the family Galeocerdonidae, is a circumglobally cosmopolitan predator vital in ecosystem regulation but is experiencing population declines. Here, we generated the first chromosome-scale haplotype-phased reference genome for the tiger shark and integrated comparative and population genomics with methylomics to characterise its genome architecture and evolutionary history. This assembly presented the first evidence of male heterogamety in this species. Comparative analyses revealed lineage-specific transposable element expansions across the chondrichthyan class suggesting ongoing genome restructuring in Carcharhiniform sharks. We report the first hydroxymethylome in a chondrichthyan, higher than that of other vertebrates, hinting at novel DNA evolutionary and regulatory pathways in an early-diverging lineage of jawed vertebrates. We identified genomic signatures of prolonged population decline that correlated with historical climate fluctuations and have resulted in sustained low levels of genetic heterozygosity in this species. These findings offer new insights into shark and broader vertebrate genomic and epigenomic evolution while providing valuable resources for conservation genomics of one of the world's most widespread top-order predators in the face of accelerating environmental change.

papers.title: Trunk muscle activity across various trunk-limb coordination patterns in centipede locomotion
papers.abstract: Animals coordinate movements of their limbs and flexible bodies, yet how trunk muscle activity changes across locomotor patterns remains unclear. We simultaneously recorded electromyograms from trunk muscles (deep dorsal oblique muscles) and trunk-limb kinematics in two centipede species exhibiting retrograde and direct locomotor waves during swimming and walking. During swimming, trunk muscle activity followed a similar phase relationship with trunk bending in both species despite opposite wave directions and different involvement of limbs, suggesting common active generation of undulation. During fast walking, trunk muscle activity was strongest around the ipsilateral swing phase in the undulatory retrograde-wave gait of Scolopendra mutilans, but weaker and associated with the ipsilateral stance phase despite the nearly straight trunk in the direct-wave gait of Scolopocryptops rubiginosus. Together, our findings suggest that the same trunk muscles serve two contrasting mechanical roles depending on locomotor mode: either generating trunk undulation or actively straightening the trunk against limb-induced deformation.

papers.title: PCB-Exposed Gut Microbiota Recapitulate Neurobehavioral Deficits and Reprogram Hippocampal Transcriptomic Signatures
papers.abstract: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent environmental pollutants associated with developmental neurotoxicity and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, whether PCB-induced alterations in gut microbiota contribute to neurodevelopmental toxicity independently of direct chemical exposure remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether transplantation of PCB-associated gut microbiota produces early neurobehavioral alterations and disrupts brain molecular pathways in offspring. Gut microbiota from conventional dams exposed to the Fox River PCB mixture (FRM; 6.0 mg/kg/day) or vehicle were transplanted into germ-free recipient females without direct PCB administration. At postnatal day 7 (P7), offspring underwent ultrasonic vocalization (USV) testing, whole-brain RNA sequencing (n = 4/sex/group), and untargeted serum metabolomics. Untargeted serum metabolomics were also performed in donor dams. PCB-associated fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) significantly reduced offspring USVs, reproducing effects observed following direct maternal PCB exposure. Brain transcriptomics in offspring identified substantially more differentially expressed genes in males (9,339) than females (1,082), including 512 shared genes. Concordantly regulated genes revealed downregulation of neurotransmitter signaling and ion channel pathways alongside upregulation of RNA processing pathways. Male-associated responses involved altered protein synthesis and neuronal signaling, whereas female-associated responses involved DNA repair and extracellular matrix remodeling. Despite these molecular differences, behavioral responses showed no significant sex-dependent effect. Maternal metabolomics revealed increased bile acids and decreased indole-3-propionic acid, highlighting potential AhR-NF{kappa}B and bile acid-associated signaling mechanisms. Offspring metabolomics further identified alterations in lipid-associated metabolites and metabolic profiles. Collectively, these findings show that transferring PCB-exposed microbiota reproduces early neurobehavioral alterations and induces shared and sex-biased molecular responses, identifying the maternal gut microbiome as a candidate mediator linking PCB exposure to developmental neurotoxicity.

papers.title: Early visual cortex is not functionally necessary for temporal attention: A TMS study
papers.abstract: Temporal attention enhances the selective processing of information at a specific point in time and improves perception. Previous neuroimaging studies investigating its neural mechanisms have either conflated temporal attention with temporal expectation or provided correlational evidence. Thus, whether early visual cortex is functionally necessary for temporal attention remains unknown. Here, we combined psychophysics with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to examine whether V1/V2 are functionally necessary and play a causal role in temporal attention. Observers performed an orientation-discrimination task in which two consecutive stimuli, T1 and T2, were presented in the periphery, preceded by a precue providing either valid or neutral temporal information. Double-pulse TMS was delivered under four conditions: at T1 (T1-TMS), at T2 (T2-TMS), at both T1 and T2 (both-TMS), or not at all (none-TMS), to assess its effects on temporal attention and the efficacy of the stimulation was verified by pupil size analysis. Behavioral results revealed robust temporal attention benefits on d', reaction time, and the Balanced Integration Score (BIS) across all four TMS conditions, indicating that the benefits of temporal attention were unaffected by occipital TMS. Furthermore, pupil dilation was largest in the both-TMS condition, followed by the T1-TMS and T2-TMS conditions, and smallest in the none-TMS condition, providing physiological verification of the stimulation protocol. Together, these findings reveal the first causal evidence that the early visual cortex is not functionally necessary for endogenous temporal attention.

papers.title: MorphoANOVA: Dissecting Histology-Gene Expression Relationships in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures the expression of hundreds to thousands of genes within tissue architecture, often accompanied by histology images. However, it remains challenging to systematically characterize which genes exhibit associations with tissue morphology, whether these associations vary spatially, and which genes show additional spatial expression patterns beyond those captured by morphology. Here we introduce MorphoANOVA, a gene-wise statistical framework for characterizing morphology--expression relationships across genes measured by ST. Using nested spatially varying coefficient models and sequential ANOVA, MorphoANOVA assesses slide-wide associations with an H\&E-derived morphology feature, location-specific changes in these associations, and additional spatial variation after accounting for the selected feature. The resulting statistics enable gene prioritization and pathway enrichment analysis, while spatial component maps support the interpretation of individual genes. Simulations demonstrate MorphoANOVA's ability to distinguish the modeled components and recover their spatial patterns. Applications to human cortex and breast cancer identify biological programs associated with different morphology--expression patterns and reveal distinct relationships with cell composition. Across three HER2-positive breast cancer patients, invasive-cancer marker genes consistently exhibit stronger evidence of location-specific morphology associations. MorphoANOVA thus provides a framework for systematically interpreting spatial gene-expression patterns in relation to tissue morphology.

papers.title: A cohesin acetylation complex that recognises nicked DNA
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic DNA replication products are held together by cohesin to enable their faithful inheritance during cell division. The establishment of stable sister chromatid cohesion requires replication-coupled acetylation of two conserved lysines on the cohesin Smc3 ATPase head. Here, we use AlphaFold 3 to predict the existence of a budding yeast cohesin acetylation complex, consisting of the replication protein PCNA, the cohesin subunit Pds5 and the Eco1 acetyltransferase. The predicted complex specifically contacts nicked DNA, a replication fork determinant that controls acetylation. Furthermore, cohesin engagement results in predicted conformational adaptations that bring acetyl-CoA in striking distance of the Smc3 target lysine. We perform biochemical and genetic experiments that confirm anticipated features of this reaction trajectory. Related cohesin acetylation complexes are predicted to form in other eukaryotes, including humans. Our study combines AI-assisted structure predictions and wet-bench experimentation to reveal the likely mechanism of replication-coupled cohesin acetylation during sister chromatid cohesion establishment.

papers.title: Programmable interphyla communication for Staphylococcus aureus by transferability of homoserine lactone sensors between Bacillales bacteria
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen of the order Bacillales and a frequent member of human-associated microbiomes. Despite its clinical relevance, engineering S. aureus and the communities it inhabits remains limited by a shortage of well-characterized genetic tools for precise control of gene expression and intercellular signaling. Biosensors for homoserine lactones (HSLs) are widely used in Gram-negative bacteria, as HSLs are small, passively diffusible signaling molecules for and their sensors are tightly regulated. Here, we show that synthetically designed HSL sensors using LuxR-family regulators are highly functional in S. aureus. Notably, synthetic designs previously built for the Gram-positive model Bacillus subtilis, a distantly related Bacillales, transferred functionally and establish repurposing the genetic toolbox as an effective strategy for importing these functions into S. aureus. Sensor performance correlated strongly between the two Bacillales, and activation in S. aureus reached 55-fold, exceeding the dynamic range of reported inducible systems. We further demonstrate tightly regulated, programmable interphyla communication between Gram-negative Escherichia coli and S. aureus via HSL signaling. These results provide a new toolset for engineering interbacterial communication and open a route to extending programmable HSL signaling to other tough-to-engineer bacteria.

papers.title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
papers.abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.

papers.title: Nutrient Availability as a Driver of Transcriptome Reprogramming in Osteosarcoma
papers.abstract: Background: Gene expression in mammalian cells is intricately regulated by environmental and metabolic cues. Among these, nutrient availability represents a key feature of the tumor microenvironment and has recently emerged as a potent modulator of oncogenic signaling networks. In this study, we employed a cell-line model of osteosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive bone malignancy affecting both humans and dogs. We demonstrate that altering the concentration of a single nutrient can profoundly reprogram gene expression in osteosarcoma cells, revealing a previously underexplored phenomenon: nutrient-dependent gene regulation. This finding highlights potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention and underscores the broader implications of metabolic regulation for personalized medicine and nutrition. Methods/Results: We performed bulk RNA sequencing of an established osteosarcoma cell line cultured under varying concentrations of two key nutrients, glucose and glutamine. Differential gene expression analysis revealed a pronounced nutrient-dependent transcriptional response. The identified genes were functionally associated with pathways involved in cancer, development, nervous system regulation, metabolism, cellular signaling, and immune responses. We identified seven distinct expression patterns, one of which exhibited a striking correlation with cell growth rate and resembled a FOS-like transcriptional signature. Notably, the proto-oncogene FOS was among the identified genes and displayed a strong growth-rate-dependent expression pattern. Conclusion/Impact: Our findings demonstrate that modulation of nutrient availability profoundly reshapes the gene expression landscape of osteosarcoma cells, revealing nutrient-responsive targets with potential therapeutic relevance. This work expands our understanding of metabolic regulation in cancer and suggests that nutrient-based interventions may provide a controllable means of influencing tumor progression. Beyond oncology, such approaches may also have broader implications for developmental biology, autoimmune disorders, and nervous system function. More broadly, this study highlights the potential of metabolic interventions as a strategy for targeted modulation of gene expression programs.

papers.title: A Standalone PD-1 Chimeric Switch Receptor T-Cell Platform Expands the Therapeutic Window of PD-L1 Targeting in Solid Tumors
papers.abstract: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) is a promising therapeutic target owing to its broad expression on tumor cells and immunosuppressive myeloid cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), providing an opportunity to target both cellular compartments. However, physiological PD-L1 expression in normal tissues poses a substantial risk of on-target/off-tumor toxicity, limiting the therapeutic window and clinical translation of PD-L1-targeted cellular therapies. Here, we developed a standalone programmed death-1 (PD-1) chimeric switch receptor (CSR) T-cell platform designed to preserve the therapeutic advantages of PD-L1 targeting while improving tumor-normal discrimination. Iterative receptor engineering, with antitumor activity and normal-cell reactivity evaluated as parallel selection criteria, identified two lead PD-1 CSR T-cell candidates. Compared with our previously developed antibody-based PD-L1 CAR T cells, the lead candidates retained potent PD-L1-specific cytotoxicity against tumor cells while exhibiting markedly reduced cytotoxicity against primary human small airway epithelial cells, astrocytes, renal epithelial cells, hepatocytes, and cardiomyocytes. They also efficiently eliminated PD-L1-positive immunosuppressive myeloid cells and mediated dual-compartment targeting of tumor and myeloid cells in three-dimensional (3D) multicellular tumor organoids. In vivo, both candidates suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic breast cancer and patient-derived glioblastoma models after systemic and intracranial administration, respectively. Collectively, these findings establish PD-1 CSR T cells as a standalone therapeutic platform that expands the therapeutic window of PD-L1-targeted cellular therapy by preserving dual-compartment targeting of tumor and immunosuppressive myeloid cells while reducing normal-cell reactivity, providing a foundation for further clinical translation across solid tumors.

papers.title: Inference of cell division parameters in bacteria under transient growth conditions
papers.abstract: Most quantitative models of bacterial cell division assume steady-state growth, yet natural environments are highly dynamic. Here, we infer division control parameters of E. coli from single-cell size trajectories under nonsteady growth. We describe growth as a continuous process interrupted by stochastic divisions, whose propensity depends on cell size and on the size added since birth. Combining an estimation of time-dependent single-cell growth rates with a maximum-likelihood estimator that we previously validated on synthetic data, we obtain time-resolved estimates of the mean added size at division, its noise, and a strategy parameter that measures how added size depends on birth size. This parameter vanishes for the adder, in which cells add, on average, a fixed size regardless of their size at birth, and is negative for sizer-adder control, in which larger-born cells add less size. We apply this approach to published single-cell data covering steady exponential growth, gradual nutrient depletion, and exit from starvation. We implement a time-resolved model selection based on the Akaike information criterion, concluding that the adder is sufficient during steady growth, whereas size dynamics during entry into and exit from stationary phase are better explained by transient deviations toward sizer-adder control. The framework provides a general method to quantify time-resolved changes in the scale, stochasticity, and strategy of division in nonsteady environments.

papers.title: Quantitative Head-to-Tail Analysis Reveals Heterogeneous Cellular Organization and Connexin Expression in the Porcine Sinoatrial Node
papers.abstract: Background: The sinoatrial node (SAN) is an integral component of the cardiac conduction system that dictates heart rhythm. Optical mapping studies have demonstrated functional differences between the superior and inferior leading pacemaking sites in the human SAN; however, the mechanistic connections between structure and function in the SAN through intra-tissue and inter-tissue current source-sink relationships have not been fully resolved. Methods: Porcine SAN longitudinal cryosections along the head-to-tail axis were immunostained and analyzed for regional cell organization and connexin (CX) isoform expression. Results: Quantification of pacemaking cardiomyocyte (PCM) density revealed >9-fold more PCMs within a SAN volume than suggested by a widely cited estimate, assuming comparable PCM densities across species. The SAN head region consisted of large PCM clusters with low aspect ratios, high PCM density, low fibroblast density, and PCMs with the highest HCN4 expression and lowest CX40 and CX43 expression. These characteristics are consistent with an electrically well-insulated, strong current-source that supports pacemaking function. Although the SAN tail also exhibited high local PCM density, its smaller PCM clusters, lower HCN4 expression, and higher CX40, CX43, and CX45 expression rendered it a weaker current source. The SAN mid-region exhibited large PCM clusters aligned in the head-to-tail axis and the highest expression of CX40 and CX45, an expression profile that suggests a fast-conducting intra-tissue pathway that electrically links the leading pacemaking sites at the head and tail. The peripheral SAN at the head and tail also exhibited higher CX expression of all isoforms than the central subregions, an organization consistent with enhanced inter-tissue coupling required for proper pacing function. Conclusions: Our data provide novel insights into the distinct regional micro-organization of the SAN along the head-to-tail axis, which through intra-tissue and inter-tissue coupling, likely modulates the balance of current source-sink relationships that supports robust pacemaking and pacing functions.

papers.title: PROST: An Open Toolbox, Harmonised Multi-Lab Dataset, and Meta-Analysis of Ankle-Foot Roll-Over Shape
papers.abstract: The ankle-foot roll-over shape (ROS) is the sagittal-plane path of the centre of pressure (CoP) during the stance phase of walking, expressed in a shank-based coordinate system. It describes the effective rocker geometry that emerges from both the shape and the elastic deformation of the ankle-foot system during walking, and informs prosthetic and orthotic design. Previous studies characterised ROS in small samples with differing laboratory protocols, so they have not systematically assessed inter-individual variability or its relation to anthropometrics. We developed the open-source Public ROS Toolbox (PROST) for standardised ROS computation, and used it to harmonise marker trajectories, ground reaction forces and CoP data from four public gait datasets collected in independent laboratories. For each leg, we fitted a circular arc to the pooled ROS of all its stance phases. In a one-stage individual-participant data meta-analysis, linear mixed-effects models, with dataset as a fixed effect and participant as a random intercept, related the arc radius and the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre to anthropometrics, and, in the two self-selected-speed datasets, to walking speed. The harmonised dataset comprises 249 participants and 5,667 stance phases at walking speeds of 0.7-8.5 km/h. Circular arcs fitted the ROS closely (mean RMS radial residual 1.9 mm). The radius had a median of 410.3 mm (interquartile range, IQR, 237.6 mm), and the circle centre lay posterior to the ankle (median -20.6 mm, IQR 49.5 mm). Between-participant differences, quantified by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), accounted for 42% of the variance in log radius (95% CI 25-57%) and 47% of the variance in the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre (95% CI 24-65%). Anthropometrics explained a negligible share of this variance (radius: pseudo-R2 -0.001, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.12), and height normalisation did not reduce radius variability (robust coefficient of variation 43% with and without normalisation). Faster self-selected walking was associated with a larger radius and a more posterior circle centre. To our knowledge, this study provides the first harmonised multi-lab ROS dataset. Together with the open-source toolbox, it is publicly available to support reproducible research in gait biomechanics, rehabilitation device design and clinical gait assessment. ROS geometry was participant-specific but was not predicted by age, sex, height or mass. A device ROS scaled from anthropometrics is therefore unlikely to match an individual's ROS, motivating studies of whether matching it, through device geometry and stiffness, improves gait mechanics.

papers.title: A Human Tumor Virus Recruits HSP70 Chaperone to Remodel Its Replisome on DNA
papers.abstract: Human Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV) large T (LT) protein functions as a replication helicase analogous to the cellular MCM complex but requires a second MCV protein, small T (sT), for efficient LT-initiated replication. Both LT and sT encode highly-conserved DnaJ domains that bind to the cellular refolding molecule, heat shock protein 70 (HSP70). Using single-molecule imaging and FRET, we find that sT recruits dimeric HSP70 to serve as a molecular bridge between sT and LT on DNA and that this complex facilitates remodeling LT into a functional double-hexameric helicase. Disruption of LT-HSP70-HSP70-sT interaction with HSP70 inhibitors or by mutations to the LT-sT DnaJ domains collapse the LT-HSP70-HSP70-sT complex, abolishing sT-enhanced LT dodecamerization and ATP-dependent DNA unwinding. Assembly of virus-free mammalian MCM3, MCM4 and MCM6 in nuclear extracts similarly recruits HSP70 to DNA suggesting that Hsp70 remodeling is used for efficient eukaryotic assembly of the multi-protein replication machinery.

papers.title: Benchmarking foundation models for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series in cognitive aging research
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets could help smaller studies investigate cognition from brain recordings. However, whether the foundation model-derived representations improve assessment of current cognition, prediction of follow-up cognition, or characterization of cognitive change remains unclear. We evaluated nine configurations from five model families that process regional resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series, using 3,103 scans from 1,653 participants across two observational and five intervention aging cohorts. Primary frozen representations showed no consistent superiority over conventional functional connectivity for concurrent cognitive associations or diagnostic classification. Changing the readout improved selected concurrent cognitive associations without updating model weights, indicating that performance depended partly on how representations were extracted. Additional post-training and embedding alignment yielded gains in selected settings but did not consistently improve performance across outcomes. In the primary longitudinal analyses, imaging representations did not establish added value beyond baseline clinical measures. These findings show that readout choice influences concurrent cognitive associations, while the added value of these representations for longitudinal outcomes remains unestablished.

papers.title: Structural determinants underlie the essentiality of the m-type thioredoxin TrxA in Synechocystis
papers.abstract: Thioredoxins are central regulators of thiol-based redox signaling in photosynthetic organisms, where multiple isoforms with partially overlapping functions coexist. Among them, TrxA is the cyanobacterial homolog of chloroplast m-type thioredoxins and the only thioredoxin known to be essential in cyanobacteria. However, it is unclear whether this essentiality is due to its high intracellular abundance or to its specific molecular properties. Here, we evaluated the ability of different thioredoxins to functionally replace TrxA and used TrxA/TrxB chimeras to identify the structural determinants underlying its functional specificity. Overexpression of TrxB, TrxQ or TrxC did not support complete segregation of a disrupted trxA locus, although the proteins accumulated to levels comparable to those of endogenous TrxA. Similarly, heterologous expression of NTRC did not rescue the phenotype associated with reduced TrxA levels. Comparative structural analysis revealed differences in surface electrostatics and structural features surrounding the catalytic site of TrxA compared with the other thioredoxins. Analysis of TrxB/TrxA chimeras showed that determinants required for functional complementation are primarily located within the C-terminal region of TrxA. Chimeric variants also differed in their ability to activate cyanobacterial FBP/SBPase and pea chloroplast FBPase in vitro, supporting a role for this region in target-specific interactions. Together, these results demonstrate that the essential function of TrxA cannot be explained by protein abundance alone and requires molecular determinants located primarily within its C-terminal region.

papers.title: Choline kinase A is required for alkylating agent resistance via lipid droplet formation
papers.abstract: Tolerance of DNA damage promotes cellular fitness, particularly in cancer cells under chemotherapeutic pressure. However, the biology and regulation of DNA damage responses remain incompletely understood. Using an unbiased genetic screen, we found that choline kinase A (CHKA) is required for alkylating resistance in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). CHKA is best-known as a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the first step in phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, but alkylating agent resistance was mediated by a nuclear function of CHKA. We found that CHKA positively regulates transcription of the DNA repair factor RAD51 via formation of lipid droplets. Restoring lipid droplet formation or RAD51 expression was sufficient to confer alkylating agent resistance despite CHKA inactivation. Our findings link lipid droplet formation to transcriptional control of the DNA damage response, providing a mechanism through which cellular lipid metabolism can control the maintenance of genome integrity.

papers.title: Engineered microvessel networks -- Longitudinal transcriptomic profiling validates chip-grown tissues as a robust model for studying vasculature
papers.abstract: Vascularised Organ-on-Chip (OoC) models are promising New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), but their translation requires validation for defined Contexts of Use (CoU). Here, we combine microfluidic microvessel networks (MVNs) with longitudinal bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing to determine how cell provenance influences engineered vascular phenotype. Stromal cell identity produced distinct network architectures and transcriptional trajectories, demonstrating that support cells, commonly treated as interchangeable, represent an important CoU variable. Primary human pancreatic microvascular endothelial cells failed to form stable perfusable networks, but supplementation with 10% Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) or Blood Outgrowth Endothelial Cells (BOECs) rescued self-assembly. Single-cell transcriptomics identified specialised endothelial populations associated with vascular morphogenesis, including tip, stalk, phalanx, endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) and pericyte-like endothelial cells. Failed networks lacked coherent endothelial specialisation, whereas rescued networks restored stabilising cell states and revealed FLRT2--UNC5B signalling within pericyte-like HUVECs, recapitulating a pathway implicated in angiogenic development in vivo. These findings establish cell provenance as a critical determinant of microvascular NAM performance and demonstrate how transcriptomic validation can define and strengthen the biological relevance of microvessel-on-chip models for specific CoUs.

papers.title: Vasopressin V2 receptor phosphopeptide reshapes the conformational landscape of arrestin-2 beyond C-tail detachment
papers.abstract: Binding of phosphorylated GPCR tails influences arrestin conformation, but the contribution of this interaction to the interdomain rotation associated with activation remains incompletely characterised. In particular, it remains unclear whether displacement of the arrestin C-tail is sufficient to favor larger interdomain rotations or whether the bound phosphotail exerts an additional effect on the conformational landscape. Here, we used enhanced-sampling simulations to characterise the conformational free-energy landscapes of basal (unbound) and V2Rpp-bound arrestin-2. We find that V2Rpp binding broadened the range of energetically accessible interdomain rotation angles relative to basal arrestin-2. However, the pronounced rotation observed in the experimental structures, while accessible, was not strongly favored. Strikingly, C-tail displacement alone does not reproduce this effect, as arrestin-2 retains a strong preference for small interdomain rotation angles in the absence of V2Rpp. Moreover, the C-tail-detached state is energetically unfavorable in the absence of V2Rpp. Together, these findings quantify the effects of V2Rpp binding on the interdomain rotation of arrestin-2 and disentangle the effects of phosphopeptide binding from those of C-tail detachment.

papers.title: Modular assembly of mitochondrial complex III from a dynamic matrix domain pool
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial complex III is a central component of the cellular energy metabolism. It is an obligate dimer of catalytic and accessory subunits that are encoded by two genomes. How its large matrix domain, formed by the core proteins Qcr1 and Qcr2, is built and joined to the membrane part and during assembly is not known. Here we show that Qcr1 and Qcr2 preassemble independently of complex III into matrix domain modules. Cryo-EM structures from a cardiolipin-deficient yeast strain and of recombinant protein resolved single, double and triple matrix domains, which are linked by the C-terminal tail of Qcr1. In the mature complex III, the same tail binds cytochrome b and cardiolipin. The modules form a dynamic pool, in which assembly species interconvert and exchange subunits. Mutations at the module interfaces, including mimics of human disease variants, reshape this pool and deletion of the Qcr1 tail impairs respiratory growth. Substitution of a tyrosine residue linked to parkinsonism exposes a conserved cysteine residue to oxidation. A cryo-EM structure of an assembly intermediate shows a cap of two matrix domains bound to a monomeric membrane module of cytochrome b, Qcr7, Qcr8 and cytochrome c1. We propose that complex III receives its matrix domain from a dynamic pool of prebuilt modules, which organizes the dimerization of the complex.

papers.title: Tfcp2l1 recruits Thrap3 to sustain ESC self-renewal via Jmjd1c exon-5 splicing and DNA repair choice
papers.abstract: How embryonic stem cells (ESCs) maintain genomic integrity while sustaining self-renewal remains poorly understood. We find that transcription factor CP2-like 1 (Tfcp2l1) recruits Thrap3 in mouse ESCs, where this complex maintains RNA polymerase II activity and promotes transcription of Tfcp2l1 target genes. In addition, Thrap3 supports mESC self-renewal. Interestingly, knockdown of either Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 induces highly overlapping alternative-splicing changes, including reduced inclusion of exon-5 in Jmjd1c. Further studies reveal that skipping of Jmjd1c exon-5 weakens the association between Jmjd1c and Mdc1, accompanied by elevated Mdc1-associated dimethylation, leading to reduced Mdc1 and Rnf8 interaction and diminished K63-linked ubiquitin signalling. These alterations impair chromatin recruitment of the Rap80 and Brca1 repair complex and increase Rad51 foci formation, indicative of a shift in DNA repair pathway preference. Accordingly, loss of Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 results in accumulated DNA damage, hypersensitivity to genotoxic stress, compromised ESC self-renewal and enhanced apoptosis. Similar phenotypes can be recapitulated in human ESCs. Together, our findings provide new insights into how ESCs coordinate genome maintenance with self-renewal.

papers.title: Tree cavities as attractors: an experimental test of the effects of woodpecker legacy on local bird activity and species richness
papers.abstract: Tree cavities, whether excavated by birds or formed through wood decay, are key structural features of forest ecosystems. They are critical resources for secondary cavity users and influence breeding bird assemblages by affecting the occurrence and abundance of certain species. However, the effect of an individual cavity on fine-scale bird activity, independently of the surrounding habitat context, remains poorly understood. Here, we experimentally tested the effect of cavity presence on bird activity in a coniferous forest in southern Poland. We installed pairs of standardized, debarked snags, each consisting of one snag with an artificial entrance resembling a woodpecker-excavated cavity and one control snag without a cavity entrance. Bird presence and activity were monitored using camera traps and vegetation structure was quantified around each snag. The presence of a cavity entrance had a positive effect on visitation rates and species richness. Snags with cavity entrances received 114% more bird visits than control snags (4.5 [95% CI: 3.1-6.5] vs 2.1 [1.4-3.2]) and were visited by 48% more species (2.0 [1.5-2.6] vs 1.3 [0.9-1.9]). In addition, greater canopy closure around snags was associated with higher visitation rates and species richness. Our study demonstrates that a single cavity can act as a fine-scale attractor for forest birds. These findings highlight the role of cavities and cavity-bearing trees in shaping spatially heterogeneous patterns of fine-scale habitat use by birds.

papers.title: Disease dynamics during ecosystem restoration and faunal reassembly
papers.abstract: Biodiversity recovery is increasingly promoted as a strategy for restoring ecosystem services, including the regulation of infectious diseases. However, it remains unclear how the potential for pathogen transmission interacts with the timing of biodiversity recovery and the life history of the recovering species to shape the disease dynamics during restoration. Here, we developed a stochastic multi-host metacommunity epidemic model to investigate how the timing of the establishment of slow life history species, pathogen transmissibility, and host-community succession jointly influence disease outcomes in recovering ecosystems. Pathogen transmissibility (R_0) was the dominant predictor of epidemic intensity, whereas the delayed timing of establishment of slow life history species during restoration emerged as a major ecological determinant of pathogen persistence. Delayed establishment of slow life-history hosts consistently increased disease prevalence and persistence by prolonging the dominance of highly competent fast life-history hosts. Generalized additive models revealed a strong interaction between delayed timing of slow life-history species establishment and pathogen transmissibility, explaining more than 90% of the variation in pathogen persistence. The influence of timing of establishment of slow life history species was weak for pathogens with low transmission potential but increased markedly as R_0 increased. Sensitivity analyses further showed that, once pathogen transmissibility was controlled, timing of establishment became the strongest predictor of persistence, whereas among-host spillover transmission primarily influenced the speed of epidemic spread. In contrast, maximum species richness had comparatively little influence on disease outcomes, indicating that the functional composition and assembly timing of recovering communities may be more important than richness alone for predicting disease dynamics. Together, these results demonstrate that disease regulation during ecosystem restoration depends not only on pathogen transmissibility, but also on the life history traits and the timing of establishment of species within recovering communities. Our findings identify life history traits and the timing of when functional communities are restored as a key ecological lever influencing long-term pathogen maintenance in restored ecosystems.

papers.title: Two decades of EU pesticide substitution have not reduced impacts on stream invertebrates
papers.abstract: Chemical regulation assumes that withdrawing hazardous substances and replacing them with alternatives reduces environmental harm. We tested this premise within the EU pesticide regulatory framework using a 23-year record of event-driven pesticide exposure and stream-invertebrate communities from 152 German agricultural streams sampled between 1998 and 2021. Neither pesticide toxic pressure nor pesticide-related invertebrate impairment showed a detectable decline over time, and an improvement equivalent to one ecological status class can be excluded. Dominant toxicity drivers shifted from organophosphates to neonicotinoids and subsequently to pyrethroids, yet the relationship between toxic pressure and community effects remained consistent despite their distinct modes of action. Sustained toxic pressure reflected three mechanisms: successive chemical substitution, prolonged approval periods, and continued exposure to substances no longer authorised as plant protection products. Substitution thus changed which chemicals harm streams, not how much. Measured field outcomes must become the benchmark of pesticide regulation.

papers.title: Age-dependent mechanical stress underlies unexpected vestibular differentiation and regeneration patterns
papers.abstract: Loss of inner-ear sensory hair cells (HCs) is a major cause of hearing and balance disorders. Promoting HC regeneration offers a potential therapeutic strategy, but regenerative capacity is limited in adult mammals and declines rapidly during early postnatal development in mice. HCs can regenerate through trans-differentiation of neighboring supporting cells in a process controlled by Notch mediated lateral inhibition. However, the factors underlying the decrease in regeneration capacity are poorly understood. Here, we combine live imaging with single-HC ablation in mouse vestibular explants to track the dynamics of HC development and regeneration. We reveal unexpected age-dependent deviations from the classical lateral inhibition model, in which new HCs differentiate adjacent to existing HCs. We find that mechanical stress changes with age and that perturbing it alters the observed differentiation patterns. A mathematical model incorporating local mechanical regulation of Notch signaling captures both HC differentiation and regeneration patterns across ages. Together, these findings identify mechanical stress as a crucial regulator of HC differentiation and support an underlying mechanism in which the interplay between local mechanics and Notch signaling shapes regenerative responses. This coupling offers a framework for understanding the age-dependent decline in HC regeneration and motivates investigation of mechanical regulation as a potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Bioinformatic pipeline for functional inference of Rickettsia akari hypothetical proteins reveals virulence-associated and effector candidates
papers.abstract: Background Rickettsia akari, the causative agent of rickettsialpox, is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a highly reduced genome encoding numerous hypothetical proteins (HPs) of unknown function. Many of these HPs are expressed during host-cell infection, yet their roles in bacterial physiology and potential contribution to virulence remain unclear. Methodology/Principal Findings We performed an integrative in silico characterization of 54 R. akari HPs previously identified by mass spectrometry in purified bacterial cells. Using a benchmarked computational workflow, we predicted their physicochemical properties, subcellular localization, putative secretion signals, protein folds, potential interaction partners, and evolutionary conservation. Most HPs were predicted to be thermostable. The majority of HPs were predicted to be cytoplasmic (37.00%) or membrane-associated (29.63%). Predicted features associated with the type IV secretion system were more frequent than those associated with type I secretion. Network and structural analyses identified candidate HPs with features consistent with potential roles in outer membrane assembly, host-cell interaction, and immune modulation, including predicted peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases, oxidoreductases, methyltransferases, and putative E3 ubiquitin ligases. Several HPs were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis supported the plausibility of selected predicted protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. Evolutionary analyses indicated predominant purifying selection among the analyzed HPs. A8GP20 showed elevated sequence divergence and warrants further investigation as a potential effector candidate. Conclusions/Significance Our findings prioritize A8GPG8, A8GP63, A8GNV4, A8GMM8, A8GM41, A8GMJ7, A8GMI5, A8GP20, A8GN23, A8GMB4, A8GM08, and A8GM39 as promising candidates for experimental validation of their predicted functions and potential roles in R. akari biology and pathogenicity. This work provides an integrative and reproducible bioinformatic framework to guide functional discovery in R. akari and related neglected intracellular pathogens, and identifies candidate proteins for future studies of rickettsial pathogenesis, antigen discovery, and therapeutic target development.

papers.title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
papers.abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.

papers.title: Choice of annotation data significantly impacts automated reconstruction of genome-scale metabolic networks
papers.abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models are valuable tools for studying metabolism in many applications, such as metabolic engineering or understanding human disease. However, curated models are available for only a limited number of organisms, and generating high-quality models for additional organisms remains a challenge. To help address this challenge, several software tools have been developed that can produce draft models in an automated fashion, but the quality of these draft models lags behind manually curated ones. Thus, there is still a need to improve these tools. Previous work has focused primarily on developing better methods for each step in the reconstruction process, such as gene annotation and gap-filling. Here, we focus on the data that underlies these methods, such as known connections between protein sequence and function. We find that changing the source of reconstruction data has a substantial impact on the contents and predictions of generated models. In fact, the source of data can have a bigger impact than the choice of reconstruction method. Additionally, we show that the reconstruction process is sensitive to the accuracy of gene annotations in the reconstruction data. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of having functional annotation data from an organism that is closely related to the one for which a model is being built. These observations highlight the importance of reconstruction data and identify principles that should be considered when selecting data for reconstruction tools.

papers.title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
papers.abstract: Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish (Danio rerio), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model's floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30-43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful.

papers.title: Synergy-informed bilevel optimization reveals joint-specific benefits for realistic exoskeleton torque prediction
papers.abstract: Simulation-driven optimization can guide exoskeleton control design, but its utility is limited by the accuracy with which muscle coordination is predicted. Strict effort-minimization formulations predict non-physiological muscle shutdown under high exoskeleton assistance, leading to peak assistive torques that exceed values reported in human-in-the-loop experiments. We evaluated the accuracy of synergy-informed simulations at predicting assistance across four single-joint exoskeleton configurations: ankle plantarflexion, knee extension, hip flexion, and hip abduction. We implemented a bilevel optimization to predict a parameterized assistive torque that minimizes metabolic cost, with assisted muscle dynamics estimated via either effort-minimization simulations (minimizing muscle effort only) or synergy-informed simulations (minimizing muscle effort constrained to a synergy structure). We used experimental data from five unimpaired adults walking at their preferred speed and compared results descriptively between the two formulations within each subject. Assistance based on effort-minimization simulations shut down agonist muscle activations and overestimated peak assistive torque compared with experimental values. In contrast, constraining muscle controls to a synergy structure prevented non-physiological muscle shutdown and yielded assistive torques closer to those measured in human-in-the-loop experiments. This benefit was not observed equally across all assisted degrees of freedom or subjects, emerging only where no single synergy could be suppressed to unload the assisted muscles. Synergy weights can therefore be interpreted as joint-specific predictors of when simulations can reliably inform wearable robot design.

papers.title: Glycine-Proline driven flexibility and interface-dependent conservation of six-residue {Omega}-loops in protein complexes
papers.abstract: {Omega}-loops are six- to sixteen-residue, non-regular structural motifs that occur in protein structures, connecting regular regions and forming a well-defined, ordered structural segment. They are functionally important because of their strategic location on the protein surface, where they are often associated with molecular recognition, ligand binding, and catalytic activity. Their non-regular nature enables them to adopt different conformations, which makes them important in protein dynamics and allosteric communication. In this work, we have curated six-residue {Omega}-loops from diverse protein-protein complexes of varying stability and found them to be abundant across all. We identified 1205 hydrogen-bonded and 6518 non-hydrogen-bonded {Omega}-loops, leading to an average of ~1.7 {Omega}-loops per structure. Glycine and proline were the most enriched residues in the loop, with proline preferentially positioned at the fourth position and glycine distributed across multiple positions, supporting their roles in chain reversal and conformational flexibility. Using ProteinMPNN-based sequence-design modelling and Rate4Site evolutionary-rate analysis, we show that {Omega}-loops occupy a relatively constrained sequence space, with interface loops in obligate homodimers and heterodimers more conserved than non-interface loops; the opposite trend was observed in transient and crystal dimers. Mapping known pathogenic and benign mutations onto the {Omega}-loop present in human proteins, together with a case study of the TEM1 {beta}-lactamase {Omega}-loop, further illustrates how small sequence changes within these loops can produce crucial structural and functional consequences, leading to altered enzyme activity and antibiotic resistance. Altogether, we report that {Omega}-loops are not merely connectors of secondary structure but are structurally constrained, evolutionarily significant elements that contribute to protein folding, stability and function.

papers.title: The ants (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) of Iceland
papers.abstract: The native terrestrial biota of Iceland required long oceanic journeys to colonize the island. Human colonization of Iceland, however, has allowed many less vagile species, such as ants, to reach the island. We compiled published, unpublished, and new records of ants from Iceland and evaluated the probable origin and current status of each species. We analyzed 565 records compiled by the Icelandic Institute of Natural History (1974-2020) and 84 new records (2019-2023) representing 25 species. Only five species were found living outdoors: Hypoponera ergatandria (507x indoors and 9x outdoors, mostly in geothermal areas), Lasius niger (24x indoors and 12x outdoors away from heated buildings), Hypoponera eduardi (5x only in geothermal areas), Lasius platythorax (1x near a small greenhouse and 1x in imported plant material), and Myrmica rubra (1x in an urban garden). Three ant species were exclusively found inhabiting heated buildings: Monomorium pharaonis (41x), Tapinoma melanocephalum (10x), and Monomorium nr. pharaonis (3x). Records of the remaining 17 species all appear to be based on temporary infestations, found on recently imported plant material. Previous records from Iceland of Hypoponera punctatissima appear to be based on misidentifications. Although it is possible that some ants were present before human arrival, all 25 ant species may have arrived accompanying humans.
