In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

papers.title: Tandem clustering of toxin genes exceeds gene-family-size expectations in four venomous bilaterians
papers.abstract: Toxin genes of venomous animals often lie in tandem arrays, which are commonly read as a signature of venom-specific evolution. However, large gene families of any function also cluster, so how much of this architecture is specific to toxins remains unclear. In this study, we compared toxin clustering in five venomous genomes with random genes and with size-matched non-toxin families. It is anchored on a new chromosome-level genome of the centipede Scolopendra mutilans, whose venom-gland proteome (12 individuals) detected 163 of 188 curated toxins and resolved 141 to single loci. Against random genes, the odds of a toxin gene having another toxin gene within 100 kb were 14-31 times higher in four bilaterians (centipede, snake, spider and scorpion). Against size-matched non-toxin families, the odds ratio fell to about 2-6 but remained above 1 under three gene-family definitions and, under the primary definition, for windows of 25-200 kb, after matching on within-family sequence similarity and, in the snake, with published venom-gene annotations. In the sea anemone, evidence for an excess was insufficient. The excess was spread across many toxin families and was carried mainly by adjacent homologous copies. Duplication topology and expression did not distinguish toxin from control tandem families, and in a congener toxin arrays were recovered less often and copy-number comparisons were uncertain. Thus, a random-gene baseline overstates the exceptionality of toxin clustering, but toxin families keep more homologous copies in local arrays than equally sized families; whether such arrays form more often or persist longer remains open.

papers.title: One placement, many fields: robust voxel-wise mapping with multichannel TMS
papers.abstract: Understanding the human brain at the individual level is central to understanding its function and a prerequisite for personalized therapy. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can map structure-function relationships at high resolution by regressing trial-wise variation in the TMS-induced electric field (E-field) against a response such as motor evoked potentials (MEPs). This requires distinct E-fields across pulses at different cortical locations, which single-coil TMS (sTMS) achieves by physically repositioning the coil (typically supported by neuronavigation software such as InVesalius Navigator; Souza et al., 2018)--increasingly reliant on robotic guidance and capped by the coil geometry. Multichannel TMS (mTMS) instead steers the E-field electronically via independent currents in several coils, opening a design space of high variability without physical repositioning. We adapt determinant-based sequence optimization from discrete sTMS coil-placement sets to the continuous mTMS current space (D-optimal design), identifying pulse sequences whose induced cortical E-fields are as mutually dissimilar as biophysical constraints allow. We benchmarked optimized mTMS sequences against random baselines and optimized sTMS placements in virtual motor mapping across multiple head models, assessing three mTMS array geometries (5-channel planar, 6- and 12-channel spherical), two figure-of-eight sTMS coils, and varying pulse counts, response noise, and cortical depth. D-optimal mTMS currents substantially outperformed random currents and optimized sTMS at matched pulse counts. The gain was modest without noise but increased significantly with it: at the highest noise level, optimized sTMS failed to converge after 100 pulses (~20-22 mm error), whereas all mTMS arrays reached median errors at or below 6 mm. mTMS also recovered deep targets better than sTMS (up to 35 mm skin-cortex distance, versus 25 mm) and performed uniformly across the region of interest. A coil-space scheme based only on the magnetic vector potential, precomputable once per array without per-subject MRI, captured most of the benefit, matching subject-specific optimization at 100 pulses. mTMS thus makes voxel-wise mapping robust throughout a region of interest without coil repositioning.

papers.title: Drought-induced changes in sex-specific floral chemistry reshape interactions with a nursery pollinator across life stages
papers.abstract: Nursery pollination systems provide unique models for studying the chemical ecology of plant-insect interactions, as specialized insects act as both pollinators and seed predators across life stages. How climatic stress alters the plant chemistry underlying these interactions remains unknown. To address this gap, we use the dioecious plant species Silene latifolia and its nursery pollinator Hadena bicruris. We investigated how water limitation affects visual floral traits, scent and nectar chemistry in male and female plants along with associated moth behaviour, as well as female seed chemistry along with associated larval performance. Water limitation broadly compromised floral traits, with particularly pronounced reductions in nectar metabolites in male plants eroding sexual dimorphism in nectar chemistry. Correspondingly, moths preferred well-watered flowers for oviposition and lost their adaptive preference for female flowers under water limitation, while feeding behaviour remained unaffected. Water limitation also compromised seed traits, including reductions in defence-associated metabolites. In parallel, larvae grew faster on seeds from water-limited plants despite consuming similar amounts. Our findings provide first evidence that climatic stress broadly compromises the multimodal phenotypes underlying nursery pollination, particularly chemical traits, and that these changes coincide with contrasting insect responses across life stages, with potential consequences for fitness and coevolution.

papers.title: How AlphaFold 3 helps with multiscale drug discovery
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) predicts protein ligand complexes, but the utility of its confidence scores for drug discovery remains unclear. We benchmarked AF3 interaction scores against BANDOCK+, an experimentally informed approach, using approved drugs and human protein libraries. AF3 ipTM achieved slightly higher observed aggregate disease ranking scores in a matched 1,103 protein comparison, with performance varying among individual indications. BANDOCK+ enabled substantially broader protein coverage using a computationally less demanding approach, including a 20,158 protein reference library. These findings highlight the potential of AF3 confidence scores for computational drug discovery and the tradeoffs between predictive performance and scalability.

papers.title: Dehydration-Responsive Left-Handed G-Quadruplexes Expandthe Sequence Repertoire
papers.abstract: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are widely studied noncanonical nucleic-acid structures that carry important biological functions. Typically, G4s form from G-rich sequences containing at least four tracts of more than two consecutive guanines, yet a plethora of unconventional G4-forming sequences have been identified, including sequences that fold into G4s only under specific conditions. These G4 states remain poorly resolved. Here we identify dehydration-responsive left-handed G4s (drLHG4s), a class of left-handed G4 (LHG4) structures accessible under dehydrating conditions. Using d(GT)n repeats, we show that left-handed folding depends on repeat length, salt condition and solvent conditions. Systematic mutational analysis reveals a broader but register-constrained sequence space, while high-resolution crystal structures of d-GTGGTGTGTGGTG, a sequence that folded robustly under dehydrating conditions, establish a bulged LHG4 architecture and reveal a distinctive hydration sphere. We further show that selected peptides and a cationic zinc phthalocyanine derivative, ZnTEGQPyrPc, containing four triethylene glycol methyl ether tails can induce LHG4 states. Together, our findings reveal a dehydration-responsive G4 landscape and expand the experimentally accessible sequence space of LHG4 folding.

papers.title: Sex Differences in Human Subcortical Anatomy are Robust and Replicable in Adulthood, Already Evident Prepubertally, and Aligned with Sex Chromosomal and Gonadal Influences
papers.abstract: The existence and mechanistic bases of sex effects on human subcortical anatomy remain unclear. To address these gaps, we combined structural neuroimaging of sex differences in subcortical volume and shape across three independent cohorts (combined N=2,886) with neuroimaging maps of sex chromosomal and endocrine effects from three clinical cohorts (combined N=313, including sex chromosome aneuploidies and isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency). We found that human subcortical anatomy shows focal sex differences of moderate-strong effect size during young adulthood (male-biased surface area overlying lateral/ventral putamen and pallidum, nucleus accumbens, ventral posterior complex of thalamus, anterior hippocampus, and medial and central nuclei of amygdala; female-biased surface area overlying caudate head, posterior/dorsal pallidum, mediodorsal, lateral dorsal, lateral geniculate, and medial geniculate nuclei of thalamus, posterior hippocampus, and basolateral and lateral nuclei of amygdala). These regional sex differences show strong within-sample reproducibility at modest sample sizes (N[≥]200) and are replicable in a fully independent mid-adulthood cohort. Strikingly, we find that the topography of adult subcortical sex differences is already established by pre/early puberty (age 9 years), and the same holds for cortical sex differences. Comparison with neuroimaging data from rare disorder cohorts reveals that subcortical sex differences show a statistically significant spatial and directional congruence with the anatomical effects of X-chromosome dosage in the striatum and effects of testicular hormones in the amygdala. Together, these findings provide a reference map for the fine-grained spatial patterning of sex differences in adult subcortical shape, demonstrating its replicability, establishment before pubertal progression, and spatial concordance with potentially causal sex chromosomal and gonadal effects.

papers.title: Freshwater Microbiomes Shape Viral Inactivation in Continuous Cultures
papers.abstract: In freshwater environments, bacteria are known to enhance the removal and inactivation of human viruses. Rates of inactivation differ across freshwater ecosystems, though the influence of community diversity and composition on this process remain poorly understood. Here, we used dilution-to-extinction to generate 64 distinct freshwater communities from three lakes and three aquifers. After establishing freshwater communities in chemostat cultures, each community was challenged with two viruses, coxsackievirus B5 and human adenovirus 2. Both viruses were inactivated more rapidly in lake-derived than in groundwater-derived communities, and adenovirus was inactivated faster than coxsackievirus in both freshwater types. Community-level parameters (e.g., cell numbers, richness) were not significant predictors of viral inactivation. Instead, differential abundance analyses identified bacterial OTUs associated with inactivation: Acidovorax sp. were associated across sources and Brevundimonas sp., Sphingopyxis sp., and Hydrogenophaga sp. showed source-specific associations. Together, these findings provide new insights into the ecological drivers of viral stability and suggest that viral inactivation may depend more strongly on specific microbial taxa and their environmental context than on overall community diversity. Identifying these associations improves our understanding of the factors governing viral stability in freshwater environments.

papers.title: Structural conservation of the gabapentinoid binding site in human and Caenorhabditis elegans α2δ subunits: a docking and molecular dynamics perspective
papers.abstract: Pain is a global health burden requiring effective therapeutic strategies. Gabapentin (GBP) and pregabalin (PGB), used for neuropathic pain, act primarily through alpha2delta subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels. Caenorhabditis elegans expresses UNC-36, an ortholog of mammalian alpha2delta proteins involved in calcium-channel function and nocifensive behavior. However, whether UNC-36 retains the features essential for gabapentinoid recognition remains unclear. We compared human alpha2delta-1 and UNC-36 using sequence and structural analyses, docking, one 500-ns molecular dynamics trajectory per complex, distance-based contact profiling, principal component and free-energy landscape analyses, and MM/GBSA calculations. The modeled proteins showed C-alpha correspondence within a selected 13-residue pocket core (RMSD 0.53 Angstrom), whereas the complete 14-residue mapping yielded 9.07 Angstrom. All four trajectories showed recurrent ligand-protein proximity contacts with residue-level patterns. Aromatic-residue contacts accounted for a larger fraction of contact records in human trajectories, whereas basic-residue proximity was more frequent in UNC-36 trajectories, including recurrent Arg501 and Arg503 contacts. Human alpha2delta-1/PGB showed the lowest ligand RMSD, while alpha2delta-1/GBP showed greater positional variation. In UNC-36, PGB deviated more from its initial pose than GBP. The first two principal components accounted for more conformational variance in UNC-36 complexes than in human complexes. MM/GBSA estimates, without an explicit conformational-entropy contribution, were more negative for PGB than GBP in human trajectories and for GBP than PGB in UNC-36 trajectories. These simulations suggest that selected pocket-core correspondence coexists with differences in modeled contacts, sampled motions, and estimates. They provide hypotheses for investigating gabapentinoid recognition by UNC-36 and its pharmacological relevance.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN: Phase-lag-dependent modulation of interhemispheric β-band functional connectivity by dual-site tACS
papers.abstract: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript because a bug was discovered in the code used for the main analysis, which had a major influence on the reported results. Additionally, the authors realised that the primary metric (DKL) is not defined for negative values, and the transformation applied to avoid negative values was not appropriate. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author

papers.title: phyB photobodies display molecular memory, regulating light signaling transcriptional states through phase separation.
papers.abstract: Phytochrome B is a crucial red and far-red light sensor, which controls plant development and environmental responses to light and temperature. In the nucleus, phyB forms phase separated condensates, also called photobodies, consisting of various transcriptional regulators and transcription factors. phyB photobodies can form or disperse depending on the amount of light, the light quality, or ambient temperature. However, the biological relevance for forming photobodies is still unclear. In recent years the study of condensates has given rise to the idea that condensates can act as molecular memory, either due to long equilibration timescales arising from strong interactions that can kinetically trap a mixture in a phase-separated state beyond the equilibrium coexistence line, or from phase-separation dependent modification processes or transcriptional regulation. Here, we hypothesize that the formation of phyB photobodies and the associated sequestration of signaling molecules allows for the formation of cell-type specific memory about light conditions. To address this hypothesis, we first developed a live imaging setup of phyB photobodies which shows that they do not follow classic liquid-liquid phase separation dynamics, but instead have a restriction on their size, intensity and minimum number. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) then showed that photobodies between cell types have different levels of mobilities and diffusivities, suggesting that they are more stable in darkness or high red light, versus low red light. These differences in phyB photobody stability between cell types were also confirmed through whole-mount confocal imaging and single-nucleus transcriptomics in the same light-perturbation series. Through sci-Seq single nucleus spatial transcriptomics of the cotyledon in this light perturbation series, we identify a photobody-associated transcriptional cluster of nuclei that regulates photosynthesis, circadian rhythm, and RNA processing; the phyB photobody likely promotes its own stability by regulating TZP expression. The correlation between photobodies and transcriptional regulation shows how phyB condensates can provide cell-type specific light responses and exhibit signaling memory in changing environmental conditions.

papers.title: A nuclear targeting approach enables efficient transgenesis in the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus
papers.abstract: Insects show extreme diversity and have long intrigued biologists. Although gene editing and transgenesis should enable the use of almost any insect species for biological research, species-specific challenges remain and conditions must be optimized carefully. Here, using the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus, we first generate a useful eye- and body-color mutant strain by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing. Using this strain, we develop an efficient piggyBac-mediated transgenesis system with a nuclear targeting approach. Incorporating 1x and 3x nuclear localization signals into piggyBac mRNA substantially enhances overall transformation efficiency in O. fasciatus. Taking advantage of the mutant strain and the efficient transgenesis system, we integrated multiple expression cassettes ranging from 1.8 to 7.2 kb, including attP strains for phiC31-mediated integration and histone-labelled strains for live imaging. We further show that the Q system, a binary expression system, is functional in this species, paving the way for sophisticated genetic manipulations. Together, our results expand the genetic toolkit of O. fasciatus as a comparative model insect and provide a practical framework for developing efficient transgenesis in other non-traditional model organisms.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN: Age-Related Increases in 40Hz Neural Synchrony Are Specific to Typical Development: A Cross-Sectional Study of Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript because of re-evaluation of clinical data. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.

papers.title: Ecological connectivity modelling for memory-constrained compute environments
papers.abstract: Circuit theory has been successfully applied to ecological connectivity modelling, notably via the Circuitscape software, which is typically run locally on a laptop, or on a dedicated server. However, for some applications, such web apps, automated pipelines, or high-throughput parallel analyses, backend infrastructure is often required. These systems can be costly, complex to operate, and introduce privacy and data governance concerns. Recent developments in WebAssembly (Wasm) now also allow fast C++ or Rust code to be run directly in a sandboxed browser environment. However, these are also contexts in which memory is limited. In order to make connectivity analysis feasible under memory constraints, we developed a Rust/WebAssembly toolset with a geospatial data pipeline and efficient, memory-optimised implementation of connectivity analysis. This approach may be useful for geospatial modelling software where raster sizes and memory are constrained, such as in the browser context. We also demonstrate that lower memory presents opportunities for parallelism, such as in the context of algorithms that require sampling, enabling previously constrained analyses. Our approach has the potential to reduce backend operational complexity, resource requirements, and overall cost.

papers.title: A cross-frequency architecture links biological and behavioral periodicities
papers.abstract: Spontaneous behaviors, e.g., walking and speaking, are thought to rely on an internal sense of time that provides a scaffold for precise temporal coordination. Yet endogenous rates of many behavioral processes often diverge from arbitrarily defined unit of objective time, raising a fundamental question: what temporal reference frame coordinates behavior? Using high temporal resolution multimodal recordings, we show that endogenous body-brain periodicities (including pupil fluctuations, saccadic eye movements, respiration, cardiac activity and neural oscillations) as well as spontaneous behaviors such as tapping, walking, and speaking, form a cross-frequency architecture organized as an arithmetic progression in a natural logarithmic frequency space. Successive rates are spaced by about {varphi} (golden ratio {approx} 1.618 1), while the ratio between rhythm classes are captured by e (e {approx} 2.72 2). The absence of power law scaling and harmonic anchoring to individual heart rates excluded the possibility that the frequency architecture scales to, and depends uniquely on, a single pacemaker. Rather, the irrational scaling suggests each rate to be principally independent and maximally de-coupled from others, yet capable to dynamically engage in cross-frequency interactions. We propose that the body-brain frequency architecture may provide an emergent temporal reference frame to scaffold perception and action.

papers.title: From junk to deleterious: Natural subtelomeric repeat amplifications impact fitness and cellular phenotypes in yeast
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic genomes exhibit astounding levels of complexity. Much of this complexity resides in repetitive DNA thought to evolve neutrally, meaning that its impact on fitness is so small that natural selection cannot act efficiently to favor or purge it. Yet, repetitive DNA greatly facilitates the generation of structural variants (SVs), which fuel evolution with both adaptive and deleterious variation. How SVs involving initially neutral repetitive DNA can bring new evolutionarily meaningful impacts is not well understood. This is in part because finding and interpreting molecular signatures of these transitions using comparative genomics over long evolutionary timescales is challenging. Here, we document one such transition over a microevolutionary timescale using budding yeast population genomics. We characterize multiple massive amplifications of the Y' element, a highly polymorphic and dispensable subtelomeric tandem repeat. We uncover extreme structural diversity in Y' tandem amplifications among near-isogenic strains, and show that these amplifications bring a significant fitness cost. We further link Y' amplifications with transcriptome rewiring, heightened DNA replication stress sensitivity and DNA damage response activation. Together, our results support a model by which massive subtelomeric tandem amplification pushed a repetitive DNA family outside of effective neutrality to become deleterious.

papers.title: Elementary Dynamics of Neural Microcircuits
papers.abstract: In neural circuits with multiple excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) cell types, qualitatively new dynamics arise when one population is silenced by the others, an effect linear theories cannot capture. Using threshold-linear networks, the simplest nonlinear population model, we derive closed-form conditions for multistability, oscillations, and paradoxical responses across microcircuits. In E-I circuits, strengthening E-to-I rather than I-to-E connections controls runaway excitation without silencing E cells. In a canonical neocortical circuit, two distinct gamma-oscillation mechanisms reproduce optogenetic silencing experiments, reconciling conflicting models. In hippocampal E-I-I circuits, cross-inhibition determines whether transitions between gamma rhythms are gradual, abrupt, or non-oscillatory. Two E populations or assemblies can cooperate, compete, or suppress each other depending on cross- versus self-excitation. Balanced inhibition prevents competition between E-I assemblies, unless I-to-I connections are more specialized than I-to-E ones, whereas lateral inhibition yields winner-take-all dynamics even without assemblies. These testable conditions link connectivity to dynamics across brain areas.

papers.title: When can a joint species distribution model capture biotic interactions? A simulation study across interaction mechanisms and levels of model integration
papers.abstract: Joint species distribution models (JSDMs) describe the composition of communities by the response of each species to the environment and by the residual dependence between species, which can be read as a network of associations. These associations are not biotic interactions, but interactions are one of the processes that can produce them, and it remains unclear how much of a set of interactions an estimated network retains, and under which conditions. We address this question with a virtual ecologist approach. Communities are simulated along an environmental gradient with a known network of competition and facilitation, under three interaction mechanisms: a lottery for space (the VirtualCom model) and two models of population dynamics, Gompertz and Ricker. We compare four estimators of increasing integration, from a Gaussian graphical model on log-transformed counts to PLNnetwork, a Poisson log-normal model that estimates a sparse network of partial associations while it is fitted. Each estimated network is scored for two uses: ranking all the pairs of species, and shortlisting a fewpairs. Each score is compared with the one obtained on a paired simulation without interactions, so that what an estimator owes to the niches alone is not counted. Within the assumptions of these simulators, five results emerge. (i)When the niches are narrow, interacting species seldom meet and there is little to capture, whatever the estimator. (ii) Partial associations do better than marginal ones, mostly among the best-ranked pairs. (iii) What a JSDM brings depends on the use and on the mechanism: its model for counts improves the ranking of all the pairs under the loglinear mechanism (Gompertz) only, mostly when counts are small or sampling effort is unequal, whereas estimating the sparse network together with the model improves the shortlist under the three mechanisms. (iv) Under the lottery and the Ricker mechanism, the Gaussian graphical model does as well over the whole ranking. (v) These gains require a covariate measured almost without error, no unmeasured gradient, a suitable representation of the abiotic effect of the covariate in the model, and enough latent factors. The scores remain modest throughout: a network inferred by a JSDM is at best a shortlist of candidate interactions, under conditions that this study makes explicit.

papers.title: Decoding the BRCA2 reversion principles underlying PARP inhibitor resistance
papers.abstract: Reversion mutations that restore BRCA2 function represent a major mechanism of resistance to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) in BRCA2-mutant cancers. Predicting these events could inform treatment strategies, identify patients at increased risk of acquiring PARPi resistance, and improve interpretation of secondary variants. Here, we use an isogenic cell system and CRISPR editing to define the principles governing BRCA2 reversion. We show that local sequence context shapes the spectrum of reading-frame restoration events, whereas domain architecture determines which of these events are selected as PARPi-resistant reversions. We characterize two routes of BRCA2 restoration that operate both within and across exons: DNA-level reading-frame restoration and transcript-level rescue via alternative splicing. Lastly, we identify distinct exon 11 restoration mechanisms, including large genomic deletions and recurrent splice isoforms that can bypass the loss of the canonical splice donor. These findings provide a basis for defining a predictive code for BRCA2 reversions that confer PARPi resistance.

papers.title: Effectiveness and efficiency of temporary fences as mitigation measures for preventing amphibians roadkill
papers.abstract: Temporary fences are used to prevent amphibians from accessing dangerous areas. These fences can be built out of different materials and field studies have shown that some of them still allow for trespassing. In this study we compared, in controlled conditions and using experimental arenas, the effectiveness and efficiency of the three most commonly used materials for temporary amphibian fences (polyethylene tarp, polyethylene netting, and wire meshing) and of the presence of an overhang, on two amphibian species with distinct modes of locomotion (Bufo bufo for walker/short-distance jumper and Rana dalmatina for long-distance jumper). The polyethylene tarp fence, and fences equipped with an overhang, were the only designs able to stop every individual for three consecutive trials. Fences that were not smooth nor equipped with an overhang could be crossed at any height by both species. For non-climbable fences (smooth or equipped with an overhang), long-distance jumper species required a 60 cm high fence to be stopped while the walker/short-distance jumper species only required 20 cm. The walker/short-distance jumper individuals interacted 1.7 times more with the polyethylene netting and wire meshing than the polyethylene tarp, this difference is likely due to the tarp being opaque and impossible to climb, deterring the amphibians from interacting with it. The long-distance jumper species was not deterred by the tarp fence and interacted equally with all materials. When considering price, durability and ease of use while maintaining effectiveness, the polyethylene netting fences equipped with an overhang were the most efficient option for long-term use, while polyethylene tarp is the best option for short-term use. These fences should systematically be equipped with a 10 cm overhang at their top to ensure their effectiveness.

papers.title: Collateral effects of drug resistance evolution: explaining repeatability and directionality patterns
papers.abstract: Drug resistance evolution is hindering the treatment of various diseases where new drug development cannot keep pace. One possible solution to this problem could be to exploit trade-offs in resistance to already existing drugs. One such trade-off is collateral sensitivity, where resistance to one drug increases susceptibility to another. Contrarily, cross-resistance means that resistance to one drug implies resistance to another. However, the evolution of these two collateral effects is not always repeatable, nor is it always independent of drug order (i.e., bidirectional). Understanding what drives repeatability and directionality would help define the clinical applicability of collateral sensitivity and avoid cross-resistance. Nevertheless, the genetic and evolutionary mechanisms causing non-repeatability and unidirectionality patterns are not yet fully understood. In this study, we aim to define which drug concentrations, population dynamics, and genetic architectures give rise to these patterns of collateral effects. We describe minimal examples of the fewest loci and conditions needed for repeatable and non-repeatable, uni- or bidirectional cross-resistance and collateral sensitivity to occur. We show that clonal interference can explain unidirectional cross-resistance and can increase repeatability, whereas a strong selection, weak mutation regime increases non-repeatability. Additionally, we show how drug concentration can change the collateral effect and/or its pattern. Overall, we show how non-repeatability and unidirectionality of collateral effects are not properties solely of a drug pair but also of the selection regime: drug dose and population dynamics. We suggest that further studies, combining mathematical modelling with measurements of mutations and full dose-response curves for drug pairs with known patterns of collateral effects, are needed to understand this problem.

papers.title: Natural selection on synonymous genetic variation in the major histocompatibility complex
papers.abstract: Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. Synonymous variation has recently been shown to coevolve between viruses and their natural hosts, but its potential role in host immune defenses has not been explored. Here, I present evidence of natural selection on synonymous variation in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), a highly polymorphic multigene locus that plays a crucial role in pathogen recognition by the adaptive immune system of vertebrate species. Using data from a wild population of Great Reed Warblers, I show that codon usage in exon 3 of MHC class I (MHC-I) genes is under strong purifying selection in 57 out of 87 codon sites. Scanning the Great Reed Warbler genome for tRNA genes revealed that, for most amino acids, bias towards preferred codons was associated with abundances of tRNA isotypes, indicating that the purifying selection is likely driven by selection for increased translational efficiency. However, spikes of synonymous variation appeared in 30 of the 87 sites in the MHC-I exon 3, and in those sites, codon usage bias and correlations with tRNA abundances were reduced. About half of these sites fall in CpG contexts, where cytosine deamination elevates the mutation rate; the other half do not, leaving the driver of much of the variation unexplained. The distribution of the spikes of synonymous variation showed no consistent association with structural domains of the MHC-I protein, nor with sites under positive selection for amino acid change, which are considered important for antigen binding properties. Intriguingly, the amount of synonymous variation in genotypes showed a positive correlation with Darwinian fitness, indicating that important evolutionary forces are at play that neutralize purifying selection in the 30 sites. From an ultimate perspective, the release of purifying selection among certain sites in MHC genes may indicate an arms race with pathogens, and I propose that the spikes of synonymous variation reveal a footprint of natural selection to escape inhibitory molecular interactions targeting MHC mRNA. I advance this RNA-level arms race as a novel axis of host-pathogen coevolution and a hypothesis to be tested directly. The fitness association is specific to synonymous variation, independent of amino-acid differences and the number of MHC alleles in genotypes, implicating selection on the synonymous variation itself rather than linked protein-level diversity. These results expose a previously unrecognized layer of selection in a key immune gene family and highlight the potential functional importance of synonymous variation in host-pathogen coevolution with direct implications for understanding susceptibility to infectious diseases.

papers.title: I err, therefore I am: Neural signature of error-monitoring predicts self-awareness in infants
papers.abstract: Self-reflection is central to human cognition and arguably a defining feature of human consciousness, yet the mechanisms enabling our mind to reflect upon itself and to construct a sense of self are unclear. Specifically, whether metacognition implies self-awareness, is independent of it, or emerges because of it, remains a subject of debate, fuelled by reports of metacognitive-like behaviour in preverbal infants and non-human animals. Building on evidence that 12-month-old infants show neural signatures of internal error-monitoring, we follow infants longitudinally from 12 to 18 months, when infants first start exhibiting evidence of a conceptual self-representation. Using a gaze-contingent match-to-sample paradigm with concurrent eye-tracking and EEG, we confirm that infants exhibit a neural signature of internal error-monitoring (error-related negativity, ERN) after making an incorrect decision (saccadic eye-movement) and before receiving visual feedback. Critically, we find that ERN at 12 months developmentally predicts which of the infants will evidence self-representation (mirror self-recognition) six months later. Infants' self-recognition was predicted specifically by internal error-monitoring, and not by external feedback-monitoring (FRN), nor by infants' age or general development. Moreover, we show that only infants who later self-recognised adjusted their behaviour post-error, by slowing their decisions and increasing visual exploration. Thus, internal error-detection, if available, can be utilised for online adjustments in information-seeking and decision-making as early as 12 months of age. These converging neural and behavioural findings support the idea that, rather than presupposing a self, early metacognition may be functionally involved in building conceptual self-awareness in humans.

papers.title: An atlas of human histological diversity
papers.abstract: Descriptions of tissues by histopathologists rest on verbal statements limited by quantitative inaccuracies and personal cognitive biases. Here we propose an unsupervised computational framework that transposes to histology the concepts and methods of RNA-seq gene expression analysis, setting histology on an unbiased quantitative ground. Leveraging this framework and the GTEx dataset, we built an atlas surveying the histological diversity of 40 organs from 946 non-diseased individuals and documenting 11,125,747 associations between 2,560 morphemes - the histological analogs of genes in our framework - and 9 layers of patho-clinical and multi-omic molecular data, providing a rich context to interpret histology. In contrast with the ideally healthy normal specimens depicted in histology textbooks, the atlas reveals the influence of age, sex, genetics and sub-clinical pathologies on tissue structures. For example, we report that female eccrine sweat glands are surrounded by more adipocytes than their male counterparts, and that distinct calcification-associated aorta morphemes are driven by either smoking or genetic polymorphisms. Cross-organ analyses also delineate the systemic histological impact of diabetes and other conditions and establish the power of blood gene expression to predict disease-related morphemes. The atlas is released as an interactive web resource aimed at researchers.

papers.title: COTree: A Statistical Framework for Deciphering Cell-Resolved Multi-Omics Trajectories
papers.abstract: Recent advances in whole-cell modeling enable the computational tracking of the temporal evolution of thousands of molecular species across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic layers. These models provide a complementary perspective for studying cellular dynamics, offering continuous, system-wide observations that are difficult to obtain from experimental technologies, which are often destructive and yield only static measurements from limited modalities. While whole-cell models generate multi-omic simulation trajectories with high temporal resolution, analyzing and interpreting such complex data remains a major challenge that limits their potential to elucidate cellular dynamics. To address this challenge, we propose COTree, a statistical framework that learns integrated multi-omic representations and constructs a trajectory principal tree to summarize cellular progression patterns. COTree enables a broad range of downstream analyses, including cell classification, fate prediction, developmental time detection, and driver species identification, that provide new insights into how cells develop and differentiate. To demonstrate its practical utility, we apply COTree to a multi-omic trajectory dataset generated from the whole-cell model of JCVI-Syn3A, revealing cell types, characterizing long-term cellular dynamics, and identifying key driver species associated with cell death and replication.

papers.title: Preemptive SOD1 Silencing via Neonatal Intramuscular AAV Therapy Modifies Disease Trajectory in an ALS Mouse Model
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder with limited therapeutic options. A major challenge for developing effective therapies is the safe and efficient delivery of genetic cargo to the spinal motor neurons that degenerate in the disease. This is particularly pertinent for SOD1-linked familial ALS, where gene silencing approaches are promising but remain constrained by suboptimal delivery. Here, we establish a gene delivery platform that overcomes this barrier by combining the retrograde transport of rAAV2-retro with an artificial miRNA to achieve pan-spinal SOD1 silencing. A single intramuscular injection of rAAV2-retro-miRNA into neonatal SOD1G93A mice achieved widespread transduction of spinal motor neurons, significant reduction of mutant SOD1 protein, and conferred multifaceted therapeutic benefits. Treated mice exhibited delayed disease onset, extended lifespan, preserved motor function, reduced neuroinflammation, and protection of neuromuscular junctions and spinal motor neurons. These findings establish the rAAV2-retro-miRNA platform as a versatile and efficient tool for spinal motor neuron-targeted gene silencing, addressing the delivery challenge and providing a foundation for further development in motor neuron diseases.

papers.title: SoluProtMut: Siamese Deep Learning for Predicting Solubility Effects of Protein Mutations with Experimental Validation
papers.abstract: Protein solubility is an attractive engineering target because it is a critical property influencing the scalability of protein production and the success of therapeutic proteins in biomedical applications. However, predicting in silico solubility changes upon mutation is challenging due to data heterogeneity and protein bias. Here, we explore how different sources of solubility data can be used for machine learning and present SoluProtMut, a Siamese deep geometric neural network trained to predict the impact of mutations on protein solubility. Our final model was trained exclusively on deep mutational scanning data derived from recombinant protein expression assays in bacterial and yeast systems. We compare our model with five established solubility prediction methods. On an independent set of 44 proteins, the model achieves the highest informedness among the methods compared, with the largest margin for multipoint mutations (a ternary informedness of 26.5%, 8.8 percentage points above the next-best method). Our findings also reaffirm that the scarcity of solubility data continues to hamper progress in this field. To address this limitation, we experimentally quantified solubility changes for 277 single-point and multipoint mutants of haloalkane dehalogenase. Complemented by recent deep-mutational-scanning data on myoglobin, we employed both datasets for external validation. We identify protein-level generalization, rather than model capacity or training-set size, as the main limiting factor in the domain. Integrating high-throughput assays with deep learning nonetheless offers a route to improving the accuracy and scope of solubility prediction.

papers.title: Flagellotropic bacteriophage selects for evolutionary remodeling of cell motility and chemotaxis in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Bacteria can evolve resistance to bacteriophage attack via mutations that alter phage receptors on the cell surface. Flagellotropic phages bind to motility-enabling flagella, creating a potential evolutionary trade-off, since losing flagellar function can reduce fitness in many environments. Phage-resistance studies typically characterize this trade-off using population-mean phenotypes, but selection can act on, and reshape, the underlying single-cell distribution of a trait in ways that mean values alone do not capture. Here, we exploit the well-developed and experimentally tractable model system of Escherichia coli-phage {chi} (chi) to ask how evolved resistance to a flagellotropic phage reshapes single-cell motility phenotypes, not just their population averages. We experimentally evolved E. coli populations under selection by {chi}, on soft-agar swim plates which favor motility. Whole genome sequencing revealed early emergence of non-motile mutants with disrupted motility genes, followed by motile, {chi}-resistant mutants carrying flagellin mutations. Swim-plate assays and single-cell tracking revealed heterogeneous motility outcomes among resistant lineages: some recovered or exceeded ancestor-level motility while others swam slower than ancestors, demonstrating that trade-offs and trade-ups can both arise from selection by the same phage- an outcome rarely captured in a single phage-resistance study. Single-cell tracking further showed that resistant lineages evolved increased tumble bias and altered swimming speed distributions, revealing shifts in trait heterogeneity invisible to mean-based measures. At the ensemble level, resistant mutants also showed remodeled kinase-response output in the upstream chemotaxis signaling pathway, indicating that resistance reshapes motility behavior both through receptor-level and signaling-level adaptation. Together, these findings demonstrate that evolved phage-resistance reshapes the receptor-linked (motility) phenotype across multiple phenotypic scales: from single-cell behavioral distributions to signaling network output, producing diverse and previously undocumented evolutionary outcomes under combined selection pressures.

papers.title: Precon_all: A species-agnostic automated pipeline for non-human cortical surface reconstruction
papers.abstract: Cortical surface reconstruction has transformed the study of brain morphology and cortical geometry in human neuroimaging. Here we present precon_all, an open-source structural imaging pipeline that generalizes reconstruction of the neocortical surface to multiple species. Adopting a modular framework that mirrors FreeSurfer's recon-all in humans, precon_all produces surfaces for non-human species compatible with FreeSurfer and Connectome Workbench. Precon_all reduces the dependencies of surface reconstruction to an image with T1-like contrast and five user-defined masks. This removes the dependence on species-specific atlases and tissue priors, and in turn extends surface reconstruction to species where these resources do not yet exist. The pipeline supports a wide range of imaging conditions, including in-vivo and post-mortem data, and has thus far been used to reconstruct the cortical geometry of primates, carnivores, and ungulates across multiple sites, spanning both highly gyrified and lissencephalic brains. Precon_all can be automated for high-throughput processing, and its template construction module can build surface-based common spaces to enable group-level analysis of cortical morphometry in new species. In short, precon_all is a flexible, modular pipeline that enables the comparative neuroimaging community to study brain evolution through cortical geometry in an ever-growing number of species.

papers.title: Mu opioid receptor expression by nucleus accumbens inhibitory interneurons promotes affiliative social behavior
papers.abstract: Mu opioid receptors in the nucleus accumbens regulate motivated behavior, including pursuit of natural rewards like social interaction as well as sensitivity to exogenous opioids. However, the specific circuit elements where mu opioid receptor expression promotes these motivated behaviors remain unclear. In mice of both sexes, we used a suite of genetic and viral strategies to conditionally delete mu opioid receptor expression from major neuron types in the nucleus accumbens, as well as monosynaptic inputs to this brain region. We pinpointed local inhibitory interneurons as an essential site of mu opioid receptor expression for typical social behavior. Mu opioid receptor deletion from inhibitory interneurons decreased both social interaction and preference, while shifting the ratio between synaptic excitation and inhibition onto medium spiny projection neurons, but did not alter exogenous opioid sensitivity. Conversely, mu opioid receptor deletion from medium spiny neurons altered exogenous opioid sensitivity but not social interaction, revealing a double-dissociation in the behavioral functions of mu opioid receptors expressed by nucleus accumbens projection neurons versus interneurons. Chemogenetic activation of inhibitory interneurons in the nucleus accumbens also decreased social interaction, mimicking the effect of mu opioid receptor deletion from these cells. Our findings suggest that circuit-specific engagement of mu opioid receptors could circumvent the risk of misuse associated with conventional exogenous opioids, with important implications for the pathophysiology and treatment of neuropsychiatric conditions involving social differences.

papers.title: Proliferation and mutation as humoral immune response
papers.abstract: The affinity maturation process, through which antibodies acquire relatively high affinity for an invading pathogen, involves complex mechanisms whose relative importance is not yet fully understood. This study proposes an analytical model of this process, to investigate the main factors governing proliferation and mutation and assess their respective roles. The model suggests that the immune system should not be expected to follow a single, rigid evolutionary pattern, as a wide range of proliferation and mutation strategies can yield nearly optimal outcomes. Keywords: Antibody, antigen, affinity, B-cell, mutation, proliferation

papers.title: StableProt: Structure-Aware Deep Learning for Protein Thermostability (Tm) and Environmental Adaptation (OGT) Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting protein melting temperature (Tm) and organismal optimal growth temperature (OGT) is essential for enzyme engineering, biocatalyst design, and metagenomic bioprospecting, yet computational prediction faces several fundamental bottlenecks: sequence-only representations miss tertiary packing; dual-task coupling induces destructive gradient conflict; natural database skew (>87% mesophiles) drives mesophilic collapse; and existing tools produce uncalibrated point predictions. To address these challenges, we present StableProt, a structure-aware framework that couples amino acid sequences with Foldseek 3Di structural tokens via a frozen SaProt backbone to capture 3D contacts. Disjoint heads condition thermodynamic stability on ecological context without gradient conflict, while targeted 14% mesophilic subsampling expands thermophile representation to eliminate mesophilic collapse. Calibrated ensemble modeling reduces calibration error to 1.92%, providing dependable 95% confidence intervals. Evaluating models across 10{degrees}C temperature intervals reveals severe baseline collapse at thermal extremes, whereas StableProt maintains robust accuracy across regimes. On ProThermDB and zero-shot FireProtDB, StableProt achieves state-of-the-art probabilistic accuracy (CRPS = 4.52{degrees}C and 8.71{degrees}C) while recovering 92.0% of hyperthermophiles ([≥]80{degrees}C), and in prospective validation, its calibrated intervals capture both enzyme stability (75.3% coverage) and host environmental growth temperatures (78.1% coverage). StableProt is freely accessible as an interactive web server at https://stableprot.dixitlab.org/.

papers.title: Three-dimensional mapping of human lung fibrosis identifies spatial coupling between tissue microarchitecture and maladaptive repair states
papers.abstract: Human lung fibrosis progressively destroys three-dimensional tissue architecture, yet how the structural microenvironment shapes cellular states remains unclear. Integrating 3D X-ray histology with spatial omics, we generate a volumetric multimodal atlas of human lung fibrosis that enables direct interrogation of relationships between tissue microarchitecture and spatial molecular programmes. We identify collapse of the alveolar-capillary unit - the coupled loss of alveolar type 1 epithelial cells, capillary endothelial cells, and basement membrane integrity - as a structural transition associated with early fibrogenesis. Surrounding transitional zones exhibit aberrant epithelial differentiation and proteolytic matrix remodelling, with epithelium shifting toward bronchiolised, airway-like states. Stromal activation converges on spatially restricted fibrogenic cores, sites of maximal collagen maturation and matrix stabilisation that function as signalling hubs within surrounding perifocal and vascular microenvironments. Molecular signatures of atlas-defined tissue states were associated with lung function and mortality across independent patient cohorts. Together, these data support a model in which fibrosis emerges as a spatial tissue-state process, with alveolar-capillary collapse redirecting repair towards mechanically stabilised niches that reinforce pathological remodelling.

papers.title: Citrobacter rodentium infection disrupts colonic mucus barrier function via ablation of intercrypt goblet cells
papers.abstract: The colonic mucus barrier, composed of distinct layers maintained by specialized goblet cell (GC) subtypes, forms the first line of defense against enteric pathogens. However, the individual contributions of inner (IML) and fecal (FML) mucus layers to barrier integrity, and how these layers and the GC responses are dynamically modulated during infection remain incompletely understood. Using Citrobacter rodentium infection in mice, we show that early colonization disrupts the inner mucus layer, increases mucus penetrability and drives alterations in faecal mucus layer thickness. Spatial imaging revealed progressive crypt infiltration and concurrent accumulation of pathogen clusters within the FML. Transcriptomic and functional analyses identified Spdef-dependent intercrypt goblet cells (icGCs) as essential for sustaining IML integrity and limiting epithelial access. Spdef-deficient mice exhibited delayed clearance and enhanced crypt invasion, highlighting the protective role of icGCs. Infection selectively depleted icGCs, collapsing the intercrypt mucus and creating permissive niches for colonization. Mechanistically, C. rodentium leveraged its type III secretion system, specifically the EspF effector to reprogram GC transcriptional responses, inducing metabolic stress and promoting apoptotic signatures in GCs specifically. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized virulence strategy in which EspF-driven GC remodeling compromises intercrypt mucus defenses, potentially facilitating pathogen persistence and transmission.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structures of an Acinetobacter baumannii podovirus reveal a canonical capsid maturation
papers.abstract: Phages that hunting multidrug resistant bacteria represent a promising approach in precision medicine nowadays, including these infecting Acinetobacter baumannii. To data, a large number of A. baumannii phages has been isolated, however, complete structural information remains not adequately released. Previously, we reported a podovirus, AbP20, that infects A. baumannii with potent efficacy in mouse model. In the present work, we further report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of AbP20 and its procapsid. The near-atomic resolution reveals that AbP20 is composed of five distinct structural subunits, i.e., capsid, portal, nozzle, fiber, and adaptor. We then characterized the assembly mechanisms of molecular interactions within capsid and portal-tail complex. By co-expressing the scaffold protein and the capsid protein of AbP20, we constructed the self-assembled DNA-free procapsid of AbP20. A near-atomic resolution reconstruction reveals it a double-layered concentric spherical architecture with a nearly 1:1 ratio of these two proteins. Comparison between the mature and apo-form of the capsid of AbP20 uncovers a canonical model of conformational switch from procapsid to capsid. Altogether, the present work reports the first whole atom structure of a podovirus infecting A. baumannii, providing a reference for structure-based phage engineering and editing.

papers.title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease
papers.abstract: Background Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. Methods We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity. Results A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099. The mitigation of degenerative neuropathology was linked to targeted inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2 and complemented by reduced levels of gliosis in astrocytes and microglia in the SN. Single-microglia segmentation analysis suggested URMC-099 treatment preserved dynamic effector state switching in microglia to enhance autophagic flux to reduce the overall burden of pathologic aSyn. Transcriptomic analysis of a complementary in vitro microglia model corroborated the retention of a homeostatic-like effector state with URMC-099 treatment that was unique to MLK3/LRRK2 dual inhibition. Conclusions Unilateral injection of low dose AAV-haSyn successfully resulted in a lateralized model of early, progressive PD. Dual inhibition of aberrant MLK3 and LRRK2 activity with once-daily i.p. URMC-099 therapy significantly mitigated the development of PD pathology and progression in an early manifest phenotype. Our results present a potential mechanism of therapeutic action dependent on the dual inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2. This presents a novel therapeutic modality that may be beneficial to a broad population of etiologic PD patients.

papers.title: Identification and characterization of new P. aeruginosa phages using a surface receptor platform
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages are of increasing interest for their potential use as alternatives to antibiotics for treating drug-resistant infections. Phage steering, specifically receptor-based steering, involves use of phages that bias the development of resistance in bacteria towards phenotypes such as reduced fitness. Phage therapy typically involves administering cocktails of phages with different targets to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging. To ensure effective steering and cocktail design, there is a need to identify the receptors used by phages of interest, and to isolate phages that use diverse receptors. Here we describe a SURFAce Receptor (SURFAR) platform consisting of a set of defined Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains and mutants for rapid characterization of phage receptors. This platform can also be used to enrich for and isolate diverse phages from environmental samples, yielding novel phage genomes from wastewater. Using the SURFAR platform, two new phages were isolated and characterized: Dalewood, which targets both flagella and the conserved LPS outer core, and Bowman, a biofilm targeting phage capable of supressing growth of a subset of carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates. This tool helps to standardize the laborious but important task of phage receptor characterization, with the goal of expanding the known repertoire of P. aeruginosa phage receptors and phages.

papers.title: Frequency-Dependent Structural Responses of Amyloid-β Fibrils to Terahertz Pulses: A Nonequilibrium Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: The abnormal aggregation of amyloid proteins into fibrils is closely associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, highlighting the importance of developing effective strategies to modulate fibril structural stability. Here, we employed nonequilibrium molecular dynamics(NEMD) simulations to examine the effects of intense terahertz-to-mid-infrared pulses on three amyloid fibrils (2LMP, 2MXU, and 5OQV), focusing on the combined effects of pulse frequency and electric-field strength. Frequency scans from 0.5 to 60 THz in 0.5 THz steps revealed frequency-dependent losses of {beta}-sheet content, with several common response patterns in these fibrils. Comparisons at 2, 23, 33, and 50 THz showed that pulse-induced changes in secondary structure differed from those in high-temperature controls. Hydrogen-bond analysis showed that total hydrogen-bond counts could partially recover even as interchain hydrogen bonds continued to decrease, with distinct responses among representative chain pairs. We therefore propose a two-threshold electric-field framework for fibril disruption: Eth1 describes the onset of structural perturbation, whereas Eth2 indicates persistent structural loss after the pulse. This framework offers a testable approach for characterizing amyloid structural responses to external fields, although the underlying energy-coupling mechanisms, quantitative thresholds, and long-term recovery require further validation. These findings may provide a theoretical basis for exploring external-field-based strategies to modulate protein aggregation.

papers.title: Shikonin alleviates bone cancer pain through suppression of spinal IGF2-associated p38 MAPK signaling
papers.abstract: Background Bone cancer pain (BCP) is a debilitating complication of advanced cancer that substantially impairs physical function and emotional wellbeing. Current pharmacological treatments often provide incomplete analgesia and may be limited by adverse effects. Shikonin, a bioactive naphthoquinone derived from Lithospermum erythrorhizon, exhibits analgesic and anti inflammatory activities, but its effects and underlying mechanisms in BCP remain unclear. Methods A rat model of BCP was established by intratibial inoculation of luciferase labeled MADB106 cells. The analgesic and behavioral effects of intrathecal Shikonin were evaluated using mechanical and thermal nociceptive assays, CatWalk gait analysis, the open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), light/dark box (LDB) test, and rotarod testing. Bioluminescence imaging and hematoxylin eosin staining were used to characterize tumor development and bone pathology. Spinal dorsal horn transcriptomic sequencing was performed to identify candidate molecular pathways. Western blotting, quantitative PCR, and ELISA were used to examine IGF2 associated p38 MAPK signaling and proinflammatory cytokines. The functional involvement of IGF2 and p38 associated signaling was further evaluated using intrathecal IGF2 siRNA and the p38 inhibitor Adezmapimod (SB203580). Results Intrathecal Shikonin produced dose and time dependent antinociceptive effects in BCP rats, with an estimated ED50 of 29.80 g/kg, and did not produce an apparent impairment of rotarod performance. Shikonin also improved gait abnormalities and pain related anxiety like behaviors. Transcriptomic analysis identified Igf2 as a candidate gene responsive to Shikonin treatment, and spinal IGF2 and p38 phosphorylation were increased during BCP development. Shikonin significantly reduced IGF2 expression and p38 phosphorylation in the spinal dorsal horn, accompanied by decreased IL 6, IL 1{beta};, and TNF ; expression in spinal tissue. IGF2 knockdown reproduced the analgesic and behavioral effects of Shikonin and reduced p38 phosphorylation, whereas p38 inhibition reproduced key behavioral effects without a marked change in IGF2 expression. Combined treatment with Shikonin and either IGF2 knockdown or p38 inhibition produced no significant additional behavioral benefit. Conclusion Intrathecal Shikonin alleviates nociceptive hypersensitivity, functional impairment, and pain related anxiety like behaviors in rats with MADB106 induced BCP. The phenocopying and non additive effects of IGF2 knockdown and p38 inhibition support the involvement of an IGF2 associated p38 MAPK signaling axis in the analgesic actions of Shikonin.

papers.title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
papers.abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.

papers.title: Magnetic organelle gene clusters enable bacterial growth and ATP homeostasis under oxidizing conditions
papers.abstract: Biological organisms can produce magnetic nanoparticles made of magnetite to detect the Earth's magnetic field for orientation. The evolutionary mechanisms that led to the acquisition of this capacity remain unknown. The most ancient organisms known to perform magnetic orientation are magnetotactic bacteria. Under tight genetic control, they produce chains of magnetite nanoparticles in dedicated organelles to allow efficient navigation in aquatic environments containing molecular oxygen. Yet, these bacteria have been proposed to emerge before molecular oxygen became abundant on Earth, at a time when this navigation system could not have served its current function. Here, we show that gene clusters responsible of magnetite formation and organization enable resistance against hydrogen peroxide, a toxic oxygen-derived compound that was produced during the early stages of Earth's oxygenation when iron oxidation consumed molecular oxygen. Characterization of the nanoparticle's oxidation state supported the involvement of magnetite in resistance to hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress. These findings are compatible with an early emergence of magnetotactic bacteria, before natural waters became oxygenated. We propose a conceptual framework to explain the origin of magnetic orientation in bacteria, and offer tools to identify the initiation of Earth's oxygenation in a time-resolved manner.

papers.title: Identification of Kinome Biomarkers and Therapeutic Rescue in cGMP-Linked Retinal Degeneration
papers.abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations, such as Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) and Leber's congenital amaurosis (LCA), are major causes of progressive and irreversible vision loss. The large number of genes associated with these disorders makes their clinical and molecular characterization difficult, while systemic biomarkers for disease progression or treatment response remain limited. These challenges were addressed by targeting cGMP-associated mechanisms shared by RP and LCA and integrating systemic biomarker profiling with retinal outcomes. Kinase activity analysis (kinome analysis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells distinguished healthy and diseased states and captured therapy-associated signatures in rd10 mice treated with LP-CN03, a liposomal formulation of the cGMP analog CN03. This first systemic analysis in a therapeutically responsive animal model highlights kinome analysis as a potential translational readout. Given shared cGMP signaling in RP and AIPL1-associated LCA, LP-CN03's therapeutic potential was further evaluated in a new CRISPR-Cas9-generated Aipl1-/- mouse model. Treatment with LP-CN03 preserved retinal structure and function, as shown by electroretinography, longitudinal optical coherence tomography, fundus imaging, optomotor testing, and photoreceptor-specific gene expression. Together, these findings provide independent in vivo evidence for the neuroprotective effect of LP-CN03 in both cGMP-related RP and LCA, also highlighting the translational value of kinome profiling.

papers.title: Feasible closed-loop stimulation for neural latent dynamics control
papers.abstract: Modern neuroscience benefits from powerful computational and experimental methods for studying neural populations, including latent dynamics models that predict behavior with few dimensions. But despite their explanatory utility, latent factors are seldom targeted explicitly with experimental perturbations, leaving causal relationships to behavior and inferred dynamical landscapes untested. A promising solution is closed-loop, multi-channel optogenetic control, which, when paired with model predictions, could steer neural trajectories in real time--a feat impossible for traditional, hand-designed stimulation. However, because closed-loop latent control has not been demonstrated in vivo, the hardware and software requirements remain unclear--particularly the necessary stimulation dimensionality and how limited resources such as implant volume and bandwidth should be allocated between stimulation and recording capabilities. Preliminary experiments would thus help guide ongoing technological development. As large-scale exploration of these design spaces in vivo is prohibitively expensive, we conducted a high-throughput simulation survey using biophysically grounded spiking neural networks. We found that low-dimensional actuation is sufficient: in the reference configuration, ~20% of the stimulation channels achieved ~85% of peak control performance, far fewer than the number of neurons. Furthermore, allocating channels roughly equally between stimulation and recording optimized behavioral control, whereas pairing many electrodes with a single light source--the prevailing practice in experimental labs--performed poorly. Even without heavily optimizing modeling or control, we obtained >60% tracking error reduction and >90% evoked behavior accuracy on average for optimal channel counts. These results held across extensive parameter variations, suggesting that closed-loop latent control is feasible with accessible channel counts and establishing design principles for future tool development and in vivo experiments.

papers.title: Epidermal Langerhans Cells Act as Neuroimmune Regulators of Pain and Itch
papers.abstract: Neuroimmune interactions in the skin coordinate immune defense and somatosensory perception, yet how immune cells shape sensory signaling remains poorly defined. Here, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), epidermal antigen-presenting cells, function as local immune-derived amplifiers of cutaneous sensory signaling. Anatomical and transcriptomic analyses reveal preferential LC association with non-peptidergic sensory neurons. LC activation increases neuronal and behavioral responses to thermal, mechanical, and pruritic stimuli without directly exciting sensory neurons, whereas LC inhibition or ablation selectively reduces pruritogen-evoked itch. We identified semaphorin 7A as a candidate LC-expressed mediator. Semaphorin 7A sensitized cultured sensory neurons to chloroquine and histamine, and neutralizing semaphorin 7A abolished the increase in chloroquine-evoked scratching produced by LC activation. Its receptor PlexinC1 was expressed by most MrgprA3 pruriceptors and blocking PlexinC1 reduced semaphorin 7A-evoked neuronal responses. Together, these findings identify epidermal LCs as local immune-derived amplifiers that regulate the responsiveness of cutaneous sensory circuits and identify semaphorin 7A as a mediator of LC-induced itch potentiation.

papers.title: The methionine cycle sustains the mesenchymal phenotype of tumor cells and drives PDA progression
papers.abstract: Mesenchymal traits are associated with poor prognosis in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDA), but direct targeting of mesenchymal tumor cells remains a challenge. Metabolic profiling of tumor cells isolated from murine PDA and liver metastases (LM) revealed that LM rely more on the methionine cycle than does primary PDA. This metabolic shift was specifically associated with increased activation of the methionine cycle in mesenchymal tumor cells compared to differentiated tumor cells. We show that the targeting of the key enzyme of the methionine cycle S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (SAHH) in mesenchymal cells lowers the levels of homocysteine (Hcy) and glutathione, resulting in reduced antioxidant capacity, deregulated intracellular calcium homeostasis, and ultimately loss of mesenchymal markers. Together, these events decrease cell proliferation and invasion, blunting the tumorigenic and metastatic potential of SAHH-deficient cells, eventually impeding tumor growth and progression of the metastatic disease. Clinically, the high expression of SAHH in patients with mesenchymal PDA is correlated with poor survival, positioning SAHH as a potential therapeutic target to impede the pro-metastatic, mesenchymal phenotype of PDA.

papers.title: Fatty Acid Synthase Binds Cellular mRNAs and its Depletion Reduces Translational Efficiency
papers.abstract: Metabolic enzymes with non-canonical RNA binding activity have drawn a growing interest, due to their implications for basic biology and disease. Here we present the first endogenous RNA interactome of fatty acid synthase (FASN), an emerging oncological and virological target. Utilizing crosslinking-based approaches, we characterize the direct RNA association of FASN in two human cell lines, identifying over 6000 binding sites across over 3500 protein-coding genes, with a striking preference for the 5' UTR. We provide a functional cross-screen on the effects of FASN depletion on cellular translation. This integration with ribosome profiling indicated a preferential reduction in the translational efficiencies of FASN-associated mRNAs - an effect shown to be dependent on binding location and site number. Associated transcripts were enriched for morphogenic and cell division-related functions, as well as palmitoylated proteins. This correlative work primes further investigation of FASN as a regulator of translation of its target mRNAs.

papers.title: Proteome-wide discovery of novel diagnostic antigens for coccidioidomycosis
papers.abstract: Coccidioidomycosis, commonly called Valley Fever (VF), caused by Coccidioides spp., is an understudied fungal disease that accounts for a substantial fraction of pneumonias in endemic areas. Diagnosis remains challenging because the mainstay of diagnosis is serology, and current assays have modest sensitivity in early infection. Discovery of new antigens could improve serologic detection early in disease. Here, we use PepSeq, a DNA-programmable serology platform, to represent the complete proteome of Coccidioides within a library of 244,000 DNA-barcoded peptides. By profiling antibody reactivity at the protein and epitope levels in VF patients, naturally infected pigtail macaques, and healthy controls, we identify numerous previously-unrecognized antigens and epitopes, including some shared between humans and macaque responses. When translated into a pooled peptide ELISA, we show that a subset of identified antigens can discriminate VF cases from controls in an independent cohort with high accuracy (AUC = 0.91). These findings establish high-dimensional peptide serology as a scalable approach for fungal antigen discovery and identify new targets for improved VF diagnosis.

papers.title: Sequential pathways preserve kinetochore integrity in meiosis
papers.abstract: Kinetochores connect chromosomes to spindle microtubules, but how their integrity is maintained as they are remodelled during meiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify three distinct pathways linking centromeric chromatin to the outer kinetochore in budding yeast, mediated by the Ctf19 complex (Ctf19cCCAN), Mif2CENP-C and binding of Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U to the Cse4CENP-A essential N-terminal domain (END). Although partially redundant during mitosis, all three connections are required during meiosis, with distinct temporal requirements. The assembled Ctf19cCCAN and Mif2CENP-C-dependent pathways maintain kinetochore integrity from meiotic entry, while Cse4CENP-A-Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U binding becomes critical during prophase and the meiotic divisions. We further show that Ipl1Aurora B maintains kinetochore integrity independently of Ctf19cCCAN and provide evidence for an outer kinetochore-associated Ipl1Aurora B pool. Strikingly, Cse4CENP-A phosphomimetic mutations that restore kinetochore integrity upon Ipl1Aurora B depletion instead exacerbate defects in cells lacking Ctf19cCCAN. Our findings suggest that phosphorylation of the Cse4CENP-A N-terminal domain (NTD) by Ipl1Aurora B may regulate the use of alternative centromere-kinetochore connections to adapt to the changing requirements of meiosis.
