papers.title: A subtype-specific gene regulatory program controls differential circuit integration of deep CA3 pyramidal neurons
papers.abstract: How closely related neuronal subtypes integrate into different circuits remains poorly understood. Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

papers.title: LplA-mediated rescue of lethal myopathy and cardiomyopathy in mitochondrial lipoylation-deficient mammalian caused by Lipt1
papers.abstract: Inherited mitochondrial metabolic disorders impair cellular energy generation and often lead to fatal metabolic crises. Mitochondrial lipoylation defects represent a severe case of such disorders that can lead to lethality but lacks effective treatment so far. In this study, we generated a viable mouse model with muscle-specific deficiency of the lipoyltransferase coded by Lipt1 to provide an in vivo preclinical model that overcomes embryonic lethality. Using this model, we examined a bacterial lipoate protein ligase A (LplA)-mediated gene therapy via adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery. By introducing LplA alongside lipoic acid supplementation, we reconstituted a salvage pathway that bypasses the mammalian endogenous lipoylation pathway. The intervention rescued premature lethality, recovered motor function and reversed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the Lipt1-deficient mouse model. Mechanistically, AAV-LplA reconstitutes mitochondrial protein lipoylation and oxidative phosphorylation in situ. This energetic rescue suppresses phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt hyperactivation, thereby restoring autophagic clearance and subsequently contributing to the recovery of the pathological phenotype. This study established AAV-LplA as a promising gene-delivery strategy for rescuing lethal mitochondrial lipoylation disorders.

papers.title: SF3b inhibitors suppress proliferation of nonsmall cell lung cancer cells irrespective of EGFR mutation status
papers.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are standard care for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but acquired resistance limits their durability, and alternatives that do not depend on EGFR kinase activity are needed. We asked whether inhibitors of SF3b, a core component of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle, act on NSCLC cells regardless of EGFR genotype. Three lung adenocarcinoma lines were treated with pladienolide B or herboxidiene at 0.01, 0.1 and 1 uM: PC9 and HCC827, both carrying an EGFR exon 19 deletion and both inhibited by gefitinib at nanomolar concentrations, and A549, which is EGFR wild type and gefitinibin sensitive. Proliferation was followed for three days by crystal violet staining, EGFR intron 2 retention was assayed by RTPCR, and EGFR protein was measured by western blotting. Both compounds produced a concentration-dependent increase in the intron 2 retained product in all three lines, and both held proliferation at or near the day 0 cell number in all three, at concentrations down to 0.01 uM. EGFR protein was lost in PC9, reduced in A549, and only partly reduced in HCC827, where a residual band persisted in lanes whose growth was fully suppressed. Since A549 is EGFR wild-type, and published knockdown data show that removing EGFR does not suppress proliferation of wild-type lines, the growth inhibition cannot be attributed to loss of EGFR alone. We read EGFR intron 2 retention as a marker of target engagement rather than as the mechanism of the growth effect. These are the results of single experiments without replicates or statistical testing and should be read as preliminary.

papers.title: Global failure to track international biodiversity targets on islands
papers.abstract: Islands harbour exceptional biodiversity but face severe threats, making their conservation crucial to achieving the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. To evaluate progress toward its 23 targets across islands worldwide, we screened 504 biodiversity and socioeconomic indicators, and retained 47. We modelled historical time series from 1950, then projected to 2030. Progress was uneven: nine targets improved across all available indicators, while nine displayed conflicting trends. Critically, 15 of 23 targets (65%) lacked a suitable headline indicator, and five had none. Furthermore, 29 of 47 indicators (62%) were reported nationally, potentially obscuring island conditions. Most targets also lacked quantitative objectives, limiting evaluation of whether change rates suffice for 2030. Overall, progress toward halting island biodiversity loss remains insufficient and unlikely to meet the Framework targets.

papers.title: High-throughput identification of chromatin-opening transcription factors
papers.abstract: Cell fate transitions involve major changes to the chromatin landscape, some of which are thought to deepen the basin around a newly adopted cell state, stabilizing gene expression programs that might otherwise be transient. Transcription factors (TFs) are central to this process, binding only a subset of the genome-wide occurrences of their cognate motifs to create accessible regions that can act as cell type-specific enhancers. However, apart from a few well-studied cases, it is not clear which of the ~1,600 mammalian TFs can directly or indirectly initiate newly accessible sites, nor why only some motif occurrences gain accessibility. Here, we performed pooled CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) screens to upregulate endogenous developmental TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and assess their impact on the chromatin landscape. Following a pre-screen of 240 developmental TFs for their capacity to elicit strong changes to the transcriptome, we prioritized 60 TFs for a well-powered CRISPRa multiome screen in which we jointly profiled gene expression and chromatin accessibility across ~140,000 single cells. We identify TFs that appear to initiate new chromatin accessibility on their own ("autonomous"), others whose chromatin-opening activity appears dependent on coincident binding of co-TFs heterogeneously expressed across mESCs ("opportunistic"), and yet others which appear to induce a co-TF and then act alongside it ("hierarchical"). Taken together, our findings suggest that the ability of a TF to "pioneer" chromatin opening, when it is newly expressed at physiological levels, strongly depends on the cell state and gene regulatory network it lands in. Looking forward, a comprehensive charting of such dependencies will inform how cell fate transitions are initiated in development, homeostasis and disease, and how to engineer them in silico, in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: CryoSHIELDs: tunable amphipathic peptide additives for cryo-EM
papers.abstract: While cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has transformed structural biology, sample preparation remains a major determinant of success. Specifically, the air-water interface (AWI) can damage complexes, impose preferred orientation, and reduce particle density. Here, we introduce cryoSHIELDs, a library of peptide additives designed to modulate the AWI and improve cryo-EM grid preparation. Across 24 diverse protein systems, cryoSHIELDs improved particle distribution, angular sampling, complex integrity, and, in selected cases, map quality and resolution. CryoSHIELDs enabled structure determination of the OSMR{beta}-Vixarelimab complex, the multi-subunit CCAN kinetochore complex without chemical cross-linking, and membrane proteins including ABCC6 and the -opioid receptor-Gi complex, the latter resolved at 2.3 A using tenfold lower protein concentration without compromising map quality. CryoSHIELDs provide a simple, tunable, and broadly applicable platform for more reliable cryo-EM in discovery biology and structure-based drug development.

papers.title: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus in summer of 2026 shows antigenic advance of H3N2 subclade K region D mutants and H1N1 D.3.1.1 Sa mutants
papers.abstract: Human seasonal influenza evolves rapidly, necessitating twice yearly decisions about whether to update the strains in the vaccine. To help inform this decision, we have been using high-throughput sequencing-based neutralization assays to make twice yearly measurements of how recent human sera neutralize current human H3N2 and H1N1 strains. Here we provide the third installment in this series of measurements by reporting 52,268 titers representing neutralization of 148 viral strains by 355 human sera collected between April and August of 2026. Our measurements show that new H3N2 subclade K strains with mutations in antigenic region D and new H1N1 subclade D.3.1.1 strains with mutations in antigenic region Sa (such as G155E) have reduced neutralization by human sera, with notable heterogeneity in the impact of some of these mutations across sera from different individuals. This paper is accompanied by an interactive summary (https://jbloomlab.github.io/flu-seqneut-2026/summary.html) that enables detailed exploration of the results, and all titer data are publicly available for further analysis to aid vaccine antigen selection and studies of viral evolution.

papers.title: Learning to play with spikes: characterizing, predicting, and engineering unsupervised plasticity rules for spiking reservoir computing
papers.abstract: Spiking reservoir computing, and reservoir computing more generally, is a powerful and efficient framework for neuromorphic and biological applications, in which a fixed random reservoir drives a trained readout. Its performance depends critically on the reservoir initialization, so that enriching the reservoir with adaptive, unsupervised plasticity rules offers a natural solution to this limitation. However, it is unclear which rules work, or why, and how to find the best-suited rules for specific tasks without exhaustive and expensive search. Here, we learn how to play the Atari game Pong in a plastic spiking reservoir network. We systematically characterize a large family of local plasticity rules that were meta-learned in prior work. We then show that their performance is predictable and structured: high-scoring rules are characterized by strong differentiation between neurons encoding the ball trajectory and the background, with stable weight dynamics, and consistent readout alignment across time. These mechanistic signatures are not task-specific and transfer to a delayed-match recognition task. Rule performance can be estimated from rule parameters alone. Finally, conditioning simulation-based inference (SBI) on high scores allows us to sample directly from promising regions of the rule space, to discover rules that exceed the performance of those found in the prior distribution and reveal stable, high-performing configurations. Together, these results offer competitive performance against classical reservoir computing while providing a transparent, interpretable account of what makes a plasticity rule useful for neuromorphic hardware and biological computing.

papers.title: Open-source benchmarking of dairy and dairy-free products
papers.abstract: Dairy-free products offer opportunities to reduce the environmental impact of food. However, they must reproduce the diverse sensory and functional properties of conventional dairy, from foam stabilization in a latte to acid-gel structure in yogurt and melt--stretch behavior in mozzarella. Yet, large-scale, open-source sensory benchmarks across dairy product categories remain scarce. Here we show that the sensory gap between dairy and dairy-free products varies substantially across ten categories: barista milk, butter, cheddar, cream cheese, creamer, ice cream, fluid milk, mozzarella, sour cream, and Greek-style yogurt. We analyze the NECTAR Taste of the Industry 2026 dataset, which includes 1,437 respondents, 3,220 overall-liking ratings, and 79,027 recorded survey responses, including 35,762 product-linked responses. Leading dairy-free beverages, barista milk ($+0.17$), fluid milk ($+0.02$), and creamer ($-0.06$), closely approach their dairy benchmarks in overall liking on a seven-point scale. In contrast, mozzarella shows the largest deficit ($-1.46$), followed by Greek-style yogurt ($-0.68$) and butter ($-0.54$). All three deficits remain statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Across categories, descriptive penalty analysis identifies off-flavor (1.85 points), stale or cardboard notes (1.81 points), and artificial or chemical notes (1.80 points) as the sensory attributes associated with the largest reductions in overall liking. Together, these results establish the first open sensory benchmark for dairy and dairy-free products, identify beverage categories that approach conventional dairy in overall liking, and reveal the sensory attributes and product categories with the greatest opportunities for future innovation.

papers.title: R-pyocin-mediated selection restores aminoglycoside sensitivity in a pan-drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
papers.abstract: The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged not as conventional biocides but as precise selective forces to drive an evolutionary trap. We subjected the laboratory strains PAO1 and PAK and the clinical pan-drug-resistant (PDR) wound isolate MRSN 6220 to R-pyocin selective pressure. Under sustained R-pyocin pressure, every pyomelanogenic variant we recovered evaded R-pyocin killing through large-scale chromosomal deletions spanning 250-388 kbp. These deletions encompass a conserved region harboring the galU gene (essential for LPS synthesis), the hmgA gene (yielding a pyomelanogenic brown phenotype), and the mexXYZ multidrug efflux operon. While the loss of galU confers broad cross-resistance to R-pyocins by likely truncating the LPS receptor, the concurrent excision of mexXY induces profound collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides. These deletions also eliminate critical virulence factors and biofilm clusters, including the hcnABC, exoY, phzABCDEFG, and cup operons. In a Galleria mellonella model, the resulting brown mutants were non-lethal, and in infected murine wound tissue treated ex vivo with gentamicin they exhibited a significant 3-log reduction in bacterial load, whereas the pan-drug-resistant ancestor did not. This work establishes a framework for utilizing R-pyocins as evolutionary steering agents that couple the acquisition of R-pyocin resistance to the reversion of multidrug resistance into an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state.

papers.title: Integrated genomics and transcriptomics reveal molecular insights into extreme dietary adaptation in vampire bats
papers.abstract: Vampire bats are the only tetrapods that feed exclusively on blood. To uncover the molecular changes associated with this extreme dietary specialization, we generated six new reference genomes, including genomes of all three vampire bat species, and integrated comparative analyses of gene sequence evolution (selection signatures, duplications, and losses) with transcriptomic data from six major organs to identify shifts in gene expression. Our integrative analyses reveal sequence or expression changes in 150 genes that provide insights into the molecular biology of sanguivory. Through comparative analyses and experiments, we show that the enlarged vampire bat stomach has increased connective tissue content, likely facilitating extreme expansion, is pH-neutral, and exhibits reduced mucus production, together providing molecular insights into its shift from a digestive to an absorptive organ for water, electrolytes, and vitamins. We further uncover pathway-level molecular changes associated with altered gastrointestinal motility; trypsin-dependent protein digestion; upregulated amino acid catabolism with key aspects diverging from other mammals; impaired dietary fat digestion counterbalanced by increased fatty acid synthesis; defective sugar metabolism and natural insulin deficiency; enhanced heme iron absorption; and adult splenic erythropoiesis. Together, these findings provide an integrated view of molecular changes associated with one of the most extreme dietary transitions among vertebrates.

papers.title: FMRP safeguards long mRNA expression by opposing repressive RNP states
papers.abstract: Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) is widely viewed as a translational repressor, yet its loss paradoxically compromises expression of exceptionally long, dosage-sensitive neurodevelopmental mRNAs. First shown in Drosophila oocytes, this selective loss extends to mouse cortex and hippocampus, but its mechanism remains unknown. Here, we uncover a protective function for FMRP: shielding long mRNAs from repression by Me31B/DDX6, a conserved RNA helicase that organizes repressive RNP complexes. In Drosophila oocytes, FMRP loss redirects target mRNAs into Me31B-marked P-bodies. Transcriptome-wide binding maps reveal extensive FMRP-Me31B co-occupancy, preferentially concentrated on long coding sequences whose translation depends on FMRP. Strikingly, disrupting Me31B-dependent repression preferentially enhances translation of FMRP targets in FMRP-deficient oocytes. We identify Rin/G3BP, Caprin, and Lig/UBAP2L as FMRP-associated cofactors supporting expression of distinct targets. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing view of FMRP as a translational repressor, revealing instead a mechanism that safeguards vulnerable neurodevelopmental mRNAs from inappropriate cytoplasmic silencing.

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
papers.abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children's Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

papers.title: Uncovering the latent structure of interwoven population and temporal codes
papers.abstract: Population analysis methods have become standard for navigating the complexity of neural data. However, these methods often assume a rate code, neglecting information encoded in the precise timing of spikes. Critically, additional information encoded in bursts of action potentials may be missed. Here, we develop a probabilistic latent-variable framework that disentangles the factors associated with bursts and individual spikes. This enables burst codes to be investigated directly from the structure of the data, without requiring external covariates. We demonstrate that analyzing firing rates alone obscures the latent structure and factors underlying bursts. Applying our method to simulated and experimental data, we show that it can infer the correct latent structure and be used to test for the presence of burst coding. By merging the population and burst coding perspectives, we provide a framework for linking changes in bursting to internal variables involved in attention, perception, and learning.

papers.title: Integrated omics analysis reveals reorganization of nitrogen and lipid metabolism in a toluene-degrading bacterium in the gas phase
papers.abstract: Gas-phase bioprocesses, in which microbial cells are immobilized on solid carriers exposed to the gas phase, enable efficient conversion of poorly water-soluble compounds for biodegradation and bioproduction. However, operation without a surrounding bulk aqueous medium can constrain the replenishment of water and nonvolatile nutrients. The metabolic mechanisms that sustain cellular activity in these low-water environments remain largely unknown. Here, we elucidated the metabolic alterations in the highly adhesive bacterium Acinetobacter sp. Tol 5 degrading toluene in the gas and aqueous phases. Polyurethane carriers bearing cells from independent cultures were assigned to the gas phase or to two aqueous media, nitrogen-depleted basal salt medium and phosphate-buffered saline, so that the conditions differed only in phase and nutrient availability. In cells actively degrading toluene, integrated metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics (97 metabolites, 108 lipids, and 3,899 genes) revealed a metabolic state specific to the gas phase. Under gas-phase conditions, amino acid and nucleotide degradation was enhanced while the intracellular glutamate pool was maintained at a high level, and citrulline specifically accumulated. Membrane lipids were remodeled, and the storage lipid triacylglycerol was consumed, suggesting that it serves as an endogenous carbon and energy source and may also contribute to metabolic water production under nutrient- and water-limited gas-phase conditions. These findings highlight nitrogen metabolism and lipid mobilization as features of gas-phase adaptation, providing a rational basis for designing robust gas-phase bioprocesses and selecting suitable microbial chassis.

papers.title: Body size and fruit handling ability explain frugivory patterns among Asian mammals
papers.abstract: Aim Frugivore traits influence the diversity of fruits that frugivores consume. While well studied in birds, trait-based drivers of frugivory remain less understood in mammals despite their considerable morphological, physiological, and ecological diversity. We compiled a comprehensive dataset of mammalian frugivory across Asia, and compared the species diversity and morphological traits of fruits consumed across major mammal guilds. We examine the importance of traits such as body size and fruit handling ability in explaining observed frugivory patterns among Asian mammals. Location Asia. Time period 1964 to 2023. Major taxa studied Herbivores (Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Proboscidea), Primates, Carnivora Methods We compiled frugivory data for three major non-volant, terrestrial Asian mammals from 518 sources, comprising 5276 unique plant mammal interactions between 142 mammal species and 2,234 plant species. We compared fruit taxonomic composition, diversity and morphological traits (fruit size, colour, type, growth habit, seed number) among three mammal groups. Using Phylogenetic Generalized Least Squares (PGLS) and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, we tested relationships between mammal body size, fruit handling behaviour and the mean and maximum fruit size consumed by different mammal groups. Results Focal mammal groups differed in taxonomic diversity of fruits consumed. They also differ in fruit colour, fruit type and the growth habit of fruits consumed. Mammal body size was generally associated with the mean and maximum size of consumed fruits. Fruit handling ability was an important factor for the maximum size of non-fig fruits consumed but not for figs, potentially because figs may be consumed piecemeal. Main conclusions Our findings highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of mammalian frugivory patterns due to differences among mammal groups in fruit consumption patterns, range of body sizes and fruit handling abilities. In the context of frugivory interactions, mammals are better considered as different functional groups rather than a single entity.

papers.title: Hierarchical organization in sparse gene regulatory networks shapes structural coherence and emergent regulatory coordination
papers.abstract: A fundamental challenge in systems biology is understanding how regulatory coordination is maintained within extremely sparse gene regulatory networks (GRNs). While traditional unsigned network metrics can quantify the overall magnitude of influence a specific node or edge exerts over the network, they cannot predict the functional direction and consistency of these regulatory changes. To address this gap, we introduce the coherence matrix. This topology-based framework for signed, directed GRNs computes a strictly bounded, interpretable measure of directional regulatory coordination between gene pairs. Using synthetic network ensembles, we demonstrate that architectures with low intrinsic structural coherence suffer severe density-driven scaling penalties. Such structures cannot scale without requiring biologically unrealistic edge densities. Applying this framework to six whole-organism GRNs reveals how biological topologies overcome these limitations. Whole-organism GRNs exhibit lower overall coherence and more fragmented structures than expected, avoiding rigid global co-regulation to maximize regulatory degrees of freedom. Furthermore, these systems resolve the scaling penalties of complex, low-coherence architectures by restricting dense regulatory crosstalk to a compact intermediate core. Modeling synthetic hierarchical networks confirms that this architecture, a compact core within a globally feed-forward scaffold, neutralizes scaling penalties by minimizing nodes requiring dense connectivity. This allows GRNs to efficiently route decisions despite extreme sparsity. Finally, validation with transcriptomic data confirms that coherence matrix accurately predicts empirical co-regulation directionality. By moving beyond unsigned connectivity, the structural coherence framework provides a quantitative tool to map how the intrinsic behavior of localized interactions scales into macroscopic, system-wide coordination.

papers.title: Global Proteomic Analysis of Colorectal Cancers Stratified by Microsatellite Instability Subtype Reveals Protein Differences
papers.abstract: Lynch syndrome, historically known as hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, is caused by germline mutations in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, MLH1, MSH2 (EPCAM), MSH6, and PMS2. While the genetic changes associated with Lynch syndrome have previously been characterized, there have not been studies of the associated proteomic alterations, in part because of the limited availability of primary samples and the absence of in vitro model systems. In this study, the first large-scale tissue proteomic assessment of Lynch syndrome samples as well as three other subtypes of colorectal cancer was completed with specimens from the Ohio Colorectal Cancer Prevention Initiative. The cohort contained three groups of microsatellite unstable (MSI-high) colorectal cancer (CRC) patients (Lynch syndrome, double somatic MMR mutation, and MLH1 hypermethylation) and a group of microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC patients. A total of 122 tumor and complimentary normal mucosa samples from 61 patients were evaluated using label-free bottom-up proteomic analysis identifying 7,352 proteins. Hierarchical clustering analysis of the global proteome showed that the MSS group was significantly different than the three MSI-high groups. Of the 1,607 proteins found to be dysregulated within CRC patients, 648 proteins were specific to Lynch syndrome and 260 proteins were dysregulated across all four subtypes studied. Further examination of dysregulated proteins in response to age of diagnosis and patient's sex assigned at birth were also evaluated. This study fills a critical gap as the first proteomic characterization of Lynch syndrome samples to date. Data are available via ProteomeXchange with identifier PXD073693.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

papers.title: Glycolytic enzymes form membrane-less condensates in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum by sensing glucose levels
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in cells can regulate essential cellular events, including metabolic processes. Glycolytic bodies (G-bodies) are biomolecular condensates formed through the LLPS of glycolytic enzymes, and they accelerate glycolysis to overcome hypoxic stress in several organisms. Although the asexual blood stage (ABS) of the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum highly depends on glycolysis for energy production, there have been no reports of the formation of such G-bodies throughout the parasite's lifecycle. Using fluorescence tagging and live imaging, we found that G-body-like condensates containing phosphofructokinase 9 (PFK9) and phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) were formed in the parasite cells after long-term culture under conditions of low glucose. These G-body-like structures appeared stable, but membrane staining and osmotic stress experiments suggested that the observed condensates were not associated with a lipid membrane. Notably, PFK9 and PGK formed spatially distinct, non-overlapping condensates, indicating that these structures were formed with different mechanism as compared to the shared, multi-enzyme G-bodies described in other organisms. Whether the condensation of these enzymes enhances or restrains glycolysis under low-glucose stress remains to be determined. These results suggest that the formation of glycolytic enzyme condensates may be an enzyme-specific cellular response that helps the parasite adapt to reductions in blood glucose levels in the host during the ABS.

papers.title: Somatic Structural Variant Discovery from Tumor Specific Strings Computed Against a Draft Composite Germline Reference
papers.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) are among the most clinically relevant genomic alterations in cancer. However, their accurate detection remains challenging due to complex genomic rearrangements, repetitive genomic regions, difficulties in distinguishing somatic variants from germline variation and sequencing artifacts, and limited sequencing support for low-frequency events. Existing mapping-based somatic SV callers are susceptible to alignment ambiguities in repetitive regions and near complex SV breakpoints, while approaches relying on comparisons of independently generated tumor and normal variant callsets may propagate errors from both callsets. Building on the concept of specific strings, previously applied to germline SV discovery, we introduce VESPA-SS, a novel approach for detecting somatic SVs from paired tumor-normal long-read whole-genome sequencing data. VESPA-SS directly extracts somatic SV signals using specific strings computed from tumor reads against a Draft Composite Germline Reference, without requiring initial read mapping or a high-quality germline assembly. These signals are subsequently clustered and refined through consensus sequence generation and alignment-based procedures to identify somatic SVs. Evaluation on real PacBio HiFi datasets demonstrates that VESPA-SS outperforms state-of-the-art somatic SV callers, achieving F1 scores exceeding 0.92 and 0.90 on the well-characterized HG008 and COLO829 cancer cell lines, respectively, compared with the highest F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.85 achieved by the evaluated methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of specific string based signal extraction for accurate somatic SV discovery and establish a new computational paradigm for identifying complex genomic alterations in cancer. VESPA-SS is freely available at https://github.com/dcmonti/VESPA.

papers.title: Massive inter-animal horizontal gene transfer contributes to stress tolerance in the fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila
papers.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in animals is thought to be rare and largely restricted to transfers from non-animal sources. In contrast to this expectation, we discovered that 9.2% of the protein-coding genes in the genome of the dark-winged fungus gnat Bradysia coprophila (order: Diptera, family: Sciaridae) are of potential HGT origin. Most of these genes have phylogenetic affinity with sequences from other distantly related arthropods that inhabit a shared soil-dwelling niche with B. coprophila. We show that these findings are inconsistent with genomic contamination or widespread gene loss and instead suggest a level of inter-animal HGT that is, to our knowledge, unprecedented. Consistent with their potential functional importance, ~75% of putative B. coprophila horizontally transferred genes (HTGs) are transcribed, and nearly all are shared across multiple sciarid fungus gnat species that diverged tens of millions of years ago. Further, domain annotations suggest that HTGs participate in diverse processes potentially important to B. coprophila ecology. We tested the functions of eight putative B. coprophila HTGs through transgenic expression in the fly Drosophila melanogaster and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and found evidence that HGT has likely endowed B. coprophila with the novel capability to biosynthesize NAD+, as well as enhanced capacity to withstand stressors imposed by arsenic, cyanide, alkylating agents, and reactive oxygen species. Our findings reveal a previously underappreciated contribution of inter-animal genetic exchange to the evolution of genomic, physiological, and ecological novelty.

papers.title: CauloBrowser 2.0: an AI powered update
papers.abstract: CauloBrowser is a systems-biology database for Caulobacter crescentus that organizes the largest repository of experimental data for this model bacterium. The original CauloBrowser provided a web interface for accessing these data, but the growing number of experimental datasets and advances in AI chatbots motivated an updated resource. We developed CauloBrowser 2.0 (CauloBrowser.org) as an open-source application that broadens access to RNA-seq, microarray, ribosome profiling, Tn-seq, ChIP-seq, and genome annotation data. The CauloChat AI interface allows users to query these datasets in natural language, generate visualizations, and achieve complex biological insights. While the database is hosted freely on the web, users may also download the database and run it locally, reducing dependence on the web-hosted service and allowing laboratories to use compatible unpublished datasets. Altogether, CauloBrowser 2.0 provides a significant update for exploring diverse systems biology data in C. crescentus.

papers.title: scCircaSim: A Circadian Simulator for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Motivation: Simulated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets that capture circadian dynamics while providing known ground truth remain scarce, limiting systematic evaluation of circadian analysis methods. Results: We developed scCircaSim to generate circadian single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from a single-time-point reference. The framework combines phase progression with reference-derived network propagation of anchor gene rhythms and incorporates neighborhood effects for spatial simulation. Outputs retain reference heterogeneity and provide known cell or spot phases, rhythmicity labels, and gene-level mesor, amplitude, and phase values. Validation showed retention of reference structure and recovery of specified temporal patterns. Benchmarks of four cell phase inference methods and three rhythmic gene analysis methods revealed differences in phase accuracy, rhythmicity detection, and parameter recovery. scCircaSim supports reproducible method evaluation and preliminary experimental planning. Availability and Implementation: scCircaSim is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/Liwei-DynamicsLab/scCircaSim.

papers.title: Analysis of reproductive traits associated with lipoprotein(a) deficiency in participants from the Pakistan Genome Resource
papers.abstract: Aims. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, driving development of LPA-targeting therapies that markedly lower circulating Lp(a). Because LPA?the gene encoding apolipoprotein(a)?is absent in most model organisms, preclinical studies have limited value for assessing effects such as reproductive safety. Therefore, naturally occurring human LPA ?knockouts? were analyzed to evaluate reproductive outcomes of on-target Lp(a) lowering. Methods and Results. Individuals carrying high-confidence LPA loss-of-function (LoF) variants which reduce Lp(a) in a gene-dosage?dependent manner within the Pakistan Genome Resource were identified. LoF variants showed no depletion of homozygotes relative to Hardy?Weinberg expectations. LPA LoF associations with fertility-related traits (ever having a child and number of children) under additive and recessive models were assessed using regenie-based burden testing, including sex-stratified analyses, and no significant associations were observed. A recall-by-genotype study of female LoF homozygotes alongside heterozygous and non-carrier family member controls was performed, surveying reproductive histories and offspring outcomes. Across 107 pregnancies and 87 children in 19 homozygous LoF women, rates of miscarriage, maternal complications (including preeclampsia, hypertension, and gestational diabetes), delivery complications, neonatal intensive care admission, birth defects, and child health problems were comparable across genotypes with no statistically significant genotype?outcome associations. Conclusions. These genetic and by-genotype analyses indicate that complete lifelong LPA deficiency due to high-confidence LPA loss-of-function variants is not associated with overt adverse maternal fertility, pregnancy or child health outcomes. These findings offer human genetic reassurance regarding reproductive and developmental safety in the context of sustained Lp(a)-lowering, with implications for long-term therapies targeting Lp(a).

papers.title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
papers.abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV-associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.

papers.title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis of the Angiogenesis-EMT Interface in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) are key hallmarks that contribute to the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but whether the two programs vary simultaneously across tumors and how much of this reflects tumor composition remain unclear. We scored predefined, non-overlapping 20-gene angiogenesis and EMT signatures with a rank-based method in 342 primary oral cavity tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-OSCC). The two programs were strongly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.809, P = 2.7 x 10^-80), and 2,396 bridge genes were associated with both programs across the transcriptome. The bridge genes were enriched in pathways associated with focal adhesion and extracellular matrix-receptor interaction. In the cellular case, fibroblast and endothelial marker scores were prominent and correlated with the program scores. The coupling was attenuated but remained positive after joint adjustment for tumor purity and stromal and immune scores (partial rho = 0.406) and with an epithelial-restricted EMT score (rho = 0.710). Further correlation was performed with a partial EMT (pEMT), which shows a significant positive correlation (rho = 0.59) and an inverse correlation with tumor purity (rho = -0.70). 146 final gene candidates were found using multi-omic evidence and candidate-level testing on the external cohort GSE30784; after adjusting for inferred cell fractions, 101 of these candidates supported the dual program. For thorough characterization, three candidates with an emphasis on OSMR, MICAL2, and LHFPL2 were chosen. Additional CPTAC data were used to confirm protein-level support, which was strongest for MICAL2. No significant connection was seen between the Interface score and overall survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.78-1.08). These results describe a coordinated angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in OSCC that is attenuated but retained after accounting for tumor composition, and nominate candidate genes for experimental study.

papers.title: Genome-wide Analysis of the VQ Gene Family and Expression Profiling in Sorghum bicolor
papers.abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts agricultural productivity, making the stress-tolerant sorghum an ideal model for studying crop adaptation. VQ motif-containing proteins are plant-specific transcriptional co-regulators vital for stress responses, yet their roles in sorghum remain underexplored. Here, we identified 35 VQ genes in sorghum, classifying them into seven subfamilies. Evolutionary analysis indicated that the family's expansion was primarily driven by segmental duplication. Notably, synteny analysis revealed a lack of collinearity between sorghum and Arabidopsis VQ genes, suggesting significant functional divergence during monocot evolution. Expression profiling showed distinct patterns among VQ members, with SbVQ34, SbVQ39 adn SbVQ40 significantly upregulated under salt stress. Furthermore, protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted SbVQ39 as a potential key regulator in sorghum salt tolerance. This study provides novel insights into sorghum's salinity tolerance mechanisms and establishes a foundation for utilizing VQ genes in breeding salt-tolerant crops.

papers.title: Lineage-specific histories rather than shared drivers shape olfactory evolution in New World monkeys
papers.abstract: Variation in primate olfactory receptor gene repertoires has been linked to shared ecological and sensory drivers, including diet, diurnality, and colour vision. Yet within anthropoids, each link rests on a single lineage, leaving unclear whether this variation reflects a shared response to these drivers or lineage-specific histories. Here, we combine genomic data from 80 New World monkey species with CT-based olfactory anatomy and ecological data to investigate the evolutionary processes underlying repertoire variation. Ecological and sensory variables explain little of this variation; even routinely trichromatic, leaf-eating howler monkeys have repertoires of unremarkable size. Instead, convergent reductions in repertoire size arose through distinct genomic routes: extensive gene inactivation in titi monkeys and large structural deletions in squirrel monkeys. Owl monkeys, the only anthropoids that reverted to nocturnality, retained rather than expanded a large ancestral repertoire shared with diurnal capuchins, and instead enlarged their olfactory bulb. Repertoire size covaries with olfactory bulb volume across the radiation, but only partially within lineages: squirrel monkeys show the converse, losing receptors without a matching bulb reduction. Thus, olfactory evolution in New World monkeys reflects historical contingency rather than a shared response, with convergent changes in repertoire size and partial decoupling of genomic and anatomical evolution.

papers.title: Confidence: Its Measurement, Relation to Behavior, and Neural Representation
papers.abstract: Confidence (certainty/uncertainty about one's own decision) has attracted considerable attention in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Yet its relation to behavior remains unclear: Some treat confidence as a cause of behavior whereas others view it as a state controlled by environmental variables. The unobservable nature of confidence makes its measurement validation and analyses difficult. To tackle these issues, we developed a novel procedure combining a decision-making task, risk choices, and a post-task open-ended questionnaire. Point-gain/loss amounts for correct/incorrect decisions varied depending on choices between high-risk/high-return and low-risk/low-return. In the questionnaire, 90% of 16 participants reported feelings interpretable as certainty/uncertainty when making those risk choices despite no instruction about confidence, whereas 8% did so when the choices led to identical outcomes/returns. This suggests confidence is a state controlled by environmental contingencies rather than a cause of behavior. We also decoded changes in the state from electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging.

papers.title: FUSION PORE CLOSURE DETERMINES SUBQUANTAL KISS-AND-RUN SEROTONIN RELEASE FROM FULLY LOADED DENSE-CORE VESICLES
papers.abstract: During kiss-and-run exocytosis, a transient fusion pore opens, releases part of the vesicular quantum, and closes without full fusion. This report investigates two questions: first, whether dense-core vesicles undergoing kiss-and-run contain the same number of molecules as those undergoing full fusion; second, whether subquantal release results from pore closure or vesicle depletion. We analyzed amperometric recordings of extrasynaptic serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in cultured leech Retzius neurons. Full-fusion events released 91,585{+/-}34,428 molecules (n=14), whereas kiss-and-run events released 58,344{+/-}20,759 molecules, 64% of the quantum. We analyzed the biexponential dynamics of the filtered amperometric current using Ohmic equations for cylindrical and toroidal pores. Hydrated flux packing (HFP) independently estimated the minimum peak pore diameter from the number of hydrated serotonin molecules crossing the pore. Kiss-and-run peak diameters were 2.1 to 3.2 nm, corresponding to the passage of 4 to 10 hydrated molecules. The vesicular serotonin content of individual kiss-and-run events was estimated by a frozen pore extrapolation (FPE), in which pores were kept at the peak HFP diameter. FPE yielded 102,650{+/-}10,989 molecules per vesicle (n=15), similar to the quantum obtained by integrating full-fusion events. Therefore, kiss-and-run subquantal release did not reflect a smaller quantum. We then compared the decay of serotonin flux with that estimated through the frozen pore at its peak diameter. In every event, the flux decayed faster, reaching half its peak in 0.59 (0.23 to 0.95) of the time taken by the frozen pore flux. We conclude that subquantal release during kiss-and-run exocytosis is governed by fusion-pore closure rather than vesicle depletion.

papers.title: Stoichiometric Encoding of Amplification Kinetics Enables High-Level Multiplexing in Single-Channel TaqMan Real-Time PCR
papers.abstract: Multiplexing in TaqMan real-time PCR (qPCR) is limited to four-six targets per reaction by fluorophore spectral overlap. Amplification curve analysis (ACA) can discriminate several targets within one fluorescence channel from amplification curves (AC) kinetic features, but has been confined mainly to digital qPCR (dqPCR) and is sensitive to domain shifts between instruments and specimen types. Here, we co-design biochemical encoding of target-specific information into ACs and their computational decoding to achieve single-channel 8-plex TaqMan qPCR on a standard thermocycler. Using asymmetric PCR, we show that forward primer, reverse primer and probe concentrations act as a programmable encoding mechanism, generating a 27-condition design space of reproducible non-canonical ACs, conserved from digital to bulk qPCR. Applying this stoichiometric encoding to an 8-plex central nervous system pathogens panel increased inter-target separability, raising the mean silhouette score from 0.329 to 0.711. To decode ACs without labelled target-domain bulk qPCR data, we pretrained a transformer encoder by self-supervised learning on more than 170,000 unlabelled dqPCR curves and aligned source and target domains using conditional domain adversarial training. On contrived clinical specimens, the framework classified a canonical 7-plex respiratory virus panel with 83.6% accuracy (versus 67.7% for a supervised baseline) and the encoded 8-plex panel with 89.8% accuracy. Furthermore, stoichiometric encoding enabled resolution of double- and triple-target co-amplification events with 98.7% accuracy in controlled dqPCR experiments. This approach expands the information capacity of existing qPCR instrumentation without new hardware, fluorophores or oligonucleotides, offering a low-cost route to syndromic molecular diagnostics.

papers.title: Sex differences in agonistic social behavior: Effects of exercise and ovariectomy
papers.abstract: Aggressive behavior encompasses a range of offensive and defensive responses that may be differentially influenced by sex, ovarian hormones, and physical activity. However, much of the existing research has focused on males and utilized paradigms designed to elicit aggression, leaving the expression and regulation of offensive and defensive behaviors during other forms of social interaction poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of sex, voluntary wheel running (VWR), and ovariectomy (OVX) on agonistic behavior during juvenile social exploration in adult Sprague-Dawley rats. Males exhibited greater offensive aggression, characterized by increased aggressive grooming and pinning, whereas females displayed more defensive kicking, darting, and avoidance. OVX selectively reduced defensive kicking without significantly affecting offensive aggression or avoidance, suggesting that distinct behavioral responses differ in their sensitivity to ovarian hormone removal. In contrast, VWR did not significantly alter any of the behaviors examined. Importantly, exploratory composite analyses revealed a significant sex difference in offensive aggression that was no longer detected when defensive behaviors were incorporated into the measure. Together, these findings demonstrate that sex differences in agonistic behavior extend beyond overall levels of aggression to distinct patterns of offensive and defensive responses. Distinguishing these behavioral categories may therefore be important for identifying how various manipulations, such as sex, ovarian hormones, and physical activity, influence agonistic behavior.

papers.title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
papers.abstract: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph's response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 m pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q < 0.05), against one gene behind the membrane, and the number of differentially expressed genes rose from 20 on day 4 to 91 and 127 on days 6 and 8. Nine regulatory programs (iModulons), mainly nitrogen and photosynthesis, responded in mixed co-culture and none behind the membrane. Reactor configuration alone changed 40 genes in axenic culture. These results suggest that co-localization, in addition to metabolite exchange, was required for the heterotrophic partner to trigger a response in the phototroph. Co-culture studies that infer interactions from shared metabolites may miss effects that depend on spatial structure. Importance Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.

papers.title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
papers.abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

papers.title: Real-time detection of N2 and N3 sleep from scalp and intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep rhythms such as slow oscillations and spindles arise predominantly during N2 and N3 sleep (N2+N3). Closed-loop stimulation targeting these rhythms is a promising strategy to enhance memory. Such stimulation requires online sleep stage classification. Conventional staging labels completed 30-s epochs using past and future data and cannot support online staging. We developed a causal tracker that, every 2 s, estimates the current stage from the preceding 10 s of scalp or intracranial EEG. We also evaluated a simulated rule that permits stimulation after three consecutive estimates indicating N2+N3 sleep. In six adults with drug-resistant epilepsy with simultaneous scalp EEG and stereo-EEG, real-time N2+N3 discrimination remained close to offline scoring of the same recordings (scalp AUC 0.953 versus 0.958). Thalamic channels alone reached AUC 0.934 and exceeded mesial temporal channels in every patient, and scalp plus thalamus performed best (0.967). The scalp tracker, retrained in 28 healthy adults, reached 0.976. When patients transitioned into N2+N3 sleep with stimulation initially disabled, the rule permitted stimulation within 5 min in 63-73% of transitions, with a median delay of 42-64 s among those detected. After leaving N2+N3, stimulation was disabled after a median of 19-22 s. The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. These findings show that both scalp and thalamic EEG can support real-time N2+N3 detection and inform when stimulation is permitted. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.

papers.title: Mutant Isocitrate Dehydrogenase 1 Alters Extracellular Vesicle Secretion and Cargo Composition in Cellular Models
papers.abstract: Somatic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) define major subtypes of adult diffuse gliomas and occur across a broad spectrum of cancers. These mutations ablate the conventional turnover of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate and confer the neomorphic production of D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D2HG), which drives epigenetic remodeling. Growing evidence suggests this neomorphic activity may also affect how tumor cells communicate; small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are elevated in gliomas, though how mutant IDH1 shapes sEV production and cargo remains poorly understood. Using glioblastoma and chondrosarcoma cell models, we show expression of mutant IDH1 correlates with a trend of increased sEV secretion, and that D2HG is packaged into sEVs that are taken up by cells. Cell-permeable D2HG treatment dose-dependently increased sEV release from IDH1 wild type cells. Untargeted proteomics showed that mutant IDH1 expression remodeled sEV cargo in a cell type-specific fashion, with mutant chondrosarcoma sEVs enriched in one-carbon metabolism enzymes, and mutant glioma sEVs in lysosomal luminal proteins and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) chaperones. Mutant IDH1 glioma cell transcriptomics suggested expanded ER folding capacity and reduced ribosomal pathways, and sEVs from these cells decreased nascent protein synthesis in IDH1 wild type recipient cells. Together, this suggests sEVs can serve as carriers of mutant IDH1 phenotypes.

papers.title: TGF-b/TIF1g signaling restrains CD8+ T cell expansion while preserving cytotoxic competence
papers.abstract: Transforming growth factor b exerts complex and often opposing effects on CD8+ T cell biology, yet the molecular mechanisms that distinguish these functions remain poorly understood. Here, we identify TIF1g (TRIM33) as a critical signal threshold regulator that couples TGF b signaling to CD8+ T cell activation and cytotoxic function. In the presence of TGF b, TIF1g deficient CD8+ T cells bypass canonical suppressive signals and acquire a transcriptional program characterized by enhanced activation and proliferation. Despite this hyperactivated state, TIF1g deficient cells fail to acquire full effector function, exhibiting markedly reduced Granzyme B and Perforin expression under TGF b signaling. We confirmed this functional uncoupling in vivo using a secondary Listeria monocytogenes challenge model, in which TIF1g deficient CD8+ T cells underwent robust expansion yet failed to efficiently control bacterial infection because of impaired cytotoxic activity. In a lymphopenic homeostatic proliferation model, TIF1g deficiency disrupted cellular quiescence, leading to excessive proliferation and spontaneous effector differentiation. Consistent with these findings, loss of TIF1g accelerated B16 melanoma growth and was associated with reduced Perforin expression in tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells. Together, these findings identify TIF1g as a key regulator of TGF b mediated CD8+ T cell responses, uncoupling activation from cytotoxic differentiation and revealing a mechanism by which TGF b independently regulates proliferative and effector programs.

papers.title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
papers.abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.

papers.title: Broad Cognitive and Motivational Enhancement through M4-Selective Muscarinic Modulation
papers.abstract: The muscarinic M4 subtype of acetylcholine receptors is part of agonist compounds considered treatment options for Schizophrenia and Alzheimers disease, but how M4-subtype selective modulation affects cognition and motivation is largely unknown due to dose-limiting side effects, a scarcity of receptor-selective compounds, and missing multi-domain assessments of cognition. Here, we surmount these constraints by utilizing a M4-selective positive allosteric modulator (PAM) to assess in nonhuman primates a broad array of endpoints spanning motivational effort control and multiple executive function domains. We found broad dose-dependent performance improvements of set shifting indexing cognitive flexibility, visual search indexing selective attention, antisaccade performance indexing inhibitory control, visuospatial maze learning, and temporal order serial object learning, while working memory span was non-systematically modulated. In addition, the M4 PAM reduced effort avoidance in an effort-based choice task documenting a pro-motivational effect. Task-composite performance scores showed pro-cognitive effects across multiple doses and an effective dose range for individual subjects in the absence of adverse dose-limiting cholinergic side effects. Together, the broad pro-cognitive and pro-motivational multi-task profile of M4 PAM modulation suggests that the M4 receptor is a master regulator of executive cognitive functioning, possibly acting on domain-general neural processes across the prefrontal-striatal circuits.

papers.title: Tools for genetic mapping and gene identification in Caenorhabditis briggsae
papers.abstract: The nematode Caenorhabditis briggsae serves as an important companion species for Caenorhabditis elegans for comparative studies. Because C. briggsae exhibits androdioecious reproduction and ease of laboratory culture similar to C. elegans, it has long been used for genetic studies in cross-species comparisons of mutant phenotypes to uncover the evolution of gene function. Here, we provide an updated toolkit for C. briggsae genetic experiments, leveraging the resource of recently improved C. briggsae genome sequence assemblies with variant mapping tools and gene identification methods. We identify and validate a set of indel variants between CGC2 (AF16) and two divergent strains, HK104 and VX34. We then use these variants to genetically map 10 previously isolated mutations and identify the impacted genes using high-throughput sequencing. We combine these new genes with others curated from the literature into an updated map with 73 genes, providing an enriched resource for C. briggsae genetic studies.

papers.title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
papers.abstract: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.

papers.title: Preferential Isoform Usage and Isoform Switching in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Patients with Distinct Autoantibody Profile
papers.abstract: RNA sequencing has advanced our understanding of molecular heterogeneity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), yet most studies have focused on differential gene expression (DGE), which overlooks transcript-level complexity. Alternative splicing and polyadenylation generate multiple isoforms from a single gene, and their dysregulation may contribute to autoimmune pathogenesis, including through the production of non-canonical isoforms with potential autoantigenic properties. To explore this underexamined dimension, we analysed differential isoform usage (DIU) and major isoform switching (MIS) across SLE subgroups stratified by autoantibody profile: anti-dsDNA+, anti-ENA+ and anti-dsDNA+ENA+. Subgroup-specific DIU and MIS events were enriched in RNA-binding and transcription-related functions. In the anti-dsDNA+ subgroup, the T-cell receptor adaptor GRAP2 showed isoform switching accompanied by expansion of a non-coding retained-intron transcript. In the anti-ENA+ subgroup, IGHM switched from the membrane-bound to the secretory form, consistent with an antibody-secreting cell signature; NACA, a reported IgE autoantigen, showed isoform switching; and BRI3, linked to TNF--induced cell death, switched toward its protein-coding transcript. In the anti-dsDNA+ENA+ subgroup, TNFAIP2, a TNF--induced gene, showed isoform redistribution with loss of a uORF-containing transcript. These findings highlight isoform regulation as a distinct, subgroup-specific and functionally relevant layer of transcriptomic dysregulation in SLE.

papers.title: Tyrosine hydroxylase deletion in Ntsr1 neurons confers resistance to diet-induced weight gain: an energy-balance analysis
papers.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD) disrupts circadian feeding rhythms and promotes diet-induced obesity (DIO), but the neural mechanisms linking diet to energy balance remain unclear. Previously, we demonstrated that dopamine production in neurotensin receptor 1 (Ntsr1)-expressing neurons was required for HFD-induced daytime overfeeding and DIO. Here, we tested whether DIO resistance in Ntsr1Cre;Thflox conditional knockout (cKO) mice was explained by altered energy expenditure. We replicated resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and assessed food intake, indirect calorimetry, activity, body temperature, fecal energy, fecal nonesterified fatty acids, and the gut microbiome. Indirect calorimetry on standard chow diet (SCD) was confounded by reduced intake and body weight loss, whereas HFD-fed cKO mice consumed food readily and resisted weight gain. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets. In the replication cohort, HFD fecal output was lower in cKO mice, whereas the independent bomb-calorimetry cohort showed no genotype difference in fecal mass; fecal energy density and nonesterified fatty acid concentration were unchanged. Preliminary analysis of the microbiome was consistent with an obesity-resistant gut profile. Together, these findings indicate that the feeding phenotype is diet- and experiment-dependent and that DIO resistance is not explained by increased energy expenditure, activity, thermogenesis, or detectable changes in fecal energy or fat content.

papers.title: Primary vitamin B12 limitation and widespread stress in Antarctic phytoplankton
papers.abstract: Iron is considered the dominant limiting or colimiting nutrient for phytoplankton growth in the Southern Ocean. However, strong competition and limited biosynthesis capabilities for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) within the microbial community creates conditions suitable for cobalamin limitation. Through a nutrient enrichment experiment in the Amundsen Sea, we show that growth in a phytoplankton community comprising diatoms and prasinophytes was limited primarily by cobalamin and secondarily by iron. Protein biomarkers across a broad area of the Southern Ocean further indicate widespread cobalamin stress within diatoms and Phaeocystis. As warming-induced melting of ice-shelves increases iron supplies in the coastal Southern Ocean, shifts from iron to cobalamin limitation favor mixotrophic flagellates with low cobalamin requirements, altering community composition and function.

papers.title: Brief visual oddball events evoke CSF flow in the spinal canal
papers.abstract: The measurement of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow with fMRI, made possible by exploiting edge artifacts of spin saturation when the bottom acquisition slice lies in a CSF reservoir, allows researchers to investigate an aspect of brain health that has been increasingly linked to cognitive aging and neurodegenerative disease via its role in glymphatic clearance. The initial demonstration of this technique used the fourth ventricle, but recent reports show it can also be done when the bottom acquisition slice lies in the spinal canal in the foramen magnum. We present a method to automatically identify the spinal canal without manual tracing, and measure CSF flow with high confidence using multi-echo acquisition to separate out BOLD-like and non-BOLD-like signal components, along with physiological regression to improve signal to noise ratio. Using these methods we found that CSF flow correlated with decreases in BOLD activity in 70 adults aged 19-76. We further found that brief, infrequent salient stimuli (visual oddballs, requiring a button press) were capable of provoking measurable CSF flow.

papers.title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
papers.abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries. GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once.
