On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.

papers.title: Network analysis of mouse brain proteomes resolves molecular and cellular endophenotypes of aging and Aβ pathology
papers.abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology exert both shared and distinct effects on the brain, yet their relative contributions to molecular alterations remain poorly defined. Here we performed tandem mass tag proteomics across the lifespan in wild-type and 5xFAD mice and integrated these data with human brain proteomic networks to resolve aging- and amyloid-beta (A{beta}-associated molecular programs. We quantified 8,535 proteins and identified 51 co-expression modules representing neuronal, mitochondrial, glial, vascular and proteostatic pathways. Aging emerged as the predominant driver of proteomic remodeling, with widespread alterations in RNA metabolism, protein translation, and neuronal pathways occurring independently of A{beta} pathology. In contrast, A{beta} selectively modified a subset of age-dependent processes, including suppression of mitochondrial ATP biosynthetic machinery and amplification of astrocytic and microglial activation states. These key aging and disease-related molecular signatures were highly conserved in human AD brain proteomes. Together, our findings establish aging as the primary determinant of brain proteome organization while revealing specific mechanisms through which A{beta} pathology reshapes age-associated biological processes. Our results also highlight molecular mechanisms of human aging and AD pathology that can be modeled in mouse models.

papers.title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
papers.abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.

papers.title: Regenerative epithelial spike cells instruct immune niche homeostasis in zebrafish fin epidermis
papers.abstract: Epithelia comprise diverse specialized epithelial cells that interact with immune cells, yet how these interactions sustain immune cell pools remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis with transgenic assays in zebrafish and discovered a previously unrecognized epithelial population marked by advillin (avil). We identified epithelial cells exhibiting unique morphology and localization, characterized by an apical spike projecting outward from the body - which we term spike cells. These cells exhibit features reminiscent of mammalian tuft cells. Notably, avil+ spike cells exhibit close spatial association with a subset of mpeg1+ immune cells. Following fin amputation, spike cells are replenished de novo from precursors and undergo dynamic changes in density, morphology, and orientation, and their regeneration depends on Alk signaling. Moreover, spike cells dynamically interact with mpeg1+ immune cells to maintain the immune cell population. Together, our findings identify a unique epithelial population in zebrafish fins and define their roles in maintaining immune cell niche dynamics.

papers.title: Hub labeling makes exact distance calculation practical for large human pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Pangenome graphs are now a standard reference representation, and tools built on them depend on fast minimum-distance queries between graph positions, for example, when clustering seed matches during read alignment. The baseline distance index, previously used by the vg toolkit, answers such queries based on a decomposition of the graph into nested subgraphs called "snarls". Within each snarl, the index uses a dense all-pairs distance matrix. Because such a matrix is quadratic in a snarl's number of children, the large, complex snarls that often occur in many pangenome graphs dominate the overall index size. This means whole-genome graphs can be impractical to index. To mitigate this, the baseline distance index does not fully index the largest snarls, and thus cannot itself answer certain queries involving them. We replace the dense matrix with a hub labeling for snarls above a size limit. Because hub labeling and associated methods are defined for directed graphs, we introduce a directed representation of a snarl's bidirected internal "net graph", whose shortest path lengths are the net graph's minimum walk lengths. Hub labels are built using pruned landmark labeling, ordered by a contraction hierarchy. On four human chromosome pangenomes, our hub-labeling-based distance index indexes every snarl in 0.9 GB to 3.0 GB at a snarl limit of 500, an estimated 28x to 119x less space than dense distance matrices would need for those snarls with more than 500 children, and supports the 3-18.6% of node-to-node queries that the previous index cannot answer by itself. On the queries both indexes can answer, query time distributions broadly overlap. We explore the snarl limit parameter space and are able to build indexes under 50 GB for four human whole-genome pangenomes in under 6 hours, where we estimate dense matrices could have required multiple terabytes.

papers.title: Human organoid screen links transient translational modulation to progenitor progression in corticogenesis
papers.abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived models are increasingly used to recapitulate aspects of human corticogenesis, including the emergence of diverse cortical cell types and their progression through developmental states. These systems offer an opportunity to dissect the molecular mechanisms regulating transitions between cell states, but methods for perturbing them systematically at scale remain limited. Here, we developed a semi-automated culture and high-throughput arrayed screening platform for human cortical organoids. Using a library of 1,280 small molecules designed to systematically target major signaling and regulatory pathways, we screened for modulators of EOMES, which encodes for the transcription factor TBR2, and identified Emetine, an inhibitor of translation elongation, as the top hit. The effect of Emetine on cortical cell-state progression was reproduced across human pluripotent stem cell lines, non-human primate cortical organoids, and primary human cortical tissue but not broadly across translation inhibitors. Moreover, transient exposure resulted in a shift from dividing radial glia towards cortical glutamatergic neurons. Mechanistically, nascent-proteome profiling revealed an early and coordinated remodeling of newly translated proteins that preceded detectable transcriptional changes, placing translational regulation upstream of the ensuing cell-state transition. Together, these findings highlight a role for specific translational inhibitors in promoting cortical cell-state progression and establish a scalable platform for systematic perturbation and discovery in human neural organoids.

papers.title: Seed Amplification Assay-Based Detection of Alpha-Synuclein Aggregates Outperforms Immunohistochemical Analysis in the Intestinal Mucosal Biopsies of Parkinson's Disease and Multiple System Atrophy Participants
papers.abstract: Objective: To determine whether an -synuclein (-Syn) seed amplification assay (SAA) detects seeding-competent aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies, differs by gastrointestinal region, registers pathology more frequently than immunohistochemistry (IHC), and associates with Parkinson disease (PD) diagnosis, disease duration or severity. Design: This cross-sectional, proof-of-concept diagnostic accuracy study analyzed duodenum, ileum, and sigmoid biopsies from PD participants, age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), plus exploratory multiple system atrophy (MSA) subtypes [parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar (MSA-C)]. Ileal and sigmoid PD and HC biopsies were assessed using proteinase K-resistant phospho-Ser129 IHC. SAA positivity was evaluated against clinical and biological measures. Results: In PD, SAA detected seeding competent -Syn aggregates with high observed specificity (97.5-100%) and region-dependent sensitivity (18/37, 48.65% in ileum and 36/56, 64.29% in sigmoid). Sigmoid SAA positivity increased significantly with PD disease duration (40.00% at <5 years, 73.33% at 5-10 years, and 93.75% at >10 years), independent of motor severity, whereas ileal positivity remained stable across disease stages. In 37 paired sigmoid biopsies, SAA detected -Syn aggregates 2.8-fold more frequently than IHC. Sigmoid seeding activity was detected in all five MSA-P, but not in two MSA-C. IHC did not detect aggregates in any MSA. Conclusions: In PD, -Syn SAA detected seeding-competent -Syn aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies with high observed specificity, moderate sensitivity, and approximately 2.8-fold higher detection rate than IHC in sigmoid. Positive SAA in MSA patients supports GI involvement across synucleinopathies. SAA detection in PD differed by intestinal region and disease duration, supporting further validation of intestinal SAA as a PD biomarker.

papers.title: Sex-dependent and region-specific morphological adaptations in astrocytes following early-life stress
papers.abstract: Astrocytes are structurally heterogeneous, with cell morphology providing a valuable readout of experi-ence-dependent plasticity. Despite this, single-cell reconstruction including complete cellular territories remains challenging to compare across brain regions and experimental groups. We used unilateral retro-orbital delivery of PHP.eB-GfaABC1D-eGFP as a practical method for sparse astrocyte labeling and ap-plied it to evaluate regional, sex, and early-life-stress comparisons in the mouse amygdala. Systemic vi-rus delivery to broadly target astrocytes across the brain produced eGFP-positive cells throughout cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and amygdala with spatially isolated cells suitable for intensity projection, three-dimensional surface reconstruction, filament tracing, and Sholl analysis. In naive females, we report relatively homogenous morphological features between lateral amygdala and basal amygdala. In naive males, basal amygdala astrocytes had greater volume and a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, while surface area, soma diameter, territory, and arborization measures did not differ significantly. Interestingly, early-life stress produced sex-specific morphological responses in the basal amygdala. Females showed increased perimeter, area, and Feret diameter without significant changes in three-dimensional volume or resolved filament measures. Males instead showed reduced surface area and volume, with no significant changes in projected territorial dimensions, soma diameter or resolved filament measures. S100{beta}-positive cell density was unchanged in the displayed regional and stress comparisons. These findings es-tablish systemic sparse eGFP labeling as an efficient route to single-cell astrocyte morphometry and re-veal a sex-dependent and region-specific dissociation between territorial expansion and three-dimensional volumetric contraction after early-life stress.

papers.title: Generative 3D Spatial Reconstruction of Cellular Organization from Single Cell Expression
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles cellular states at scale but removes their three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization. Reconstructing this organization requires recovering not only individual cell positions but also the physical size, geometry, and neighborhoods of an entire tissue. Existing methods either map cells onto measured spatial references or reconstruct two-dimensional sections independently, leaving the joint reconstruction of a new 3D specimen unresolved. Moreover, predicting the average plausible position of each cell can reduce per-cell error while compressing tissue geometry. We introduce ORBIS, a generative framework that jointly reconstructs whole 3D specimens from single-cell gene expression without requiring a spatial reference at inference. ORBIS learns spatial organization through flow matching in a shared physical coordinate frame, using training views sampled from sparse serial sections, tissue blocks, and whole specimens. At inference, a shared spatial state is iteratively updated through dynamically regrouped windows, enabling the generation of millions of cell positions without independently reconstructing and stitching tissue regions. We evaluate physical size, cell-population shape, per-cell placement, and neighborhood organization separately to distinguish accurate tissue geometry from low per-cell error. Across eight held-out specimens spanning whole mouse brains, thick brain blocks, and Drosophila embryos, ORBIS achieves lower cell-population shape error than all five evaluated baselines on every test and reconstructs specimens containing up to 3.7 million cells. On a single GPU, ORBIS samples million-cell brains in 0.9-2.8 minutes, approximately 38 times faster than the sampler of LUNA-3D, our 3D extension of the state-of-the-art generative spatial reconstruction method LUNA. On two held-out brain tests, sampling reduces size error by 3.3-fold and shape error by 1.8-fold compared with a single-call variant. On an independent dissociated single-cell brain atlas, ORBIS returns on average 37.9% of each region's cells to their dissection region across 23 regions, compared with 28.5% for LUNA-3D.

papers.title: Motivation-dependent communication between cortex and brainstem
papers.abstract: Neurons in the medullary brainstem exhibit movement-related patterns of activity, but the neuronal population codes that specify distinct actions, and the mechanisms by which cortex may shape these codes as a function of motivational state, remain unclear. To explore whether coupling between cortex and medulla depends upon motivational context, we trained mice to make both pre-reward "appetitive" licks that served to trigger water availability and rapidly attenuated with satiety, and "consummatory" licks, which occur post-reward release and more slowly attenuated with satiety. Simultaneous recordings from secondary motor cortex and motor medulla revealed that medullary activity was more time-locked than cortical activity to individual licks and exhibited a phase-based population code that encoded lick direction. Correlations between cortex and medulla were stronger during appetitive licks than during consummatory licks, with causal dependency established by optogenetic intervention and supported by multi-region recurrent network models. Population codes underlying behavior shared across the central nervous system, exemplified by cortico-medullary coupling, thus may depend upon the motivational context underlying action.

papers.title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells
papers.abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate therapeutics regimens of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2, encoded by EPAS1) but not HIF-1 in NK cells. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2 was not dependent on limited oxygen availability. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2 protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2 transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2/HIF-1{beta} heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolism. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1{beta} independent, HIF-2 pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2 to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies.

papers.title: Deprivation of dietary fiber promotes low-grade neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior in mice
papers.abstract: Background: Intestinal health is an important determinant of brain function in that an array of gut perturbants, especially those targeting microbiota, influence behavior. Fermentable dietary fiber nourishes gut microbiota and, consequently, promotes gut health. We hypothesized that depriving mice of fermentable dietary fiber would impact their brain and behavior. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed standard grain-based chow (GBC), a compositionally defined diet (CDD) which mimics macronutrient content of GBC but lacks fermentable fiber, or CDD supplemented with the fermentable fiber inulin (CDD+INU). Mice were subjected to behavioral testing 6-8 weeks later followed by analysis of the gut brain axis. Results: Relative to GBC-fed mice, CDD-fed mice exhibited low-grade gut inflammation and a reduction in open-field center exploration, signaling heightened anxiety-like behavior. CDD+INU fully reversed these abnormalities arguing they were a consequence of fiber deprivation. Analysis of the gut microbiome and serum metabolome showed that CDD+INU increased oxidative phosphorylation and immune suppressive metabolites. Flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses of the brain revealed an array of pro-inflammatory alterations in myeloid cells, CD4+ T-cells, microglia and astrocytes in mice fed CDD but not CDD+INU. Most notably, microglia and astrocytes from mice fed CDD, but not CDD+INU, displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration and greater glycolytic activity. CDD, but not CDD+INU consumption also reduced the abundance of oligodendrocytes and neurons, and increased hippocampal pro-inflammatory gene expression. Conclusions: Deprivation of fermentable fiber results in coordinated changes in brain immune composition and glial metabolic state that is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.

papers.title: Therapeutic Potential of Melatonin, Erythropoietin, and TRPV4 Antagonism in a Preclinical Model of Genetic Hydrocephalus
papers.abstract: Symptomatic hydrocephalus is a neuropathological disorder of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis characterized by abnormal accumulation of CSF and progressive ventricular enlargement. Current treatment relies primarily on surgical CSF diversion, which is invasive and associated with substantial rates of treatment failure and surgical revisions. Congenital hydrocephalus can be caused by genetic pathologies; for example, a point mutation in the Meckel-Gruber type 3, Tmem67, gene produces a congenital hydrocephalus phenotype in rats, characterized by progressive ventriculomegaly. Here, we evaluated a combinatorial cocktail therapeutic strategy consisting of erythropoietin (EPO), melatonin (MLT), and the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) antagonist, RN1734 (RN), in the Tmem67-- rat model of congenital hydrocephalus. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated marked progression of ventriculomegaly in untreated Tmem67-- rats between postnatal (P) 7 and P15. RN1734 and EPO+MLT+RN1734 (triple therapy) from P7-P14 prevented further ventricular expansion. Hydrocephalus is associated with structural disruption of the periventricular white matter (WM) and ependymal lining (EL), accompanied by regionally increased TLR4 and NLRP3-associated inflammatory signaling. EPO+MLT, RN1734, or triple therapy differentially attenuated these inflammatory responses. The triple combination reduced both TLR4 and NLRP3 protein abundance within the affected periventricular region and ameliorated the structural alterations. These findings support a combined therapeutic approach that addresses ventricular pathology, inflammation and periventricular structural consequences of congenital hydrocephalus.

papers.title: Label-free flow operators and stability operators from single-cell time courses: what local dynamical operators can and cannot identify
papers.abstract: Local Jacobians of single-cell dynamics are used to locate unstable cells along trajectories, but what they identify from measured data has rarely been tested against independent truth. We present scJDO2, which separates two per-cell operators by the time information they require: a score operator, the Hessian of a score-matched log density, available from any snapshot; and a flow operator, the Jacobian of a drift fitted to a measured velocity, here estimated label-free from a sampled time course by entropic optimal transport. Both are summarized in a shared operator space of magnitude-free descriptors, with the invariance of each stated, and evaluated with pre-registered tests. On synthetic data calibrated to six real datasets, the flow operator from the time course alone separated fate-bifurcation cells from committed cells on held-out seeds (AUC 0.89-1.00) with a-priori settings; tuning on development seeds overfit. On LARRY lineage-traced hematopoiesis, its fitted drift predicted the clonal displacement of barcoded cells beyond population movement (Spearman 0.56, permutation p < 0.001; 0.50 after removing the mean shift) and a held-out sampling day better than mean-displacement and no-movement baselines (energy distance 0.69, 95 % CI 0.66-0.73, vs 0.87 and 0.88); lineage thus validates the velocity, not {lambda}. Mini-batch transport reproduced dense transport (velocity cosine 0.9998) and scaled to all 130,887 cells (transport 5 min and 2.5 GB; drift fit and Jacobians 21 min and 1.3 GB). On an independent simulator it detected two of three bifurcations and two of three cycles and never reported instability on linear trajectories. Several readings failed. Neither operator recovers the values of the true Jacobian; the flow operators leading eigenvalue ranks branching cells empirically. The flow operator depends on the transport metric and inverts on Factor Analysis. Operator archetypes isolated bifurcation cells but did not outperform expression clustering and were unstable across fit seeds. The score operator did not predict CRISPRi knockdown responses or sister-cell fate coherence. A confirmatory test of transition timing could not be constructed, and diffusion is not identifiable at typical sampling intervals. The released software reports these diagnostics.

papers.title: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
papers.abstract: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

papers.title: Neurons entrain and shape an intrinsic arteriole rhythm that distributes blood across the cortical mantle
papers.abstract: The cerebral arteriole network distributes blood across cortex through branches whose diameters oscillate near a frequency fvaso ~ 0.1 Hz. We asked whether the spatiotemporal pattern of these vaso-oscillations reflects neuronal entrainment of an intrinsic vascular oscillation. Three findings support this: First, suppressing endothelial hyperpolarization left resting-state oscillations intact but weakened the vascular response to neural activity, showing that vasomotion originates within the arteriole network rather than following neuronal drive. Second, arterioles amplify sensory drive selectively rather than faithfully: neural activity near 0.1 Hz is resonantly enhanced to form a strong peak in the vascular response. Third, neuronal frequency sets spatial reach, and areas compete: when two neighboring cortical areas are driven simultaneously, the one nearer fvaso captures more vascular territory. Neurons therefore entrain an intrinsic vascular rhythm and stimulation frequency governs how vasomotion distributes blood, shapes functional brain images, and may influence interstitial fluid transport.

papers.title: Structural Basis of Second-Generation HIV-1 Maturation Inhibitor Activity by Magic Angle Spinning NMR
papers.abstract: The CA-SP1 junction of HIV-1 Gag forms a six-helix bundle (6HB) within the immature Gag lattice, sequestering the CA-SP1 cleavage site. Maturation inhibitors (MIs), such as Bevirimat (BVM) and its analogs, are an emerging class of HIV-1 antiviral compounds that stabilize Gag maturation intermediates by interfering with CA-SP1 proteolytic processing. Here, we report the binding modes of a potent second-generation BVM analog with an extended scaffold, HRF-4467, in crystalline CACTD-SP1-NC11 assemblies with inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), as determined by magic-angle-spinning solid-state NMR (MAS NMR) spectroscopy. The atomic-level structure reveals that HRF-4467 binds asymmetrically in the SP1-NC11 six-helix bundle and stabilizes its helical conformation in the immature lattice, in both the wild-type and the BVM-resistant SP1-V7A Gag variant. Additionally, in the presence of HRF-4467, IP6 adopts distinct conformations in the wild-type CACTD-SP1-NC11 and the SP1-V7A variant. Taken together, our results establish a molecular basis for HRF-4467's improved antiviral activity relative to BVM and suggest strategies for designing inhibitors with enhanced performance against MI-resistant HIV-1 variants for potential therapeutic use.

papers.title: Toward space-optimal approximate colored indexes at scale
papers.abstract: Searching current petabase-scale sequence repositories requires indexes that combine compact storage with high query throughput. Although exact colored indexes retain complete sequence information, their construction and storage costs can become substantial for highly diverse collections. Indexes based on approximate membership query (AMQ) filters offer a compact alternative with fast construction and queries. Being hash-based, these indexes support different seeding schemes without structural changes, while sampling can reduce storage requirements, construction time and query time by an order of magnitude. Within the AMQ framework, querying many independent filters causes scattered memory accesses, reducing throughput. This motivates interleaved filters, which address this weakness by storing filter slots contiguously by position, enabling cache-friendly access and simultaneous membership queries. However, existing implementations face a trade-off between guaranteed construction and space-efficiency. Here, we introduce a new indexing framework based on interleaved ZOR filters, fingerprint-based structures with guaranteed construction that require only approximately 1% more space than the theoretical minimum for AMQ. To exploit redundancy between genomes, we introduce a color-preserving merging mechanism that extends fingerprints with membership bits, allowing multiple genomes to share a filter while retaining their individual identities. Together with a lightweight, sketch-based layout planner, this mechanism yields a compact index structure that accommodates collections with widely varying genome sizes and degrees of similarity. Our third contribution extends the AMQ framework beyond contiguous -mers through a low-density minimizer scheme alongside efficient implementations of sensitive seeds, including gapped -mers and randstrobes. We implement these methods in Zindex, a parallel, SIMD-accelerated Rust index that scales to millions of genomes while supporting diverse seeding and sampling schemes. Zindex indexes the latest RefSeq release of 564,401 assembled genomes in under 22 hours, producing a 289.5 GB index. It further scales to all 2,763,297 genomes of AllTheBacteria, producing a 406.3 GB index in four days with a peak memory footprint of 43.8 GB. Availability. Zindex is available at https://github.com/Malfoy/Zindex

papers.title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.

papers.title: Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.

papers.title: Isocaloric restriction of a high-fat diet under TAK-242 administration: metabolic and gut microbial responses in mice
papers.abstract: High-fat feeding promotes obesity in mice largely by increasing energy intake, so diet composition and energy intake are hard to separate without pair-feeding. We previously showed that isocaloric restriction normalizes body weight, glycemia and plasma lipids but not visceral adiposity, adipose inflammation or the fecal microbial community. We hypothesized that, during administration of the TLR4 signaling inhibitor TAK-242, matching energy intake to that of low-fat controls would normalize adiposity, intestinal barrier gene expression and the fecal microbial community. Male C57BL/6 mice (n = 8 per group) received a low-fat diet, a high-fat diet ad libitum, or a high-fat diet pair-fed to controls from week 0 or week 5 for 12 weeks; TAK-242 (3 ug/g, three times weekly) was given to every group from week 0.4, with no vehicle-injected arm. Intake did not differ among groups during a three-week low-fat acclimation (P = .88); over the 12 weeks on the assigned diets the ad libitum high-fat group ate 5.5% more than controls (P = .50). Over the full trajectory the ad libitum high-fat group gained 0.48 g/week more than controls (group x week, P = .012); both pair-fed groups had lower fasting glucose than that group. Adipocyte diameter, visceral fat proportion, ileal barrier genes, CCK-induced satiation and microbial alpha diversity did not differ significantly among groups. Adipose Ccl2 expression differed (P = .043, exploratory), as did fecal community composition (PERMANOVA P = .022), although no pairwise contrast survived correction. Energy restriction did not return the microbial community toward the low-fat profile.

papers.title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
papers.abstract: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica, reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ~275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

papers.title: LAP-TLR2 Axis Drives Inflammatory Pathology during Listeria monocytogenes Gastroenteritis
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) causes acute gastroenteritis that precedes systemic invasive listeriosis, yet the molecular mechanisms coordinating bacterial virulence with host inflammatory responses during the enteric phase remain poorly understood. We show that Lm-associated gastroenteritis is dose-dependent, and a high infectious dose (~1x10^10 CFU/mouse), reflecting epidemic cases, recapitulates hallmark features of gastroenteritis in a mouse model, including early onset, epithelial erosion, and profound inflammatory cell infiltration. We identify Listeria adhesion protein (LAP), rather than classical virulence factors such as internalin A and listeriolysin O, as the primary mediator of enteric pathology, driving epithelial cell death and neutrophil recruitment. Transcriptomic (mRNA-seq) profiling implicates LAP-driven engagement of the TLR2-MyD88 pathway. Using the HEK-Dual hTLR2 (NF-kB) reporter cell line and TLR2 knockout mice, we show that LAP engages TLR2 to activate TNFalpha; NF-kB signaling and compromises the gut epithelial barrier. Disease severity correlates with myeloid hyperactivation and intestinal ion channel dysregulation, as CD11b-; mice exhibit attenuated diarrhea despite elevated bacterial tissue loads. Finally, studies in MLCK knock-out mice confirm that this myeloid-driven pathology requires MLCK-dependent tight junction opening for paracellular neutrophil migration, which works in concert with LAP-TLR2 signaling during Lm-induced gastroenteritis.

papers.title: Metatranscriptomic Profiling of Viral Diversity in Aquatic Environments with a Focus on Microalgal Viruses
papers.abstract: Freshwater microeukaryotes contribute to aquatic productivity, yet the RNA viruses associated with these communities remain incompletely characterized compared with their marine counterparts. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to profile viral diversity across five Finnish freshwater sites (one river and four lakes) and one coastal marine sample from Hiroshima Bay in the Seto Inland Sea, Japan. We recovered 399 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), of which 285 (71.4%) represented RNA viruses distributed across five viral phyla and putatively associated with fungal, plant or algal, metazoan and bacterial hosts. DNA viruses formed a smaller component of the dataset, including bacteriophage-like vOTUs with transcripts encoding replication, structural, packaging, and lysis proteins. Two vOTUs, which were detected in the Vantaanjoki river sample, were putatively classified within the family Marnaviridae, which comprises RNA viruses that infect protists in marine and freshwater environments. Both vOTUs encoded conserved replication and picornavirus-like capsid domains, and one represented a near-complete dicistronic genome. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) -based phylogeny placed these vOTUs in a strongly supported lineage outside the currently recognized genera within the family Marnaviridae, supporting their provisional assignment to the candidate genus Vandarnavirus proposed here within Marnaviridae. Whole-genome comparisons using the IMG/VR v4 database revealed genetic similarities between the vOTUs representing the candidate Vandarnavirus genus and picorna-like virus sequences from freshwater, wetland, saltmarsh, and estuarine metatranscriptomes. These findings expand the known ecological range of marnavirus-like RNA viruses and identify freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgae-associated viral sequences.

papers.title: Quantum Entanglement as a Physical Determinant of Genomic Instability in TP53
papers.abstract: Abstract Mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene are among the most frequent alterations in human cancers, but whether quantum mechanical effects such as DNA entanglement, influence mutation patterns remain unexplored. Here, we applied a coupled quantum harmonic oscillator model to compute von Neumann Entropy (VNE), a proxy for quantum entanglement, across the TP53 sequence. We found that known mutational hot spots exhibited significantly elevated VNE compared to non-hot spot regions, suggesting that local quantum coupling may reflect structural instability or altered repair accessibility. CpG sites, traditionally linked to methylation-driven mutability, did not exhibit elevated VNE, indicating that quantum properties captured by our closed model are distinct from classical biochemical mechanisms. While these computational results raise the possibility that quantum effects could contribute to genomic instability in TP53, we caution that the analysis is limited by the small number of validated hot spots (n=6) and lacks biological validation. our findings are exploratory and should be interpreted carefully. If confirmed in a larger, multi-gene studies with biophysical measurements, a quantum informed framework could open new avenues for predicting mutation hot spots and understanding cancer mutagenesis. We advocate for interdisciplinary efforts bridging quantum physics and oncology to explore these possibilities further.

papers.title: Temporal changes in genetic variation during the invasion of Lygodium japonicum in North America
papers.abstract: Premise of the study. Invasive species are now widespread and have detrimental ecological and economic impacts. They also offer opportunities to investigate rapid evolution in colonizing populations. Here, we leverage nuclear DNA from herbarium specimens of Lygodium japonicum, an invasive fern to 1) identify the putative source(s) of its invasion, 2) test for climate adaptation in its invaded range, and 3) characterize the effects of genetic bottlenecks on adaptive and neutral variation during its establishment. Methods. We use low-coverage genome skimming data from specimens spanning 1905 through 2017 to identify the source region(s) of the L. japonicum invasion of North America. We use a genotype-environment analysis of invaded range samples to identify genomic regions associated with local adaptation to variation in five bioclimatic variables. Finally, we compare heterozygosity between native and invasive individuals and their changes through time in non-coding, coding, and putatively adaptive loci. Key results. We identify mainland Asia as the most likely source region for this invasion. Our genotype-environment analysis found 144 candidate SNPs significantly associated with climatic variation in the invaded range, with precipitation of the driest month associated with the greatest number of SNPs, suggesting rapid genomic adaptation in the invaded range. Finally, we found conflicting trends in individual-level heterozygosity over time when analyzing different types of genetic variation: in non-coding loci, there was a small, yet significant decrease in genetic diversity, but in putatively adaptive loci we did not find evidence of a genetic bottleneck. Conclusions. Natural history collections provide exceptional opportunities to explore evolutionary processes, by capturing genomic sequences across time. Here, herbarium specimens reveal rapid evolution, maintenance of adaptative variation, and accumulation of noncoding diversity in the Lygodium japonicum invasion, highlighting the potential for adaptative variation to fuel the success of invasive species.

papers.title: Concussion decreases brain signal variability
papers.abstract: Sports-related concussion represents a major public health concern, with millions of cases diagnosed annually. Despite significant methodological advances in functional brain imaging, a clinically meaningful neuroimaging biomarker of concussion has yet to be established. This may be due in part to a reliance on traditional measures. For example, approaches examining mean activation across trials reduce responses to a single measure of central tendency and therefore fail to capture important individual differences. In contrast, blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) variability offers a promising new approach to measuring brain function, Specifically, it captures individual differences in the temporal variability in the BOLD signal over time. Further, it is sensitive to neural, vascular, and neurovascular coupling changes that accompany concussion. We collected baseline (prior to injury) and post-concussion (within 48 hours of injury) neuroimaging data in 56 collegiate athletes. Within this longitudinal dataset, we investigated changes in BOLD variability across multiple spatial scales. In addition, we examined their relationships with self-reported symptoms and cognitive performance. As expected, symptoms increased following concussion while computerized cognitive performance declined. BOLD variability decreased from baseline to post-concussion, particularly in the somatomotor and language networks. Moreover, changes in BOLD variability were related to changes in symptom reporting and cognitive performance. Together, these findings advance our understanding of how concussion affects brain function and highlight BOLD signal variability as a promising biomarker to aid ongoing efforts to improve the diagnosis and treatment of sports-related concussion.

papers.title: Isoform diversity as a complementary dimension of gene expression
papers.abstract: Most human genes produce multiple mRNA isoforms through alternative splicing and alternative transcription start and end sites. Isoforms of the same gene can differ in function, and their relative abundance varies between tissues and conditions. However, gene expression analysis is often restricted to the gene level, masking its diversification into mRNA and protein isoforms with potentially distinct functionality. Here we show, using an adaptation of Shannon evenness applied to 4,814 GTEx samples from 25 tissues, that isoform diversity constitutes a distinct dimension of gene expression, complementary to gene-level abundance and whole transcriptome diversity. Isoform diversity separated tissues based on non-differentially expressed genes and changed with age in a gene- and tissue-specific manner, most strongly in the brain and often without changes in overall gene expression levels. During neuronal differentiation, it increased most notably in RNA processing and splicing genes. Our results suggest that isoform diversity represents an independent dimension of gene expression and may help explain functional differences between tissues and cell states that are not captured by analyzing expression levels alone.

papers.title: Multimodal cellular context enables molecular phenotyping from single-molecule trajectories
papers.abstract: Single-molecule tracking (SMT) provides direct measurements of molecular dynamics in living cells, but motion alone rarely specifies the underlying biological process, without accounting for the cellular environment in which that motion occurs. Here, we present MIST (Multimodal Interpretation of Single-molecule Trajectories), a framework that brings the paradigm of image-based profiling to single molecules by integrating trajectory dynamics, emitter properties and cellular context into a common, reusable phenotype space. Using a reference panel of nine proteins in live Escherichia coli, we show that multimodal context more than doubled protein-specific information relative to trajectory features alone, a gap that learned trajectory representations did not close. MIST allowed de novo identification of shared transcription-translation phenotype at the nucleoid periphery. A fixed reference space detected effects of previously uncharacterized MukB ATPase mutations without retraining. MIST provides an interpretable and extensible framework for comparing proteins, mutants and conditions within a common space of molecular phenotypes.

papers.title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2-related disorders
papers.abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1, finding ~50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: Plumage diversity without differential expression of pigmentation genes in a rapid avian radiation
papers.abstract: Uncovering the molecular basis of reproductive traits is key to understanding species divergence. Capuchino Seedeaters ( Sporophila ), a radiation of genetically similar birds differing mainly in male reproductive plumage color, can be leveraged to study how such traits evolve. Outlier scans identified candidate pigmentation variants primarily in noncoding sequence, implying regulatory changes. However, RNA-seq of growing feather follicles generally did not show differential expression of pigmentation genes among different colors, with only ASIP downregulated in crown feathers. Gene expression patterns instead varied by body region. The largest difference between dimorphic sexes was the upregulation of the carotenoid-degrading gene BCO2 in males, accompanied by lower carotenoid content in male feathers. An improved genome annotation assigned 9.5% of candidate variants into coding and untranslated sequence. This suggests species-diagnostic variants lie within transcribed sequence and could act post-transcriptionally, rather than through transcript abundance, leading to a revised hypothesis for plumage divergence in this radiation.

papers.title: scCont: Interpretable Contrastive Learning for Functional Characterization of Cellular State Transitions
papers.abstract: Timecourse single-cell RNA (scRNA) datasets have become indispensable biological tools for studying and uncovering the underlying regulatory processes driving continuous cell-state transitions such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, these highly fluid, non-linear gene program dynamics remain difficult to disentangle. While deep neural network models can effectively map complex topologies, they are biological black boxes, lacking the gene-level interpretability required by experimental practitioners. Here, we introduce scCont, a fully unsupervised contrastive learning framework for extracting interpretable functional transition units from scRNA-seq data. Rather than relying on explicit temporal labels or clustering priors, scCont uses an unsupervised k-nearest neighbors approach to project local transcriptomic neighborhoods into a low-dimensional embedding. During post-training analysis, scCont employs Shapley network attribution to determine gene-latent relationships, mapping latent dimensions directly into functional gene programs. We quantitatively and qualitatively validate this representation by demonstrating that scCont captures biologically interpretable dynamics more effectively than baseline methods such as LDVAE. Evaluated across 13 diverse EMT timecourse datasets and four simulated datasets, scCont exposes interpretable functional dynamics and effectively maps context-dependent functional groups, helping to bridge the gap between deep learning representation and translational biological utility. scCont is an open source software available on GitHub (https://github.com/nramani611/scCont).

papers.title: How mutation rate evolves: Gene expression shapes genome-wide mutation rates in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Mutation rates vary across the genome, linked to biochemical properties of local DNA sequences. However, mutation rate variation also associates with functional genomic features, raising the possibility that intragenomic mutation rate variation is shaped by adaptive evolution. In particular, recent studies in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana suggested that highly conserved genes under strong purifying selection also have reduced de novo mutation rates, suggesting that natural selection may have acted to reduce mutation rate specifically at important genes. However, whether this is true for wider taxa, including animals, remains unknown. Here we repurposed published mutation accumulation datasets from Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the determinants of de novo single nucleotide variant (DNV) rates genome-wide under minimal selection. Loci under stronger purifying selection accumulated fewer mutations, including intronic and synonymous mutations. Various sequence-specific (i.e. GC content) and regulatory features (e.g. chromatin modifications) were strongly correlated with mutation rate, but gene expression best explained the depletion of mutations within strongly conserved loci, even after accounting for correlations amongst variables. Using excision repair (XR)-sequencing data we determined that higher levels of transcription- coupled repair (TCR) were associated with reduced mutation rates, strongly suggesting that TCR lowers mutation rate of highly conserved genes. Furthermore, by comparing orthologs between C. elegans and its close relative Pristionchus pacificus, we found that altered gene expression across evolutionary time correlated with altered mutation rate. These findings support a model whereby developmental transcription modulates local mutation rates through TCR. A corollary is that adaptive mutation bias may emerge indirectly, downstream of gene regulation evolution, providing a mechanistic framework that reconciles non-random local mutation rate variation with established evolutionary theory.

papers.title: Genomic signatures distinguish isolates of Salmonella Typhimurium from humans and livestock
papers.abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a major cause of human salmonellosis and livestock represent an important reservoir for human infection through the food chain. However, it remains unclear whether isolates recovered from human disease reflect the broader livestock population or constitute a subset of livestock-associated isolates characterized by specific genetic features. Here, we analysed 1,398 S. Typhimurium genomes from human, poultry, bovine and swine isolates to evaluate whether isolates associated with human disease can be distinguished from those circulating in livestock and to identify the genetic features underlying this discrimination. Whole-genome multilocus sequence typing profiles were converted into a gene presence/absence matrix and analysed using four machine-learning algorithms, which showed high and consistent discriminatory performance. Model performance was influenced by the phylogenetic structure of the population and by the variable distribution of human- and livestock-associated isolates across lineages of sequence type (ST) 19, the most prevalent S. Typhimurium ST. Nevertheless, within ST19, 97 genes were significantly enriched and 36 were significantly depleted in human-associated genomes relative to genomes from each of the three livestock sources. Human-enriched genes included 14 genes required for biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide core, the O-antigen, the T1 antigen, and six virulence factors. These genes were consistently absent from livestock-associated genomes across ST19 lineages. Conversely, human-depleted genes included the galactitol utilisation cluster and five virulence genes, which are predominantly absent in specific ST19 lineages. Overall, our findings support the existence of host-associated genomic signatures that distinguish isolates associated with human disease from those sampled from the livestock reservoir.

papers.title: A biomimetic deep encoder for auditory restoration by cortical stimulation
papers.abstract: Cochlear and auditory brainstem implants are the primary treatments for profound deafness. However, the inherently low resolution of electrical stimulation used by these devices limits information transfer to a small number of independent stimulation channels and results in perceptual difficulties. An alternative approach is to target the auditory cortex, a brain region large enough to accommodate hundreds of stimulation channels and whose stimulation evokes sound percepts. Although modern brain interfaces offer large channel counts and spatial resolution, developing encoding algorithms capable of accurately transmitting interpretable sound information remains challenging. Here we introduce Braincodec, a deep network that optimizes both sound information transmission and the alignment of stimulation patterns with the spatial, temporal, and high-level properties of the auditory cortex neural code. Braincodec operates online and requires only a few hundred channels to transmit sufficient information for the reconstruction of natural sounds with high fidelity, a performance inaccessible to cochlear implant encoders. Moreover, mice equipped with a Braincodec-driven auditory cortical prosthesis matched the accuracy of non-implanted mice in discriminating real sounds. Braincodec therefore enables the development of high-throughput cortical neuroprosthetics with the potential to overcome the limitations of current auditory implants and provides a generic framework applicable to other sensory modalities.

papers.title: Rapid, accurate, and memory-frugal sub-gene-level quantification of probe-based, multiplexed single-cell data
papers.abstract: Probe-based, multiplexed single-cell assays enable accurate transcriptome profiling while processing multiple samples in parallel. Their predefined probe sequences and additional sample barcodes introduce computational requirements that differ from those of poly(A)-based assays, for which many existing single-cell quantification tools were developed. We extend simpleaf to enable efficient demultiplexing and quantification of probe-based single-cell libraries. A new, cache-friendly dictionary specializes lookup to small probe references, while a shared thread budget balances parallel decompression and mapping. We extend RAD and downstream tools with reusable sample-scoped correction plans and external-memory collation of hierarchically barcoded data, retaining probe identities through quantification to enable rapid mapping and quantification with a small working memory budget. Across five 10x Genomics Flex datasets comprising 44 samples, simpleaf had the shortest runtime and lowest peak memory use of the three tools on every library, while producing gene-expression estimates, cell clusters, and marker genes concordant with cyto and Cell Ranger. Compared with cyto, simpleaf was on average 2 times faster and used approximately one-thirteenth as much memory. simpleaf also exports probe-level quantification results, allowing a range of analyses at sub-gene resolution. Here, we show that individual probe counts reveal expression changes obscured by gene-level aggregation, identify the transcript groups contributing to gene-level changes, and provide insight into splicing dynamics across cell types. These results demonstrate the computational and biological value of retaining probe-level information in multiplexed singlecell analysis.

papers.title: A Framework for SPICE MRSI Reconstruction Posterior Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Purpose: Low-rank reconstruction methods such as SPICE substantially improve Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) reconstruction quality. However, SPICE does not provide an estimate of reconstruction uncertainty. A framework for posterior uncertainty estimation in SPICE reconstruction is proposed, hereafter referred to as the framework. Theory and Methods: A Laplace approximation is used to estimate the covariance of the reconstructed spatial coefficients. This covariance is propagated through the spectral basis and spectral fitting to obtain metabolite concentration uncertainty. Matrix-free Hessian--vector products and voxel-wise conjugate-gradient estimation are used to avoid explicit construction or inversion of the full Hessian, making the method tractable. Results: Validation using repeated in vivo 7 T MRSI acquisitions showed that the estimated posterior uncertainty exhibited spatial and spectral patterns similar to those of empirical repeated-scan uncertainty. Experiments further demonstrated how spatial regularization and k-space undersampling affect the estimated uncertainty. Conclusion: The framework provides a practical framework for uncertainty quantification when using SPICE reconstruction of MRSI. It could be adapted to other regularised low-rank reconstruction methods.

papers.title: Towards an analytical framework for investigating the neurophysiological influence of social context in speech perception
papers.abstract: Social information plays an important role in everyday speech communication, yet existing neurophysiological approaches provide limited means of isolating its contribution during naturalistic speech perception. Here, we present an analytical framework that combines the large language model (LLM) Mistral-Instruct, fine-tuned on conversational language, and temporal response functions (TRFs) to investigate the influence of social context on word-level speech processing. The framework disentangles local context (LC) from speaker-specific social context (SC) when generating LLM-derived lexical expectation measures, enabling such predictions to be generated under either matching or mismatching speaker contexts for the same speech material. This provides a direct way of isolating the contribution of social information to lexical predictions. We first show that speaker-related social context carries information about speech register and conversational role beyond that available from previous local context alone by interrogating Mistral-Instruct. We then demonstrate that lexical expectations generated from socially congruent contexts produce small but reliable improvements in EEG prediction relative to expectations generated from incongruent social contexts. These effects were observed despite identical acoustic input and neural recordings, indicating that the influence of social context on lexical expectations explains dissociable variance in neural responses to speech. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept for using LLM-derived lexical expectations to isolate and measure the influence of social context on speech processing. More broadly, the proposed framework offers a flexible approach for generating and testing hypotheses about how different forms of contextual knowledge shape neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension.

papers.title: QRAFT: Scaling coalescent-based species tree inference to one million taxa
papers.abstract: Species tree inference from multi-locus data under the multispecies coalescent has not kept pace with phylogenomic datasets that now span hundreds of thousands of species. We present QRAFT, a statistically consistent method for estimating species trees by maximizing quartet support on phylogenomic datasets at unprecedented scales. For n taxa and k gene trees, QRAFT achieves near-linear running time of O(kn log^2 n) when its recursion is balanced, which is within a polylogarithmic factor of the O(kn) time required simply to read the input. It also achieves asymptotically optimal O(kn) memory, so its memory requirements grow only linearly with the input size. QRAFT infers a million-taxon species tree from 1,000 genes in just three hours using only 298 GB of RAM, 64 CPU threads, and no GPUs. We estimate that the same analysis with ASTRAL-MP, a scalable parallel implementation of the widely used method ASTRAL, would take about 36 years (>100,000 times longer) and require prohibitive amounts of memory, far beyond practical computational limits. QRAFT maintains accuracy comparable to, and in many cases better than, leading species tree estimation methods. Notably, QRAFT reconstructed a microbial tree of life comprising 199,330 genomes in just a few hours using modest CPU resources. Thus, QRAFT brings highly accurate statistically consistent coalescent-based species tree inference to the unprecedented million-taxon regime and enables phylogenomic analyses towards the scale of the tree of life. QRAFT is publicly available at https://github.com/risenfromashes/qraft.

papers.title: Personality and dominance shape core area use and territory-related signalling in a feral ungulate
papers.abstract: Space use strategies determine how animals acquire resources and encounter competitors, which ultimately influence their survival. Instead of utilising their entire range uniformly, animals typically concentrate activity in locations where resources are most valuable, and these 'core areas' provide key insights into the behavioural strategies underlying space use. Although competitive ability is often expected to influence core area use, substantial individual-level variation remains unexplained. Consistent behavioural differences among individuals, or personality, may contribute to this variation, but their role in shaping spatial behaviour under natural conditions is poorly understood. To address this gap, we observed adult males (n=24) from a free-ranging, semi-urban population of Asian water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis). We quantified individual core area size and territory-related signalling behaviour, and assessed personality from >9,300 minutes of observations. Most males (79%) shared overlapping core areas with one to five other males but with clear dominance relationships. Social engagement, reflecting a social personality, was positively associated with core area size in subordinates, but not in dominant males. Social engagement was also positively associated with territory-related signalling frequency. By contrast, a non-social personality labelled as activity-maintenance did not influence with core area size or signalling behaviour. We also found that dominant males exhibited lower signalling frequencies than subordinates. Overall, we show that personality and dominance are associated with distinct aspects of spatial behaviour. These findings demonstrate that individual spatial strategies emerge from the interplay between behavioural phenotypes and social lives, highlighting the spatial-social interface as a source of variation in animal space use.

papers.title: Continental scale genetic diversity supports geo-clustered ecoregions connectivity
papers.abstract: Connectivity is fundamental to ensuring that ecosystems can recover after impact. The genetic information in DNA metabarcoding can provide insight into connectivity at different timescales. We compared structural connectivity, represented by an adjacency matrix of ecoregions, and functional connectivity at different levels of organization, represented by the {beta}-diversity of exact sequence variants and species, between ecoregions, focusing on benthic arthropods. While structural and functional connectivity were correlated, there was a distinct divide between eastern and western ecoregions that approximately aligned with the Rocky Mountains. Within the western ecoregions, species {beta}-diversity was not correlated with ecoregion adjacency and had higher intraspecific genetic differentiation. This implies that gene flow is more restricted in this area. Understanding how gene flow can be limited is important to conservation planning.

papers.title: Measuring American black bear genetic load in fixed structural variants and runs of homozygosity
papers.abstract: Populations living in geographically isolated regions are expected to have reduced gene flow, increased genetic drift, and elevated levels of inbreeding, influencing both genetic load and possibly the distribution of structural variants. The American black bear (Ursus americanus) is widely found across Ontario, Canada, where populations inhabit diverse landscapes ranging from relatively intact contiguous forested landscapes to isolated regions such as the Saugeen Peninsula. Here, we investigated the population genomic history across five Ontario black bear populations using a combination of short-read (SR) and long-read (LR) sequencing data. We compared population genetic metrics including nucleotide diversity ({pi}), Tajimas D, runs of homozygosity (ROH), and genome-wide structural variants (SVs) to assess population health and identify signatures of isolation. Our results showed that the isolated Saugeen Peninsula population is genetically distinct and exhibited reduced nucleotide diversity, greater ROH and SV abundance compared with mainland populations. The population also showed elevated genetic load in all genomic features, suggesting increased exposure of deleterious variation that are expressed in ROH and population specific SVs. We further discuss the integration of ROH, SVs and genetic load in conservation assessments.

papers.title: Growing a Root from Its Genome : Emergent Tissue Layers and Zones in a GPU-Native Simulation of the Arabidopsis Root Tip
papers.abstract: Models of the Arabidopsis root tip usually take its cell identities as given. Here we grow a root tip from a single genome. In a two-dimensional median section, every cell reads the same network of 62 genes (26 core genes from an earlier, unpublished model of callus and 36 added for the root) and starts with the same expression; the only spatial cues are the polarity of auxin transport, auxin from the shoot and the free surface. Identities and zones are never given to the simulation; they are read from gene expression. Cells are polygons of a shared mesh, relaxed towards mechanical equilibrium under turgor at every step. In 48 simulated hours, a tip-shaped template grows into a root of 3 000-4 500 cells with epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and stele in order along most of its length, SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW in the endodermis, an auxin maximum, a quiescent centre and a cap at its tip, and meristem, elongation and mature zones. A WOX5 gate built from published interactions and one hypothesis keeps a quiescent centre to 48 h in 17 of 20 simulated roots that were not used for tuning (85%; Wilson 95% interval 64-95%; criteria fixed before the run), against 9 of 20 roots used for tuning, before the gate. The niche is not maintained beyond 48 h: grown on to 73 h, only 6 of these 20 roots still have a quiescent centre (30%; 15-52%). All pre-registered criteria hold in only 1 of 20 roots, because the quiescent centre is too wide at 0 h; without that count, 12 of 20. The meristem is too long, and cortical cells made after the start of growth elongate only three- to four-fold instead of eightto thirty-fold, a limit set in large part by the numerical growth scheme. Mutants are a major weakness: several look like their published phenotype, but an exploratory re-run of a mutant benchmark fixed in advance for our first model passes one of nine predictions. Nor does the root regenerate: cut near its tip, it re-forms an auxin maximum and a columella but no quiescent centre. On a first, simpler model and without any polarity cue, a mass of identical cells still sorts into concentric layers and, when PIN carriers follow the auxin flux, concentrates auxin into a few foci, but forms no stem-cell niche: the genome lacks a lateral inhibition between foci. We state the limitations and the next stages.

papers.title: Apparent sequential effects due to trial-to-trial fluctuations in decision criterion
papers.abstract: Decision making is shaped by sequential effects, whereby preceding stimuli and responses influence current decisions. Computational models typically explain these effects by assuming that decision parameters are causally updated as a function of experimental history. Here, we challenge this assumption by showing that several hallmark sequential effects can instead emerge from slow fluctuations in the decision criterion. Using simulations based on Signal Detection Theory (SDT), we demonstrate that trial-to-trial criterion fluctuations, independent of experimental history, generate three commonly observed sequential effects: the repulsive effect of the previous stimulus (i.e., a tendency to alternate), the influence of previous response (i.e., choice history bias), and the modulation of choice history bias by previous confidence. To disentangle causal effects from effects driven by criterion fluctuations, we used the Hierarchical Model for Fluctuations in Criterion (hMFC), which simultaneously estimates both processes. Applying hMFC to 14 empirical datasets revealed that the repulsive effect of the previous stimulus was fully explained by criterion fluctuations. Accounting for criterion fluctuations also substantially altered choice history bias estimates: attractive biases disappeared in all four affected datasets, while three datasets revealed a previously masked tendency to alternate and two showed stronger alternation. In contrast, the modulation of choice history bias by previous confidence was largely unaffected by concurrent estimation of criterion fluctuations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that criterion fluctuations account for a substantial portion of sequential effects and highlight the importance of explicitly modeling them to avoid confounded interpretations of behavioral and neuroimaging data.

papers.title: Moving Heads, Moving Sounds: Systematic Errors in Auditory Motion Perception
papers.abstract: The movement of moving objects seen during self-motion is incorrectly perceived as a result of errors in parsing the visual motion arising from the retina and from information about the movement of the head and eyes in space1. The perception of motion of auditory targets may be even more challenging as previous research suggests that the auditory system lacks dedicated low-level speed processing mechanisms. This study investigates how the perception of a moving auditory sound source is influenced by concurrent head movements, drawing comparisons with established visual motion perception findings and illusions, such as the Filehne Illusion. Participants were asked to move their heads at a fixed speed, either horizontally (left to right or right to left) or vertically (up to down or down to up), while indicating the perceived direction of a moving sound source by using a joystick. A physical sound source was moved silently at a constant speed in fronto-parallel 2D space using a 3x3x3m cable robot. Results showed that head movements created a perceptual bias of the perceived direction of the moving sound source in the opposite direction to the head movement. Responses were less precise during horizontal than vertical head movement, whereas overall directional accuracy did not differ reliably between movement planes. The magnitude of the directional error also depended on the direction of head movement, consistent with the different cues available for horizontal and vertical localization (binaural vs. spectral cues). These findings suggest that similarly to how visual motion perception is distorted by extraretinal signals and the movement of the eyes, so too is auditory motion perception influenced by movement of the ears, revealing errors in the integration of proprioceptive, vestibular and auditory cues that distort the perceived direction of a moving sound source.

papers.title: SNAzzy: an image processing pipeline for investigating global Synchronous Network Activity
papers.abstract: Genetically encoded fluorescent indicators are powerful tools for monitoring biological processes in live samples (Lin and Schnitzer 2016; Nakai, Ohkura, and Imoto 2001).
