When combined with a large field of view, a single time-lapse recording has the potential to capture many specimens, facilitating high-throughput data collection. However, this approach generates large, multidimensional datasets that are challenging to process and analyze. We present SNAzzy, a Python package for studying synchronous network activity (SNA) in Drosophila embryos via high-throughput microscopy. SNA is a hallmark of developing nervous systems (Wu, Kourdougli, and Portera-Cailliau 2024; Blankenship and Feller 2009; Akin and Zipursky 2020), often studied using genetically encoded calcium indicators to monitor neural activity in vivo. SNAzzy processes and analyzes time-lapse datasets taken from live samples using fluorescent widefield microscopy. Each dataset contains dozens of individual specimens in the same field of view and thousands of time points. The software offers individual specimen cropping for optimization of storage and processing, adaptive regions of interest for quantification of fluorescence and changes in morphology over time, a custom peak detection algorithm, and a graphical user interface for data visualization, curation, and dataset comparison. The code is available at https://github.com/ACRLab/snazzy.

papers.title: Organism-dependent ecotoxicological effects of transition metal-containing layered double hydroxides
papers.abstract: Due to low environmental stability of certain molecule classes, such as phytohormones and RNA interference, layered double hydroxides (LDHs) have been investigated as nanocarriers capable of protecting and transporting molecules of interest in natural systems. Herein, the ecotoxicological effects of LDH nanoparticles composed by different transition metals (Al-Ni, Al-Co, and Al-Cu) were evaluated in maize (Zea mays), tomato (Lycopersicum esculentum), and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, two important crops and one soil organism found in agricultural systems. Plants were exposed to the nanoparticles through foliar spraying (5, 50, and 500 ug/mL), and physiological parameters were evaluated. In C. elegans, lethality, locomotion, larval development, and body length were analyzed. The nanoparticles exhibited high colloidal stability and characteristic lamellar morphology. The results demonstrated low phytotoxicity for all formulations, without significant changes in photochemical activity, effective quantum yield of photosystem II (psi-PSII), stomatal conductance (gs), and chlorophyll index (Chl a+b; ICF) in plants. In contrast, C. elegans exhibited greater sensitivity, showing reduced motility, developmental delay, and decreased body length, although mortality remained below 12% under all evaluated conditions. Toxicity was dependent on the metallic composition, following the order Al-Cu > Al-Ni > Al-Co. Collectively, the results indicate that LDHs exhibit high compatibility with those two crops but may cause sublethal effects in soil organisms. These findings highlight the importance of multispecies ecotoxicological assessments for the safe development of nanocarriers intended for agricultural applications.

papers.title: QUANTA: A quantum annealing framework for species tree estimation using weighted quartet amalgamation
papers.abstract: Reconstructing species trees from genome-scale data is challenging due to pervasive gene tree discordance. Maximizing quartet consistency is a widely used approach for species tree inference from multi-locus data. Quartet amalgamation approaches, such as Quartet Fiduccia-Mattheyse (QFM) and Quartet MaxCut (QMC) families, have emerged as highly accurate quartet-based species tree inference techniques, but their reliance on computationally expensive classical bipartitioning heuristics, such as Fiduccia-Mattheyses (FM) and MaxCut, limits their scalability. Here, we introduce QUANTA, a quantum annealing-based quartet amalgamation method that, to our knowledge, represents the first quantum formulation of quartet-based approaches and the first species tree estimation method for multi-locus data that runs on real quantum hardware. At the core of QUANTA is a novel, general formulation of weighted quartet bipartitioning as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem that enables quantum annealing to replace the classical bipartitioning strategies underlying the QFM and QMC families of methods. We prove that our formulation uses the minimum possible number of qubits to represent bipartitions and that its energy function correctly orders satisfied, deferred, and violated quartets for any positive penalty weights. We implemented QUANTA on real D-Wave quantum annealing hardware, and evaluated it on a wide range of simulated and biological datasets. QUANTA achieves accuracy comparable to the state-of-the-art methods, including ASTRAL and wQFM, under challenging evolutionary conditions. We also reanalyzed several biological datasets, including the avian phylogenomic dataset comprising 14,446 genes across 48 genomes, on which QUANTA reconstructed a species tree with a higher quartet score than wQFM. Remarkably, despite running on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, QUANTA's bipartition technique achieved 4100x speedup over the FM bipartitioning technique in wQFM on bipartition containing 90-200 taxa, while maintaining comparable tree accuracy. By establishing a theoretically grounded, hardware-independent quantum optimization framework for weighted quartet amalgamation, QUANTA opens a new direction for quantum-assisted phylogenomics and provides a foundation for increasingly scalable and accurate species tree estimation as quantum computing hardware advances. QUANTA is publicly available at https://github.com/QuitttCat/QUANTA-Phylogenomics.

papers.title: Phase-locked dual-band vibration bursts strengthen anti-kindling by vibrotactile coordinated reset stimulation in a spiking network model
papers.abstract: Parkinsons disease and related movement disorders are accompanied by pathologically synchronized neuronal activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits. Coordinated reset (CR) stimulation was derived computationally as a means of suppressing such activity at its source, by resetting the phases of the subpopulations of a synchronized network at staggered times. Under spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), the resulting decorrelated firing depresses excitatory coupling and establishes a weakly coupled, desynchronized state that outlasts stimulation, a process termed anti-kindling. Sustained post-stimulation benefit has been demonstrated for electrical CR stimulation in parkinsonian primates and in proof-of-concept patient studies, and vibrotactile CR (vCR) stimulation realizes the same principle non-invasively through bursts of fingertip vibration. The deployed vCR protocol employs a carrier frequency of 250 Hz, which preferentially recruits Pacinian afferents. Because Pacinian receptive fields extend substantially beyond the stimulated digit, inputs originating at adjacent fingertips converge on overlapping regions of the target population, which degrades the spatial separation on which CR depends. Here we examine whether the spectral composition of the individual burst, independent of the stimulation schedule, governs the magnitude of anti-kindling. In a Hodgkin-Huxley network with STDP, driven through a two-channel model of fast-adapting afferents, a dual-band burst superimposing a 30 Hz component on the 250 Hz carrier yielded the lowest post-stimulation coupling among eleven vCR patterns, at one third of the carriers drive power. Recruitment of focal Meissner afferents by the 30 Hz component restricts part of the drive to the stimulated subpopulation, and phase locking of that component to the burst envelope generates post-burst pauses that reset the phase of the stimulated neurons. Spectral composition therefore determines both the spatial selectivity of vCR stimulation and its capacity for phase resetting.

papers.title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in gel environments
papers.abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different in vitro systems of interest. In this work, we present a genome-scale, metabolism-informed continuum model (GEM-CM), a computational framework for coupling a reaction-diffusion model to a surrogate GEM representation that generates metabolic rate predictions informed by flux balance analysis outputs. A key feature of GEM-CM is its application of random forest regression, or ensembles, to coarse-grain the interface connecting the GEM and reaction-diffusion models down to a small set of input metabolites methodically chosen through the random forests evaluation of feature importance. To demonstrate GEM-CMs utility, we evaluated simulation predictions against P. aeruginosa PA14 populations radially propagating in low weight percentage agar gels. In addition to biomass growth, we simulated PA14 populations producing the cytotoxic secondary metabolite pyocyanin (PCN). GEM-CM could capture PA14 growth dynamics in agar gels when ensembles were provided with three carbon source inputs describing the simulated growth media. Bacterial motility parameters and the random forest ensemble allowed GEM-CM simulations to accurately predict spatial biomass distributions for PA14 populations over time and probe their PCN production dynamics. Ensembles also demonstrated robust performance for single gene knockout conditions with GEM-CM simulation accurately capturing the partial or total biomass and PCN inhibition observed in transposon mutant screenings. When evaluating transposon mutant population development, the GEM-CM framework additionally suggested that metH may be a promising target to inhibit the spatial propagation of PA14. This works proof-of-concept applications illustrated GEM-CM utility as an early stage multi-scale modeling tool for interrogating in vitro metabolic behavior in microbial populations.

papers.title: Starve, stress, and mate: Activation of the CCAAT-Binding complex overrides sterility of mating-type heterozygous Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Sexual reproduction in the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans is typically restricted by a strict genetic lock: the a1-2 repressor present in standard mating-type heterozygous (MTLa/) diploid strains, which actively represses mating competency. While severe environmental pressures are known to influence fungal development, the molecular mechanisms that allow cells to override this genetic sterility block remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the highly conserved CCAAT-binding complex (CBC) as the critical developmental hub that integrates environmental stress to unlock mating in heterozygous diploids. By combining proteomic mapping (ChIP-SICAP) and transcriptomics (RNA-Seq) to define the regulatory network of the core CBC subunit Hap5, we demonstrate that CBC hyperactivation completely overrides the a1-2 repressor. This activation triggers a robust white-to-opaque phenotypic switch and initiates a mating-competence program in MTLa/ strains genetically locked in a sterile state. Crucially, this developmental transition is antagonized by the iron-regulatory partner Hap43, but is strictly dependent on physical interaction at the chromatin level with Cap1, the master regulator of the oxidative stress response. Our findings reveal that the CBC and Cap1 couple metabolic starvation (glucose and iron limitation) and oxidative stress to a core reproductive program, providing a mechanistic basis for how C. albicans bypasses genetic constraints on sexual reproduction to generate genetic diversity under hostile host conditions.

papers.title: Cross-excitation in dorsal root ganglia redistributes coding capacity from stimulus intensity to stimulus location
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of cross-excitation between neurons of dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) of mammals is widely known, yet its exact mechanism remains underexplored. In this work, we analyze the phenomenon as part of the signal processing performed by the body's somatosensory system. We argue that, if the mechanism is indeed as prevalent as it is reported in experimental works, it should provide a significant computational advantage. Here, we created a model network in which sensory A-type neurons are interconnected only via a chemical agent and showed that such a connection, when fitted with parameters similar to those observed in experiments, improves the stimulus-localization properties of the ganglia at the expense of intensity-encoding accuracy. Although this exchange is near-neutral in raw bits, it becomes favorable once the logarithmic compression of intensity perception - the Weber--Fechner law - is taken into account, since the sacrificed intensity capacity is largely perceptually redundant. We therefore propose that cross-excitation is not an imperfection of somatic isolation but an effective, chemically mediated pre-processing stage that sharpens spatial localization.

papers.title: Towards a foundation model for raw nanopore signal through discrete tokenization
papers.abstract: Nanopore sequencing reads nucleic acids as changes in ionic current that carry information beyond the base sequence. Self-supervised pretrained models have advanced genomic sequence modeling and single-cell analysis, but remain underexplored for raw nanopore signals, which are continuous and lack a native token vocabulary. Here we present Brieno, an approach combining reconstruction-based tokenization through residual vector quantization with a Transformer for contextual representation learning. We pretrain the Transformer using masked-token prediction on raw nanopore signals from 118 million reads. With frozen or fine-tuned features, the model identifies species without requiring reference genomes. It complements Dorado by accurately classifying reads left unclassified in native-barcode demultiplexing, approaches Dorado's basecalling performance across six genomes, and exceeds Dorado's specialized 5-methylcytosine model as well as a dedicated 6-methyladenine caller. Brieno also supports accurate CpG methylation detection with limited labeled data. Across tasks, pretrained contextual representations improve downstream performance over non-pretrained baselines and generalize across sequencing runs. Together, these findings support self-supervised pretraining as a basis for transferable representations of raw nanopore signals.

papers.title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
papers.abstract: Background Residual barcode-like sequences after preprocessing are a quality-control concern in multiplexed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing data, particularly in low-biomass, host-dominated samples such as blood. Using blood datasets spiked with a microbial mock community and prepared with the Native Barcoding Kit 96 V14 (SQK-NBD114.96), we compared Dorado 1.1.1, Dorado 2.0.0, and Barbell 0.3.2. Results Dorado demultiplexing reduced barcode-positive reads to approximately 2% of reads, with internal barcode-like matches in 0.17-0.19% of reads. Barbell 0.3.2 applied to untrimmed Dorado basecalls yielded an approximately 50-fold lower detector-defined internal-match rate (0.0035-0.0037%) while retaining 91.2-91.8% of input reads. In the NCBI core_nt release of 12 September 2026, the focused screen identified complete, ungapped 24 nt identity for 64 of the 96 barcodes (66.7%), comprising 505 distinct barcode-accession pairs across 482 accessions and 195 exported TaxID groups of mixed taxonomic ranks. Records annotated as rRNA genes, chromosomes/genomes, and plasmids accounted for 35.6%, 23.2%, and 22.4% of the pairs, respectively. The barcode was located within its native ligation flanks in 224 pairs (44.4%), including 170 (33.7%) with the complete Dorado barcode search window and 3 (0.6%) with the full adapter construct. Conclusion Barbell combined 91-92% read retention with lower detected internal barcode signals. After demultiplexing, barcode-like sequences remained in sample data. Moreover, kit barcode sequences, often within their native ligation flanks, were detected in reference records. Both findings call for careful preprocessing, reference inspection, and downstream validation. Further research should determine whether barcode-associated artifacts in reads and reference records affect taxonomic classification in clinical metagenomic workflows.

papers.title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase.
papers.abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription-replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription-replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of a diverse range of influenza virus evolution.

papers.title: Genomic signatures of positive selection and relaxed selective constraints associated with convergent dietary specialisation
papers.abstract: Island radiations provide ideal frameworks for studying the molecular basis of convergent evolution. The rapid diversification of Dysdera spiders in Canary Islands provides a striking example, with repeated dietary shifts towards specialisation on woodlice, accompanied by morphological, metabolic, and behavioural modifications that facilitate the exploitation of this heavy-metal-rich prey. Here, we investigate two independent events of dietary specialisation on different islands. By analysing six high-quality genome-assemblies, including three newly generated in this study, we investigate the genomic signals of positive selection and relaxed selection in protein-coding genes, upstream regulatory regions, and gene family turnover rates. We detected signatures of positive selection associated with the two specialists, accompanied by a twofold increase in gene loss rates relative to generalist ancestors. Notably, positive selection targeted a smaller, functionally coherent set of genes, potentially involved in detoxification likely through heavy metal excretion. In contrast, relaxation of selection affected a broader set of genes associated with functions that may have become dispensable under the new dietary regime. Furthermore, we found contractions in gene families associated with vesicular transport, potentially reflecting a reduced reliance on vesicle-mediated metal accumulation. Overall, our findings suggest that similar ecological pressures can drive parallel, yet non-identical, adaptive and non-adaptive responses, pointing to partially predictable evolutionary trajectories in an island radiation.

papers.title: Hyperactivity preferentially disrupts scotopic retinal circuits in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy
papers.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness worldwide. In this disease, visual impairments result from neurovascular dysfunction in the retina. However, the specific retinal circuits and the mechanisms underlying their dysfunction remain unclear. Here, in mouse models of diabetes, we evaluated scotopic (night vision) and photopic (day vision) retinal circuit function in the early stages of the disease. Using a combination of immunohistochemical, behavioral and electrophysiological techniques, we show that vision impairments early in the disease are not associated with widespread degeneration of the retinal circuitry but with abnormalities localized to scotopic circuits. Specifically, we observed swelling of axon terminals in rod but not cone bipolar cells. Importantly, these abnormalities were closely linked with bipolar cell activity, as rod bipolar cells showed higher intrinsic activity than cone bipolar cells, and inducing hyperactivity in control retinas was sufficient to recapitulate the pathology in diabetic rod bipolar cells. Further, the swollen rod bipolar cell terminals exhibited an increase in oxidative stress, consistent with cellular dysfunction. In line with this notion, electrophysiological measurements demonstrated that the contrast sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells was preferentially attenuated under scotopic conditions. Finally, behavioral experiments showed that visual sensitivity under scotopic conditions was affected earlier in disease progression compared to photopic conditions. Together, these findings reveal that scotopic circuits are preferentially affected in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy and that hyperactivity is sufficient to drive these abnormalities.

papers.title: Maltose-driven carbohydrate status and early raffinose synthesis enhance maturation efficiency in hybrid fir somatic embryogenesis
papers.abstract: Somatic embryogenesis (SE) is a critical biotechnological tool for the large-scale propagation of the Abies genus, which faces significant threats from climate change and high commercial demand. While sucrose is a first-choice energy source among conifers, firs often exhibit a dramatic preference for maltose. Using hybrid fir (Abies alba x numidica), we have shown an order-of-magnitude higher amount of mature cotyledonary embryos cultivated on maltose compared to sucrose. Determination of endogenous carbohydrate balance during maturation and post-maturation phases revealed fundamental difference in spectrum between sucrose (S) and maltose (M) variants, notably massive presence of hexoses in S variant and, remarkably, an earlier accumulation of raffinose in M variant, pointing to establishing a "mature" biochemical profile. After post-maturation desiccation treatment, though both variants accumulated raffinose family oligosaccharides (RFO), their proportion of in total carbohydrate content remained higher in M variant. Based on the results, we propose, that specific features of fir carbohydrate processing machinery (degradation and transport) resulted in slower but steady C and energy supply in M variant and represent the base of maltose superiority.

papers.title: A hierarchical Bayesian model for dynamic phenotypes in multi-environment trials with genotype by environment interaction
papers.abstract: New phenotyping tools produce longitudinal phenotypes that describe plant growth and development. Estimates for the parameters that describe the dynamics of such longitudinal phenotypes can be incorporated as predictors in models for static target traits like yield and biomass. Within a hierarchical Bayesian context, we present a differential equation (DE) model for log-logistic growth in longitudinal traits for sets of genotypes across multiple environments. The DE parameters coincide with a midpoint, a slope, and an asymptote at the end of growth and development, i.e., final biomass. Each DE parameter in our hierarchical model results from contributions of genotype, environment, and G x E. This formulation allows one to assess and quantify the genotype-specificity of the DE parameters. When none of the DE parameters in our model requires a G x E term, the dynamic parameters characterizing the particular trait will be useful features for inclusion in prediction models for yield or biomass. We fitted a DE model to APSIM-simulated longitudinal wheat biomass data and quantified the contribution of genotype, environment and G x E to the phenotypic variation in the DE parameters. Only the upper asymptote showed clear G x E. Estimates for genotypic and G x E parameters within the DE parameters were used to characterize genotypes. Estimates for environmental and G x E effects formed inputs for environmental characterization.

papers.title: Signatures for conserved phenolic-based acclimation responses to UV in a unicellular algal sister of land plants
papers.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) light is a major stressor that particularly comes to bear in the terrestrial habitat. As such it is among the major challenges that the earliest land plants had to overcome. The closest algal relatives of land plants, the zygnematophytes, are single celled and filamentous algae that - in the context of their terrestrial and freshwater habitats - have diverse adaptations to UV irradiance. As such, contextualized with data on land plants, zygnematophyte algae harbor important information for inferring how the earliest land plants have acclimated to UV. Here we exposed the unicellular zygnematophyte model Mesotaenium to daily UV irradiance and assessed its response through microscopy, untargeted metabolomics, and global gene expression profiling using transcriptomics. Our data reveal cell biological acclimation by formation of lipid droplets. Further, we find that the cells accumulated chemodiverse coumarin-like derivatives. Altogether, our data suggest that acclimation to long-term UV exposure is composed of building blocks of a molecular chassis conserved with that of land plants, underpinned by phenolics and genes that are tied to their biosynthesis. From this chassis, divergent evolutionary trajectories have assembled them into a divergent conformation - one of which ushering in the emergence of the phenylpropanoid pathway.

papers.title: Clinical relevance of diffusion tensor imaging-based parameters estimated with deep learning: the effect of model retraining
papers.abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based approaches have recently become powerful tools for characterizing microstructural properties of brain tissue from diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging data. These techniques enable depicting microstructural features with significantly reduced acquisition schemes while preserving relatively high image-quality metrics compared with non-DL-based approaches. Learning-based methods have increasingly been applied to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and more advanced multi-compartmental biophysical models, with the potential to facilitate multiparameter analyses of brain microstructure in clinical settings. However, independently trained DL models-while maintaining image-quality properties-do not appear to preserve the statistical properties of groupwise analyses across independently trained models. In this study, we systematically evaluate the statistical properties of DL-based DTI parameters across independently trained neural networks under the same architecture to preserve group-level effects in bipolar disorder. We examine the impact of model retraining and its dependence on reducing the number of gradient directions compared with the nonlinear least-squares (NLLS) procedure. Our results show that initializing model weights randomly from a uniform distribution, while keeping the network architecture and training hyperparameters the identical in the experiment, leads to significant variation in the statistical properties of DTI measures inferred from independently trained models. The analyses showed that the true positive rate in groupwise analysis using the DL-based DTI parameters ranges from 0\% to 100\% compared with the NLLS-based analysis. As the number of gradient directions increased, the NLLS procedure yielded more stable groupwise statistical results, whereas independently trained DL models showed greater variability despite similar image-quality agreement with reference maps. The results indicate that the DTI maps retrieved from a single trained network should be treated with great caution before drawing clinical conclusions.

papers.title: Theoretical prediction of assembly contiguity
papers.abstract: Theoretical methods for predicting the performance of assembly algorithms have the potential to guide experimental design on a scale that simulations cannot. A fundamental question of experimental design is how deep to sequence in order to obtain an assembly with long-enough contigs. More precisely, given a certain read length and coverage, what is the expected contig length that an assembler would produce on a given genome? The foundational work of Lander and Waterman tackled this question, but their method is not applicable to modern high-throughput sequencing. In this paper, we derive what we call a Z-value, which is a formula that takes as input the read length, coverage, and basic properties of the genome, and returns a prediction of the mean contig length produced by a simple single-k assembler on error-free data. We show on a benchmark of 14 genomes that the Z-value is highly accurate, with a mean absolute prediction error of less than 2 percent. We further show how this formula can be used to determine the best choice of k for the assembler and how to choose a coverage level that gives contig lengths within a desired fraction of the optimal. Finally, we show how the Z-value can also predict the performance of a more complicated assembler like Velvet and how it can be used to guide the choice between instruments when there is a tradeoff between coverage and read length and the budget is limited.

papers.title: Maximum Likelihood Localization Maps
papers.abstract: Single-molecule localization microscopy commonly reconstructs images from estimated emitter coordinates. We calculate maximum-likelihood localization maps (MLLM), a non-iterative approach that evaluates positional likelihood from measured data and a supplied point-spread function. The MLLM of each detected single molecule image is added into a final upsampled image representing the overall molecular probability map, preserving the positional likelihood structure and obviating separate coordinate-based rendering. MLLM calculation is noniterative, fast, supports any calibrated point-spread function, accounts for local background variation, supports two- and three-dimensional reconstruction, and can be calculated in parallel.

papers.title: Microglial AhR Drives Sex-Biased Amyloid Pathology
papers.abstract: Microglia integrate local and systemic signals that can modify their response to amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), but the molecular pathways connecting these signals to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a sensor of microbiota- and host-derived metabolites, as a microglial regulator of amyloid pathology. Sustained administration of the AhR agonist indoxyl-3-sulfate (I3S) exacerbated cortical A{beta} deposition and plaque-associated neuritic damage in APPNL-F mice. Conversely, constitutive AhR deficiency reduced amyloid burden, promoted plaque compaction, and preserved behavioural performance, whereas inducible deletion of AhR in microglia was sufficient to reduce plaque accumulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that AhR loss reprogrammed microglia toward phagolysosomal and A{beta}-recognition states and enhanced microglial A{beta} uptake, with markedly stronger effects in females. APPNL-F mice also exhibited sex-dependent remodelling of the gut microbiota and tryptophan-derived metabolites. Circulating indole-3-aldehyde (IAld) robustly activated AhR and was associated with cortical amyloid pathology. AhR-activating bioactivity was increased in mouse serum, cortex and faecal extracts and was higher in serum from the COGNIBIO12 analytical subcohort than in independently recruited cognitively unimpaired H2H participants. Among amyloid-positive patients, higher serum AhR bioactivity was associated with lower CSF A{beta}42 concentrations. Together, these findings identify microglial AhR as a metabolically responsive regulator linking systemic ligand availability, biological sex, and microglial control of amyloid pathology.

papers.title: Ribosomal Remodeling and Translational Suppression in the Post-Arrest Heart
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest (CA) is a leading cause of death and disability in the United States, and no pharmacologic therapies improve post-arrest outcomes. Acute myocardial dysfunction is a highly prevalent CA complication that contributes to post-arrest mortality, yet the molecular mechanisms that drive this dysfunction remain incompletely understood. Prior work in our laboratory has suggested that ribosome-associated pathways are altered after CA in the heart and that translational dysregulation may be a central feature of post-arrest myocardial injury. Objectives: To define the impact of CA on myocardial ribosome biology and protein synthesis across experimental models of CA and determine how transcriptome, ribosome-bound transcriptome, translational efficiency, and proteome changes evolve after CA in the heart. Methods: We studied complementary porcine and murine models of CA. In pigs, left ventricular myocardium was collected from naive controls, cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation (Arrest), and cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA) re-arrest in a myocardial infarction-induced CA model and analyzed tissue by RNA sequencing. In mice, left ventricular tissue was collected at various time points after potassium chloride-induced asystole and resuscitation for ribosome activity and multi-omic profiling including RNA sequencing, ribosome profiling, and proteomics. Results: In the porcine model, myocardial transcriptomes demonstrate enrichment of cytosolic ribosomal protein transcripts and translation-related pathways that increase with ischemic burden. In contrast, a functional assay of ribosome activity in mice demonstrates suppression of protein synthesis after CA with gradual recovery over days. Multi-omic profiling in the mouse model demonstrates that ribosome- and translation-related pathways are among the most consistently altered programs across time points and modalities. While 6 h studies note prevalent inflammatory signals, 24 h studies find disruptions to ion homeostasis and conduction-related pathways that are likely related to translational suppression. Conclusions: CA induces marked remodeling of myocardial ribosome biology, characterized by increasing ribosomal transcripts with ischemic burden in the pig model. However, functional studies in the mouse model demonstrate that ribosome activity is suppressed following CA and remains suppressed for at least 24 h after resuscitation, contributing to reduced nascent protein synthesis and may limit critical functions of the heart. These findings identify translational control as a central feature of post-arrest myocardial injury and suggest that ribosome-dependent recovery pathways may represent a novel therapeutic target in post-arrest cardiac dysfunction.

papers.title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

papers.title: Historical contingency is revealed by trade-offs upon sequential adaptation to different infection routes
papers.abstract: Past adaptation can shape how populations respond to subsequent selection. Because host-pathogen interactions vary widely in their ecological and physiological context, they provide a powerful system for testing the role of historical contingency in adaptation. Here, we evolved replicate populations of Drosophila melanogaster, previously adapted to systemic infection with Pseudomonas entomophila, under oral exposure to the same pathogen. Both evolutionary histories evolved increased survival under oral infection, but previous systemic adaptation altered the trajectory of this response in a sex-dependent manner. Females with a history of systemic selection began with lower oral-infection survival, yet adapted more rapidly than controls, whereas males showed weaker history-dependent differences. These contrasting trajectories could not be attributed simply to an overall loss of standing genetic variation in the founder populations. Adaptation to oral infection also incurred a trade-off, reducing survival under systemic infection, whereas the fecundity cost of infection did not differ between evolutionary histories. Finally, sex- and generation-specific changes in bacterial clearance revealed that adaptation to oral infection involved distinct mechanistic responses alongside shared genetic components. Together, our results show that past selection shapes both the tempo and mechanism of adaptation, revealing that responses to different infection ecologies are built on partially shared, but also route-specific, genetic architectures.

papers.title: Predicting Transcriptional Responses to Unseen Compounds through Context Modeling and Multi-View Transfer
papers.abstract: Predicting drug-induced transcriptional responses could support in silico screening of new compounds, yet existing models barely use the compound: on a drug-blind L1000 benchmark, removing the drug input from seven published models changes accuracy by at most 0.012 Pearson correlation. They capture shared cellular and experimental variation while overlooking the compound-specific signals that distinguish drug effects. We present UnDetect, a framework that separates contextual variation from compound effects to predict responses to transcriptionally unprofiled compounds. UnDetect integrates chemical structure, annotated targets, mechanisms of action and Cell Painting morphology into a normalized multi-view kernel that accommodates incomplete compound information, and transfers residual responses within and across profiled cell lines, so that pharmacological and phenotypic relationships inform predictions beyond chemical similarity. On a drug-blind benchmark, where the paired control reveals the assay plate, UnDetect is the only model to beat a network that ignores the compound, in every fold; on a within-plate score that is zero for any compound-blind prediction, it reaches 0.117 against 0.092 for the strongest published model. On DeepCE's benchmark it reaches 0.602 Pearson correlation against the reported 0.491. Transfer across cell lines improves 28 of 28 LINCS L1000 and, at the two higher doses, 47 and 49 of 50 Tahoe-100M cell-line evaluations. These results show that separating context from compound effects and integrating complementary compound information improves transcriptional prediction and extends the utility of perturbation atlases for virtual screening.

papers.title: Multi-Criteria Evaluation of Hibiscus mutabilis Cultivars for Food Development Using Delphi and Analytic Hierarchy Process
papers.abstract: This study evaluated 11 Hibiscus mutabilis cultivars from Chengdu Botanical Garden to assess their quality for food use and identify promising cultivars. An evaluation framework was developed using the Delphi method to select indicators and the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) to determine their weights. Overall scores ranged from 2.5785 to 3.6043, and the cultivars were classified into three grades. Grade I included Hibiscus mutabilis 'Bairi Huacai', Hibiscus mutabilis 'Chongbanbai' and Hibiscus mutabilis 'Jinqiusong'; Grade II included Hibiscus mutabilis 'Jinqiuhong', Hibiscus mutabilis 'Zuifurong', Hibiscus mutabilis 'Danbanhong', Hibiscus mutabilis 'Jinxiuzi', Hibiscus mutabilis 'Jinbiyu' and Hibiscus mutabilis 'Caixia'; whereas Grade III included Hibiscus mutabilis 'Mudanfen' and Hibiscus mutabilis 'Jinrui'. In summary, Hibiscus mutabilis 'Bairi Huacai', Hibiscus mutabilis 'Chongbanbai' and Hibiscus mutabilis 'Jinqiusong' are the preferred cultivars for food processing and development. The framework provides a basis for cultivar screening and further evaluation of H. mutabilis flowers for food use.

papers.title: Curved geometry shapes the observability of hippocampal oscillations
papers.abstract: Curved neural architectures reshape the spatial distribution of field oscillations, complicating the identification of their underlying generators. To test these principles experimentally, here we resolve the paradoxical poor expression of theta oscillations in the hilus of the folded dentate gyrus (DG), a region that otherwise exhibits some of the largest FPs in the brain. Using laminar recordings across both hippocampi and computational modeling, we show that theta is locally masked by cancellation of phase-coherent contributions. Theta generators in CA1 and DG produce volume-conducted fields that, due to the curved geometry of the DG, exhibit opposite dipolar orientations in the hilus, leading to regional cancellation. In contrast, beta and gamma generators are only weakly coordinated across hippocampal regions and therefore remain prominently expressed despite the same geometry. These results demonstrate that theta amplitude, local observability, spatial segregation and apparent translocation emerge from the interplay between geometry and temporal coherence among distributed generators, with tissue geometry acting as a spatial filter for coherent activity.

papers.title: The enemy of my enemy: A bacterial antagonist rescues Chlamydomonas by inactivating a toxin from a rival
papers.abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bacteria that coexist in the same soil habitat. In pairwise cultures, all three interactions are amensalistic (-like): Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 antagonizes both C. reinhardtii and Pseudomonas fluorescens HKI0770 without benefit, while P. fluorescens inhibits C. reinhardtii without profiting from the alga. However, in a tripartite culture, P. fluorescens protects C. reinhardtii from P. protegens and promotes algal recovery. This protection is not stopped when the used carbon source, acetate, is supplemented. The P. fluorescens rescue effect is associated with reduced levels of the polyyne toxin protegencin produced by P. protegens. Protegencin levels, detected by Raman microspectroscopy, are decreased by application of spent medium or protein extracts from P. fluorescens, while heat- and protease-treatment abolish this activity. A heat-sensitive, proteinaceous factor, likely an enzyme(s), appears to contribute to protegencin inactivation. Our results show that P. fluorescens rescues C. reinhardtii by inactivating protegencin, despite being inhibited by P. protegens. These findings demonstrate the importance of investigating higher-order effects, since additional community members can transform pairwise antagonistic interactions into conditional protection through toxin inactivation.

papers.title: Genomic and Epigenomic Relationships Capture Different Patterns of Genotype-by-Environment Interaction in Grapevine Clones
papers.abstract: Genotype-by-environment interaction (GEI) challenges selection in clonally propagated perennial crops by reducing the consistency of clone performance across years. In perennial crops, both genetic and epigenetic variation are likely to contribute to complex trait variation among clones. However, the extent to which each molecular source contribute to GEI remains poorly understood. Here, we used UMR-seq, an assay that recovers SNPs and unmethylated-region (UMR; DNA methylation) profiles from a single library, to generate paired genomic and epigenomic profiles for 206 Riesling (Vitis vinifera L.) clones phenotyped for yield and juice quality traits across nine growing seasons. We then partitioned the contribution of each omic layer to clonal variation and GEI, and examined the genomic distribution of their effects. In models without explicit GEI, environmental and residual effects were the largest source of phenotypic variance and the clonal main effect was modest. Genomic relationships accounted for most of the clonal variance in four of five traits, and adding an epigenomic relationship matrix (ERM) to the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) had little effect. In contrast, when GEI effects were modelled using factor-analytic covariance structures, the epigenomic layer captured a substantial proportion of GEI variance and exceeded the genomic contribution in four of five traits. The two omic layers differed not only in the amount of GEI captured, but also in the pattern of clone re-ranking across years. When back-solved effects were aggregated into genomic windows, the largest genomic and epigenomic effects tended to fall in different regions, with overlap no greater than expected by chance. Together, these results show that genomic and epigenomic relationships capture complementary components of year-to-year variation in clone performance, with the epigenomic contribution expressed primarily through GEI. These findings provide a basis for investigating the molecular drivers of GEI and for testing whether genomic and epigenomic information can inform selection for stable clonal performance across variable environments.

papers.title: Lysenin Induced Membrane Curvature on Erythrocytes and Nanoporous Mica Free Standing Membranes
papers.abstract: Beta porin toxins are virulence factors that oligomerize in host cell membranes, forming beta-barrel pores that permeabilize target cells, leading to osmotic imbalance, cell lysis, and immune evasion. Despite extensive research on beta-pore-forming toxins (PFTs), significant gaps remain in understanding their role as actors of large-scale supramolecular membrane remodeling. While beta-PFTs are traditionally viewed as passive cylindrical conduits, their biological efficacy is fundamentally tied to an evolved ability to structurally alter the host cell membrane. In this study, we combine erythrocytes, model membranes and a novel engineered nanopores on mica substrates. We overcome the limitation of traditional mica substrates and demonstrate that lysenin pores do not merely permeabilize the membrane; they curve it into rigid, dome-like supramolecular structures. Moreover, to gain biophysical insight beyond the standard membrane models which do not directly consider the membrane insertions, we propose a hybrid model combining the biophysical models and the architectural models of pendentive domes, where the intrinsic wedge-shaped geometry of the monomers is considered. Experimental mechanical assessment of the lysenins domes shows a non-linear mechanical of stiffness with respect the radius of curvature as predicted by our hybrid model. Collectively, our work suggests that the beta-PFTs induce membrane curvature by the assembly of wedges. Beyond their pore-forming function, this membrane-bending activity may represent an additional mechanism by which beta-PFTs interfere with host-cell membrane repair.

papers.title: CD300f is required for efficient lipid handling during cuprizone-induced demyelination
papers.abstract: Microglia play a crucial role in central nervous system homeostasis and response to demyelination, yet the mechanisms that coordinate the sensing and processing of myelin-derived lipids remain poorly understood. CD300f is a lipid-sensing innate immune receptor expressed by myeloid cells that has been implicated in tissue damage sensing, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. Here, we investigated the role of CD300f in the cuprizone-induced demyelination model. Using CD300f-deficient mice, we demonstrate exacerbated demyelination, increased lipid droplet accumulation, impaired microglial responses, and reduced remyelination accompanied by motor coordination deficits. Bulk RNA sequencing of the corpus callosum at the peak of demyelination revealed enrichment of homeostatic, disease-associated (DAM), and foamy microglial signatures, together with increased expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, phagocytosis, inflammation, and lipid metabolism. Notably, these transcriptional changes were associated with marked lipid droplet accumulation in microglia and enrichment of microglial states previously linked to chronic demyelinating lesions. These findings suggest that CD300f is required for efficient handling of myelin-derived lipids and for microglial metabolic adaptation during demyelination. Our study identifies CD300f as a critical regulator of microglial function and lipid homeostasis and highlights this receptor as a potential therapeutic target in demyelinating diseases.

papers.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics
papers.abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distinguish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

papers.title: Opposing Roles of Cholesterol and Cholesterol Sulfate in Proton Transfer and Diffusion at Membrane Interfaces
papers.abstract: Sterols are fundamental components of biological membranes that modulate membrane fluidity and organisation, yet their role in governing interfacial proton dynamics remains underexplored. Here, we elucidate how cholesterol (Ch) and cholesterol sulfate (ChS) regulate excited-state proton transfer (PT) and long-range proton diffusion (PD) using a complementary dual-approach experimental framework combined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Using a membrane-anchored photoacid in small unilamellar vesicles, we demonstrate that Ch accelerates local PT dynamics in gel-phase phosphatidylcholine membranes by inducing a fluid, liquid-ordered phase. Surprisingly, ChS inhibits local PT despite its negative headgroup. MD simulations reveal this inhibition stems from deeper probe embedding within ChS containing bilayers and the reduced basicity of sulfate relative to phosphate. Conversely, solid-state electrical measurements on supported lipid bilayers show a stark reversal for long range proton conduction (lateral PD): ChS increases lateral proton conductance by 400 fold under controlled relative humidity, whereas Ch decreases conductivity. This divergence arises mainly because ChS supplies titratable sulfate charge carriers, whereas Ch dilutes key phosphate proton mediators that promote a percolating interfacial hydrogen bonding network without providing charge carriers. Our findings demonstrate that sterols exert scale-dependent control over membrane PT/PD, revealing how headgroup chemistry, membrane fluidity, and hydration synergistically govern bioenergetic proton dynamics.

papers.title: Integrative identification of Tetratostichococcus sp. CCAH0201 (Trebouxiophyceae, Chlorophyta) from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam
papers.abstract: A microalgal strain from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam, was examined by light microscopy and three molecular markers. Thirty-six cells from 22 micrographs measured 6.68-12.74 by 3.49-4.79 micrometres. Homologous phylogenetic windows comprised 550 nucleotides for SSU rDNA, 711 for ITS and 1,170 for rbcL. CCAH0201, P1 and Tetratostichococcus jenerensis SAG 2138 shared the SSU 3-prime sequence, whereas ITS and rbcL placed CCAH0201 with P1 (SH-aLRT/UFBoot 87/94 and 96.9/99). CCAH0201 differed from P1 at 22/711 ITS and 4/1,170 rbcL sites. Structure-guided ITS2 comparison identified one strict CBC, one two-sided change from a wobble pair and three hemi-CBCs relative to P1. CCAH0201 is thus identified as Tetratostichococcus sp. in a lineage close to P1.

papers.title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (Mapping of Cryptic Hidden Intronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.

papers.title: LeadWeaver: Topology-Aware Masked-Lead Modeling for Robust 12-Lead ECG Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Clinical electrocardiography is organized as a structured set of correlated leads, yet most neural ECG classifiers assume that all twelve leads are present, correctly ordered, and acquired under the same device conditions at training and deployment. We propose LeadWeaver, a topology-aware ECG representation model designed for diagnosis under missing, corrupted, or device-shifted leads. LeadWeaver represents each lead as a temporal token stream, couples leads through a fixed-plus-learned physiological lead graph, and performs masked-lead latent completion rather than waveform synthesis. A reliability router estimates which observed leads should dominate each diagnostic decision, while a consistency objective aligns complete-lead and incomplete-lead predictions. We evaluate the model on PTB-XL and CPSC-style settings using complete-input diagnosis, arbitrary missing-lead subsets, lead corruption, cross-dataset transfer, calibration, and selective prediction. The central hypothesis is that robust ECG diagnosis requires explicitly modeling both inter-lead topology and uncertainty about unavailable evidence, rather than treating missing channels as zero-valued inputs.

papers.title: Development of a Pan-Proteome Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Nipah Virus Using Reverse Vaccinology and Immunoinformatics Approaches
papers.abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a high-consequence zoonotic pathogen for which no licensed human vaccine is currently available. This study applied a consensus-guided pan-proteome immunoinformatics framework to design and prioritize a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using sequence information from all nine NiV proteins. A total of 901 NiV protein sequences were retrieved, of which 842 passed quality filtering and were processed through clustering, multiple-sequence alignment, and protein-specific consensus generation. Consensus-derived fragments were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte, helper T-lymphocyte, and B-cell epitopes, followed by multi-criterion filtering based on antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservancy, class-specific immune-response properties, and human-proteome similarity. Ten epitope-selection strategies were combined with two adjuvant candidates and three construct architectures to generate 60 vaccine constructs. Shortlisted candidates were subsequently evaluated for physicochemical properties, HLA population coverage, structural characteristics, conformational B-cell epitopes, TLR3 docking, molecular dynamics, immune-response simulation, and expression-oriented optimization. VC033_V6_BD_L03 construct was prioritized as the lead candidate and showed combined predicted population coverage of 99.78% worldwide and 99.96% in South Asia. Docking against human TLR3 structure 1ZIW yielded a ClusPro score of -1624.8. During a 100-ns molecular-dynamics simulation, the complex underwent early conformational reorganization followed by lower late-phase structural variation and persistent interchain hydrogen bonding. MM/GBSA analysis yielded a mean interaction-energy estimate of -20.52, 15.42 kcal/mol. C-ImmSim predicted coordinated humoral and cellular responses, while codon optimization generated a 1,539-bp expression sequence compatible with virtual cloning into pET-28a(+). These analyses prioritize VC033_V6_BD_L03 as a consensus-derived, pan-proteome NiV multi-epitope vaccine candidate for experimental evaluation of expression, immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy.

papers.title: Evolutionary dynamics of the pan-centromere architecture in oaks
papers.abstract: Centromeres ensure faithful chromosome segregation and genome stability, yet their DNA evolves rapidly, presenting a long-standing centromere paradox. Here we characterise the genomic and epigenomic architecture of >1,300 candidate centromeres from 111 high-quality Quercus (oak) genomes. We show that lineage-specific expansion of QuCEN146 satellite drives centromere turnover in oaks by displacing ancestral LTR-rich sequences into flanking regions, with genetic drift facilitating fixation of satellite-rich centromeres. Population-scale analyses in Q. serrata reveal extensive variation in satellite rich centromeres, generated by array expansion and contraction, strand-orientation shifts, and interspecific introgression. By contrast, LTR rich centromeres of Q. variabilis exhibit extremely low polymorphism and high collinearity across populations, sustained by suppressed local recombination, linked selection, and constrained LTR dynamics. We further demonstrate chromosome-independent evolutionary patterns for both satellite-rich and LTR-rich centromeres. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how evolutionary processes drive centromere turnover and shape contrasting centromeric sequence landscapes in forest trees.

papers.title: Highly conserved talin isoforms encode distinct mechanical responses and ligand-binding capabilities
papers.abstract: Talin is a central mechanosensitive adaptor that links integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and converts mechanical force into biochemical signals. Vertebrates express two highly homologous talin isoforms, talin-1 and talin-2, yet the molecular basis for their nonredundant functions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how isoform-specific sequence differences alter the mechanical response and ligand-binding capabilities of the talin rod. Using single-molecule force spectroscopy and biochemical binding assays, we show that talin-2 preserves the overall mechanical architecture of talin-1 but exhibits distinct mechanical responses in key rod regions. Talin-2 R7-R9 exhibits a previously unobserved three-domain cooperative unfolding pathway, while an alternative sequential pathway reveals early unfolding of R9 at substantially lower force than in talin-1. Strikingly, talin-2 R4-R6 has acquired two additional mechanically regulated interactions: a previously unrecognized vinculin-binding site in R5 and an A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP) region within R5-R6 that recruits protein kinase A (PKA). Together with the conserved R9 AKAP site, this establishes two spatially separated, mechanically regulated PKA-anchoring regions within the talin-2 scaffold. These findings establish that isoform-specific sequence divergence not only reshapes the mechanical response of the talin scaffold but also expands its repertoire of force-regulated interactions, providing a mechanism for the assembly of different structural and signaling complexes in an isoform-dependent manner.

papers.title: Deep transcriptomic analysis of molecular mediators of complex traits in heterogeneous stock (HS) rats
papers.abstract: Rats are a powerful model organism for genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of physiological and behavioral traits. Heterogeneous Stock (HS) rats, which were created by intercrossing 8 inbred rat strains, are heavily used for this purpose because of their genetic diversity and accumulated recombinations due to over 100 generations of outbreeding, which improves mapping precision. However, functional genomics resources for post-GWAS interpretation of genomic findings have been limited. We processed 3,160 RNA-seq samples, 1,932 of which were previously unpublished, from 13 tissues as part of RatGTEx. We used Pantry to quantify six modalities of transcriptome regulation (expression, isoform ratio, intron excision ratio, alternative transcription start site (TSS), alternative poly(A), and RNA stability) in each sample, which allowed us to identify 144,876 independent quantitative trait loci (QTL) for 22,599 genes. We performed a transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) with 19,796 unique genes across tissues and transcriptional modalities and 308 traits collected from 14 studies using FUSION, which identified 7,473 significant gene-trait associations. This work presents a significant expansion of the RatGTEx resource in terms of samples, modes of transcriptome regulation, and genetic analyses. Our findings provide molecular evidence for the involvement of specific genes in mediating GWAS signals through a range of transcriptome regulatory mechanisms. These gene-to-phenotype relationships can be easily applied to genetic analyses in humans and other species. Further experiments can use this evidence to confirm these molecular mediators and target them for the treatment of behavioral and physiological traits and disorders. To facilitate use of these results, we have updated results on RatGTEx.org and provided a new interactive TWAS web portal (twas.ratgtex.org).

papers.title: A novel KIR3DL2-directed CAR T-cell therapy for cutaneous and systemic T-cell lymphomas
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but its extension to T-cell lymphomas (TCLs) has been constrained by the paucity of antigens that can be safely targeted. While targeting pan-T antigens broadens the therapeutic reach across various TCLs, it carries a substantial risk of immunosuppression and infection. Here, we report killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, three Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 2 (KIR3DL2/CD158k) as a viable target for CAR T-cell therapy against a wide range of TCLs. Using single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and flow cytometric phenotyping, we observed that KIR3DL2 expression is restricted to a subset of mature NK cells and a minor fraction of CD8 T cells, with negligible expression in other healthy adult tissues. Among TCLs, KIR3DL2 expression was noted in various subtypes of cutaneous and systemic TCLs. Anti-KIR3DL2 CAR constructs (3DL2CARs) efficiently and selectively redirected T cells against antigen-positive cell lines but not isogenic KIR3DL2-negative counterparts, with antigen-specific signaling, cytotoxicity, proliferation, and cytokine production. Importantly, 3DL2CART cells produced sustained tumor regression and prolonged survival in two distinct cell line-derived xenograft models of cutaneous TCL and in one patient-derived xenograft model of hepatosplenic TCL. 3DL2CART cells exhibited minimal off-target activity against bystander immune cells and showed no appreciable fratricide. To mitigate the risk of tumor cell contamination in autologous CAR T-cell products, we established a two-tiered strategy that integrates immunomagnetic depletion of KIR3DL2-positive tumor cells with in vivo activation of a safety switch if inadvertently transduced malignant cells contribute to immune escape. Together, our results establish the preclinical efficacy and safety of 3DL2CART-cell therapy and support its clinical translation. This approach may offer a targeted alternative to pan-T-cell-directed CAR T-cell strategies for patients with relapsed/refractory cutaneous and systemic TCLs, addressing a critical unmet clinical need.

papers.title: Multi-omics integration reveals candidate genes and molecular mechanisms associated with resistance to sugarcane smut
papers.abstract: Sugarcane smut, caused by the fungus Sporisorium scitamineum (Syd.), is one of the main diseases affecting sugarcane and is capable of causing severe yield losses in susceptible varieties. Given the limitations of classical breeding, mainly due to the genetic complexity of sugarcane cultivars, molecular and omics approaches have gained increasing prominence for studying the genetic basis of traits such as disease resistance. In this context, we investigated sugarcane resistance to smut through the integration of association mapping methods and transcriptomics. A panel of 155 genotypes was genotyped with 33,335 SNP markers and inoculated with S. scitamineum generating three phenotypic variables. These data were jointly analyzed through genome-wide association analyses to identify marker-trait associations. In addition, transcriptomic analyses were performed using publicly available datasets from four studies evaluating sugarcane responses to smut. The integration of these multi-omics data enabled the identification of candidate genes involved in structural reinforcement, immune signaling, redox homeostasis, genome maintenance, and cellular adaptation. These findings provide valuable molecular resources for functional validation and breeding strategies aimed at developing sugarcane cultivars with enhanced smut resistance.

papers.title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
papers.abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.

papers.title: Developmental interactions between oscillatory and spontaneous neural activity support improvements in inhibitory control from adolescence into adulthood
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period of development marked by improvements in cognitive control driven by maturation of executive brain systems. Neural mechanisms supporting inhibitory control (the ability to suppress a prepotent response in favor of generating a goal-directed response) mature into adulthood in parallel with refinements in frequency-specific neural oscillations and broadband spontaneous activity, supporting more accurate and reliable performance on response inhibition tasks, such as the antisaccade oculomotor task. Prior work has established that the maturation of neural circuitry contributes to age-related decreases in spontaneous activity, supporting higher-fidelity transmission of task-relevant activity, such as frequency-specific neural oscillations, which are crucial for antisaccade performance. Using longitudinal electroencephalography (EEG) data from 146 participants (72 F, ages 10-34, 253 total sessions) collected while participants performed an antisaccade task, we sought to understand the interplay between frontal oscillatory and spontaneous activity during cognitive processing and how it supports developmental improvements in inhibitory control. We found that spontaneous activity decreased developmentally during the preparation of an inhibitory response, and that this was associated with reduced trial-to-trial variability in response latency, indicating that reductions in spontaneous activity may increase the reliability of inhibitory control processing. Furthermore, performance-related decreases in broadband spontaneous activity were associated with the suppression of preparatory high-beta oscillations in an age-dependent manner, such that this relationship became more pronounced through development. Together, these results illustrate how developmental enhancements in the coordination of frequency-specific oscillations and spontaneous activity during inhibitory response preparation support developmental improvements in inhibitory control, providing a potential mechanism through which inhibitory control becomes more accurate and reliable from adolescence into adulthood.

papers.title: Stepwise assembly and mechanical stability of nsP3 Helical Scaffolds in Chikungunya Virus
papers.abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus that replicates its genome through a viral replication complex (RC) essential for successful infection. The RC consists of four non-structural proteins: nsP1, nsP2, nsP3, and nsP4. In this study, we focused on nsP3, which comprises three distinct domains: the alphavirus unique domain (AUD), the long and intrinsically disordered hypervariable domain (HVD), and the enzymatic macrodomain (MD). Notably, nsP3 assembles into helicoidal macrostructures, termed helical scaffolds (HSs), which are components of the CHIKV replication complex and are involved in the formation of macromolecular traps in the cytoplasm of the infected cell called Alphagranules (AGs). HSs form tubular helical scaffolds assembled through the AUD, with the MD and HVD flexibly deployed to the scaffold exterior. Despite their functional importance, the mechanisms governing HS formation remain poorly understood. Using High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy (HS-AFM) and Electron Microscopy (EM) we achieved new findings on the structure, mechanics and assembly of these macrostructures. Our results show the nsP3 monomers follow intermediate steps before completing the assembly into full helical scaffolds, with each nsP3 domain contributing differently to this process. The macrodomain (MD) provides mechanical stability, yet it fractures under tens of piconewtons of force. This rigidity acts as a mechanical regulator that constrains the position of the HVD, which in turn mediates interactions with host factors and neighboring HSs. Through this interplay, nsP3 achieves both structural cohesion and functional adaptability, promoting the higher-order organization of HSs into honeycomb-like networks.

papers.title: Breaking the bottleneck: semi-automated quantification of actin filament dynamics
papers.abstract: Actin reconstitution assays visualized by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy have been crucial for defining mechanisms of filament assembly, disassembly, and higher-order organization. Yet quantitative analysis remains slow, labor-intensive, and subject to investigator bias. We developed SMAUG (Single filament Measurement and Analysis Using a GUI), a semi-automated image analysis interface that extends TSOAX filament segmentation and tracking with user-verified trace analysis of time-lapse TIRF images. SMAUG generates kymographs and quantifies filament nucleation, elongation, pausing, junctions, and filament-associated fluorescence while retaining measurements at the individual filament level. We tested the approach across actin reconstitution assays producing concentration-dependent polymerization, formin-stimulated elongation, capping-induced arrest, Arp2/3 branching, and fascin-mediated bundling. SMAUG reproduced manual measurement while reducing analysis time and revealed where dense networks and bundled filaments require user validation. Together, TSOAX and SMAUG provide a semi-automated approach for quantitative analysis of actin filament dynamics.

papers.title: Asymmetric division and polar growth define a non-canonical cell cycle in Bradyrhizobium.
papers.abstract: Bradyrhizobia are widely used as plant growth promoters in agriculture, yet their cell biology remains poorly understood. Here, we described for the first time, nucleoid segregation dynamics and the cell cycle of Bradyrhizobium at the cellular level.
