In PiB+ older adults, higher tau burden was associated with a task-induced collapse of network segregation across large-scale networks. These findings reveal dissociable influences of dopamine and tau on rest-to-task network organization, highlighting the value of integrating neuromodulatory and pathological markers in aging research.

papers.title: Global repression of mesenchymal genes in epithelial cells by the histone demethylase LSD1
papers.abstract: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is an essential process in development, tissue repair, and tumour metastasis, and is triggered by SNAI, ZEB and TWIST transcription factors, that recruit lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) to repress epithelial genes such as E-cadherin. In mesenchymal cells, LSD1 inhibition restores E-cadherin expression and reduces migration and invasion, consistent with LSD1 inhibition reverting EMT, and offering a therapeutic modality for EMT-associated disease. Recent data, however, suggest context-dependent roles for LSD1, as its inhibition in epithelial cells increases mesenchymal marker expression, potentially promoting EMT. To investigate this discrepancy, we mapped genome-wide binding of LSD1 in HCT116 epithelial cells and used rapid degron-mediated ablation of endogenous LSD1 to measure changes in nascent and steady-state transcription and chromatin accessibility. In epithelial cells, LSD1 binds constitutively-accessible, primed mesenchymal promoters. These are rapidly derepressed after LSD1 ablation, with activation of SNAI2 and ZEB1, which repress epithelial hallmarks such as E-cadherin. Re-introduction of LSD1 downregulates SNAI2 and ZEB1 but, surprisingly, further represses E-cadherin, indicating sustained loss of epithelial characteristics. Collectively, our results show that LSD1 maintains epithelial identity by repressing mesenchymal genes, questioning the therapeutic utility of LSD1 inhibition for EMT control.

papers.title: Proteome-wide profiling reveals compartment-specific RNA buffering of protein aggregation during stress
papers.abstract: Cellular adaptation to stress requires extensive remodeling of RNA metabolism. The rewiring of the RNA-protein interaction landscape and the assembly of biomolecular condensates are central to this response, yet the global stress-induced reorganization of macromolecular RNA-protein assemblies remains incompletely characterized. Here, we apply R-DeeP, a density gradient approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry, to profile the RNA-dependent sedimentation behaviour of the Saccha-romyces cerevisiae proteome during heat and salt stress. We demonstrate that stress triggers a profound, stress-specific reorganization of the RNA interactome. Many proteins undergo pronounced, selective shifts into high-molecular weight fractions, indicative of aggregation. RNase treatment markedly exacerbates this aggregation, consistent with the model that RNA acts as a general chaperone that keeps proteins with intrinsically disordered regions soluble. Strikingly, our data demonstrate that this protection is compartmentalised. Nuclear proteins are partially shielded from stress-induced aggregation. This protection coincides with the nuclear accumulation of RNA caused by a block of RNA export during stress, and RNase treatment abolishes this protection. Nuclear RNA retention may therefore act as a buffer that actively increases the local chaperoning capacity of the nucleus. In contrast, cytoplasmic proteins, including translation factors and ribonucleoprotein granule components, exhibit increased aggregation under stress. Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that increased biochemical aggregation in density gradients reflects changes in assembly state in vivo. For many stress-induced aggregators, these changes are visible as spatial reorganisation in stressed cells, such as the formation of foci. Our findings suggest that cells use subcellular RNA distribution to tune the condensation and/or aggregation threshold of proteins in a compartment-specific manner.

papers.title: Genomic features and instability of linezolid resistance in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecalis ST525
papers.abstract: This study investigated the mechanisms of oxazolidinone resistance and genomic background in clinical ST525 Enterococcus faecalis isolates, a poorly characterized lineage reported in Brazilian hospitals as either vancomycin-resistant (VRE) or linezolid- and vancomycin-resistant (LVRE). Five LVREfs from intensive care unit patients (linezolid MICs, 8-32 mg/L; vancomycin MICs, >256 mg/L) carried only G2576T and G2505A (in three of four rrl copies) as known linezolid resistance determinants, despite variable linezolid MICs. During serial in vitro passages without antibiotic pressure, isolates with initial MICs of 8-16 mg/L exhibited progressive MIC reductions accompanied by reversion of mutant to wild-type rrl copies, whereas the isolate with an initial MIC of 32 mg/L maintained high-level resistance without reversion. Additional domain V substitutions emerged during MIC decline, while growth kinetics remained broadly similar. Whole-genome sequencing of a representative isolate (LVREfs L7) revealed a ~2.8-Mb chromosome enriched in mobile genetic elements (~8.6%), lacking a functional CRISPR-Cas system. A plasmid-borne prototype Tn1546 carrying vanA, devoid of internal insertion sequences, was found inserted into a Tn3-family transposase gene, a platform not typically associated with vanA mobilization. Together, these findings indicate that ST525 LVREfs, whose genomic features are consistent with long-term persistence in hospitals, may pose a challenge to routine susceptibility testing. A single mutational mechanism can yield variable linezolid MICs, and the ratio of mutated vs wild-type rrl copies can become heterogeneous in the absence of antibiotic pressure, without correlating directly with these values, contrary to the well-documented copy number-MIC correlation.

papers.title: Learning Strand-Equivariant Tokenizations of DNA with MirrorDNA
papers.abstract: DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer. Yet DNA language models are tokenized, trained and tested on one strand at a time. We show that this makes them inconsistent. BPE and $k$-mer tokenizers split 92--100\% of transcription-factor motifs differently on the two strands, and NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA change 25-31\% of their predictions when the test sequences are reverse-complemented. We introduce {\model}, a compact DNA language model with a learned tokenizer that guarantees mirror-symmetric token boundaries across reverse-complement sequences, regardless of its learned parameters. We prove that this symmetry holds through the whole model. As a result, the same model can give identical answers on both strands when the label does not depend on the strand, and can still tell the strands apart when it does, which no strand-blind model can learn. Counting only predictions that are correct on both strands, \model\ more than doubles the MCC of NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA. With 2.3M parameters, it is more accurate than the Caduceus models trained on the same data, and not significantly different from NT-v2 (98M parameters) on Genomic Benchmarks or from DNABERT-2 (117M) on the Nucleotide Transformer tasks. It also stays accurate on inputs sixteen times longer than those it was trained on. The same model trained with reverse-complement augmentation instead still changes about one prediction in ten with the strand, unless its outputs are averaged over both strands. Without any annotation, the tokenizer learns to keep the splice-donor signal \texttt{AGGT} in a single token. Code: https://github.com/NIRJHOR-DATTA/MirrorDNA.

papers.title: Structural Basis for Human Milk Oligosaccharides Recognition by Evolutionarily Dominant Norovirus Genogroup II Genotypes
papers.abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of acute gastroenteritis. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) contain glycan motifs similar to histo-blood group antigens and may act as soluble decoys that reduce viral attachment. However, the molecular basis of HMO recognition by the P domain of the major capsid protein VP1 of different norovirus genotypes is not fully understood. Here, we combined ligand-based and protein-based NMR experiments with X-ray crystallography to study HMO binding to the P domain of the latent GII.2, dominant GII.4 and emerging GII.17 noroviruses genotypes. Screening of 12 HMOs by STD NMR showed binding of all fucosylated HMOs to GII.4 and GII.17 and none for non-fucosylated HMOs. In contrast, GII.2 showed little or no detectable binding under the same conditions. Seven crystal structures of GII.4 or GII.17 with complexed HMOs supported fucose anchoring via five conserved residues. The remaining sugar moieties formed genotype-specific secondary interactions with an extended, shallow and solvent exposed binding surface whose shape is dictated by divergent surface loops. GII.4 recognition is mainly driven by hydrogen bonds whereas GII.17 relied more strongly on water-mediated interactions. Chemical shift perturbation from NMR titrations (CSP NMR) of GII.4 corroborated the fucose interactions and gave dissociation constants of 20-33 mM, consistent with weak and rapidly exchanging interactions.

papers.title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. In this paper, we have measured the Raman spectra of microtubules and their constituent protein tubulin in dry powder form for a range of temperatures, from nitrogen liquid T=77 K up to room and physiological temperature T=310 K, to determine if molecular bond vibrations present potential Fano resonance asymmetry. We have found nontrivial persistence of Fano resonances, q<5, at room and physiological temperatures for some specific vibrational modes.

papers.title: LinearRaccess: linear-time approximation of RNA accessibility without base-pair span limits
papers.abstract: Motivation: RNA accessibility is the probability that every nucleotide in a contiguous interval is simultaneously unpaired; it is widely used to predict binding sites for RNA-binding proteins and other RNA-RNA interactions, often in the form of the opening energy, an equivalent measure on a logarithmic scale. Existing tools restrict the maximum base-pair span, discarding long-range base pairs that matter biologically. Others sample structures, introducing statistical variance, or compute accessibility exactly without a span limit, at cubic time cost. No existing method computes the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically in linear time while preserving long-range base pairs. We present LinearRaccess, which computes accessibility directly in linear time via beam-pruned inside-outside dynamic programming with a difference-array aggregation step, without restricting base-pair span. Results: For a sequence of length N and a fixed beam width b, LinearRaccess runs in O(N) time and O(Nb) memory. Against exact accessibility on 12,872 bpRNA-1m(90) sequences of 100-1,000 nt, its median opening-energy error is below 0.001 kcal/mol (0.14 kcal/mol for 700-1,000 nt), and it distinguishes windows of very small accessibility, including 35-nt windows, below the resolution of sampling-based estimates. LinearRaccess analyzes the full 29,903-nt SARS-CoV-2 genome in 419 seconds. Conclusion: LinearRaccess is the first method to compute the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically (without sampling) in linear time without restricting base-pair span. Availability: https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearRaccess, archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598502).

papers.title: Active eye modeling: a tool for estimating retinal image quality across the visual field in everyday life
papers.abstract: Purpose: The "visual diet," the totality of visual experience, shapes retinal image formation and thereby refractive development, but measuring retinal image statistics during everyday behavior is challenging. Limits in mobile eye tracking, egocentric video, and full-field optical measurement leave gaps in our understanding of how environmental and behavioral factors shape image quality across the retina. Methods: We introduce active eye modeling, a computational platform combining optically validated, wide-field, accommodating eye models (Hastings et al. 2024) with realistic three-dimensional virtual environments and gaze behavior derived from human data. This approach enables systematic estimation of retinal blur across the visual field under parametrically controlled conditions, including varying viewing distances, ambient light levels, and environmental depth structure. Inputs may be simulated and/or drawn from real-world measurements: scene depth, video, and gaze/pupil recordings. Results: During simulated far work, peripheral image quality is depth-tolerant, owing to wide depth-of-field from off-axis aberrations. Near work under dim indoor lighting substantially increases peripheral blur, reducing contrast at mid and high spatial frequencies. This contrast reduction is comparable in magnitude to a moderate diffusing filter (Bangerter 0.4 strength) that affects eye growth when imposed experimentally in animal models. A consistency check with eye-tracked virtual driving confirms peripheral depth-tolerance during far work. Conclusions: Active eye modeling provides a flexible framework for investigating how visual experience shapes the retinal image, relevant to refractive development, display and lens design, and peripheral vision. Applied to common visual behaviors, the platform identifies optical conditions during indoor near work that warrant empirical investigation, complementing measurement-based approaches.

papers.title: Global homeostatic forces shape the composition of a hyperdiverse tropical insect fauna
papers.abstract: Despite comprising the bulk of terrestrial biodiversity, we know surprisingly little about insect faunas, particularly in the tropics. Here, we characterize the insect fauna of Madagascar, a global biodiversity hotspot, based on extensive DNA metabarcoding of Malaise trap and leaf litter samples. We estimate that the fauna comprises at least 250,000 species, only 5% of which are currently recorded. The ecological and taxonomic composition is surprisingly similar to that of temperate forests. We show that this is likely caused by global homeostatic forces shaping net diversification rates after colonization of Madagascar rather than by the composition of colonizing lineages. Features differing from temperate forests include the dearth of parasitoids and richness of beetles. Understanding the forces shaping these patterns is key in sustainable management of tropical insect faunas.

papers.title: Genomic analysis of the Streptococcus anginosus group; taxonomic implications, evolutionary insights and clinical considerations
papers.abstract: Background: The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) (S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group's diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods: Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results: Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa (S. anginosus, S. hominis, S. whileyi and S. vaginalis). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex-S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ~15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity (S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions: Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.

papers.title: Distinct lifespan trajectories of cortical intrinsic timescales and neural oscillations
papers.abstract: The brain integrates information over time through the persistence of neural activity, yet how this persistence changes across the human lifespan and the mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear. Using resting-state magnetoencephalography from three independent cohorts (n = 1,156; ages 6-88 years), we systematically examined lifespan changes in neural temporal dynamics, focusing on cortical intrinsic timescales and alpha oscillatory frequency. We found that cortical intrinsic timescales shortened from approximately 29 ms in childhood to 9 ms in late adulthood, with the steepest decline occurring before age 30. This compression was reproducible across cohorts and observed in all cortical regions, while the sensory-to-association hierarchy of timescales remained preserved throughout life. By contrast, alpha frequency followed a distinct trajectory, peaking in early adulthood before declining after midlife. Individualized corticothalamic models linked timescale compression to stronger intrathalamic inhibition, whereas increased conduction delays partly accounted for alpha slowing. Further network simulations indicated that intrinsic timescales primarily reflect collective network dynamics rather than single-neuron kinetics. Together, these findings reveal distinct lifespan trajectories of neural persistence and oscillatory rhythms, implicating collective corticothalamic dynamics in the temporal organization of the human brain across development and ageing.

papers.title: Plate design confounds donor variation and model evaluation in single-cell perturbation screens
papers.abstract: Single-cell screens of immune cells from many donors are used to study why individuals respond differently and to benchmark response models. Each donor-perturbation combination typically occupies one well, controls are grouped, and donors share one layout, so technical effects can look biological. Using a 90-cytokine screen, two compound screens, four cohorts and simulations, we show that well effects explain most replicate-control variation in abundant cell types, controls carry a shared offset, and identical control wells differ by hundreds of differentially expressed genes at a standard threshold, about as many as two receptor-negative proteins do. Negative controls, design-aware estimators and perturbation-specific evaluation change the interpretation of four recent analyses. A deep-learning model that scores below a perturbation-agnostic predictor under standard evaluation outperforms a simple baseline on perturbation-specific differences in two of three cell types (significantly in one with stricter controls), but predicts less well the component shared with inert wells.

papers.title: Mutually Repressive Transcription Factors Drive Intestinal Maturation for Weaning
papers.abstract: In mammals, rapid neonatal growth depends on specialized intestinal enterocytes that absorb nutrients from milk. These cells exhibit distinct functions, morphologies, and gene expression programs that support neonatal nutrition before transitioning to an adult state at weaning. However, the transcriptional mechanisms that establish neonatal enterocyte identity and coordinate their maturation remain poorly understood. Here we show that the transcription factors BLIMP1 and CASZ1 form a central switch in the timing of enterocyte maturation. While BLIMP1 marks and promotes neonatal enterocytes, CASZ1 is expressed in adult enterocytes and is required for the proper timing of their emergence. Genetic analysis indicates that these neonatal and adult factors are mutually repressive, forming a genetic switch underlying weaning. This regulatory mechanism also controls glucocorticoid-induced maturation, a process relevant to both normal weaning and the clinical use of corticosteroids to promote epithelial maturation in preterm infants. We show that corticosteroids act directly on the intestinal epithelium and require CASZ1 to induce maturation. Together, these findings reveal a transcriptional mechanism that coordinates intestinal epithelial identity with the changing nutritional demands of early life and mediates the response to maturation-promoting hormones.

papers.title: Prenatal THC exposure alters metabolic gene expression and KEAP1 regulation in the mouse placental labyrinth
papers.abstract: Introduction: Prenatal cannabinoid exposure may influence fetal development through changes in placental biology, yet its effects on metabolic gene regulation remain poorly understood. We examined the effects of {Delta}9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) on the mouse placental labyrinth zone. Methods: Pregnant C57BL/6JRj mice received THC (5 mg/kg), CBD (5 mg/kg), or vehicle daily by intraperitoneal injection from gestational day 5 to 17.5. Targeted NanoString profiling and pathway analysis were combined with RT-qPCR and protein measurements. Results: THC exposure reduced glutaminase (Gls), Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1), and FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (Flt3) expression (false discovery rate = 0.0904 for each). Pathway analysis identified transcriptional changes in the nine-gene arginine-metabolism set (false discovery rate = 0.0527). No genes or pathways met the significance criteria following CBD exposure. RT-qPCR confirmed lower Keap1 expression with sexes pooled and identified lower Gls and Flt3 expression in male samples. KEAP1 protein abundance increased despite lower Keap1 mRNA, while nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 localization and heme oxygenase 1 (Hmox1) expression showed no significant differences. Discussion: These findings identify amino acid metabolic gene expression and KEAP1 regulation as complementary components of the placental response to prenatal THC exposure, connecting transcriptional changes with protein regulation within the placental exchange region.

papers.title: hAM-pe soluble extract increases human keratinocyte HaCaT cell-line mobility in scratch assays
papers.abstract: We have studied the impact of human amniotic membrane (hAM-pe) on wound closing speed in a scratch assay of human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Though not without limitations, scratch assays are useful for studying collective cellular displacement as a model of wound healing. We show that the treatment is effective in decreasing the average time that the cells need to completely close the wound, in agreement with previous \emph{in vivo} experiments. We developed an automated segmentation software, and verified that a linear fit, though not completely describing the wound edge dynamics, is a robust method for comparing treatments and control measurements. By tracking the individual motion of a subset of cells, we found that individual treatment does not cause an increase in individual speed enough to explain the effect of the treatment at the collective (wound edge) level. Instead, the mean squared displacement and numerical simulations of a simple model of interacting active Brownian particles support the view that the main effect of the treatment at the individual level is to increase the persistence of cellular motion.

papers.title: Extensional Flow Microfluidics Reveal Size-Dependent Core-Shell Mechanical Heterogeneity in Pancreatic Tumor Spheroids
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanical behavior of cancer cell aggregates is important for investigating metastatic potential and developing effective therapeutics. Tumor cell clusters are major contributors to metastasis and can undergo extreme deformation to migrate through capillaries smaller than the cluster size, suggesting complex multicellular mechanics. Despite their clinical significance, the mechanics of multicellular spheroids remain underexplored. In this study, the mechanical behavior of spheroids formed from the pancreatic cancer cell line PANC-1 was investigated using a cross-slot microfluidic device. Suspended spheroids from two size ranges were stretched in non-contact extensional flow (small spheroids mostly 40 < D0 < 75 m, large spheroids mostly 90 < D0 < 145 m). Digital image correlation analyses of intra-spheroid strains revealed strong deformation differences for small and large spheroids while analyses based on 2D projected contours of the spheroid shape did not show trends. Smaller spheroids deformed relatively homogeneously and exhibited significant overall stretching. In contrast, larger spheroids displayed heterogeneous deformation characterized by a stiff central core and a deformable outer shell. To investigate the origin of these mechanical differences, cellular morphology and the expression of stiffness-associated proteins, including vimentin and E-cadherin, were assessed from confocal microscopy. Larger spheroids display significantly lower nuclear sphericity than small spheroids, indicating more cellular packing with increasing spheroid size. Additionally, vimentin expression was concentrated in the outer shell of large spheroids, whereas small spheroids exhibit vimentin expression throughout the aggregate. Thus individual cell morphology and cytoskeletal networks seemed to contribute to the core-shell biomechanical behavior of the large spheroids and lack thereof for small spheroids. Taken together, this study suggests that as spheroids grow, they transition from an irregular and disorganized cluster at low cell numbers to a coordinated and hierarchical structure at sufficient cell numbers that corresponds to diameters {gtrsim} 100 m.

papers.title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition
papers.abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.

papers.title: A Dynamic Stem Cell State Links Environmental Cues to Skeletal and Regenerative Fates
papers.abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.

papers.title: Residual Hearing Loss After Chronic Cochlear Implantation in Guinea Pigs is Primarily Conductive
papers.abstract: It is desirous to preserve residual low-frequency hearing in cochlear implant recipients, as dual stimulation using electrical and acoustic signals results in superior speech-in-noise processing and musicality. However, cochlear implant recipients commonly lose their residual acoustic hearing gradually following surgical placement of the array. The governing mechanism is not understood and is likely due to multiple factors including surgical trauma, inflammation, and the foreign body induced immune response to the array, including formation of intracochlear fibrosis. Normal mechanical function of the cochlea is expected to underpin residual hearing but has not been directly studied. This function includes efficient transmission of sound to the cochlea via the middle ear, sound propagation via the basilar membrane travelling wave, mechanical tuning characteristics, and the non-linear cochlear amplification of responses to low-frequency stimulation. Here, we examined these features in cochleae and middle ears of unimplanted, acutely and chronically implanted guinea pigs using our minimally invasive preparation and optical coherence tomography vibrometry. We observed that mechanical tuning and amplification is not significantly altered by either acute or chronic implant. However, the response threshold was raised and proportional to middle ear responses. Additionally, the organ of Corti phase, and its sound intensity dependent changes, are unaltered by CI. Finally, a cluster analysis revealed sensitivity loss in chronically implanted animals is caused by middle ear dysfunction. Hence, in the guinea pig model, the dominant etiology of residual hearing loss is conductive. More research is required to establish whether residual hearing loss in humans similarly shares conductive elements.

papers.title: A mammalian fibroblast zoo reveals barriers to cross-species virus replication and differential regulation of antiviral immunity
papers.abstract: Virus zoonosis represents a continual threat to humans. Viruses emerge in humans directly or indirectly through interactions with mammals. However, our understanding of virus-host susceptibility across the diversity of mammals is limited and experimental model systems are restricted to a very small set of model organisms. Mammals are highly diverse and different habitats, lifestyles, diets, and exposures to different pathogens have driven substantial genetic diversity. We generated a library of primary fibroblasts across 86 mammalian species and used these cells to build an atlas of virus-host susceptibility across a panel of arboviruses that infect diverse mammals including humans. Perturbing the innate immune system revealed some virus-host pairs where restriction is controlled by the immune system and others where there is an incompatibility with host factors. Transcriptomic profiling of the library in response to virus sensing mimicked by poly(I:C) or antiviral signaling with type I interferon reveals a core set of conserved genes that respond as well as substantial species- and order-specific responses. Together these data provide a comparative atlas of innate immune responses across mammals and offer a window into how these systems have evolved across animals.

papers.title: γδ T cell-derived IL-17A aggravates experimental epidermolysis bullosa acquisita in response to IL-1β
papers.abstract: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is a mucocutaneous autoimmune blistering disorder mediated by autoantibodies against type VII collagen and subsequent splitting of the dermal-epidermal junction. Interleukin (IL)-17A promotes the production of chemokines and cytokines involved in neutrophil recruitment and activation, suggesting that IL-17A may contribute to EBA pathogenesis. We aimed to clarify the role of IL-17A in experimental EBA. Using an antibody transfer-induced EBA mouse model, we demonstrate that IL-17A promotes disease development, as pharmacological blockade of IL-17A with a neutralizing antibody ameliorated skin lesions. Gamma-delta ({gamma}{delta}) T cells were identified as the predominant cellular source of IL-17A, supported by the attenuated disease phenotype observed in {gamma}{delta}TCR-deficient mice. In addition, CD4+ T cells and neutrophils contributed to IL-17A production in experimental EBA. Mechanistically, IL-1-beta, rather than IL-23, was identified as a critical mediator of IL-17A production by {gamma}{delta} T cells in vitro, consistent with our in vivo findings. Whereas EBA severity was not reduced in IL-23p19-deficient mice, disease was markedly attenuated in IL-1R-deficient animals. Together, our study provides the first evidence that {gamma}{delta} T cell-derived IL-17A plays a pivotal role in experimental EBA and identifies a previously unrecognized IL-1{beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell/IL-17A axis that expands current understanding of EBA immunopathogenesis.

papers.title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya virus
papers.abstract: Langya virus (LayV) was recently discovered in infected individuals with febrile illness and classified as a Parahenipavirus, a group of poorly understood pathogens. LayV is distantly related to Nipah henipavirus which causes recurring outbreaks with case fatality rates reaching up to 90%. No vaccines or therapeutics are approved for use in humans for any parahenipavirus or henipavirus despite their broad geographic distribution and pandemic potential. Here, we discovered that human endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is an entry receptor for LayV and that the tetrameric LayV attachment glycoprotein (G) binds EPCR avidly. We reveal the molecular basis of LayV G recognition of the EPCR receptor and provide a blueprint of the determinants of receptor ortholog usage. We found that human and shrew EPCR orthologs promote cell entry of LayV and of the closely related Mojiang pseudoviruses. These results along with the detection of several Parahenipaviruses in shrews set these pathogens apart from Henipaviruses, which use Pteropid fruit bats as reservoir hosts. Our data support future surveillance efforts, by enabling prediction of EPCR utilization among newly discovered Parahenipaviruses, and the development and evaluation of countermeasures targeting this emerging group of human pathogens.

papers.title: Secondary growth in the tomato stem is suppressed by the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3
papers.abstract: Herbaceous eudicot crops such as tomato accumulate substantial amounts of secondary xylem in their stems, particularly in the basal part. As plants progress from the vegetative phase to flowering and fruit development, secondary growth continues to provide mechanical support and facilitate transport. To uncover how secondary growth is regulated in the tomato stem, we used laser capture microdissection RNA-seq to establish tissue-specific transcriptomic profiles. This revealed that key regulators associated with wood formation in poplar are also acting in tomato. Furthermore, we found that the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3 are substantially expressed in xylem tissue. Subsequent functional analysis identified FUL2 and STM3 as key repressors of secondary growth, with ful2 or stm3 knock-out mutants exhibiting strongly increased secondary growth in older tomato stems. Notably, a higher order mutant in which both ful2 and stm3 were knocked out displays a similar non-additive phenotype, indicating, together with yeast two-hybrid data showing physical interaction, that FUL2 and STM3 act together in a complex. The expression levels of both genes remain low until after the floral transition but strongly rise during subsequent stem development. Transcriptomic analyses in ful2, stm3, and wild-type stems at stages before and after detectable anatomical differences, showed that the FUL2-STM3 complex represses distinct sets of NAC and MYB candidate regulators associated with xylem development. Interestingly, FUL2 and STM3 control these regulators in a stage- and position-dependent way, with candidates showing upregulation only at later stages in mid-height stems being already upregulated at earlier stages in basal stem regions. Our findings provide a tissue-resolved transcriptomic resource for tomato stems and reveal a role for FUL2 and STM3 in limiting secondary xylem accumulation as stem development progresses.

papers.title: Temporal Structure in Resting-State fMRI under Marginal and Cross-Spectral Surrogate Controls
papers.abstract: Resting-state functional MRI is commonly analyzed using correlations between regional signals and their frequency spectra, which characterize average connectivity and spectral properties but may miss other aspects of temporal organization. Measures of temporal complexity offer complementary information about the recurrence of signal patterns, how fluctuations vary across timescales, and signal roughness. These properties may reveal disease-related alterations in brain activity, offering opportunities for biomarker discovery and insights into mechanisms of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here we examined sample entropy (SampEn), multifractal de-trended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA), and Higuchi curve shapes in 732 scans from 270 ADNI participants, including cognitively normal individuals, people with mild cognitive impairment, and people with dementia. Using the seven Yeo resting-state networks (Yeo-7), we compared recordings with randomized signals preserving either each networks amplitude distribution and approximate spectrum (IAAFT), or the complete cross-spectrum across networks. If these properties fully explained temporal complexity, real recordings should resemble their randomized references. We therefore counted how often each real recording was the strongest outlier among itself and 20 references. This occurred in 21.7%, 12.7%, and 44.2% of 5,124 network-visits for SampEn, MFDFA, and Higuchi, versus 5.5%, 5.1%, and 6.3% in surrogate-only controls. Cross-spectrum-preserving references yielded 39.8%, 17.5%, and 49.8%. Simulations showed that changes in sampling or signal processing, including abrupt changes in signal amplitude, can produce similar differences without changing the underlying dynamics. The measures showed repeatability across visits but did not improve retrospective prediction of changes in Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. These findings identify temporal features not reproduced by the tested spectral controls and provide a basis for evaluating their potential as disease biomarkers.

papers.title: Personalized Prediction of Differences in fMRI Connectivity Estimates Across Preprocessing Pipelines
papers.abstract: Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently. We examined whether we could use earlier scans to predict how preprocessing would affect a later scan. In 69 ADNI (Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) participants scanned three times, we measured how nuisance regression and filtering, alone and in sequence, changed the measured FC. A ridge regression model combined these responses with baseline FC from the third scan to predict the effect of reversing the processing order. Just four coefficients were shared across 79,800 connections. In leave-one-participant-out testing, mean squared error was 0.012, compared with 0.017 for predicting the same average response for everyone. It outperformed the best of seven alternative predictions chosen for each participant (0.013; normalized gain 0.069, 95% bootstrap interval 0.006-0.134), with lower error in 44 of 69 participants. About half the benefit of using each persons earlier responses, rather than the average across participants, came from which connections changed. This advantage persisted after accounting for acquisition variables. The ADNI-trained model reduced mean error in ten Midnight Scan Club participants without refitting. These results support using personal preprocessing history to predict changes in connectivity estimates on newly acquired scans.

papers.title: The structures of two intermediates en route to DNA repair within a (6-4) photolyase
papers.abstract: Pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts (6-4PPs) are mutagenic DNA lesions produced when UV light crosslinks two adjacent pyrimidine bases. These lesions must be repaired to maintain genome integrity, a function executed by the (6-4) photolyase enzymes. This repair chemistry is complex, involving the transfer of a hydroxyl group from one base to another, accompanied or followed by cleavage of an interbase bond. It remains unclear how the enzyme orchestrates this reaction. Typically, models invoke a stepwise process in which an oxetane intermediate is transiently populated, but despite over thirty years of investigation, such an intermediate has never been definitively observed. Conducting dose-controlled X-ray crystallography on the (6-4) photolyase from Vibrio cholerae, we observed the transformation of 6-4PP into an oxetane species. Furthermore, we identified a previously unanticipated hemi-cleaved intermediate. The progressive transformation of 6-4PP into oxetane, hemi-cleaved, and fully repaired species requires a reexamination of the existing models of DNA repair by (6-4) photolyases.

papers.title: Endothelial Cell Specific Thioredoxin 1-Dependent Signaling in Oxygen-1 Induced Retinopathy
papers.abstract: Purpose: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of childhood blindness, characterized byoxidative stress and dysregulated angiogenesis in preterm infants with immature antioxidant systems.This study aimed to investigate the specific role of endothelial cell-specific thioredoxin 1 (TXN1), a crucial oxidoreductase, in oxygen-induced retinopathy, hypothesizing that the absence of endothelial TXN1 directly impairs angiogenesis and exacerbates hyperoxia-induced injury. Methods: We generated tamoxifen-inducible, endothelial cell-specific Txn1 knockout mice (Txn1-iECKO) and utilized the oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) model, exposing litters to 85% oxygen from postnatal day 7 (P7) to P12. Retinal vascular morphology during vaso-obliteration and neovascularization phases, endothelial cell proliferation, and apoptotic cell death were assessed. Furthermore, human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs) with TXN1 knockdown were subjected to hyperoxic conditions, followed by comprehensive gene expression profiling using RT2 Profiler PCR arrays and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Results: Deletion of endothelial Txn1 significantly enhanced vascular regression during the hyperoxic vaso-obliteration phase at P12 and markedly exacerbated pathological neovascularization at P17. Txn1-deficient retinas exhibited significantly impaired endothelial cell proliferation during the vaso-obliteration phase, while apoptotic cell death remained unchanged. Transcriptomic analysis of TXN1-deficient HRMECs under hyperoxia revealed an enhanced activation of NRF2-mediated oxidative stress response pathways. Conclusions: These findings identify endothelial TXN1 as an essential and oxygen-dependent regulator of vascular development in ischemic retinopathy, primarily influencing endothelial proliferation and redox signaling. This suggests TXN1's crucial protective role and highlights its therapeutic potential to mitigate ROP progression by modulating endothelial cell responses to oxidative stress.

papers.title: Circuit and cell-type mechanisms of the spectrolaminar motif of cortical oscillations
papers.abstract: Oscillations are a key feature of cortical activity, coordinating spike timing across areas, layers, and cell types. Recent work suggests these rhythms follow a stereotyped organization across cortical depth, the spectrolaminar (SL) motif, with higher-frequency gamma prominent in superficial layers and lower-frequency alpha/beta in deep layers, yet the mechanisms generating it remain poorly understood. Using a bio-realistic model of mouse primary visual cortex, we reproduced the SL motif and found it preserved across diverse visual stimuli. Systematic cell-type- and layer-resolved perturbations showed that the alpha/beta component was intrinsic to every layer, whereas the 50-80 Hz gamma component was predominantly generated within layer 4 (L4) and propagated network-wide through inter-laminar connections. Pvalb interneurons were the principal regulators of gamma, Sst cells shaped low-frequency power, and Vip cells controlled oscillation magnitude. The temporal properties of L4 Pvalb-to-excitatory synapses were especially influential in generating the SL motif. These models and simulation results thus offer a plausible description of circuit mechanisms underlying cortical oscillations and the SL motif and are publicly available to facilitate further studies.

papers.title: Invasion analysis for structured populations: analytical principles and numerical workflows
papers.abstract: All real populations show some form of structure--differences among individuals, such as life stage or physiological condition, that shape a species' ability to persist. Yet it remains challenging to incorporate population structure into models of species interactions. We provide a general framework for studying competition in structured populations by quantifying species' invasion growth rates. The crux of our approach is separation of timescales: the initial dynamics of a structured population depend on how exactly it is introduced, but these transient differences do not affect long-term invasion success. Depending on the research question, the relevant long-term growth rate when rare may equivalently be derived using analytical separation of timescales, matrix population theory, or numerical simulations. Using case studies spanning developmental stage, environmental state, and infection status, we illustrate how our methodology derives simple, ecologically meaningful invasion conditions for a variety of systems. Finally, we extend the approach to fluctuating resident dynamics, showing how to use simulations or a general mathematical framework known as Floquet theory to correctly quantify invasion growth. By unifying the quantitative methods of population biology and community ecology, our framework will allow ecologists to study species persistence and coexistence across a greater variety of demographically complex systems.

papers.title: Contrastive Learning Improves Generalization on M2OR Olfactory Binding Dataset
papers.abstract: Olfaction-based biosensors stand to have profound impacts in fields such as medical diagnostics, national security, and drug discovery. A promising mode of vapor phase biodetection mimics volatile organic compound-olfactory receptor (VOC-OR) interactions with target-specific protein or peptide probes; however, lack of experimental coverage remains a core bottleneck. Current computational approaches aim to improve prediction of VOC-OR binding to reduce experimental burden, and current machine learning approaches fail to demonstrate a level of generalization that addresses current engineering challenges. Here, using the Molecular to Olfactory Dataset (M2OR) and Insect Olfactory Binding Protein Database (iOBPdb) datasets, data partitioning methods and their performance are evaluated on a neural network and contrastive learning framework on such VOC-OR binding datasets, varying: model training, architecture, and structure of the input data distribution. It was found that holding out certain chemical or proteomic motifs from the training data diminished model performance with a two layer neural network model. The model was able to generalize to state of the art performance (0.88 AUCROC) on every data split by applying a contrastive learning objective defined by shared molecular constituents and a stochastic sampler. This suggests the contrastive objective provides a strong inductive bias for neural networks to predict novel VOC-OR pairs. These findings highlight that model performance on pairwise biological interaction datasets can be inflated through identity leakage from constituent overlap, and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we show contrastive regularization mitigates dataset degeneracy through enforcement of compatibility in the models latent geometry that may extend to other binder target-datasets where identity leakage confounds evaluation.

papers.title: Preserving Nanotherapy-Induced Allogeneic Murine Islet Graft Tolerance During Distal Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Skin Infection
papers.abstract: Eliminating lifelong immunosuppression can make islet transplantation a durable alternative to insulin therapy for type 1 diabetes. As short-course tolerogenic regimens are developed to replace lifelong immunosuppression, it is critical to test their robustness against perturbations such as hospital-acquired infections, which transplant recipients routinely encounter. Herein, we investigated whether rapamycin-loaded polymersomes (rPS), a subcutaneous nanotherapy that induces long-term murine islet allograft survival, can preserve host defenses in a Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) skin infection, and whether the resulting immune response from this distal infection relative to graft location erodes rPS-induced tolerance. rPS maintained neutrophil antibacterial activity despite inhibiting oxidative mechanisms in vitro, and rPS-treated mice demonstrated normal recovery following MRSA challenge. However, MRSA skin infection caused a decline of ~43% in recipient survival for rPS-treated mice, despite surviving recipients retaining glucose-stimulated insulin responsiveness. This erosion of allograft acceptance coincided with a burst of IL-6 within 24h of the infection followed by elevated TNF-[a] and neutrophilia at 13 days post-infection. Combining rPS with a single dose of methylprednisolone reduced IL-6 and TNF- without altering neutrophilia, nearly doubling survival among infected recipients to 80%. Our findings demonstrate that partial dampening of inflammatory insults can restore superior islet allograft acceptance following perioperative infection.

papers.title: Sexual interactions and local selection shape reproductive gene diversity and divergence
papers.abstract: Genes involved in genotype x genotype coevolution display unique patterns of nucleotide diversity and population divergence. In Drosophila melanogaster, Sex Peptide is a key sperm competition gene that is an outlier for both pi within populations and Fst between populations. This pattern is not predicted by current theoretical expectations of selective sweeps highlighting the need to develop predictions to identify genes experiencing balancing selection. We compared pi and FST in D. melanogaster populations to identify other genes following a co-evolutionary model that generates divergence and diversity. Multiple male and female genes that interact with Sex Peptide exhibited elevated FST x pi values. Genome-wide analyses also revealed an enrichment of genes critical for neuronal development, pointing to courtship evolution. Specifically, fruitless, its interacting genes, and a female behavior gene were identified as outliers. These parallel findings indicate that both sperm competition and mating behaviors are subject to co-evolutionary selection.

papers.title: Long-read DNA sequencing reveals global hypomethylation and focal hypermethylation in SDHx-deficient pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
papers.abstract: Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGL) are highly heritable neuroendocrine tumors of the autonomic ganglia. Genomic DNA in most cancer cells is hypomethylated. However, DNA in PPGLs secondary to mutations in succinate dehydrogenase complex (SDHx) genes is reportedly hypermethylated due to succinate-mediated inhibition of DNA demethylases. We used nanopore long-read sequencing to characterize the methylome of tumor and white blood cell DNA from SDHx and non-SDHx PPGL patients, alongside normal adrenal medulla. We find that both SDHx and non-SDHx PPGLs are globally hypomethylated, particularly at centromeres. In normal adrenal medulla, CpG islands marked by H3K4 methylation are hypomethylated, whereas CpG islands lacking H3K4 methylation are hypermethylated. In SDHx-related PPGL, some H3K4me-marked CpG islands are hypermethylated, but most are not. We propose that DNA methylation in SDHx-related PPGL reflects the global hypomethylation generally observed in tumors, partly offset by succinate-mediated inhibition of TET DNA demethylases. Opposing effects of succinate may alter the balance between DNA methylation (indirect inhibition of the DNMT3A/B DNA methylases via inhibition of H3K4me demethylases) and DNA demethylation (inhibition of TET DNA demethylases) at active CpG islands.

papers.title: A three-factor model can explain symmetry breaking and the n-1 rule during X-chromosome inactivation
papers.abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is a mammalian gene regulatory process that via chromosome-scale transcriptional silencing, leaves active a single X chromosome per diploid genome complement. The mechanisms that enable cells to select the appropriate number of X chromosomes to inactivate while leaving others active remain unclear. We demonstrate that all known chromosomal counting scenarios during XCI can be accounted for by a three-factor mathematical model that includes (1) Xist, the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) responsible for gene silencing during XCI in eutherians, (2) an X-linked transcriptional activator of Xist, and (3) the autosomally-encoded SPEN, an Xist RNA-binding protein that is essential for gene silencing during XCI. In our model, symmetry between active X chromosomes is broken by stochastic differences in the number of Xist molecules that associate with the X chromosomes at the onset of XCI. Subsequently, integrated positive and negative feedback loops amplify then propagate superstoichiometric assemblies of SPEN complexed with Xist on the inactive chromosome(s), and select for levels of X-linked activator that enable only one X chromosome per diploid genome complement to remain active. Thus, asymmetric propagation of the SPEN-Xist ribonucleoprotein complex may play an essential role in symmetry breaking and chromosomal counting during XCI, independently of or in concert with cis-acting networks of DNA regulatory elements. Our results also have conceptual implications for gene regulatory circuits on autosomes.

papers.title: Squalene as a Candidate Signalling Molecule: Computational Evidence for a Predicted KEAP1 Interaction and Implications for Stress-Induced Altruistic Stem-Cell Niche Protection
papers.abstract: Stem and progenitor cells exposed to cytotoxic stress must preserve both their own viability and the functional integrity of their surrounding niche. Previous investigations from our laboratory have described stress-adapted altruistic stem-cell phenotypes and demonstrated the cytoprotective potential of squalene in normal haematopoietic and mesenchymal progenitor cells through preservation of glutathione homeostasis. More recent studies have associated hypoxia-driven changes in squalene metabolism with intracellular squalene accumulation and protection against lipid peroxidation, while independent experimental evidence has implicated NRF2 in squalene-mediated cytoprotection. However, the molecular basis through which squalene may engage the NRF2 regulatory pathway remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the structural feasibility of a potential interaction between squalene and the KEAP1 Kelch domain using molecular docking across three human KEAP1 crystal structures (PDB IDs: 6TYM, 6SP4 and 5CGJ). The docking protocol was evaluated through native-ligand redocking, yielding RMSD values of 0.826, 0.277 and 0.303 A, respectively. Squalene was consistently accommodated within the canonical hydrophobic cavity, with predicted docking scores of 7.905, 7.513 and 6.756 kcal/mol. The predicted interaction environment was predominantly hydrophobic and involved residues including Arg415, Arg380 and Asn414, without conventional hydrogen-bond formation. These findings support the structural feasibility of squalene accommodation within the KEAP1 Kelch domain and provide a testable hypothesis connecting stress-responsive squalene metabolism with potential KEAP1 NRF2 regulation. However, docking alone does not establish direct binding, physiological accessibility, KEAP1 inhibition or functional NRF2 activation. Further biophysical, molecular-dynamics and cellular investigations are required to establish the biological significance of the predicted interaction.

papers.title: An integrated workflow for dual-guide CRISPR-Cas9 targeting and amplicon-based genotyping of Pla2g6 in primary mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 editing in primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMD-M{phi}s) requires coordinated assessment of cellular morphology, target modification, and sequence-level editing outcomes. We describe a workflow for dual-guide targeting of murine Pla2g6 that integrates guide design, ribonucleoprotein nucleofection, PCR-heteroduplex mobility analysis (PCR-HMA), and targeted amplicon sequencing. At 24 h after nucleofection, cells receiving ribonucleoproteins assembled with chemically synthesized single-guide RNAs preserved the elongated, adherent morphology, whereas cultures receiving in vitro-transcribed guides contained predominantly poorly adhered, rounded cells and appeared less densely populated; both guide preparations generated indels and deletions, so the difference observed was in cell appearance rather than in target modification. PCR-HMA provided a simple, qualitative screen for sequence heterogeneity and for a putative deletion product, which was subsequently characterized by sequencing. In two independent BMDM samples, one each from C57BL/6 and NOD mice, breakpoint-based analysis identified editing-associated indels in 54.7% and 44.5% of analyzed reads, compared with 0.28% and 0.07% in matched Cas9-only controls. Deletions spanning both target sites represented 33.1% and 26.2% of analyzed reads; none were detected among 4,383 analyzed control reads. The modal spanning deletion was 137 bp, the size predicted from precise joining of the two blunt Cas9 ends. Sequence interpretation depended on verified guide coordinates, deletion-aware analysis settings, and matched controls: scored permissively, the same control reads returned 22-23% apparent editing. Modest-depth Nanopore sequencing recovered the major editing classes, although low-frequency variants and small indels required additional caution. This workflow supports a simple and streamlined screening and sequence-based genotyping of edited BMDM populations, allowing the discernment of the comprehensive mutation spectrum arising from CRISPR-Cas9 gene targeting.

papers.title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
papers.abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.

papers.title: Ranging and territoriality in African Apes
papers.abstract: Intergroup relations vary strikingly among African apes, with only chimpanzees showing intense, often lethal territoriality. The economic defendability hypothesis proposes that such territorial behaviour is favored where home ranges can be economically defended, as indexed by the ratio of daily travel distance to home range diameter. To test this idea, we compiled and analyzed comparable data on yearly home range size, daily travel distance and defendability indices from one population of each nonhuman African ape species and integrated these with comparable published data. We find that bonobos had substantially larger home ranges and longer daily travel distances than chimpanzees and gorillas, contradicting a prevailing assumption that bonobos experience higher or more reliable food abundance. Defendability indices were higher in chimpanzees and bonobos than in mountain gorillas, but did not differ significantly between chimpanzees, bonobos, and western gorillas. Overall, our results indicate that economic defendability alone cannot explain interspecific variation in territoriality and that our current understanding of ecological differences between the species of the genus Pan have to be revised. Possible additional factors shaping space use of neighboring groups include mate competition within groups.

papers.title: Generalizable virtual staining from histopathology to spatial proteomics across biological scales
papers.abstract: Large histology archives capture morphological correlates of molecular tissue states but lack direct spatial protein measurements. In this study, we show that routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology can provide a queryable, morphology-based representation of spatial protein expression that remains informative from pixels to patients. To achieve this, we developed QUEST, a model framework that represents protein markers as semantic queries for flexible multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF) prediction. Trained on a heterogeneous atlas of paired H&E and MIF images comprising over 10,000 tissue regions, QUEST captured morphological patterns associated with protein markers and reconstructed their expression intensities across diverse tissue types and cohorts. Its utility extended beyond image reconstruction and preserved biologically meaningful information across multiple scales: virtual staining preserved protein marker expression at the cellular and tissue scales, supported cell phenotyping, cellular neighborhood analysis, and characterization of spatial tissue organization, retained clinically relevant signals for patient stratification, and enabled H&E-based queries to retrieve MIF references with similar molecular profiles. These findings position virtual staining not simply as image generation but as a flexible interface between routine histology and spatial proteomics, expanding the analytical value of existing H&E archives.

papers.title: Epigenetic Rescue of Disuse Muscle Atrophy by Histone Deacetylase Inhibitor Trichostatin A
papers.abstract: Mechanical unloading rapidly induces skeletal muscle atrophy and functional deterioration, yet how the loss of mechanical input influences nuclear architecture, chromatin organization, and associated transcriptional programs remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs) using Trichostatin A (TSA) could attenuate the consequences of continued mechanical unloading in a murine hindlimb suspension model. Following 14 days of unloading, mice exhibited impaired locomotor activity, altered muscle architecture, and widespread transcriptional reprogramming characterized by increased expression of atrophy associated genes, inflammatory mediators, and extracellular matrix remodeling pathways, alongside suppression of mitochondrial metabolic programs. Super resolution imaging further revealed irregular Lamin A/C organization and disruption of discrete H3K9me3 associated heterochromatin foci. Systemic TSA treatment significantly attenuated the decline in locomotor activity, accompanied by trends toward reduced body weight loss, and preservation of muscle morphology. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated a substantial shift toward the baseline expression profile, with high-dose TSA attenuating FOXO associated catabolic programs, inflammatory, and extracellular matrix-related signatures, while enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Quantitative gene level and pathway analyses further revealed dose dependent and selective reversal of unloading associated transcriptional changes. Notably, TSA treatment also partially preserved nuclear lamina organization and the focal distribution of H3K9me3 associated heterochromatin. Despite these muscle specific benefits, TSA did not prevent trabecular bone loss over the 14-day unloading period, although several muscle-expressed genes potentially involved in muscle to bone communication were altered by treatment. Together, these findings demonstrate that HDAC inhibition counteracts multiple functional and molecular consequences of skeletal muscle unloading and is associated with partial preservation of nuclear and heterochromatin organization. This study supports a link between mechanical unloading, nuclear architectural remodeling, and HDAC sensitive transcriptional regulation, providing a foundation for epigenetic strategies to counter disuse induced muscle deterioration.

papers.title: Establishing an ex vivo platform for molecular profiling of skin structural cells using frozen human skin biopsies
papers.abstract: Skin structural cells, including keratinocytes, melanocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts, play critical roles in the development of chronic inflammatory skin disease. Inflammatory stimuli induce transcriptional reprogramming and epigenetic changes in skin structural cells, which contribute to disease pathogenesis. Although two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) skin culture models have been widely used to investigate inflammatory responses in skin structural cells, ex vivo systems that maintain skin structure and cellular composition remain limited. To address this gap, we explored using frozen skin biopsies as an experimental platform to study the responses of skin structural cells to inflammatory stimuli. Using a simple air-liquid interface culture method on permeable Transwell inserts, we showed that viable skin structural cells that retain cell-type-specific transcriptional profiles can be recovered from frozen skin biopsies after prolonged in vitro culture. Stimulation with IFN-{gamma} induced robust transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes that were largely resolved after stimulus removal, with transcriptional responses to secondary stimulation comparable to the primary stimulation. Treatment of cultured skin biopsies with histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors effectively altered global histone modification levels, but did not substantially affect the transcriptional resolution of IFN-{gamma}-induced responses. Collectively, these findings establish cryopreserved human skin biopsies as a scalable ex vivo platform that enables mechanistic studies of inflammatory responses of multiple populations of skin structural cells.

papers.title: Deducing splicing events from transcript sets with splicelogic
papers.abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures a greater proportion of full-length transcripts, enabling more accurate isoform identification, discovery of novel isoforms, and more precise differential transcript usage analysis. However, comparing transcripts, whether between conditions or between sets such as novel and annotated isoforms, yields complex isoform changes that are hard to manipulate, summarize, and visualize. This is compounded by vertical integration of some tools, where downstream analysis depends on the specific output of a particular upstream tool. To address this gap, we have developed splicelogic, an R/Bioconductor package that makes transcript-set comparisons biologically interpretable by turning them into discrete splicing events, such as exon skipping, alternative splice sites, intron retention, and alternative transcription start and end sites. We designed splicelogic to integrate easily with existing RNA-seq workflows and tools. The splicelogic functions are modular, readable, and extensible, making it easy for users to adapt core logic to their own custom scientific questions or novel splicing definitions. By obtaining interpretable splicing events from transcript changes, splicelogic enables downstream analyses, including annotation of RNA-binding protein recognition sites, alongside summary statistics and visualization. The splicelogic package is publicly available and distributed through Bioconductor.

papers.title: Persistent hippocampal traces of lifelong spatial memory
papers.abstract: Memory presents a biological paradox: the brain changes continuously, yet a brief experience can influence behavior for a lifetime. How such memories are stored in brain circuits remains unclear. Here we show that two days in a binary-tree maze leave mice with spatial memories that survive repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year. Across return visits, mice explored the maze more efficiently than when naive and resumed direct runs to a reward location sooner, both by a factor of 3. Chronic calcium imaging of the same hippocampal CA1 neurons showed that although most neurons had changed their preferred locations, the population activity at a given maze location still resembled the pattern from 90 days earlier. Furthermore, even when a neuron's place fields changed location, they tended to remain at the same branching level of the binary tree, reflecting the local geometry of the maze. In return sessions where the neural tuning for branching level was preserved more accurately, the mouse explored the environment more efficiently. Population patterns were best preserved near the reward location, and more reliable neural activity there accompanied earlier direct runs to the reward. With repeated experience, spatial representations changed less, both within a visit and across the long absences. A brief experience thus left selective hippocampal traces that survived months of absence despite drift, grew more durable with each return, and were correlated with memory in navigation behavior.

papers.title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
papers.abstract: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-m-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. By shifting optical sectioning from instrumentation to gene expression, SPress makes kilohertz cellular resolution voltage imaging accessible across mesoscopic scales.

papers.title: RoDPAA: A Robust Dissimilarity-Based Principal Angle Analysis Framework for Multi-View Microbiome Data Integration
papers.abstract: Multiview microbiome studies profile the same participants across body sites or molecular layers, but integration is hampered by sparse, compositional data, modest sample sizes and methods that recognize only exact sharing. We present RoDPAA (Robust Dissimilarity-based Principal Angle Analysis), a framework that represents each view through any data-appropriate dissimilarity, such as Bray--Curtis, without log-ratio transformation or likelihood assumptions. RoDPAA aligns view-specific signal subspaces through principal angles, captures complete and partial sharing, and tests by permutation how many components are shared, using only eigendecomposition and little tuning. In Gaussian simulations, RoDPAA matched JIVE and MOFA given true ranks, ran faster and alone recovered the shared dimension in every replicate. In two inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) cohorts with sparse, zero-inflated data, Bray--Curtis-based RoDPAA recovered shared structure that was stable to prevalence filtering, whereas log-ratio-based alternatives were not. Its leading microbiome--metabolome factors, learned without disease labels, were the only ones associated with IBD.

papers.title: Regionalisation of muscle nucleus heterogeneity in foetal skeletal muscle
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle is organized into functional domains with attachments at both extremities to tendons via the myotendinous junction (MTJ) and innervation in the middle via the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). In adult muscle, the molecular heterogeneity of muscle domains is described at the level of myonuclei with specialized MTJ and NMJ myonuclei at the tips and middle of muscle fibre. However, the regionalisation of molecular heterogeneity remains poorly understood during development. Combining single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing approaches with in situ hybridization experiments to limb muscles of chicken embryos, we uncover transcriptionally distinct muscle nuclei according to tip and central domains, in both myofibres and mononucleated myogenic cells. At early foetal stage, all myonuclei display either a tip or a central domain identity. Immature mononucleated myogenic cells are enriched in the tip domain. Tip myonuclei of foetal muscles show a robust transcriptional signal transduction signature, which highlights molecular crosstalks with adjacent tendon fibroblasts but also with adjacent immature myogenic cells. We propose that the tip muscle domain is a signalling centre interacting with tendon fibroblasts to regulate muscle/tendon attachment and with adjacent mononucleated muscle cells to regulate myogenesis in limb foetal muscles.

papers.title: A noncanonical function of Dicer fuels self-dsRNA-driven inflammation
papers.abstract: Self-derived double-stranded RNA (self-dsRNA) acts as potent triggers of autoinflammation and damage-associated molecular patterns in cancer and infection. However, the upstream processes controlling self-dsRNA homeostasis remain unclear. We uncover a non-canonical role for human Dicer in driving cell-intrinsic immunity to self-dsRNAs that arise from editing or splicing defects, epigenetic deregulation or mitochondrial stress. Dicer loss abolishes type-I interferon induction, PKR activation, and OAS-RNase L activation in response to self - but not exogenous - dsRNA in multiple cell types, including a clinically-relevant hiPSC model of neuroinflammation. Dicer interacts with G3BP1 and LGP2 to regulate self-dsRNA availability and recognition, respectively, independently of miRNAs. As immunostimulatory self-dsRNAs fail to accumulate and activate dsRNA sensors in absence of Dicer, these findings position Dicer as a central regulator of self-dsRNA sensing.

papers.title: Neural Bases for Working Memory of Natural Sound Textures
papers.abstract: Holding sound objects in mind is critical to understanding the sound world around us.
