Auditory texture perception is thought to rely on extracting statistical properties of sounds over time, raising the question of how encoding duration influences subsequent maintenance of auditory texture information. We investigated this question using behavioural performance and fMRI while participants performed two delayed match-to-sample tasks: a texture discrimination and a comparison loudness discrimination task. In the texture task, participants judged whether two sequentially presented sounds belonged to the same texture type, whereas in the loudness task, participants judged whether the sounds, drawn from the same texture type, had the same loudness. Stimuli were presented for either 0.1s or 2s. Discrimination sensitivity increased with duration in both tasks, but more strongly for texture discrimination. fMRI analysis revealed distinct effects of duration on univariate and multivariate activity in the auditory cortex and medial temporal lobe (MTL) during maintenance. We found no univariate duration effect in the auditory cortex during maintenance, but multivariate patterns encoded texture category more strongly for longer stimuli, regardless of task. In contrast, MTL activity was modulated by sound duration in both tasks, but there was no effect of duration on texture category decoding. There was a task effect in MTL where multivariate patterns in posterior hippocampal and parahippocampal regions distinguished texture from loudness tasks following 2s stimuli. Together, these findings show effects of duration on sound texture representations during maintenance and that MTL representations reflect the behavioural context in which that information is maintained.

papers.title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
papers.abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

papers.title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
papers.abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Yet, how all these concurrent mechanisms unfold in time remains underexplored. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in participants listening to stochastic tone sequences with periodically shifting inferential statistics, we modelled the temporal, spatial, and spectral dynamics of stimulus-specific repetition suppression, surprisal, model updating, and prior precision. By concurrently tracking these computational parameters within this dynamic auditory environment, we revealed a distinct chronological hierarchy governing predictive and adaptive processing. Prior precision states - reflecting expectations - emerged earliest, followed by rapid and concurrent repetition suppression and surprisal - reflecting local acoustic attenuation and global mismatch detection. These initial dynamics culminated in subsequent, distributed model updates within fronto-parietal networks. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

papers.title: Stochasticity in Metabolism: Oxidative Stress Response Phenotypes As Emergent Consequences of Network Topology
papers.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are ubiquitous yet elusive due to their reactivity and short half-lives, making simulation essential for mechanistic insight. Traditional ROS modeling has been confined to small ODE frameworks limited by kinetic-parameter scarcity. Here, we recast ROS dynamics as a flux-balance analysis (FBA) optimization problem using COBRA and CPLEX, augmenting the Escherichia coli iJO1366 genome-scale model with 84 spontaneous oxidation, 14 redox, and 9 detoxification reactions, targeting three ROS species: hydroxyl radicals, superoxide, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). We also formalize five fundamental rules of oxidation biology in the form of mixed-integer linear constraints, allowing us to dynamically incorporate reaction rate constants and let complex behavior emerge from first principles. Among these phenomena is the bimodal killing pattern under H2O2 stress, first announced over 40 years ago and never computationally recapitulated until now. We observe it by stochastically sampling our models with GapSplit, simulating bet-hedging and partitioning solutions into growers, persisters, and non-survivors. In our simulations, this killing effect arises solely from the metabolic network topology during random exploration of alternative metabolic configurations. The conservation of steady state creates a stochastic bias for detoxification when central carbon metabolism reaches its metabolic capacity to deal with ROS, causing the famous survival recovery phase. The recovery phase is thus part of Mode 1 metabolism, characterized by spare detoxification capacity and fulfilled by the Ahp reaction in E. coli. Mode 2 has no spare detoxification. We anticipate this to be an overlooked universal principle.

papers.title: Tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
papers.abstract: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles that move the eyes contain specialized nerve endings found in frontal-eyed species. Based on this suite of evidence, we conclude that lateral eyes do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.

papers.title: Mapping the THESEUS1 interactome links cell wall integrity and stress signalling in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: The receptor kinase THESEUS1 (THE1) activates responses to impairment of cell wall integrity (CWI). However, the interaction partners enabling THE1 to mediate the responses remain underexplored, impeding a mechanistic understanding of THE1. We produced a set of THE1 GFP fusion constructs in which THE1 is either wild type, mutated in its kinase domain, has a loss of function mutation in its ectodomain, or lacks the kinase or extracellular domain. We used these constructs to perform localization studies and immunoprecipitation liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry under control and stress conditions (isoxaben induced cell wall damage and sorbitol induced hyperosmotic stress) to identify the THE1 interactome. The interactome of THE1 changed in a context dependent manner, linking THE1 to known signaling components in CWI maintenance and phytohormone response (such as proton pumps, calcium pumps, other receptor kinases or cellulose synthesis regulators). Moreover, we identified novel interactors, associating THE1 with hitherto unexplored signaling pathways in response to CWI impairment. Our results also suggest that the THE1G37D protein (corresponding to the the1 1 allele) is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum, explaining its loss of function phenotype. The THE1 interactome and localization data provide the foundation to build a mechanistic understanding of THE1 mediated CWI maintenance.

papers.title: Scalable high-density tactile arenas for measuring ground-contact forces in freely moving animals
papers.abstract: Understanding how animals physically interact with their environment is fundamental to studying movement, sensorimotor control, and neurological function. Yet most behavioral measurement systems primarily capture movement and posture, while direct measurements of contact forces often require specialized instrumentation or involve trade-offs among spatial coverage, resolution, and acquisition speed. Here, we introduce a scalable tactile sensing platform that transforms the surface beneath freely moving animals into a high-resolution contact-imaging instrument. By combining modular sensor arrays with adaptive compressive tactile sampling, the platform provides 16,384 tactile sensing elements at 2-mm pitch across a 512 x 128-mm runway, with nominal 1 kHz acquisition. Rather than exhaustively scanning the entire array, the system concentrates measurements around active contacts, enabling high-speed sensing across an extended behavioral surface. Synchronized overhead video and a camera-assisted analysis pipeline enable paw-resolved measurements of contact loading, stance dynamics, footprint morphology, interlimb weight redistribution, and center-of-pressure trajectories. In a longitudinal rat model of sciatic nerve injury, the platform detected reduced loading of the injured hindlimb and increased loading of the contralateral limb, including changes that conventional gait timing measures underestimated. The modular architecture, together with openly available hardware designs, software and data, provides an accessible framework for studying the mechanical interactions underlying freely moving behavior, with potential applications across neuroscience, injury, and motor recovery research.

papers.title: Sex-specific dynamics of activity-dependent regulation of synaptic CaMKII
papers.abstract: Similar behavioral outcomes in males and females can mask substantial differences in the mechanisms underlying neuronal function. However, to what extent sex influences the abundance and activity-dependent changes of proteins that govern neuronal plasticity remains poorly understood. Here we investigated sex-specific regulation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), an evolutionarily conserved regulator of synaptic stability and plasticity in fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. We find that the steady state levels and activity-driven changes in CaMKII protein differ between female and male at both third instar larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and in adult fly mushroom body (MB). These sex-specific differences are downstream of the sex determination pathway, implicating somatic sex identity in the regulation of CaMKII abundance and its activity-dependent dynamics. Despite the differences in CaMKII levels between female and male flies, we observed no impairment of plasticity in either sex. Overall, our findings reveal sex-dependent regulation of both steady-state and activity-dependent levels of a highly conserved neuronal plasticity-associated protein across distinct neuronal contexts and development stages. These results further support the idea that females and males can achieve similar behavioral outcomes through different molecular mechanisms. Growing evidence that sexually dimorphic molecular responses contribute directly to sex differences in vulnerability to stress and disease underscores the importance of identifying these mechanisms and understanding their consequences.

papers.title: Expanding Therapeutic Target Space from Genes to Disease-Relevant Molecular Forms with Agent3Diso
papers.abstract: Therapeutic targets are commonly defined at the gene or canonical protein level, yet therapeutic effects are ultimately exerted through specific molecular states operating in specific biological contexts. Alternative splicing generates diverse RNA and translated protein forms whose functional consequences, disease relevance, and therapeutic vulnerabilities can differ substantially within the same gene. Resolving these disease-relevant molecular forms creates opportunities for selective intervention across complementary RNA- and protein-directed modalities, but requires reasoning across tightly coupled molecular layers, heterogeneous evidence, explicit biological constraints, and modality-specific therapeutic requirements. Here, we present Agent3Diso, a hybrid deterministic--agent multimodal framework for molecular-form-resolved therapeutic discovery. Agent3Diso establishes cross-layer molecular coherence from transcript identity and translation to structure, function, and disease context; enforces explicit molecular and therapeutic constraints through deterministic computation; and applies specialized agentic reasoning to evidence synthesis, mechanistic interpretation, conflict resolution, hypothesis critique, and experimental design. The framework evaluates therapeutic opportunities across multiple intervention modalities and translates prioritized disease-relevant molecular states into traceable hypotheses linking molecular identity, therapeutic rationale, modality, concrete intervention, uncertainty, and experimental validation. By integrating molecular resolution with constraint-aware and modality-conditioned agentic reasoning, Agent3Diso provides a framework for extending therapeutic discovery beyond gene-level targets toward disease-relevant molecular forms.

papers.title: VoroTIDE: Protein domain segmentation through independent hierarchical searches using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
papers.abstract: Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein-protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce VoroTIDE (Voronoi-based Two-way Independent Domain Exploration), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. VoroTIDE applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of elementary structural units until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH-ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, VoroTIDE achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

papers.title: Graph-Based Classification of Penetrating Cortical Arteries and Veins in Whole-Mouse Vasculature Datasets
papers.abstract: Advances in whole-brain imaging have produced large-scale vascular datasets, yet most lack artery-vein annotations. However, this is essential for quantitative analysis of whole brain vascular structure, blood flow simulation and translational cerebrovascular research. For unlabelled datasets, manual labelling is infeasible at network scale, and surface-vessel tracing is hampered by reconstruction artefacts, limiting the insights that can be gained from these datasets. Here, we focus on penetrating vessel trees, i.e. descending arteries (A) and ascending veins (V). A supervised Random Forest classifier is trained on graph-derived morphological and topological tree features, including persistent homology. Training uses datasets from two imaging modalities: Light sheet (LS) microscopy with arterial staining and two-photon (TP) micrscopy with manual labelling in smaller samples. Classification reached 96% balanced accuracy on independent TP dataset and 93% on LS datasets. Topological features alone achieved competitive accuracy without relying on diameter measurements, demonstrating cross-modality portability. Arteries exhibit larger diameters and longer inter-bifurcation segments, likely facilitating their functional task of directed blood delivery. The veins show greater branching complexity, allowing low-pressure drainage. These signatures are stable across modalities, supporting their physological relevance. The framework enables A-V label transfer to unlabelled whole-brain TP graph datasets, validated through the V:A ratio as a function of middle cerebral artery (MCA) distance. Operating on graph representations derived from any volumetric imaging modality and requiring no retraining, the approach is applicable to LS, TP, and likely other imaging platforms, providing a scalable foundation for A-V quantification, vascular topological analysis, and haemodynamic modelling.

papers.title: Recording proteome dynamics in the late-stage embryo at hour-timescale, spatial, and single-cell resolution with MEMBRYO
papers.abstract: Cell fate during development is directed by new gene expression states that replace prior ones. When and where a protein is first translated, and how long it will remain in the cell, dictate the timing and extent of a gene's phenotypic effect. Accessing protein synthesis and turnover information in the rapidly developing embryo remains a major challenge. Here we present MEMBRYO: a method for continuous stable isotope labeling (SILAC) of newly synthesized proteins throughout the live embryo at the hour-timescales of developmental phenotypes. We extend embryo culture into the late stages of organogenesis, thereby accessing the proteome of neurogenesis in the forebrain ex utero. Variations in protein synthesis and turnover activity lead to expression patterns that diverge from the corresponding transcripts, impacting molecular pathways and key milestones of cortical neuron differentiation. The high labeling depth enabled both spatial and single-cell SILAC proteomics analysis of cortical cells, revealing distinct layers of post-transcriptional gene expression regulation in progenitors and neurons. By continuous metabolic labeling in the live embryo, MEMBRYO tracks the past, present, and future of the developmental proteome.

papers.title: Interrogating contrastive learning embeddings for structure-based virtual screening: a case study on DrugCLIP
papers.abstract: Virtual screening has become central to early-stage drug discovery, and structure-based approaches have recently been reframed as a retrieval problem through contrastive learning methods such as DrugCLIP, which project protein pockets and ligands into a shared embedding space. However, what these abstract representations encode and how they relate to conventional notions of structural and chemical similarity remain unclear. Here we present a systematic dissection of DrugCLIP's latent space. We show that its pocket embeddings, despite not being explicitly trained for this task, achieve state-of-the-art performance in pocket similarity search while running over 10,000 times faster than existing structural descriptors. We further demonstrate that this embedding space is structurally coherent and robust to conformational variation. Ligand embeddings, by contrast, capture a pocket-aware notion of chemical similarity that extends beyond conventional fingerprint-based measures. Using a rigorous de-leakage benchmark, we show that DrugCLIP generalises beyond its fine-tuning set, retrieving the crystallographic ligand within the top 1% of a library of 48,999 compounds for 56.5% of 223 pockets with low protein sequence identity (SI [≤] 30%) and limited ligand chemical similarity (TS [≤] 0.7) to the fine-tuning set. Nevertheless, performance declines under increasingly realistic screening conditions, primarily due to differences in sidechain orientation across apo, holo and AlphaFold-predicted structures, and mismatches in pocket residue composition when using predicted pockets. These findings delineate the practical limits of DrugCLIP's applicability, highlight accurate pocket identification and representation as key factors for improving performance, and provide a transferable framework for interpreting the latent spaces of related contrastive pocket-ligand models. Together, these results offer insight to guide the refinement of existing methods and the development of future contrastive screening approaches.

papers.title: Intravital microscopy and statistical image analysis of early engraftment of haematopoietic stem cells reveal dynamic and evolving cellular behaviours linked to progressive differentiation.
papers.abstract: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) have long been used in the clinic for bone marrow transplantation applications, critical for the survival of an increasingly wide range of patients with haematological, oncological and immunological pathologies. Despite this, little is known about the mechanisms through which relatively few stem cells are able to regenerate the entire haematopoietic tissue of transplant recipients. To gain insights on this biological process, we used intravital microscopy of calvarium bone marrow, collecting tissue-wide images and a total of 850 hours of tracks of engrafting haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells from 24 hours to 8 days following injection in lethally irradiated recipients. Analysis of the data revealed that regenerating HSCs and their immediate progeny are highly dynamic, migrating through the parenchyma at both the microscopic and near-macroscopic scales, i.e. within and in-and-out of fields of view. HSC-derived cell clusters, expanded locally between day 2 and day 4 post-transplant, leading to patches of densely populated bone marrow by day 8. Single cell level analysis highlighted increasingly heterogenous cellular behaviours over time. Track clustering based on migration and niche interaction parameters combined with post-tracking whole mount immunostaining revealed that persistence in the vicinity of nestin-GFP perivascular cells and relatively slow movement correlated with stemness, while more heterogeneous niche interactions coupled with slowest or faster migration correlated with differentiation, validated through flow cytometry analysis and functional studies. The findings presented here shed light on the fundamental principles driving haematopoietic regeneration in transplantation settings.

papers.title: Gelato streamlines reproducible and auditable assembly of Western blot figures
papers.abstract: Western blotting has been widely used for decades, yet figure preparation remains unstandardized, error-prone and difficult to audit. Gelato is a free Fiji/ImageJ plugin that streamlines intuitive figure preparation, logs processing coordinates, provides a straightforward audit platform and enables reproduction from raw images. By making these capabilities simple and accessible, Gelato facilitates robust Western blot reporting, reducing a substantial burden on authors and reviewers while strengthening scientific rigor.

papers.title: Metastable Dimeric Intermediate Drives Native-like Spidroin Fibrillogenesis, while Dehydration Promotes Cross-β Transition
papers.abstract: The exceptional mechanical properties of spider dragline silk originate from hierarchical spidroin self-assembly, yet mimicking this process to generate native-like structures remains challenging. Here, we report a metastable dimeric intermediate as an essential molecular factor for fibrillogenesis. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) revealed a compact core stabilized by solvent-excluded "dry interfaces" surrounded by extended random coil regions. Within the core, a subset of the polyalanine blocks is held by side-chain packing rather than by main-chain {beta}-sheets; the majority remain exposed in the surrounding coil regions. Upon lowering the denaturant concentration, these exposed polyalanine segments pair with their counterparts at a fibril end, forming intermolecular {beta}-sheets that act as linkers and drive the stepwise end-to-end polymerization of the dimeric particles. In solution, the resulting fibrils exhibit an ordered {beta}-structure in which the polypeptide chains run parallel to the fibril axis, in contrast to amyloid-like cross-{beta}, in which the strands lie perpendicular to it; this matches key features of native silk nanofibril architecture. However, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis demonstrates that these native-like nanofibrils undergo an effectively irreversible transition toward amyloid-like cross-{beta} structures upon drying. Native-like fibrils are thus achievable by self-assembly, but structural control is lost during the final dehydration step. Accordingly, we propose a general principle for decoupling self-assembly from dehydration: native-like nanofibrils are formed first, then dried under conditions that restrict molecular-chain mobility (for example, mechanical constraint or immobilization on a surface), which we expect to suppress thermodynamic relaxation into cross-{beta} structures.

papers.title: One Molecule, Multiple Histories: Comparative Phylogenomics of Glutamate Metabolism, Transport and Receptor Families Across 89 Eukaryotic Proteomes
papers.abstract: Glutamate links cellular metabolism with excitatory neurotransmission, yet the evolutionary histories of its metabolic enzymes, transporters, and receptor paralogues have not been compared within a common human-reference-anchored phylogenomic framework. Here, we traced human UniProt/Swiss-Prot-associated protein lineages across 89 eukaryotic proteomes using homology searches, sequence and domain filtering, maximum-likelihood phylogenies assessed with transfer bootstrap expectation (TBE) and ultrafast bootstrap (UFBoot), sequence-stability analyses, and GeneRax gene-tree/species-tree reconciliation under a duplication-loss model. Metabolic enzyme homologues showed the broadest distributions: GLUD, GOT, and GPT were recovered across multiple eukaryotic supergroups, whereas GLS-associated sequences were detected in metazoans and the ichthyosporean Capsaspora owczarzaki. SLC17 and SLC1 transporter homologues were recovered only from sampled metazoans. Receptor distributions varied among families: GRM and GRIN sequences were detected across sampled cnidarians and bilaterians, GRIA and GRIK across bilaterian groups, and GRID only in seven sampled vertebrate species. Reconciliation mapped numerous paralogue-associated duplications to early vertebrate, gnathostome, and osteichthyan ancestral nodes, alongside independent lineage-specific expansions. Although many local phylogenetic relationships were supported, deeper relationships in some transporter and receptor families remained uncertain, with TBE and UFBoot providing different support values. These findings characterize the human-associated glutamatergic repertoire as an evolutionary mosaic of gene families with distinct taxonomic distributions and duplication histories. Because homology searches were anchored on human reference proteins, the inferred distributions represent detectable lineages in the sampled dataset rather than definitive evidence of gene-family origins or absence.

papers.title: Genome-resolved metatranscriptomic analysis of arsenic demethylation and detoxification in a methanogenic rice paddy soil
papers.abstract: Microbial methylation and demethylation of arsenic in rice paddy soils influence the speciation and toxicity of arsenic in rice, with implications for human health and rice yields. Here, we combine genome-resolved metatranscriptomics with arsenic speciation analysis in methanogenic paddy soil incubations to elucidate microbial pathways regulating As demethylation, with emphasis on: (i) evaluating links between methyltransferase gene transcription by methylotrophic methanogens and arsenic demethylation; and (ii) assessing how toxicity-induced microbial responses regulate As demethylation and the resulting distribution of As species. Experiments with dimethylarsinic (DMAs) and 2-bromoethanesulfonate as a methanogenesis inhibitor confirm an important role of methanogens in anaerobic arsenic demethylation. Amendment of the methylotrophic substrate trimethylamine accelerated arsenic demethylation and induced an association between arsenic demethylation rates and the transcription of diverse methylotrophic methyltransferases. Six Methanosarcina metagenome assembled genomes dominated methyltransferase transcription and concurrently transcribed genes involved in multiple (methyl)arsenic oxidation and efflux pathways, illustrating a link between putative demethylation and arsenic detoxification at the genome level. Paddy soil incubations also demonstrated toxicity-driven feedbacks between DMAs concentrations and demethylation rates, wherein higher DMAs concentrations inhibited methanogenesis and decreased pseudo first-order demethylation rate constants. These findings provide new insights into links between methylotrophic methanogenesis and arsenic demethylation in anaerobic conditions, with implications for biogeochemical control of arsenic speciation in rice paddy soils.

papers.title: MAXWELL: Calibrating the probabilistic outputs of protein language models to the mutation-induced stability change landscape
papers.abstract: Designing mutations that enhance protein stability is a central goal in protein engineering. However, experimentally screening large numbers of candidate mutations is costly and time-consuming, creating a strong need for computational methods that can identify potentially stabilizing mutations. Among these approaches, protein language models are particularly promising because they learn context-dependent amino acid preferences from large-scale sequence and structure datasets. Nevertheless, most existing stability prediction methods use these models primarily as feature extractors and do not fully exploit the amino acid probability distributions they encode. Here, we introduce MAXWELL (Matrix-wise Landscape Learning), a novel post-training method that calibrates the probabilistic outputs learned by protein language models during pretraining to generate mutational landscapes that quantify the effects of individual amino acid substitutions on protein stability. When applied to ProteinMPNN, MAXWELL yields a state-of-the-art predictor of the effects of protein mutations on stability, outperforming ThermoMPNN and other representative methods on a curated benchmark of experimentally measured stability changes. We next applied MAXWELL to the design of ten single-point mutations in the DhaA dehalogenase, seven of which (70%) increased thermal stability. Among them, G171W showed the largest improvement, with a measured {Delta}T of 4.91 . These experimental results establish MAXWELL as a novel post-training strategy for protein language models and a practical framework for designing stabilizing mutations.

papers.title: β-cell NCK1 is reduced in type 2 diabetes, impairing the unfolded protein response and insulin secretion while revealing sex-specific adaptation
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by failure of pancreatic {beta} cells to adapt insulin secretion to metabolic demand, causing {beta} cell function and reduced {beta} cell mass. The unfolded protein response (UPR) is central to adaptation by maintaining endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and supporting insulin biosynthesis, secretion, proliferation, and survival. NCK1, is an adaptor protein that regulates insulin biosynthesis and UPR activation, positioning it at the crossroads of several processes essential for {beta} cell function. We found in mouse and human islets that NCK1 expression was upregulated by glucose and reduced in individuals living with type 2 diabetes. We thus explored the importance of {beta} cell NCK1 in endocrine function and glucose homeostasis using INS 1 cells, mouse and human islets, and {beta} cell specific knockout male and female mice (NCK1{beta}KO). Loss of {beta} cell NCK1 disrupted the UPR and impaired insulin gene expression, insulin content, and glucose stimulated insulin secretion in vitro. Unexpectedly, these intrinsic {beta} cell defects triggered sex-specific adaptive responses at the organismal level, revealing distinct strategies to reshape glucose homeostasis. Under high fat/high sucrose diet, both NCK1{beta}KO female and male mice increased pancreatic insulin content, but females exhibited impaired insulin secretion associated with an increased number of small islets and reduced PERK pathway activation resulting in mild glucose intolerance. In contrast, males NCK1{beta}KO mice had improved insulin secretion associated with islet expansion, {beta} cell proliferation, and increased PERK pathway activation leading to enhanced glucose tolerance. These findings identify NCK1 as a regulator of {beta} cell insulin synthesis, secretion, and UPR signaling, and reveal sex specific adaptive mechanisms to metabolic stress. Thus, reduced NCK1 in islets from people living type 2 diabetes may contribute to {beta} cell dysfunction.

papers.title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
papers.abstract: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.

papers.title: From exact gradients to exact standard errors: third- and fourth-order sensitivities for the Laplacian population likelihood family
papers.abstract: Asymptotic standard errors for the parameters of a nonlinear mixed effects model fitted by Laplacian estimation, first-order conditional estimation (FOCE), or FOCE with interaction (FOCEI) require the observed (Fisher) information, the negative second derivative of the population objective at the optimum. The gradient of this objective can be computed exactly from sensitivity equations, but the observed information is still formed by finite differencing, which is less accurate, step-size dependent, and requires empirical Bayes reoptimization. These perturbed individual optimization problems can fail even after a successful fit. Our objectives are to (1) extend the exact-gradient sensitivity framework by one differentiation and give the observed information of the Laplacian population likelihood family in closed form and (2) illustrate covariance calculation without further empirical Bayes optimization in a case example. Writing the objective as a data term plus the log-determinant of the inner Hessian, the population Hessian splits so that the data term reuses second-order sensitivities, whereas the log determinant term requires third-order sensitivities for FOCE/FOCEI and fourth-order sensitivities for the full Laplacian method. We illustrate this on a two-compartment oral model with first-order absorption fitted to simulated data. The analytic covariance involves no differencing step and uses the fitted empirical Bayes estimates without reoptimization, avoiding this source of covariance-step failure. Implemented for FOCE/FOCEI in the open-source R package nlmixr2, the construction provides exact, reproducible standard errors for the approximate likelihood, limited by numerical solution accuracy and conditioning. This supports more dependable confidence intervals, identifiability assessment, and uncertainty propagation.

papers.title: MintCNA: A Unified Framework for Integrative Copy Number Profiling with Single-Cell Multi-Omics Data
papers.abstract: Chromosomal copy number alterations (CNAs) are key drivers of tumor evolution, disease progression and therapeutic resistance, and their identification is critical for delineating tumor clonal structure. However, accurately detecting CNAs from single-cell data remains challenging as most existing CNA callers still analyze a single omics layer and are susceptible to assay-specific noise. Recently, single-cell multi-omics techniques have enabled joint sequencing of multiple molecular layers (e.g., genomics and transcriptomics) simultaneously in the same cells, yet computational methods that fully exploit such complementary multi-omics data for CNA analysis remain limited. Here, we present MintCNA, a unified framework for CNA detection from paired single-cell multi-omics data. MintCNA integrates deep-learning based denoising with a missingness-adjusted multivariate change-point detection procedure to enhance CNA profiling across omics layers. In simulations, MintCNA outperformed existing single-cell CNA callers across all evaluated scenarios. MintCNA showed the highest correlation with bulk whole-genome sequencing in a colorectal cancer dataset and revealed progressive loss of chromosome 17 during metastasis. In an IDH-mutant glioma cohort, MintCNA generalized to paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data and identified copy number subclones corresponding to distinct malignant cell states. MintCNA provides an advanced multi-omics integrative single-cell CNA analysis tool for better delineating the mechanisms underlying disease progression and tumor evolution.

papers.title: A Mathematical Model of Reliability-Dependent Sensory Reweighting in Quiet Standing
papers.abstract: Human quiet standing relies on vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual information whose contributions change with sensory context. Posturography characterizes this reweighting through responses to visual and support-surface perturbations, but a compact account of how sensory reliability propagates from state estimation to postural action remains incomplete. We develop a minimal quiet-standing model in which sensory reliability is encoded by channel-specific precision parameters that weight sensory prediction errors. A one-link inverted pendulum with intrinsic ankle stiffness estimates posture by minimizing an active-inference free-energy objective and selects ankle torque by minimizing the same objective under a restorative sensory goal. A fixed-point analysis predicts in closed form the perturbation-induced belief bias, each channel's state-update contribution, the steady posture, and a linear stability condition from the precisions, goal dynamics, and intrinsic stiffness. Closed-loop simulations in 115 trials matched the predicted equilibria to within 0.001degrees wherever the loop settled, and the two conditions predicted unstable diverged or drifted. Reducing an unreliable channel's precision eightfold reduced perturbation-driven posture shifts by 82%, with a matching decrease in that channel's state-update contribution; intrinsic stiffness left this reduction essentially unchanged for visual and sensory-only perturbations but bounded it for physical support tilts; a global precision reduction did not reduce the shift; and a within-trial precision switch showed belief updating, not a separate action gain, carrying the change to ankle torque. The results give a compact mathematical account of postural sensory reweighting as relative, context-selective precision control in a closed multisensory loop.

papers.title: Molecular diffusion and binding kinetics are sufficient to explain condensate-like nuclear clustering
papers.abstract: Many key transcriptional regulators form clusters in cell nuclei that are proposed to promote transcription by concentrating reactants. These clusters exhibit emergent biophysical properties consistent with biomolecular condensates such as high local densities, spherical morphologies, fusion, and rapid molecular exchange kinetics. Whether these properties are specific hallmarks of condensation or can arise from simpler mechanisms is unclear. Here we developed SPARK (Simulation of Protein Accumulation from Reaction Kinetics), a computational framework parameterized by genomic, and molecular diffusion and binding kinetics data, to simulate the spatial distributions of chromatin-binding proteins as they would appear under an optical microscope. These simulations recapitulate key reported features of Brd4, Nanog, Sox2, and Bicoid clusters, without including any higher-order protein-protein interactions or phase separation. We demonstrate that commonly used signatures of condensates instead emerge directly from molecular scale binding and diffusion kinetics. Through systematic variation of nuclear concentrations and enhancer binding-site composition, we show that distinct combinations of molecular kinetics can result in similar spatial distributions of transcription factors. These analyses establish that imaging-based features of protein clusters cannot uniquely define the underlying physical mechanism of their formation. We therefore conclude that condensation is not required to drive transcription factor occupancy and that protein-protein interactions off chromatin are not required to explain cluster formation. Our results instead imply that mechanisms other than clustering are sufficient for target-search acceleration and robust occupancy. SPARK thus provides a quantitative null model for identifying which molecular mechanisms are necessary to explain experimental observations of nuclear protein clustering.

papers.title: Do plasmid-dependent phages enable the survival of costly plasmids?
papers.abstract: Plasmids store auxiliary genes that address environmental challenges such as antibiotics. In the short term, plasmid loss can be advantageous to hosts if plasmid benefits are temporary but costs are permanent. However, this loss can proceed to plasmid extinction, with access to plasmid-derived benefits permanently lost. We consider a worst-case scenario: a plasmid that yields benefits only infrequently, imposes heavy costs that cannot be alleviated, and whose host population faces a competitor that cannot acquire the costly plasmid. Thus, horizontal transmission of this plasmid is detrimental to the host population when the plasmid does not provide benefits. Using population models, we demonstrate that -- counterintuitively -- plasmid-dependent phages can enable high-cost plasmid survival. Phage predation pins the plasmid at low abundance, effectively neutralizing the plasmid cost at the population level and boosting persistence time. When the costly plasmid becomes beneficial, it spreads and survives by vertical transmission until benefits subside.

papers.title: Pollinator specificity among three co-flowering Mediterranean Aristolochia species pollinated by Diptera
papers.abstract: Attracting species-specific pollinators can be favoured by natural selection to avoid reproductive interference between sympatric plant species. However, the ways in which fine differences in floral traits lead to the attraction of species-specific pollinators are diverse and unknown in most pollination interactions. We surveyed pollinators on three Aristolochia species that can occur in pairs in sympatry (A. clematitis-A. rotunda and A. pistolochia-A. rotunda) and are pollinated by Ceratopogonidae and Chloropidae (Diptera), to investigate the extent to which pollinator assemblages differ among plant species. To assess whether specificity in pollinator assemblages may be mediated by differences in floral odour composition, we characterised the volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted by receptive flowers and highlighted those VOCs electrophysiologically detected by pollinators of A. rotunda and A. pistolochia. Among the most abundant pollinators, females of Forcipomyia monilicornis were specific pollinators of A. pistolochia while males and females of two Dasyhelea species were specific pollinators of A. clematitis. Females of Forcipomyia aristolochiae and of Trachysiphonella ruficeps were the main pollinators in A. rotunda but also pollinated the other two species. The floral odours of A. rotunda and A. pistolochia differed significantly from each other and elicited specific electrophysiological responses in their respective pollinators. Although several pollinator species visit more than one Aristolochia species, those pollinators are preferentially found in one Aristolochia species. Selective attraction is likely mediated by specific VOCs.

papers.title: Robust lesion network mapping reveals symptom-specific circuits
papers.abstract: Lesion network mapping (LNM) is a powerful tool for linking distributed brain lesions to symptom-relevant networks, but similar LNM maps across unrelated symptoms have raised concerns about its statistical validity and specificity. Here we introduce robust LNM (rLNM), a statistically principled framework that combines two complementary controls: an anatomy-preserving spatial null model to account for connectome-derived hub bias shared across symptoms, and hypothesis-driven contrasts to resolve selective specificity among related symptoms. rLNM effectively controls both false positives and negatives. Across 10 lesion datasets (384 lesions) and two task-fMRI meta-analyses (339 experiments), rLNM recovers distinct symptom-specific networks (mean r = 0.044), which show significantly reduced similarity to the connectome hub pattern (r = 0.12 vs. 0.33 in conventional LNM). In 56 patients with neurosurgical lesions, rLNM predicts postoperative language decline at the single-patient level. rLNM thus resolves these concerns and lays a unified statistical foundation for network-symptom inferenc.

papers.title: A fine-tuned genomic language model captures nucleotide-level information overlooked by missense variant impact predictors
papers.abstract: Established missense variant impact predictors primarily capture protein-level consequences, yet missense-annotated variants can also act through nucleotide sequence context. We developed GLM-Missense by systematically optimizing the fine-tuning of a genomic language model for missense variant impact prediction. GLM-Missense contributed the most complementary information to seven established predictors on held-out ClinVar variants and independent RAD51D saturation genome editing data. The complementary signal partly reflects splicing disruption, including disrupted exonic splicing regulatory elements largely missed by SpliceAI, and possibly codon-level effects on mRNA stability. These findings suggest fine-tuned genomic language models capture nucleotide-level information overlooked by current missense variant impact predictors.

papers.title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
papers.abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

papers.title: Evolutionary tuning of rhodopsin-mediated light protection
papers.abstract: Visual sensitivity introduces the inherent risk of blinding photodamage. Rhodopsin directly mediates this vulnerability, as activation drives excessive signaling via the Meta-II (MII) state, which subsequently releases the toxic, desensitizing agonist all-trans retinal (atRAL). In dim-light specialists, slow atRAL release is assumed to reflect extended MII signaling; however, this model ignores that arrestin quenches signaling in milliseconds and that apparent release reflects reversible atRAL rebinding. Here we reveal that extended post-bleach lifetimes, including an atRAL-driven shift toward non-signaling Meta-III (MIII), evolved independently of intrinsic G-protein signaling to dually protect retinal cells against photochemical toxicity and shield neighboring receptors from agonist noise. Dim-light specialists whose rod-dense retinas experience daytime solar flux, such as megabats, possess an extremely cytoprotective rhodopsin that retains nearly 60% of atRAL at equilibrium by partitioning into MIII, validating long-standing predictions that MIII buffers retinoid toxicity while explaining why bat rhodopsin signals more weakly than faster-releasing human or bovine orthologs. To definitively uncouple sequestration from intrinsic signaling, we engineered an active-state-locked, signaling-null rhodopsin that achieves 100% atRAL sequestration and confers extreme cytoprotection in retinal cells. Mimicking partial bleaches with heterogeneous active and inactive receptor populations, co-incubation reveals that this signaling-null sink acts in trans to boost wild-type rhodopsin regeneration and signaling by shielding neighboring dark-state receptors from agonist interference. Lastly, while consensus human rhodopsin is non-protective, alleles restoring cytoprotective sequestration emerged in high-irradiance geographies, conferring a 38% reduced risk of blindness in modern populations. Our findings redefine rhodopsin as a tunable light buffer shaping adaptation and human disease.

papers.title: On the intra-laboratory replicability of results in animal cognition research, obtained in animals that were not exposed to, or unaffected by, experimental manipulations - Exemplified by spatial learning in pigs (Sus Scrofa Domesticus) across 12 holeboard studies
papers.abstract: The replicability of experimental results is considered a cornerstone of empirical research. However, the reproducibility of results from groups that have not undergone experimental manipulation - the standard against which comparisons in an experiment are made - has been almost entirely neglected in animal research. Our aim is to address this gap by exemplarily determining within-laboratory replicability using research in pigs, an increasingly popular large animal model species. Drawing on data from twelve independent porcine holeboard studies conducted in our laboratory, we examine the replicability of groups that were not subjected to experimental manipulation (typically the control group), eventually including groups on which the experimental treatments had no effect. These analyses were also performed on all eight studies involving the Terra x Finnish Landrace x Duroc pig breed, with all other breeds excluded to increase genetic uniformity. The holeboard is a complex spatial discrimination task in which an animal must learn to find food at four of sixteen possible locations (holes) arranged in a 4 x 4 matrix. The main variables measured are spatial working memory (WM), reference memory (RM) and the inter-visit interval (IVI), which serves as an index of motivation. All studies showed predominantly linear improvements in WM and learning rates across successive trial blocks. IVI showed greater variation across trialblocks, but this did not affect WM and RM learning, which are robust and replicable indices of spatial learning in pigs. Assessing replicability provides relevant information, such as whether behavioural and physiological traits in a model species are stably expressed and robust across studies. Including replicability research and publishing its results can stimulate the development and use of more replicable methods and workflows, thereby increasing scientific rigour. Provided the data are available and accessible, the next step should be to expand replicability studies to include those conducted in different laboratories.

papers.title: Altered neurodevelopment, CSF volume, and emotional reactivity following postnatal Zika virus infection in infant macaques
papers.abstract: Although congenital Zika virus (ZIKV) syndrome is well-characterized, the neurodevelopmental consequences of postnatal infection are understudied. We used a rhesus macaque (RM) model to investigate the consequences of postnatal ZIKV infection on brain and behavior. Male and female infant RMs infected with ZIKV at 1 month of age were compared to sex-, age-, and rearing-matched controls: uninfected and treated with Poly-IC as an innate immune control. ZIKV-infected infants showed poor state control in early infancy and increased hostility during an acute stressor. They displayed sex-specific behavioral alterations during caregiver separation though attachment bonds were preserved. MRI at 3 months revealed larger total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume, reduced visual processing region volumes, and sex-specific brain structural alterations: males exhibited amygdala hypertrophy, whereas females had volumetric reductions in temporal-limbic and temporal-auditory cortices. These findings indicate that postnatal ZIKV infection is associated with alterations in sensory, social and emotion-regulatory systems and in CSF volume, that may warrant long-term monitoring of exposed children.

papers.title: Non-canonical peptidoglycan cross-linking is essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis acid resistance
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis withstands acidic conditions to survive and replicate within macrophages. To define the genetic determinants of this adaptation, we performed a transposon screen in a lipid-rich, acidic medium that mimics the host environment and supports robust M. tuberculosis growth. This screen identified ldtB, encoding an L,D transpeptidase, as essential for growth and survival under acid stress. Loss of LdtB decreased 3-3 peptidoglycan cross-linking, disrupted cell wall architecture, and impaired intrabacterial pH homeostasis, resulting in increased susceptibility to cell wall-active antibiotics. Notably, M. tuberculosis lacking LdtB displayed heightened sensitivity to meropenem within macrophages, suggesting that targeting this enzyme could potentiate beta-lactam efficacy during infection. These findings establish LdtB as a key mediator linking peptidoglycan homeostasis to acid stress resistance and underscores the importance of in vitro culture models that recapitulate the host microenvironment for uncovering new in vivo active therapeutic targets.

papers.title: PREMISE: A Quality-Aware Probabilistic Framework for High-Resolution Source Assignment in Metagenomic Sequencing
papers.abstract: Metagenomic applications, from influenza A virus (IAV) subtype tracking to bacterial strain resolution, frequently require sub-species resolution.However, traditional $k$-mer-based methods fragment reads into short $k$-mers and discard per-base quality scores.By omitting both intra-read linkage and error information, these methods confound closely related genomic variants, thereby impeding real-time pathogen surveillance and containment.We introduce \premise (Pathogen Resolution via Expectation-Maximization In Sequencing Experiments), a probabilistic, alignment-based framework implemented in Rust for high-resolution source assignment against near-complete reference databases.\premise aligns whole reads using a bidirectional run-length FM-index and quantifies reference abundances with a quality-aware Expectation-Maximization algorithm mapped over a taxonomy.This framework applies an optional sparsity penalty to resolve ambiguous assignments, which is particularly important when sparse samples are mapped against reference databases rich in highly homologous candidate references.On ten dense CAMI II strain-madness samples, \premise achieves the highest species-level read classification F1 score ($0.992$) among eight evaluated methods, with no false-positive or missed species.At the strain level, \premise maps reads to their source genome with top precision ($0.80$ vs. at most $0.64$ for competing methods), achieves 100\% recall, and estimates abundances as accurately as the best competing tool.These results demonstrate \premise's ability to provide rigorous, uncertainty-aware source resolution across both dense and sparse metagenomes, accurately resolving targets ranging from viral subtypes to bacterial strains.\\textbf{Availability:} \url{https://github.com/sriram98v/premise} under an MIT license.\\textbf{Contact:} \href{sriramv@iastate.edu}{sriramv@iastate.edu}\\

papers.title: Polar Marine Microbial Communities as Reservoirs of Polyester Degrading Enzymes
papers.abstract: Background: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is one of the most widely used plastics and a major contributor to marine pollution. While the diversity of PET hydrolases (PETases), which degrade PET into mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET), terephthalate (TPA) and ethylene glycol, has been documented in temperate and tropical waters, their potential presence in polar oceans remains unascertained. Results: Here, we systematically screened polar and non-polar marine metagenomes using Hidden Markov models (HMM) generated using experimentally validated PETases. We identified >680 putative PETase-like sequences, with Antarctic and Arctic candidates enriched in high-fidelity motifs associated with PETase-like activity. Phylogenetic and structural analyses defined a high-confidence PETase-like clade comprising both Type I and Type II enzymes, differing in thermostability-related features and PET-binding motifs. Experimental assays confirmed polyesterase activity in 5/9 candidates from this clade, including polar-derived variants active at 14-25{degrees}C. Downstream enzymes for PET consumption were also widespread, detecting 209 putative MHET hydrolases and 442 TPA-catabolyzing enzymes. Further, we reconstructed 112 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) carrying at least one enzyme of the PET degradation pathway, 89 of them carrying a PETase-like gene. Notably, 15 MAGs encoded multiple PETase-like enzymes, nine of them from polar datasets, and one polar MAG harbored a complete PETase-MHETase-TPA pathway, suggesting the genomic potential for a fully integrated degradation potential in cold-adapted taxa. Conclusions: Together, these results demonstrate that polar oceans act as previously overlooked reservoirs of taxonomically and functionally diverse plastic-degrading enzymes. The enrichment of PETase-like enzymes and downstream pathways in polar microbial communities expands the global biogeography of plastic biodegradation and highlights cold-active enzymes as promising candidates for developing low-temperature plastic bioremediation strategies.

papers.title: PIKfyve inhibition induces LRRK2 activation through phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and CASM
papers.abstract: LRRK2 is a Parkinson's disease (PD)-associated kinase that phosphorylates Rab GTPases. Hyperactivation of LRRK2, which is thought to cause PD, occurs on stressed endolysosomal membranes via CASM (conjugation of ATG8 to single membranes) and Rab, whereas the involvement of specific membrane lipids remained unclear. Here, we found that the inhibition of PIKfyve that metabolizes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) induces hyperactivation of LRRK2, and that additional inhibition of the class III phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) that generates PI3P suppressed LRRK2 hyperactivation. Cellular PI3P levels were indeed elevated when LRRK2 was activated. CASM-induced activation of LRRK2, but not CASM itself, was suppressed by PI3K inhibitors, whereas inhibition of CASM or Rab12/Rab29 suppressed LRRK2 activation induced by PIKfyve inhibitors. LRRK2 and phospho-Rab10 were co-localized with PI3P on LAMP1-positive enlarged vacuoles, and LRRK2 directly bound PI3P in vitro via its N-terminal positively charged amino acids. Together, we propose an updated mechanism of LRRK2 hyperactivation that simultaneously requires CASM, Rab and PI3P-rich membranes.

papers.title: Experience shifts value updating from synaptic plasticity to neural dynamics
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires durable value memories and rapid updating. Experience in dynamic environments accelerates value updating, but the underlying neuronal mechanisms remain unclear. Mice exposed to repeated reversals of odor-outcome contingencies acquired faster value updating at the cost of faster memory decay. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained with continual plasticity revealed two routes to faster learning, one through more efficient synaptic plasticity and one through a transition to value computation by neural dynamics. Only the latter reproduced the trade-off between updating speed and memory persistence observed in mice. Consistent with this transition, inhibiting dopamine neurons at reward delivery or pharmacologically inhibiting CaMKII in the amygdala impaired initial learning but largely spared expert reversal learning. In vivo recordings in the amygdala and hippocampus revealed representations of cue value and latent context necessary for rapid value updating. Context and value signals decayed over prolonged inter-trial intervals, paralleling behavioral forgetting. Conditional deletion of CaMKIIa in Emx1-cre-expressing neurons spared initial associative learning but impaired expert reversal performance, as did freezing the recurrent weights of RNNs, suggesting distinct loci for initial value learning and meta-learning. Together, these findings reveal how experience shifts value computation from synaptic plasticity toward neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for the trade-off between memory stability and behavioral flexibility.

papers.title: Small RNA-mediated genomic silencing promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase in C. elegans
papers.abstract: We previously found that small RNAs with perfect homology to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats are very rare. Here we use long read sequencing to reveal that most N2 wild type C. elegans strains have few telomere mutations at 5 prime ends of telomeres, where the telomeric lncRNA TERRA is transcribed. Therefore, telomere mutations cannot explain the absence of perfect small RNAs to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats. We show that the heterochromatin mark H3K9me2 is enriched at C. elegans sub-telomeres and that the HP1 protein HPL-2 that binds H3K9me2 promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase. Small RNA silencing can promote H3K9 methylation, and telomere stability in the absence of telomerase requires germ granule proteins MUT-7 and MUT-14 that promote small RNA biogenesis and also WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 Argonaute proteins that bind subtelomeric small RNAs. Loss of telomerase induced biogenesis of small RNAs from the subtelomeric 5 prime end of the telomeric lncRNA TERRA but not from telomere repeats of TERRA. Loss of both telomerase and small RNA-mediated genome silencing induced TERRA expression, telomere damage and accelerated sterility. We propose that small RNA-mediated heterochromatin formation and telomerase function redundantly to repress a form of telomeric DNA damage that is coupled to TERRA expression and subtelomeric small RNA biogenesis. However, telomere repeats of TERRA strongly resisted RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity in telomerase mutants, revealing an exceptional quality of telomere repeat RNA.

papers.title: The G-protein coupled receptor GPR34 maintains the homeostatic state of microglia and restrains the disease-associated microglial response in an Alzheimers disease model
papers.abstract: Expression of the G protein coupled receptor GPR34 is highly enriched in microglia and is downregulated in various brain diseases, including Alzheimers disease (AD) and multiple sclerosis (MS). GPR34 function is poorly understood, as is its role in regulation of microglial states. Using RNA-sequencing, we find that microglia from Gpr34 knockout (KO) mouse brains exhibited a transcriptomic shift toward disease-associated microglia (DAM) and inflammatory profiles, partially resembling the microglial phenotype seen in 5xFAD AD model mice. Moreover, when Gpr34 KO mice were crossed with 5xFAD mice, the DAM transcriptional profile of microglia and glial pathology were further exacerbated beyond the already robust DAM signature driven by 5xFAD alone. This occurred without affecting amyloid plaque burden. Human stem cell-derived microglia (iMGLs) lacking GPR34 showed reduced calcium (Ca2+) and phosphorylated ERK (pERK) signaling in response to stimulation with known GPR34 agonists (lyso-phosphatidylserine (lysoPS) and myelin), as well as transcriptomic changes in immune regulation and cell proliferation related pathways. Interestingly, GPR34 KO iMGLs were selectively impaired in phagocytosis of myelin but not amyloid-B; (AB) or E. coli, and showed a diminished transcriptional response elicited by myelin. Together, these findings suggest that GPR34 is important for maintaining microglia in a homeostatic state, promotes phagocytosis of and transcriptional response to myelin, and limits microglial reactivity in neurodegenerative disease conditions.

papers.title: Microfluidic sieve and detector for rapid ultrasensitive assays with single-molecule sensitivity
papers.abstract: The advent of ultrasensitive assays enabled many new research and clinical applications, but the time-to-result is hours and has not significantly improved over time, limiting their potential. We introduce the microfluidic sieve and detector (MFSD) that can sieve 200 microlitres in just one minute, and quantify captured analytes in four minutes, down to zeptomolar (10^-19M) concentration. The MFSD comprises half a million 8-m-diameter pores that bind analytes upon Brownian motion-induced wall collision. Conventional ensemble models and a stochastic Brownian agent dynamics introduced here reveal rapid, predictable and tuneable analyte capture under flow. Digital sandwich assays are completed by sequentially flowing the sample and reagents, partitioning the pores, and digitally revealing single trapped analytes by enzymatic amplification. The MFSD tests are specific and reproducible, exhibit a large dynamic range, and are simple, tuneable and versatile, enabling measurement of different proteins including influenza A nucleoprotein in clinical samples, and even nucleic acids while being both faster and more sensitive than PCR. As such, the MFSD could open a new chapter for analysis and diagnostics.

papers.title: Murine Toll-like receptor 8 is a functional sensor of nucleic acid fragments
papers.abstract: Toll-like receptors 7 and 8 (TLR7 and TLR8) detect nucleic acid degradation products to initiate innate immune responses, although their ligand-sensing functions differ between species. Whereas human TLR8 is a well-established nucleic acid sensor, murine TLR8 (mTLR8) has long been considered unable to detect nucleic acids. Here, we show that mTLR8 is an active receptor that responds to the synthetic agonist TL8-506 and the endogenous cyclic nucleotide 2',3'-cGMP, with signalling potentiated by cooperative binding of nucleic acid fragments at the secondary ligand-binding site. Using Tlr7-deficient mice expressing mTlr8 under control of the Tlr7 promoter, we demonstrate that mTLR8 partially restores TLR7-dependent tonic transcriptional programs in splenocytes, indicating responsiveness to physiological ligands in vivo. Comparison with a chimeric human-mouse TLR8 knock-in model expressing human TLR8 from the endogenous murine Tlr7 locus demonstrated that the mTLR8 ectodomain is intrinsically less sensitive, consistent with sequence divergence in the LRR11-12 region that links agonist recognition to antagonist regulation. Collectively, these findings establish mTLR8 as a functional nucleic acid sensor specialized for combinatorial detection of nucleic acid degradation products, extending the murine endosomal nucleic acid-sensing repertoire beyond TLR3, TLR7, TLR9, and TLR13.

papers.title: A Gαq/11-IP3R1-ANO1 pacemaking axis underlies pressure-induced lymphatic chronotropy
papers.abstract: The frequency of spontaneous lymphatic contractions is exquisitely sensitive to changes in intraluminal pressure, enabling lymph transport to be matched to the filling state of the lymphatic capillary network. The mechanistic basis of this mechanosensitive response was investigated using ex vivo contraction assays of mouse popliteal collecting vessels. Based on electrophysiological and transcriptional similarities between lymphatic muscle cells (LMCs) and arterial smooth muscle, we hypothesized that pressure-dependent chronotropy shares a parallel signaling process with pressure-induced arterial depolarization/constriction. Thus, we probed two potential mechanisms: 1) pressure-induced activation of mechanosensitive cation channels and 2) mechano-activation of GNAQ/GNA11-coupled G-protein receptors (GPCRs) that would generate second messengers to activate those channels. Contraction assays were combined with scRNAseq analysis of the respective targets and use of transgenic mice. Our findings rule out significant roles for the mechanosensitive channels implicated in arterial myogenic constriction as well as channels implicated in ionic pacemaking of other tissues. In contrast, smooth-muscle specific knock out or inhibition of ANO1, IP3R1 or GNAQ/GNA11 significantly abrogated pressure-induced chronotropy. These results support a scheme whereby mechano-activation of one or more GNAQ/GNA11-coupled GPCRs generates IP3, inducing sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release through IP3R1, which drives depolarization through the activation of ANO1 Cl- channels. The major GPCRs expressed in LMCs were identified and ranked by scRNAseq analysis but individual inhibition or knock out the top 7 candidates failed to significantly impair pressure-induced chronotropy. Our results implicate one or more GNAQ/GNA11-coupled GPCRs in mediating this mechanosensitive process, but the specific GPCRs remain to be identified.

papers.title: Long-Term Neurovascular Dysfunction and Altered Placenta-Derived EV miRNA Profiles in a Rat Model with Preeclamptic Features
papers.abstract: Objective: Preeclampsia increases long-term cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and cognitive risk but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We examined cerebrovascular function, cognitive performance, and placenta-derived extracellular-vesicle (PD-EV) microRNA profiles in a transgenic rat model with preeclamptic features (TGA-PE) at 2 months after delivery (2M). Methods: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) hemodynamics were assessed by transcranial Doppler (TCD), and cerebral oxygenation was measured by photoacoustic imaging (PAI) in TGA-PE and Sprague-Dawley control rats. Blood pressure was measured using a tail-cuff method. Touchscreen-based cognitive tasks evaluated learning and reward-directed responding, while histological assessment evaluated MCA structure. MicroRNA sequencing was performed on circulating PD-EV, and miRNA target networks were analyzed using KEGG-based NEST-Scoring (Node, Edge, System, Topology). Validation of miR-363-3p was performed in PD-EV, plasma, non-PD-EV, and human brain endothelial cells (HBEC-5i). Results: TGA-PE rats were hypertensive and exhibited lower MCA resistance and pulsatility indexes with unchanged blood flow velocities. Cognitive testing revealed impaired associative learning and reduced motivation to respond on a progressive-ratio schedule. Temporal brain oxygen saturation was higher in TGA-PE rats with unchanged total hemoglobin, lower brain HIF-2, and unchanged VEGF levels. MCA elastin content was reduced in TGA-PE rats without changes in total collagen. PD-EV sequencing identified 29 differentially expressed miRNAs, including reduced miR-363-3p in non-placental EVs and plasma at 2M. Inhibition of miR-363-3p in human cerebral endothelial cell line HBEC-5i upregulated NOX4, p21, and {beta}-galactosidase levels. NEST-Scoring highlighted pathways involving MAPK, Ras, TNF, focal adhesion, cytoskeletal regulation, and cellular senescence. Conclusions: The exposure to experimental preeclampsia resulted in altered MCA flow resistance, cerebral oxygenation, vascular structure and behavioral performance. Although direct mechanistic studies are needed to establish the role of miRNA363-3p in neurovascular health, the increased endothelial oxidative stress and senescence-associated markers in HBEC-5i cells in response to miRNA363-3p inhibition suggest a potential protective role for miRNA363-3p. A novel NEST-Scoring analysis also identified potential pathways for future mechanistic investigations. Overall, the TGA-PE model provides a useful experimental system for investigating candidate mechanisms that may contribute to long-term maternal neurovascular changes following hypertensive pregnancy and sequelae of preeclamptic pathophysiology.

papers.title: Striatal Value Signals Track Progress Toward a Goal During Planning
papers.abstract: When making decisions, we often weigh immediate gains against long-term goals, and the value of the same choices can change over time. We used a novel task in which participants repeatedly chose between two cards, each with an immediate point value and an uncertain prospective value, with the latter reflecting the collection of card sets. Computational modeling showed that the prospective value captured how close participants were to completing a set. This goal gradient could be explained by both a simple progress-weighted heuristic and a forward-simulating planner. Using fMRI, we found that striatal and precuneus activity increased with the prospective value of the chosen card but not with its immediate point value. Activity in the dorsomedial and insular cortices instead increased with the value of the card given up and was highest when participants chose against the model-based value of the options. Activity in all regions of interest provides stronger support for the goal gradient rather than a full forward-planning model. These results refine the role of the valuation and cognitive control networks in goal-based decision-making.

papers.title: Application of nucleoside analogue labelling to study the cell cycle of xenografted PDAC cell lines in the chorioallantoic membrane model.
papers.abstract: The chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) model is an underutilised alternative model for the research into tumour xenografts. We demonstrate that in the pancreatic cancer cell lines BxPC-3 and AsPC-1, nucleoside labelling with 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) can be multiplexed with other human cell cycle markers, (e.g., cyclin B1 and Ki-67), particularly when combined with digital image analysis, allowing human versus chicken cell classification. Furthermore, starting from the embryonic day of development 14 (ED14), we observe embryonic cells exhibiting substantial apparent cytoplasmic accumulation of synthetic nucleosides. This was observed for (F-ara-)EdU as well as for the halogenated analogues BrdU and IdU. Characterisation of these cells suggests that they are non-proliferating and possess granules and can be found in the embryonic liver of (non-)grafted embryos, as well as in the CAM itself and within xenograft sections. Importantly, these cells are unlikely to represent activated professional antigen presenting cells as they lack MHC II expression, nor do they express CD41/CD61, ruling out thrombocyte origin. Together, our findings demonstrate that the CAM model constitutes a valuable platform for studying tumour cell cycle dynamics in vivo.
