Our findings establish endocytosis as a critical regulator of Hiw/Phr1-dependent JNK signaling, with implications that extend beyond synaptic morphogenesis to axon injury and degeneration pathways.

papers.title: Neural representations supporting reuse of abstract structural knowledge in humans
papers.abstract: A human ability to adapt to the dynamics of novel environments relies on abstracting and generalizing from past experiences. Previous research focused on how humans generalize from isolated sequential processes, yet we know little about mechanisms that facilitate adaptation to more complex dynamics, including those that govern much everyday experience. Here, using a novel sequence learning task based on graph factorization, coupled with simultaneous magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings, we ask whether reuse of experiential "building blocks" is reflected in neural representations that could support inference and generalization. Behavioral results were consistent with participants decomposing task experience into subprocesses, both abstracting their dynamical structure away from their sensory specifics and reusing these in a new task environment. Neurally, this was accompanied by a learning-induced, condition-specific, increase in neural similarity among stimuli conditional on their shared structural role in abstract subprocesses across distinct task phases. Consistent with this, a complementary dynamical role decoding analysis revealed enhanced neural decodability, across experiential contexts, for stimuli that adhered to identical structural transition types, specifically when prior experience included the relevant graph structure. Decoding strength for these role representations was positively related to behavioral success in reuse of subprocess knowledge, a relationship that will require future independent replication. The findings provide neural evidence consistent with the notion that abstract role representations may contribute to the reuse of experience within new contexts.

papers.title: Programmed mineralization of metal-oxides by de novo designed protein templates
papers.abstract: We describe a coupled de novo design and screening approach to identify protein interfaces which guide the mineralization of specific metal-oxides, including technologically relevant materials that are not found in biological systems. We identify two interfaces promoting hematite growth in conditions typically yielding magnetite, and three interfaces promoting heterogeneous ZnO nucleation under conditions where traditional ZnO-binding peptides and control proteins are ineffective. Cryo-electron microscopy analysis of a designed nanocage with ZnO nucleating interfaces lining interior cavities revealed atomic density, likely corresponding to growing ZnO, directly adjacent to the designed interfaces. Our findings suggest that designed proteins can template mineralization through modes beyond electrostatics, likely by ordering ions and water molecules, and provide a route to protein-metal-oxide hybrid materials with tunable structure and function.

papers.title: Disrupted sleep-wake regulation in the MCI-Park mouse model of Parkinson's Disease
papers.abstract: Disrupted sleep has a profound adverse impact on lives of Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients and their caregivers. Sleep disturbances are exceedingly common in PD, with substantial heterogeneity in type, timing, and severity. Among the most common sleep-related symptoms reported by PD patients are insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, and sleep fragmentation, characterized by interruptions and decreased continuity of sleep. Alterations in brain wave activity, as measured on the electroencephalogram (EEG), also occur in PD, with changes in the pattern and relative contributions of different frequency bands of the EEG spectrum to overall EEG activity in different vigilance states consistently observed. The mechanisms underlying these PD-associated sleep-wake abnormalities are poorly understood, and they are ineffectively treated by conventional PD therapies. To help fill this gap in knowledge, a new progressive model of PD - the MCI-Park mouse- was studied. Near the transition to the parkinsonian state, these mice exhibited significantly altered sleep-wake regulation, including increased wakefulness, decreased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, increased sleep fragmentation, reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and altered EEG activity patterns. These sleep-wake abnormalities mirror those identified in PD patients. Thus, this model may help elucidate the circuit mechanisms underlying sleep disruption in PD and identify targets for novel therapeutic approaches.

papers.title: Phenotypic Plasticity in Sub-Antarctic Plants: Costs, Environmental Complexity, and the Facilitative Role of Trait Integration
papers.abstract: Phenotypic plasticity is one plant response to climate warming, but it may incur costs and be either limited or facilitated by trait integration or simultaneous environmental shifts such as shading. Empirical studies addressing these costs and limitations across populations or maternal lineages, and how they vary with environmental context, remain scarce. We studied three plant species from the sub-Antarctic Kerguelen Islands, a region undergoing rapid warming, growing seeds from multiple source populations under different temperature and light treatments. We measured plasticity, performance, and morphological integration in young plants. Plants from more plastic source populations performed worse, while those from more integrated populations were more plastic, consistent with the facilitation hypothesis. Shading reduced plasticity in response to warming, and combined shading and warming reduced performance more than single treatments, contrasting with recent findings in Mediterranean plants, where multiple stressors did not limit adaptive plasticity. Our results suggest that phenotypic integration may favour rather than limit plasticity. However, plasticity under climate warming may also be constrained by increased shading from competitors, and does not guarantee success given induced performance costs.

papers.title: Drug combination prediction for cancer treatment using disease-specific drug response profiles and single-cell transcriptional signatures
papers.abstract: Developing novel cancer treatments is a challenging task that can benefit from computational techniques matching transcriptional signatures to large-scale drug response data. Here, we present 'retriever,' a tool that extracts robust disease-specific transcriptional drug response profiles based on cellular response profiles to hundreds of compounds from the LINCS-L1000 project. We used retriever to extract transcriptional drug response signatures of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell lines and combined these with a single-cell RNA-seq breast cancer atlas to predict drug combinations that antagonize TNBC-specific disease signatures. After systematically testing 151 drug response profiles and 11,325 drug combinations, we identified the combination of kinase inhibitors QL-XII-47 and GSK-690693 as the topmost promising candidate for TNBC treatment. Our new computational approach allows the identification of drugs and drug combinations targeting specific tumor cell types and subpopulations in individual patients. It is, therefore, highly suitable for the development of new personalized cancer treatment strategies.

papers.title: RBM25 selectively stabilizes XBP1s mRNA independently of splicing factor activity
papers.abstract: The unfolded protein response (UPR) preserves endoplasmic reticulum (ER) proteostasis through coordinated transcriptional and translational programs that promote adaptation and prevents apoptosis. A central component of this response is the IRE1-XBP1 signaling axis, in which IRE1-mediated unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA generates the active transcription factor XBP1s. While the mechanisms governing IRE1 activation and XBP1 splicing have been extensively characterized, the post-transcriptional processes that sustain XBP1s expression remain poorly understood. Here, we identify RNA-binding motif protein 25 (RBM25) as a key post-transcriptional regulator of the UPR that selectively stabilizes spliced XBP1 mRNA during ER stress. RBM25 binds the XBP1s 3' untranslated region and prolongs XBP1s mRNA half-life without affecting unspliced XBP1u transcripts or IRE1-dependent regulated decay (RIDD) targets. Consequently, RBM25 depletion diminishes XBP1 transcriptional output, compromises adaptive UPR signaling, and sensitizes cells to ER stress-induced death across multiple stress paradigms. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized RNA-based regulatory checkpoint that amplifies and sustains XBP1 signaling, thereby tuning the magnitude of the adaptive UPR and cellular survival under proteotoxic stress.

papers.title: High-density environmental DNA metabarcoding reveals fine-scale three-dimensional structure of a fish community in a semi-closed bay
papers.abstract: Coastal fish assemblages are influenced by environmental heterogeneity across horizontal and vertical dimensions, yet their fine-scale three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. We investigated spatial variation in fish assemblages using environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding at 100 stations across three depth layers (300 samples) in Maizuru Bay, a semi-enclosed coastal bay in Japan. Concurrent hydrographic measurements were used to examine associations between fish assemblage composition and environmental conditions. We detected 216 fish species, with mean species richness decreasing from 28.4 at the surface to 16.4 at the bottom. Thirty-three species were detected exclusively below the surface. Fish assemblage composition differed significantly among depth layers and exhibited pronounced horizontal turnover along the bay axis. Although depth, geographic position, and measured environmental variables were associated with assemblage composition, they collectively explained only 13.0% of the variation. The independent contribution of spatial position (2.9%) exceeded those of depth (0.8%) and measured environmental variables (0.9%). These findings demonstrate substantial three-dimensional heterogeneity in coastal fish assemblages that cannot be fully explained by conventional hydrographic measurements. Our study highlights the importance of integrating horizontal and vertical sampling to characterize coastal fish biodiversity and improve marine ecosystem monitoring.

papers.title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
papers.abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920-0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875-0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672-0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

papers.title: Virus coinfection in plants determined by ecological responses to environmental heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Community ecology is acknowledged as a relevant causative agent of epidemiological processes of plant viruses and has consequences for coinfection and virus and host evolution. Plant virus coinfection is common, but factors that promote non-random virus interactions above the population-level are unknown. Here, we analyse intrinsic and extrinsic factors in virus-host and virus-virus interactions by eighteen generalist virus species of a diverse multi-host-multi-virus system. Coinfection among viruses with broad host ranges, diverse modes of horizontal transmission, and interspecific variation in responses to environmental heterogeneity is expected to be shaped by ecological as well as evolutionary constraints. We analyse patterns of coinfection from 1,931 individual plants in 94 species from multiple plant communities of distinct habitat types and show that above 50% of plants were coinfected by 2-8 viruses. To analyse the role of environmental variables on the observed virus associations we used Markov and conditional random fields modelling. Results showed that a large majority of coinfections were random interactions, consistent with ecological fitting, and only a minor fraction being non-random associations. Random field models underscored the relevance of common responses to environmental heterogeneity driving coinfection, and strongly suggest mode of horizontal transmission as a causal agent. Results highlighted a major role of between-host, rather than within-host processes in driving coinfection. This study is a considerable addition to the understanding of drivers of virus coinfection and, hence, of virus community ecology and epidemiology.

papers.title: Temporal genomic imprinting regulates grain filling in barley
papers.abstract: In cereals, the persistent endosperm accumulates starch and storage proteins, making their grains a major source of food and feed. Early grain development is epigenetically controlled through the parent-of-origin-specific expression of imprinted genes in the endosperm that regulate endosperm proliferation, nutrient accumulation and embryo nourishment. Imprinted genes have been identified in several major cereals, and a few have been functionally characterized. However, it is unclear how imprinted genes regulate the accumulation of storage compounds in cereal grains. Through spatiotemporal transcriptome analysis of 255 imprinted genes in barley (Hordeum vulgare), we identify endosperm transfer cells in grains as a hotspot of expression of imprinted genes. Furthermore, we show that transcription factor LYS3 dynamically regulates grain filling in barley through early expression of the maternal allele, followed by partial activation of the paternal allele.

papers.title: A red fluorescent sensor for intensity-and lifetime imaging of cAMP in living cells
papers.abstract: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) is a crucial intracellular messenger involved in neuromodulation and plasticity, but more information on its spatiotemporal regulation is desirable. Here we constructed a red fluorescent indicator based on a truncated cAMP binding site derived from a regulatory PKA subunit of protozoan origin. It contains a single binding site for cAMP highly specific for cAMP over cGMP. chILI (cAMP highly-responsive Intensity and Lifetime Indicator) can be imaged as an intensity-based probe, but alternatively also offers options for fluorescence lifetime imaging. When expressed in the mouse brain using AAV-vector mediated gene transfer, it reports spontaneous and evoked cAMP transients from CA1 neurons in the hippocampus of awake mice. chILI will add valuable options for monitoring cAMP in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Platelet-endothelial crosstalk drives distinct endothelial dysfunction in bicuspid aortic valve disease
papers.abstract: Background: Bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) predispose individuals to premature development of aortic stenosis (AS). The abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV affects both platelets and valvular endothelial cells (VECs), but whether platelet-derived signals contribute to valve morphology-specific endothelial dysfunction remains unknown. Methods: Platelets and VECs were obtained from patients with BAVs or tricuspid aortic valves (TAVs) undergoing valve replacement for AS. Platelets were activated to generate platelet releasate (PR). PR composition and its effects on VECs were investigated using complementary molecular, multi-omic, functional, and computational approaches. Results: BAV and TAV patients exhibited markedly distinct PR profiles, which translated into differential endothelial responses. Strikingly, BAV-derived PR elicited a substantially more pronounced endothelial dysfunction phenotype, characterized by widespread molecular reprogramming and functional alterations. Integrated multi-omics uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction as a central feature of BAV PR-induced endothelial injury, accompanied by activation of pathways spanning endothelial remodeling, migration, and immune-cell recruitment. These molecular signatures translated into mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced VEC migration, and increased neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis. Finally, computational ligand-receptor and ligand-target analyses identified candidate signaling axes linking platelet-derived mediators to endothelial reprogramming, highlighting potential therapeutic targets. Conclusions: We provide the first direct evidence that platelet activation contributes to AS initiation through the induction of endothelial dysfunction and that these effects are amplified in BAV. These findings identify platelet-VEC crosstalk as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking abnormal valve hemodynamics to disease onset. Targeting platelet-derived mediators may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for AS, specifically in BAV.

papers.title: A Bias Correction Method for Substructure Estimation with Small Reference Sample Sizes
papers.abstract: Reference data are important for accurate estimation of population substructure, yet sufficiently large reference samples are often unavailable for some populations. This limitation is especially important for methods that estimate population substructure from genetic summary data using reference allele frequencies derived from reference samples, such as Summix2. Here, we systematically evaluated how reference sample size for five continental reference groups [African (AFR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Indigenous American (IAM), and South Asian (SAS)] affects Summix2 substructure estimates in simulated Latino-like, African American-like, and Peruvian-like populations, as well as real African American genetic data. We show that small reference sample sizes introduce systematic bias in substructure proportion estimates. We identified a sample size threshold of 150 individuals per reference group for accurate estimates with a mean estimation error below 0.05. We also developed two bias corrections: a simple inverse sample size correction and a flexible power-law correction. The power-law correction provided the greatest reduction in mean estimation error when all reference groups had small reference sample sizes, whereas the simple inverse sample size correction performed better when a single reference group had a small reference sample size. These findings provide practical guidance and bias adjustments for reliable population substructure estimation from genetic summary data, particularly when reference populations have small sample sizes.

papers.title: Floral scent diversity and evolution in deceptive Cypripedium, and post-pollination effects on floral scent and its biosynthesis in C. henryi
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Floral scent is a primary driver of pollinator attraction and reproductive isolation in deceptive orchids. Yet, little is known about the variation and evolution of scent in a phylogenetic framework and how pollination affects the biosynthesis and emission of scents in these lineages. This study characterizes scent diversity across Cypripedium, a genus of deceptive orchids, examines phylogenetic constraints, and investigates post-pollination effects on scent composition in one of the species. Methods: Floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were sampled from 31 Cypripedium taxa using dynamic headspace techniques, and analysed by gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC/MS). Uni- and multivariate methods were used to analyse intra- and interspecific scent variation and test for phylogenetic signal in floral scent. Post-pollination effects on scent composition were experimentally tested in C. henryi using four pollination treatments, combined with RNA-seq analyses of floral tissues to examine transcriptional responses in VOC biosynthetic pathways. Key results: We detected 258 floral VOCs, revealing a high chemical diversity dominated by terpenoids, aliphatics, and aromatic compounds. Floral scent composition was highly species-specific, and closely related taxa often shared only few compounds. Scent composition differed among pollination groups, but these groups explained only a limited proportion of overall scent variation. We detected a significant but weak phylogenetic signal, suggesting limited evolutionary constraint in floral scent. Pollination had limited effect on C. henryis floral scent and volatile biosynthesis gene expression, despite a significant decrease in total scent emission after pollinium deposition. Transcriptional changes predominantly occurred in the petals rather than the labellum and staminode. Conclusion: Floral scent evolution in Cypripedium is characterized by high chemical diversity, and a weak phylogenetic constraint, consistent with variable selection in food-deceptive systems. The pollination study further suggests the absence of a strong, directed post-pollination effect on the floral scent of C. henryi. Keywords: Cypripedium; deceptive pollination; floral scent; volatile organic compounds (VOCs); phylogenetic signal; linalool; post-pollination effects; transcriptome profiles; differential gene expression; floral organs

papers.title: Antibiotic-induced protein mislocalization drives hypervesiculation in Salmonella
papers.abstract: The incorporation of cytosolic proteins into bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) has remained mechanistically unresolved, as these proteins are normally excluded from vesiculation sites by the inner membrane (IM) barrier. Here, we show that antibiotic-induced envelope perturbation compromises this spatial barrier, enabling an aberrant interaction between proteins that are ordinarily segregated across cellular compartments and thereby promoting MV formation in Salmonella. Exposure to non-lethal cephalexin (LEX) induced robust hypervesiculation, accompanied by inhibition of the essential division penicillin binding protein (PBP) 3 and accumulation of the PBP5. Under envelope perturbing conditions, PBP5 accumulated at lateral sites associated with MV emergence and promoted periplasmic crowding independently of its catalytic activity. A cytosolic acyl carrier protein (ACP) emerged as a PBP5 interacting partner under LEX exposure, coinciding with cryogenic electron microscopy detected IM perturbation and aberrant ACP mislocalization. Formation of the PBP5 ACP complex promoted PBP5 accumulation, resulting in periplasmic crowding, progressive weakening of outer membrane peptidoglycan tethering, and ultimately MV formation. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism whereby stress-induced disruption of subcellular compartmentalization enables a non-canonical interaction between normally segregated proteins, driving hypervesiculation in Salmonella.

papers.title: Error-Controlled Discovery of Protein Interactions via Conformal Calibration
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Electrostatic control of conformational dynamics drives proton translocation in respiratory Complex I
papers.abstract: Complex I is a large membrane protein that transduces redox energy into a proton motive force across a biological membrane, powering cellular respiration. Yet, despite significant experimental and computational efforts, its long-range proton translocation mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we combine nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and site-directed mutagenesis experiments with multiscale classical and hybrid quantum/classical (QM/MM) simulations to probe how conformational dynamics is linked to proton transfer reactions in the terminal antiporter module (Nqo12/NuoL/ND5) of Complex I. We show that protonation of a conserved proton-loading site (Lys329/His241Nqo12) in the terminal antiporter-like module gives rise to conformational changes that result in opening of the proton pathway. We further show that this protonation reaction is controlled by buried ion-pairs that modulate the barrier for proton translocation by intrinsic electric field effects. On a general level, our combined findings reveal how bioenergetic machines combine conformational dynamics with hydration transitions to establish efficient redox-driven proton pumps.

papers.title: MoALE1, an ART-like effector, contributes to rice blast virulence through host immune suppression
papers.abstract: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .

papers.title: Phosphate-responsive ornithine lipid biosynthesis remodels outer membrane composition and contributes to polymyxin tolerance
papers.abstract: Bacteria frequently encounter environments in which essential nutrients are limiting. Phosphate limitation constrains phospholipid synthesis and challenges maintenance of the cell envelope. While many Gram-negative bacteria respond by producing phosphorous-free membrane lipids, the mechanisms and consequences of this remodeling remain poorly understood in Enterobacterales. Here, we characterize the genetic and physiological basis of ornithine lipid (OL) biosynthesis in the opportunistic pathogens Enterobacter cloacae and Klebsiella pneumoniae. We show that OL biosynthesis depends on OlsF, a bifunctional acyltransferase that catalyzes both acylation steps required for OL synthesis. Phosphate limitation promotes OlsF-dependent OL accumulation through the PhoBR two-component system. Membrane fractionation revealed that OlsF-derived OLs are present in both membrane compartments but are enriched in the outer membrane. OlsF-dependent OL production enhances polymyxin tolerance during phosphate limitation, linking nutrient availability to changes in antimicrobial susceptibility. Together, these findings identify OlsF-dependent OL synthesis as a phosphate-responsive membrane remodeling pathway that reshapes outer membrane composition and influences the physiological properties of the Gram-negative cell envelope.

papers.title: Functional genomic characterization of anti-phage defense systems in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
papers.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a significant public health threat, demonstrating high rates of antibiotic resistance and frequently causing hospital-acquired infections. Bacteriophages (phages) are a promising adjunctive therapy to reduce bacterial load and manage VREfm infections. Many bacteria encode anti-phage defense systems--groups of genes that can counteract phage infection--but these systems have not been characterized in VREfm. Here we explored the diversity of anti-phage defense systems within clinical VREfm isolate genomes and examined their impact on phage susceptibility. We first used two available bioinformatic tools (DefenseFinder and PADLOC) to identify putative anti-phage defense systems in 21 hybrid-assembled VREfm clinical isolate genomes, and observed that most anti-phage defense systems were located on plasmids, defense islands, and prophages. Combining this information with functional testing of phage susceptibility did not reveal robust associations between specific defense systems and resistance to four VREfm-targeting lytic phages. Due to inherent limitations of phage susceptibility testing, we next developed an assay to assess phage survival after co-incubation with bacteria, and identified over two dozen genes associated with phage killing, including a potentially novel defense island. Lastly, we attempted to functionally validate 10 candidate anti-phage defense systems, only four of which were ultimately tested in enterococci. Expression of one of these candidates, AbiE, decreased bacterial susceptibility to two Enterococcus-targeting phages. As VREfm-targeting phage therapy becomes more widely available, identification of genes contributing to phage resistance can aid in streamlining the provision of phages to patients who could benefit from this new therapeutic modality.

papers.title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
papers.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. Existing segmentation methods focus on delineating cell boundaries, yet transcripts that diffuse beyond their cell of origin, fall where cells overlap, or lie in bins that cells only partially cover are still misassigned. Here we present Tracel, a two-stage optimal transport framework that assigns spatial observations to cells under the guidance of a matched single-cell RNA-sequencing reference. Tracel first aligns reference cells to spatial cells to estimate the expected expression profile at each cell location, and then maps transcripts to cells against these profiles. The same formulation assigns transcripts from imaging-based platforms (e.g., Xenium, CosMx) and bin counts from sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Visium HD). Across five human datasets spanning three platforms and three tissues, Tracel improves the separation of cell types over existing methods, assigning cell-type markers to their correct cells, retaining more cell-intrinsic transcripts and reducing contamination from neighboring cells. Tracel also preserves variation within cell types, yielding more accurate differential expression across spatial locations, and its expression profiles attribute ligand-receptor interactions to the correct cell-type pairs in cell-cell communication analysis. Tracel can enter the segmentation workflow at different stages, either refining an existing segmentation or segmenting cells starting from nucleus segmentation.

papers.title: Structural and evolutionary insights into FcαμR recognition of polymeric immunoglobulins
papers.abstract: Polymeric immunoglobulins (pIgs) are central to adaptive immunity in jawed vertebrates. FcR is a bispecific pIg receptor that recognizes both IgM and IgA, but the molecular basis has been unclear. Here we determine cryo-EM structures of mammalian FcR bound to IgM or IgA and show that FcR engages each ligand in a 1:1 stoichiometry, with higher affinity for IgM. The FcR-binding site overlaps with those of pIgR, and also with the preferred FcR-binding site on IgM, yet distinct features distinguish FcR from both pIgR and FcR. Functionally, FcR efficiently internalizes both IgM and IgA through a pathway independent of the di-leucine motif. Structures of amphibian pIgR and FcR bound to IgM further shed light on the evolutionary diversification of the FcR/pIgR family. Together, these findings define the structural basis of FcR-mediated pIg recognition and provide a framework for understanding the evolution of pIg receptors.

papers.title: Inosine Triphosphate Pyrophosphatase as a Candidate Associated with White Matter Abnormalities in Chronic Heart Failure
papers.abstract: Background: White matter hyperintensities (WMHs) are common with normal brain aging and frequently observed also in chronic heart failure (CHF). However, the relationship between CHF and white matter abnormalities and the biological factors remain unclear. We investigated WMH and associated white matter microstructural changes, such as fractional anisotropy (FA), in CHF and explored candidate molecular factors. Methods: We conducted a longitudinal prospective observation including brain T2-FLAIR magnetic resonace imaging for 32 asymptomatic Stage B (mean age 63.3{+/-}10.5 years; 25% women) and 23 symptomatic Stage C CHF patients (mean age 67.3{+/-}7.1 years; 30% women). Plasma proteomics and Mendelian randomization (MR) were used to identify candidate proteins associated with both CHF and WMH. The association of candidate proteins was further investigated using complementary analyses in CHF rats, cultured cortical neurons, and community-based genetic data in UK Biobank. Results: Global WMH volume increased more in Stage C than Stage B patients, predominantly near the anterior periventricular white matter, despite comparable cardiac indices (4,717{+/-}5,335 mm3 vs. 2,116{+/-}3,134 mm3, P=0.027). SomaScan-based proteomic analysis of plasma samples from this patient cohort revealed that 44 proteins are significantly associated with both Stage C CHF and WMH progression (P<0.05). Of these 44 proteins, two-step Mendelian randomization analysis identified inosine triphosphate pyrophosphatase (ITPA) as the only candidate protein, further supported by an association between rare variants in ITPA and FA. In CHF rats, the anterior pericallosal cortex showed decreases in myelin basic protein density and FA and an increase in ITPA expression compared to sham rats. In cultured cortical neurons, recombinant ITPA exposure reduced total axonal length. Conclusions: Symptomatic CHF was associated with WMH and impaired white matter integrity. ITPA emerged as a candidate factor across human, animal, and cellular analyses. These findings provide a basis for investgating the biological pathways linking CHF and white matter injury.

papers.title: brisc: a multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets have grown from tens of thousands of cells to tens of millions. At this scale, standard toolkits like Scanpy and Seurat need hours per analysis, hindering iterative exploration. We present brisc, the first end-to-end multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis, spanning dimensionality reduction, integration, label transfer, clustering, embedding, differential expression and plotting. Unlike GPU-based counterparts, brisc strictly guarantees reproducibility: identical results between runs, regardless of thread count. Algorithmic innovations include a blocked inverted-file-index-based nearest-neighbors algorithm that makes 81-98% fewer errors than Scanpy and Seurat. On a 192-CPU node, brisc ran a standard workflow on 10 million cells in 3 minutes, 116x faster than Scanpy at under half its peak memory usage and 236x faster than Seurat with BPCells. On 96 CPUs, it matched the speed of rapids-singlecell on four H100 GPUs. brisc enables near-real-time, reproducible analysis of tens of millions of cells without specialized hardware.

papers.title: A conserved thermodynamic signature links transcriptome organization to growth state
papers.abstract: Living systems operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, sustaining complexity through continuous free-energy influx and heat dissipation. Yet the higher-order functional constraints imposed by non-equilibrium dynamics remain largely unexplored. To formalize how changes in cellular entropy production constrain intracellular organization across proliferative state transitions, we developed a stochastic-thermodynamic model linking reduced dissipative drive to transient increases in intracellular configurational entropy. Within this framework, we examined abundance-weighted predicted RNA folding stability as a transcriptome-level projection of the intracellular configurational remodelling. Consistent with the model, transcriptome reorganization across the cell cycle produces coordinated, phase-dependent changes in the distribution of transcript-level RNA folding free energies. Extending this analysis to stress adaptation, we find that human cancer cells exposed to molecularly targeted agents and nutrient-limited Escherichia coli converge on expressed RNA pools enriched for transcripts with less negative RNA folding free energies, despite marked heterogeneity in the transcriptional responses within each system. Opposing shifts during acquired resistance under continued drug exposure and bacterial recovery from starvation further support an association with growth state. Together, these findings suggest that transcriptome organization extends beyond gene-regulatory programs to collective biophysical properties that may reflect non-equilibrium constraints shaping cellular-state transitions.

papers.title: Peptorama: Structure creation and exploratory data analysis for non-ribosomal peptides
papers.abstract: Non-ribosomal peptides (NRPs) are a diverse family of compounds with many clinical and biotechnological uses. NRP biodiscovery increasingly focuses on biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), and NRP structures can generally be predicted from BGCs. Despite their chemical connection, there is no individual research tool which quickly analyses NRPs and BGCs in combination. Here, we present Peptorama, which simplifies drawing diverse NRP structures and allows rapid comparisons between known and predicted NRPs. We show the utility of peptide comparisons and interactive analysis for biodiscovery, exemplified by retrospective analysis of calcium dependent antibiotics and biodiscovery of novel pyoverdine producing candidate strains. Peptide comparisons are computationally more efficient than BGC comparisons, substantially cutting runtimes without loss of biodiscovery functionality. Peptorama can therefore enhance existing pipelines with a rapid method for comparing peptide-level diversity. It is available online at https://peptorama.com/ and is also available to be run locally.

papers.title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
papers.abstract: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

papers.title: Representation-aware calibration enables statistically reliable protein structure search
papers.abstract: Searching large databases of predicted protein structures can reveal remote homologs, but reliable discovery requires accurate significance estimates. We show that native E-values reported by protein structure search tools such as Foldseek and Reseek can be unreliable, leading to false discoveries or missed homologs. To address this problem, we introduce Struct-Caliper, which provides reliable query-specific p-values for protein structure search. The method uses representation-aware query randomization to generate background queries and compares observed alignment scores with the highest scores from randomized searches of the same database. In simulations, SG p-values generally kept reported false positive at or below the chosen cutoff under the evaluated randomization procedures. In searches of 15,177 ASTRAL40 structures, SG p-values increased Foldseek homolog recovery by 18.2% with slightly fewer false discoveries compared with native E-values at a cutoff of 0.01. For Reseek, false discoveries even decreased by 99.5%. Across 73 queries searched against more than two million AlphaFoldDB structures, SG p-values increased the mean recovery of DALI-supported matches by 23.5% at the same cutoff. These results show that Struct-Caliper can improve the reliability of structure searches and help prioritize discoveries for further biological analysis.

papers.title: Multispecies transport shapes electrochemical environments in perforated cells
papers.abstract: Cells maintain asymmetric electrochemical environments across selectively permeable plasma membranes. Ion channels on plasma membranes redistribute small ions, whereas large openings such as gasdermin pores allow both ions and proteins to cross the membrane, generating a multispecies transport regime. The transport of charged ions and proteins shapes electrochemical environments, leading to osmolarity changes, which in turn promotes water influx and cell swelling. Although biologists have observed the phenotypic progression from pore formation to cell swelling for decades, the molecular transport events underlying this progression remain elusive. To elucidate how pore formation drives downstream cellular effects, we establish quantitative multispecies transport frameworks to investigate gasdermin-perforated cells. We start by developing a reductionist model and benchmarking it against analytical Donnan predictions. We then explore three-dimensional geometries containing individual pores or pore clusters that form either simultaneously or sequentially. We reveal that ion-protein timescale separation generates non-canonical Donnan-like states, pore and cargo properties tune local transport, pore clustering modulates osmotic gradients, and sequential pore formation produces feedback-dependent dynamics. This work deepens our mechanistic understanding of cellular responses to membrane damage and informs the therapeutic design of pore-forming proteins with tunable cellular effects.

papers.title: Discovering compositional, interpretable structure in social behavior
papers.abstract: Quantitative assessment of behavior is vital for rigorous analysis of how animals interact in the world and how behavior is generated from brain activity. Recent advances in automated pose detection have made possible data-driven discovery of movement action sequences. While many algorithms have been developed for this purpose, their categorical nature, i.e., the assumption that behavior is one action at a time, prohibits expressive quantification of social behavior. Such behavior is combinatorial and compositional, with multiple animals performing actions that may be either independent or coordinated over time. Here we show how developments in decomposed linear dynamical systems (dLDS) can instead represent action-generating dynamics as a signed, graded mixture of shared linear operators acting directly on keypoint positions. We demonstrate our approach across both single-mouse and two-mouse datasets, comparing against a state-of-the-art switching model, keypoint-MoSeq. In single-mouse data, we find that a composition of three operators can capture the full repertoire of 21 keypoint-MoSeq syllables, showing that even for a single animal, the action space is more parsimoniously described by a continuous subspace than clustered motifs. In a two-mouse resident--intruder assay, we identify, without behavioral labels, separate primitives for self-action, inter-animal-geometry, and social-action. The latter couples an animal's action to its partner's relative bearing, enabling the action to incorporate the social geometry in which it occurs. dLDS further decodes human-labeled social behaviors (i.e., "attack", "investigation", "mount", and "other") more accurately than behavior-selective keypoint-MoSeq syllable sets using fewer units. Together, these results demonstrate that compositional, time-varying linear dynamics can provide a path towards flexible and interpretable modeling of action-level behavior for both individual and social behavior.

papers.title: A new Serratia taxon found in a trombidiform mite shows genomic evidence of host adaptation but is phylogenetically distinct from Serratia symbiotica
papers.abstract: Abstract The evolutionary transition from free-living bacteria to host-adapted symbionts is typically accompanied by substantial genomic changes. Within the genus Serratia, this transition has so far been documented only in the aphid-associated species, Serratia symbiotica, whereas all other Serratia species are free-living. In this study, we identify a putatively new Serratia taxon using metagenomic approaches in the trombidiform mite, Halotydeus destructor. We provide genomic evidence for a possible transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in this new Serratia sp., which sits phylogenetically within a clade of free-living Serratia species. The genomic signatures of evolving toward a host-adapted lifestyle include a reduced genome size and coding capacity, an elevated transposase fraction, and detectable chromosomal rearrangements, relative to other free-living Serratia species. However, the species does not show the same structure of genome reduction as S. symbiotica. Functional gene content analyses including COG categories and virulence factor repertoires also showed that our new Serratia sp. had a distinct gene profile from both free-living Serratia and S. symbiotica. Additional genomic screening suggests that infections of the new Serratia sp. are common in wild populations of H. destructor across its invasive Australian range, warranting future investigations on the possible role this symbiont plays in the evolutionary ecology of its mite host. Our work not only highlights a potential parallel transition to a host-adapted lifestyle in the Serratia genus, but also represents the first characterisation of a possible host-adapted Serratia taxon in a trombidiform mite.

papers.title: Non-equilibrium cyclic conformations of DNA under electrokinetic confinement
papers.abstract: Classic nanofluidic devices harness geometric confinement to modulate single polymer conformation and control chain dynamics. While classic nanofluidic devices have given rise to a range of applications, they are fundamentally limited by the static nature of their construction, which restricts real time control over molecular conformations. The reversible electrokinetic confinement (RECON) technique enables time-dependent control of DNA conformations in nanowells via dynamic modulation of field-induced confinement. Here, we demonstrate that applying dynamically varying confinement using stochastic and periodic signals can drive the confined polymer to access a range of non-equilibrium states, with the distinct configurations quantified via their radius of gyration tensor. For periodic driving, the device allows controlled cycling across conformational states, with distinct hysteresis observed in the shape anisotropy modulation. We quantify the interplay between the driving frequency, driving amplitude, and resulting hysteresis. Overall, our results establish RECON as a platform for active manipulation of single molecules, opening new avenues for studying non-equilibrium polymer physics and developing high-throughput, dynamically tunable nanofluidic devices.

papers.title: Comparative Transcriptomic Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Neutrophils from Rheumatoid Arthritis and COVID-19
papers.abstract: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective: To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods: Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results: In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions: RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.

papers.title: Monoaminergic changes are associated with impaired neurogenesis along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus in ageing and dementia
papers.abstract: Neurogenesis persists in the adult human hippocampus and is thought to support memory and emotional regulation. Both normal ageing and Parkinson disease dementia (PDD) are associated with reduced hippocampal neurogenesis, but why this occurs and how this might change across the across the hippocampal axis remains unclear. Here, we quantified the expression of genes regulating neurogenesis from stem cell production to neuron maturation and examined their relationship with monoaminergic activity throughout the post-mortem hippocampus in young and aged individuals, as well as in individuals with PDD. DCX and MKI67 expression were markedly reduced in PDD cases throughout the hippocampus, while GFAP and GFAP{delta} were elevated in aged control individuals but not in PDD. Dopamine and serotonin levels were unchanged but reduced levels of the dopamine metabolite DOPAC, and increased levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA, were present across the hippocampal axis in PDD. Hierarchical regression analysis identified DOPAC and 5-HIAA as significant predictors of DCX and MKI67 expression independent of diagnostic group. Coupling between stem cell markers and proliferative output was preserved in the hippocampus of young controls but was absent in aged controls and in PDD. These data suggest changes in monoaminergic systems are linked to stage-specific deficits in neuronal proliferation and maturation, identifying a potential mechanistic bridge to cognitive decline in PDD.

papers.title: Gene expression in Anolis sagrei suggests conservation of patterning mechanisms drives formation of two high acuity areas
papers.abstract: As humans we enjoy high acuity color vision. A specialized area in our retinas, the fovea, endows us with this ability. Some vertebrates, such as the Anolis sagrei (brown anole), have two such areas. Whether different species use conserved developmental mechanism(s), and whether the same mechanism is used in one organism to pattern both foveae, are herein addressed in the brown anole. We observed that the expression of canonical axis patterning genes is conserved in the anole retina. Retinoic acid and Fgf signaling pathways were found to define two discrete domains corresponding to emerging foveae. Comparative spatial analyses of early gene expression patterns among anole, chick, and human revealed conserved patterns in the anlage of the high acuity areas of each species. Variation in foveal number could arise through spatial redeployment of conserved patterning programs.

papers.title: Atmospheric pollution contributed to destabilizing a small mammal community amid four decades of environmental changes
papers.abstract: In the recent decades, climatic and land-use changes paralleled major decreases in atmospheric pollution, but unclear is how these concomitant changes shape ecological dynamics. We analyzed 39 years (1986-2024) of semiannual abundances for six small-mammal species in the Black Triangle of Europe (Czechia), a region historically-marked by acidic rains causing forest diebacks and toxic lead (Pb) deposition. We combined these small-mammal data with monthly time series of atmospheric pollution, vegetation index (NDVI), meteorology and soil moisture. We used Empirical Dynamic Modelling (EDM) to infer chaos, recover species-species and environment-species causal relationships, recover time-varying interactions, and perform out-of-sample forecasts. Small mammal populations were causally affected by atmospheric pollution, and its abrupt decline in the late 1990s likely triggered a delayed critical transition of community composition. Pollution primarily affected the dominant omnivores and strengthened the interactions among species, a hallmark of instability. We identified a second route to chaos with a role of vegetation dynamics and soil moisture that was especially strong on shrews. Our feedback-loop analysis suggests how pollution and other environmental changes favored destabilizing, positive feedbacks. Forecasting of these chaotic dynamics improved when adding the relevant environmental predictors, demonstrating that the unpredictability of chaotic systems can slightly improve when we identify the main drivers of interactions in a network, offering hope for anticipating the future of complex ecosystems. Our study offers a unique retrospective of the destabilizing effects of pollution, an overlooked macro-ecological driver.

papers.title: Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov. sp. nov., a new gut genus isolated from the stool of a healthy donor
papers.abstract: Strain Marseille-QA0792 (=CSUR QA0792, CECT 31199) was isolated from the feces of a healthy person using the culturomics method. The fecal sample originated from leftover material collected for a fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) procedure, obtained during a routine screening in accordance with the guidelines of the French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM). This strain is Gram-stain-negative, rod-shaped, non-motile, and non-spore-forming. It is strictly anaerobic, with optimal growth at 37{degrees}C. Strain Marseille-QA0792 presented its highest 16S rRNA identity, 96.2%, with ''Merdibacter massiliensis'' strain Marseille-P3254 (not validly published) (accession number LT598590) and ANI similarity of 75.0% with the same species. Among validly published species, strain Marseille-QA0792 showed its highest 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (91.5%) with Faecalicoccus acidiformans strain 37-2a (accession number HQ452864), whereas all computed average nucleotide identity (ANI) values were below 75%. Genome sequencing revealed a genome size of 2.67 Mb and a G+C content of 50.01%. This species is classified within the Erysipelotrichaceae family in the Bacillota phylum. Thus, we isolated for the first time a novel genus named Sarrella massiliensis gen. nov., sp. nov., strain Marseille-QA0792. This discovery highlights the importance of continuing culturomics efforts to explore the human microbiome.

papers.title: Immersion as inference: An active inference account of induced realities and its relation to the two-competitor model
papers.abstract: Immersive technologies are designed for a single target: the human perceptual system. Engineers of virtual and augmented reality have long recognized that a display does not have to replicate the physical world, it only has to provide the inputs that satisfy the senses at the level at which the brain samples them. This engineering intuition is, in fact, a statement about brain function. Here we develop it into a formal account of immersion within the active inference framework. We treat an induced reality (a virtual, augmented, or mixed reality, but also a book or a daydream) as a candidate generative model that competes with the model of the actual reality for the explanation of a shared sensorium and for the control of action. Immersion is then defined as the ensuant belief that the induced reality best explains the current sensory signals and supports the current perceived reality of the winning model, despite any break in immersion by Bayesian model switching driven by a high-precision prediction error that the induced model cannot absorb. Exogenous and endogenous attention, implemented as weights governing stream selection in our earlier two-competitor model, which treated attention as necessary but not sufficient for immersion, appear as two routes of precision allocation: likelihood precision of evolutionarily entrenched sensory events, and precision that follows the expected free energy of policies. Affect and motivation enter through the pragmatic and epistemic value of remaining in the induced reality and through the rate of change of free energy. We show that the two-competitor attentional focus vector and its angle are recovered from the active inference variables, and we reproduce the two scenarios of the original model, a rewarding and a fatiguing activity interrupted by a slamming door, in a minimal simulation. The account links presence, embodiment, cybersickness, and narrative absorption to a single quantity, and it yields concrete predictions for the psychophysiological assessment and closed-loop control of immersion. We discuss implications for neuroergonomic design in which the evolutionarily entrenched core of perception is non-negotiable while its experience-dependent periphery can be trained.

papers.title: Inferring modularity in genotype-phenotype maps using patterns of epistasis and pleiotropy
papers.abstract: Methods for inferring the relationship between genotype and phenotype often search for low-dimensional structure, motivated by the hypothesis that genetic loci can be organized into a small number of groups representing biological processes. These methods typically group genetic loci based on which other loci they interact with (epistasis) or based on how their effects covary across environmental conditions (patterns of pleiotropy). Here, we present two complementary methods that combine epistasis and pleiotropy to infer modular structure. The first, Sparse, Low-dimensional, Epistatic Decomposition (SLED), parametrizes the genotype-phenotype map in terms of a small number of modules: loci contribute sparse additive and epistatic effects to modules, and modules contribute sparse additive and epistatic effects to multiple phenotypes. The second method, Graph Tensor Decomposition (GTD), represents the epistatic interactions in each environment as a combination of shared basis graphs, each capturing a pattern of epistasis that recurs across environments. Since GTD does not use additive effects, learned graphs are not restricted to include only loci whose additive effects covary across environments. We validate SLED and GTD on synthetic data, then apply both methods to an experimental dataset consisting of the growth rates of yeast segregants from an F1 cross, measured across 101 environments with a hub-and-spoke structure. We evaluate the biological structure of the inferred modules and show that both models generalize well to held-out environments. Finally, we compare the modules inferred by SLED, GTD, and a previously established method that infers sparse modular structure from a locus-by-environment matrix of additive effects (SSD) and find that all three methods yield highly similar modular architectures. This suggests that the genetic architecture underlying this dataset is consistent across additive effects (SSD), epistatic effects (GTD), and both jointly (SLED). Together, our methods provide a framework for combining two sources of information, epistasis and pleiotropy, to infer interpretable low-dimensional structure in genotype-phenotype maps, expanding on previous work that has traditionally treated each independently.

papers.title: MHCII+ cancer-associated fibroblasts promote antitumor immunity in pancreatic cancer
papers.abstract: The functions of major histocompatibility complex class II molecule-expressing cancer-associated fibroblasts (MHCII+CAFs) in pancreatic cancer remain controversial. MHCII+CAFs are primarily described as immunosuppressive, as MHCII allows for direct interaction with, and support of, regulatory T cells (Tregs). However, MHCII+CAF functions may be more complex depending on their origins and their cellular interactions within the tumor microenvironment. Here, using orthotopic models of pancreatic cancer, we show that conventional CD4+ T cells and their production of Interferon gamma (IFN{gamma}) increased MHCII+CAFs in tumors. Acute depletion of Tregs using Foxp3DTR mice revealed that Tregs suppress the abundance of MHCII+CAFs in tumors by inhibiting CD4 T cell responses that can directly control primary tumor growth and metastatic progression. Functionally, MHCII expression on fibroblasts was required for CD4 T cell control of PDAC progression upon Treg ablation. Collectively, our findings identify an IFN{gamma}-driven, antitumor activity of MHCII expression on CAFs and reveal that CAFs may be harnessed to promote adaptive immunity to PDAC.

papers.title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps
papers.abstract: Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool-using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.

papers.title: Social copying drives spatial allocation in gregarious herbivores
papers.abstract: Resting patch selection in free-ranging social cattle (Bos taurus) inhabiting steep, rugged, mountain valleys is critical, because the recurrent use of flatter resting patches may reduce energetic costs and enhance fitness prospects. As these patches may constitute a limited resource, understanding their pattern of use dynamics may help explain resting patch selection. We therefore combine empirical data with a theoretical modelling framework to investigate the processes underlying resting patch selection. Using high-resolution GPS tracking data from 144 cows collected over three seasons, we identify several recurrently used resting patches located on significantly gentler slopes than expected in the valley. We then build a simple, memory-free agent-based model, which suggests that the dynamics of resting patch selection arise from social copying and, to a lesser extent, from individual heterogeneity. The model quantitatively reproduces three empirical observables: a slowing (sub-linear) discovery of new sites through time, heterogeneous occupancy across resting patches and similarity in patch use among individuals. These results suggest that collective dynamics in social species can emerge primarily from a simple social mechanism with weaker modulation from inter-individual heterogeneity, such as age, without explicitly incorporating individual memory to reproduce the aggregate patterns.

papers.title: Long read sequencing reveals changes in measured isoform structure and abundance due to RNA processing
papers.abstract: Oxford Nanopore Technology enables direct RNA sequencing without reverse transcription (RT) and cDNA sequencing without PCR amplification, allowing investigation of how RNA preparation protocols bias sequencing data. PCR amplification is known to introduce biases related to expression levels, transcript lengths, and GC content. However, biases introduced by RT have been described more recently and their quantification remains more elusive. Using seven cell line datasets from SG-NEx, we compared nanopore sequencing of direct RNA, direct cDNA, and PCR-amplified cDNA. We identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and isoforms between protocols, indicating significant changes in observed expression. Differentially expressed isoforms displayed expected amplification biases, and further we observed decreased PCR counts associated with higher m6A methylation levels on native RNA. We also found differential transcript usage in hundreds of genes across cell lines, showing substantial changes in measured isoform proportions between protocols. Analysis of structural differences between isoforms that switch dominance revealed that while some events involve simple RNA fragmentation, most involve complex structural differences including novel junctions (e.g. exon skipping, intron retention). Compared to non-DTU genes, inserted introns (exitrons) were significantly more common after RT and amplification. Furthermore, visualisation of raw coverage data proved crucial for qualitative validation of experimental findings.

papers.title: Replication-coupled maturation of readthrough late transcripts by a polyomavirus small T antigen
papers.abstract: Productive polyomavirus gene expression requires the maturation of long, non-polyadenylated "wraparound" transcripts generated by late-strand readthrough of the polyadenylation signal on the circular genome, giving rise to structural protein mRNAs and microRNAs. In Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), small T (sT) antigen, along with large T (LT) antigen-mediated DNA replication, drives this process. Deletion of sT (MCV{Delta}sT) attenuates late gene transcription, abolishes splicing, eliminates VP1 expression, and traps unspliced transcripts in the nucleus. Exogenous sT restored transcription and splicing in an aphidicolin-sensitive manner, requiring domains that activate DNA replication and bind chromatin. RNA sequencing revealed that sT promotes splicing and polyadenylation of wraparound transcripts, thereby increasing cytoplasmic VP1 and VP2 mRNA levels. A dual-fluorescence reporter confirmed that the leaky late poly(A) signal (LpA) was used more efficiently upon sT expression, indicating enhanced polyadenylation. Co-expression with LT abolished this effect, likely by overwhelming the capacity of the polyadenylation machinery. sT from HPyV7 and HPyV9 could similarly rescue this defect, indicating that this regulatory activity is conserved in a subset of sT proteins. Together, these findings define sT as a replication-coupled regulator of late transcript expression, splicing, and polyadenylation, revealing how a compact DNA virus converts readthrough transcription into productive gene expression.

papers.title: Proteome-Wide Serology Identifies Secreted IgD against RSV Fusion Glycoprotein as a Signature of Broadly Elevated Antibody Response
papers.abstract: Serological evaluation of antibody response using conventional indirect immunoassays cannot capture the full depth, diversity, and functional complexity of human polyclonal antibodies. Here, we developed mass spectrometry-based Proteome-Wide Serology (ProWiSe) assays for the identification and absolute quantification of antigen-specific human antibodies across isotypes, subclasses, and variable-region repertoires. Using ProWiSe, we measured the depth and diversity of serum antibodies to multiple antigens of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a pathogen associated with repeated reinfections and skewed immune response. IgG1 antibodies targeting the fusion glycoprotein F (RSVF) dominated the antibody response, with a background-corrected median level of 1,700 ng/mL across 214 healthy maternal serum samples from the general population. ProWiSe identified reproducible co-enrichment of complement component 1q complexes, revealed the usage of several dozen IGHV variable-region germline genes in the anti-RSVF polyclonal response, and suggested limited IGHV repertoire diversity in some individuals. In addition to IgG1, we discovered a complex antibody response characterized by significantly elevated levels of nearly all human immunoglobulin isotypes and subclasses, including previously unexplored IgG4 and IgD. The identification of high-affinity IgD against prefusion and postfusion RSVF, but not against other antigens studied, was the most unexpected observation, occurring in 52% of the healthy maternal serum samples. ProWiSe unambiguously identified the secreted IgD isoform P01880-1 and supported the IgD paradox of preferential {lambda} light-chain usage in secreted IgD. Detectable anti-RSVF IgD levels ([≥]0.11 ng/mL) correlated with broadly elevated antibody responses across all other isotypes and subclasses, except IgE. ProWiSe assays offer a versatile platform for quantitative serological diagnostics, exploration of depth, diversity, and dynamics of polyclonal antibody response, and discovery of rare antibody isotypes.

papers.title: Scn2a-deficient mice exhibit serotonergic dysfunction and altered behavioral responses to psilocybin
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prominent neurodevelopmental disorder affecting approximately 3.2% of children in the United States. Although ASD has traditionally been considered a polygenic disorder, advances in genetic testing have identified individual genes that can contribute to its development. Large-scale whole-exome sequencing has identified variants in SCN2A, which encodes the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2, as a leading monogenic cause of ASD. Social deficits are a core feature of ASD, and the serotonergic system has been implicated in the regulation of social behavior. Recent studies have demonstrated that serotonergic psychedelics, such as psilocybin, can increase sociability in mouse models of ASD. However, whether underlying genetic alterations associated with ASD influence behavioral responses to psilocybin remains poorly understood. Therefore, we investigated how Scn2a deficiency affects behavioral responses to psilocybin and whether these differences are accompanied by alterations in the serotonergic system. We found that Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited differential responses to psilocybin compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Specifically, psilocybin increased sociability in Scn2a-deficient mice without affecting anxiety-like behavior, whereas WT mice exhibited decreased anxiety-like behavior without increased sociability. Further behavioral evaluation revealed a reduced head twitch response in Scn2a-deficient mice following psilocybin administration compared to WT mice. To further investigate these differences, we examined serotonin levels and receptor expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a brain region implicated in social behavior and psychedelic action. Although baseline serotonin levels in the mPFC did not differ between genotypes, Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited altered serotonin receptor expression. We further characterized the serotonergic system by evaluating neuronal activity in the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus, a major source of serotonergic projections to the mPFC, and found increased spontaneous firing in Scn2a-deficient mice. Together, these findings highlight serotonergic alterations associated with SCN2A deficiency and the potential for serotonergic interventions to alleviate social deficits associated with SCN2A-related ASD.

papers.title: Gain Control of Peripheral Input by Core Brain Thermosensors Drives Drosophila Thermoregulation
papers.abstract: Temperature affects all aspects of animal physiology, rendering thermoregulation critical for survival. In Drosophila larvae, well-established peripheral thermosensors detect temperature changes and mediate thermotaxis over a broad innocuous range, but how larvae seek a specific preferred body temperature within this range remains unknown. Here we show that core thermosensors in the brain (LPBT neurons) establish this setpoint by mediating warming-evoked turning at temperatures above it. LPBTs express the warmth-activated thermosensor TrpA1(A), but are not simply cell-autonomous thermosensors. Rather, sustained LPBT responses above setpoint require both peripheral thermosensory input and TRPA1-dependent thermosensing within LPBTs. TRPA1-dependent core thermosensing provides gain control that defines the homeostatic setpoint by tuning the behavioral weights of peripheral inputs. This new conception of thermal preference reveals parallels between Drosophila and mammalian thermoregulation.

papers.title: A microstructural analysis of water intake patterns associated with light phase food and water restriction in male and female rats.
papers.abstract: Water intake is influenced by both eating and circadian rhythms, and the available literature is mixed regarding which variable exerts greater control. Previous reports primarily focused on short term manipulations, however, one study using long term light phase food restriction found that water intake patterns primarily retained circadian characteristics in male rats. To further characterize this behavioral effect, water intake and lick microstructure was analyzed in male and female rats with food access restricted to the light phase. In addition, food and water intake and lick microstructure were analyzed when water access was restricted to the light phase. In support of the previous short term, but not long term, food manipulation studies, when food access was restricted to the light phase most water intake shifted to this time frame. This shift was medicated by increased lick burst number, suggesting altered satiety signaling underling this intake pattern. When water access was restricted to the light phase, food intake was equally distributed across the light and dark phases. There was no effect of sex on the patterns of intake during any test condition. These results further our understanding of the mechanisms underlying food and water-associated and circadian intake patterns by suggesting that altered satiety signaling underlies changes in water intake.
