Our results demonstrate senMAGIC as a robust automation-friendly whole-genome evolution tool and highlight limitations of the method, providing a roadmap for future multifunctional CRISPR screens to optimize host metabolism for efficient bioprocesses.

papers.title: CTLA-4 checkpoint signalling modulates germinal centre dynamics and antibody avidity during Borrelia burgdorferi infection in mice.
papers.abstract: Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme borreliosis, persists in mammalian hosts despite robust activation of innate and adaptive immunity. A hallmark of murine infection is the production of low-avidity antibodies, yet the immunological mechanisms underlying this defective humoral response remain poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing of draining lymph node cells from Borrelia-infected mice at days 7 and 14 post-infection, comparing transcriptional profiles with those from mice immunised with heat-killed Borrelia or with a potent germinal centre-inducing protein immunisation. Borrelia infection induced a rapid germinal centre response, however, light zone B cells displayed diminished expression of co-stimulatory and T-B cell interaction molecules while maintaining core germinal centre identity markers, suggesting impaired positive selection. T follicular helper cells upregulated multiple inhibitory checkpoint receptor genes, most prominently Ctla4, alongside an active germinal centre engagement programme. Foxp3? regulatory T cells upregulated genes associated with follicular-homing and suppressive function, including those implicated in CTLA-4-mediated trans-endocytosis. To test whether inhibitory signalling contributes to the impaired humoral response, infected mice were treated with anti-CTLA-4 blocking antibody. CTLA-4 blockade significantly increased plasma cell numbers and enhanced both the magnitude and avidity of Borrelia-specific IgG responses, including the induction of complement-fixing IgG2a. These findings reveal that CTLA-4-dependent inhibitory signalling contributes to defective antibody quality during Borrelia infection, identifying a mechanism by which dysregulated T cell responses may facilitate impaired humoral control of a persistent spirochaetal pathogen.

papers.title: Whole methylome changes in Barrett's metaplasia, dysplasia, and cancer
papers.abstract: The clinical management of Barrett's esophagus (BE) and the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is dependent on the presence or absence of dysplasia. The histopathological diagnosis of dysplasia is unreliable however, and would benefit from additional diagnostic criteria. Here, we obtained EM-seq whole-genome methylation profiles from 86 samples across the BE/EAC disease spectrum, notably supplementing the scant existing methylation evidence for low-grade and high-grade dysplasia. While the bulk of methylation changes occur in the transition from normal squamous epithelium to intestinal metaplasia (non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus), we identified a smaller set of changes that mark the onset of dysplasia and progression to EAC. Methylation changes were broadly independent of copy number variation. They were tightly anticorrelated with RNA-seq expression for some genes. Deconvolution of the bulk methylation signatures into constituent cell types revealed four sample groupings enriched with a particular cell type (squamous, columnar, lymphoid and erythroid cells), somewhat reflecting existing clinical classifications. We outline potential markers that could improve the diagnosis of metaplasia and dysplasia in EAC.

papers.title: Seesaw configuration of the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 axis governs sensitivity to polyamine-targeting inhibitors of breast cancer cells
papers.abstract: Polyamines are endogenous metabolites crucial for various cellular functions, and maintaining their cellular levels is critical for normal cell survival and fate. Polyamine homeostasis is managed by a complex metabolic network, wherein the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 protein-protein interaction axis plays a central role in regulating polyamine synthesis and membrane transport. While existing research has established that polyamine-targeted inhibitors (PTIs) significantly perturb this axis in various cancers, and that different breast cancer subtypes display distinct PTI sensitivities, the fundamental mechanism of drug sensitivity difference has remained poorly understood. Here, we combine large-scale bioinformatic analysis with comprehensive experimental verification to reveal a polarized seesaw configuration of the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 axis across diverse tumor types, including breast cancer. We show that this seesaw configuration is not only distinct across breast cancer subtypes but also associated with unique cellular states. Furthermore, we reveal that this configuration underpins the distinct sensitivity profiles of these subtypes to both single and combination treatments of PTIs. Crucially, we demonstrate that targeted re-configuration of this axis can shift the drug sensitivity of resistant cells. This study provides the first systematic mechanistic framework linking the configuration of the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 axis to PTI sensitivity, thereby providing a configuration-based framework for rational selection of PTI combination regimens and new personalized therapeutic strategies in breast cancer.

papers.title: Dissecting Genetic Variability and Multi-Trait Performance in Cucumber
papers.abstract: Cucumber improvement requires the simultaneous enhancement of yield, earliness, fruit quality, and postharvest performance, yet many breeding studies rely on single-season or single-trait evaluations. This study therefore assessed 18 diverse cucumber genotypes across two consecutive Rabi seasons (2025 and 2026) using 23 agronomic, phenological, yield, fruit-quality, and postharvest traits, of which 12 non-redundant core traits were retained for the principal genetic and multivariate analyses. Genotypic variability, GCV, PCV, broad-sense heritability, genetic advance, interannual correlation, principal component analysis, hierarchical clustering, and multi-trait selection using MGIDI and MTSI were evaluated. Genotype effects were highly significant for nearly all estimable traits in both years (P<0.001). CU-10 produced the highest yield in both years (6.90 and 7.69 t ha-1), followed by CU-11 (4.38 and 4.89 t ha-1) and CU-09 (4.12 and 4.59 t ha-1). Yield showed high GCV (51.80%), PCV (52.21%), broad-sense heritability (98.46%), and GAM (106.04%). Fruit number plant-1 and fruit weight also exhibited high heritability (97.57% and 95.91%) and GAM (80.75% and 59.46%). Interannual repeatability was strongest for fruit number plant-1 (r=0.987), yield (r=0.986), and plant mortality (r=0.981), whereas shelf life was less stable (r=0.426, P=0.078). The first two principal components explained 57.29% of total variation, increasing to 70.92% with PC3. MGIDI selected CU-09, CU-11, and check variety Anuska, whereas MTSI selected CU-11, CU-01, and CU-06. Overall, CU-11 was the only genotype selected by both MGIDI and MTSI, indicating a favourable balance of multi-trait performance and relative interannual stability, while the other selected genotypes provided complementary breeding value for hybridization and further validation. These findings provide an integrated framework for improving productivity, stability, and postharvest performance in cucumber breeding programs.

papers.title: Anorectal care products cause variable inflammation and adverse barrier effects in a mucosal epithelial model
papers.abstract: Introduction: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and colorectal cancer (CRC) are rising in the United States, yet their shared mucosal environment remains underexplored. Rectal douching, a common practice among individuals engaging in receptive anal intercourse, has been epidemiologically linked to increased STI and HPV risk, but biological mechanisms are unclear. Methods: Using a human colorectal epithelial co-culture model (Caco-2/HT29-MTX-E12), we compared the effects of common douching products on cell viability, barrier integrity, and cytokine response. Results: Hyperosmolar or surfactant-containing solutions, including saline enemas, detergents, and soaps, caused rapid declines in metabolic activity and transepithelial electrical resistance, coupled with IL-6 and TNF- upregulation. In contrast, isotonic formulations maintained epithelial viability and barrier function comparable to buffered controls while reducing inflammatory signaling. Discussion: These findings provide mechanistic evidence that many consumer douching products compromise mucosal health and highlight the feasibility of harm-reduction designs for safer anal hygiene and sexual preparation.

papers.title: GSET: Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories select compact contexts for mechanistic GRN inference
papers.abstract: Mechanistic inference of gene regulatory networks from temporal transcriptomic data can become computationally prohibitive at transcriptome scale, making gene selection an important determinant of which regulatory relationships can be recovered. However, gene selection for GRN inference commonly relies on static expression or co-expression structure, rather than prioritizing dynamically informative genes whose temporal patterns capture how transcriptional programs change and relate to one another. We introduce GSET (Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories), an upstream retrieval framework that extracts dynamic information from temporal gene embeddings using two complementary signals: an optimal transport residual, which captures gene-specific deviations from global embedding movement, and a KL divergence, which detects changes in local co-expression neighborhoods. Temporal gene-embedding similarity identifies static transcriptional programs, whereas vectorial GSET signals represent coordinated temporal changes among genes, complementing this static structure. Lagged comparisons of these signals further prioritize temporal relationships between programs and candidate bridge genes associated with their transitions. Integrated with CardamomOT, GSET combines static program cores with dynamically retrieved bridge genes into compact, program-informed gene sets for mechanistic GRN inference. In synthetic benchmarks, at equal gene budget these sets recover more of the regulatory links between programs than static selections of the same size, and inference on the edges within the set is comparable to that of the full-gene model on the same gene pairs. On a time course of mouse fibroblasts reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells, GSET traces the transition from the fibroblast program to the cell-cycle program. By providing a dynamic retrieval layer upstream of GRN inference, GSET nominates bridge genes as candidate regulators of cell-state transitions, which, once refined by a mechanistic model such as CardamomOT and confirmed by perturbation experiments, could open the way to controlling these transitions.

papers.title: Polycomb Marked Promoter Methylation Gains in Aging and Cancer are Independent of Replication
papers.abstract: DNA methylation alterations are hallmark features of aging and cancer, occurring early during tumor initiation. Yet how these changes evolve during early tumorigenesis, and whether oncogenic signaling actively drives them, remains poorly understood due to limitations in resolving this at the longitudinal and clonal level. Here we developed a genome-wide DNA methylation profiling method for low DNA amounts and applied it to single stem cell-derived clones from a BRAFV600E -inducible mouse colon organoid model, tracking nucleotide-level methylation heterogeneity over time. BRAFV600E induction produced stepwise methylation divergence consistent with progressive clonal takeover, in contrast to gradual epigenetic drift in uninduced controls. Strikingly, while the specific CpG sites altered differed between BRAFV600E and control lineages, they converged on the same genomic elements. Particularly, Polycomb-marked promoter CpG-island methylation gains were not induced or accelerated by BRAFV600E, challenging models in which oncogenic signaling or cell proliferation actively instructs de novo methylation of Polycomb-targeted promoters. Instead, these gains tracked with "biological aging" independent of replication, which was validated across independent aging, cancer, and cell-line datasets. BRAFV600E -induced clones additionally showed progressive loss of intestinal lineage-specification transcription factor programs, consistent with selection for cells adapted to oncogenic stress. Together, these findings show that epigenetic trajectories during early tumor development, are rooted in baseline, age-dependent drivers of epigenetic alterations, and that oncogenic signaling acts primarily by selecting and expanding clones bearing pre-existing, age-associated epigenetic drift rather than instructing new methylation. Our findings have implications for how promoter methylation is interpreted as a cancer biomarker and for identifying upstream aging-associated processes as targets for early intervention.

papers.title: Amyloid/RNA Condensates with Germ Granule Characteristics Are Present in Rat Epididymal Spermatozoa and Exhibit Prion-Like Propagation Activity
papers.abstract: Environmental exposures to the germline can alter its epigenome resulting in new traits being acquired by offspring. While the epigenetic carrier in mammalian spermatozoa remains unknown, studies in C.elegans show that amyloids and sperm-specific populations of germ granules, phase-separated biomolecular condensates enriched in RNA-binding proteins and small noncoding RNAs, transmit heritable epigenetic phenotypes to descendant cells. Here we discovered that rat epididymal spermatozoa contain germ granule-like condensates in the head perforatorium, a cytoplasmic derived structure that participates in early post-fertilization events. The perforatoria condensates contain evolutionarily conserved germ granule markers and small noncoding RNAs and are enriched in amyloid, including those of the clinically relevant amyloidogenic proteins androgen receptor (AR) and TDP43. Further, perforatoria extracts exhibit prion-like propagation behavior by functioning as molecular seeds to template amyloid assembly in recombinant AR and TDP43. We propose that nature has conserved sperm germ granule-like structures throughout evolution to allow an organism to respond and adapt to a changed environment by passing environmentally encoded information to the embryo via a non-Mendelian protein-based mechanism of inheritance.

papers.title: Structural Determinants of Ligand-Mediated Hmg2 Mallostery
papers.abstract: The sterol pathway is a conserved eukaryotic process that produces essential metabolites. Hmg-CoA reductase (HMGR) is a key rate limiting enzyme of the sterol pathway and is the most successful clinical target for managing cholesterol levels. However, determination of the structural features that are essential for its regulation remains elusive. Because of the conservation between mammals and yeast, for many years we have studied the structural features of a yeast Hmg2 isozyme of HMGR. Hmg2 is regulated by the mevalonate pathway isoprenoid GGPP. GGPP acts similarly to an allosteric ligand and appears to bind to a specific site on Hmg2, causing Hmg2 to undergo reversible misfolding. Misfolded Hmg2 is then recognized by the protein quality control mechanism known as the HRD pathway. Due to its similarity to allosteric regulation we have termed this ligand-dependent misfolding mallostery. In this work, we systematically probe each residue of the Hmg2 lumenal domain as well as assess the transmembrane domain and lumenal domain as independent domains and use in vivo and in vitro techniques to assess what regions are important for GGPP response. We identified stabilizing mutations within each loop of the lumenal domain but did not find mutants that were completely unresponsive to GGPP. When assessing the transmembrane domain and lumenal domain as two independent structures, we found that only the transmembrane domain responded to GGPP specifically in vitro. Our results suggest that GGPP binding occurs within the Hmg2 transmembrane domain and that the loops in the lumenal domain are required for transducing a mallosteric response to GGPP. Taken together, these data suggest a new model of Hmg2 regulation.

papers.title: HYphlow: bringing end-to-end flow to HyPhy selection analyses, from taxon reconciliation to trait-based foreground assignment
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic analyses of molecular evolution often require repeated manual preparation to reconcile taxa, annotate trees, execute models, and summarize results. These steps become increasingly time-consuming and difficult to standardize as the number of taxa, genes, and analytical hypotheses increases. We present HYphlow, an open-source graphical workflow developed in Python that integrates data preparation, trait-based foreground branch assignment, HyPhy execution, and structured result extraction within a single interface. HYphlow reconciles taxon labels across alignments, trees, and trait data; reconstructs ancestral states using parsimony and maximum likelihood; generates alternative foreground annotations; executes HyPhy analyses locally or through portable scripts for high-performance computing; and records analytical decisions and settings throughout the workflow. We evaluated HYphlow using simulations and two published datasets comprising cryptochrome analyses in pigeons and doves and visual opsin analyses in skinks. A name-similarity threshold of 80 reliably recovered simulated spelling variants, while consensus foreground assignment increased precision relative to parsimony or maximum likelihood alone (0.928 vs 0.891 and 0.907, respectively), with a corresponding reduction in recall (0.875 vs 0.921 and 0.918). In the empirical datasets, HYphlow reconciled taxon labels, reconstructed or reproduced foreground hypotheses derived using different approaches, and generated selection results consistent with the principal conclusions of the original studies. HYphlow therefore provides a reproducible framework for carrying comparative molecular evolutionary analyses from independently prepared sequence, phylogenetic, and trait data through branch assignment, model execution, and results summary while retaining researcher control over analytical decisions. HYphlow is freely available under the MIT licence from GitHub at: https://github.com/Schott-Lab/HYphlow.

papers.title: Making sense of chaos: replication and segregation defects in the yeast mcm4Chaos3 mutant
papers.abstract: Genome instability is a defining feature of cancer and is strongly influenced by alterations in the fidelity and timing of DNA replication. The conserved Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM 2-7) helicase is a central component of the eukaryotic DNA replication machinery, playing critical roles in origin licensing and activation. Genetic screens for genome instability mutations in mice identified mcm4Chaos3, a hypomorphic allele of MCM4 associated with the formation of micronuclei and tumorigenesis, suggesting that the mcm4Chaos3 allele causes genome instability. To define the mechanistic basis of this instability, we examined the effects of the corresponding mutation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We found that mcm4Chaos3 selectively compromises origin firing at a subset of early S-phase origins, with pronounced effects at many centromere-proximal origins. Chromosome V, containing the sensitive centromere-adjacent ARS510, exhibited elevated loss rates that were rescued by replacement with the robust early-firing origin ARS305, restoring both origin activity and chromosome stability. Together these findings demonstrate that mcm4Chaos3 compromises genome stability by impairing a subset of early, centromere-proximal origins that are intrinsically sensitive to origin activation capacity. Our results establish that robust origin function near centromeres is critical for accurate chromosome segregation and reveal how subtle perturbations in helicase function can lead to chromosome instability.

papers.title: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy of optically cleared human head-and-neck organs: three-dimensional tissue assessment and histological correlation
authors: van den Hout, M. F. C. M.
papers.abstract: Conventional histology provides detailed cellular information but only a partial view of the three-dimensional (3D) organisation of head-and-neck tissues. We investigated whether optical tissue clearing combined with light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) could visualise the microanatomy of large head-and-neck specimens and relate volumetric features to conventional histology. Non-neoplastic human palatine tonsil, cervical lymph node, tongue and parotid gland specimens were cleared with a solvent-based protocol, labelled with small-molecule dyes and imaged by LSFM, with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology as a morphological reference. LSFM visualised the characteristic architecture of each tissue, including lymphoid follicles and crypt epithelium in tonsil, cortex, paracortex and follicles in lymph node, epithelium and intrinsic muscle fibres in tongue, and lobules, ducts and adipocytes in parotid. Following structures through successive optical sections revealed their continuity and branching over long distances, information not available from single sections. Tongue epithelial measurements were comparable with H&E, and segmentation enabled volumetric quantification of structures such as the tongue epithelium and parotid adipocytes. Optical clearing and LSFM thus provide a feasible single workflow for volumetric investigation of human head-and-neck microanatomy. These data establish a 3D morphological reference with potential applications in cancer research and staging, computational image analysis and anatomical education, to be further developed through larger donor cohorts and specific labelling.

papers.title: Inherited maternal memory T cells protect offspring from respiratory viral infection through disease tolerance
papers.abstract: Maternal immune transfer is a powerful mechanism for early-life protection from infection, yet the full repertoire of protective factors remains unknown. We discovered that maternal memory T cells are both necessary and sufficient to protect offspring from lethal respiratory infection. This antigen-specific protection operated independently of maternal antibodies and offspring T cell responses and required IL-10 produced by maternal T cells. Transfer of protective maternal T cells reduced offspring inflammatory responses and lung tissue damage without affecting viral burdens, indicating that maternal memory T cells directly suppress pathogenic innate inflammatory responses to preserve offspring health. Critically, maternal vaccination similarly protected offspring in a T cell-dependent manner. These findings reveal maternal antigen-specific T cell transfer as a complementary immunological defense mechanism to protect offspring against pathogens that escape maternal antibodies, with broad implications for maternal vaccination strategies.

papers.title: Cigarette smoke extract and palmitic acid exposed patient-derived iPS- RPE cells as a model for AMD
papers.abstract: Purpose: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a multifactorial disease in which dysfunction and loss of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells contribute to disease progression. Besides genetics, cigarette smoking and high fat diet are important environmental and metabolic risk factors for AMD and are associated with RPE dysfunction. However, the effects of combined environmental and metabolic stress on AMD-derived RPE cells remain poorly understood. In this study, we used patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (iPSC-RPE) cells to examine the effects of cigarette smoke extract (CSE) and palmitic acid (PA) on RPE cell function. Methods: iPSCs derived from non-AMD and AMD donors were differentiated into RPE cells and characterized based on morphology, RPE-specific marker expression, polarity, gene expression, and barrier function. Mature iPSC-RPE cells were exposed to different concentrations of CSE and PA to determine experimental conditions. Cell death, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-like morphological changes, stress-related gene expression, RPE polarity, TEER, VEGF-A and PEDF secretion, and intracellular lipid accumulation were then evaluated following CSE, PA, or combined CSE and PA exposure. Results: Differentiated iPSC-RPE cells developed typical pigmented, hexagonal morphology, expressed RPE-specific markers, and formed polarized monolayers. Both CSE and PA increased cell death in a dose-dependent manner in the control and AMD-iPSC-RPE, with AMD-iPSC-RPE exhibiting greater susceptibility, particularly those from patients with dry AMD. CSE and PA also induced also induced EMT-like morphological changes and increased the expression of ZEB1, NQO1, and IL8. Furthermore, CSE and PA disrupted the polarized distribution of ZO-1 and Best1, significantly reduced the polarity ratio, decreased PEDF and VEGF-A secretion and increased intracellular lipid accumulation. Combined CSE and PA treatment produced more pronounced effects than either treatment alone in AMD lines. Conclusions: AMD- iPSC-RPE cells, particularly those derived from dry AMD donors, exhibit increased susceptibility to environmental and metabolic stress. Exposure to CSE and PA revealed this vulnerability through alterations in cell survival, stress responses, epithelial morphology, polarity, secretory function, and intracellular lipid accumulation. These findings highlight the effects of CSE and lipid stress on RPE metabolism and underscore the utility of patient-derived iPSC-RPE cells as a model for investigating how environmental and metabolic factors contribute to RPE dysfunction and AMD pathogenesis.

papers.title: Quantitative Donor Histology and Transcriptomics Link Pancreatic Composition and Precancers Across the Adult Lifespan
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) is the primary precursor to invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). While PanIN is common in the general population, PDAC is rare. PDAC risk rises with age, diabetes mellitus, and obesity, but whether this increased risk reflects a greater precancer burden is unknown, as previous studies assessed PanIN presence and grade. We aimed to quantify pancreatic composition and PanIN burden across the adult lifespan to identify demographics of donors carrying disproportionate precancer burden. Methods: We applied CODAvision, a deep-learning segmentation pipeline, to 410 high-quality pancreas sections from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) donors aged 21 to 70 years. We screened twenty-seven donor phenotypes against 14 compositional measures, applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. We further related tissue composition and donor phenotype to bulk gene expression in 281 donors to understand which demographics are associated with a compositional or transcriptional fingerprint. Results: PanIN was present in 83% of donors. Acinar proportion declined with age, offset by fat and stroma. Median PanIN burden did not change with age, though the fitted 90th percentile rose from 0.21% to 0.72% of exocrine tissue (uncorrected P=.002). The 39 sections (10%) with high-outlier PanIN burden came disproportionately from donors with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension and had greater stromal proportion and higher fibroblast and immune-cell densities. Both cell types were denser in peri-PanIN stroma than in the surrounding pancreatic parenchyma. PanIN abundance was associated with a gastric transcriptional signature including VSIG1, TFF1, and MUC5AC. Conclusions: Most donors carried little PanIN at any age, whereas high burden was concentrated in a minority of donors more likely to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and inflamed, fibrotic stroma. Because PanIN was present in most donors, its presence did not distinguish high-risk groups, whereas quantitative burden did, concentrating on the metabolic phenotypes already under consideration for pancreatic surveillance.

papers.title: Singular Value Decomposition for the Automated Analysis of NMR Fraction Libraries
papers.abstract: Identifying and quantifying molecular components of biological fluids offers great potential for the diagnosis of disease, detecting environmental contaminants, and process monitoring. The use of simple 1D 1H NMR spectra to accomplish this task offers advantages in terms of broad applicability and quantitative output. However, it also encounters obstacles in extracting individual components from complex superimposed spectra and in compound identification through comparison with limited database entries. Here, we present a new protocol that includes automatically separating component spectra using singular value decomposition (SVD) and matching them to database entries that carry both chemical shift and scalar coupling information. The procedure is illustrated by application to a fungal extract from Neurospora crassa that is chromatographically fractionated to form a two-dimensional spectral fraction library. Results are compared to a previous analysis that used a semi-manual curation of separated spectra followed by chemical shift matching.

papers.title: Particle-based representation of phytoplankton modulates emergent coexistence and biogeography in a model ocean
papers.abstract: Phytoplankton communities sustain the marine food web through primary productivity. These communities sustain a high diversity of species, all of which must draw from the same finite nutrient supply. The mechanisms driving phytoplankton biogeography and succession, as well as those enabling high diversity, remain incompletely understood. Here, we compare emerging patterns of biogeography, richness, and diversity in a size-structured phytoplankton community as it is advected and diffused within an idealized North Atlantic double-gyre circulation, using both Eulerian and Lagrangian (particle-based) modeling (PBM) frameworks. When a sufficient number of particles is modeled, the PBM, which resolves mortality at the particle level, produces stronger seasonal variability in biomass in the northern gyre and less stable and higher biomass in the southern gyre, while reproducing large-scale chlorophyll patterns observed by satellite. These contrasting dynamics are accompanied by distinct regional diversity patterns: local richness and diversity are generally higher in the PBM than in the Eulerian model in the northern gyre, with differences depending on the mortality threshold, whereas in the oligotrophic southern gyre, PBM local richness increases with particle number, while Eulerian richness is more sensitive to the mortality threshold. The PBM also produces a dynamic and emergent biogeographical structure that is more robust to the mortality threshold than the Eulerian model. Finally, Lagrangian variability in environmental conditions experienced by particles shows a stronger impact compared to the local Eulerian variability in the Northern gyre and stresses variable sensitivity to environmental histories. Together, these results suggest that the discrete representation of biomass fundamentally alters mortality, biogeography, and emergent coexistence patterns in model plankton ecosystems.

papers.title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes
papers.abstract: Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators (R1-R5). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1, R2, R3, and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1-R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

papers.title: Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Modeling Reveals CO2-Dependent Growth Control in Picochlorum celeri
papers.abstract: Picochlorum celeri grows 11.6 times faster at elevated CO2 than in air, yet the abundance of its metabolic enzymes is only 17% higher. To explain this, we reconstructed iPiccel954, a genome-scale metabolic model with 3525 reactions, 2973 metabolites and 954 genes, and eciPiccel954, its enzyme-constrained version limited by the measured enzyme abundance in air and at elevated CO2. Calibrating the enzyme-constrained models against the measured proteome showed that a similar protein budget supports very different growth depending on how it is allocated. With urea as the nitrogen source, urea carboxylase was the only step whose relaxation alone raised growth, by 627% in air and 78% at elevated CO2. Bottleneck analysis showed that growth is limited by many enzymes spread across the network in both conditions, that the limiting enzymes differ between the two, and that control over starch metabolism seen in air disappears at elevated CO2. Measured proteomes agreed with these predictions, since the predicted bottleneck enzymes were more abundant than other enzymes. Rapid growth in P. celeri therefore reflects how the protein budget is allocated more than how large it is. Therefore, eciPiccel954 provides a quantitative basis for engineering this alga for biotechnological application.

papers.title: HER3 mediates metabolic reprogramming in metastatic colorectal and pancreatic cancer
papers.abstract: Liver metastases are a major cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the oncogenic signals that shape tumor metabolism in the hepatic niche remain poorly understood. Here, we show that HER3 activation drives a liver metastasis-specific glycolytic program in both cancer types. Genetic or pharmacological HER3 inhibition suppresses cancer glycolysis while increasing dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), rendering liver metastases vulnerable to OXPHOS inhibition. Combining the HER3 inhibitor sapitinib with distinct OXPHOS inhibitors led to in vitro synergy and durable tumor-free survival in orthotopic CRC and PDAC liver metastases models, with further validation in patient-derived xenografts. Mechanistically, HER3 promotes glycolysis through activating PFK2 and reduces OXPHOS through activating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial remodeling, both pathways were activated in liver metastases compared to matched primary tumors. Together, our findings identify the HER3-AKT/RSK-PFK2 axis as a driver of glycolysis and metastatic growth and reveal an OXPHOS dependency induced by HER3 inhibition that may be exploited through combined HER3 and OXPHOS targeting in metastatic CRC and PDAC.

papers.title: CO2-concentrating nanoparticles drive progressive photosynthetic and cell-wall remodelling in Arabidopsis thaliana cells
papers.abstract: Plant cells offer a distinctive platform for biohybrid engineering because they combine growth and proliferation with photosynthetic carbon acquisition and the continuous fabrication of structurally complex biomass. Harnessing these capabilities could enable living systems in which synthetic functionality develops together with cellular physiology and material organization. Yet nanomaterial engineering of proliferating plant cell populations remains largely unexplored. Here, we establish a biohybrid system combining photosynthetically active Arabidopsis thaliana suspension cells with chitosan-modified polyethyleneimine (gPEI-Chi) nanoparticles, a synthetic CO2-concentrating nanomaterial. By supplying fresh nanoparticles at each subculture, newly generated cell populations were successively functionalized, driving progressive changes in cellular and multicellular phenotypes. Nanoparticle functionalization reduced net headspace CO2 accumulation, increased chlorophyll content and induced stage-dependent reorganization of photosynthetic function and carbon-handling pathways. These physiological changes were accompanied by altered cell wall regeneration and progressive remodelling of cell wall composition, spatial organization and ultrastructure, ultimately promoting more cohesive multicellular aggregates. Our findings establish successive nanomaterial functionalization as a strategy to steer the evolving physiology and structural organization of proliferating plant cell populations, opening opportunities for plant biohybrid systems and engineered living materials.

papers.title: Sodium arsenite requires redox sensitization to cause developmental dopaminergic neurotoxicity in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Environmental pollutants can disrupt mitochondrial function through many pathways and mitochondrial dysfunction is often linked to neurotoxicity, particularly of dopaminergic neurons. However, there are many mechanisms of mitochondrial toxicity. Remarkably, despite the centrality of the Krebs cycle to mitochondrial bioenergetics, there is very limited evidence regarding whether pollutants that inhibit the Krebs cycle can cause neurotoxicity. We exposed Caenorhabditis elegans through its whole development to Krebs cycle inhibitors sodium arsenite and fluoroacetic acid, and evaluated neuronal morphology and function as well as dopaminergic ATP levels and redox state. Both chemicals impaired growth and reproduction, but neither caused morphological damage nor functional deficits in dopaminergic, glutamatergic, or cholinergic neurons at concentrations causing mild organismal toxicity. Sodium arsenite, but not fluoroacetic acid, decreased dopaminergic ATP levels; neither caused significant changes in mitochondrial redox state. However, developmental exposure to sodium arsenite caused dopaminergic neurotoxicity when mitochondrial quality control or redox stress response was compromised by loss of pink-1/PINK1 or sod-2/SOD2, by co-exposure to rotenone, antimycin A, or buthionine sulfoximine, or secondary challenge to 6-hydroxydopamine. These conditions also led to dopamine-associated behavioral deficits. Thus, developmental exposure to sodium arsenite required an additional mitochondrial or redox stress challenge to cause dopaminergic neurotoxicity, and we did not find evidence that inhibition of the Krebs cycle broadly defined causes developmental neurotoxicity.

papers.title: Serotonin signals through ciliary 5-HT6 to control insulin secretion
papers.abstract: In the pancreatic islet, serotonin (5-HT) functions basally to modulate glucagon secretion, but its contribution to beta-cell signaling and function remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the Gs-coupled serotonin receptor 6 (5-HT6), previously thought to be expressed almost exclusively in the brain, localizes to the primary cilium and plasma membrane of islet cells and augments insulin secretion. Utilizing a transgenic model of beta-cell cilia loss, along with approaches to perturb cilia-specific 5-HT6 function without disrupting the native cilium architecture, we show that 5-HT6 action in beta cells is dependent on the primary cilium. Critically, the plasma membrane pool of 5-HT6 cannot stimulate insulin release when the cilium is absent, representing an instance of whole-cell regulation by a cilia-localized GPCR. These findings establish subcellular localization as a determinant of GPCR function in beta cells and identify ciliary 5-HT6 signaling as a distinct pathway for modulating insulin secretion.

papers.title: Integrative taxonomy of the North American pink flat-backed millipedes (Polydesmidae: Pseudopolydesmus Attems, 1898)
papers.abstract: Millipedes of the genus Pseudopolydesmus Attems, 1898 are common millipedes in North America. They are the largest, in terms of body size, and most geographically wide-ranging of the family Polydesmidae, and are ubiquitous in eastern and central North American forests. Eight species have been named based on the morphology of the genitalia, but these have not been investigated genetically. Here, we take an integrated taxonomic approach, using five genes to infer a molecular phylogeny of Pseudopolydesmus species, and analyze a dataset of 15 morphological characters in an effort to delimit species in the genus. 1,148 Pseudopolydesmus specimens were newly collected for this study, and all known species were sampled. These specimens were used for analysis, and were combined with museum specimens and literature records into a database of 3,462 unique specimen records. This database was used to produce distribution maps for each species in the genus. The maximum likelihood phylogeny found support for the eight species in the genus, supporting previous morphological species hypotheses. However, previous morphology-based hypotheses regarding evolutionary relationships between the species were not supported by the analysis. The morphological analysis, performed with a modified PCA, did not delimit species clusters as well as the genitalic and genetic differences did, due to comparatively uniform somatic morphology in the genus. However, our results show that genitalic morphology, combined with genetic analysis, provide congruent species delimitation hypotheses for Pseudopolydesmus, and these lines of evidence may prove useful in delimiting species and generic boundaries in other Polydesmidae worldwide.

papers.title: Serum Calprotectin as predictor of Rheumatoid Arthritis disease severity and Mortality
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the clinical utility of serum calprotectin (sCAL) as a biomarker of disease activity, disease severity, cardiovascular risk, and mortality in inflammatory rheumatic diseases (IRDs). Methods: Serum calprotectin was measured in 2677 patients with IRDs, including 1472 rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 771 axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), and 434 psoriatic arthritis (PsA) patients enrolled in the Swiss Clinical Quality Management in Rheumatic Diseases registry, as well as 248 healthy blood donors. Associations with disease activity, radiographic progression, cardiovascular biomarkers, incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and mortality were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic, Cox regression, and Kaplan-Meier models. Results: sCAL concentrations were significantly higher in RA than in axSpA, PsA, or healthy blood donors. Although diagnostic discrimination between IRDs was modest (Area under the curve (AUC): 0.56), elevated sCAL identified a subset of patients with RA characterized by higher disease activity, higher autoantibody levels, and accelerated radiographic progression, performing better than CRP for the assessment of inflammatory activity, particularly for the discrimination of active synovitis (SJC28[≥]4, AUC 0.67 vs 0.62, p=0.012), even in patients with normal CRP concentrations. Elevated sCAL was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR:2.99; 95% confidence interval (95%CI):1.87-4.78), cardiovascular mortality (HR:7.49;95%CI:1.50-37.55), respiratory mortality (HR: 5.89; 95%CI:1.97-17.62), and incident MACE (HR: 2.10; 95%CI: 1.04-4.24). Furthermore, sCAL correlated with high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T and NT-proBNP concentrations, independently of lipid profile. Conclusions: Serum calprotectin is a clinically relevant biomarker in RA that reflects both disease activity and severity, independently identifying patients at increased cardiovascular risk and mortality, supporting its potential role in disease monitoring and risk stratification.

papers.title: Ancient U/V sex chromosomes reveal slow expansion of recombination suppression in Polytrichaceae mosses.
papers.abstract: Sex chromosomes evolving in haploid versus diploid life cycles provide complementary systems for testing theories of sex chromosome evolution, yet haploid sex chromosomes remain poorly studied. In dioicous bryophytes, females and males carry non-recombining U and V chromosomes, respectively, providing a unique opportunity to examine the consequences of long-term recombination suppression independently of diploid heterogamety. Here, we characterize the U/V sex chromosomes of Polytrichaceae using chromosome-scale genomes from ten species. We identify homologous U/V chromosomes across the family and show that their non-recombining sex-determining regions (SDRs) originated early in Polytrichaceae evolution, approximately 124 million years ago. Despitetheir ancient origin, however, the SDRs have undergone limited expansion and are consistently flanked by large pseudoautosomal regions (PARs). The SDRs nevertheless show strong genomic signatures of recombination suppression, including reduced gene density, transposable-element accumulation, reduced diversity, high synonymous divergence, and altered codon usage. Yet they retain hundreds of genes and show limited evidence of functional degeneration. Their gene content is dynamic, with frequent lineage-specific gains and losses, while a conserved core of 60 orthogroups has persisted across all ten species for more than 100 million years. Comparisons across sex chromosome systems suggest that haploid U/V chromosomes retain more genes than similarly old diploid X/Y or Z/W chromosomes, consistent with a role for haploid selection in limiting degeneration. However, haploid selection alone cannot explain the limited SDR expansion observed in Polytrichaceae, suggesting that other factors also shape SDR evolution. Together, these results reveal an ancient U/V system in which recombination suppression has strong genomic consequences but has not driven extensive SDR expansion or functional degeneration. By decoupling recombination suppression from diploid heterogamety, U/V chromosomes provide a powerful framework for distinguishing the consequences of recombination arrest from those of ploidy in sex chromosome evolution.

papers.title: Genome-wide loss of chromatin accessibility coexists with selectively elevated RNA abundance in nutrient-starved U2OS cells
papers.abstract: Background Chromatin accessibility is widely used as a proxy for regulatory potential and is often interpreted together with RNA-seq to infer gene-regulatory responses. However, the quantitative relationship between chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance may become difficult to interpret, particularly under acute cellular stress. Metabolic challenges such as nutrient deprivation are known to induce extensive chromatin remodelling and transcriptional reprogramming, raising the question of whether changes in transcript abundance are directly governed by chromatin accessibility in these contexts. Clarifying this relationship is critical for interpreting epigenomic data under stress conditions, and requires careful distinction between Tn5 accessibility, relative steady-state RNA abundance and transcriptional output. Results We integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses in human U2OS osteosarcoma cells following 18 h of severe nutrient deprivation. We found that starvation was associated with a genome-wide reduction in accessibility and almost all significantly altered accessible regions showed reduced signal relative to actively growing cells. This decrease affected promoter- and enhancer-associated regions alike, including housekeeping-gene promoters and CTCF-motif sites. In contrast, RNA-seq revealed a more selective change in relative steady-state RNA abundance: only a minority of expressed genes were differentially regulated, and approximately 64% of differentially expressed genes showed increased relative RNA abundance. Changes in accessibility and transcript abundance were modestly correlated at promoters (Pearson r = 0.25) and weakly at enhancers (r = 0.10), and together explained only ~6% of the variance in transcript abundance changes. The relationship was graded: genes with the smallest promoter losses were about four times as likely to show increased RNA abundance as genes with the largest losses, independently of baseline promoter accessibility. Within-condition analyses similarly showed only modest relationships between promoter accessibility and RNA abundance in both actively growing and starved cells. Pathway-level analysis of mRNA abundance revealed the expected repression of biosynthetic and growth-related programmes, including ribosome biogenesis, translation and cellular growth, together with a less anticipated relative activation of stress-adaptive programmes, including extracellular matrix organisation, lipid and cholesterol metabolism, small GTPase signalling and developmental processes. For genes within these activated programmes, increased steady-state mRNA abundance was observed despite reduced ATAC-seq accessibility at associated regulatory regions. Exon-intron analyses of RNA-seq data indicated that these changes predominantly reflect altered RNA production. Metabolic labelling of nascent RNA at selected loci confirmed increased transcription of genes involved in adaptive programmes despite reduced promoter and enhancer accessibility, alongside with reduced production of biosynthetic transcripts and rRNA. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that chromatin accessibility and steady-state RNA abundance are only modestly coupled during severe nutrient deprivation, against a baseline of similarly modest promoter accessibility-abundance coupling. This underscores the limited ability of ATAC-seq accessibility to predict transcript abundance under this stress condition and supports a model in which chromatin accessibility acts as a permissive rather than deterministic layer of gene regulation. The selective induction of adaptive programmes, confirmed here at the level of RNA production, shows that transcriptional activation can occur despite genome-wide loss of ATAC-seq accessibility. Because ATAC-seq reports Tn5 accessibility rather than physical chromatin compaction, we interpret compaction as a plausible mechanistic model compatible with the current observations, which will require direct orthogonal validation.

papers.title: A cotranslational role for selenocysteine in productive protein folding
papers.abstract: Selenocysteine (Sec) is generally regarded as the catalytic determinant that distinguishes selenoproteins from their cysteine (Cys)-containing counterparts. Consequently, the biological significance of Sec has largely been attributed to its unique chemical properties within mature proteins. Here, we uncover an unexpected role for Sec in protein biogenesis. Using the endoplasmic reticulum selenoprotein SELENOM as a model, we show that replacement of Sec with Cys redirects the protein into an alternative assembly pathway, resulting in formation of a stable domain-swapped homodimer. Biochemical and structural analyses demonstrate that this phenotype cannot be explained solely by altered active-site chemistry, as dimerisation persists following extensive active-site mutagenesis. Remarkably, reintroduction of Sec at alternative positions suppresses dimer formation, including when Sec is placed within a cleaved signal peptide and is absent from the mature protein. Thus, identical protein sequences can adopt distinct folding outcomes depending on whether Sec incorporation occurred during biosynthesis. These findings reveal a previously unrecognised role for Sec in productive protein folding and raise the possibility that evolutionary retention of the Sec incorporation pathway reflects advantages not only in catalysis but also in protein folding.

papers.title: Calcium and actomyosin pulses drive tricellular zipping to remodel epithelial cell-cell junctions and facilitate cell packing
papers.abstract: Epithelial morphogenesis requires coordinated changes in cell geometry, neighbor cell arrangement, and cell packing to generate functional tissue architectures. However, the spatiotemporal regulation of upstream signals that drive local junctional remodeling in highly proliferative developing epithelial tissues remains unclear. Here, we characterize a new junction remodeling process, which we call "tricellular zipping". It resolves long, thin cell extensions generated by cell-division forces that terminate at transient higher-order vertices. We show that tricellular zipping facilitates epithelial cell packing in blastula-stage Xenopus laevis embryos through asymmetric displacement of a tricellular vertex and formation of a de novo bicellular interface. Similarly, we observe tricellular zipping in developing mouse embryos. Combining modeling and live imaging approaches, we find that displacement of the remodeling vertex depends on actomyosin-dependent asymmetric force generation and on enrichment of adaptor proteins coupling actomyosin to junctions, which enables effective force transmission. In contrast, the stationary vertex remains close to mechanical equilibrium and therefore undergoes no net displacement. Furthermore, we find that calcium flashes drive the localized, pulsatile actomyosin contractility required for efficient tricellular zipping. Extending our observations, we show that disrupting transient calcium signaling also affects cell packing in Drosophila embryos, thereby impairing mesoderm internalization. Overall, by combining multidisciplinary and multisystem approaches, we uncover a new mode of junctional remodeling and highlight the importance of spatiotemporally regulated calcium signaling in driving local junctional rearrangements to facilitate morphogenesis.

papers.title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation reverses adolescent alcohol-induced cellular and behavioral deficits.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol is commonly consumed by adolescents in a binge-like pattern that can produce persistent cognitive impairments. Previous work found that adolescent intermittent ethanol (AIE) exposure reduces parvalbumin expressing (PV+) interneurons and increases perineuronal net (PNN) expression in brain regions critical for cognition. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for treating psychiatric disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether AIE exposure alters PV+ interneurons and PNN expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and impairs cognition, and whether mPFC-targeted gamma tACS can reverse these effects. METHODS: Sprague Dawley rats (N=139, 50% female) underwent AIE or control exposure during adolescence and received Active or Sham mPFC-targeted gamma tACS treatment for three consecutive days in adulthood. Following stimulation, rats either underwent immunohistochemical assessment of PV+ and PNN expression or behavioral testing using the novel object recognition (NOR) task. RESULTS: AIE exposure reduced PV+ cell counts in the prelimbic cortex, an effect that was reversed by active tACS. In contrast, AIE exposure did not alter PNN measures. Interestingly, active tACS affected the prelimbic and infralimbic cortices more than the anterior cingulate cortex. AIE exposure also reduced recognition memory of a novel object, and this deficit was ameliorated by active tACS when assessed one week after stimulation. Additionally, active stimulation decreased anxiety-like behavior in the open-field test. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these results confirm that adolescent alcohol exposure produces lasting cellular and cognitive alterations and supports mPFC-targeted gamma tACS as a potential intervention for alcohol-induced dysfunction.

papers.title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia
papers.abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and 2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Results Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by 1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced 2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Conclusions Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.

papers.title: Sublingual Buprenorphine/Naloxone Film in Unanesthetized Rats: Feasibility, Tolerability, and Plasma Exposure
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Buprenorphine/naloxone sublingual film is first-line treatment for opioid use disorder, yet preclinical rodent studies use routes that do not match clinical dosing. We tested sublingual film administration in unanesthetized rats. Methods Male Sprague-Dawley rats received film delivering 3.2 mg/kg buprenorphine, scaled from the 16 mg/day clinical dose by body surface area and corrected for species differences in sublingual bioavailability. Plasma buprenorphine was measured by LC-MS/MS after a single dose. Body weight, liver weight, serum AST, ALT and ALP, and liver histopathology were compared with controls after 21-days of once-daily dosing. Results Plasma buprenorphine peaked at 4.0 ng/mL at 2 h and was 0.9 ng/mL at 24 h, with an AUC(0-24h) of 39.0 h ng/mL, spanning concentrations reported as therapeutic in patients. Repeat dosing reduced absolute and relative liver weight and relative liver weight, with no change in serum enzymes or liver histology. Conclusions Sublingual film dosing is feasible and tolerated in unanesthetized rats and achieves clinically relevant buprenorphine exposure, enabling route-matched preclinical studies of buprenorphine pharmacology and opioid-related behavior.

papers.title: Optimizing the efficiency of assisted reproduction procedures in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) improved IVF outcomes
papers.abstract: The marmoset has emerged as a model species for genetic studies of complex neurodevelopmental conditions because of their brain development, behavior, communication, and compact size. IVF has been used to generate wild-type and transgenic marmoset embryos, but inefficiency of IVF in the marmoset compared to other primates poses challenges for genetic manipulation. To address this limitation, we analyzed the association between variables of age, number of cycles, and progesterone levels for IVF and embryology outcomes. Longitudinal data collected over 2 years indicated that the progesterone levels 24 hours after Cloprostenol sodium (Estrumate) administration, the number of days of ovarian stimulation during an IVF cycle, and the number of oocyte retrievals that an animal had undergone all influenced IVF cycle outcomes. Higher serum progesterone levels at cycle start were negatively correlated with the likelihood of fertilized eggs progressing to the cleavage stage of embryo development. Additionally, a shorter duration of ovarian stimulation (ranging 7 to 14 days of medication) coupled with a GnRH antagonist correlated with an increased percentage of fertilized eggs. We observed a trend that a shorter hormonal stimulation cycle length was associated with a higher percentage of embryos reaching the cleavage stage. The optimization of stimulation cycle protocol and embryology has led to a high percentage of implantation after embryo transfer regardless of whether the embryo was fresh or cryopreserved. These findings suggest that shorter IVF cycles and a progesterone level <10 ng/mL at cycle start were correlated with an increased likelihood of a cleavage stage embryo development.

papers.title: Impact of acoustic property uncertainty on transcranial ultrasound simulation
papers.abstract: Subject-specific simulations of wave propagation are commonly used to plan and report acoustic and thermal exposure during transcranial ultrasound (TUS) interventions. Their accuracy depends on acoustic and thermal tissue property assumptions, including sound speed, density, and attenuation. Reported property measurements vary widely across the literature, precluding consensus point estimates for simulation. How this property uncertainty affects estimated exposure has not been quantified. We compile literature-based bounds for seven acoustic and thermal properties of skull and brain tissue and assess their individual impact on simulated intensity and temperature rise using two independent simulation platforms (PRESTUS/k-Wave and BabelBrain). Variations in skull attenuation and absorption produced the largest outcome uncertainty: peak intensity in the brain varied roughly threefold across the reported range of skull attenuation alone, while absorption most strongly affected temperature rise within the skull. The direction of each parameter's effect was consistent across platforms and, with one exception, across skull thickness. This allowed bounds to be combined into setups that bracket transmission and temperature rise. Compared to these extremes, default property sets of three simulation toolboxes (k-Plan, BabelBrain, PRESTUS) yielded similar brain intensity but divergent skull heating, driven mainly by differing assumptions on skull absorption and heat capacity. These results indicate that uncertainty in skull acoustic properties is a major source of variability in TUS exposure estimates, and that refined measurements of these properties, together with explicit reporting of exposure uncertainty, are needed to support safe, effective, and reproducible transcranial ultrasound planning.

papers.title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.

papers.title: Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM): An open-source tool for the harmonisation and analysis of batch effects in MRI-derived measures.
papers.abstract: Technical differences between scanners, acquisition protocols, machine hardware and processing pipelines can introduce systematic variation into MRI-derived measures. Numerous harmonisation methods have been developed to reduce these effects. However, validation of these methods is often performed using different criteria depending on the method itself, the datasets used and the study design. Consequently, determining whether harmonisation is required, selecting an appropriate method and establishing whether or not technical variation has been sufficiently removed without compromising biological signal remain challenging. In this manuscript, we introduce Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM), an open-source Python toolbox for diagnosing batch effects, applying harmonisation and evaluating harmonisation performance in cross-sectional and repeated-measures settings. DHARM is user-friendly, comes with GUI-based and command-line interfaces, and has graphical reporting. It provides standardised reporting workflows combining complementary measures of batch-associated differences in feature location, scale, empirical distributions, covariance and multivariate structure, together with measures assessing preservation of biological covariate effects and repeated-measures consistency. The framework includes several established harmonisation approaches, but its evaluation workflow is method-agnostic: users can also supply data harmonised using external or newly developed methods and benchmark their outputs using the same common set of diagnostics. We demonstrate DHARM using multisite cross-sectional MRI measures from UK Biobank, Cam-CAN and OxBAC as well as travelling-heads data from the ON-Harmony dataset. Across the cross-sectional datasets, harmonisation substantially reduced additive batch effects, while residual differences in variance and empirical distributions varied between methods. Multivariate diagnostics further demonstrated that reduction of batch-associated structure can coexist with preservation or increased detectability of biologically relevant variation. In the repeated-measures example, harmonisation reduced batch-associated and within-subject variability, while broadly preserving subject-level and biological relationships. DHARM provides a reproducible framework for diagnosing batch effects, applying different harmonisation methods and evaluating harmonisation as a multi-criteria problem rather than relying on a single measure of success. By jointly characterising technical variation and preservation of biologically meaningful information, DHARM can support dataset- and objective-specific selection, benchmarking and validation of harmonisation strategies.

papers.title: Fast rate coding in heterogeneous spiking networks
papers.abstract: A network of spiking neurons is said to operate in the rate coding regime if its dynamics can be accurately described by a continuous rate network. But how can discrete spike-based communication between neurons give rise to continuous rate-based dynamics? Computational studies showing that heterogeneous spiking networks can approximate the dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a special case of rate network, assume that spikes are approximately Poisson or that network dynamics are slow. Here, we show that neither assumption is necessary: heterogeneous networks of non-Poisson neurons can produce fast rate-based dynamics. To demonstrate this, we show that signal transmission in feedforward networks of integrate-and-fire-type neurons can be described by a history-dependent rate network that is asymptotically exact as network size grows, even if heterogeneity persists, while linear-nonlinear rate networks fail. By providing a constructive model of fast rate coding in heterogeneous networks, this work lays the foundation for extending rate-based analyses of neural recordings beyond the assumption of slow dynamics or Poisson rate codes.

papers.title: Tropical Peatlands as Hotspots of Hidden Arcellinida Diversity: Insights from Maludam National Park, Borneo (Sarawak, Malaysia)
papers.abstract: Recent investigations on tropical peatlands have shown their extremely high efficiency as carbon sinks, far beyond better studied boreal bogs. The microbial diversity found in those ecosystems, as well as their corresponding ecological and metabolic processes, are just starting to be revealed, and differ considerably from high latitudes systems. However, these efforts have been concentrated almost exclusively towards prokaryotes and fungi, leaving protist communities virtually unknown. Arcellinida (testate amoebae) are well acknowledged to play an important role in boreal and temperate peatland ecology by driving microbial community composition as top predators, but also as nutrient recyclers and carbon fixers. Yet, to our knowledge, no community-level study has addressed their diversity and its drivers in tropical peatlands. In this study, we surveyed Arcellinida communities' diversity across five functionally distinct vegetation-hydrological zones situated along a hydrological transect in a coastal tropical peatland in the Maludam National Park, Malaysia. Taxonomic composition of Arcellinida communities, characterized by a high diversity of Trigonopyxis-related taxa, indicated fundamental differences in diversity and community composition from extratropical ecosystems. Species richness was significantly higher in the zones with developed understory vegetation. Furthermore, the composition of diversity varied significantly among vegetation-hydrological zones. Altogether, this study shows unique Arcellinida communities in a Southeastern Asian peatland and suggests the importance of vegetation-hydrological characteristics for protist diversity.

papers.title: Submembrane geography dictates GPCR signalling compartmentation and physiological function
papers.abstract: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are key mediators of intercellular signalling and targets for the vast majority of current therapeutics. Numerous biochemical and biophysical studies have uncovered that individual GPCRs activated at different subcellular locations can mediate distinct functional effects due to compartmentalization of the downstream second messengers in subcellular nanodomains. However, the reasons why a single receptor subtype activated at the same subcellular compartment such as plasma membrane leads to various functional responses have remained poorly understood. Here, we used beta1-adrenergic receptor and cardiomyocytes as classical examples of a therapeutically relevant GPCR and highly compartmentalized cell, to study communication between membrane receptors and subcellular cAMP nanodomains based on a combination of nanoscale scanning ion conductance microscopy assisted local receptor activation with Foerster resonance energy transfer based live cell imaging of the cAMP pathway. Unexpectedly, this approach revealed that beta1-adrenoceptors located in cardiomyocyte T-tubular membrane are strongly coupled to the regulation of cardiac contractility, whereas receptors residing in the outer non-tubular membrane preferentially engage nuclear nanodomains linked to hypertrophy. This unique mechanism of spatially segregated signalling was maintained in failing rodent and human hearts, indicating that it is conserved across species and preserved in disease. Finally, we explored potential therapeutic targeting of this mechanism by generating submembrane-specific beta-blockers acting exclusively at the outer non-tubular membrane. These improved compounds could ameliorate hypertrophy and cardiac remodeling without reducing contractility in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings uncover an unexpected level of spatial organization of GPCR signaling within the same subcellular compartment and show that not only its identity but also its submembrane location determines cellular signaling and functional response engaged by the same GPCR.

papers.title: Sedimentary ancient DNA analysis from the Iron Age courtyard and cooking pit site of Rodskjaer in Troms, Northern Norway
papers.abstract: Courtyard sites, which are Iron Age structures unique to Norway, are often associated with cooking pit fields suggesting feasting practices, but little is known about the main purpose of these sites. To address this, a framework for sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) metabarcoding sampling was undertaken at the site of Rodskjaer, northern Norway. Of the 63 sediment samples from cooking pits, fire pits, a hearth, a fireplace, the natural shell-sand and topsoil, 52 successfully detected plant and animal sedaDNA. The plant diversity was high with 41-100 taxa. SedaDNA identified archaeologically significant taxa that were not detected by other methods, including Avena (oats), Quercus (oak), Equus (horse), and Salmo salar (salmon). Additionally, from inter-sample comparison, and with reference to worm sedaDNA we identified the archaeological contexts that were affected by partial bioturbation and root penetration that restricted interpretation of spatial or temporal differences in use of these features. This pioneering study shows the importance of taking many samples from modern and natural sediments as well as using multi-proxy analysis when conducting sedaDNA metabarcoding studies at open-air archaeological sites. If these factors are taken into consideration, sedaDNA from cooking pits can be a valuable resource for investigating uses of courtyard and cooking pit field sites.

papers.title: Assessing reinforcement learning and vigor with an online decision-making battery
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning and vigor are two fundamental aspects of decision-making modulated by dopamine. Although vigor is highly relevant for mood disorders, it has been overlooked by previous batteries characterizing decision-making abilities. We developed a test battery with two RL tasks (RL/working memory, go/no-go task) and two vigor tasks (physical effort discounting, foraging task) and administered it to an online community sample (N = 162). We used computational modeling and factor analysis to identify two factors reflecting RL and vigor. The RL factor reflected participants' general decision-making ability, while vigor corresponded to a motivational propensity to obtain rewards. Both factors demonstrated moderately strong test-retest reliability (ICC(2,1) = .65 and .67, respectively) over a one-to-two-week interval. Moreover, both factors were meaningfully related to self-report scales. The RL and vigor factors were negatively and positively associated with mania, respectively, although further analyses revealed that vigor was not fully independent of RL. Neither factor was significantly associated with depression symptoms. Collectively, we present preliminary evidence that vigor may represent a separate factor from RL in line with the putative dopamine hypothesis, paving the way for future longitudinal assessments of RL and vigor in mood disorders.

papers.title: Single Molecule Diffusion Studies Reveal Rapid Translations Across Target Membrane Surfaces for both p40Phox PX domain and Class III PI3K VPS34 Complex 1, the Autophagy Lipid Kinase
papers.abstract: Single molecule analyses are providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms by which peripheral membrane proteins approach and translate across a target bilayer surface before stable docking. Here we compare and contrast the translational movements of four diffusers on a representative supported lipid bilayer: (i) the fluorescent lipid LRB-(DO)PE, (ii) the G-protein Rab1A anchored to (DO)PE; (iii) the PI(3)P sensor p40Phox PX domain, and (iv) the autophagy lipid kinase VPS34 Complex 1. The latter enzyme is a Class III PI-3-Kinase and its unusual architecture exhibits two distinct membrane-docking "feet" unique to Class III PI3Ks. Notably, the membrane contact surfaces of the PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase each possess multiple positive charges suitable for electrostatic interactions with their anionic target membrane. The present single molecule tracking studies reveal that both the fluorescent lipid and the lipid-anchored G protein Rab1A exhibit 2-dimensional translation typical of simple lipid diffusion in the bilayer. Single molecule density measurements indicate both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit significantly reduced membrane docking when the bilayer negative charge is decreased, confirming the importance of their protein-bilayer electrostatic interactions. Single molecule tracking studies reveal that both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit hopping movements across the bilayer surface during their initial bilayer contacts, yielding a significantly higher frequency of long range displacements than allowed by lipid 2-D diffusion. After transitioning from hopping to a stable bilayer-docked state, both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit 2-D diffusion slower than lipid diffusion indicating the appearance of increased frictional drag against the bilayer due to new protein-bilayer contacts.
