Using pooled NHANES 2011-2014, we then examined, at the individual level, how reported TBI history among US adults aged 40 years and older varied by income, education, health insurance and food security, and whether dietary differences between adults with and without a TBI history persisted after socio-economic adjustment. The age-standardised TBI disability rate was almost twice as high in the high SDI quintile as in the low SDI quintile (113.68 versus 57.55 per 100,000 in 2023), a gap essentially unchanged since 1990. Moderate or severe injuries accounted for 72.5% of the TBI disability burden in the high SDI quintile versus 84.0-84.6% in the other four quintiles, rising in every quintile between 1990 and 2023. Among US adults, reported TBI history rose with educational attainment (11.9% below high school versus 17.3% above) and was most common in very food-insecure households (23.4%; adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.39-2.09); income showed no unadjusted gradient but a negative association after mutual adjustment. Unadjusted dietary differences between adults with and without a TBI history largely attenuated after socio-economic adjustment, with only fibre density remaining marginally lower (-0.35 g/1,000 kcal, 95% confidence interval -0.64 to -0.06). The moderate or severe share of the disability burden is a tractable, mortality-free monitoring indicator for injury prevention, and nutritional risk among food-insecure TBI survivors warrants clinical attention.

papers.title: Genetic diversity and population structure of Ethiopian taro Colocasia esculenta (L.) Schott) as revealed by SSR markers
papers.abstract: Abstract Taro (Colocasia esculenta (L.) Schott) is an important root and tuber crop that contributes to food security and livelihoods, but its genetic diversity remains poorly characterized in Ethiopia. This study assessed Ethiopian taro genetic diversity and population structure using simple sequence repeat (SSR) markers. We analyzed 119 accessions, 79 collected from farmers fields and 40 from the Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute (EBI), representing three regional populations: South Ethiopia Regional State (SERS), South West Ethiopia Peoples Regional State (SWEPRS), and Oromia. Fifteen polymorphic SSR markers produced 199 reproducible polymorphic loci, with 100% polymorphism. Polymorphism information content (PIC) ranged from 0.300 to 0.888 (mean 0.583). Diversity based on scored binary marker states was relatively low, with a mean effective number of alleles (Ne) of 1.077 and expected heterozygosity (He) of 0.066. Across populations, He ranged from 0.047 to 0.061, and the percentage of polymorphic loci ranged from 37.14% to 82.57%. Analysis of molecular variance showed that 98% of molecular variation occurred within populations and 2% among populations. Genetic differentiation ({Phi}PT, proportion of molecular variation among populations) was weak but significant ({Phi}PT = 0.016, P = 0.016). Principal coordinate analysis, neighbor-joining (NJ), and unweighted pair-group method with arithmetic mean (UPGMA) clustering showed extensive overlap among accessions and no clear geographic structuring. Bayesian clustering identified two groups as the strongest partition according to the {Delta}K criterion, but substantial admixture occurred, and groups did not correspond clearly to geographic populations. Despite relatively low diversity at individual scored loci, all 119 accessions had unique multilocus genotypes, indicating high multilocus genotypic diversity. Most molecular variation occurred within rather than among regional populations, potentially reflecting planting-material exchange and predominantly clonal propagation. These findings provide a basis for conserving, characterizing, and utilizing Ethiopian taro germplasm in crop improvement.

papers.title: Stochastic and Heritable Responses in Cell-Size Regulation and Survival to pH Stress in C. glutamicum
papers.abstract: Bacterial survival in fluctuating environments depends on the ability of individual cells to maintain physiological homeostasis under stress, yet how single cells recover from transient pH fluctuations remains poorly understood. We tracked the cell-size dynamics and survival of Corynebacterium glutamicum cells exposed to short, strong acid (pH 4, 20 min) or alkaline (pH 11, 15 min) pulses. Acid stress considerably increases the size added during the stress cycle, whereas alkaline stress increases it only modestly. Nevertheless, surviving cells maintain their division strategy and restore size homeostasis in the next cycle. Coordination between relatives is short-lived: sister cells have similar cell-cycle durations after stress, but durations become uncorrelated once the last division shared by two cells precedes the stress by more than about 1.5 generations. Survival of acid stress favors larger cells and is largely stochastic, with no detectable lineage heritability. In contrast, survival of alkaline stress favors smaller cells and is transiently heritable: co-survival probability remains high among relatives separated by up to two generations. These findings provide insight into pH survival in C. glutamicum and present statistical methods to study cell-size regulation and survival under transient, severe environmental fluctuations.

papers.title: LOTUS: lineage-aware optimal transport reconstructs continuous clonal fate dynamics
papers.abstract: Destructive sampling in single-cell sequencing obscures ancestor-descendant relationships, limiting the continuous reconstruction of cell-fate dynamics. Here we present Lineage-aware optimal transport for unbalanced single-cell dynamics (LOTUS), a framework that integrates time-resolved transcriptomic snapshots with clonal lineage information from engineered barcodes or endogenous T cell receptor clonotypes. LOTUS couples clone-level optimal transport with neural unbalanced transport to model continuous cellular state change, population growth and clonal propagation under lineage-consistent constraints. In branching simulations, LOTUS reduced lineage-inconsistent transport relative to benchmark methods, lowering off-target routing from 4.94-14.84% to 1.10%. On LARRY lineage-barcode scRNA-seq of hematopoiesis, LOTUS reconstructed branching trajectories, improved early neutrophil-monocyte fate-boundary prediction, and inferred multi-fate progenitors and fate-biased meta-clones, linking their distinct fate potentials to inferred epigenetic priming. On CellTagging scRNA-seq of fibroblast reprogramming, it distinguished reprogrammed from failed trajectories and prioritized fate-associated perturbation genes. In longitudinal scRNA-seq and TCR-seq of malaria-responsive memory (CD45RA-) CD4+ T cells, it preserved endogenous clonotype structure and reconstructed TR1 dynamics and regulatory networks. LOTUS thus converts lineage-resolved single-cell snapshots into interpretable, continuous models of fate dynamics and their regulatory programs.

papers.title: A Physics-Constrained Marcus-Theory Optimization Framework Restores Parameter Identifiability in Deep-Pocket Oncogenic Drug Kinetics: A KRAS G12C and STAT3 Case Study
papers.abstract: Background: More than 90% of drug candidates fail preclinically, partly because empirical dose-response models such as the Hill equation ignore microenvironmental effects inside the deep binding pockets of targets such as mutant KRAS G12C and STAT3. Bulk water is hypothesized to raise the reorganization energy (lambda_ext). Objective: To develop a physics-constrained framework, the Cluchagues-Marcus Framework, that links local dielectric permittivity to ligand-pocket kinetics, and to determine which constraints restore parameter identifiability. Methods: Non-adiabatic Marcus kinetics were coupled to a Hill-type equation derived from a steady-state scheme, and water exclusion was modeled as a collapse of epsilon_local from 80.4 to 2.0. Pocket radii and published reference constants were used for two pockets (KRAS G12C, PDB 6UT0; STAT3 SH2, PDB 6NJS). Three propositions were proved and checked with synthetic data and a global sensitivity analysis, and the identifiability result was numerically stress-tested on real napabucasin viability curves from 701 cancer cell lines. Results: Water exclusion lowered lambda_ext by 90%. At dG = -0.10 eV, k_C rose 8.0-fold (KRAS) and 3.6-fold (STAT3). Acceleration occurs if and only if |dG| < sqrt(lambda_s x lambda_u). The model has exactly two non-identifiable parameter directions: fixing nu_eff removes one and anchoring K_d removes the other. In real curves, fits were unchanged by the K_d anchor (SSE change < 10^-7 %) while the fitted k_off,q varied by 3.5 log units, as predicted. Conclusions: A dissociation-constant anchor makes the framework identifiable. The real-data stress test is not biological validation of the dielectric mechanism, which requires experiments.

papers.title: BioResearchBench: 50 Long Horizon Biological Research Tasks
papers.abstract: AI models are used in biology research to study disease mechanisms, discover potential treatments, analyze experimental data, troubleshoot problems, and plan next steps. Useful assistance depends on working with data in various scientific formats, interpreting results, and deciding what to test next. We present BioResearchBench, a benchmark of 50 research questions developed by PhD biologists drawing on their deep research expertise to reflect realistic problems encountered in their fields. Questions were refined through expert review and iterative model testing. The collection spans 10 diverse biology subdomains and includes sequencing data, proteomic measurements, microscopy images, assay readouts, and clinical datasets. We compared recorded outcomes and examined model responses in depth across the 50 tasks on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Meta Muse Wonder, and SpaceXSI Grok 4.7. Success across our benchmark was 18% for Claude Opus 5.5, 13% for Gemini 4 Argon, 11% for Meta Muse Wonder, 4% for GPT-6 Astra, and 4% for Grok 4.7. These results describe a deliberately challenging collection selected through expert review and model testing. Despite low whole task success, the selected responses met most rubric requirements on average: the average fraction of criteria missed ranged from 18% to 32% across models. Across models, the proportion of eligible tasks with at least one category failure was highest in computation and data handling (66.9% failure), followed by uncertainty and identification (55.3% failure), reporting and completeness (54.7% failure), biological interpretation (39.0% failure), controls and causal claims (37.2% failure), and choosing the next experiment or decision (31.0% failure). Gemini 4 Argon had the highest proportion of reviewed tasks without a recorded category failure in computation and data handling (45% success) and biological interpretation (69% success). Claude Opus 5.5 led in controls and causal claims (72% success) and choosing the next experiment or decision (75% success). GPT-6 Astra led in uncertainty and identification (56% success) which included judging the precision of estimates and recognizing when measurements could not distinguish between biological explanations. GPT-6 Astra and Meta Muse Wonder tied for the highest proportion of answers with no recorded omissions or reporting failures (51% success). Five case studies presented here show how top AI models can perform many analytical steps correctly yet misinterpret what results signify. For example, some answers described cells as fully recovered when oxygen consumption improved even though mitochondrial membrane potential and cell number remained below control levels. These model answers therefore overstated the extent of cell recovery. Other answers incorrectly called a protein a direct microRNA target, although the experiment had not tested whether the microRNA acted directly on its mRNA or affected it through another process. In a protein turnover task, some model answers misestimated protein half-lives because they did not account for the gradual labeling of amino acids used to make new proteins. These model errors can lead researchers to pursue the wrong explanation even when individual analytical steps are completed correctly. This matters for major scientific goals such as drug discovery, where progress depends on choosing useful experiments and tools, interpreting unexpected results, troubleshooting failed approaches, and deciding which direction is most worth pursuing. Evaluating AI research assistance therefore requires checking whether its explanations, conclusions, and proposed experiments follow from the data and experimental design. These cases highlight continuing challenges in scientific reasoning for frontier AI models: bringing together different types of biological data, analyzing them with appropriate tools and databases, and using the results to draw appropriate conclusions and guide the next steps in research. The observed errors suggest training priorities in data analysis, biological interpretation, and experimental judgment and motivate evaluations that follow researchers and models through iterative scientific work.

papers.title: Dog and Human Brains Represent Human Emotional Bodies with Asymmetric Encoding of Happiness and Anger
papers.abstract: Dogs live in an environment rich in human emotional signals, yet most of what we know about their visual emotion perception comes from faces. Our study shifts this focus to the body, a central channel of emotional communication in dogs and a source of social information when they observe human emotional expressions. Here, we investigated how the brains of dogs and humans represent emotions conveyed by human bodies. Using fMRI, we examined 24 awake companion dogs and 40 humans viewing videos of bodily happiness, anger, and neutral actions, alongside phase-scrambled controls. Both dogs and humans showed occipito-temporal sensitivity to human bodies, with emotional modulation in the right caudal suprasylvian gyrus in dogs and the right extrastriate body area in humans. Multivariate response patterns also differentiated bodily happiness from anger in both dogs and humans. Emotion-specific RSA further showed a similar representational asymmetry: happiness showed consistent category-specific neural patterns, whereas anger showed no comparable category effect but could still be differentiated from happiness and neutral actions. Despite this shared representational asymmetry, the anatomical distribution differed, with happiness represented across more distributed regions in dogs, whereas anger differentiation involved a broader cortical network in humans. No corresponding effects were found for phase-scrambled controls. Together, these findings provide the first direct neural evidence of how the dog brain represents affective information conveyed by human bodies, while leaving open whether emotions expressed by conspecific bodies evoke similar neural representations. More broadly, our results suggest similar representational relationships between bodily emotions in dogs and humans, despite differences in the anatomical distribution of these effects, while highlighting the role of human bodily expressions in dogs' social cognition, and advancing our understanding of the neural basis of emotional communication across species.

papers.title: A phase decoder for reconstructing missing muscle activity
papers.abstract: Upper-limb assistive devices are commonly controlled with electromyographic (EMG) signals, but nerve injury, muscle loss, or practical limits on electrode placement can leave only a few usable signals, which constrains the decoding of intended movements. Here, we introduce a decoder that reconstructs missing muscle activations from sparse EMGs using a two-stage real-time approach: (1) estimating ongoing movement phase from available signals, and (2) retrieving corresponding muscle activations from a library of pre-recorded muscle activity templates. In proof-of-concept tests, neurologically intact participants (N=4) performed object-transfer tasks under simulated denervation conditions. The decoder accurately estimated movement phase (median root-mean-square error [RMSE] <0.17 of movement duration) and reconstructed missing muscle activations (RMSE 0.08-0.34; correlation up to 0.97) within ~2 ms, in a previously unseen participant. The results indicate that template based reconstruction could leverage sparse EMG for low latency control of assistive technology.

papers.title: A generative network model reveals hierarchical structural memory guiding post-mitotic 3D genome inheritance
papers.abstract: How three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is reestablished after mitosis to preserve gene regulatory programs and cell identity remains unresolved. We asked whether mitotic chromosome architecture contributes to cellular memory by preserving structural information while maintaining the flexibility required for cellular adaptation. Here we introduce HiCONA, a generative Bayesian framework that infers hierarchical genome organization and quantifies the structural contribution of individual interactions through an Entropy Impact Score. HiCONA resolves genome organization across multiple scales, revealing structure-defining interaction patterns underlying chromatin architecture, independently of experimental modality. We identify structurally impactful chromatin interactions retained during mitosis delineating distinct trajectories of post-mitotic genome reassembly. These mitotically preserved interactions are enriched for active, transcriptionally competent regulatory elements, consistent with a cis-encoded architectural memory subsequently remodeled by trans-acting regulators. Together, our findings suggest that molecular information retained on mitotic chromosomes guides structural trajectories, providing an architectural basis for epigenetic memory and post-mitotic genome inheritance.

papers.title: A comparison of two culture and three sequencing methods for detection of the urobiome
papers.abstract: Standard urine culture (SUC), the clinical reference method, is optimized for fast-growing aerobes and misses much of the urinary microbiota. Enhanced culture and sequencing methods have rarely been compared on the same specimens. We compared five methods (SUC, expanded quantitative urine culture [EQUC], short-read V4 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read near full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and PCR-free long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing) on parallel aliquots of urine from pregnant participants screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Of 98 cultured samples, 98 (100.0%) were EQUC-positive while 85 (86.7%) SUC-positive. EQUC detected 102 species, but SUC only detected 41. Short-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and shotgun sequencing were positive for 188/188, 186/188 and 139/139 samples, detecting 195, 69 and 528 species, respectively. In the 79 samples positive by EQUC and all three sequencing methods, sequencing profiles resembled each other more than culture profiles, and SUC captured only a subset of taxa detected by every other method. Shotgun sequencing gave the broadest taxonomic coverage and was the only sequencing method to identify Escherichia coli to the species level. With EQUC, it outperformed both 16S sequencing methods in detecting Gardnerella vaginalis and distinguishing Lactobacillus species, and it resolved six Gardnerella species, three detected by no other method. Long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing gave the most confident amplicon-based species assignments, whereas culture better recovered Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species. No single method was best across all endpoints, but long-read shotgun metagenomics provided the broadest species-level view. Method choice should match the research or clinical question; outcome-based studies are needed to establish clinical utility.

papers.title: A Comparison and Validation of BIDS Apps for Preprocessing of UCB-J PET data
papers.abstract: Background Preprocessing of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) data can be performed in many different ways and often involves manual steps, resulting in reduced comparability across analyses and pipelines. Apps working on PET data organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) seek to automate preprocessing, enabling the application of standardized pipelines that increase comparability and reproducibility. In this study, two of these apps were validated against in-house software. Methods Data were acquired in-house from 14 subjects who received placebo in a randomized controlled clinical trial and underwent two PET measurements using the radioligand [11C]UCB-J. Preprocessing was performed with two BIDS Apps, PETPrep and PICNIC, as well as an in-house software. Arterial blood data were processed using Bloodstream, and [11C]UCB-J total distribution volume (VT) values were calculated using a 1-tissue compartment model using kinfitr. Results VT values for all 9 regions of interest were highly consistent across tools with estimates of Intraclass Correlation Coefficients for consistency ranging between 0.94 and >0.99, although bias between tools measured as signed Percentage Difference was present, ranging from 0.1% - 10.2% depending on the region. Tools performed similarly on test-retest metrics. We observed a negative test-retest bias in [11C]UCB-J VT of unknown origin. Conclusion BIDS Apps produce reliable and consistent results when compared both with each other and with an in-house software optimized for processing and analysis of our in-house data. Region-dependant bias between tools warrants caution for direct comparison of VT between tools. The usage of these apps could enable better comparability across publications

papers.title: Follow-up availability and the robustness of immune transcriptomic recovery after myocardial infarction
papers.abstract: Background: Longitudinal blood transcriptomes describe immune changes after myocardial infarction, but later assays do not necessarily represent the population sampled at admission. We examined whether recovery summaries depend on observable selection and assumptions about unavailable assays. Methods: We reanalyzed official processed data from GSE59867, linking 111 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction across admission, discharge, one month, and six months. Seven fixed Hallmark programs were scored on a common 17,590-gene vocabulary using a bounded within-sample rank statistic. The primary endpoint was the six-month inflammatory-response score. We separated paired-completer change from the observed follow-up mean minus the entire baseline mean; fitted cross-fitted availability and outcome models; and evaluated full-support completion bounds and prespecified missing-mean scenarios. Artificial deletion tested estimators in the 83 observed six-month participants. GSE123342 provided unlinked marginal comparisons and explicitly conditional completion scenarios. Results: GSE59867 contained 101, 95, and 83 follow-up assays. At six months, inflammatory-response change was -0.00893 among paired completers and -0.00999 for the marginal contrast (95% participant-bootstrap interval -0.01217 to -0.00783). Augmented inverse-probability weighting gave -0.01004 (-0.01556 to -0.00727). The full-support completion interval was [-0.16460,0.08765], but eliminating the negative change required an unavailable-assay mean 4.42 observed-follow-up standard deviations above the observed mean. The primary direction remained negative throughout the prespecified {+/-}2-SD scenarios; interferon and coagulation directions were less stable. Under artificial outcome-dependent deletion, all evaluated estimators retained bias. The unlinked external cohort had 65 admission, 64 day-30, and 37 year-one MI assays; the year-one inflammatory contrast was -0.00459, with a conditional tipping shift of 1.70 SD. Conclusions: The observed inflammatory-response rank-score decline was stable to baseline-score adjustment and the prespecified {+/-}2-observed-SD missing-mean scenarios, while unrestricted completion did not identify its direction. Robustness varied across programs and data settings. These findings concern relative transcriptomic scores and assay availability, not clinical recovery, survival, or intervention efficacy.

papers.title: How multilevel competition drives cooperation in stigmergic systems
papers.abstract: Cooperation through stigmergy relies on reliable information left in a shared environment, yet individuals may benefit from misleading others. How competition within and between groups shapes this conflict remains unclear. We investigated this question using the Stigmer Game, in which human participants interact exclusively through ratings that modify a shared informational environment, under seven payment rules. Participants were classified as collaborators, neutrals or defectors. Between-group competition produced the highest collaboration, whereas within-group competition favoured defection. Adding between-group competition partly restored cooperation despite continued rivalry within groups, although this effect depended on reward distribution. A quantitative analysis showed that within-group and rank-based competitive pressures best described differences in behavioural composition across payment rules. A genetic algorithm further revealed distinct stationary strategy compositions under each payment rule that were largely independent of initial conditions and robust to perturbations. These results reproduced the opposing effects of between-group and within-group competition observed experimentally, while highlighting differences between immediate behavioural responses and the strategy distributions favoured by each rule's incentive structure. Defectors remained present under the mutation regime, illustrating the vulnerability of shared information to exploitation. Our findings show how the organization of competitive incentives shapes cooperation and information reliability in decentralized collective systems.

papers.title: Multimodal longitudinal prediction of alcohol-use trajectories in adolescents and young adults: Social context, real-life social affective benefit, and fronto-striatal involvement
papers.abstract: Escalating alcohol use during adolescence and young adulthood confers substantial risk for later substance misuse and adverse mental health outcomes, yet the factors that determine early drinking trajectories remain poorly understood. Here, we examined alcohol use across social, affective, and neural domains in a cohort of 378 community-based young drinkers using a combination of longitudinal phenotyping, ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and functional neuroimaging. Across different levels of analysis, higher baseline alcohol consumption (standard drinks per week) was associated with immediate substance-use social context, greater social-affective benefit in daily life, and heightened engagement of the fronto-striatal reward circuitry. In a one-year longitudinal follow-up, individual social-affective benefit and substance-related social environmental factors showed the strongest predictive value for drinking trajectories in a follow-up of 219 individuals after one year. Our findings identify key social and neural reward-related determinants of youth drinking behavior, informing the development of evidence-based risk detection and prevention measures.

papers.title: An LRH-1 agonist reverses hepatic metabolic dysfunction in obesity
papers.abstract: Liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1; NR5A2) is a nuclear receptor that controls metabolic gene programs important for liver health. Here, we address two challenges with dissecting ligand-driven LRH-1 metabolism in vivo. First, we generate ME610, a potent LRH-1 agonist with favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Second, we engineer Nr5a2humLBD mice, edited to recapitulate the ligand response of the human receptor. ME610 dose-dependently induces LRH-1 target genes and reduces triglycerides in livers of Nr5a2humLBD mice. In a mouse model of diet-induced obesity (DIO), ME610 dramatically improves insulin sensitivity and reduces liver fat. Multi-omics integration of transcriptomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics data demonstrates a coordinated reversal of DIO-induced hepatic metabolic stress via changes in lipid, amino acid, and energy metabolism, with peroxisomal lipid metabolism emerging as a central process correlated to efficacy. These studies uncover new pathways through which LRH-1 regulates metabolism and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of synthetic LRH-1 agonists in obesity-associated metabolic diseases.

papers.title: Material-driven fibronectin assembly enables low-dose BMP-2 to regenerate structurally mature bone in critical-sized load-bearing defects
papers.abstract: Bone grafts for critical-sized load-bearing defects are usually judged by how much bone forms, and rarely by whether that bone is structurally and mechanically competent. Here, degradable ceramic monetites coated with poly(ethyl acrylate) (PEA) and functionalised with fibronectin (FN) and rhBMP-2 at 10-25 g/mL, 60-150-fold below the approved clinical concentration, are assessed across length scales. MicroCT showed that only monetites functionalised with rhBMP-2 bridged the defect, with a significant increase in new bone volume in both the monetite vicinity and the whole defect volume. In contrast, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) functionalisation significantly reduced bone formation relative to FN, showing that the identity of the adhesion cue, and not merely its presence, determines the outcome. Monetite degradation and increased interconnected porosity favoured bone ingrowth and produced a continuous interface between monetite and new bone. The multiscale analyses of quantitative polarised light microscopy, SAXS and nanoindentation show that PEA-coated monetites functionalised with FN and 25 g/mL rhBMP-2 promoted structurally and mechanically more mature bone, with a hierarchical organisation and local mechanical properties approaching those of native cortical tissue. In the bridged region this group recapitulated the preferential collagen fibre orientation of native cortical bone and reached an elastic modulus and hardness that were not statistically distinguishable from it, although mineral particles throughout the regenerated tissue remained thicker and less aligned than in cortical bone. Synchrotron microCT in an ovine model extended these findings to a clinically relevant scale, supporting the translational potential of the system. Taken together, these findings position PEA-coated monetites functionalised with FN and low-dose rhBMP-2 as a strategy for the structural and functional regeneration of large bone defects.

papers.title: Transplantation of human iPSC-derived retinal cells in the cone-dominant Northern tree shrew
papers.abstract: Abstract: Purpose: To characterize the transplantation and survival of photoreceptors generated from human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids in the Northern tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri, TS). Methods: TS eyes were injected with retinal cells dissociated from GFP-expressing hiPSC-derived retinal organoids (12 animals; n=22 eyes). 15 eyes had prior damage induced by either experimental retinal detachment (n=11) or ATP-induced retinal damage (n=4), and seven eyes were undamaged. Retinal organoids were treated with Notch pathway inhibitor 2 days before transplant. TS retinal structure and cellular details were assessed post-transplantation for up to 8 weeks using scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and adaptive optics SLO (AOSLO). Histological analysis was done at the end of the experiment. Results: Cell transplants in eyes treated with a simple immunosuppression treatment failed to survive for more than 2 weeks (n=10 eyes). Robust cell survival was observed in the eyes treated with a complex immunosuppression cocktail for up to 8 weeks (n=12 eyes). The transplanted cells were confirmed to be subretinally located using OCT imaging and the cell fate was confirmed to be human photoreceptors by histology. Finally, AOSLO imaging captured structures resembling photoreceptor inner segments. Conclusions: Our results demonstrate survival of transplanted cells using a species-specific immunosuppression treatment. Future studies should aim to explore the long-term survival and function of the transplanted cells.

papers.title: FastaGuard: FASTA preflight QC for modern bioinformatics pipelines
papers.abstract: Summary: FastaGuard is a streaming, explainable FASTA preflight QC tool that validates assembly FASTA files, detects structural and composition red flags, and emits a versioned multi-format report with an explicit pipeline gate before expensive downstream analysis. We evaluated v1.1.0 in four analyses whose design was fixed before data collection. On 700 public NCBI assemblies the pipeline gate stopped 19.7% (1.9% weighted to the population), always on its high-N rule and mostly in scaffold-level genomes; the NCBI submission gate stopped 2.0%, and an independent recount confirmed every stop. Among 1,040 faults injected into real assemblies, the NCBI gate flagged 520 of 520 in 13 error classes (table2asn: 280 at error level) and blocked none of 120 benign changes. Across seven downstream tools, 46 of 182 defect cells failed and 12 altered the records without a warning, all in classes the pipeline gate blocks. Stopping a mismatched reference at the gate avoided about 54-62 s of mapping and sorting at a cost of 0.05-0.06 s. Availability and Implementation: Source code and documentation are freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/ehsanestaji/FastaGuard (release tag v1.1.0: https://github.com/ehsanestaji/FastaGuard/releases/tag/v1.1.0; archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23728753). Install via Bioconda (mamba install -c conda-forge -c bioconda fastaguard=1.1.0), BioContainers, or GitHub release binaries. Implemented in Rust; supported on Linux and macOS, including Bioconda builds for linux-64, linux-aarch64, osx-64, and osx-arm64. Contact: ehsan.estaji@umu.se; jianfeng.mao@umu.se Supplementary information: Supplementary Note (designs, all results, deviations from the pre-registered protocol); scripts, manifests and result tables at Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23729530.

papers.title: Topographic reference modelling of white matter hyperintensities across the adult lifespan
papers.abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are among the most common MRI findings in older adults. They are widely regarded as markers of brain aging and cerebral small-vessel disease, and associated with risk for cognitive decline, Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD), and stroke. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are typically interpreted by total lesion burden, but lesions with similar volumes can occupy different anatomical locations, potentially reflecting distinct pathological processes. Here we present voxelwise topographic reference modelling (vTRM), a framework for characterizing individual WMH masks against age- and sex-stratified frequency maps derived from cognitively unimpaired individuals. Using 42,469 FLAIR-derived lesion masks from twelve adult cohorts, we mapped population-level WMH spatial vulnerability, characterized age-related changes in its distribution across periventricular, lobar and arterial-territory compartments, and constructed paired percentile charts for lesion burden and spatial typicality. A quadrant-based classification defined by these two percentile dimensions revealed graded relationships with ADRD pathophysiology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, while identifying WMH patterns differentially associated with ageing-related, vascular and neurodegenerative processes among individuals with similar lesion volumes. These reference charts establish a benchmark for normative WMH ageing, enabling quantification of individual deviations from typical age-, sex- and burden-related patterns and identification of WMH phenotypes associated with vascular, neurodegenerative or mixed etiologies. The framework, together with a deployable 3D U-Net model trained on these data for automated WMH segmentation, is available through the Brain Lesion Analytics platform (https://brainlesionanalytics.org/).

papers.title: Genetically restricted human antibodies recognize a conserved β-hairpin in postfusion influenza hemagglutinin
papers.abstract: A public class of broadly protective, human antibodies (Abs) binds a conserved {beta}-hairpin exposed in the postfusion conformation of influenza virus hemagglutinin (HA). We here describe use of in vitro immunoassays and high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy analysis of Ab:HA complexes to explain the apparent genetic restriction of these Abs and the wide range of influenza A and B subtypes they recognize. We show that recognition of the {beta}-hairpin epitope requires 1) germline-encoded residues unique to certain alleles of the human immunoglobulin heavy chain gene IGHV1-2, 2) a short (<14-residue) HCDR3 to avoid steric clash with HA, and 3) several Ab light chain residues that are germline-encoded by various IGLV2-family genes or IGLV7-46. Despite the genetic restrictions, the capacity to make {beta}-hairpin Abs is widespread among humans. We recovered examples of these Abs from 14 genetically unrelated donors, and a previously reported analysis of the IGHV genotypes of ~2,500 individuals sampled from major ethnic populations estimates that >75% of people have the necessary IGHV1-2 alleles to make these Abs. We conclude that an immunogen that displays the {beta}-hairpin epitope might reliably elicit broadly protective influenza antibodies in most humans.

papers.title: Deep-intronic variants in USH2A: the importance of model selection in variant interpretation and pathogenicity assessment
papers.abstract: Interpreting splice-altering USH2A variants is challenging when these result in the alteration of splicing in only a fraction of transcripts. We investigated two deep-intronic USH2A variants from a single case, the inherited variant c.5573-834A>G and the de novo variant c.11047+345A>G, using a minigene splice assay and transcript analysis in patient-derived photoreceptor precursor cells and nasal epithelial cells. The minigene assay revealed the inclusion of a pseudoexon in the presence of the c.11047+345A>G variant, but did not reproduce previously reported aberrant splicing for c.5573-834A>G. In patient-derived cells, c.5573-834A>G resulted in the inclusion of a pseudoexon in part of the transcripts, whereas c.11047+345A>G did not result in detectable levels of aberrantly spliced transcripts. To assess the impact of residual wildtype transcripts on retinal function, we used the previously developed humanized ush2aPE40+M1 knock-in zebrafish model which allows the modeling of the impact of mixed wildtype and pseudoexon-containing ush2a transcripts. This model demonstrated that detectable levels of usherin expression are maintained even when only a fraction of wildtype transcripts lacking pseudoexon inclusion remain. Collectively, these findings advocate for a more nuanced classification of partially splice-altering USH2A variants. The mere presence of alternative transcripts should not be considered sufficient evidence for pathogenicity. Within this framework, data on the c.5573-834A>G variant do not support a (likely) pathogenic classification, and findings related to the c.11047+345A>G variant are consistent with a likely benign classification.

papers.title: CD40 ligand and IFN-γ induce proinflammatory activity and microglia-mediated neurodegeneration in human stem cell models
papers.abstract: The cluster of differentiation 40 (CD40)/CD40 ligand (CD40L) co-stimulatory pathway plays a critical role in the activation and regulation of immune networks involving both adaptive and innate immune cells. Dysregulation of this pathway has been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration driven by compartmentalized neuroinflammation within the central nervous system (CNS), sustained low-grade T cell infiltration at the blood-brain barrier, and T cell reactivation at CNS border tissues. CD40L-expressing T cells can activate CD40-expressing microglia, which are a critical effector cell that contribute to neurodegeneration in MS. However, the consequence of this functional interaction in the brain remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the combination of CD40L and interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a cytokine produced by activated T cells, induces a robust inflammatory response and cell death in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived microglia. Stimulation with CD40L elicited microglial clustering, morphological transformation, and robust release of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-), and IL-6. Anti-CD40L antibody treatment reversed both cell death and inflammatory response and partially normalized the associated transcriptional changes. Furthermore, using an hiPSC-derived tri-culture system comprising neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, we demonstrated that CD40L and IFN-{gamma} trigger microglia-dependent neuronal dysregulation and death. Anti-CD40L treatment substantially attenuated neuronal injury. Finally, transcriptomic enrichment analysis identified CD40L-mediated microglial gene expression signatures that correlated with CD40 expression in primary progressive MS brain tissue but not in the normal-appearing white matter of healthy controls. Collectively, these findings support a role for the microglial CD40/T cell CD40L axis in MS pathology and suggest CD40L blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy warranting further investigation.

papers.title: Individual differences in Game Transfer Phenomena are associated with creativity and positive schizotypy but not with perceptual priming
papers.abstract: Game Transfer Phenomena (GTP) refer to involuntary experience of video-game elements as part of gamers everyday perception, cognition, and behaviour. Although previous research has identified Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD), positive schizotypy, and spontaneous cognitions (e.g., mind-popping, daydreaming) as key predictors of GTP, the role of implicit memory processes and creativity remains unclear. The present study examined whether these cognitive processes are associated with GTP frequency while replicating established predictors such as IGD, involuntary cognitions, and schizotypal traits. A total of 85 video game players (53% males; Mage = 24.89, SD = 5.87) completed a word fragment completion task to assess individual differences in perceptual implicit memory (priming). To measure creativity, participants completed the Alternate Uses Task (AUT) as a measure of divergent thinking, and a free association task to estimate forward flow, a robust predictor of creative cognition. Results showed robust priming effects at the group level (M = .23, SD = .14), however, individual differences in perceptual priming were not associated with GTP frequency. In contrast, AUT scores were positively associated with GTP and contributed uniquely to its prediction. A hierarchical regression model explained 58.2% of the variance in GTP frequency, with IGD, daydreaming, and positive schizotypy as the strongest predictors, alongside hours played per session and AUT scores. These findings suggest that GTP may not be driven by domain-general perceptual implicit memory processes but may be more strongly linked to individual differences in spontaneous cognitions and conceptual associative priming processes.

papers.title: Improving real-time search through deep learning-enhanced fragment ion indexing
papers.abstract: The fragment ion indexed database searching approach enables highly efficient tandem mass spectrometry database searches, including real-time search workflows. However, the index can require tens of gigabytes of memory, often exceeding the free memory available on instrument acquisition computers running the search. This restricts the size of the searchable database, the variable modification space, and the number of searches that can run concurrently. To address this problem, we developed an index-pruning pipeline within the Comet database search tool using Carafe, a deep learning tool that predicts fragment ion intensities based on peptide sequences. In our approach, only fragment ion positions that are predicted to be observable are written in the index, eliminating entries that are unlikely to contribute to spectrum detection. We evaluated this approach on two search spaces in three index configurations to demonstrate that masking significantly reduced the number of fragment ion index entries and, consequently, peak search memory use. Masked searches were also faster than unmasked searches and identified a comparable number of peptide-spectrum matches. Because all prediction and masking steps are performed before searching, their cost is amortized across repeated, future searches of the same database and modification configuration, introducing no per-spectrum search overhead. The complete implementation is open source with an Apache license.

papers.title: Standard touchscreen test procedures shift circadian rhythms in mice: a modified protocol to minimize circadian confounds
papers.abstract: Touchscreen based cognitive testing for rodents offers considerable experimental benefits, including a semi automated battery approach and the use of appetitive rather than aversive reinforcement. However, food reward and touchscreen illumination introduce potential confounds, as both food and light can shift, entrain, or disrupt circadian rhythms, which in turn can affect learning and memory. The potential for the test apparatus to impact endogenous circadian rhythms is particularly problematic when probing relationships between sleep, circadian disruption, and cognitive performance. After observing phase shifting of circadian rhythms in nocturnal mice tested using standard touchscreen test procedures, which include testing during the active period (early lights off), we evaluated the relative contributions of the illuminated screen and the appetitive food reward. Our results indicate that light emitted by the touchscreen chambers is responsible for the circadian phase shifting effects, with standard screen conditions inducing a ~3.5 h phase delay in daily activity rhythms when training is conducted early in the dark period for 7 consecutive days. We then modified lighting in the test environment and the home cage to identify parameters that would minimize circadian shifting without impairing visual discrimination or performance on a widely used cognitive test (Trial Unique Nonmatching to Location, TUNL). From the 10 conditions tested, we offer specific recommendations for modifying touchscreen test protocols to minimize circadian confounds, without impacting task acquisition or performance.

papers.title: Cognitive reserve depends on cortical neurochemistry to predict memory after partner-inflicted brain injury
papers.abstract: Memory problems are commonplace following brain injury (BI). However, it remains unclear why some report memory problems while others do not, especially following repeated neurotrauma. Cognitive reserve has been widely hypothesized to account for this variation, but testing this account has yielded inconsistent results and proven difficult, likely as it requires a sample spanning a wide range of BI burden with concurrent neuroimaging and cognitive measurement. Here, we combined a wide range of cognitive assessments with measures of neuronal health using magnetic resonance spectroscopy across three brain regions in 62 women who had experienced physical intimate partner violence. Partner-inflicted BI counts ranged from 0 to 420, yet we found that the number of BIs alone did not explain the variance in memory outcomes. Among a small subset with high BI exposure ([≥]10 BIs; n = 11), BI count explained 5% of the variance in delayed recall, the primary memory outcome, whereas cognitive reserve, inferred from a measure of premorbid functioning, explained almost half (unadjusted in-sample associations). In the full cohort, cognitive reserve predicted memory only among the most heavily injured participants. In a separate model, cognitive reserve predicted memory only when creatine-referenced total N-acetylaspartate, a marker of neuronal health, was lower in the posterior cingulate gyrus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Ultimately, our findings provide behavioral and neurochemical evidence consistent with the cognitive reserve hypothesis and shed new light on why, despite a high burden of neurotrauma, memory may remain resilient.

papers.title: Dyskinesia induced by a dopamine 2 receptor-like agonist, but not a dopamine 1 receptor-like agonist, is blocked by sub-anesthetic ketamine
papers.abstract: L-DOPA remains the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease, but chronic administration is frequently complicated by L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Our prior work has established that sub-anesthetic ketamine can reduced LID acutely and has a long-lasting neuroplastic effect. This study tested whether low-dose ketamine reduces dyskinesia induced specifically by dopamine D2R-like or D1R-like receptor activation. Male Sprague Dawley rats were primed with daily L-DOPA to establish dyskinesia and then challenged with quinpirole, a D2R-like receptor agonist, or SKF-81297, a D1R-like receptor agonist, to induce abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs). After stable AIM baselines were established, animals received agonist plus vehicle or agonist plus ketamine. Limb, axial, and orolingual AIMs were scored on the acute treatment day (D0) and after washout on D4 and D7. Quinpirole and SKF-81297 reliably produced stable total LAO AIM scores following L-DOPA priming. Ketamine significantly reduced only quinpirole-induced, but not SKF-81297-induced, total AIMs compared with vehicle on D0, demonstrating an acute anti-dyskinetic effect. This reduction persisted after washout, with ketamine-treated animals continuing to show significantly lower AIMs on D4 and D7. Time-course analyses further showed reduced AIMs expression across the post-quinpirole observation period on D0 and at multiple time points on D7. These findings demonstrate that ketamine suppresses quinpirole-induced dyskinesia in L-DOPA-primed male rats and suggest that D2R-like receptor-mediated or indirect pathway-related mechanisms, but not direct pathway-related mechanisms, may contribute to ketamine's anti-dyskinetic effects. Together, these results extend prior work on ketamine by linking its sustained anti-dyskinetic effects to dyskinesia driven by D2R-like receptor stimulation in vivo.

papers.title: The anti-dyskinetic and the anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine are also present in female preclinical models
papers.abstract: Biological sex is an important determinant of neuropharmacological response, yet females remain underrepresented in preclinical studies of Parkinson's disease (PD) and L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). We previously demonstrated that sub-anesthetic ketamine reduces established LID, attenuates dyskinesia development, and produces anti-parkinsonian effects in male unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) rat models. However, whether these therapeutic effects extend to females remained unknown. Here, we evaluated the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine in female Sprague-Dawley rats using the attenuation and established models of LID. In the attenuation paradigm, unilateral 6-OHDA-lesioned females received repeated L-DOPA administration with either ketamine (20 mg/kg, i.p.; 10-h dosing paradigm) or vehicle. Ketamine significantly attenuated the progressive development of dyskinesia, indicating that early intervention modified the trajectory of LID expression. In the established LID paradigm, ketamine produced robust significant acute reductions in abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs) after dyskinesia had fully developed, and these significant effects persisted for up to 49 days following treatment, demonstrating sustained suppression of dyskinesia severity. To determine whether ketamine altered therapeutic motor function, forelimb adjusting steps testing was performed in female unilateral 6-OHDA rats. Ketamine did not impair L-DOPA-mediated motor improvement suggesting compatibility with the gold standard medication. Ketamine was also by itself associated with significantly improved stepping performance during ketamine treatment conditions, indicating acute anti-parkinsonian motor benefit. Together, these findings demonstrate that the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of ketamine extend to female preclinical models and strengthen the translational rationale for repurposing sub-anesthetic ketamine as a potential therapeutic strategy for individuals with LID.

papers.title: Predicting cortical signal mixing in coarse-resolution fMRI: a forward-operator analysis of surface mapping and the conditional benefit of correction
papers.abstract: Surface-based fMRI projection can mix signals from cortical locations that are close in the volume but distant along the folded cortical sheet. We constructed an anatomy- and acquisition-informed linear forward operator to estimate this mixing and evaluated a regularised surface reconstruction that inverts it. In HCP 7T geometry, the operator-predicted net far-cortex contribution to a standard surface value exceeded 5% in 4%, 10% and 22% of the group-average cortex at 1.6 mm and at emulated 2.4 and 3.2 mm resolution. Including the modelled far component improved predictions of emulated coarser maps and of real coarser StudyForrest sessions in high-leakage regions. Against finer-resolution, cross-run fMRI references, the regularised reconstruction reduced the residual error in HCP development data (n = 15) and in a pre-specified, family-independent confirmatory analysis (158 participants in 86 families). The improvement increased with a response-weighted contamination measure in HCP and in an independent 3T dataset (35 test participants), although a coarse-data-only version of the measure did not generalise to 3T, where an anatomical atlas predicted the gain at twofold coarsening. Overall performance improved at twofold, but not 1.5-fold, coarsening in the 3T sample. Ablation and data-reduction analyses were consistent with an important contribution from local deconvolution but did not uniquely identify the mechanism. Benefits were smaller or absent for multi-run averages, and no robust improvement across separately acquired sessions was established. The leakage maps characterise model-predicted, signed mixing rather than directly measured signal origins, and every gain is measured against an fMRI reference rather than against the true cortical response. Code, analysis plans and group leakage maps (7T and 3T) are provided in a public repository.

papers.title: Cerebrovascular Structure-Flow Gradients Revealed by Volumetric Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
papers.abstract: Characterizing the joint organization of microscale cerebrovascular structure and flow in vivo is challenging. Volumetric ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) provides spatially resolved measures of microvascular structure and flow from the same acquisition, but how these features are jointly organized across brain networks remains unclear. Here, we characterized local vascular phenotypes from transcranial volumetric ULM in mice and examined whether they contained reproducible low-dimensional organization. Local measures of vascular structure and flow dynamics were summarized within corresponding brain regions across mice. Subject-specific vascular phenotype similarity matrices were combined into a group-consensus graph and analyzed using diffusion embedding. Two leading gradients, showing distinct spatial distributions across brain networks, were reproducibly recovered across subject and spatial scales. The principal gradient was associated with local vascular density and flow complexity, defining a vascular structure-related axis. The secondary gradient was associated with flow speed and acceleration, defining a flow-dynamics-related axis. These gradients provide a low-dimensional representation of the cerebrovascular structure and flow and provide a reference for studying coordinated vascular changes across disease, aging, and intervention.

papers.title: Age-related biological dysregulation quantified using metabolomics is composed of distinct subsystems with synergistic associations to health outcomes: An analysis of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
papers.abstract: Resilience is a fundamental component of healthy aging, whereby an organism can efficiently respond to external stressors and return to a resting biological and physiological state, known as homeostasis. This capacity declines with age in a heterogenous manner and is aggravated by biological dysregulation, a detrimental state broadly associated with health risk factors and poor outcomes. However, the underlying structure of dysregulation remains unclear, particularly in the context of older adult health trajectories. Here, we take a novel systems-based approach to the quantification of dysregulation using metabolomic data from n=9,992 older adults enrolled in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. We show that dysregulation across different biological systems is heritable, and exhibit distinct associations with health risk factors, indicators and outcomes, and DNA methylation patterns. Importantly, the effect of systems-specific dysregulation is cumulative, resulting in a significantly higher risk of disease incidence and death in older adults. Our findings broaden our understanding of biological dysregulation as a health state and demonstrate the value of system-specific dysregulation for effective strategies in personalized medicine and risk stratification.

papers.title: Reaction-time asymmetry covaries with shifts in hand choice in macaques
papers.abstract: How primates choose which hand to reach with remains poorly understood. Humans prefer the hand on the target's side of the body midline, and that preference shifts with biomechanical cost and with head and gaze direction. Earlier monkey studies used only two targets, one per side, too few to fit a psychometric function. Reaction time may also reflect the choice; in humans it is longest at the point of subjective equality (PSE), the target position at which either hand is equally likely to be chosen. We measured hand choice at ten horizontal target positions in two male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) that chose freely on each trial. For peripheral targets, both animals used the hand on the same side of the body midline, with a well-defined transition in between. Displacing the hands, rotating the head, or displacing gaze to one side each moved the PSE toward that side. Reaction time was longest near the PSE. Hand displacement slowed the hand on the displaced side, and gaze displacement slowed the hand opposite the gaze. In every condition, the farther the PSE lay toward one side, the slower that side's hand was relative to the other. Macaque hand choice thus resembles human hand choice, making the macaque a tractable model for studying how the brain chooses a hand.

papers.title: PHASOR: An Open-Source Pipeline for Hidden Markov Model Analysis of Stimulus-Locked Retinal Multielectrode-Array Population Activity
papers.abstract: Multielectrode-array recordings of the retina reveal neural population activity at cellular resolution, but relating recurring population states to stimulus timing and single-unit responses requires several linked analysis steps. We present PHASOR (Population HMM Analysis of Stimulus-locked Output in the Retina), a pipeline that combines stimulus-clock alignment, Fourier-based response classification, hidden Markov modeling with Chow-Liu tree emissions, model-order selection, and state visualization. We evaluated the workflow with synthetic populations and demonstrated its use in ten ex vivo recordings from three wild-type retinas (two male, one female) and one male rd1 retina, including 2 Hz full-field sinusoidal stimulation. Across ten synthetic datasets containing seven generative states, selected model orders ranged from seven to nine, with a mean of 7.9, matching the generative count exactly in three of the ten datasets. A representative confusion matrix showed a near one-to-one correspondence between generative and decoded states, with a single additional low-occupancy state, illustrating the distinction between recovering temporal structure and recovering the exact state count. In a representative retinal recording, response classes differed in stimulus phase and contrast dependence, and decoded states differed in occupancy, dwell time, and active-unit composition. Recordings during L-AP4 application, without projected stimulation, and in a photoreceptor-degenerate rd1 retina illustrated changes in the resulting population-state descriptions. PHASOR integrates established analysis methods into a reusable workflow for relating stimulus-associated population activity to functional response classes. The selected states provide a descriptive model of population activity; their number and correspondence to biological assemblies require separate validation.

papers.title: ConfUSIus: an accessible and scalable toolkit for functional ultrasound imaging analysis
papers.abstract: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) maps brainwide hemodynamics at high resolution, yet analysis requires expert knowledge as pipelines remain fragmented across laboratories. We introduce ConfUSIus, an open-source Python package and graphical interface for accessible, scalable, and reproducible fUSI analysis. Its common data model unifies heterogeneous fUSI recordings across beamformed IQ processing, motion correction, registration, denoising, and statistical analysis. ConfUSIus lowers barriers and facilitates method development, comparison, and sharing.

papers.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
papers.abstract: Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

papers.title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
papers.abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.

papers.title: Donor Aware Reanalysis of Neuronal Nuclei Supports STMN2 Depletion Associated with Nuclear TDP 43 loss in FTD and ALS
papers.abstract: Background. Nuclear TDP-43 depletion is a central pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), but donor-to-donor variation can obscure transcriptomic associations in small postmortem cohorts. We reanalyzed public RNA-seq data from FACS-isolated NeuN-positive frontal-cortex neuronal nuclei to quantify gene-expression changes associated with nuclear TDP-43 loss while explicitly accounting for donor structure. Methods. The supplied GSE126542-derived matrix contained 62,754 genes across 12 libraries from seven donors, including five complete matched pairs. Source labels TDP-43 positive and TDP-43 negative were harmonized as nuclear TDP-43 retained and lost, respectively. After validation against featureCounts-assigned read counts, 44,225 genes with at least 10 total counts were analyzed using PyDESeq2. The primary model was ~ donor + nuclear_status; status-only and diagnosis-adjusted models were sensitivity analyses. The contrast was TDP-43 loss minus retained. Results. The donor-aware model identified 3,442 genes at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05: 1,865 lower and 1,577 higher in TDP-43-loss nuclei. STMN2 was consistently depleted (log2 fold change = -1.813, 95% Wald interval -2.229 to -1.396; FDR = 6.22e-15), corresponding to approximately 71.5% lower expression. Normalized STMN2 counts were lower in TDP-43-loss nuclei in all five complete donor pairs. TARDBP expression was also lower (log2 fold change = -0.606; FDR = 4.98e-6). In contrast, UNC13A whole-gene expression was modestly higher in the donor-aware model (log2 fold change = 0.372; FDR = 0.00622) and was not significant in either sensitivity model. Conclusions. Donor-aware analysis supports a robust association between nuclear TDP-43 loss and STMN2 depletion in this neuronal-nuclei cohort, alongside extensive but model-dependent transcriptomic variation. Whole-gene UNC13A expression cannot be used to infer UNC13A cryptic-exon inclusion or functional UNC13A depletion. No splice-junction, percent-spliced-in, isoform, or protein measurements were available; mechanistic claims therefore require junction-level and experimental validation.

papers.title: Intrinsic fluctuations modulate thalamic gating during the emergence of human conscious perception
papers.abstract: Human conscious perception is not determined solely by external sensory input but is also shaped by moment-to-moment fluctuations in intrinsic brain states. However, how these intrinsic states directly function after stimulus onset to shape the emergence of conscious perception remains unclear. We recorded sEEG activity in thalamus and five other consciousness-related cortical regions, while 32 patients (n= 2,023 recording sites) conscious percept a near-threshold visual stimulus. Preceding the extensively evoked consciousness-related activities, there are early activities (0-200ms after stimulus onset) exclusively appeared in high-order thalamus. These early activities inversely associated with stimulus strength, which reflected an intrinsic state that compensated for the stimulus-evoked response to reach the conscious threshold. These early activities were closer to the critical state in conscious trials, which enables more efficient information processing. These results suggest that intrinsic fluctuations in the high-order thalamus directly modulate thalamic gating during the emergence of conscious perception.

papers.title: Glider compositionality and information capacity in an E/I-balanced neuronal automaton
papers.abstract: In cellular automata, localized activity patterns called gliders propagate and interact to carry and transform information. Whether neuronal networks can harness this computational power remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that a cortical network model with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations, graded cellular activity and uniform local connectivity spontaneously generates diverse, interacting gliders. An analytical reduction identifies the cellular conditions sustaining propagation of the dominant G-glider. Distinct gliders can assemble into growing structures that emit other glider types. Near excitation/inhibition balance, sparse glider dynamics coexist with high computational capacity, measured by input differentiation and generalization, with local capacity varying across space and time. Strong mutual inhibition between interneurons instead permits metastatic proliferation with low computational capacity. These findings connect cellular automata to neuronal information processing and identify interacting gliders as a candidate mechanism for dynamic plasticity: the reorganization of computation within an unchanged synaptic architecture.

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Why probe registration is crucial for infant fNIRS and HD-DOT? An evaluation across 49 newborns
papers.abstract: Source-detector probe registration, i.e., the mapping of optode positions on the scalp to their true anatomical locations in head/brain space, is crucial for brain imaging with fNIRS or HD-DOT. While individual, MRI-based registration is desirable, it is not always feasible, motivating the development of alternative registration approaches. This study uses the STORM-Net registration protocol and quantifies the variation of cap alignment in a cohort of 49 newborns to evaluate how this affects reconstructed images using HD-DOT. Relative to a centrally aligned template, the cohort showed a median probe-position error of 10.12 mm, while the least and most misaligned subjects exhibited mean errors of 4.41 mm and 20.60 mm, respectively. The results demonstrate that the level of cap misalignment typically observed in newborn imaging can affect the spatial accuracy of reconstructed functional images, particularly in cases with larger probe displacements. These findings provide a quantitative basis for adopting more conservative interpretations of group-level functional brain activity and functional connectivity results, and strongly support the routine use of registration methods in infant HD-DOT studies.

papers.title: Negative sampling shapes benchmark discrimination and experimental retrieval in synthetic-lethality prediction
papers.abstract: Benchmarks for synthetic-lethality prediction compare known interactions with sampled negatives. Does performance under degree matching predict which gene pairs a model can prioritize? Across five gene-disjoint folds, matching test negatives by degree in the full labelled graph brought four methods near chance. SLMGAE states selected by benchmark test F1 had a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.501 on matched negatives. The same states retrieved 21 experimental hits among 198 SPIDR selections, versus 8.00 expected by chance. Comparable enrichment was not established in three other screens. Changing training negatives increased HAP1 retrieval from 3.6 to 15.8 hits for logistic regression; swapping 28 endpoint coefficients transferred most of this difference. Rewiring positive pairs while keeping the original matched negatives reduced HAP1 retrieval for logistic regression and gradient boosting. This preserved individual gene degrees but also changed their joint distribution, limiting attribution to partner identity. A density-ratio estimate closed 55-65% of the logistic-regression shortlist gap across four previously evaluated pools, with limited transfer to nonlinear models. Frozen predictions met the shortlist criterion for one of two new graph relations. Benchmark discrimination and experimental retrieval therefore warrant separate evaluation at the intended screening budget.

papers.title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
papers.abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altoslabs/scRM.

papers.title: A vagal-to-sympathetic reflex controls lung vascular leak
papers.abstract: Dynamic regulation of the vascular barrier is required for innate immunity, yet excessive leak endangers vulnerable organs like the lungs, where edema stiffens tissue and threatens breathing. Using a chemogenetic screen, we discover a vagal-to-sympathetic reflex that controls pulmonary vascular leak. The reflex originates in a previously-uncharacterized population of polymodal, alveolus-innervating vagal sensory neurons marked by Cysltr2. Stimulating CYSLTR2 neurons increases lung fluid within minutes, whereas sustained activation elicits perivascular edema and respiratory dysfunction. Silencing them during allergen challenge reduces leak and improves lung mechanics. Rather than acting locally, CYSLTR2 neurons relay centrally to sympathetic efferents to broadcast effects throughout lung vasculature. This pathway thus forms an axis of organ defense that can go awry in disease, suggesting new ways to control lung fluid balance.

papers.title: Practical Identifiability of a Minimal Adaptive Learning-Gain Model for Binary Feedback: A Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Social learning is shaped by distinct computational components--baseline beliefs (prior mean), feedback sensitivity (learning gain), and temporal uncertainty (drift)--that empirical designs rarely disentangle.
