Therefore, assessing neuronal specific disease biomarkers, including cell death markers, without the bias of non-neuronal or cancerous cells, could provide a more biologically accurate neurodegeneration profile. In this study, we developed the Neuronal cEll death Prediction Tool for Understanding Neurodegenerative Events (NEPTUNE), a user-friendly tool for researchers that bioinformatically identifies neuronal cell death markers from user provided differentially expressed gene lists obtained by single cell RNA sequencing data. We applied NEPTUNE to a publicly available single cell RNA sequencing dataset and analysed the progression of photoreceptor degeneration in the rd1 mouse model of severe retinitis pigmentosa. The analysis interpreted the dataset in a neuronal-specific manner and showed that late-stage photoreceptor death is not purely apoptotic but possibly engages overlapping cell death programmes. From the analysis, the user is provided with publishable graphs and a list of cell death markers with fold change, type of impact, cell death type and a strength score. Overall, our tool provides markers specific to neurodegeneration, allows mapping to known WikiPathways and KEGG pathways, performs GO and KEGG enrichment analysis and plots the data for further analysis, greatly facilitating the study of neuron specific degeneration. The tool can be found at: https://neptune.rgtcarvalholab.com/.

papers.title: When touch leads vision: flexible sensory leadership during active texture exploration
papers.abstract: Vision can sample objects remotely and over a broad field, whereas touch is restricted to contacted skin and is often spatially serial however might outperform vision in resolution by transforming spatial information to a temporal code. This raises the question on how multisensory exploration is coordinated. We recorded gaze and or touch location in exploration of 60 three-dimensional surfaces with locally varying textures during visual, haptic and bimodal exploration while participants performed a same/different task, judging whether a second texture matched the first. In bimodal exploration, gaze and touch became more spatially similar than during unimodal exploration, while touch changed less than vision between unimodal and bimodal contexts. A temporal overlap analysis further showed that touch preceded gaze on average during the first 5 s of bimodal exploration. We then increased visual discriminability of the textures using cast-shadow illumination. A psychophysical pilot confirmed improved texture discrimination, and a new participant group showed a strong shift towards vision-leading exploration. Thus, sensory leadership during active visuo-haptic exploration is not fixed: touch can lead vision when texture information is important, but the balance adapts when visual information becomes more diagnostic.

papers.title: Probing bacterial fitness in virtual chemostats
papers.abstract: The growth rate of a bacterial population is a fundamental quantity in microbiology, but hard to predict from mechanistic single-cell models. Simulating exponentially growing cell populations is computationally infeasible, and single-lineage estimates are biased as they do not account for phenotypic selection between cells. We present computational algorithms to efficiently estimate growth rates with arbitrary accuracy by combining ideas from branching processes and particle filtering. These can be used with general agent-based cell models at a cost quadratic in the desired accuracy, bypassing the exponential complexity of naive approaches. Applying these methods to single-cell models of Escherichia coli, we study how single-cell heterogeneity in antibiotic responses shapes population dynamics, and how bacterial locomotion and chemotaxis in fluctuating environments affect their long-term growth.

papers.title: Why development time matters: temperature influences plasticity while nutritional stress reshapes selection and evolutionary potential
papers.abstract: The time it takes organisms to reach adulthood is often considered a central life-history trait that influences fitness and is highly plastic across environments. Despite its importance, direct estimates of how selection on development time varies across combinations of environmental stressors remain rare, limiting our understanding of its role in population responses to environmental change. We reared 68 full-sibling families of the vinegar fly, Drosophila melanogaster, at two temperatures (14{degrees}C and 28{degrees}C) on two diets (standard and low-calorie), and measured development time, body size (mass and wing size), egg-to-adult viability and productivity (number of offspring). Temperature caused the largest plastic response, with development taking 4-5 times longer at 14{degrees}C, whereas the low-calorie diet extended development by 20-30%. Yet diet, not temperature, changed directional selection on development time. On the standard diet, faster development was associated with higher fitness at both temperatures. On the low-calorie diet, this advantage disappeared, and at 14{degrees}C slower-developing females tended to produce more offspring. Viability selection showed consistent patterns. The low-calorie diet also increased evolvability in development time c.10-16-fold at both temperatures, and genetic correlations between diets were close to zero, indicating strong genotype-by-environment interactions. Plasticity in development time was not associated with fitness in any treatment. Overall, we provide evidence that development time is a functional trait whose relationship with fitness depends on the environment. Nutritional stress induced a smaller plastic response in development time than temperature, but had a larger effect on directional selection and evolvability. The stressor causing the greatest plastic change in a functional trait is therefore not necessarily the one that shapes its selection and evolution.

papers.title: Revamped transposon-induced hepatocellular carcinoma model reveals deep similarities of cancer-driver landscapes across mice and humans
papers.abstract: Genome-scale cancer-driver discovery is limited by statistical uncertainty in driver calling and by experimental constraints on mutations available for selection. We developed 3xfOnc3 - a three-frame Sleeping Beauty (SB) mutagenesis system designed to broaden functional perturbations and reduce integration biases of traditional SB screens - and tested it in vivo in mouse liver. Within 12 months, 60% of mice developed heterogeneous hepatocellular tumors. Tumor-selected integrations were interpreted against an empirical reference from SB-based therapeutic gene delivery to hepatocytes, enabling correction for gene targetability. Background-aware filtering prioritized 315 driver candidates, including 243 protein-coding genes. Tumors were multiclonal, and identical integration-marked lineages expanded differently across lesions, supporting context-dependent clonal expansion. SB hits within young L1 subfamily members were selectively enriched in tumors. Human orthologues of candidate drivers were enriched for Cancer Gene Census genes and protein-altering pan-cancer mutations. Together, 3xfOnc3 reveals a background-corrected driver landscape linking driver selection to clonal tumor evolution and cross-species cancer relevance.

papers.title: Prefrontal cortex transcriptomes distinguish Alzheimers disease from asymptomatic amyloid pathology, neuropeptide loss, immune-complement activation and glial remodelling
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now defined biologically by cortical amyloid-{beta} (A) and tau (T) pathology, yet the transcriptional programmes that separate symptomatic AD (A+T+) from amyloid-positive, tau-negative pathology ageing (A+T-) and from pathology-free controls (A-T-) remain incompletely resolved in the association cortex. We re-analysed bulk RNA-sequencing data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of 15 donors (BioProject PRJNA1017546; 87 sequencing runs aggregated to donor level): Normal (n = 2), pathology ageing (n = 5) and AD (n = 8). Differential expression was tested with DESeq2 (adjusted P < 0.05, |log2 fold change| > 1), and up- and down-regulated gene sets were analysed separately by Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG over-representation. APOE and TREM2 p.Arg47His contrasts were treated as exploratory. AD versus Normal yielded 341 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 223 up, 118 down) and AD versus pathology ageing yielded 496 (358 up, 138 down), whereas pathology ageing versus Normal yielded only six. Genes reduced in AD were dominated by neuropeptide and hormone signalling (VGF, VIP, CRH, GRP, TAC1, PENK; neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, adjusted P = 8.8 x 10-5; neuropeptide hormone activity, adjusted P = 6.3 x 10-8), most of which also differed from pathology ageing. Genes increased in AD were enriched for interferon-{gamma} response, myeloid activation, adaptive immunity and classical complement (C1QA, C1QB, C1QC). Relative to pathology ageing, AD additionally showed induction of gliogenesis, oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination programmes (gliogenesis, 21 genes, adjusted P = 2.6 x 10-6; SOX10, MYRF) and of the microglial purinergic receptor gene P2RX7 (log2FC = 1.46, adjusted P = 1.5 x 10-5). All six pathology-ageing DEGs, including the myeloid genes VSIG4 and CD163, were also DEGs in AD, and 50 DEGs shared by the two AD contrasts moved in the same direction. Genotype-stratified analyses were underpowered or confounded with diagnosis. In the DLPFC, AD is therefore characterised by a graded loss of neuropeptidergic signalling, myeloid-complement activation that begins at the pathology-ageing stage, and an AD-specific glial/oligodendrocyte response. These signatures nominate candidate biomarkers and mechanisms for early intervention, but the small cohort demands replication in larger, covariate-annotated datasets.

papers.title: Putrescine-responsive post-transcriptional feedback regulation of Arabidopsis ADC2 mediated by 5'-UTR elements
papers.abstract: Putrescine (Put) is a bioactive polyamine that contributes to plant growth, development, and stress responses, whereas excessive Put accumulation impairs growth. However, how plants maintain Put levels within an appropriate range remains poorly understood. In Arabidopsis thaliana, expression of the arginine decarboxylase 2 (ADC2) gene is a major determinant of Put abundance. Here, we show that the 5' untranslated region (5'-UTR) of ADC2 mediates Put-responsive feedback regulation and contributes to Put homeostasis in Arabidopsis. In transient expression assays using an emerald luciferase (Eluc) gene placed downstream of the ADC2 5'-UTR (ADC2 5'-UTR:Eluc), Eluc activity was reduced by exogenously applied Put but increased when endogenous Put biosynthesis was impaired by adc2 mutations or treatment with an arginine decarboxylase inhibitor. In transgenic plants carrying ADC2 5'-UTR:Eluc, Put treatment modestly decreased Eluc mRNA abundance but substantially reduced Eluc activity and translation efficiency, suggesting that this Put-responsive repression occurs mainly at the translational level. Among the cis-regulatory elements in the ADC2 5'-UTR, mutations affecting either the conserved AUU/CUG-initiated upstream ORF or the predicted RNA secondary structure in the ADC-box, a conserved GC-rich motif, abolished Put-responsive repression, indicating that these elements are required for this regulation. Two genome-edited lines carrying deletions spanning these elements exhibited delayed germination and impaired growth, and the more severely affected line showed increased Put accumulation. Together, these findings reveal a feedback mechanism that regulates ADC2 expression through its 5'-UTR and support a role for this mechanism in Put homeostasis in Arabidopsis.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Signatures Suggest Epigenetic Programming of Molecular Defense in Biochar-Exposed Formica japonica
papers.abstract: Previous transcriptomic analyses revealed that exposing the ant species Formica japonica to biochar induces a priming effect that is sustained under heavy metal stress and enhances the ants' resilience. Re-evaluation of the data shows that biochar exposure acts as an epigenetic switch, programming the ants' defense mechanisms and enhancing their resilience to various environmental stressors. Exposure to humic-like substances, such as biochar leachate, prepares insects to withstand not only heavy metals but also other environmental challenges, such as exposure to xenobiotics, pathogens, and parasites.

papers.title: Quantum Barcoding Bridges High-Dimensional Immune Phenotyping with Signaling Responses across Species
papers.abstract: Cross-species immune profiling is limited by marker-panel size and antibody cross-reactivity. We benchmark Quantum Barcoding (QBC), a split-pool oligo-antibody assay, against mass cytometry in human and rhesus macaque blood and integrate separately measured cells using MARIO. The resulting computationally matched profiles carry 174 protein features. Population-frequency concordance was higher in humans (Pearson r = 0.92) than rhesus macaques (r = 0.55), and fusion resolved complementary lineage subsets. Unstimulated signaling conservation varied by lineage, with B-cell profiles correlated across species (Spearman {rho} = 0.70). In the primary PBMC-reference analysis, GM-CSF increased pSTAT5 in human monocytes and dendritic populations and rhesus dendritic cells. Network inference identified convergent pSTAT5-centered connectivity changes in human monocytes and rhesus dendritic cells, including pSTAT1-edge reversal and gained pSTAT3/pERK coupling. These results connect broad surface phenotypes to inferred signaling organization while retaining species- and population-specific differences.

papers.title: Beyond Direct Binding: Serotonin Rewires Model Brain Plasma Membrane-Mediated Communication Pathways in Y4R
papers.abstract: Serotonin, an endogenous neurotransmitter, modulates pancreatic polypeptide (PP) recognition by the neuropeptide Y4 receptor (Y4R), a mechanism relevant to altered serotonergic signaling associated with metabolic disorder and anxiety. Although recent experiment demonstrates serotonin modulated PP dissociation kinetics of Y4R through membrane allostery, the molecular mechanism of serotonin induced lipidomic reorganization of the brain plasma membrane (BPM) relevant for Y4R activation is unknown. To this end, a total of 825.9 ns long all atom molecular dynamics simulations at 310 K elucidate the concentration-dependent coupling between serotonin partitioning, selective lipid reorganization, and PP binding and Y4R activation relevant intra-receptor communication in a heterogeneous, asymmetric model BPM. In the absence of serotonin, Y4R preferentially associates with the anionic lipids. Serotonin preferentially localizes at the lipid water interface over the PP binding and activation-associated regions of Y4R. At 6 mM, serotonin preferentially contacts phosphocholine species depleted from Y4R, whereas at 50 mM, phosphatidylinositol 4,5 bisphosphate dominates both microenvironments. These changes align with the selective remodeling of lipid networks, enhanced lipid chain ordering, and modest bilayer compaction. Weighted implementation of suboptimal paths analysis reveals concentration-dependent reorganization of communication pathways between experimentally implicated PP binding and activation associated Y4R residues. Collectively, these findings connects serotonin dependent selective lipid redistribution to altered intramolecular communication between Y4R residues associated with PP binding and G-protein coupling, and provide a framework for future experiments investigating membrane-mediated neuromodulation and neuronal signaling. These findings provide a basis for exploring lipid-targeted pharmacology as a complementary strategy to modulate GPCR allostery by altering membrane composition rather than directly targeting the receptor.

papers.title: Structure of Bacillus cereus ZmaM, a peptidase-ABC transporter that secretes and activates zwittermicin A
papers.abstract: Bacteria engage in microbial warfare by secreting toxic molecules. These toxins can serve as therapeutics or drug discovery starting points, motivating investigations of their production. Bacteria that produce these toxins must protect themselves, and a common strategy is to synthesize an inactive prodrug that is activated upon secretion. Some prodrugs are capped with N-acyl-[x1D05]-asparagine motifs, which are removed by two types of prodrug peptidases. Type I peptidases are membrane-bound S12 hydrolases; type II peptidases have an additional C-terminal half-ABC transporter module. Recent structures of a type I peptidase revealed how its transmembrane domain completes the substrate-binding site, but little is known about type II peptidases. Here, we show that the B. cereus type II peptidase ZmaM is responsible for both the export of prezwittermicin and its activation into zwittermicin. The structure of homodimeric ZmaM reveals a central type IV ABC transporter flanked by peptidase modules. The periplasmic hydrolase domains interact over the transporter's open outer vestibule. Mutations to intermodule interfaces impact both peptidase and ATP hydrolysis activities, indicating the peptidase and transporter modules are interdependent. Together, our findings reveal an evolutionary strategy to coordinate toxin activation with its export and inform future efforts to harness these systems in biotechnology.

papers.title: Pharmacological activation of mitophagy prevents calcific aortic valve disease by targeting dysregulated mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication
papers.abstract: Abstract Background and Aims: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) lacks pharmacologic therapy. Mitophagy impairment contributes to various degenerative diseases, but whether it occurs in calcified aortic valves and during human valvular interstitial cell (hVIC) osteogenic differentiation remains unknown. We therefore investigated the role of mitophagy in CAVD and whether its pharmacological treatment prevents disease progression. Methods: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on human aortic valves and hVICs. TJ0113, a novel orally available mitophagy activator from our previous screening, was tested in two CAVD mouse models. Multi-omics analyses and functional rescue experiments were performed to elucidate the mechanism. Results: Mitophagy was impaired in calcified human aortic valves and during hVIC osteogenic differentiation. TJ0113 activated MCL1-mediated mitophagy and attenuated disease progression in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, the mitophagy receptor MCL1 anchors a fraction of PRMT3 on mitochondria. During osteogenic differentiation, a dysregulated mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication is initiated by the increased release of PRMT3 into the cytosol, where it interacts with BACH1 and impairs BACH1 nuclear translocation. This leads to a widespread loss of BACH1 genomic occupancy, relieving BACH1-mediated transcriptional repression of the pro-osteogenic factor PARM1 and promoting hVIC osteogenic differentiation. Mitophagy activation by TJ0113 restored MCL1-PRMT3 binding and reversed these alterations. Conclusions: Mitophagy impairment drives CAVD through dysregulated mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication mediated by the MCL1-PRMT3-BACH1-PARM1 axis. Pharmacological mitophagy activation by TJ0113 corrects this communication and attenuates disease progression, representing a promising therapeutic strategy for CAVD.

papers.title: A conserved pituitary response to tissue loss controls regeneration across vertebrates
papers.abstract: Regenerating complex tissues requires coordination between local cellular responses and body-wide systemic signals. As a central endocrine regulator, the pituitary is well positioned to coordinate this process. Here, we identify the pituitary as an injury-responsive regulator of axolotl limb and tilapia fin regeneration. Limb loss triggered sustained transcriptional responses in the axolotl pituitary. Single-cell transcriptomics linked pituitary loss to altered gene expression in prolactin- and growth hormone-responsive limb cells. Local disruption of the prolactin receptor impaired digit formation, whereas combined hormone treatment partially restored regeneration in hypophysectomized axolotls. In tilapia, pituitary removal impaired fin regeneration and prolactin-related signaling. Mouse digits differed from axolotls and tilapia in how and when they received pituitary signals during regeneration, suggesting pituitary-dependent regrowth is evolutionarily divergent among highly regenerative vertebrates.

papers.title: Phloem conductance from leaf to fruits in avocado during development
papers.abstract: Reproductive function in seed plants depends on efficiently allocating nutrients from sources to developing fruits. Hydraulic transport of carbohydrates largely depends on phloem architecture, but how phloem structure in fruit pedicels changes with development remains unexplored for most seed plants. Using the one-year phenology of avocado trees, we quantified water content, dry matter, and non-structural carbohydrates (NSCs) in mature leaves, flowers, young fruits, and fully developed fruits. Concomitantly, we measured phloem conduit geometry in different vein orders of leaves and in flower-fruit pedicels over time, including sieve tube numbers in cross sections. NSCs were below 5% in leaves and fruits but reached the highest concentrations in flowers, especially fructose (20%) and glucose (35%), and the pedicels of these flowers showed the smallest conduits. While sieve tube elements in leaves scaled their geometry from the minor veins to the petioles, in fruit pedicels, their geometry changed only from flower to initial fruit set, increasing their number linearly up to fruit maturation. Our models show that phloem transport toward the flowers is impaired, but total conductance increases gradually due to phloemogenesis.

papers.title: The small ORF (smORF)-encoded polypeptide MIRINE promotes neuronal differentiation in vertebrate brain development
papers.abstract: The vertebrate brain expresses an extensive repertoire of long-noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), an emerging source of small open reading frame (smORF)-encoded polypeptides (SEPs) whose functions remain largely unknown. Using ribosome profiling and proteomics of zebrafish and mouse brain, we identified hundreds of translated smORFs. We characterized MIRINE, a SEP of 83 amino acids conserved across 205 vertebrate species. MIRINE contains a transmembrane domain that targets it to the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles, and is enriched in cortical and hippocampal neurons, with expression rising during neurogenesis. Downregulation of Mirine increased cell proliferation and impaired neuronal maturation in neuroblastoma cells, in mouse primary cortical neurons and cortex, and in the zebrafish forebrain, identifying MIRINE as a regulator of the balance between neuronal proliferation and differentiation. Mechanistically, MIRINE associates with the synaptic-vesicle protein Synaptogyrin-3 and related membrane proteins. Our findings define a conserved, membrane-associated SEP controlling neuronal maturation and illustrate the functional potential of brain SEPs.

papers.title: CYP123, a sterol C4-methyl oxidase, acts with CYP51 to initiate mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism
papers.abstract: Mycobacteria exploit host cholesterol, both as a carbon source and as a source of catabolites proposed to modulate host immunity, but their capacity to catabolise other host sterols has not been established. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate of host cholesterol biosynthesis, accumulates in the activated macrophages these bacteria infect. Here we define the initiating steps of mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism, combining genomic enzymology, transcriptional profiling, mutagenesis, biochemistry, NMR and crystallography. We identify the cytochrome P450 CYP123 as a sterol C4-methyl oxidase. It is encoded with the lanosterol 14-demethylase CYP51 in a co-oriented region conserved across most Mycobacteriaceae. The region carries no binding site for the cholesterol-responsive regulators KstR or KstR2, and in M. abscessus lanosterol induces both genes while cholesterol does not. CYP123 oxidises the C4-methyl group of C14-demethylated sterols in three steps to the carboxylic acid, yet acts on neither lanosterol nor cholesterol, because Met82 excludes the C14-methylated precursor. An M82A variant binds and oxidises lanosterol. In a single reaction containing both recombinant M. smegmatis enzymes, CYP51 converts lanosterol to FF-MAS, which CYP123 then oxidises to the C4-carboxylic acid, so the two act in sequence. M. smegmatis, M. phlei and M. abscessus grow on lanosterol as a sole carbon source. Growth slows in M. smegmatis cyp123 and cyp51 mutants. Mycobacterial sterol catabolism therefore extends beyond cholesterol, and blocking the cholesterol route alone may not deprive these organisms of host sterols. Induction where lanosterol confers no growth advantage raises the possibility that the pathway also serves functions beyond carbon acquisition.

papers.title: Decoding antibody-antigen recognition: the BL8 language and its application in calibrating deep learning predictions
papers.abstract: Antibodies are central to immunology and therapeutics, and understanding how they recognize antigens is essential to rational drug design. This recognition depends on the interplay of interface geometry, physicochemical interactions, sequence context, and complementarity-determining region (CDR) conformation. However, traditional analyses often oversimplify this complexity, which becomes particularly problematic when evaluating the massive and frequently overconfident structural hypotheses generated by modern deep learning models. Here, we introduce BL8, an interpretable, eight-view structural language that comprehensively parameterizes interfaces across topology, shape, interaction, CDR conformation, flexibility, interfacial area, amino-acid-pair composition, and sequence background. Using 15,396 experimental interface records from the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab), we built a fixed reference atlas containing 1,498 discrete BL8 signatures. The atlas shows that natural interfaces occupy a diverse, long-tailed structural space in which similar geometric scaffolds can be associated with different chemical and sequence features. Furthermore, we projected 28,501 predicted complexes involving programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), generated using AlphaFold 3 (AF3), Protenix-v2, and OpenDDE, into the reference space. Acting as a robust underlying calibration layer, BL8 successfully decoupled physical viability from native confidence illusions, revealing cross-target hallucinations and filtering out 15.3% to 20.1% of highly deceptive false-positive predictions. Crucially, by benchmarking distinct generative behaviors across models, it enabled the extraction of highly reliable, multi-model consensus out-of-distribution binding paradigms. Together, BL8 bridges foundational biophysics with large-scale computational predictions, providing an essential benchmarking framework for discovering novel mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Divergent Pontine and Cerebellar Pathology in Preterm Infants With Necrotizing Enterocolitis
papers.abstract: Importance: Preterm survivors of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) face substantial neurodevelopmental impairment, but the regional biology and timing of associated brain abnormalities remain poorly defined. Objective: To define the regional, cellular, molecular, and temporal features of NEC-associated brain pathology. Design: Prospective multimodal clinical cohort study (2012-2024), complemented by postmortem tissue analyses. Setting: Level IV neonatal intensive care unit at Children's National Hospital, Washington, DC. Participants: Of 400 infants screened, 253 preterm infants born before 37 weeks' gestation (128 with NEC and 125 without NEC) were included across neuroimaging, plasma metabolomic, and postmortem cohorts. Exposures: Medical or surgical NEC (modified Bell stage [≥]II). Main Outcomes and Measures: Primary outcomes were term-equivalent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities and serial ultrasound hindbrain growth; secondary outcomes were postmortem histopathology, brain and intestinal transcriptomics, and plasma metabolomics. Results: Among 179 infants with term-equivalent MRI (89 NEC, 90 controls; 102 [57.0%] male; mean [SD] gestational age, 26.3 [2.2] weeks), NEC was associated with a higher prevalence of pontine abnormalities (12.4% vs 1.1%; adjusted prevalence ratio, 9.14; 95% CI, 1.16-71.92), alongside white matter, callosal, and cerebellar abnormalities. In postmortem tissue (n = 27), white matter pathology qualitatively resembled that of prematurity, whereas the hindbrain showed distinct regional phenotypes. The cerebellum exhibited external granular layer contraction (42% reduction; P = .04), while the pons showed neuronal injury with increased morphological apoptotic burden (P [≤] .05). Brain and intestinal transcriptomics (n = 14), complemented by plasma metabolomics (n = 29), revealed divergent inflammatory and metabolic signatures. The pons showed increased neuroinflammatory and reduced mitochondrial programs, whereas the cerebellum showed reduced metabolic and cell-cycle programs alongside circulating lysophospholipid depletion. Serial ultrasonography (n = 159), anchored to the cohort mean NEC onset age of 29 weeks' postmenstrual age, identified earlier cerebellar dimensional deficits (P = .015) and later pontine growth deceleration (P < .001). Conclusions and Relevance: In this cohort study, NEC-associated hindbrain pathology showed asynchronous growth patterns accompanied by distinct cellular and molecular phenotypes. These findings support investigation of regional vulnerability and stage-specific neuroprotection; individual injury timing and causal mechanisms remain unresolved.

papers.title: A new tool for quantifying mitochondrial RNA processing intermediates reveals increased levels of immature mRNA species under oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial gene expression in mammals requires the processing of polycistronic transcripts into mature RNAs, generating multigene maturation intermediates. Yet these species and their potential association with mitochondrial stress remain poorly characterized. We analyzed intact RNA species in healthy mouse hearts using direct RNA sequencing and identified polyadenylated mitochondrial transcripts containing complete mRNA sequences with uncleaved tRNA extensions, which we termed immature mRNAs (imRNAs). Guided by these findings, we developed a new computational tool to estimate imRNA levels using conventional short-read RNA-seq datasets. Analysis of mouse hearts deficient in mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), a model of mitochondrial oxidative stress, revealed selectively elevated levels of imRNAs retaining 5' tRNA extensions, without increases in those with 3' tRNA extensions. Comparative analyses of several mouse models with defects in mitochondrial respiration, transcription, translation, or proteostasis did not reproduce this pattern. In fact, a mouse model of mitochondrial import stress with reduced ROS generation exhibited decreased levels of imRNAs retaining 5' tRNA extensions. Conversely, human induced pluripotent stem cells treated with rotenone, which elevates mitochondrial ROS, showed increased levels of imRNAs retaining 5' but not 3' tRNA extensions, reproducing the pattern observed in SOD2-deficient mouse hearts. These findings identify an imRNA signature potentially associated with mitochondrial oxidative stress. The presence of imRNAs described here suggests that widely used transcriptome analysis pipelines may count these species as mature mRNAs, overestimating mitochondrial mRNA levels and overlooking defects in RNA maturation. By enabling retrospective analysis of processing intermediates, our tool provides access to previously unexamined information in existing RNA-seq datasets.

papers.title: Systems-level imaging reveals assembly and synaptic delivery of a multi-organelle ensemble during T cell killing
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) undergo a dynamic intracellular polarisation of their secretory compartments as they recognise and destroy cancerous cells. How multiple organelles are coordinated in space and time during this process is unknown. To enable high-dimensional systems-level imaging of multiple organelles and their relationships at high spatiotemporal resolution we use multispectral super-resolution microscopy and volumetric live-cell imaging of CTLs interacting with their targets. Organelle polarisation is initiated by perinuclear endoplasmic reticulum (ER) contacting the immune synapse, while calcium signalling promotes multi-organelle clustering around the centrosome at the rear of the cell. This creates a multi-organelle ensemble that then translocates around the nucleus to the synapse. We track organelle interactions during dynamic polarisation revealing a shift from ER-dominated to Golgi-dominated contacts as organelles reach the synapse. These findings show that CTL polarity is built through staged, calcium-driven formation of a multi-organelle assembly. More broadly, this work establishes a framework for systems-level imaging of the organelle network in cells as they deliver effector functions.

papers.title: Cross-species structure-mechanics prediction in the intervertebral disc
papers.abstract: Despite long-standing uncertainty regarding the suitability of animal intervertebral disc (IVD) models for the study of human IVD pathophysiology, few cross-species studies have integrated hierarchical structure with mechanical function. In this study, we present a multiscale structure-mechanics framework combining synchrotron computed tomography (sCT), fibre tracing, digital volume correlation (DVC) with structure-based mechanical inference and finite-element modelling. Rat, mini-pig and human IVDs (n = 3/species) were imaged by sCT, with rat and mini-pig discs additionally subjected to in situ uniaxial compression and DVC. A Structure Index (SI), integrating local structural anisotropy and fibre orientation, was developed to regionally pinpoint the location of mechanically vulnerable regions. Cross-species comparison showed scale-dependent structural conservation: gross disc and lamellar organisation retained common regional features, whereas fibre-bundle architecture exhibited greater species- and regional divergence. Despite these differences, lower SI was consistently associated with elevated deformation in rat and mini-pig discs across multiple strain measures. Structure-strain inverse correlations became tighter within progressively higher-strain domains, reaching Spearman p values of approximately -0.5 to -0.7 for several strain components. Synthetic fibre phantoms confirmed that SI reflects a coupling of fibre orientation and organisation, with additional sensitivity to fibre number in poorly organised configurations. In human discs with varying degrees of degeneration, SI revealed spatial heterogeneity and redistribution of structurally vulnerable regions. Fibril-informed homogenisation provided anisotropic material properties for organ-scale finite-element modelling that independently supported SI-based predictions. Overall, these findings establish a cross-species framework linking hierarchical collagen architecture to mechanical vulnerability and provide a basis for non-invasive, structure-driven biomechanical assessment of human IVD degeneration and mechanical risk.

papers.title: SACHET: seeded contour tracking measures Rab conversion kinetics on individual endosomes in live cells
papers.abstract: Membrane-labeled endosomes appear as hollow rings in a projection; they move, deform and exchange their coat, which population trackers (tools that detect every object of one kind and link the detections across frames) are not designed to follow. Here we introduce SACHET (Seeded Adaptive Contour & Hollow Endosome Tracking), a human-supervised Fiji tool that tracks one endosome at a time. On simulated ground truth it localizes the center to 10 nm, recovers transition time constants and lags without bias and holds the target among touching neighbors; comparisons with tuned TrackMate and Cellpose delineate where each is superior. In crowded spinning-disk projections, TrackMate followed one of seven marked Rab5-to-Rab7 conversions; supervised SACHET followed all 37. SACHET thus provides a stable per-endosome frame in which membrane morphology and protein exchange can be quantified: in five cell lines the conversion toggles like a digital switch within seconds to minutes, differing between lines.

papers.title: An Integrated Experimental and Informatics Strategy Enables Large Proteoform Identification in Top-Down Proteomics
papers.abstract: Top-down proteomics enables identification and characterization of intact proteoforms, preserving information on co-occurring sequence variations and post-translational modifications. However, identifying large proteoforms remains challenging due to an exponential decrease in signal-to-noise ratio with increasing molecular weight, interference from coeluting smaller species, unresolved precursor isotopic envelopes, difficulty obtaining informative MS/MS spectra, and limitations of current informatics tools. To address these challenges, here we present an integrated experimental and informatics strategy combining protein separation, data acquisition, precursor mass assignment, and MS/MS interpretation. First, we demonstrate that online two-dimensional liquid chromatography coupling size-exclusion and reversed-phase separations enables facile detection of large proteoforms. We then utilize a precursor mass correction strategy to enable conventional database searching of data-dependent acquisition (DDA) data containing isotopically unresolved precursors. Finally, we use data-independent acquisition (DIA) optimized for large proteins to enhance fragment signal and enable identification through intact-mass-guided candidate discovery and MS/MS validation. Applied to human heart tissue, the integrated strategy identified 703 nonredundant proteoforms from 236 unique proteins, including 65 proteins >30 kDa and 22 proteins >50 kDa, with identifications extending to 223 kDa. This integrated strategy bridges the detection-to-identification gap for large proteins and expands the accessible mass range of discovery top-down proteomics.

papers.title: Bone Response to Mechanical Loading is Highly Heritable and Correlates with Osteocyte Lacunar Morphology in Genetically Diverse Mouse Strains
papers.abstract: Skeletal loading is a key regulator of bone formation. Studies using in vivo loading of rodent bones have established many mechanical and biological factors that regulate bone response to loading. However, most studies have been performed in a small number of inbred rodent strains, and there are few data on effects of genetic background on the loading response. In the current study we employed two murine models of genetic diversity, the Diversity Outbred (DO) and their eight founder inbred strains, to assess the influence of genetic background on skeletal response to tibial loading. Loading-induced periosteal bone formation rates and formed bone volumes varied significantly among inbred mouse strains. DO mice, which each carry a unique mixture of alleles of the inbred founder strains, were more responsive to loading, on average, than the the inbred founder strains. Additionally, bone response to mechanical loading was highly heritable; broad-sense heritability for measures of periosteal formation were near or above 80%. Furthermore, osteocyte lacunar morphology correlated with loading response across inbred strains. Inbred 129S1 mice had the most elongated lacunae and exhibited the highest magnitude of response on both periosteal and endocortical surfaces. 129S1 also demonstrated a robust transcriptional response to loading, although the pathways induced by loading were largely conserved with lab-standard C57Bl/6. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic background significantly contributes to bone response to loading and establish DO mice as a platform for discovery of genes that regulate skeletal mechanoresponsiveness.

papers.title: Investigating the therapeutic potential of soluble TREM2 interactions with Transgelin-2 in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a regulator of microglial function in Alzheimer's disease (AD), and its soluble ectodomain (sTREM2) has emerged as a potential neuroprotective factor. Recent work shows that sTREM2 exerts protective effects through direct interaction with neuronal transgelin-2 (TG2) and modulates downstream tau pathology, yet the molecular basis of this interaction remains unknown. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to define the structural mechanisms of sTREM2-TG2 binding. We identify an electrostatically driven interface centered on the TG2 calponin homology domain. This surface is engaged by a binding motif on sTREM2 in which charged anchoring residues are flanked by hydrophobic contacts. We further show that the AD-risk TREM2R47H variant maintains a more open, solvent-exposed CDR2 loop that redistributes interfacial contacts while preserving overall binding affinity, offering a structural explanation for reports that R47H does not exacerbate tau pathology in tauopathy models. Leveraging these insights, we design optimized sTREM2-derived peptides that outperform a previously reported therapeutic peptide in binding persistence, energetics, and recapitulation of native TG2 contacts, supporting engagement at the epitope through which sTREM2 suppresses tau phosphorylation. Taken together, our results define a mechanistic framework for the sTREM2-TG2 axis in AD and establish a structure-guided strategy for developing peptide modulators of this interaction.

papers.title: Feasibility of an anterior abdominal electrode array for non-invasive measurement of uterine contractions across the menstrual cycle
papers.abstract: While traditionally associated with pregnancy and labor, uterine contractions (UC) also occur throughout the menstrual cycle. Abnormalities in UC frequency and/or direction throughout the cycle are correlated with many uterine disorders, which can have downstream impacts on overall health, necessitating continuous monitoring throughout the cycle. Current UC monitoring technologies are invasive or bulky, and not suitable for routine monitoring. The most promising approach uses non-invasive surface abdominal electrodes in a method known as electrohysterography (EHG). However, current EHG methods remain unsuitable for longitudinal monitoring due to bulkiness and reliance on patient-specific anatomical scans. Furthermore, there are no simulations of non-pregnant UC to aid in resolving these limitations. In this work, we evaluate the feasibility of EHG using an electrode array placed only on the anterior abdomen of size 6.35 x 14 cm and without any knowledge of patient anatomy for non-invasive measurement of UC across the menstrual cycle though both simulation and experiment. We identify a signal-to-noise ratio necessary to resolve frequency, amplitude, and direction of UC in simulation. In experimental data, all recordings met the coherence criterion identified in simulation, and we find patterns across the menstrual cycle which are congruent with previous literature. These results demonstrate the feasibility of an anterior abdominal electrode array for monitoring UC across the menstrual cycle, a step towards wearable EHG.

papers.title: Tiled base editing screens uncover rare second-site mutations that rescue a misfolded disease protein
papers.abstract: Therapeutic base editing can directly revert ~30% of disease-causing missense mutations to the wild-type sequence. One strategy to broaden its reach is to install second-site corrector mutations that improve protein stability or function across multiple pathogenic alleles. Here, we use tiled adenine and cytosine base editing screens to identify such corrector mutations in NPC1, a lysosomal cholesterol transporter whose misfolding causes Niemann-Pick type C disease. Tiling mutagenesis of the endogenous NPC1 locus in haploid human cells carrying the prevalent NPC1I1061T disease allele, combined with phenotypic reporters for cholesterol transport and protein abundance, uncovered rare intragenic suppressor mutations distributed across multiple domains. Unexpectedly, we identified a promiscuous second-site variant that can correct many different pathogenic NPC1 mutations. These correctors improve protein stability, promote ER exit and lysosomal trafficking, and restore cholesterol clearance in patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons. Our results establish in situ base editing screens for the discovery of second-site corrector mutations that are actionable for therapeutic base editing when the original mutation cannot be corrected.

papers.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships1. Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

papers.title: Cell-in-drop genotyping detects megabase-scale loss of heterozygosity as a quantitative marker for CRISPR-Cas9 on-target toxicity
papers.abstract: Targeted DNA double strand breaks catalyzed by CRISPR-Cas9 have been demonstrated to cause megabase-scale segmental deletions and whole chromosome losses in a wide variety of mouse and human cell lines. This raises safety concerns for CRISPR-Cas9 based therapeutics and highlights the need for scalable methods to assess its on-target genotoxicity in clinical contexts. In this report, we present cell-in-drop genotyping, as a high throughput approach that combines single cell encapsulation with droplet-based PCR genotyping of endogenous polymorphisms to detect loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at a targeted chromosome without any genome manipulation. With this approach, we detected megabase scale LOH induced by Cas9 DSBs, mostly frequently by segmental loss. This approach also detected LOH from loss of a critical DNA repair factor, BLM helicase, and LOH induced by other genotoxic conditions, in particular, the chemotherapeutic drugs Paclitaxel and Mitomycin C, which were demonstrated to induce LOH by different mechanisms. A modified version of the assay also captured rare local short range LOH arising from DSB-induced interhomologue recombination. Because it requires no genome manipulation, cell-in-drop genotyping offers a practical, scalable tool for evaluating genotoxic risk of CRISPR-Cas9 and other agents in research and clinical development.

papers.title: Repeated Transitions in Migratory Behavior Across a Songbird Radiation Are Not Driven by Selection on Shared Variation in Candidate Genes
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms facilitating the repeated evolution of traits is a core question in evolutionary biology. While repeated evolution has been observed across many systems, behavioral phenotypes have been less well studied than morphological traits. Migration is a behavioral adaptation to seasonality that has evolved independently in many animals, and repeated gains and losses of migratory behavior have been especially prevalent throughout the diversification of birds. While migratory traits are heritable in many taxa and candidate genes underlying intraspecific variation in migratory behavior have been identified, whether similar genetic changes are responsible for the repeated evolution of migration remains poorly understood. We used a phylogenomic approach to investigate the relationship between variation in candidate genes and migratory propensity across nearly all species in the parulid warbler radiation (n = 101), a group of songbirds in which migratory behavior has been lost and gained multiple times. Comparisons of candidate gene tree topologies to the parulid warbler species tree revealed cases of discordance, though these were explained by differences in the number of phylogenetically informative sites among genes rather than by elevated genetic similarity among species sharing migratory strategies. Testing models of coding sequence evolution identified sites with elevated dN/dS in five candidate genes, suggestive of positive selection; however, variation at these sites showed no clear association with migratory strategy, nor did we detect recurrent selection across lineages where transitions in migratory behavior most likely occurred. Together, these results contradict the hypothesis that selection on shared variation (ancestral polymorphisms or introgressed alleles) facilitated the repeated evolution of migration in this clade.

papers.title: Optimal Conservation Prioritization for Waterfowl and Other Birds in Eastern Canada
papers.abstract: Conserving and restoring high-quality habitat is widely recognized as one of the most effective means of supporting migratory and wetland bird populations. To advance this objective at a regional scale, the Eastern Habitat Joint Venture (EHJV) coordinates conservation planning for 22 focal bird species across the eastern provinces of Canada. Optimization approaches to support conservation planning are increasingly common, and can be especially valuable in large areas where resources are limited. We present an optimized geospatial prioritization scheme designed to identify regions of primary importance to species coverage objectives within the EHJV. We apply linear programming methods to species abundance data products to maximize population coverage using an adaptable variable-target approach, whose outputs generalize readily to delivery projects of any budget or coverage goal. Our base results highlight areas of high conservation value for priority waterfowl and non-waterfowl species, and we present additional examples of how region-wide solutions can be subdivided based on jurisdictional boundaries, land ownership, or existing protected status. We also address methodological decision points, with attention to how available species abundance data sources were evaluated and what considerations were involved in formulating the optimization computations. We emphasize possibilities for future work to incorporate additional conservation values, such as carbon storage and flood mitigation, and costs, such as land value, and feasibility.

papers.title: Genetic and Epigenetic Landscape of Self-Identified Hispanics/Latino in All Of Us
authors: All of Us Research Program Long-Read Work
papers.abstract: Human genetic studies still underrepresent many populations, limiting discovery and interpretation of medically relevant variation. Extensive admixture in self-identified Hispanic/Latino populations increases the need for representative reference data and ancestry-aware interpretation of medically relevant variation. We used long-read sequencing to analyze genetic variation, ancestry, and DNA methylation in 1,490 self-identified Hispanic/Latino participants from the All of Us Research Program. We identified 10 million novel variants and more than 100 candidate phenotype associations, with fine-mapping prioritizing structural variants over nearby single-nucleotide variants in more than half. We linked 3,329 tandem repeats to DNA methylation, resolved widespread allele-specific methylation, and identified ancestry-linked regulation across paralogous genes. These results reveal previously inaccessible genetic and regulatory variation and show the value of long-read sequencing for diverse populations.

papers.title: Nuclear speckles comprise hierarchical nanoscale interaction networks that shape molecular dynamics
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates organize essential cellular processes, but how their internal architecture regulates molecular behavior in living cells remains poorly understood. Here, we use MINFLUX nanoscopy for quantitative single-molecule imaging and live-cell tracking to resolve the organization and dynamics of specific macromolecules within nuclear speckles. Rather than behaving as uniform liquid-like compartments, nuclear speckles are hierarchically organized into dynamic nanoscale interaction networks. Proteins and RNAs assemble into molecular clusters that generate transient interaction nanodomains, where individual molecules alternate between diffusion and confinement while exploring higher-order networks. Physiological and genetic perturbations selectively remodel molecular clustering and nanodomain organization, and these changes are not consistently coupled to changes in the abundance of the measured components. Together, these findings reveal a multiscale organization of nuclear speckles in which molecular clustering, transient confinement, and dynamic exchange represent distinct but interconnected features of condensate architecture in living cells.

papers.title: Caspase-1 and -11 defend against environmental but not host-adapted pathogens in genetically complex mice
papers.abstract: Caspase-1 and -11 are inflammatory caspases that trigger pyroptosis, yet in most infection models they confer only a modest survival benefit. We have proposed that caspase-1 and -11 evolved primarily to defend against ubiquitous environmental microbes that have not been under selective pressure to evade them, whereas host-adapted pathogens have evolved evasion strategies. Testing this idea is complicated because the inbred mouse strains used in most infection studies carry mutations in innate immune genes: i.e., C57BL/6 (B6) mice carry a loss-of-function Nramp1 allele, and 129 mice lack functional caspase-11. Here we generated B6 x 129 F1 hybrid mice, which are gene-sufficient at both Nramp1 and Casp11, and used them to measure the fold change in lethal dose ({triangleup}LD100) caused by caspase-1 and -11 deficiency for four pathogens on the B6, 129, and F1 backgrounds. Caspase-1 and -11 conferred little or no survival benefit against the host-adapted pathogens Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella Typhimurium on any of the three backgrounds, apart from a modest benefit at the lowest S. Typhimurium inoculum in F1 mice. In contrast, caspase-1 and -11 were required to survive infection with the environmental pathogens Burkholderia thailandensis and Chromobacterium violaceum, where caspase-1 and -11 deficiency lowered the lethal dose by up to six orders of magnitude. The failure of caspase-1 and -11 against host-adapted pathogens therefore persists on a genetically robust hybrid background, supporting the view that a major evolutionary role of caspase-1 and -11 is defense against environmental microbes that have not been selected to evade them.

papers.title: Identifying the source population of naturally recolonised rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) in Laokhowa-Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuary, Assam, through multidisciplinary methods
papers.abstract: Megaherbivore population recovery largely depends on restoring connectivity between fragmented protected areas to facilitate natural dispersal, gene flow, and range expansion. The Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) has recovered from severe population decline in the past, but several populations remain spatially restricted. Recent conservation efforts and the expansion of protected areas in Assam have coincided with natural rhino recolonization in Laokhowa-Burhachapori Wildlife Sanctuary (WLS). This has occurred from nearby regions of Orang NP and Kaziranga NP after the species was locally extinct in the 1980s. Identifying the source population of these recolonised rhinos is crucial for managing this emerging metapopulation. We used non-invasive genetic sampling, genetic assignment and a landscape connectivity model to investigate the origin and potential movement routes of the recolonising rhinos. We identified eight unique individuals from Laokhowa-Burhachapori WLS and assigned them to the potential source population using Bayesian and frequency-based approaches against a reference dataset of 365 individual rhinos across the rhino-bearing areas of Assam. Habitat suitability was modelled using 161 spatially thinned presence points and eight environmental variables. We applied least-cost path (LCP) analysis to assess landscape resistance between protected area nodes. All eight recolonising rhinos were assigned to Orang NP with high Bayesian assignment probabilities (q = 0.97-0.99). The connectivity model identified two least-cost pathways, with the Orang NP-Laokhowa-Burhachapori WLS linkage showing lower landscape friction than the Kaziranga NP linkage. These findings provide genetic evidence that the recolonisation occurred through natural dispersal, most likely from Orang NP, and indicate that recent landscape restoration has re-established the structural connectivity across this floodplain. Maintaining these linkages will be essential to promote natural range expansion and the long-term persistence of Indian rhinoceros in Assam.

papers.title: Filament assembly confers the mechanical resilience of the IFI16 restrictosome
papers.abstract: Interferon-inducible protein 16 (IFI16) is a mammalian innate immune sensor composed of a filament-forming pyrin domain (PYD) followed by tandem HIN200 domains that bind nucleic acids. First recognized as a major regulator of inflammatory responses against cytosolic double-stranded (ds)DNA, IFI16 filaments have been implicated in several key mechanical processes involving both host and pathogens, including viral replication restriction, latency regulation, replication-stress responses, and DNA-damage responses. Moreover, IFI16 filaments are ultra-stable, a key trait believed to drive its autoantigenicity. Although recent studies reported that IFI16 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via disordered linkers and multivalent protein-dsDNA interactions, whether such a metastable entity provides a framework for the mechanical activities of IFI16 remains unknown. Here, we show that PYD-driven filament assembly confers the mechanical stability of IFI16 condensates by compacting DNA into ultra-stable tangles capable of withstanding forces sufficient to induce duplex deformation. By contrast, HIN200-dsDNA complexes are much more sensitive to ionic perturbation, DNA pretension, and mechanical interference. Together, we demonstrate that filament assembly allows IFI16 to act as a mechano-sensitive restrictor.

papers.title: The galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain maintains plasma membrane phosphatidylserine required for KRAS function
papers.abstract: KRAS is a small GTPase essential for cellular proliferation, differentiation, and survival. It is predominantly localized to the plasma membrane (PM), where it forms nanoclusters essential for signal transduction. This PM binding and nanoclustering strictly depend on phosphatidylserine (PtdSer), an anionic phospholipid enriched in the inner PM leaflet. Galectin-3 (Gal-3), a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin implicated in cell growth, migration and tumor progression, has been shown to regulate KRAS PM binding and nanoclustering. Here, we demonstrate that Gal-3 knockout (KO) or inhibition of its carbohydrate recognition domain (CRD) depletes KRAS and PtdSer from the PM. Exogenous PtdSer supplementation fully restores PM PtdSer and partially restores KRAS PM binding, indicating that Gal-3 promotes KRAS PM binding in part by maintaining PM PtdSer content. Total cellular PtdSer, PM PI4P, cholesterol and GM3 are unchanged, excluding these established regulators of PM PtdSer. Instead, Gal-3 CRD inhibition disrupts the cellular balance of sphingomyelin (SM) and ceramide, alters intracellular SM distribution, and impairs the endocytic and recycling transport of PtdSer, SM, and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Together, our findings demonstrate that Gal-3 CRD activity sustains PM PtdSer content through endocytic trafficking, providing the PM lipid composition required for KRAS PM spatial organization.

papers.title: BSG.S regulates ionocyte radial intercalation and function in the developing Xenopus mucociliary epithelium.
papers.abstract: Mucociliary epithelia (MCE) line multiple vertebrate organs, including the mammalian airways, and rely on coordinated interactions among specialized cell types to clear pathogens and maintain epithelial homeostasis. Proper MCE function requires the appropriate specification and spatial organization of ionocytes, multiciliated cells, secretory cells, and basal cells. Ionocytes regulate ion transport and pH homeostasis, yet the mechanisms governing their integration and function within the developing epithelium remain incompletely understood. Basigin (BSG), also known as CD147 or EMMPRIN, is a conserved transmembrane glycoprotein implicated in cell migration, adhesion, and signaling. However, its role in mucociliary epithelial development remains unclear. Here, we show that the short isoform of BSG (BSG.S) is expressed in ionocytes of the Xenopus laevis MCE. Our findings demonstrate that BSG.S depletion impairs ionocyte radial intercalation, alters intracellular pH, and disrupts epithelial organization. Furthermore, BSG.S loss alters epithelial cell-type composition, decreasing the number of basal cells and increasing the number of multiciliated cells. These findings suggest BSG.S as a regulator of ionocyte integration, epithelial organization, and cell-type composition during mucociliary epithelial development.

papers.title: Conformation governs cellular behaviors of LRRK2 Parkinson's disease variants
papers.abstract: Gain-of-function of leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is a common cause of Parkinson's disease (PD). In its autoinhibited state, the leucine-rich repeats of LRRK2 block the kinase active site, preventing substrate phosphorylation. Displacing the repeats ('unlatching') primes LRRK2 for activity. Preferential unlatching causes increased substrate phosphorylation of the PD allele LRRK2[R1441H], but not LRRK2[G2019S]. Here, we define a large class of PD-associated 'unlatching' mutations based on their effect on LRRK2 conformation. Unlatching mutants show increased localization to membranes, the site of LRRK2's Rab substrates. Unlatching mutants are also characterized by decreased LRRK2 S935 phosphorylation, which we define as a biomarker of conformation. This framework resolves the mechanism of variants such as I2020T, which structural studies could not predict. Overall, we establish unlatching as a unifying mechanism for most PD-linked variants and describe measurable readouts for identifying LRRK2-driven disease.

papers.title: Ultra-precision 3D Printed Sample Tubes of Complex Cross Section for Enhanced Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Sensitivity of AqueousSamples
papers.abstract: This paper discusses the applications of ultra-precision 3D printing in developing EPR sample tubes for X-band measurements of aqueous samples. The seed idea of this work started from the flat cell idea discussed in Mett and Hyde et al.(2003), Sidabras et al. (2005), and Sidabras et al. (2017), where placing multiple aqueous flat cells perpendicular to the electric field in the microwave cavity reduce RF losses and improve EPR signal sensitivity. In this work, we present the 3D printed aquastar sample holders for dielectric resonators and the aquasun sample holders for cavity resonators. Even though the ultra-precision 3D printing enables the fabrication of complex cross-sections at 25um resolution, the photopolymer material has comparatively higher dielectric losses compared to the conventional materials like glass and PTFE. To reduce the RF losses due to the inherent dielectric properties, we introduced the latticing approach in reducing the amount of plastic without compromising the structural stability. In addition to this, we present the slicing and dielectric approximation approach in reducing the computation cost for these complex cross-sections. The novel sample tubes discussed here present signal improvements through both simulation and experiments, which were validated through power saturation experiments. The sample tube development methodology presented here provide a general framework for designing and implementing 3D printed EPR sample holders, based on resonator electromagnetic field distribution and dielectric properties of the photopolymer material.

papers.title: Patient-Derived Synovium-on-a-Chip Recapitulates Disease and Treatment Response and Permits Study of Resistance
papers.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disease with substantial interpatient heterogeneity in synovial pathology and therapeutic response. Reliable methods to predict drug efficacy for a given patients remain a critical unmet need. We developed a vascularized, immunocompetent synovium-on-a-chip platform that integrates patient-derived fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) with matched peripheral blood leukocytes to provide a physiological human model of RA. The platform reconstructed the lining-sublining synovial architecture, recapitulated key features of RA inflammation, and exhibited transcriptional profiles resembling those of patient synovial tissue. Across patients spanning low, mixed, and high inflammatory endotypes, stromal-vascular organization was associated with distinct immune cell positioning and activation patterns, and on-chip immune phenotypes correlated with histological joint inflammation scores. We then tested infliximab, tocilizumab, and tofacitinib in parallel and integrated cytokine secretion, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune cell survival and immune cell recruitment into a composite treatment response score. On-chip scores for clinically matched treatments correlated with clinical improvement measured by {Delta}DAS28-ESR (Pearson r = 0.844). To investigate the cellular basis of heterogeneous drug responses, single-cell RNA sequencing identified SFRP1 remodeling FLS that persisted under treatment and exhibited high inflammatory programs in poorly responding chips. Cell-cell communication analysis linked reduced FN1-CD44 signaling toward SFRP1 remodeling FLS to higher NF-{kappa}B activity and drug resistance. We tested the functional relevance of this finding in chips derived from an independent TNFi-nonresponsive patient, where fibronectin supplementation reduced IL-6 secretion and restored the composite treatment response. Together, these findings support patient-derived synovium-on-a-chip as a platform for individualized drug evaluation and identify ECM-mediated niche signaling as a potential therapeutic target for overcoming drug resistance in RA.

papers.title: The cell polarity landscape in Arabidopsis male and female gametophytes
papers.abstract: Plant cell polarity underlies the capacity to directionally transport auxin and other small molecules, but also precedes asymmetric cell division in the stomatal lineage. Except for specific contexts, mechanisms underlying cell polarization are poorly understood. Most insights on plant cell polarity have come from studies on flowering plant sporophytes, while no polar protein localization has yet been reported in flowering plant gametophytes, despite clear anisotropic growth and asymmetric cell divisions in this generation. Inspired by the identification of deeply conserved SOSEKI proteins and their associated partners that mark polar domains in bryophyte gametophytes and Arabidopsis sporophytes, we here investigate cell polarity in Arabidopsis gametophytes. We discover a rich landscape of polar domains throughout male and female gametophyte development, marked by one or more polar proteins. We find that successive steps in male gametophyte polarization can be mechanistically uncoupled, and the first polarization step precedes asymmetric cell division. Using ectopic expression, we find that there is a near-universal capacity for polar protein localization in gametophytes through a single polarity system. Our work offers the first insight into gametophyte cell polarity in Arabidopsis, identifies novel polar domains, and presents a starting point for future dissection of mechanisms underlying plant cell polarity.

papers.title: Natural predator-associated chemosignals evoke distinct spatiotemporal patterns of risk assessment and vomeronasal population responses
papers.abstract: Natural predator-associated chemosignals elicit diverse defensive behaviors, yet it remains unclear how complex natural cues shape the spatiotemporal organization of risk assessment and activate vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) and downstream circuits in the mammalian accessory olfactory system. Here, we investigated odor-dependent behavioral organization and VSN sensory representations using three-dimensional behavioral tracking, integrative machine-learning analysis, volumetric calcium imaging, and whole-brain FosTRAP2 mapping. We developed a pose-based integrative machine-learning analysis pipeline (PIMAP) to identify behavioral signatures based on posture, spatial exploration, state transitions, and temporal dynamics. We found that common behavioral states were expressed in multiple odor conditions, but their expression rates, spatial positions, and temporal sequencing distinguished responses to snake, tortoise, lizard, and mouse fecal cues. Snake fecal cues elicited sustained direct investigation and distinct patterns of spatial exploration, behavioral transitions, and grooming in both two-chamber and multiple-choice assays. Volumetric calcium imaging in the vomeronasal epithelium revealed distinct patterns of VSN activation by different reptilian cues. Whole-brain microscopy of FosTRAP2 transgenic mice indicated potential differential activity patterns in AOS-associated circuits following snake and tortoise exposure. Furthermore, Trpc2 deletion altered snake-associated behavioral signatures, while odor-discriminative behavioral patterns remained detectable. Together, these findings show that reptilian predator cues activate distinct AOS components and bias exploration patterns towards threat assessment and vigilance.

papers.title: Butyrate reverts Chlamydia pneumoniae -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
papers.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extra intestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of C. pneumoniae or C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with C. trachomatis-infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated. C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping Chlamydia-host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Characterisation of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei hybrids for oenological applications
papers.abstract: The Saccharomyces genus present as a genetically diverse set of microorganisms capable of tolerating a range of environmental stressors, demonstrating high fermentation capacity and producing interesting flavour compounds. Such diversity can be exploited in a single organism by producing interspecies hybrids, overcoming the limitations of a single species. Here, as proof of principle, we exploited a library of F12 interspecies diploid hybrids between Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei (Sc/Sj), to identify new strains harbouring traits of oenological relevance, such as ethanol and glycerol production, superior tolerance to acetic acid, limited production of H2S, and optimal growth on fructose. Moreover, we calculated robustness across strains tested on solid media comparing the trade-off between performance on a single conditions and overall robustness. Progeny from a range of robustness values with favourable H2S production profiles were isolated for further analysis via micro and small-scale fermentations. Micro-scale fermentations in synthetic grape must containing individual wine-associated stressors were performed, and the robustness of the selected strains was confirmed. The wine characteristics of the hybrids were tested in small-scale fermentations in synthetic grape media. We found that both ethanol and glycerol production across our selected progeny matched or exceeding that from the commercial wine strain, and most hybrids produced less acetic acid and more fatty-acids, including higher quantities of associated esters. Overall, we were able to identify suitable Sc/Sj hybrids with interesting aroma profiles to develop further for wine fermentation.

papers.title: Homoplastic evolution of proximal podomere patterning across Arthropoda
papers.abstract: The jointed arthropod leg is often credited as a key innovation spurring the evolutionary success of the phylum. Across lineages, each territory of the appendage has served as the substrate for myriad adaptations and structural innovations. While much of the available data has supported a conserved suite of transcription factors responsible for the initiation and patterning of the arthropod appendage, recent works have begun to highlight instances of lineage-specific shifts in expression dynamics, particularly amongst the chelicerates, correlated both with the emergence of novel structures and developmental system drift in the specification of plesiomorphic structures. These works confound efforts to align or homologize the leg segments across arthropod lineages, an effort already challenged by ground plan differences in segment number between the subphyla. An even more unusual architecture of leg segments occurs in sea spiders (Pycnogonida), which alone among Arthropoda are considered by systematists to bear three coxae (proximal segments), in contrast to the single coxa of the remaining arthropods. Here, we examined proximal podomere patterning in the developing appendages of a sea spider and an arachnid. We find that a particular spatial arrangement of Lim1 and SoxNeuro characterizes the developing coxa and trochanter of the harvestman Phalangium opilio (Opiliones) throughout appendage formation, with RNAi depletions of Lim1 yielding deletions of coxa and trochanter. Comparison of expression patterns across taxa shows that Lim1 and SoxNeuro have a similar spatial arrangement in the harvestman and sea spider, but these suggest conflicting interpretations of leg segment homology. We show that this is attributable to homoplastic patterns of evolution in SoxNeuro across Arthropoda. Expanding our surveys of prominent PD axis-patterning transcription factors supports additional instances of homoplasy in the domains of Sp6-9 and Irx2. The pervasiveness of homoplasy in gene expression patterns demands measured skepticism of homology statements and careful comparisons of multiple patterning genes, toward achieving falsifiability in the homology of structures.

papers.title: Harmonizing Repeated Multi-Platform Optical and LiDAR Observations for Continental-Scale Terrestrial Carbon Cycle Data Assimilation.
papers.abstract: Accurate monitoring of terrestrial carbon has attracted considerable attention due to the impacts of rapid climate change, disturbance, and land use on carbon storage and the growth of new global carbon markets and reporting requirements. While uncertainties in C estimates remain nontrivial, crucial opportunities exist to reduce uncertainty by rigorously harmonizing models and monitoring through data assimilation (DA). LiDAR has received considerable attention for its potential to inform carbon monitoring, and while there have been a number of papers on how to initialize models using LiDAR data, it has yet to be integrated into DA systems. In this study, we integrate GEDI LiDAR into an established DA system that already assimilates optical observations of aboveground biomass (AGB) and leaf area index (LAI), microwave soil moisture (SM), and ground-based soil organic carbon (SOC) to constrain C cycling processes across the entire North American continent. Notably, this is the first time both optical and LiDAR AGB products have been iteratively harmonized within a DA system. Results show that by assimilating both optical and LiDAR observations, we reduced the uncertainty in woody biomass by 63.7% relative to unconstrained model simulations and 18% relative to our previous DA system, and achieved an average RMSE reduction of 38.3 kg/m2 across five AGB products. Importantly, LiDAR reduces DA biases in high AGB regions where optical AGB estimates were exhibiting saturation.
