papers.abstract: Cells begin to respond to stress within minutes, but how this early response depends on cell type, neighboring cells, or cell cycle phase has been difficult to determine, because bulk assays average across cells and synchronization can induce stress. We measured 338 transcripts, 48 proteins and phosphoproteins, and six cell paint stains in situ in 1.18 million single cells from four human cell lines exposed to H2O2, alone and in co-culture, and in A549 cells exposed to TNF-, cadmium, dithiothreitol or lipopolysaccharide. In A549 cells, five distinct stressors changed the same targets in the same direction within 15 min, differing mainly in magnitude, and modestly increased JNK phosphorylation. By 30 min of H2O2 treatment, immediate-early genes (FOS, JUN, DDIT3, DUSP1, NR4A1) were induced most strongly in HCT116 and A549 cells. These changes occurred across the whole cell population rather than in a responsive subset. Cell line-specific differences persisted in co-culture, and the response of MCF7 cells did not increase with the number of adjacent, strongly-responding A549 cells. Ordering cells along the cell cycle from the same measurements identified 106 cycle-associated transcripts, and the response varied more between cell lines than among cell cycle phases. Overall, the measured regulators respond to stress within 30 minutes through a largely shared program whose magnitude depends more on cell identity than on cell cycle state or neighboring cell type.

papers.title: Endothelin-1 from Tongue Glands Gates 1 Sodium Taste and Intake
papers.abstract: Sodium is an essential nutrient. To survive sodium deficiency, animals dramatically increase their appetite for salt. However, whether and how sodium depletion impacts the taste of salt to drive sodium intake is unknown. Here we show that tongue gland-derived endothelin-1 (EDN1) regulates the amiloride-sensitive, sodium-selective salt taste. Edn1 is specifically expressed in the glands embedded within the tongue. Under normal conditions, EDN1 suppresses salt taste by acting on its receptor EDNRB on the projections of salt-sensing taste neurons innervating taste buds. When internal sodium levels drop, EDN1 expression decreases, lifting this inhibition and enhancing responses to salt. Applying EDN1 directly to the tongue, using a nonionic eutectic-based organogel (Neogel) delivery technology that we establish here, dampens the activity of the salt-sensing taste neurons and reduces salt intake and preference. Conversely, genetic deletion of Ednrb in taste neurons mimics the effects of sodium deficiency, enhancing salt-sensing neuron activity and increasing salt consumption. These findings reveal a peripheral mechanism that regulates salt taste and intake in response to internal sodium levels, highlighting a direct role of the taste pathway in maintaining nutrient homeostasis.

papers.title: Diversity in early animal communities of the Ediacaran, Avalon assemblage
papers.abstract: Diversity is an emergent property of macroecological and macroevolutionary processes. The Avalon assemblage preserves near-census snapshots of Ediacaran communities, enabling tests of the drivers of diversity. However, it remains unclear how alpha diversity varied among surfaces or whether variation reflected uneven sampling, abiotic context or biotic processes. We analysed diversity for 11,342 specimens across 22 surfaces and examined abiotic and biotic correlates. Despite compositional variation, most surfaces fell into four community types dominated by Fractofusus andersoni, F. misrai and/or Pectinifrons, Bradgatia, or upright fronds, with potential substructure within the upright-frond type, whereas Clapham's Pigeon Cove and Shingle Head communities, from the oldest and youngest formations, respectively, may indicate greater community differentiation near the sampled stratigraphic limits. Sampling effort varied widely, yet taxon-area curves showed richness was well captured on 12 of 22 surfaces, and Shannon and Simpson diversity remained consistent across sampling completeness and taxonomic treatments. Diversity showed no clear associations with locality or stratigraphic affiliation, but differed among community types and declined with increasing vertical segregation. Overall, these results suggest that, among the predominantly Newfoundland communities sampled, Avalon alpha diversity may have been shaped more by local community assembly and organisation than by broader geographic, environmental and temporal context.

papers.title: Ontogenetic and time-course transcriptomic analyses of maize leaf primordia reveal regulators of transverse vein development
papers.abstract: Leaf vein patterning varies greatly among land plants and is linked to leaf structure and function. C4 plants, such as maize, have a denser arrangement of veins than C3 plants, which is hypothesized to be a pre-adaptive trait for C4 photosynthesis. Therefore, understanding how leaf veins are patterned has implications for maximizing photosynthetic efficiency. Major maize leaf veins, called longitudinal veins, are arranged in parallel and are interconnected by transverse veins. Recent work has established molecular factors controlling longitudinal vein development; however, it is unknown how transverse veins are patterned. Here, we investigated how transverse veins establish connections within the maize vascular network. We performed anatomical analyses of transverse veins and found that despite asynchronous development, transverse veins fully integrate into the longitudinal vein network. Tracing the ontogeny of transverse vein development using the marker PIN1a-YFP, we found that two sets of two initial cells on opposing sides of adjacent longitudinal veins recruit intervening ground cells to form the provascular strand. Treatment with auxin inhibitors did not abolish transverse vein initiation, suggesting an auxin-independent pre-pattern for transverse vein initiation. Through time-course RNAseq of leaf primordia, we identified a transcriptional signature that precedes transverse vein development. Two genes that belong to this gene cluster, EREB41 and EREB114, are necessary for transverse vein formation. Together, our studies establish the ontogeny of maize transverse vein development and reveal how new vascular connections are specified, assembled, and integrated into an existing vascular network.

papers.title: Cellular context shapes the transcriptomic impact of somatic variants
papers.abstract: Somatic SNVs are commonly prioritized by recurrence or sequence annotation, leaving the molecular consequences of private variants unresolved. We developed PrismSNV and Ligo-Seq, a single-cell full-length transcriptome sequencing platform, to quantify transcriptomic displacement associated with within-cell SNV-state toggling. Across 26 samples from three cancer types, more than 60% of candidate SNVs showed significant cell-type-specific displacement with over 30% variation in magnitude. Sequence-based deleteriousness was poorly aligned with cellular displacement, and fewer than 3% of top-displacement SNVs across six tumor types were catalogued in ClinVar. Displacement was strongest in transcriptionally plastic, less differentiated states. Analysis of 655,349 CD4+ T-cell transcriptomes further showed that SNV-gene associations changed in magnitude and sometimes direction during activation. Lack of recurrence or clinical annotation does not imply transcriptomic inertness; variant impact is shaped by cellular context rather than sequence alone, establishing the variant-cell pair as a critical unit for interpreting somatic variation.

papers.title: The GSNOR1-VDAC3 complex acts as a cargo co-receptor for mitophagy in response to mitochondrial stress in plants
papers.abstract: Mitochondria are central for cellular energy metabolism, and their quality is warranted by multiple mechanisms, including mitophagy, a process of selectively removing damaged, aged, or excess mitochondria. However, the regulatory mechanism of mitophagy remains elusive in plants. Here, we report that Arabidopsis S-nitrosoglutathione reductase 1 (GSNOR1), an enzyme that has long been known to degrade S-nitrosoglutathione, interacts with the outer mitochondrial membrane protein Voltage-Dependent Anion Channel 3 (VDAC3) to mediate mitophagy. GSNOR1 translocates to depolarized mitochondria, binds to VDAC3, and interacts with Autophagy-related 8 (ATG8) via its ATG8-interacting motifs, thereby engulfing damaged mitochondria in autophagosomes for mitophagic degradation. Mutations in GSNOR1 or VDAC3 cause the accumulation of misshapen mitochondria and hypersensitivity to mitochondrial stress. We propose that GSNOR1 acts as a cargo receptor interacting with VDAC3 and ATG8 to target depolarized mitochondria to mitophagy, thereby regulating cellular homeostasis.

papers.title: TSNR: Protein-Specific Signals with Broad Molecular Context for Spatial Protein Prediction
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures transcriptome-wide gene expression while preserving tissue organization, enabling prediction of spatial protein abundance beyond directly measured antibody panels. Such prediction draws on protein-specific transcript signals at the center spot and broader molecular context from the surrounding tissue. Existing spatial methods increasingly use context, but what molecular information the context should retain and how reliably it transfers across tissue environments remain unclear.We compare predictors that share a protein-specific center representation but differ in contextual molecular scope. Their transferred risk difference admits a value-mismatch characterization: broader context is favored when its target-side value advantage exceeds the corresponding change in source-to-target transfer mismatch. For convex prediction objectives, we further relate mismatch to cross-environment estimating-score variation; squared loss yields an explicit covariance geometry. This analysis motivates broad molecular context together with bounded-score robust regression. We develop Target-Specific Niche Regression (TSNR), which combines a protein-specific center representation, compact broad molecular context, and a protein-specific Huber regressor.On the six-section Spatial-CITE-seq benchmark, TSNR achieves the highest mean macro Spearman correlation among the reproduced methods under matched biological holdout evaluation. Controlled analyses support both broader context and robust regression. Across two independent external cohorts, protein-level broad-context gains are positively rank-correlated with the value-mismatch balance in all 11 held-out biological folds.

papers.title: Predicted condensation-related signatures localize to two C-terminal regions of the prion protein across cervid PRNP variants associated with chronic wasting disease
papers.abstract: Genetic variation in cervid PRNP influences chronic wasting disease (CWD) susceptibility and progression, but it remains unclear whether disease-associated substitutions produce localized differences in sequence-derived properties relevant to prion protein (PrPC) condensation. We compared a white-tailed deer (WTD) reference sequence with 10 modeled variants on the same mature PrP scaffold (residues 24-233). For each sequence, we calculated intrinsic disorder, FuzDrop per-residue droplet-promoting propensity (pDP) and binding-mode entropy (Sbind), predicted residue-level pKa values, and a discrete-charge summary at pH 7.0. The overall profiles preserve a long N-terminal droplet-promoting region, whereas variant-associated differences are concentrated in selected intervals. In the FuzDrop outputs, residues 126-140 show allele-dependent changes in pDP near the droplet-promoting threshold, and residues 220-230 show variant-specific changes in Sbind, including lower Sbind for S225F/Y and higher Sbind for elk-like Q226E. These differences occur without large changes in overall intrinsic disorder. KaML pKa predictions identify near-neutral titratable sites that provide electrostatic context for these local predictor differences. Independent atomistic simulations of monomeric PrP further detected variant-sensitive backbone behavior and intramolecular contacts involving these intervals. Together, the analysis identifies residues 126-140 and 220-230 as computationally defined candidate intervals that overlap regions implicated independently in prion conversion or CWD fibril structure, motivating direct tests of cervid PrP condensation and maturation.

papers.title: A multi-tissue RNA-seq atlas of adult medaka (Oryzias latipes) under salinity and winter-summer sampling contrasts
papers.abstract: Medaka (Oryzias latipes) is a euryhaline and eurythermal teleost widely used in genetics and environmental biology. We generated an RNA-sequencing atlas of 11 adult tissues (brain, eye, gill, heart, intestine, kidney, liver, muscle, spleen, ovary, testis) of the strain d-rR/TOKYO, sampled under two independent environmental contrasts: salinity (freshwater versus seawater) and season (winter versus summer). The freshwater and summer groups, reared indoors and outdoors under long days, provide a third contrast between laboratory and outdoor rearing. Typically, one male and one female were sampled per condition, with ten tissues taken from each individual. Ninety libraries were quantified against the medaka RefSeq transcript set (GCF_053564925.1). The resource comprises gene-level TPM and count matrices, differential expression tables for each tissue and contrast, tissue-specificity indices, human ortholog annotations, sample metadata, and a self-contained interactive browser. Because replication is limited and each condition was sampled on its own date, the differential expression tables are intended for hypothesis generation. The dataset supports studies of gene-expression plasticity and comparisons between medaka and humans.

papers.title: Foreign Body Responses Adapt to Systemic Immunosuppression to Maintain Local Immune Homeostasis Through Decorin-Associated Signaling
papers.abstract: Foreign body responses (FBRs) involve complex interactions between pro- and anti-inflammatory signals that regulate the integration and function of implanted biomaterials. However, most mechanistic studies of FBRs have been conducted in healthy hosts, and little is known about how these immune responses are regulated under pathological conditions. Here, we investigated immune responses to porous polycaprolactone (PCL) scaffold implants in mice with endotoxin tolerance or aggressive breast tumors, which induce systemic immunosuppression through distinct mechanisms. Despite suppressed inflammatory activity in major organs, implanted scaffolds maintained locally immune-active environments characterized by increased pro-inflammatory immune-cell populations and elevated inflammatory mediators, including CXCL1. In migration assays, CXCL1 preferentially recruited neutrophils and enriched immune-cell populations with pro-inflammatory phenotypes among splenocytes derived from both endotoxin-tolerant and tumor-bearing mice. The extracellular matrix proteoglycan decorin, a damage-associated molecular pattern with TLR2/4-activating activity in myeloid cells, was enriched within scaffolds but reduced in major organs under both immunosuppressive conditions. Recombinant decorin promoted pro-inflammatory phenotypes in suppressive myeloid-cell populations and enhanced CXCL1 production through TLR2/4-associated signaling, suggesting a mechanistic link between decorin-mediated myeloid activation, CXCL1-dependent immune-cell recruitment, and the maintenance of local immune activity at biomaterial interfaces. Together, these findings reveal that FBRs are not merely passive inflammatory reactions to biomaterial implants but can dynamically adapt to systemic immune dysfunction to sustain local immune homeostasis. This intrinsic immunoregulatory capacity may represent an additional factor influencing the performance of immunomodulatory implants and should be considered in biomaterial design to optimize therapeutic outcomes across different applications and host immune conditions.

papers.title: Loss of stromal VEGFR2 protects against ischemic acute kidney injury by preserving the renal microvasculature
papers.abstract: Injury to the renal microvasculature, particularly the peritubular capillaries, is a defining feature of ischemic acute kidney injury (AKI). Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) signaling is a central regulator of endothelial cell survival, proliferation, migration, and vascular remodeling. Although VEGFR2 has been extensively studied in endothelial cells, accumulating evidence suggests that it is also expressed in non-endothelial cell populations, where it may regulate tissue-specific responses to injury. Here, using publicly available single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from human and mouse kidneys, we identified VEGFR2 expression in renal stromal populations. Immunostaining further detected phosphorylated VEGFR2 in the renal stroma of mouse kidneys. To determine the functional role of stromal VEGFR2, we utilized renal stroma-specific Vegfr2 KO mice. Stromal VegfR2 deletion attenuated kidney injury after renal ischemia/reperfusion injury (IRI), as evidenced by reduced tubular injury, preservation of renal blood flow, decreased endothelial oxidative stress, and maintenance of the renal microvasculature. Stromal Vegfr2-deficient kidneys also exhibited increased Angpt1 and Tek levels, enhanced endothelial ERK activation, and preserved endothelial adherent junctions. Taken together, these findings reveal an unexpected role for VEGFR2 in the renal stromal lineage and highlight stromal-endothelial communication as a potential therapeutic target for preserving microvascular integrity after ischemic AKI.

papers.title: Prolactin Receptor Long Isoform ΔS1 Expression is Reduced in the Dorsal Root Ganglia of Humans with Chronic Pain
papers.abstract: Prolactin receptor (PRLR) isoforms, specifically the short (PRLR-S) and long (PRLR-L), are differentially expressed in pathological conditions and may be involved in the induction and maintenance of pain in females. PRLR sex-dependent actions are well studied in rodent models of chronic pain, but the translatability of these findings have only been assessed in electrophysiology studies that found consistent results with previous sex differences described in mice. To increase our understanding of the sexual dimorphic nature of prolactin actions on sensory neurons and our knowledge of how this body of work applies to the human nervous system, we characterized the expression of the short and long isoforms of PRLR with RNAscope in situ hybridization in human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. Based on data in mice, we hypothesized PRLR-S and PRLR-L would be equally expressed in human DRG neurons, with higher expression in females. To test this, we used DRG tissues recovered from male and female organ donors and cervix as a positive control. Our results demonstrated human DRG neurons express more PRLR-L, specifically transcript variant 6 ({Delta}S1), than PRLR-S in both sexes and that female donors had a higher expression of PRLR overall. In DRGs from female organ donors with a history of chronic pain we observed less PRLR-L expression, a finding consistent with previous studies in pain models in female mice. Expression for both PRLR isoforms in cervix was consistent with previous reports. An analysis of previously published RNA sequencing studies on human DRGs revealed that PRLR expression is confined mostly to TRPV1-positive nociceptors in humans, consistent with our RNAscope-based findings. We conclude that the PRLR-L ({Delta}S1) form is the major isoform expressed in human DRG neurons, that this expression is higher in females than in males, and that PRLR-L ({Delta}S1) expression is suppressed in chronic pain conditions in females.

papers.title: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy alters Schwann cell calcium homeostasis and increases peripheral nerve inflammation
papers.abstract: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy (LAMA2-RD) affects skeletal muscle and peripheral nerves, yet the consequences of LAMA2 deficiency on peripheral nerve integrity beyond early postnatal development remain incompletely understood. We investigated sciatic nerve architecture and molecular alterations across postnatal life in hypomorphic Lama2dy2J/dy2J mice. LAMA2 localizes around the abaxonal surface of myelinating Schwann cells in control nerves. LAMA2-deficient nerves exhibited patchy regions lacking myelinated axons from early postnatal stages into adulthood, including expanded Remak bundles along with axons completely lacking normal Schwann cell ensheathment. In adult nerves, myelin infolding and reduced myelin circularity revealed abnormalities in the architecture of myelin that had formed. Bulk sciatic nerve RNA sequencing identified altered calcium-signaling and immune-related transcriptional signatures. Complementary Fura Red measurements in primary nerve-derived Schwann cell cultures demonstrated decreased intracellular calcium in LAMA2-deficient samples, while ATP-evoked responses were preserved. Older LAMA2-deficient nerves also exhibited increased CD45+CD11b+ myeloid-cell infiltration. Together, these observations extend the characterization of LAMA2-associated neuropathy into adulthood and identify calcium homeostasis and neuroimmune responses as candidate processes relevant to persistent peripheral nerve pathology.

papers.title: Immuno-Proteomic Age of Cardiovascular Etiology (iPACE) Signature Predicts Cardiovascular Risk in Elderly Patients
papers.abstract: Despite advances in clinical care, cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of disability and mortality worldwide. While age alone is a primary risk factor for CVD, accumulating evidence suggests the immune system influences the initiation and progression of CVD pathophysiology, particularly in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD). Here, using two independent cohorts of older adults, we develop a thirty-protein signature of age based on serum immune proteomics, which correlates with HFpEF and ASCVD risk and mortality (Immuno-Proteomic Age of Cardiovascular Etiology, iPACE). We find aging-related circulating immune proteins associated with ASCVD and HFpEF-specific resilience and susceptibility that may be used as potential prognostic, diagnostic, or therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Sex differences in fear extinction are conditional, not categorical
papers.abstract: Threat memories are dynamic, and their behavioral expression can change with subsequent experience and the passage of time. Extinction training can reduce conditioned fear responses, yet these responses may re-emerge over time through spontaneous recovery. Although biological sex has been implicated as modulatory factor in fear and extinction memory processes, studies have reported inconsistent findings. Here, we investigated how differences in extinction training and the timing of memory assessment influence extinction memory in male and female mice. Using contextual fear conditioning, we assessed fear acquisition and threat retention, characterized within-session and across-session extinction during repeated training, and compared shorter (3-minute) and longer (6-minute) daily extinction sessions. We subsequently evaluated extinction memory retention and spontaneous recovery at a later time point. Estrous-cycle stage in females was monitored daily throughout the experimental protocol to examine its potential association with fear and extinction behavior. We found that males and females demonstrated comparable fear acquisition and threat memory, as well as similar extinction progression across days. During longer extinction sessions, but not shorter, males showed greater within-session reductions in freezing, whereas females exhibited modestly higher overall freezing. We found no significant sex difference in the magnitude of spontaneous recovery. There was no significant association between estrous-cycle stage and freezing behavior. Together, our findings suggest that sex-dependent differences in contextual fear extinction are not uniformly expressed, but rather depend on the experimental conditions under which extinction is assessed

papers.title: Biomechanical stress in the retinal pigment epithelium surrounding laser scars in humans
papers.abstract: Purpose : The wound response of an epithelium comprises tissue-scale activation of stress fibers whose contraction regionally reconfigures the epithelium and drives closure of the wound. Recent in vitro studies have shown that similar biomechanical processes can paradoxically lead to enlargement of epithelial holes. In patients having undergone laser photocoagulation of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), laser scars may expand over years. Here, to document the implication of epithelial biomechanics in the enlargement of laser scars we analyzed the dynamic changes affecting the RPE around scars in patients and performed confocal microscopy on a RPE flat-mount from a donor eye. Methods: We analyzed the image files of five patients (age 61 to 85 years) showing enlargement of laser scars in the RPE (follow-up, 13 to 60 months). In three of them, prospective imaging was performed using transscleral illumination adaptive optics ophthalmoscopy (AOO), an imaging technology enabling visualization of RPE cells. Time-lapse sequences were analyzed to track dynamic processes in the RPE surrounding scars. A flat-mounted phalloidin-labeled RPE from a human donor eye with a history of scatter photocoagulation was examined by confocal microscopy to document the distribution of stress fibers and cell metrics. Results: Time-lapse sequences showed that enlargement of laser scars was accompanied by the displacement of microscopic features in margins of atrophy. AOO imaging suggested locally coordinated displacement of mosaic of darks spots, with a generally radial or tangent direction relative to the edges of scars. Such movements were detected up to several hundred microns from the edges of scars. On the histology sample, elongated RPE cells with stress fibers forming actin cables were found along edges of scars, which formed fascicles between adjacent scars. Conclusion: Enlargement of RPE scars may be accompanied by long-lasting, largescale changes in the distribution of microscopic features in the margins of lesions. In particular, transscleral illumination AOO showed coordinated displacement of a mosaic similar to the one described for the RPE. The finding by histology of RPE cell with a tractional phenotype along edges further suggests that epithelial biomechanics contribute to such movements and may hence contribute to scar enlargement.

papers.title: The genetic basis of extra-lobed leaves in ivyleaf morning glory (Ipomoea hederacea)
papers.abstract: Intraspecific leaf shape variation is common among angiosperms. Ivyleaf morning glory (Ipomoea hederacea) has become a useful system for studying the genetics and ecology of leaf shape variation as this species exhibits two leaf shapes: leaves with entire margins, and 3-lobed leaves. It is known that these phenotypes are controlled by a single locus, and differ in their ecophysiology, geographic distribution, ecology, and fitness. However, individuals producing leaves with 1-2 extra lobes have also been observed, but the genetic basis of these phenotypes have not been described. To investigate the genetic basis of extra-lobing, we compared phenotypic distributions of leaf shapes of an F2 generation to Mendelian ratios for a single locus trait, and conducted a bulked segregant analysis to uncover quantitative trait loci. Our results suggest that producing extra-lobed leaves has a complex genetic basis and that there are multiple QTLs underlying this phenotype containing potential candidate genes involved with auxin distribution and leaf development. Whether these extra-lobed phenotypes also differ in terms of their physiology and ecology remains unexplored.

papers.title: A minimal two-residue C-terminal truncation of AID in adult-onset hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2)
papers.abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), encoded by AICDA, facilitates class-switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM) in activated B cells. Loss of AID function causes hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2). While typically autosomal recessive, three C-terminal truncation variants have been reported to act in autosomal dominant manner. We describe a novel heterozygous AICDA nonsense variant, c.589G>T (p.G197*), that truncates the final two C-terminal residues of AID and results in adult-onset HIGM2. Single-cell sequencing of primary patient B cells revealed a complete block in CSR and a [~]10-fold reduction in SHM. AICDA mRNA expression was balanced between wild-type and variant alleles, yet AID protein abundance was reduced to [~]56% with normal subcellular localization. Remarkably, inducible germinal center (iGB) cultures restored CSR in purified naive patient B cells. CRISPR-Cas9 editing of healthy donor B cells confirmed that the iGB platform can rescue B cells harboring heterozygous, but not homozygous, AICDA variants. These results demonstrate that even a two-amino-acid truncation at the AID C-terminus is sufficient to disrupt its function and cause HIGM2.

papers.title: ToxINsight: An Integrated Web Platform for Sequence, Structure, and Ligand Binding Analysis of Snake Venom Toxins
papers.abstract: Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank , AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models . ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/.

papers.title: Peripheral Exercise Transcriptomes Do Not Converge on Glutamatergic or Neuroinflammatory Signatures: A Cross-Platform Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Executive dysfunction following physical overtraining has been linked to glutamatergic dysregulation in the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), but whether this central mechanism is reflected in peripheral gene expression is unknown. This study tested whether peripheral transcriptomic responses to exercise converge on the glutamatergic or neuroinflammatory pathways implicated in LPFC dysfunction. Three publicly available GEO datasets spanning skeletal muscle, whole blood, and circulating neutrophils were analyzed across four exercise groups using limma, with a discovery threshold of nominal p < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change above 0.5. Differential expression analysis identified 7,311 unique differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across the four contrasts, but overlap between datasets was limited: 7 genes were shared between skeletal muscle and blood, 38 between skeletal muscle and the GSE43856 contrasts, and 90 between blood and the GSE43856 contrasts, with none significant across all three studies. Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment of the DEG union identified ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, ribosome biogenesis, protein folding, and T cell activation as the dominant biological processes; no glutamatergic or neuroinflammatory terms reached significance. Cross-tissue concordance between skeletal muscle and blood was absent (r = 0). Effect sizes among the genes driving the top enriched pathways were dominated by ribosomal proteins, heat shock proteins, and translation initiation factors rather than glutamate receptors or transporters. These findings indicate that peripheral transcriptomic responses to exercise are tissue-specific and dominated by proteostasis, translational, and immune programs rather than glutamatergic signaling. Direct assessment of central nervous system tissue or fluid-based glutamatergic biomarkers may be required to link overtraining-induced fatigue to LPFC dysfunction.

papers.title: Multiple domains of Mata1 transcription factor contribute to binding site specificity
papers.abstract: Among homologous transcription factors with the same function, DNA-binding specificity can diverge. Mat1 is a high mobility group (HMG) box transcription factor in budding yeast whose Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans homologs regulate -specific genes but bind distinct cis-regulatory sequences. To identify the protein features underlying this divergence, we generated structure-guided chimeras and measured their activity using species-specific reporters. Replacing any of the four Mat1 regions reduced activation of the S. cerevisiae reporter, while all chimeras retained activity on the C. albicans reporter. Thus, all four regions of Mat - not just the HMG box domain - are important for sequence specificity.

papers.title: Local fractal dimension as an indicator of functional reorganization in molecular interaction networks
papers.abstract: Changes in protein abundance incompletely describe how molecular perturbations reshape cellular organization. Here we introduce DIFFRACT, a framework that integrates quantitative proteomics with protein-protein interaction networks to identify reorganization through changes in local fractal dimension. Molecular associations define effective distances between connected proteins, allowing the geometry of their surrounding network neighborhoods to be compared across conditions. Analyses across four organisms (E. coli, A. thaliana, C. elegans, and H. sapiens) and three interaction resources (STRING, BioGRID, and IntAct) establish heterogeneous local scaling, while controlled perturbations demonstrate sensitivity to regional changes and invariance to uniform distance rescaling. Applied to RAVER1-deficient A549 cells, DIFFRACT identifies components associated with established RNA-regulatory functions and candidate roles in tRNA biology, mitochondrial organization and ciliogenesis. Selected RNA-regulatory and ciliary themes are not significantly enriched by abundance-ranked gene set analysis, supporting complementary information from network geometry. Selected functional annotations also recur in HEK293T cells. Guided by the ciliary predictions, we show that RAVER1 depletion increases the proportion of ciliated A549 cells 2.57-fold and increases cilium length. DIFFRACT thus connects changes in molecular network geometry to experimentally testable biological responses, extending the interpretation of proteomic perturbations beyond differential abundance.

papers.title: Mapping, stacking and characterization of a novel resistance haplotype against GpaVvrn-virulent Globodera pallida derived from wild potato relative Solanum brevicaule
papers.abstract: Potato production is threatened by pests and pathogens. Among the most harmful are the potato cyst nematodes (PCN), including Globodera pallida. The major control measures are potato cultivars harbouring resistance genes. However, virulent nematode populations are breaking through the most broadly applied resistance genes, and therefore novel resistance genes are required to keep control of G. pallida. In this study we map a resistance locus in wild potato relative Solanum brevicaule to the bottom of chromosome 11 (42.83 - 42.85 Mb) using a k-mer based bulked segregant analysis and name the resistant haplotype GpaXIbrc. The presence of the GpaXIbrc marker in the potato genome significantly increases resistance against a GpaVvrn-virulent G. pallida population (AMPOP01). Furthermore, the GpaXIbrc haplotype was stacked with three other resistance haplotypes: GpaXItar, GpaVvrn, and GpaIXvrn. Stacking of the novel GpaXIbrc haplotype to these other resistance haplotypes resulted in a significant increase in resistance. The largest effect was seen in combinations with 'major' resistance haplotypes GpaVvrn + GpaIXvrn and GpaXItar + GpaXIbrc. To determine whether we are dealing with a novel allele, the resistance mechanism underlying the GpaXIbrc haplotype was described after performing an in vitro bioassay. The resistance mechanism was different from GpaXIspl as described in literature, which is also localized at the bottom of chromosome 11. Therefore, we conclude that we found a novel resistance allele originating from S. brevicaule.

papers.title: Female biases in islet cell gene expression, alpha cell number, and glucagon are present early in postnatal life
papers.abstract: Biological sex significantly affects glucose homeostasis. Sex differences in insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues play a role in this difference; however, a growing body of evidence suggests sex differences in islet cells also contribute to differential glucose homeostasis. Studies in rodent and human models have identified sex differences in alpha- and beta-cell gene expression, in islet cell composition, metabolism, and stress responses, and in circulating levels of glucoregulatory hormones. However, most of these studies used adult humans or mice, leaving the age at which these differences emerge less clear. We performed a detailed characterization of glucose homeostasis and islet biology in young male and female mice from two mouse strains widely used in diabetes research to model both Type 1 (non-obese diabetic, NOD) and Type 2 diabetes (C57BL/6J). We uncovered male-female differences in islet cell gene expression and composition, and in circulating levels of glucagon. Importantly, these differences were reproducible across both models and were present prior to diabetes-like phenotypes. Together, our data suggest sex differences in aspects of islet biology begin early in postnatal life.

papers.title: Tumour architecture inverts ARNT-dependent growth regulation and reveals CPE-mediated spheroid expansion in luminal breast cancer
papers.abstract: Tumour architecture profoundly influences cancer cell behaviour, yet functional genomic studies predominantly rely on two-dimensional (2D) cultures. Here, we performed parallel chromosome 1q focused CRISPR screens in matched 2D monolayers and three-dimensional (3D) spheroid cultures of luminal breast cancer cells, which revealed ARNT as a prominent architecture-dependent fitness regulator. ARNT depletion reduced proliferation in 2D but enhanced spheroid growth in 3D. This functional switch was reproduced in MCF7 and T47D but not in nontumorigenic MCF12A cells, indicating a tumour and architecture dependent role of ARNT. Transcriptomic profiling revealed distinct responses to ARNT perturbation in 2D and 3D and pointed to carboxypeptidase E (CPE) as a downstream effector. ARNT modulation reciprocally altered CPE expression, and genetic epistasis established CPE as required for ARNT loss driven spheroid expansion and sufficient to restore growth in ARNT overexpressing spheroids. In primary tumours, ARNT and CPE were inversely correlated in low-hypoxia TCGA Luminal A samples, and single-cell RNA sequencing revealed an inverse association within ER positive cancer cells. Together, these findings demonstrate that the growth regulatory function of ARNT depends on tumour architecture and that a functional ARNT CPE axis controls luminal breast cancer spheroid growth, underscoring the importance of incorporating 3D context into functional genomic approaches.

papers.title: Recurrent mitotic error and purifying selection shape chromosomal mosaicism across human tissues
papers.abstract: Mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs) have been extensively studied in cancer and clonal hematopoiesis but less so in healthy solid tissues. Here, we characterized mCAs in 19 tissues across 25 donors (aged 42-89+ years) by analyzing >200x whole-genome sequencing data generated by the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network. Across 722 tissue samples, we identified 1,008 autosomal mCAs >1 Mb in length and ubiquitous losses of sex chromosomes. Surprisingly, the highest levels of Y chromosome loss in males (5-10% cell fraction in elderly donors) were observed in the lung, adrenal gland, and heart. These tissues also tended to experience more X loss in females, revealing a gradient of mitotic error burden across human tissues. Autosomal aneuploidies displayed distinct tissue-specific patterns indicative of negative selection against most events, except in the adrenal gland, in which low-level aneuploidy was pervasive. In contrast to the adrenal gland, testis rarely harbored aneuploidies but frequently experienced low-level copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH), suggesting increased mitotic recombination in spermatogonial stem cells. Recurrent X chromosome losses within tissues of female donors exhibited allelic skews explained by a combination of genetic and epigenetic effects. Together, these results show that the chromosomal landscape of aging human tissues is shaped by genetics and recurrent mutations, most but not all of which are held in check by purifying selection.

papers.title: EigenBrain maps cortical molecular architecture from functional, geometric, and structural eigenmodes
papers.abstract: Neurotransmitter receptor and transporter distributions shape neural communication across the cortex and underpin mechanistic interpretations of brain function. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived eigenmodes, low-dimensional spatial patterns that capture the principal axes of cortical organization, are increasingly used to reconstruct brain maps and offer a potential route to approximating molecular topographies in large cohorts where direct measurements are unavailable. Yet whether the type of MRI data used to derive these eigenmodes determines which receptor and transporter distributions can be approximated, and which molecular systems are accessible through this approach at all, remains unknown. Using a spatial reconstruction framework applied to 23 molecular systems spanning neurotransmitter, metabolic, and pathological markers, we show that eight receptor and transporter maps, spanning serotonin, dopamine, histamine, cholinergic, and opioid markers, can be selectively approximated from functional eigenmodes but not structural or geometric ones. This selectivity also reveals that functional brain organization encodes a specific subset of neuromodulatory topographies that structural and geometric organization does not. To illustrate translational potential in clinical cohorts where molecular imaging is unavailable, we applied individual-level eigenmode decompositions of MRI data projected onto the eight validated molecular systems and detected cross-sectional differences in autism and longitudinal changes in schizophrenia. Together, these findings reveal a difference in how geometric, structural, and functional brain organization relate to molecular architecture, offering a method for approximating validated molecular profiles in population neuroimaging cohorts that lack direct molecular imaging.

papers.title: CD19-CAR T-cell therapy resets the EBV+ autoreactive B cell repertoire in autoimmune disease
papers.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reprograms autoreactive B cells into activated antigen-presenting cells that drive pathogenic T- and B-cell responses in autoimmune disease. Whether eliminating these cells contributes to durable remission after CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy is unknown. Here, using EBV B-cell sequencing (EBV-seq), we profiled EBV+ B cells from patients treated with CD19-CAR T cells (systemic lupus erythematosus, n=6; inflammatory myopathy, n=3; systemic sclerosis, n=3) or rituximab (n=15) and recombinantly expressed their antibodies to define antigen specificity. At baseline, EBV+ B cells were enriched relative to healthy donors, class-switched and hypermutated, expressed the latency III program with heightened antigen-presentation signatures, and encoded autoantibodies. CAR T cells, but not rituximab, depleted EBV+ B cells and shifted the reconstituted repertoire towards IgM+, minimally mutated, largely non-autoreactive cells, consistent with infection of newly generated B cells. After rituximab, EBV+ B cells retained a class-switched, hypermutated and autoreactive with an activated antigen-presenting phenotype. Sustained drug-free remission occurred in 8/12 CAR T-cell-treated versus 0/15 rituximab-treated patients. In vitro, EBV+ B cells resisted anti-CD20 and anti-CD19 antibodies but were killed by CAR T cells and a CD19 T-cell engager. Our findings suggest resetting the EBV+ autoreactive B-cell repertoire contributes to sustained drug-free remission.

papers.title: Leg blood flow and muscle oxygenation are reduced when exercising with loads >=40% 1RM compared to loads <=30% 1RM due to increases in contraction induced intramuscular pressure
papers.abstract: The critical occluding tension (COT) is the load at which contraction-induced increases in intramuscular pressure (IMP) collapse intramuscular vasculature and impair oxygen delivery. For knee extension resistance exercise, the COT occurs at ~30-40% 1RM, yet few studies have measured IMP alongside convective oxygen delivery. This study examined the interaction between IMP, leg blood flow, and muscle oxygenation during resistance exercise. Twelve participants completed knee extension bouts across a range of loads while vastus lateralis IMP, femoral blood flow (Doppler), blood pressure, muscle oxygenation (NIRS), and electromyography (EMG) were recorded. Mean IMP increased alongside relative load (20% 1RM=19.1(9.4) mmHg; 30% 1RM=22.4(10.4) mmHg; 40% 1RM=27.0(8.7) mmHg; 50% 1RM=31.5(11.5) mmHg; 60% 1RM=41.14(13.8) mmHg; p<0.05). Leg blood flow scaled to rest was similar between 20% and 30% 1RM (p=0.13), 40%, 50%, and 60% 1RM (p>0.05), but different between the 20-30% 1RM and 40-60% 1RM groupings (p<0.05) (20% 1RM=2.6(1.4) times rest; 30% 1RM=1.8(0.5) fold of rest; 40% 1RM=1.4(0.6) fold of rest; 50% 1RM=1.1(0.4) fold of rest; 60% 1RM=1.1(0.5) fold of rest). Muscle oxygenation was lower at 40%, 50%, and 60% 1RM compared to 20% and 30% 1RM (p<0.05). Thus, at [≤]30% 1RM exercising blood flow increased well above rest, indicating preserved microvascular perfusion, whereas at [≥]40% 1RM the rise in IMP was sufficient to impair perfusion and limit blood flow increases. Exercise at or above the COT restricts convective oxygen delivery due to contraction-induced increases in IMP.

papers.title: A molecular circuit integrates environmental cues to coordinate the exit from developmental dormancy
papers.abstract: Diapause is a reversible dormancy state that enables organisms to survive extreme environments. In annual killifishes, embryos use diapause to bridge seasonal drought, but how environmental cues are integrated to trigger exit remains unclear. Here, we combine model-based single-embryo transcriptomics with cross-clade small-molecule screening to define the molecular logic of diapause exit. In the African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri), high-resolution profiling uncovered a temporal transcriptional cascade, while transcriptomic-clock analysis revealed reduced transcriptional noise during developmental reactivation. Transcriptome-guided drug-enrichment analysis nominated overlapping compounds across two annual killifish clades, leading to a targeted chemical screen that identified shared activators and inhibitors of diapause exit. Functional assays support a model in which HSP90 integrates temperature-dependent cues with steroid-hormone signaling. Together, these findings reveal shared molecular machinery that couples environmental sensing to developmental timing, aligns diapause exit with favorable conditions, and provides a powerful comparative framework for dissecting vertebrate dormancy control.

papers.title: Why is Cyclin A degraded before Cyclin B?
papers.abstract: The Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C) ubiquitin ligase controls mitosis by targeting the mitotic Cyclins for degradation. CyclinA has evolved multiple APC/C degrons that enable its degradation as soon as cells enter mitosis while the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint prevents recognition of CyclinB until all chromosomes have attached to the mitotic apparatus. But why the rapid early degradation of CyclinA is conserved in evolution is not known. Here, we mutated two APC/C-recognition motifs in human CyclinA2 to slow down its degradation. We find that slower degradation of CyclinA induces errors in chromosome congression and chromosome clustering at mitotic exit, leading to aneuploidy and malformed daughter cell nuclei. We identify Ki67 as the candidate that interferes with chromosome clustering since its phosphorylation and behaviour are perturbed when CyclinA is degraded more slowly, and increased microtubule dynamics as a contributing factor to chromosome congression errors. We conclude that rapid early CyclinA degradation is important for genomic stability.

papers.title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
papers.abstract: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.

papers.title: Paper-Based Microfluidic Continuous-Flow Electroporation (μCEP) for Bacterial Transformation through Pore-Scale Electric-Field Enhancement
papers.abstract: Electroporation (EP) is an established method for introducing biomolecules such as DNA into bacterial cells. Commercially available cuvette-based EP systems are expensive to use and limited to small sample volumes making them impractical for high-throughput applications. Furthermore, high electric fields are required in these systems which can promote electrolysis and Joule heating, thereby reducing cell viability. Herein, we report a scalable, low-cost technique called Microfluidic Continuous-Flow Electroporation in Paper (CEP) which takes advantage of the insulating nature of glass fiber paper and its micron-sized pores to amplify the electric field strength experienced by cells. The CEP device is fabricated by sealing glass fibers between PDMS membranes using a combination of corona plasma treatment and heat-pressing. Our results demonstrate that the CEP technique enables transformation of E. coli at lower applied electric field strengths with transformation efficiencies comparable to or higher than those of cuvette-based EP under the tested conditions. The continuous-flow format and lower required applied field provides a low-cost approach to bacterial electroporation while maintaining cell viability comparable to that of conventional cuvette-based EP.

papers.title: TDP-43 amyloid conversion in cells tracks the net charge of a polyampholyte motif, not condensate solidification
papers.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation of TDP-43 is implicated in ALS and FTLD, yet how its condensates convert into pathological amyloid in living cells remains poorly defined. Here we identify a polyampholyte motif (PAM) in the linker between RRM2 and the amyloid-forming low-complexity domain as a charge-tunable determinant of fibrillization that operates independently of condensate solidification. In budding yeast expressing GFP-TDP-43{Delta}NLS, charge reversal of three PAM arginines (R268E/R272E/R275E; 3R-E) converted liquid puncta into ProteoStat-positive fibrils. Unexpectedly, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching revealed that 3R-E condensates were more mobile than wild-type condensates, whereas the least mobile condensates, in both yeast and human U2OS cells, converted least. Across 24 PAM charge variants, the proportion of fibril-bearing cells scaled linearly with net charge independently of residue identity, and charge neutralization delayed rather than abolished conversion. Phosphomimetic substitution of the PAM serines alone induced fibrils, implicating phosphorylation as a potential physiological modulator of PAM charge.

papers.title: SMARTFlexDB: a paired apo-holo RNA structure database and analysis platform for RNA conformational flexibility and small-molecule recognition
papers.abstract: RNA structures can undergo substantial conformational changes upon small-molecule binding, yet existing structural resources provide only static RNA-ligand snapshots without connecting ligand-bound (holo) RNA structures to corresponding ligand-free (apo) conformations. SMARTFlexDB is a curated database and analysis platform that uses paired apo-holo RNA structures to characterize conformational differences and RNA-small molecule recognition. Candidate pairs were identified from the Protein Data Bank by matching RNA chains with at least 90% sequence identity and coverage, and fully conserved binding pocket nucleotides. The current release contains 434 binding pockets from 266 holo structures, linked to 186 apo structures to yield 1187 pocket-level apo-holo pairs organized into 734 database entries, spanning 150 small molecules and 23 RNA functional classes. Each entry integrates RNA sequence and secondary-structure annotations, apo and holo three-dimensional structures, RNA-ligand atomic interactions, and quantitative descriptors of global and local conformational changes. An interactive web interface enables users to explore sequence alignments and structural overlays, compare secondary structures and RNA motifs, and upload paired apo-holo structures for customized analysis. By linking ligand-bound and ligand-free RNA structures, SMARTFlexDB provides a robust foundation for investigating RNA structural flexibility and supporting RNA-targeted small-molecule drug discovery. The database and analysis platform are available at https://aidd.rc.ufl.edu/app/smartflexdb/.

papers.title: Assessment of trace metals and arsenic contamination in water and sediments in a former mining area of the river basin after an ecological disaster, Slana River, Slovakia
papers.abstract: This study assessed the spatial distribution of trace metals and arsenic in the water and sediment of the Slana River (Slovakia) approximately one and a half years after the 2022 release of mine water from the former Nizna Slana siderite mine. Samples were collected in September 2023 at four river sites from Gocovo to Lenartovce (L1-L4) and at five points within 50 m of the mine-water discharge (S0-S4), and the data were evaluated using non-parametric tests, principal component analysis, contamination factors (CF) and the pollution load index (PLI). At the discharge point, the water contained 149 mg/L Fe, 27 mg/L Mn and 0.29 mg/L As; beyond this point, however, most metals in the filtered river water were below the limit of detection, and only sulphur remained clearly elevated downstream (35.7 mg/L at L2 vs. 6.4 mg/L at the reference site). In contrast, the sediment retained the contamination: As reached 7920 mg/kg and Cd 39 mg/kg at the discharge, exceeding the probable effect concentrations of freshwater sediment quality guidelines more than 200-fold and almost eightfold, respectively, and As remained above this level at the first downstream site (47 mg/kg). While As, Hg, Mn and Ni declined rapidly downstream, S and Al accumulated toward the most distant site, so that the PLI remained uniform along the river (1.06-1.16; p = 0.246). Despite the apparent recovery of the water column, the sediments of the Slana River thus remain a persistent reservoir of arsenic and trace metals and a potential source of chronic exposure for biota; repeated sampling across seasons is needed to confirm this pattern.

papers.title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation
papers.abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception. In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing. Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear. Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

papers.title: CHORUS: A proteome-scale atlas of membrane protein interaction interfaces predicted from sequence
papers.abstract: Membrane protein interactions underpin essential cellular processes, yet the residues mediating these interactions remain difficult to identify at scale due to the paucity of experimentally resolved protein complexes within hydrophobic bilayers. Here, we present CHORUS, a sequence-only framework for predicting interaction interfaces in membrane proteins without requiring structural coordinates, multiple sequence alignments, or known interacting partners. By synthesizing complementary latent representations from three protein language models, CHORUS outperforms 18 established sequence- and structure-based methods by a chain-macro average precision value of 0.643 versus 0.613 for ScanNet-MSA on an independent, homology-restricted test set of 4,655 protein chain contexts, with a particularly pronounced advantage within the membrane-embedded interior (0.746 versus 0.645). Using six mammalian mitochondrial respiratory supercomplexes with >100 independent chains, we show that CHORUS-identified intersubunit interaction interfaces accurately delineate the boundaries between buried protein-protein contact surfaces and surrounding lipid-facing regions in complex molecular systems (0.945-0.984). We subsequently applied CHORUS at proteome scale to chart a global landscape of membrane-protein interaction interfaces for 80,619 expert-reviewed membrane protein entries, 70,247 unique sequences, 4,918 species, and 33.7 million residues across the tree of life. The resulting open-access CHORUS Atlas (https://chorus.atlas.sunnylab.org) provides predicted residue interactions across the membrane proteome. Together, CHORUS establishes a sequence-based foundation for systematic investigation of membrane protein assembly and function, potentially facilitating interactome-scale knowledge discovery and allosteric therapeutic design.

papers.title: Simulating Bead-Tethered Biomolecules: Force-Probe Coupled Steered Molecular Dynamics (fp-SMD) in Optical Tweezers Force Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Interpreting single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) data from optical tweezers with steered molecular dynamics (SMD) is hindered by a severe timescale mismatch: SMD trajectories span nanoseconds to microseconds, while SMFS experiments unfold over milliseconds to seconds, forcing SMD to pull six to nine orders of magnitude faster than experiment and systematically distorting rupture forces, molecular pathways, and kinetic intermediates. We introduce force-probe coupled steered molecular dynamics (fp-SMD), which explicitly propagates the force probe (the optically trapped bead) alongside the biomolecule within a single classical Hamiltonian description of the coupled molecule-linker-bead system. A Predict-Correct Trajectory Propagation (PCTP) scheme resolves the resulting computational bottleneck by alternating a bead-propagation step, with the molecular center of mass (COM) held fixed, and a molecular step in which metadynamics and transition-state theory identify the kinetically resolved intermediate reached at each macroscopic time step. On the cholesterol--{beta}-cyclodextrin ({beta}-CD) host-guest complex, fp-SMD reproduces the experimental rupture-force histogram directly at matched conditions, without extrapolation from standard SMD. fp-SMD further resolves how applied force reshapes the molecular escape pathway: we find that cholesterol dissociates via a high-angle route at low force and a direct, small-angle route at high force--providing, to our knowledge, the first direct structural evidence for force-induced pathway switching in a small host-guest system, a mechanism believed to underlie catch-slip bond behavior.

papers.title: Divergent NUMT mimicking functional coding region of the mitochondrial genome
papers.abstract: Using long read sequencing, we report here a NUMT (nuclear fragment of mitochondrial origin) in a sawfly species Euura vittata (Hymenoptera, Tenthredinidae) that contains the entire coding region with all the genes in the same order as in the mitochondrion. The NUMT is 3.2% different from the mitochondrial sequence (4.1% divergence for COI barcode region), yet appears entirely functional when assuming mitochondrial genetic code. The NUMT is unlikely to be functional because of the usage of standard genetic code in the nuclear genome. Examination of the NUMT containing contig of the whole genome assembly revealed no assembly issues and showed depth of coverage as expected for single copy nuclear genes, strongly suggesting nuclear integration rather than heteroplasmy. Based on mitochondrial COI data, the NUMT is most similar to a cluster of sequences containing mostly Euura tillbergi and related species (but also a few E. vittata specimens). The NUMT, therefore, may result from recent mitochondrial introgression explaining its divergence and misleading functional appearance. The implications are that reports of divergent heteroplasmy need to be validated with long read or RNA sequencing, or by other appropriate experiments.

papers.title: Spatial and developmental reprogramming enables root growth under high salinity
papers.abstract: How do plant roots sustain growth under salinity levels that would normally arrest development? The extremophyte Schrenkiella parvula maintains root growth under high salinity through a previously unrecognized spatial reorganization of primary root development. The root elongation zone transitions into two distinct developmental states, the bulged and gap zones, during a transient growth pause that precedes renewed tip growth and localized lateral root emergence. In Arabidopsis, a related salt-sensitive species, the cells in the elongation zone simply burst. Jasmonic acid was found to be necessary to initiate this transition in S. parvula, while spatially coordinated jasmonic acid and auxin accumulation accompanies zone establishment and maintenance. We constructed zone-resolved transcriptomic networks to distinguish developmental from salt-responsive processes and identified their interactions under salinity stress. Salt-induced zone-specific networks revealed distinct regulatory programs coordinating hormone signaling, cell wall remodeling, and water, ion, and reactive oxygen species homeostasis. Cell layer-specific Raman spectroscopy, UHPLC-MS/MS metabolite profiling, and cellular imaging provide independent support for the transcriptomic networks, linking spatially organized cellular responses with salt stress mitigation, suppression of cell death, and continued growth. We also identified orthologous genes potentially recruited into novel regulatory roles that support growth under stress. Together, these findings establish spatial developmental reprogramming as a strategy for sustaining root growth under salinity and identify candidate mechanisms for improving crop salt tolerance.

papers.title: A rational design strategy and validation for protease-resistant fusion-inhibitor antiviral peptides
papers.abstract: Peptide-based fusion inhibitors are promising pharmaceuticals in the fight against enveloped viruses relying on membrane fusion for host infection. However, peptide therapeutic applications have long been hindered by their poor stability in vivo. Here, we discovered that peptide inhibitors with the wildtype sequence of the heptad repeat 2 (HR2) domain of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein are efficiently cleaved by Transmembrane Protease, Serine 2 (TMPRSS2), a key protease involved in the SARS-CoV-2 virus-cell fusion pathway. We then identified the corresponding cleavage sites and designed three protease-resistant peptides using ranking based on deep mutational scanning and natural occurrence. The three candidates all exhibit inhibitory activity in a cell-cell fusion assay. A high-resolution cryo-EM structure of the top candidate, HR2-NHN, bound to its HR1 target reveals the molecular basis for its potent activity. The top candidate of the cell-based screening assay showed significantly improved efficacy relative to the wildtype peptide when administered at different times before infection in both an authentic virus-cell infection assay and a mouse assay. More broadly, our results suggest that the design strategies for protease-resistant peptides could be applied to a broad spectrum of other enveloped viruses and pave the way for the development of safe, prophylactic antivirals that can be administered before exposure.

papers.title: Covalently Functionalized Click Alginate Cryogels Enable Non-Invasive Near-Infrared Sensing of Gastric pH
papers.abstract: Gastric acidity shapes mucosal injury in reflux disease, peptic ulcer, and gastritis, yet is almost never measured. Acid-suppressive therapy, taken by approximately 40% of elderly adults, is therefore titrated on symptoms alone. A gastric sensor must hold onto its reporter in a highly acidic protease-rich environment, conditions that destabilize ionically crosslinked hydrogels and leach physically entrapped dyes. Click alginates, established in biomechanics and drug delivery but not as sensors, meet this requirement with a single chemistry: bioorthogonal tetrazine-norbornene crosslinks are stable in acid and against proteases, and excess norbornene from crosslinking becomes the anchoring site for the pH-sensitive reporter, so network and reporter are installed by the same mechanism. Cryogelation adds macroporosity for rapid gastric fluid influx. A screen identifies IRDye 680RD as the only near-infrared dye responsive across the targeted pH 2-5. Dye release stays below 1.5% in simulated gastric and intestinal fluids, and the pH response remains active after nine months of storage. In rats, the orally administered NIR fluorescent cryogel resolves pH 2.0 from pH 5.0 transabdominally and discriminates esomeprazole- from saline-treated animals, with extra-gastric organ and plasma fluorescence comparable to untreated controls. Ex vivo photoacoustic imaging shows pH-dependent contrast, pointing toward deeper-tissue detection. These results establish covalently functionalized cryogels as a non-invasive sensing platform for hostile physiological environments.

papers.title: Stress-induced Metabolic Remodeling of Adipose and Brain Tissue Revealed by Positron Emission Tomography
papers.abstract: Stress impacts our health and triggers physiological adaptations, yet the metabolic programs engaged during stress remain incompletely understood. To fill this knowledge gap, we utilize total-body positron emission tomography (PET), multi-OMICS, and endocrine profiling to assess how various murine stress models affect systemic metabolic remodeling. We find that acute immobilization and surgery activate brown adipose tissue as part of the stress response, independently of hypothermia, thereby acting as a highly stress-sensitive metabolic hub. Additionally, we identify stress-specific hypo- and hypermetabolic signatures in different brain regions, and distinguish networks between brain and adipose tissue depots across the different stress groups. Our work presents a novel perspective on stress and its mobilization of metabolic resources and identifies PET imaging of brain and adipose tissue as a valuable, minimally invasive technique for tracking metabolic stress responses in mice, with relevance for animal welfare and disease models, and translational impact for mental health studies and preventive medicine.

papers.title: Cell-state-dependent responses to PLK1 inhibition reveal a non-canonical microtubule-endolysosomal vulnerability in quiescent leukemia stem cells
papers.abstract: Relapse in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is frequently driven by therapy-resistant quiescent leukemia stem cells (LSCs). We show that inhibition of the mitotic master regulator Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1), a kinase extensively pursued for antiproliferative therapy, unexpectedly eradicates quiescent LSCs through a mechanism distinct from its canonical mitotic function. In proliferating AML cells, PLK1 inhibition (PLK1i) induced G2/M arrest and mitotic catastrophe. In contrast, quiescence-enriched LSCs underwent apoptosis independent of mitotic arrest, revealing a cell-state-dependent mode of drug action. Mechanistically, PLK1i perturbed vesicle trafficking and endolysosomal homeostasis in LSC by disrupting a previously unrecognized PLK1-MAP1A interaction, leading to apoptotic cell death. Combinatorial pharmacologic perturbation studies established microtubule regulation as a critical determinant of quiescent LSC survival, while ex vivo and in vivo assays demonstrated depletion of functionally-defined LSC following PLK1i. These findings identify non-canonical effects of PLK1i in LSC and uncover a targetable vulnerability linked to microtubule and endolysosomal homeostasis.

papers.title: K2P Channels Regulate Presynaptic Organisation through a Membrane Potential-Independent Mechanism
papers.abstract: Neuronal ion channels have well-established effects on synaptic plasticity, in many cases by influencing pathways that depend on membrane excitability. Here we find that a C. elegans two-pore domain potassium (K2P) channel, TWK-40, regulates presynaptic organisation through a membrane potential-independent mechanism. Instead, this mechanism depends on TWK-40's effects on intracellular potassium levels. Loss-of-function mutations in twk-40 lead to excessive presynaptic protein accumulation, while gain-of-function mutations lead to depleted presynaptic components and cause synaptic transmission deficits. These changes in presynaptic protein abundance are phenocopied by transporter mutations predicted to alter intracellular potassium homeostasis in the same direction as TWK-40 mutations, but not by sodium channel mutations that mimic its effects on membrane excitability. This indicates that cytoplasmic potassium promotes presynaptic assembly. This process depends on pyruvate kinase PYK-1, a potassium-sensitive enzyme, and three transcription factors. These findings establish a new pathway linking neuronal potassium homeostasis to the control of presynaptic organisation and synaptic function.

papers.title: Novel, highly divergent clones in Listeria monocytogenes serotype 4b in North America: Sublineages 782 and 1039, members of the hypervirulent clonal complex 2
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive bacterial foodborne pathogen responsible for the severe illness listeriosis. Of the 14 L. monocytogenes serotypes, serotype 4b is a major contributor to human listeriosis and encompasses all four leading hypervirulent clonal complexes (CCs), including the ancient, ubiquitous CC2. CC2 is globally dominated by sublineage (SL) 2, responsible for most human CC2-associated cases. Here we describe two other CC2 SLs, SLs 782 and 1039. These SLs are newly recognized, having been reported only since 2002, and to date are encountered exclusively in North America. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that they are strikingly divergent from each other as well as from SL2. SL782 and SL1039 have been implicated in human listeriosis and have also been repeatedly isolated from surface water and wildlife in North America, with several of these environmental strains exhibiting high genomic similarity ([≤]7 core genome allelic mismatches) to strains from human listeriosis. They share an unusual resistance profile towards a panel of Listeria wide-host-range-phages and exhibit several distinct lineage-specific traits. Specifically, SL782 universally lacks a gene otherwise unique to and conserved in serotype 4b and harbors the Listeria pathogenicity island LIPI-4, while SL1039 harbors LIPI-3 and is almost always resistant to tetracycline, harboring the novel Tn916-like transposon Tn916.1039. These and other traits may have driven clonal emergence of SL782 and SL1039, potentially via adaptations in natural ecosystems.

papers.title: Lymphangiogenesis is Critical for Healing and Survival in a Murine Model of Laryngotracheal Injury
papers.abstract: Objective: Lymphatic dysfunction has been implicated in exacerbating fibrosis in numerous diseases, yet the role of the lymphatic system in laryngotracheal injury has not previously been explored. This study aims to evaluate lymphatic vascular remodeling in a murine model of laryngotracheal stenosis (LTS) and determine how pharmacologic blockade of lymphangiogenesis impacts airway healing after mucosal injury. Methods: LTS was induced in C57BL6 mice using an established chemomechanical injury model. Lymphatic density was quantified using LYVE-1 immunohistochemistry. Mice were treated with the VEGFR-3-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor SAR131675 to block lymphangiogenesis after injury. Outcomes assessed included survival, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and Evans blue dye vascular leakage. Results: Laryngotracheal injury induced a substantial increase in subepithelial lymphatic vessel density concomitant with fibrotic remodeling. Pharmacologic inhibition of VEGFR-3 signaling with SAR131675 abrogated this lymphangiogenic response and resulted in markedly increased mortality, impaired epithelial repair with obstructive sloughing, increased edema, and persistent histopathologic evidence of tissue injury. A qualitative increase in pathologic fibrocellular remodeling was also observed, though with no measurable difference in lamina propria thickness. Conclusion: These findings establish lymphatic remodeling as an essential component of successful airway repair following mucosal injury. Lymphatic dysfunction is a common feature of known risk factors for LTS including diabetes, obesity, and prematurity, and can be exacerbated by positive pressure ventilation. Disruption of the lymphangiogenic response to airway injury may lead to stasis of pro-inflammatory factors that result in chronic inflammation, maladaptive remodeling, and pathologic tissue changes. The lymphatic vasculature is a viable target for future mechanistic study and potential therapeutic intervention following airway injury.

papers.title: Reconfiguration of default mode metabolic demands and network organization during acute stress
papers.abstract: Psychosocial stress engages coordinated physiological and neural responses that enable adaptation to environmental challenges. Maladaptive stress responses and reduced resilience are major risk factors for psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. As the brain's metabolic response to stress remains largely unexplored, we used simultaneous [18F]FDG PET/MRI during performance of the Montreal Imaging Stress Task to assess cerebral glucose metabolism, BOLD activation and functional connectivity.
