The optimized production medium consisted of carbon @7.9 %, nitrogen @ 1.1% and agitation rate 180 r.p.m. This was provided by adding glucose @ 2%, ammonium nitrate @0.2%, mustard oil seed meal @10% and whey@ 10% in modified Bushnell Haas broth. The biosurfactant produced retained its properties during exposure to a wide range of pH values (5-11), high temperatures (up to 121C), high salinities of up to 5% and also five -fold concentration. Approximately three- fold increase in yield of the biosurfactant (25g/L to 68.5g/L) was obtained upon scaling-up the production from 100ml to 1500 ml in a lab scale fermenter with agitation @ 150r.p.m. and D.O. levels maintained at 6mg/L. Power calculations and the cost thereof was calculated (Rs 10.24 /L) and summed up with the cost of raw materials Rs 8.40/L and found to be Rs 18.64/L of product .Since 68.5g product is present in 1L, the cost is calculated to be Rs 271/- per kg. Comparison with selling price of currently used chemical surfactants like Linear Alkyl Benzene sulphonic acid (LAB) and sodium Lauryl sulphate and Sodium Lauryl ether sulphate (SLS and SLES) reveals that prices of these products varies from Rs 120 to 600 per kg depending on manufacturer and quality, order quantity. From the above studies it can be seen that production and use of this multiutility biosurfactant has, besides a clear advantage over chemically produced surfactants in terms of sustainability, a fairly good comparison with selling price of currently used chemical surfactants. The present study on the production costs (excluding capital costs) successfully demonstrates a break even analysis into the production of biosurfactants.

papers.title: Evolutionary rewiring of regulatory topology refines butterfly wing patterns
papers.abstract: Phenotypes evolve through changes in gene regulatory networks (GRNs), but how changes in network topology contribute to phenotypic evolution is still poorly understood. Butterfly wing color patterns provide a tractable system to answer this question. Here, we characterized spatiotemporal expression of four color pattern genes, WntA, pdm3, ivory, and Optix, in five nymphalid butterflies, and tested their regulatory connections in WntA-associated patterns through genetic perturbations in three species spanning 80 million years of divergence. We found broadly conserved 1) regulatory hierarchy linking early pattern instruction via WntA signaling to subsequent color readout via ivory and Optix, 2) positive autoregulation in WntA signaling, and 3) positive regulation from WntA signaling to pdm3. The WntA-pdm3 axis, however, produced detectable color pattern readouts only in Vanessa cardui. In this species, additional negative feedback from pdm3 to WntA signaling closes a reciprocal WntA-pdm3 feedback loop that refines spatially separated pattern elements. We show that developmental programs can evolve by rewiring internal interactions among pre-existing GRN nodes, emphasizing the importance of network topology in phenotypic evolution.

papers.title: DNA polymerase kappa supports repair-associated DNA synthesis and genome maintenance in postmitotic neurons
papers.abstract: Postmitotic neurons depend on continuous DNA repair to preserve genome integrity, yet the polymerases supporting repair-associated DNA synthesis remain poorly defined. Here, we identify DNA polymerase kappa (POLK), a Y-family translesion synthesis polymerase studied predominantly in proliferating cells, as a regulator of DNA synthesis and genome maintenance in postmitotic neurons. Using primary mouse cortical neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain neurons, we show that POLK localizes near newly synthesized DNA and repair-associated proteins, including ubiquitinated PCNA. POLK depletion reduces DNA synthesis in both mouse and human neurons and promotes nuclear and organelle remodeling, p21-associated senescence-like stress, inflammatory responses, and increased p38 MAPK immunoreactivity. In an Alzheimer's disease-risk genetic background, POLK depletion also increases cytoplasmic double-stranded DNA and tau phosphorylation. Conversely, POLK overexpression enhances neuronal DNA synthesis while reducing DNA damage-associated signals, p38 MAPK immunoreactivity, cytoplasmic DNA, and Alzheimer's disease-relevant phenotypes. These findings uncover a role for POLK in postmitotic neuronal genome maintenance, linking specialized DNA polymerase function to neuronal stress and vulnerability relevant to aging and neurodegeneration.

papers.title: BMP4 Restricts Axonal Ramification and Bouton Density in Cholinergic Projections from the Basal Forebrain
papers.abstract: Axonal projections and precise synapse formation are essential for the establishment of functional neural circuits, and their dysregulation contributes to various psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Although numerous extracellular cues secreted from surrounding tissues regulate axon guidance and synapse formation, the mechanisms by which neurons locally regulate terminal patterning within their projection fields remain poorly understood. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) is a classical morphogen that is involved in early neural tube patterning during development. However, its postnatal function remains unclear. Previous in vitro studies using hippocampal glutamatergic neurons demonstrated that BMP4 can act locally on axons to suppress synapse formation, raising the possibility that BMP4 regulates terminal differentiation after target innervation. Here, we investigated the role of BMP4 in postnatal cholinergic circuit development using cholinergic neuron-specific Bmp4 conditional knockout (Bmp4 cKO) mice, with adult analyses performed in males. Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons project extensively throughout the neocortex and are essential for higher brain functions, including arousal and attention. Bmp4 cKO mice exhibited increased cholinergic axon terminals in the neocortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, as well as increased axonal ramification in the neocortex without affecting cytoarchitectonic organization or cholinergic neuron numbers in the basal forebrain. These findings demonstrate that BMP4 functions as a negative regulator of cholinergic terminal formation and axonal arborization, suggesting that BMP4 may act locally to restrict cholinergic axonal expansion during neural circuit maturation.

papers.title: MCseg: AI agent-guided workflow search for no-code cell segmentation and transcript attribution in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-level analysis of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics depends on accurate segmentation and transcript assignment, yet current workflows often trade transcript capture for boundary purity and can require substantial image-analysis expertise. We developed MCseg, a downloadable no-code platform whose fixed segmentation engine was derived by an AI-agent-guided search in which an AI agent iteratively proposed and evaluated combinations of image-processing and segmentation operations against Xenium-derived cell boundaries. In a lung adenocarcinoma development set, fixed-parameter MCseg increased mean panoptic quality from 0.432 to 0.472 relative to an Optuna-tuned two-diameter Cellpose baseline, while a reference-guided calibration analysis reached 0.554. In an independent expert-annotated colorectal cancer region, MCseg showed higher lineage recall and micro-F1 than the StarDist-based ENACT workflow among cells covered by both methods. Across 15 colorectal cancer regions, MCseg increased neighborhood expression discordance and reduced lineage-exclusive co-expression relative to Space Ranger at similar UMI density. The fixed workflow also transferred to fresh-frozen breast cancer without tissue-specific architecture search, illustrating an agent-guided route to reproducible, locally deployable cell-level spatial transcriptomic analysis.

papers.title: Policy regularization as a unifying theory of the striatal division of labor in learning
papers.abstract: Learning novel behaviors requires balancing previously learned actions with the ability to flexibly adapt to changing reward contingencies. This trade-off is well documented in the division of labor between dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which promotes selection of cached, history-dependent actions, and dorsomedial striatum (DMS), which supports flexible learning as reward contingencies change. Here, we propose policy regularization as a general computational principle for understanding this division. Capacity-limited agents face a fundamental trade-off between maximizing reward and minimizing the cost of deviating from a default policy that caches frequently used action transitions. We formalize this trade-off as a KL-regularized reward objective in which a flexible controller (DMS) incurs a cost for diverging from a history-dependent default (DLS). The resulting optimal policy is a combination of a reward-driven action value, continuously updated by DMS, and a default policy conditioned on action history, cached by DLS. In practice, DLS consolidates the action transitions shaped by DMS's reward-driven value learning, so DLS preserves behaviors that were once optimal even when reward contingencies change, producing robust but inflexible action selection and effectively "regularizing" DMS-driven learning. We show that a single model, with a single set of learning and lesion parameters, shared across paradigms, provides a unifying explanation for the functional organization of the striatum, reproducing canonical DLS-DMS dissociations in outcome devaluation, serial spatial reversal, skilled action sequencing, and motor sequence execution tasks.

papers.title: NeuroGraphBench: Interacting with Drosophila Connectomes at Scale for Exploring the Functional Logic of Neural Circuits
papers.abstract: Drosophila connectomic datasets provide increasingly comprehensive maps of neuronal morphology and synaptic connectivity, offering an unprecedented opportunity to explore the structural organization of its neural circuits. This calls for designing automated tools to interact with connectomic datasets at scale for efficiently exploring structural features embedded in the vast amounts of data. Yet the central challenge remains the understanding of the functional logic of neural circuits. In order to formulate a connectome-grounded hypothesis for what a circuit computes, it is critical to (i) characterize the objects in the natural environment in which brain circuits operate, and (ii) formulate how brain circuits represent and process the defined objects. To develop and demonstrate a methodology for these requirements, we focus on the Drosophila looming-evoked escape pathway. We modeled the trajectory of looming objects that are on a collision course (direct-hits) or pass by the fly (near-misses): their projected images on the retina can be characterized by the subtended solid angle and center elevation. By analyzing the sub-neuronal structure and retinotopic organization of the looming pathway embedded in connectomic datasets, we devised a pathway abstraction, and mapped its structural elements into a connectome-grounded functional model. We demonstrate that (i) the expanding boundary of a looming object activates an annulus of LPLC2 neurons, and (ii) the Giant Fiber reads out this population code through its two dendritic branches, modeled as separate units whose outputs are combined to drive its axon. It is this functional separation of the dendritic branches that gives the model access to the center elevation, separating direct-hits from near-misses well before the solid angle of the two trajectories diverge. To accelerate the connectomic analysis step, we developed a Python toolset with an agentic, code-free workspace interface called NeuroGraphBench (NGB). NGB provides four composable morphology-analysis primitives and an AI Agent that composes them to interactively respond to natural-language queries aided by visualization on an interactive 3D canvas. Thus, NGB automates tedious and repetitive tasks to enable faster and scalable connectomic exploration, keeping human reasoning, instead of writing code, at the center of an open-ended research inquiry.

papers.title: Impaired formation and updating of internal predictive models in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
papers.abstract: Predictive coding frameworks propose that perception emerges from a continuous comparison of incoming sensory signals with internally generated predictions, with mismatches between the two computed as prediction errors. Disruptions to the balance between these top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory signals are theorized to contribute to sensory abnormalities in neuropsychiatric conditions like autism spectrum disorders. However, disambiguating bottom-up from top-down contributions to sensory processing remains a difficult challenge, particularly in animal models. Here we develop a probabilistic oddball detection task in which rats must track local statistics within a trial to detect a deviant stimulus, as well as global statistics across trials to anticipate when a deviant will occur. This design enables formation of experimentally specified internal models of deviant expectation that can be quantitatively derived from behavior and manipulated independently of local stimulus statistics. We used this task to characterize sensory predictive behavior in a Fmr1 KO rat model of Fragile X Syndrome, the most common monogenic cause of autism. Male Fmr1 KO rats detected deviant stimuli at wildtype levels but exhibited reduced anticipation of deviant occurrence based on cross-trial statistics and failed to adapt their behavior when these statistics changed. Computational modeling revealed that these behavioral deficits reflected an overweighting of immediate sensory evidence and temporal response pressure at the expense of learned predictive expectations, consistent with imprecise internal models skewed towards sensory immediacy. These findings provide evidence for disrupted predictive processing in Fragile X Syndrome, consistent with active inference accounts of autism, and highlight the utility of this probabilistic oddball task design for interrogating predictive coding and perceptual impairments in neuropsychiatric conditions.

papers.title: Engineered trophoblast organoids recapitulate molecular and functional features of preeclampsia
papers.abstract: Preeclampsia is a major pregnancy complication driven by placental dysfunction, yet research is limited by reliance on patient-derived tissues and models that do not fully capture human disease. Here, we develop a genetically engineered human trophoblast organoid model of preeclampsia that can be generated without access to placental tissue. Using a CRISPR-based Prime Integrase strategy, we engineered induced trophoblast stem cells to express the preeclampsia-associated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) exon 15a isoform. Engineered organoids showed a transcriptional shift towards primary preeclamptic placentae and developed several features of disease. These included reduced PlGF, increased IL-6 and soluble endoglin, oxidative stress, impaired growth and an elevated sFlt-1/PlGF ratio comparable to primary preeclamptic trophoblast organoids. These broader changes were not reproduced by adding recombinant human sFlt-1 to control organoids. Conditioned media from engineered organoids impaired endothelial network formation, demonstrating a functional effect of the altered trophoblast secretome. Treatment with sulfasalazine and metformin also restored angiogenic balance and organoid growth. Together, these findings establish a tractable human model that reproduces molecular and functional features of preeclampsia and provides a platform to study disease mechanisms and test potential therapies.

papers.title: Structure constrained spin responses of an FMN superoxide radical-pair model in mitochondrial complex I
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial complex I produces reactive oxygen species at its flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor. We combined steric sampling of oxygen positions in human complex I with radical-pair spin simulations to examine how the FMN pocket shapes reaction yield sensitivity, which provided singlet yields across FMN O2 centroid separations, magnetic fields and spin dephasing conditions. When candidate oxygen positions overlapping the FMN cofactor itself were excluded, almost no accessible positions remained within 3.3 A of the isoalloxazine centre (0.2%), and a composite score combining geometric accessibility with normalised field and dephasing responses had no near-contact maximum. In the reference structure (PDB 5XTD), the highest-scoring 10% of accessible configurations had a mean separation of 5.8 A (2.5th~97.5th percentiles, 5.6~6.0 A); in the independently determined 9TI4 structure, the corresponding mean was 7.9 A (7.7~8.0 A), reflecting differences in the modelled pocket. Within each structure, this location changed little when the dephasing model, flavin hyperfine parameters, steric radii and recombination/dephasing rates were varied. Over 2.5~20 A, the exchange only score formed a broad plateau without a localized maximum. Small prescribed fluctuations in separation produced less singlet yield variability in the high scoring configurations than elsewhere in the accessible ensemble. A near contact score maximum reported in an earlier version of this analysis arose because positions overlapping FMN had been counted as accessible. The accessibility-weighted spin-response map of the complex I flavin site is therefore set mainly by pocket geometry and should be evaluated over structural ensembles rather than a single model.

papers.title: Partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition mediates profound gap closure through growth and fluidization
papers.abstract: Epithelial gap closure is essential for maintaining tissue integrity during development and wound healing. Previous studies have shown that closure of small gaps is driven by actomyosin purse-string contraction and traction forces generated at the gap edge. Here, we show that millimeter-scale circular gap closure in mouse epicardial (MEC1) monolayers is driven primarily by growth-mediated compressive stresses. Compared with MDCK monolayers, MEC1 cells close gaps more rapidly with reduced undulation near gap edge through coordinated tissue-wide extension-contraction. The collective closing dynamics can be modulated by partial epithelial mesenchymal transition induction and Rho kinase inhibition. By integrating tissue and cell kinematic analyses, traction force mapping, and a continuum framework that decomposes tissue strain rates into growth, elastic, and fluidity related contributions, we reveal that growth-generated compression drives inward tissue flow, while elastic cell elongation and fluid-like tissue remodeling through cell cell intercalation act synergistically to accommodate deformation and promote robust collective gap closure.

papers.title: Dosimetric Characterization and Workflow Optimization of the FLASH-SARRP for Reliable Preclinical Radiobiological Studies
papers.abstract: Objective: The reliable use of preclinical small-animal irradiators requires dosimetric characterization and quality assurance (QA) protocols. This study aimed to characterize the FLASH-SARRP, a dual-tube small-animal X-ray irradiator capable of ultra-high dose-rate (UHDR) delivery, as well as to establish and validate a practical QA workflow that improves dose reproducibility for preclinical FLASH experiments. Approach: A combined dosimetric approach using Gafchromic films for spatial dose assessment and a plastic scintillating fiber for real-time temporal monitoring, was used to evaluate beam characteristics. Custom 3D-printed spacers were designed to ensure reproducible experimental configurations. The temporal pulse structure of the two X-ray tubes and their synchronization during simultaneous irradiation were investigated using scintillating fiber measurements. Based on the findings of the two dosimeters, a QA workflow was implemented and validated, which uses a cross-calibration between the Gafchromic film and the scintillating fiber in the experimental setup, followed by pre-irradiation verification with the fiber to compensate for day-to-day output variations. Main results: Simultaneous irradiation of both X-ray tubes achieved dose-rates of approximately 80 Gy/s inside a homogeneous irradiation field suitable for small-animal studies. Temporal measurements revealed an average delay of 10 ms in between the two X-ray tubes, resulting in temporal dose-rate heterogeneity throughout the delivery of the dose. Additionally, a substantial inter-session variability of approximately 11% was found, whereas the intra-session variability was relatively low around ~4%. Implementation of the proposed QA workflow reduced the inter-session variability to around 5%, approaching the intrinsic intra-session variability of the machine. Significance: This work highlights the importance of temporal dosimetry for preclinical FLASH studies, as a measurable desynchronization between the two X-ray tubes was identified, generating temporal dose-rate heterogeneity that would not be detected by integrated dose measurements alone. The proposed QA framework improves reproducibility and provides a practical approach for reliable preclinical investigations.

papers.title: Increased CA3 burst activity in Doc2α and Syt7 knockout mice
papers.abstract: The hippocampal CA3 subfield is central to associative learning and memory consolidation. CA3 pyramidal neurons execute these functions by generating hypersynchronous bursts that feed forward to the CA1. Extensive recurrent collateral connections within CA3 are crucial for the generation of this burst activity. Double C2 domain-containing protein (Doc2) and synaptotagmin 7 (Syt7) are high-affinity calcium sensors implicated in asynchronous release (AR) of neurotransmitter and in the exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (DCVs). Additionally, Doc2 is a sensor for miniature neurotransmission, whereas Syt7 is involved in synaptic facilitation and SV replenishment. Both Doc2 and Syt7 are expressed in the hippocampus, but their potential roles in spontaneously bursting networks, like CA3, remain unanswered. Using whole-cell recordings at near physiological conditions (33-34 {degrees}C and 1.2 mM Ca2+) in acute hippocampal slices obtained from juvenile (P15-21) KO mice lacking Doc2, Syt7, or both proteins, we report no changes in spontaneous inhibitory or excitatory postsynaptic current frequency or amplitude in CA1 pyramidal neurons. However, there was a marked increase in burst activity, originating in CA3, in all three KO conditions; this was not due to changes in AR or the intrinsic properties of CA3 pyramidal neurons. We propose that this novel burst phenotype in Doc2- and Syt7-KO mice is unrelated to changes in neurotransmitter release but might be mediated by changes in neuropeptide release from DCVs in the CA3 subfield, or along upstream pathways. Regardless of the underlying mechanisms, this work reveals that both Doc2 and Syt7 act to regulate network activity.

papers.title: Modeling and validation of parallel co-flows layer widths of viscous liquids in open-capillary trigger valve systems
papers.abstract: Control of fluids is a hallmark of microfluidic systems and fundamental for the successful application of microfluidic devices. Trigger valves use geometric features to autonomously control the release of fluids in microfluidic devices. Our previous work has adapted geometries used in closed trigger valve systems to enable use in open systems, allowing for open microfluidic devices with up to three trigger valves. Here, we focus on the parallel co-flows produced by sequential release of trigger valves and present a model that predicts their layer widths as a function of the geometric characteristics of the different side channels of each trigger valve. We show layered co-flows with widths as low as 50 microns. Additionally, we expand the use of trigger valves in open microfluidic devices by incorporating 1) varied step heights, 2) devices with up to seven trigger valves, and 3) use of varied fluids and plastics including an application with fibroblasts in collagen. To validate the implementation and use of these trigger valves in open systems, we have developed a theoretical framework to compare predicted outcomes (i.e., fluid travel distance, velocity, and layering width) with our experimental values. This theoretical work offers applications in various fields, including hydrogel patterning for 3D cell culture, organ-on-a-chip models, at-home sample preparation, and autonomous microfluidic systems for biosensing.

papers.title: An ecological origin of the asymmetry of human color discrimination: evidence from psychophysics, MEG, and deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Hue is a powerful cue for object discrimination, but human color discrimination is anisotropic: hue thresholds are lower than chroma thresholds for orangish colors, but nearly equal for purplish colors. Here we show that this asymmetry reflects environmental color statistics rather than being a fixed consequence of cone-opponent architecture. Across fifteen image and reflectance databases, orangish hues accounted for 62.5% of chromatic samples, compared with 5.3% for purplish hues. We replicated the hue-chroma asymmetry psychophysically in 44 participants. Magnetoencephalography revealed a corresponding neural asymmetry, with superior decoding of orangish hue differences emerging around 250 ms after stimulus onset. Deep neural networks trained on naturalistic image datasets reproduced the human-like asymmetry without explicit color supervision. Critically, training on hue-inverted images reversed the asymmetry, producing greater hue sensitivity for purplish than for orangish colors. These results suggest that the geometry of color discrimination is shaped by ecological chromatic structure.

papers.title: A collaborative submission model for building high-quality data resources at scale through partnership: lessons from single-cell genomics
papers.abstract: Community data resources that aggregate datasets across studies are critical infrastructure for modern biomedical research, accelerating discovery, and rapidly-advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) models place ever-greater demand on large, well-described data corpora. However, building these resources involves a fundamental tension: comprehensive metadata is imperative for reuse, yet capturing this information systematically requires substantial effort that limits growth. We detail how CZ CELLxGENE Discover has used a collaborative submission model, whereby data contributors partner with dedicated resource curators, to become a large, widely used single-cell genomics resource for diverse analytical applications including AI model development and integrative analysis. This partnership leverages contributors' intimate study knowledge and curators' focus on data reuse and expertise in standardization to improve data quality, metadata accuracy, and richness. This is achieved by motivating researcher participation through tangible benefits while minimizing submission burden. We contrast this collaborative model with contributor-driven and resource-driven approaches, highlighting tradeoffs in scalability, consistency across submissions, and quality assurance. The principles and practices we describe provide a framework for building high-quality community data resources across diverse biological data types.

papers.title: An agent-built, verified atlas of public spatial transcriptomics shows that breadth across studies drives transfer and reproducibility
papers.abstract: Public spatial transcriptomics data are deposited study by study, in formats that differ from one laboratory to the next, and no resource has yet indexed or verified them as a whole. Here we present SpatialDataAgent-DB, an atlas built from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) by SpatialDataAgent, a workflow in which language-model agents do the work and every output is checked rather than trusted. An assay index covering all 298,179 GEO series identifies 2,411 spatial series, which gives public spatial data an explicit denominator. For each series, an agent writes conversion code instead of editing the data directly, and a frozen, rule-based scorer recomputes every released value from the source files. In a held-out test, the scorer rejected all 1,231 corrupted copies. We also visually reviewed every released sample, including the 4,386 H&E-registered Visium samples of our earlier HESRT release. SpatialDataAgent-DB contains 12,163 samples from 12 platforms and 42 species in a single format, each with its provenance and defect flags. Its 8,211 image-paired samples are 5.9 times as many as in the next image-paired resource, and at least 71% of all samples are absent from five existing catalogues. Without batch correction, sequencing-based samples group by organ more than by platform: with platforms balanced, organ explains 32% of the variance of human pseudobulk profiles and platform 13% (mouse, 47% and 18%). We then used the atlas in two applications. Image-to-expression models trained on it transfer to unseen studies, and their accuracy rises steadily with training data and, at a fixed number of patches, with the number of training studies over the range tested (for H&E, Pearson r gains 0.0056 per doubling of training patches up to 524,288); 11 of 13 forecasts locked in advance were confirmed. Adding studies helps more than adding patches from the same studies, because each study leaves a fingerprint in its images. Intent-based search over the same index assembled 70 single-cell dementia studies, and the replication of disease signatures in held-out studies rose steadily with the number of studies (direction agreement averaged over 28 held-out studies, 63% with one study and 77% with 16). In both applications, performance kept rising with the number of independent studies, which a complete and verified atlas is built to provide.

papers.title: Stochastic failure accumulation as a foundation for exponential mortality and selective disappearance
papers.abstract: Most organisms become increasingly likely to die as they grow older, a phenomenon known as demographic senescence. We develop a general mathematical framework for modelling senescence in which individuals are viewed as comprising a fixed number of interacting intra-organismal sub-systems, each characterised by stochastic failure and repair rates. In many organisms, `failure begets failure' because sub-systems are typically interdependent. We use diffusion approximations to derive an expression for population-level mortality curves in this setting, and demonstrate that greater interdependence leads to faster rates of senescence. Since individuals who die can no longer age, observed cohorts become increasingly composed of `lucky' individuals that avoided death by (stochastically) taking paths in failure space associated with lower mortality despite no intrinsic differences in their quality. Selective disappearance of `unlucky' individuals generates deviations of population-level measurements from individual-level trajectories, causing late-life mortality plateaus. We show that while these deviations must always exist, they may often be too small to detect, either because the failure accumulation process is stereotyped or because detection requires unreasonably large cohort sizes. We provide necessary and asymptotically sufficient conditions for Gompertz-Makeham mortality in our framework, with falsifiable predictions in terms of a scaling law for mortality near complete failure. We also show that the simplest null model in our framework leads to exact Gompertz-Makeham curves. Our work establishes a general framework for modelling demographic senescence and selective disappearance from biological first principles, and provides concrete predictions for when Gompertz-Makeham mortality emerges in such models.

papers.title: The effect of a reduction in population size on mean fitness and inbreeding depression
papers.abstract: A sudden reduction in population size increases the rate of genetic drift, reducing variability and increasing the mean level of homozygosity. The resulting increase in exposure of strongly deleterious, recessive or partially recessive alleles to selection against homozygotes may lead to their being purged from the population, potentially allowing mean fitness to increase after an initial decline, and accelerating the decline in inbreeding depression associated with reduced variability. However, detailed population genetic theory on the effects of population bottlenecks on mean fitness and inbreeding depression remains limited. We develop a theoretical framework for small, randomly mating populations founded from a large population at mutation-selection-drift equilibrium, using both simulations and approximate analytical results. These provide quantitative predictions for the dynamics of the population's mean fitness and level of inbreeding depression following a bottleneck. In particular, we derive an approximate expression for the time needed for mean fitness to recover after an initial decline; such a recovery requires selection to be sufficiently strong relative to drift, and mutations to be sufficiently recessive. In contrast, weakly deleterious mutations cause reductions in mean fitness and inbreeding depression that are similar in size to those predicted from increases in homozygosity for neutral alleles, over the relatively short timescales considered here.

papers.title: Single-nucleus profiling reveals age-associated remodeling opposed by parity in the postmenopausal human ovary
papers.abstract: The postmenopausal ovary is commonly viewed as a largely quiescent organ, yet its cellular biology remains incompletely characterized. We generated a single-nucleus atlas of the aging postmenopausal human ovary comprising 439,011 nuclei across 64 ovarian samples from 28 donors. We resolved 37 cell states, revealing extensive stromal, vascular, and immune heterogeneity. We developed an interactive data explorer to facilitate interrogation of cell annotations and gene expression across the atlas. Aging was associated with expansion of stress-associated stromal states, vascular and immune depletion, and a shift toward steroidogenic and androgen-responsive programs. Several major age-associated compositional shifts were supported in an external GTEx ovary bulk RNA-seq cohort, validating relevance. Parity (1-3 versus 0 live births) was associated with transcriptional and compositional patterns broadly opposing age-associated remodeling. Our findings establish the postmenopausal ovary as an actively remodeled aging tissue and link obstetric history to molecular and cellular signatures detectable later in life.

papers.title: Box-Counting Fractal Dimensions of Cranial Suture: Effects of Measurement Conditions and Model-Based Reproduction of Fractal-Like Patterns
papers.abstract: Cranial sutures are important structures associated with skull growth, and it is widely believed that cranial sutures exhibit fractal structure. However, measurement conditions and analytical procedures have varied among studies, making direct comparison and interpretation difficult. In this study, we reviewed previous measurements and established a standardized box-counting protocol for the fractal dimension (FD) of cranial sutures by quantifying the effects of skeletonization and scale-range selection. Using this protocol, we quantified FD in 45 digitized images of human lambdoid sutures and in eight structure-formation model variants: step, Gaussian, and Mexican-hat kernels; absolute-value and sine $F_{\mathrm{base}}$ fields; low-frequency noise; a time-dependent kernel; and a given-pattern initialization. We tested whether each model can generate structures with FD values at least as high as those of real sutures using one-sided Welch $t$-tests with Bonferroni correction for eight comparisons ($\alpha_{\mathrm{adj}} = 0.00625$), and found that six of eight model variants satisfied this criterion. Analysis of scale-dependent FD further revealed that FD is close to 1 at fine scales and approaches 2 at coarse scales in both real and model-generated patterns, indicating that cranial sutures are better described as finite-range fractal-like structures than as strict fractals, and that the box-counting FD is a scale-conditioned descriptor sensitive to preprocessing choices.

papers.title: Isolation and Purification-Free Digital Single-Small Extracellular Vesicle Biosensing with Scalable Plasmonic Arrays
papers.abstract: Recent advances in plasmonic biosensing and imaging have enabled label-free analysis of single biological nanoparticles. We previously developed PlAsmonic NanOapeRture lAbel-free iMAging (PANORAMA) for isolation and purification-free, digital counting and precise localization of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), with complementary fluorescence interrogation of surface and intravesicular biomarkers for quantitative molecular profiling. The fact that no isolation and purification or isolation is needed represents a crucial advantage because various specificity, efficiency, and time-consumption issues hinder quantitatively reproducible extraction of sEVs from biological fluids. PANORAMA achieves ultrahigh refractive-index sensitivity through arrayed gold nanodisks on invisible substrates (AGNIS) fabricated by nanosphere lithography (NSL). However, despite its simplicity and low cost, NSL is frequently constrained by poor large-area uniformity, which hinders scalable fabrication. Here, we introduce nanosphere settling lithography (NSSL) as an alternative to the gold-standard Langmuir Blodgett trough (LBT) process, enabling highly uniform, large-area monolayers with reduced process stringency. AGNIS fabricated via NSSL exhibits high refractive-index sensitivity with low spatial variability across 60 mm 24 mm substrates, sufficient for 60-well in standard 384-well plate format. The platform demonstrates exquisite sensitivity through PANORAMA digital counting and sizing of 25, 50, and 100 nm polystyrene beads, as well as single-vesicle characterization of sEVs derived from H460 lung cancer cells. For the first time, combined PANORAMA and fluorescence imaging enables quantitative analysis of microRNA-21 (miR-21) expression in sEVs to identify cancer-suspicious sub-population from liver cancer patient plasma in an unbiased fashion allowing both highly sensitive detection of individual sEVs and simultaneous molecular profiling. Collectively, NSSL enables uniform, high-performance plasmonic biosensing over large areas, providing a scalable and economical pathway for high-throughput, digital single-sEV analysis and translational liquid biopsy applications.

papers.title: Temporal Phosphoproteomic Network Reconstruction of Condition-Dependent EGFR Signaling Routes Through Unmeasured Proteins
papers.abstract: Time-resolved phosphoproteomics captures fast signaling dynamics, but proteins that show no phosphorylation change, or escape detection, leave gaps the data cannot bridge. TS-BFS-BS uses the temporal order of a phosphoproteomic time course to guide a beam-pruned breadth-first search over STRING v12.5 functional, physical, and regulatory priors, returning temporally continuous routes that can pass through unmeasured bridge proteins. In EGF time courses from MDA-MB-468, EGFR Flp-In HEK293T and HeLa cells, endpoints and short routes were stable across search settings, and endpoints were largely shared across STRING priors, whereas long routes depended on settings and prior. When measured hubs CBL and SRC were removed, both were recovered as bridges and 94-99% of endpoints were retained. Incorrect temporal orders gave endpoint Jaccard indices of only 0.23-0.33 with the correct order, comparable to SHP2 inhibition (0.25-0.35), under which PTPN11 was excluded from all routes by its measured pretreatment response and returned after washout. TS-BFS-BS generates time-resolved, testable signaling hypotheses for iterative refinement.

papers.title: Differential and regionally distinct molecular responses distinguish FLASH and conventional RT in a medulloblastoma model while preserving therapeutic outcomes
papers.abstract: Background. FLASH radiotherapy might minimize treatment-related complications in medulloblastoma patients. To support its clinical translation, we investigated the therapeutic index of hypofractionated FLASH- and CONV-RT and their respective molecular determinants using an orthotopic human medulloblastoma mouse model. Methods. Five cohorts of juvenile UW228-MB-bearing nude mice were irradiated or not using 3x10 Gy (BED10 = 60 Gy), delivered 48 h apart at 0.1 Gy/s (CONV) or 5.5x10 Gy/s (FLASH) using an electron beam (eRT6). Digital spatial profiling (DSP) and immunofluorescence were performed 24h after radiotherapy in one cohort, while four cohorts were followed for long-term tumor response, cognition and neuroinflammation. Results. Both CONV- and FLASH-RT induced a long-lasting anti-tumor response in all irradiated animals. Long-term NOR performance was preserved in irradiated animals, with no significant difference compared with age-matched, non-tumor-bearing controls. A higher but non-significant proportion of very good discriminators was observed in the FLASH cohort while neuroinflammatory markers were statistically reduced. In the FLASH-irradiated mice, DSP revealed a sustained microglial activation in the cerebellar tumor micro-environment, with enhanced expression of genes with phagocytic and proteolytic activity. In the hippocampus, FLASH-induced genes involved a preferential astrocyte/neuron transcriptional crosstalk including metabolic support and synapse-glia interaction. The relevance of this metabolic support provided by astrocytes to neurons in the FLASH cohort was further supported by the enhanced expression of the astrocytic monocarboxylate transporter MCT4, a key transporter of lactate. Conclusion: The study shows that despite similar therapeutic index, hypofractionated FLASH and CONV-RT induce a distinct molecular signature in a human medulloblastoma mouse model.

papers.title: Mathematical Modeling of AA Amyloidosis: Coupling SAA-HDL Binding Dynamics with Path-Dependent Renal Aging
papers.abstract: Why does chronic inflammation cause AA amyloidosis in only some patients, even when serum amyloid A (SAA) remains elevated in many? This study proposes that disease progression is governed by two linked nonlinear processes: saturation of the finite SAA-binding capacity of high-density lipoprotein (HDL), followed by autocatalytic aggregation of amyloid A (AA) in the kidney. A hypothesis-generating mathematical model is developed that couples reversible SAA-HDL binding to renal filtration of free SAA, lysosomal cleavage to AA fragments, Finke-Watzky aggregation, oligomer deposition, and fibril turnover. As total SAA rises beyond the effective HDL binding capacity, the model predicts a disproportionate increase in free, filterable SAA available for renal amyloid formation. A dimensionless reduction reveals two kinetic regimes separated by a threshold at which autocatalytic oligomer production balances oligomer loss. Below this threshold, aggregation is nucleation-limited; above it, the system becomes supply-limited and is controlled mainly by upstream SAA delivery. In the zero-primary-nucleation limit, the two steady-state branches exchange stability at this threshold, giving a transcritical bifurcation that finite primary nucleation smooths into a continuous transition. The baseline parameter set lies in the supply-limited regime, explaining why total SAA concentration and effective HDL binding-site capacity have the largest local sensitivities, with SAA-HDL affinity and lysosomal cleavage next in rank, whereas the aggregation rate constants have small local effects but can still determine which regime applies. The model further predicts that the temporal pattern of inflammation matters: intermittent SAA flares can produce several-fold more renal damage than sustained inflammation with the same mean SAA, and earlier SAA suppression leaves a lower renal biological-age index, a calibrated measure of cumulative damage, than later suppression. Published SAA-outcome data are consistent with the predicted SAA dependence. By linking HDL buffering to renal SAA delivery, nonlinear aggregation, and cumulative injury, the model provides a quantitative framework for identifying amyloidogenic transitions and testing how SAA control can alter renal disease progression.

papers.title: Representations of semantic relations in the human cerebral cortex
papers.abstract: An essential aspect of human cognition is the ability to explicitly think about semantic relations between concepts. Neuroimaging studies have found that individual concepts are encoded by distributed patterns of cortical activity, but it is unclear how representations of semantic relations compare to concept representations in the brain. Some theoretical models suggest that relation representations are embedded within concept representations, while others suggest that relation representations are independent of any specific concept pair. We designed a study to compare how semantic relations and concepts are encoded across the cerebral cortex. To characterize how relations are encoded across cortex, fMRI was used to record brain activity while six participants each answered over one thousand questions about different semantic relations. We find that representations of relations are distinct from their relata. Our results further suggest that relations and concepts are represented in similar cortical regions, and that, within these regions, each location is preferentially selective for specific relations. Overall, these results suggest that in the human cerebral cortex, relations and concepts have distinct representations that share a common functional organization.

papers.title: BRIDGE: Biological Antimicrobial Resistance Inference via Domain-Knowledge Graph Embeddings
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global health crisis, responsible for an estimated 1.27 million deaths in 2019 alone. Traditional approaches to identifying antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) are often labour-intensive and limited in their ability to detect novel resistance mechanisms. In this study, we propose BRIDGE, a knowledge graph-based framework, to improve AMR gene prediction by integrating gene neighbourhood information and protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. Focusing on Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli, we con- struct a comprehensive and biologically grounded knowl- edge graph using curated data from CARD, STRING, and DrugBank. We apply knowledge graph embedding models which are fed into neural networks to infer novel AMR links, achieving classification accuracy of up to 97%. Our results demonstrate that incorporating biologically meaningful re- lationships, such as gene neighbourhood information and PPIs, enhances the predictive accuracy and interpretability of AMR link predictions. This work contributes to the de- velopment of scalable and data-integrated approaches for advancing antimicrobial resistance surveillance and drug discovery. BRIDGE implementation and data are available at https://github.com/GraphML-lab/BRIDGE.

papers.title: NAD boosting by CD38 inhibition drives reversal of a pathological vicious cycle of intracrine activity and inflammation in eyelid meibomian gland involution
papers.abstract: Vicious cycles--reciprocal cause-and-effect loops that progressively intensify dysfunction--are implicated in many diseases. Here, we examined whether "intracrine" steroidogenesis, a tissue-local mode of hormone production, participates in a pathological vicious cycle in eyelid meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD), the most common cause of evaporative dry eye disease with incidence increasing with age. We show that loss of meibomian intracrine androgen production triggers inflammatory remodeling of the eyelid tarsal plate. Conversely, inflammation suppresses nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent 3{beta}-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity in the meibomian gland, thereby further weakening intracrine steroidogenesis. Mechanistically, we identified inflammation-associated accumulation of the NAD-degrading enzyme CD38 as a key down-regulator for the NAD-dependent intracrine activity. Accordingly, pharmacological inhibition of CD38 (using 78c) in aged mice, restores meibomian cellular NAD levels, rescues intracrine activity, suppresses inflammatory signatures, and promotes recovery of gland size. Thus, our data suggest that boosting NAD availability not only ameliorates meibomian gland dysfunction but also induces a reciprocal "virtuous" cycle, in which suppression of inflammation and restoration of intracrine activity mutually reinforce each other. These findings constitute a previously unknown example in which the reversal of a pathological vicious cycle into a beneficial virtuous cycle underlies the therapeutic effects of NAD boosting and may help combat age-associated meibomian gland disorder.

papers.title: Metabolic dysfunction and metformin modify plasma extracellular vesicle signaling to prostate cancer cells
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is associated with altered outcomes in established prostate cancer, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We examined whether whole-body metabolic state and systemic metformin treatment are associated with changes in circulating plasma extracellular vesicle (EV) signaling to prostate cancer cells. Plasma EV-derived miRNAs were profiled in six T2D and six non-diabetic (ND) donors, selected mimics were tested in DU145 cells for effects on transcription of ZEB1, a master regulator of tumor progression. Recipient cell transcriptional responses to human EV-enriched fractions were also assessed by RNA sequencing using six T2D and two ND donors. DU145 cells were also transfected with plasma EV-derived RNA from high fat diet (HFD)-fed mice with or without metformin treatment. Human miRNA profiling identified miR-192-5p, miR-106b-5p, and miR-29b-3p as candidates with greater than two-fold elevation and nominal P<0.05; none of the 84 assayed miRNAs remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Synthetic miR-192-5p and miR-106b-3p mimics increased ZEB1, whereas miR-29b-3p had no effect on ZEB1. T2D donor EV exposure was associated with broad range of aggressive responses, including cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, mitotic, and RHO-GTPase-related pathways. Mouse EV-derived RNA from metformin-treated HFD mice induced lower DU145 migration than RNA from untreated HFD mice (12.23% versus 20.25% mean membrane coverage; n=3 mice/group; Welch P=0.0246). Matrigel invasion analysis showed less invasion for HFD+metformin than HFD alone (4.89% versus 7.89%; n=3 mice/group; Welch P=0.0302). These findings support a strong association between abnormal systemic metabolism and circulating EV signaling to drive prostate cancer progression, together with a metformin-driven reduction in the tumor progression activity of plasma EV-derived RNA. The responsible RNA species and molecular mechanisms will be central to future research.

papers.title: Germline stem cell isolation, lineage tracing, and aging in a protochordate
papers.abstract: Germline stem cells (GSCs), the source of gametes, are the only stem cells capable of passing genes to future generations making them cellular units of natural selection. Yet, factors regulating their fitness, and thus governing GSC competition, which exist in both protochordates and mammals, remain poorly understood. We study how aging affects GSC fitness in the protochordate Botryllus schlosseri, an evolutionary crosspoint between invertebrates and vertebrates. GSCs were isolated using flow cytometry and characterized by single-cell RNA sequencing, supported by a new PacBio genome assembly. GSC transplantation assays confirmed their function, further validated through a transgenerational lineage tracing strategy combining membrane-labeling dyes and single-cell transcriptomic analysis. Leveraging our method to isolate them, we uncover significant age-related changes in GSCs, while spermatids and sperm show minimal differences, suggesting that reproductive aging is influenced primarily by GSCs rather than by gametes. Reduced expression of markers like DDX4 and PIWIL1 in aged GSCs mirrors trends in mammalian datasets, suggesting conserved age-associated molecular changes in GSCs across chordate evolution. This study provides new techniques that lay the foundation to investigate further drivers of GSC fitness and highlights fertility-related genes as promising targets for therapies to preserve reproductive health.

papers.title: Sleep Renormalizes Negative Emotional Generalization
papers.abstract: Overgeneralization of negative experiences co-occurs with sleep disruption and characterizes anxiety and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A strategically-designed behavioral paradigm tested whether sleep shifts emotional generalization away from negative and toward positive representations. Participants learned positive, negative, or neutral face-outcome associations, then completed immediate and delayed generalization testing with morphed faces after sleep or wakefulness. Sleep selectively enhanced positive generalization, whereas wakefulness favored negative generalization. To uncover the underlying neural mechanisms, individual variability in generalization was examined using fMRI and high-density EEG. Amygdala and limbic activity during outcome-processing predicted both stronger immediate negative generalization and a sleep-specific shift toward positive generalization. Additionally, sleep-spindle activity positively correlated with post-sleep increases in positive generalization and reductions in negative generalization. Together, these findings identify a neural mechanism through which sleep reduces negative bias while strengthening positive representations, highlighting a pathway by which sleep may protect against maladaptive generalization associated with anxiety and PTSD.

papers.title: Charge Screening by Extracellular Ca2+ Shields Endothelial Cells from Histone Injury and Permits Membrane Repair
papers.abstract: **Background:** Extracellular histones released after trauma and in sepsis injure the vascular endothelium and contribute to coagulopathy and organ failure. Hypocalcemia frequently accompanies resuscitation with citrated blood products and predicts poor outcome, an association usually attributed to coagulation-factor dysfunction. Whether extracellular Ca2+ directly governs endothelial vulnerability to circulating cytotoxic histones, and whether the resulting membrane injury is reparable, are unknown. **Methods:** We combined live-cell spinning-disk confocal imaging of plasma membrane dynamics (FM1-43), Ca2+ imaging, flow cytometry, electric cell-substrate impedance sensing, and protein-lipid binding assays in cultured human endothelial cells, ORAI1/2/3 triple-knockout HEK-293 cells and surgically opened en face murine mesenteric arteries. Membrane repair was assessed with a sequential two-dye live-cell viability assay. **Results:** Histones evoked rapid, irregular endothelial Ca2+ elevations that were unaffected by deletion of all three ORAI homologs and were blocked by Gd3+ only at concentrations two orders of magnitude above those required to inhibit store-operated Ca2+ entry, excluding this pathway. Histones instead bound anionic membrane phospholipids, deforming the plasma membrane: lamellipodial ruffling, retraction, blebbing, extracellular vesicle release, phosphatidylserine externalization, and permeabilization in a heterogeneous subset

papers.title: A retrospective analysis of 400 publications reveals patterns of irreplicability across an entire life sciences research field
papers.abstract: The ReproSci project retrospectively analyzed the conceptual replicability of 1006 claims from 400 papers published between 1959 and 2011 in the field of Drosophila immunity. This project represents an expert assessment of the replicability 14 years later, of the replicability of nearly all publications across an entire scientific community in experimental life sciences. We found that 61% of claims were verified, while only 7% were directly challenged (not replicable), a replicability rate higher than previous assessments. Notably, 24% of claims had never been independently tested and remain unchallenged. We performed experimental validations of a selection of 45 unchallenged claim, that revealed that a significant fraction (38/45) of them is in fact non-replicable. We also found that claims from top-ranked institutions were more likely to be challenged and that claims published in trophy journals showed a similar but weaker trend. In line with the reproducibility crisis narrative, the rates of both challenged and unchallenged claims increased over time, especially as the field gained popularity. We characterized the uneven distribution of irreplicability among first and last authors. Surprisingly, irreplicability rates were similar between PhD students and postdocs, and did not decrease with experience or publication count. However, group leaders, who had prior experience as first authors in another Drosophila immunity team, had lower irreplicability rates, underscoring the importance of early-career training. Finally, authors with a more exploratory, short-term engagement with the field exhibited slightly higher rates of challenged claims and a markedly higher proportion of unchallenged ones. While limited by its reliance on published literature, this systematic, field-wide retrospective study offers meaningful perspective into the ongoing discussion on reproducibility in experimental life sciences.

papers.title: EBF1 controls an embryonic artery-forming niche that reactivates in pulmonary arterial hypertension
papers.abstract: Developmental programs that orchestrate cell fate and tissue architecture during organogenesis can cause disease when reactivated in adults. Here we identify a population of endothelial cells (ECs) defined by the pioneer factor early B cell factor 1 (EBF1) that controls both pulmonary artery (PA) morphogenesis and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). During embryonic development, the PA emerges from an endothelial niche harbored within the vascular plexus, where Aplnr+ endothelial progenitors give rise to both arterial ECs and EBF1+ ECs. Rather than incorporating directly into the PA intima, EBF1+ ECs control the branching and maturation of the PA tree through paracrine vasculotrophic signals that direct plexus expansion, arterialization, and mural cell recruitment. Although essential for development, most EBF1+ ECs disappear upon completion of PA morphogenesis, leaving only a rare residual population within the adult Aplnr+ gCap compartment. In PAH, vascular injury reactivates the EBF1 program through recruitment of the pre-existing Ebf1 lineage together with an additional contribution consistent with de novo Ebf1 induction in gCaps, reconstituting this artery-forming niche in a maladaptive reprise of PA development. Unlike their transient embryonic counterparts, these EBF1+ ECs persist within occlusive intimal lesions and express vasculotrophic signals associated with pathological PA remodeling. Combined with endothelial injury, gCap-specific Ebf1 overexpression drives a coordinated program of neo-arterialization, occlusive vascular remodeling, and severe PAH. Conversely, gCap-specific genetic deletion of Ebf1 in mice and endothelial-targeted AAV-mediated Ebf1 knockdown in rats protect against disease, showing that endothelial EBF1 is required for PAH pathogenesis. These findings demonstrate that reactivation and persistence of a transient embryonic artery-forming niche in adulthood drive pathological vascular remodeling and PAH.

papers.title: Regional species coexistence despite local priority effects: the overlooked role of dispersal-community feedback
papers.abstract: Many cases of animal-mediated dispersal are non-random, with the animals altering their movement pattern in response to the local species composition of the organisms that the vectoring animals disperse. Yet, this dispersal-community feedback has received little attention in metacommunity ecology. We use a mathematical model to show that dispersal-community feedback can promote regional species coexistence. As a well-characterized system, our model focuses on nectar-inhabiting bacteria and yeast that are dispersed by pollinators and affected by priority effects within flowers once dispersed. Model analysis suggests that bacteria and yeast coexist regionally across a wide range of regional pollinator abundances only when their occurrence in flowers influences the frequency of flower visits by pollinators. This microbe-pollinator feedback creates positive frequency dependence in each plant, causing competitive exclusion at the plant scale, but spatial partitioning across multiple plants, stabilizing coexistence at this scale. Our finding highlights dispersal-community feedback as an overlooked potential contributor to species coexistence.

papers.title: Differential Glutamatergic Inputs to Semilunar Granule Cells and Granule Cells Underscore Dentate Gyrus Projection Neuron Diversity
papers.abstract: Semilunar Granule Cells (SGCs) are sparse dentate gyrus projection neurons whose role in the dentate circuit, including pathway-specific inputs, remains unknown. We report that SGCs receive more frequent spontaneous excitatory synaptic inputs than granule cells (GCs). Dual GC-SGC recordings identified that SGCs receive stronger medial entorhinal cortex and associational synaptic drive but lack short-term facilitation of lateral entorhinal cortex inputs observed in GCs. Consistently, the probability of firing in response to medial perforant path input was greater in SGCs than in GCs. Additionally, the dendritic spine density on proximal and middle dendrites was higher in SGCs than GCs. However, the strength of commissural and supramammillary nuclear inputs and dendritic input integration, examined in passive morphometric simulations, did not differ between cell types. Activity-dependent labeling identified an overrepresentation of SGCs among neuronal ensembles in both mice trained in a spatial memory task and task-naive controls. The divergence of modality-specific entorhinal inputs to SGCs and GCs identified here can enable parallel processing of information streams and expand the computational capacity of the dentate gyrus.

papers.title: The nucleus accumbens dorsomedial column: distinct anterior-posterior inputs and activation inversely associated with opioid relapse
papers.abstract: Anatomical studies suggest that a dorsomedial region of nucleus accumbens (dmACB) forms a basal ganglia-like closed-loop circuit with medial ventral pallidum (mVP), lateral hypothalamic area (LHA), and paraventricular thalamic nucleus (PVT). The topographic organization of the circuit is unknown. We first used anterograde (Phaseolus vulgaris leucoagglutinin, PHAL) and retrograde (cholera-toxin B, CTB) tracers to map this organization. We then used immunoreactivity for Fos phosphorylated at serine 32 (pSer32-Fos-ir) as a proxy for the activation marker Fos (thus, we refer to pSer32-Fos hereafter as 'Fos') to determine whether the time-dependent increase (incubation) of oxycodone seeking after electric barrier-induced abstinence is associated with dmACB activation. In Experiment 1, we injected rats with PHAL into the anterior PVT (aPVT) and CTB into either the mVP or the anterior LHA (LHAa) to determine the distribution of their connections within the dmACB. We also injected CTB into anterior and posterior dmACB to identify afferent inputs. In Experiment 2, we trained rats to self-administer oxycodone for two weeks and counted Fos-labeled cells in anterior and posterior dmACB, the surrounding ACB, and dorsal striatum regions after drug-seeking tests on either abstinence day 1 or day 15 following electric barrier-induced abstinence. PHAL-labeled aPVT axons and CTB-labeled mVP and LHA neurons were confined to dmACB, forming a longitudinal column along the anterior-posterior axis of ACB. Inputs to anterior and posterior dmACB came from different cortical and subcortical regions. dmACB Fos+ cell counts were higher after oxycodone-seeking tests on day 1 than on day 15 and were negatively correlated with oxycodone seeking. These results characterize a connection-defined dmACB circuit and show that incubation of opioid-seeking is unexpectedly associated with reduced dmACB activation.

papers.title: BlastPhyMe: A toolkit for rapid generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: We present BlastPhyMe (BLAST, Phylogenies, and Molecular Evolution) a new application to facilitate the fast and easy generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets. The application uses a portable database framework to manage and organize sequences along with a graphical user interface (GUI) that makes the application extremely easy to use. BlastPhyMe utilizes several existing services and applications in a unique way that save researchers considerable time when building and analyzing protein-coding datasets. The application consists of two modules that can be used separately or together. The first module enables the assembly of coding sequence datasets. BLAST searches can be used to obtain all related sequences of interest from NCBI. Full GenBank records are saved within the database and coding sequences are automatically extracted. A feature of particular note is that sequences can be sorted based on NCBI taxonomic hierarchy before export for visualization using existing tools, such as fast. The application provides GUIs for automatic alignment of sequences with the popular tools MUSCLE and PRANK, as well as for reconstructing phylogenetic trees using PhyML. The second module incorporates selection analyses using codon-based likelihood methods. The alignments and phylogenetic trees generated with the dataset module, or those generated elsewhere, can be used to run the models implemented in the codeml PAML package. A GUI allows easy selection of models and parameters. Importantly, replicate analyses with different parameter starting values can be automatically performed in order to ensure selection of the best-fitting model. Multiple analyses can be run simultaneously based on the number of processor cores available, while additional analyses will be run iteratively until completed. Results are saved within the database and can be exported to publication-ready Excel tables, which further automatically compute the appropriate likelihood ratio test between models in order to determine statistical significance. Future updates will add additional options for phylogenetic reconstruction (eg, MrBayes) and selection analyses (eg, HYPHY). BlastPhyMe saves researches of all bioinformatics experience levels considerable time by automating the numerous tasks required for the generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets using a straightforward graphical interface. AVAILABILITY: Installation package and source code available from: https://github.com/ryankschott/BlastPhyMe

papers.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress
papers.abstract: Host-parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host-pathogen coevolutionary trajectories.

papers.title: Variational quantum thermalization of environment-coupled DNA sequence biases
papers.abstract: Understanding whether environmental conditions bias the statistical weight of specific genomic configurations requires a framework connecting molecular interactions, thermal fluctuations, and sequence-level observables. Here, we model DNA as an open quantum system coupled to an environmental thermal bath (represented as an external bosonic field) and parameterize the underlying molecular interaction energies (effective Hamiltonian terms) directly from prescribed nucleotide sequences. To evaluate sequence distributions at thermodynamic equilibrium, we compare two finite-temperature strategies at fixed inverse temperature ($\beta=1$): classical Bayesian optimization targeting the exact thermodynamic equilibrium distribution (the Gibbs state), and quantum simulation using a Variational Quantum Thermalizer (VQT) implemented via a nine-layer parameterized quantum circuit. Both methods optimize the same interaction energy model and target-sequence objective across short oligomers ($N=2$--$5$ base pairs), using 200 outer evaluations. Benchmarking against a uniform sequence distribution, exact-Gibbs optimization enhances target-sequence probabilities by factors of $9.11$, $25.64$, $54.51$, and $159.87$. The VQT approach similarly yields substantial target enrichment across all sequence lengths, achieving enhancement factors between $9.85$ and $62.77$. By evaluating the VQT-selected Hamiltonians against exact Gibbs calculations, we decouple optimization errors in parameter learning from approximation errors inherent to the variational quantum circuit. While concordance with the exact-Gibbs optimum is high in shorter oligomers, larger systems exhibit heightened sensitivity to variational thermal approximations. These results demonstrate that environment-induced sequence biases can be systematically captured within a variational quantum simulation framework, bridging biophysical models of DNA thermodynamics with quantum algorithms for finite-temperature state preparation. Crucially, the resulting equilibrium probabilities represent intrinsic thermodynamic biases rather than realized evolutionary substitution rates, which remain governed by kinetic activation barriers, replication fidelity, and enzymatic DNA repair.

papers.title: Joint QTL mapping reveals patterns of pleiotropy across structured environments in budding yeast
papers.abstract: Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping studies in model organisms have long been used to infer the structure of genotype-phenotype maps. However, prior work has largely focused on analyzing the genetic architecture of complex traits individually. Here, we sought to instead infer genotype-phenotype maps for a large set of related phenotypes simultaneously. To do so, we used bulk assays to measure the competitive fitness of each of 100,000 individuals from a large budding yeast QTL mapping panel across a set of 101 phenotypes related by a ``hub-and-perturbation'' pattern, and then used a forward search approach to jointly infer the genetic basis of all phenotypes together. Our results reveal complex patterns of pleiotropy in the genetic architecture of these traits. We find that these patterns of pleiotropy reflect the structure of the environmental relationships as well as functional information about individual variants and the interactions between them. This suggests that high-throughput QTL mapping across structured environments can help uncover biologically meaningful genetic interactions, along with their variation across related environmental contexts.

papers.title: Distinct labeling of host and viral genomes highlights redistribution of nuclear proteins during HSV-1 infection
papers.abstract: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) coordinates viral and cellular proteins during infection. While proteins associated with HSV-1 genomes have been identified, changes in proteins associated with the host genome during infection remain poorly understood. We adapted accelerated native isolation of proteins on nascent DNA (aniPOND) to label and purify cellular and viral DNA then identify associated proteins by mass spectrometry. Using this approach, we confirm observations that cellular transcription, DNA replication, and repair proteins are enriched on viral genomes after the onset of viral DNA replication. We assessed how protein interactions with cellular DNA change during infection relative to protein abundance. Targets of the viral E3 ubiquitin ligase, ICP0, are depleted from the nucleus and cellular genome during infection. Transcription regulatory factors, Pol II, and the proteasome are depleted from the host genome, while association with DNA damage response and nuclear pore proteins increases. We also provide evidence for HSV-1 disruption of ribosome biogenesis. Results demonstrate reorganization of the nucleus during infection and validate this technique to identify changes to host genome-associated factors during infection.

papers.title: Levodopa induced dyskinesia severity is linked to distinct microstructural alterations in nigrostriatal and brainwide neural circuits
papers.abstract: Dopaminergic replacement therapy via L-DOPA is the major medical therapy for Parkinsons Disease. Long-term L-DOPA administration is known to cause dyskinetic movements, L-DOPA Induced Dyskinesia (LID). It remains unclear if the LID related, maladaptive changes in brain structure/function are localized to neural circuits within the nigrostriatal DA system or have brainwide impact. We employed multi-shell diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and correlational tractography to investigate structural brain networks associated with daily administration of L-DOPA and the development of LID in the unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine rat model. 53% of rats receiving L-DOPA therapy developed severe LID. Tractography found brainwide statistical maps positively and negatively associated with LID severity highlighted by bilateral neural circuits contained in the lesioned nigrostriatal system as well as others including the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex. These results suggest that systemic dysfuntion in brainwide neural circuits forms the mechanistic basis the maladaptive changes underlying LID.

papers.title: Trisomy 21 Perturbs Oligodendrocyte Developmental States and Oligo-Neuron Communication in Human Forebrain Assembloids
papers.abstract: Intellectual disability is a hallmark of Down syndrome (DS), caused by the triplication of human chromosome 21. Abnormal neuronal connectivity and impaired myelination are consistently observed in DS, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we used DS-derived isogenic induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain assembloids (FAs) to investigate oligodendrocyte lineage cell (OLLC) development and neuron-glia interactions. Trisomic FAs exhibited an expansion of BCAS1+ pre-myelinating OLLCs, without a corresponding increase in myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. Transcriptomic analyses identified a euploid-enriched, trophic and maturation-supportive state (OLLC_2-TMS) and a trisomy-enriched synaptic interactions and differentiation state (OLLC_3-SID), lacking coordinated enrichment in myelination-promoting programs. Corresponding transcriptional signatures were identified in OLLCs from early postnatal human cortex. Increased excitatory neuronal contacts with pre-myelinating OLLCs accompanied ultrastructural myelin abnormalities in trisomic assembloids. Our findings suggest that trisomy redirects OLLC development toward a pre-myelinating state, uncoupling oligodendrocyte differentiation from productive myelination.

papers.title: State-dependent modulation of cross-area sensory processing in mouse neocortex
papers.abstract: Perception and decision-making rely on distributed cortical circuits that transform sensory inputs into choices and actions. Such cortical processing varies with behavioral state, such that the same inputs can be handled differently across states. However, how behavioral state shapes sensory processing across distributed brain regions remains unclear. To address this question, we trained mice to perform a two-alternative choice task that required discrimination between paired auditory and whisker cues. During task training, we simultaneously recorded neuronal population activity from the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), using two-photon imaging of neurons expressing the fluorescent calcium indicator GCaMP6f. Using a Hidden Markov Model with Generalized Linear Models (GLM-HMM), we identified three latent behavioral states, including one optimal-performing stimulus-guided state and two sub-optimal biased states. We found that the optimal state was associated with stronger sensory representation in S1 and PPC, as well as stronger bottom-up information transfer from S1 to anterior PPC (PPC-A). In contrast, biased states showed weaker sensory coding and relatively stronger involvement of rostrolateral PPC (PPC-RL). State-dependent differences were present in both task-related and task-orthogonal population activity. These results show that internal states modulate not only local sensory encoding, but also the routing of task-relevant information across cortical networks.

papers.title: A mismatch in wildfire impact reduction and ecological restoration in western U.S. fuel treatments
papers.abstract: A century of fire suppression has made historically fire-adapted forests across the western U.S. denser and dominated by fire-intolerant trees, leading to severe fires. Fuel treatments aim to reduce wildfire impact and restore fire-adapted forests. Ecological theory suggests these objectives need not align: protecting the existing, fire-maladapted stand may prevent fire-tolerant seedling recruitment. Using Forest Inventory and Analysis data on 81,621 trees and 41,328 seedlings across 11 western U.S. states, we show that fuel treatments increase tree survival, but benefits are largest for fire-intolerant trees, fade within nine years, and come with no seedling composition shift towards fire-tolerant species. Concluding, fuel reduction reduces wildfire impacts but does not restore fire-adapted forests. Without changes in treatment design, long-term resilience will require repeated intervention.

papers.title: HERC1 Loss of Function Causes a Developmental Disorder with Impaired Hippocampal Function
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in HERC1 are associated with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by macrocephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and psychomotor dysfunction. Although genetic and molecular studies suggest a loss-of-function mechanism, definitive in vivo evidence that HERC1 deficiency is sufficient to cause neurodevelopmental abnormalities is lacking. Using a HERC1 knockout mouse model, we investigated the behavioural, neuronal, and synaptic consequences of complete HERC1 loss.
