papers.title: Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) reveals the diversity and complexities of an open ocean photosymbiosis
papers.abstract: The Retaria are an abundant marine protist lineage that play a substantial role in biogeochemical cycling, primary production, and food web dynamics in open ocean ecosystems. Their impact is, in large part, due to their capacity to host photosynthetic endosymbionts. Despite the importance of these relationships in the global oceans, our knowledge about the diversity of photosymbionts associated with the planktic Retaria is still limited due to the difficulty of collecting and analyzing these cells. Here we used Fluorescence in situ Hybridization (FISH) in combination with Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) to assess the frequency and abundance of common algal photosymbiont lineages. We applied FISH probes that hybridize with the most commonly reported retarian photosymbiont lineages to environmental plankton samples and used FLIM to distinguish chlorophyll autofluorescence of retarian symbionts from FISH probe signal. By analyzing the fluorescence lifetime of 92 photosymbionts across 71 hosts, we found that the retarian photosymbiosis is far more complex than originally described, where Retaria commonly host multiple algal lineages per cell, and regularly host algal lineages outside of the two most common lineages. Similarly, the most prevalent photosymbiont species to open ocean Retaria (the dinoflagellate Brandtodinium nutricula) was only present in 34% of hosts according to our analyses. These efforts demonstrate that FLIM is an overlooked tool in the study of host-microbe associations, with significant potential to be used to distinguish chlorophyll autofluorescence from FISH probe signal in environmental samples.

papers.title: Parameters for stable Notch-independent Her6 oscillations across a frequency spectrum in neural stem cell populations
papers.abstract: Neural proliferation zones drive strong and persistent growth of the developing vertebrate brain. How Notch signaling and HES/Her transcription factors in vivo maintain stable neural stem cell (NSC) populations during brain growth is not well understood. Genetic evidence revealed Her6, a Notch-independent homolog of mammalian HES1, to be essential for maintenance of zebrafish NSCs. We recombined mNeonGreen into the her6 locus and analyzed temporal Her6-mNG fluorescence profiles in vivo. Her6 is expressed dynamically in all NSCs, with a majority revealing stable oscillation, albeit from cell to cell across a wide frequency range. Her6 oscillates cell-autonomously, unaffected by inhibition of Notch, and is robustly reinitiated after experimental perturbations. Mathematical modelling predicts, and we indeed find in vivo, that Her6 oscillations prevail only when both transcript and protein degradation rate constants are equal. These intrinsic control parameters may have evolved for the Her6 oscillator to contribute to robust maintenance of NSCs.

papers.title: A hypothalamic circuit links hunger to mesolimbic dopamine to drive feeding
papers.abstract: Hunger enhances the motivational value of food, but the neural circuits linking homeostatic hunger neurons to dopamine systems remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a hypothalamic-midbrain neural circuit through which AgRP neurons engage the mesolimbic dopamine system. We demonstrate that AgRP neuron activity is both necessary and sufficient for the potentiated dopamine response to food by hunger, and that they achieve this by reducing inhibitory drive onto midbrain dopamine neurons. Importantly, this AgRP neuron-evoked dopamine signaling is required for subsequent food intake. Mechanistically, we find that AgRP neuron projections to NPY-sensitive paraventricular hypothalamic neurons selectively amplify food-evoked dopamine release to promote feeding behavior. These findings reveal a circuit mechanism through which hunger recruits dopamine signaling to transform physiological need into motivated feeding behavior.

papers.title: mTOR signalling, not clock gene rhythms, organises daily physiology
papers.abstract: Daily rhythms in mammalian physiology are widely attributed to rhythmic transcription of "clock-controlled genes" driven by the circadian transcriptional/translational feedback loop (TTFL). Here we show that daily physiology can be uncoupled from the TTFL: inhibiting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) abolishes most daily variation in cellular and organismal physiology, whilst clock protein rhythms persist. In cultured cells and mouse liver, functional rhythms are lost, including the proteome, RNA abundance, substrate utilisation and drug metabolism. In forebrain, most daily variation in protein abundance and phosphorylation is lost, yet locomotor activity and sleep-wake architecture are largely preserved in mice and zebrafish. PERIOD2 binds mTORC1 and limits its activity, providing a route by which clock proteins shape daily mTOR signalling. mTOR inhibition preferentially suppresses output over clock gene rhythms in Arabidopsis and Neurospora. We conclude that mTOR is a conserved conduit through which circadian and environmental timing impose daily organisation on physiology.

papers.title: Mural-VISTA: A tool for mural cell-vessel interaction assessment and multiscale single-cell topo-morphological analysis
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) mural cell morphology is heterogeneous and coupled to vessel geometry, however, measurements from two-dimensional (2D) maximum intensity projections (MIP) obscure overlapping processes and cell-vessel contacts. Accordingly, we developed Mural-VISTA, a semi-automated Python workflow for mural cell-vessel interaction and single-cell topo-morphology analysis of reconstructed surface meshes. This workflow integrates mesh pretreatment, interactive centerline extraction, hierarchical segmentation of cell soma, main axis and secondary processes (branches), and extraction of 37 multiscale (cell process segment level, process level, and whole cell level) topo-morphological and vessel-referenced metrics. Mural-VISTA identified morphological changes in pericytes and vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs) with altered RhoA activity. Constitutively active RhoA (RhoA CA) over-expression reduced branch complexity and increased alignment in both cell types, while increased whole-cell and branch solidity only in vSMCs. Dominant-negative RhoA (RhoA DN) over-expression increased branch abundance and reduced branch solidity in pericytes but not vSMCs, suggesting cell-type specific effect of reduced RhoA activity. In conclusion, Mural-VISTA enables quantitative 3D profiling of mural cell architecture and its spatial relationship with the vessel.

papers.title: Elephant seal cells export iron and form lipid droplets to evade lipid peroxidation
papers.abstract: Elephant seals are remarkable breath-hold divers, capable of remaining submerged for up to two hours during diving bouts. These dives entail repeated, extreme hypoxia/reoxygenation events that would induce severe lipid peroxidation and tissue dysfunction in most species. Here, we show that primary vascular endothelial cells derived from elephant seals resist oxidant-induced lipid peroxidation and cell death without relying on canonical lipid hydroperoxide scavenging. Comparative transcriptomic profiling across seal, human, and sheep cells identified transcriptional signatures of lipid metabolism and iron handling as uniquely regulated in seal cells following hydroperoxide exposure. Mechanistically, seal cells exhibit high constitutive levels of acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 3 (ACSL3) alongside robust, seal-specific induction of the iron exporter ferroportin-1 (FPN1). Comparative lipidomic profiling revealed that seal cells are enriched in triglycerides and monounsaturated fatty acids. ACSL3 silencing and FPN1 inhibition each partially sensitized seal cells to lipid peroxidation, identifying lipid droplet biogenesis and active iron export as complementary but non-redundant axes of protection. Together, these data reveal a protective strategy based on lipid sequestration and iron export rather than hydroperoxide reduction, with implications for ischemia-reperfusion injury in non-diving mammals.

papers.title: Torsion in motion: the visual system as a three-axis gimbal
papers.abstract: Rigorously tracking eye and head behavior in space is key to building realistic models of the stimulus that reaches our retina. The motion structure of this stimulus or retinal flow is created by the relative movement of the eyes with respect to the world. Characterizing this stimulus requires tracking the eye's three degrees of freedom in the head and the head's six degrees of freedom in the world. While vertical and horizontal eye rotations have been described during locomotion in the context of gaze stabilization, the component around the line of sight - torsion - has remained difficult to quantify, and how all three rotational components jointly contribute to retinal flow during self-motion remains largely unexplored. Here, we leveraged head-mounted technology to estimate eye torsion in ten subjects as they walked towards a distant target. More specifically, we combined automatic feature tracking with gaze-constrained simulations of eye rotations and camera projection to recover torsion from image data. We then estimated the curl present in the optic-flow field in head and retina centered frames in two scenarios: torsion as estimated from our data and with no torsion. We show that the eye's torsional component compensates for the roll component of head's angular displacement, altering the incoming visual flow in ways that are relevant for the extraction of self-motion parameters from retinal flow.

papers.title: Perceptual sensitivity supports online control, while perceptual errors drive motor memory formation during locomotor adaptation
papers.abstract: To maintain stable locomotion, the nervous system must continually adapt, whether reacting to an unexpected perturbation, such as a trip on uneven terrain, or anticipating external demands, such as walking on snow, by forming and updating motor memories. Error-based learning is the dominant computational account of such adaptation, in which motor commands are updated to reduce prediction errors, that is, the mismatch between predicted and actual limb state. Yet this framework has been largely defined in reduced, single-effector paradigms, where the sensory consequences of movement are isolated and the prediction error is directly controlled by the experimenter. Whether the same principle governs whole-body, multi-segmental, multi-sensory behaviors such as walking has remained untested, owing in part to the challenge of identifying a behavioral proxy for prediction errors in this complex, dynamic setting. Here, we combined a split-belt treadmill paradigm with a novel method for quantifying perception of leg motion to address this open question. We found two perceptual contributions to locomotor adaptation: perceptual sensitivity predicted initial motor corrections during early adaptation, whereas perceptual prediction errors (i.e., the mismatch between the actual belt-speed difference and the difference perceived as symmetric) predicted the magnitude of motor aftereffects during post-adaptation. Together, these findings support error-based learning, long characterized in upper limb tasks, as a core computational principle underlying human locomotion.

papers.title: Impaired synthesis of both telomere strands and adaptive TERT reduction in RTEL1 ATPase-dead cells
papers.abstract: Regulator of Telomere Elongation Helicase 1 (RTEL1) plays a critical role in telomere replication by disassembling DNA secondary structures such as G-quadruplexes and telomeric loops (T-loops). However, its precise mechanism remains unclear. Previously, we generated HeLa cells homozygous for ATPase-dead RTEL1. Here, we found that these cells have a 50-77% reduction in the synthesis of both telomere strands, indicating that RTEL1 ATPase activity is important for both leading-strand and lagging-strand synthesis. Surprisingly, these cells also showed a substantial reduction in Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase (TERT) mRNA levels and an approximately 80% reduction in telomerase activity, without activating alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT). Forced TERT overexpression suppressed proliferation and caused late S/G2 accumulation, implying that the naturally occurring reduction in TERT provides an adaptive mechanism for cell survival. Expressing the longest RTEL1 isoform at close to physiological levels failed to rescue growth defects, suggesting other isoforms are important for cell survival. These results reveal an unexpected interplay between RTEL1 and telomerase and show how cancer cells compensate for RTEL1 dysfunction by decreasing TERT expression.

papers.title: Continuous, high-speed 3D topographic profiling of living tissue monolayers
papers.abstract: Tissue monolayers are active living matter whose three-dimensional (3D) architecture and mechanical remodeling regulate tissue function, yet fast and continuous topographic monitoring remains difficult. Here, we present FLuorescence EXclusion microscopy fOr Monolayers (FLEXOM), a microfluidic platform that combines multilayer micropillar arrays with negative-staining optics to convert wide-field images into self-calibrated 3D height maps. Geometry-anchored reference cavities maintain in-frame calibration standards even in fully confluent monolayer fields, enabling continuous 3D profiling from isolated cells to confluent sheets with sub-second temporal resolution (~250 ms), sub-micrometer axial precision (~0.37 m), and multi-day biocompatibility and operational stability (>96 h). FLEXOM reveals two distinct anisotropic signatures in tissue monolayers. First, monolayers of different cell types show distinct vertical thickness profiles despite comparable lateral footprints. Only two vertical descriptors, mean height and height variability, distinguished cell types more accurately than nine 2D lateral descriptors, including area, circularity, and convexity (95% vs. 76%). Second, under acute osmotic shock, confluent monolayers exhibit geometrically anisotropic and temporally decoupled vertical-lateral remodeling: height changes dominate the overall volume response and precede lateral remodeling. Surprisingly, cyclic isotonic-hypotonic pulses every 3 min confine remodeling entirely to the vertical axis. Overall, our work provides a high-resolution 3D profiling tool and a framework for axis-resolved analysis of topographic responses in active living matter.

papers.title: Integrative structure determination of a human mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS) sub-assembly
papers.abstract: The Mitochondrial contact site and Cristae Organizing System (MICOS) complex is an inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) assembly present at the cristae junction. It is responsible for regulating cristae formation and remodeling. However, its structure is not known. We applied Bayesian integrative structure determination to characterize the structure of the Mic60, Mic19, Mic10, and Mic13-containing MICOS sub-assembly combining AlphaFold predictions with data from crosslinking mass spectrometry, biochemical assays, electron tomography, homology modeling, and sequence alignments. The integrative structure revealed novel mutual interfaces among Mic10N,C, Mic60LBS1,LBS2,mitofilin, and Mic13central,C. Several likely-pathogenic missense mutations also localize to these novel interfaces, highlighting their importance. Further, we investigated some of these interactions using binding assays on purified proteins and demonstrated direct interactions among Mic10-Mic13-Mic60. Our results support a bridging role for Mic13 in the MICOS assembly, by binding Mic10 in the IMM-proximal region and Mic60 in the intermembrane space. Taken together, our integrative approach sheds light on the structure and assembly of the MICOS complex.

papers.title: Processing at Phrase Boundaries During Self-Paced Reading
papers.abstract: Sentence comprehension requires the incremental construction of syntactic structure and semantic interpretation. Prior neural work (Nelson et al., 2017) identified key neural events at major phrase boundaries during sentence comprehension. To investigate a behavioral correlation of these processes, we used self-paced reading to examine the impact of syntactic phase boundaries, semantic congruence, and sentence structure on sentence processing. Participants read object-relative, subject-relative, and canonical control sentences one word at a time and a subsequent comprehension task. Reading times were analyzed relative to phrase boundaries, node-closing operations, and semantic congruence. Object-relative sentences produced the greatest processing difficulty, demonstrated by increased reading times and decreased comprehension accuracy. Reading times peaked at the phrase boundaries, indicating that processing costs are tied to constituent completion rather than individual lexical categories. Reading times also increased with the number of syntactic constituents completed at a phrase boundary. Agent-patient semantic congruence produced its largest effects in object-relative sentences, suggesting that semantic information interacts with syntactic computations when processing demands are greatest. These findings demonstrate that self-paced reading is sensitive to the incremental processing associated with syntactic constituent completion. Processing costs are tied more closely to phrase completion than to individual lexical categories, scale with the amount of syntactic structure completed at a boundary and interact with agent-patient semantic interpretation during object-relative sentence comprehension. Together, these findings support a view of sentence comprehension in which syntactic structure building and semantic interpretation proceed incrementally and interact continuously throughout online language processing.

papers.title: The chemoreceptor McpA mediates aerotaxis and redox taxis in Salmonella Typhimurium
papers.abstract: Redox environments in nature are shaped by reactive oxygen species (ROS), oxygen, and metal ion chemistry, and exert profound effects on bacterial physiology and survival. In some pathogens, bacterial chemosensory zinc-binding (CZB) proteins mediate responses to inflammatory ROS that may contribute to pathogenesis, but their functions in the many environmental bacteria that also possess them remain unclear. Reports of attraction to hypochlorous acid (HOCl), repulsion from hydroperoxides (ROOH) and other ROS, and responsiveness to exogenous zinc have left unresolved whether CZBs distinguish individual effectors or reflect an underlying sensory logic. Here, using time-resolved video microscopy to directly visualize swimming and taxis behaviors, we show that the CZB-containing receptor McpA in Salmonella Typhimurium mediates attraction to O2 and biologically relevant concentrations of HOCl, H2O2, and organic hydroperoxides, three types of oxidants generated through the neutrophil oxidative burst. This identifies the CZB domain as a previously unrecognized sensory architecture for aerotaxis, distinct from, and possibly more widespread, than the FAD-dependent Aer and heme-dependent HemAT and Aer2 families. Although Zn2+ itself is not redox-active, we show that McpA-dependent taxis is controlled by Zn2+ availability and that exogenous OZn2 and ROS promote the formation of insoluble zinc precipitates, which may generate Zn2+ gradients sensed through the CZB domain. We propose these findings are consistent with a model in which CZBs use soluble, bioavailable Zn2+ as a secondary messenger for highly sensitive navigation of environmental redox landscapes.

papers.title: Determining Reliable Neural Targets for enhancing Motor Sequence Learning: A preparatory study for focal tDCS
papers.abstract: Background: Motor sequence learning (MSL) underlies the acquisition of everyday skilled movements, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has shown promise for enhancing it, although reported effects vary considerably. Before such interventions can be applied and interpreted reliably, the behavioural and neural signatures of the underlying task should be shown to be robust. This study therefore characterised an fMRI-based Serial Reaction Time Task (SRTT) protocol and evaluated the consistency of its behavioural and fMRI-based neural signatures in repeated measurements to identify potential network targets for tDCS. Methods: Twenty healthy young- to middle-aged adults (10 females; mean age 24, SD 4) performed the SRTT during 3T fMRI in two sessions about one week apart, each using one of two matched, non-overlapping task versions in counterbalanced order. We examined block-wise behaviour, task-related and sequence-specific brain activation (general task activation relative to baseline and the SEQ > RND contrast), and functional connectivity using two complementary approaches: the task and temporal dynamics of seed-based connectivity (SBC) within an a priori defined motor network (M1, SMA, PMC, putamen, and cerebellum), and whole brain generalised psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) for the SEQ > RND contrast. Results: Reaction time decreased steadily across sequence blocks and returned toward baseline during random blocks, confirming implicit sequence learning; this pattern was consistent across both sessions and both task versions. Test retest reliability was excellent for random-block reaction time (ICC = 80 to .85), and modest for sequence blocks (ICC = .29 to.53). General task activation (sequence and random performance relative to baseline) engaged the expected sensorimotor network, including the primary motor cortex (M1), premotor cortex, and SMA, with M1 more strongly engaged during sequence than random blocks. The sequence-specific contrast (SEQ > RND) additionally revealed six clusters spanning the left superior parietal cortex, bilateral supplementary and cingulate motor areas, bilateral secondary somatosensory cortex, and left ventral visual cortex together with cerebellar Crus I. The a priori defined motor network was engaged across all task phases and was anchored throughout by strong M1 to SMA coupling, with overall network coupling following a non-monotonic course across the session, consistent with successive stages of resource allocation, consolidation, and automatisation. The gPPI analysis identified four sequence-specific connectivity clusters, dominated by a right-lateralised visuomotor network and a somatosensory visual integration channel. Conclusions: Together, these findings indicate a two-component architecture for SRTT performance: a left hemispheric cortico striato cerebellar network that supports performance and acquisition of the sequence, and a right hemispheric network associated with monitoring its predictable structure. Within this protocol, the SRTT produced robust and stable group-level signatures of implicit motor learning, yielding well-defined network targets for future tDCS interventions..

papers.title: ResXR: infrastructure for quality-controlled, reproducible studies of human behavior in Extended Reality
papers.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) combines experimental control and ecological validity, yet behavioral XR research lacks shared infrastructure: building immersive experiments demands specialized engineering, and custom tools yield data in custom formats that other laboratories cannot readily reanalyze. We present ResXR (Research with XR), an open-source toolkit providing a path from immersive experiment to standardized dataset and quality report, running on standalone Meta Quest headsets. A Unity template records head, hand, eye, and face tracking with per-sample software development kit (SDK) timestamps and status flags; an independent Python pipeline checks data quality, can mask flagged intervals, and exports raw and derivative datasets in Motion-BIDS, the motion extension of the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS), with self-contained quality reports. Three ready-to-run paradigms, covering discrete choice, spatial navigation, and free visual exploration, let researchers collect and process data without programming. ResXR grounds its default schema and the signals its quality checks read in stress tests rather than in vendor documentation: when we induced tracking failures on Meta Quest Pro headsets, several status flags kept marking the data as valid. With its code, stress-test protocols and example datasets openly available, ResXR provides a transparent, community-extensible foundation for reproducible XR experimentation.

papers.title: Hill-Based Reformulation of the Hodgkin-Huxley Model for Mapping Gating Changes to Neuronal Excitability
papers.abstract: Conductance-based models link ion-channel gating to neuronal excitability, but mutation reports often provide steady-state voltage shifts without sufficient kinetic measurements to specify a unique model. We introduce a Hill-based reformulation of selected Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) gating relationships and evaluate its usefulness under this low-information constraint. The hybrid formulation retains canonical HH-like spike waveforms and frequency-current behavior after a modest remapping of applied current, while providing an explicit mapping from reported activation descriptors to model parameters under specified assumptions. An A863P kinetic-sensitivity analysis shows how steady-state constraints and kinetic assumptions jointly shape excitability predictions in both classical HH and Hill-based implementations. The Hill formulation makes this mapping reproducible through explicit parameter relations, whereas refitting classical HH rates requires additional fitting choices; both approaches still require kinetic assumptions. Retrospective benchmarks using the Nav1.7 mutations A863P, F1449V, and A1632G show that the Hill-based model captures the qualitative increase in excitability but overestimates the magnitude of threshold reduction. Classical HH comparisons for A863P demonstrate that similar qualitative predictions can also be obtained under specified kinetic assumptions. These findings support the Hill formulation as a reproducible framework for mapping reported gating changes onto HH-like excitability, without establishing superior quantitative prediction of mutation effects. Quantitative transfer to mutation-specific neuronal behavior requires additional kinetic and cellular constraints.

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics Outweigh Fungicide Treatment in Shaping the Turfgrass Phyllosphere Resistome
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) are an emerging class of environmental contaminants with significant implications for public health. Previous studies have linked fungicide exposure to elevated levels of ARGs in soil microbiomes, but research investigating the impacts of fungicide on ARGs within phyllosphere bacterial communities is limited. To address this, creeping bentgrass was treated with the fungicide active ingredients chlorothalonil, fluxapyroxad, and propiconazole and sampled at 4 hours, 96 hours, and 168 hours post-application, along with a non-treated control. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed to quantify the abundance of ARGs and a metal resistance gene's (MRG) abundance relative to 16S rRNA. Additionally, 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed to characterize bacterial community composition. Results indicated that fungicide treatments did not significantly alter the relative abundance of ARGs or an MRG within bent grass bacterial communities. However, significant changes were observed over time, with changes in ARG and MRG abundance mirroring temporal shifts in bacterial beta diversity. ARGs and the MRG relative abundance had significant correlations with Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteriadota, and Firmicutes, including with genera Pseudoxanthomas, and Dyandobacter, which contain opportunistic human pathogens. This study demonstrates that fungicides have limited influence on the abundance of ARGs and MRGs in the phyllosphere and helps guide further investigations aiming to mitigate the spread of antibiotic resistance.

papers.title: Emergence of Task-Related Motor Cortical Dysfunction in Mice with Progressive Parkinsonism
papers.abstract: The primary motor cortex (M1) exhibits substantial changes in Parkinsons disease (PD). However, the temporal relationship between midbrain dopamine (DA) neurodegeneration, M1 circuit dysfunction, and motor symptoms remains poorly understood. Using the MitoPark mice, we investigated the time course of M1 cellular dysfunction during progressive DA loss. MitoPark mice developed gradually impaired skilled movements at a moderate motor stage of Parkinsonism. The motor deficits were associated with reduced cellular activity, impaired neuronal coactivation, and decreased proportion of responsive M1 pyramidal neurons. Moreover, the corticospinal (CSp), but not the intratelencephalic (IT), neurons showed a selective reduction in cellular activity during reaches. At the population level, M1 pyramidal neurons included heterogeneous functional clusters in relation to skilled movements and their stability in longitudinal encoding of movement degraded substantially in MitoPark mice. Together, these results delineate the emergence of M1 circuit pathophysiology at cellular and neural population levels during progressive Parkinsonism.

papers.title: Accelerating drug development in infectious diseases using zebrafish disease models supported by pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic modeling as new approach methodology (NAM)
papers.abstract: The development of novel therapeutics for infectious diseases remains a global health priority. To accelerate the treatment development, innovative strategies through new approach methodology (NAM) are needed to bridge speed of in vitro with predictive power of in vivo studies, while reducing mammalian experiments. The zebrafish (Danio rerio), particularly the embryo/larva, has been established as a valuable non-mammalian in vivo model in biomedical research. We developed a standardized and streamlined workflow for the zebrafish as NAM, which consisted of 3 steps: drug selection and efficacy evaluation, internal exposure assessment, and PKPD modelling. Compounds with higher tolerated doses than minimum inhibitory concentration were selected. Drug efficacy was quantified through longitudinal individual fluorescence microscopy at baseline and 24 and 48h on treatment. Drug exposure was quantified in larval homogenates and exposure medium from 0-48h on treatment. The PKPD relationship was quantified by non-linear mixed effects modelling. For case study bedaquiline, PKPD was quantified using a one-compartment model with age-depending elimination, and an Emax concentration-response relationship on the delayed logistic bacterial growth function, with an EC50 of 26.5 g/mL and an Emax of 1.09-1.37. In the case of clarithromycin, in contrast, negligible internal exposure after waterborne treatment was observed, illustrating the risk of false negatives without internal exposure assessments. Bactericidal efficacy was confirmed by intravenous drug injections, showing a clear dose dependent antimycobacterial effect. The standardized zebrafish NAM workflow presented here facilitates the translation of drug efficacy to higher vertebrates, reducing rodent studies to confirmatory or replacing them completely, thus accelerating drug development.

papers.title: De novo lipogenesis controls antigen presentation and metastatic immune escape in triple-negative breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Metastatic dissemination is a major cause of mortality in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet how tumor metabolic state regulates immune surveillance during metastasis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify de novo lipogenesis as a tumor-intrinsic determinant of immune visibility and metastatic progression. Genetic or pharmacologic disruption of fatty acid synthase (FASN) suppresses metastasis with limited effects on primary tumor growth and enhances tumor-cell major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) antigen presentation and CD8+ T cell activation. Mechanistically, FASN-dependent lipogenesis sustains epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) palmitoylation, selectively maintaining PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling without altering EGFR abundance, cell-surface localization, or MAPK activation. Disruption of FASN-dependent lipogenesis, EGFR palmitoylation, or mTOR signaling restores peptide-MHC-I presentation and enhances antigen-specific CD8+ T cell recognition and cytotoxicity. FASN loss increases the abundance of multiple antigen-processing machinery proteins without corresponding changes in MHC-I transcript abundance, supporting transcription-independent regulation of antigen presentation downstream of PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. Tumor-cell B2M depletion substantially restores metastatic outgrowth and circulating tumor cells following FASN loss, identifying MHC-I antigen presentation as a major mediator of lipogenesis-dependent metastatic immune escape. In patient-derived TNBC organoids and independent human breast cancer cohorts, elevated lipogenic gene expression correlated with PI3K-AKT-mTOR-related transcriptional programs and reduced immune-surveillance programs, without significant differences in MHC-I transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings define a tumor-intrinsic immunometabolic circuit in which de novo lipogenesis sustains EGFR palmitoylation and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling to regulate antigen presentation, thereby modulating tumor-cell immune visibility during metastatic progression.

papers.title: Dysplastic Alveolar Basaloid Cells Provide a Protective Barrier via KRT17-Stratifin Complex during Chronic Fibrosis
papers.abstract: Understanding how lung alveolar type 2 (AT2) stem cells respond to chronic profibrotic insults in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is critical for developing therapies and determining physiological relevance of maladaptive regeneration. Using integrated snATAC/snRNA-sequencing of human lungs and in vitro models, we mapped distinct AT2 regenerative trajectories: resolvable euplastic repair and persistent dysplastic repair. Spatially restricted ITGB6/TGF{beta}1/SMAD3 signaling drives AT2-to-basaloid dysplasia via direct upregulation of KRT17 and Stratifin. Using murine models of dysplastic repair and a human precision-cut lung slice/stem cell incorporation assay, we show that KRT17 and its interaction with Stratifin are required for AT2 cell flattening, alveolar coverage, and barrier protection. AT2s leverage these mechanisms to re-epithelialize damaged tissue during chronic fibrosis, navigating a delicate balance between preventing further lung damage and driving aberrant epithelial remodeling. Collectively, we identify novel mechanisms governing alveolar metaplasia and its functional relevance, offering crucial insights for therapeutic interventions in fibrotic lung diseases.

papers.title: Double-Stranded RNA Profiling with Mass Photometry
papers.abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a potent immunogenic impurity and its detection is a critical quality attribute in characterizing mRNA therapeutics. Standard analytical methods (e.g., sandwich ELISA) are only able to resolve the bulk presence of dsRNA and cannot characterize the different sub-species that may be present within a mRNA sample.. In this study, we use mass photometry (MP) as a single-molecule analytical platform for the simultaneous detection and characterization of dsRNA impurities in mRNA samples. We demonstrate how ionic strength can interfere with the stability of the mAb/dsRNA complex and measure the binding affinity (1 nM) under a set of parameters for reproducible characterization of the complex. We then leverage the J2 antibody to identify antibody/dsRNA complexes that then resolve dsRNA-positive species within an mRNA sample based on discrete molecular weight profiles. Furthermore, we introduce a novel MP assay that harnesses the repulsive surface chemistry of uncoated glass to exclude the bulk mRNA analyte to enable the use of higher loading concentrations to sensitively profile trace dsRNA impurities as antibody-bound species. This work establishes MP as a valuable next generation mRNA analytical tool for analyzing dsRNA byproducts within mRNA samples.

papers.title: Coherence from Context - Two-Point Neuron Models for Contextual Integration in Visual Information Processing
papers.abstract: The integration of contextual information is crucial for coherent perception and cognition. The morphology and conductance properties of cortical pyramidal cells suggest that they operate as ''two-point neurons'' (TPNs), asymmetrically combining driving sensory input at basal dendrites with modulating context at apical compartments. We present a mechanistic rate-based TPN model of layer V pyramidal cell populations and their local PV, SOM, and VIP interneuron circuits. The model rests on asymmetric feedforward-feedback integration and pooled inhibition to implement local competition and global cooperation supporting the selective amplification of coherent signals. Fitted to multi-compartment pyramidal cell simulations, it reproduces their basal-apical input-output map and, unlike static transfer functions, shows how apical amplification unfolds over time under interneuron control. Asymmetric apical-basal coincidence integrates context during processing and tags TPNs for reward-driven learning with a local four-factor rule. A pool of TPNs thereby learns to use flanker context to decide ambiguous orientations. Context-driven VIP cells gate apical integration and learning through dis-inhibition. We connect TPN populations with joint spatial and feature selectivity into networks. Contextual signals from lateral recurrence and top-down feedback yield coherence formation and evidence propagation. This propagation disambiguates visual motion and requires apical-basal coupling. For larger-scale simulations, we show how established simpler models follow from reducing the TPN's complexity while retaining its core principles. Overall, context in the TPN amplifies sensory evidence but cannot create it without feedforward input. Finally, we discuss when dynamics and interneurons matter, the model's testable predictions for VIP silencing, and implications for artificial neural networks.

papers.title: Beyond single markers: bacterial synergies identified by Multidimensional Feature Selection reveal conserved microbiome disease signatures
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome encodes disease-relevant information not only in the abundance of individual taxa and functions, but in the way they co-occur and interact. Yet metagenomic analyses have largely relied on univariate approaches that evaluate features in isolation, systematically overlooking the combinatorial signals that arise from meaningful, disease-informative patterns of microbial co-occurrence. Here, we introduce a framework based on the Multidimensional Feature Selection (MDFS) algorithm to identify synergistic feature pairs - combinations of taxa and functions in which the information carried by a feature significantly increases in the presence of a partner. This includes features which carry no detectable individual information and may therefore be overlooked by univariate analyses. We first validated the approach on a meta-analysis of colorectal cancer (CRC) cohorts - one of the most competitive microbiome classification benchmarks available - using a leave-one-cohort-out cross-validation framework. Classifiers built solely on our synergy-derived features achieved performance comparable to the state-of-the-art benchmark (AUC = 0.84 vs 0.85). This confirmed that we were able to capture an informative disease signal while revealing microbial interactions not provided by univariate methods. A subset of the pairs was repeatedly selected by the models during feature selection, which indicated their stability. Post-selection effect size analysis revealed their consistent differences between cases and controls. To learn more about diseases beyond CRC, we extended our framework to 13 additional datasets spanning inflammatory bowel disease, cardiometabolic disease, liver cirrhosis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. We identified 80,790 synergistic pairs in eight of them as well as a set of candidate markers recurring across independent cohorts. Overall, synergistic pairs carried substantially more information about disease status than their individual constituents. Our framework therefore established meaningful microbial co-occurrence patterns which would not be possible with univariate methods alone. The framework is freely available at https://github.com/Kizielins/MDFS_synergies. Importance Most microbiome studies search for individual gut bacterial species associated with disease. However, bacteria do not act in isolation, and their combined presence or relative balance may be far more informative than any single microbe considered alone. This study presents a computational framework which identifies pairs of gut microorganisms whose co-occurrence or relative abundance carries significantly more information about disease status than their importance alone. Applied to stool metagenomic data from patients with colorectal cancer, as well as individuals with other conditions, we demonstrate that these synergistic interactions are: 1) widespread; 2) reproducible across independent patient cohorts; 3) and resolve disease-relevant microbial relationships which single-feature analyses do not report. Our framework offers a more complete view of how the gut microbiome is altered in disease and provides a principled basis for identifying robust, interaction-based biomarkers.

papers.title: The role of deficient action knowledge in unawareness (anosognosia) of tool-action errors after left-hemisphere stroke
papers.abstract: Many individuals with limb apraxia after left-hemisphere stroke exhibit a lack of awareness of their tool-related action errors, i.e., unawareness of apraxia (UA; also called anosognosia of apraxia). Little is known about the prevalence of UA, the relationship between UA and apraxia severity, or its underlying mechanisms. Here, we assessed both the causes and consequences of UA. Based on a mechanistic model, we hypothesized that UA may arise because of deficits in representations signaling how tool-related movements should look and feel - a component of action knowledge - and that degradation of this knowledge impedes the detection of mismatches between planned and actual tool-related actions. We further predicted that a consequence of UA is a reduction in error-correction attempts. Fifty-six individuals with chronic LCVA gestured to show how to use tools. Immediately after the gesture production task, participants were asked if they made any errors. All participants also completed an action knowledge task to measure the integrity of tool-related movement goals. Individuals were denoted as exhibiting UA if they performed below a normative cutoff for apraxia yet reported making no errors. Our sample included 21 individuals with apraxia; of these, nearly half (48%) exhibited UA. These two groups made a comparable number of gesture errors and were of equivalent stroke severity, yet individuals with UA had significantly more impaired action knowledge. Additionally, individuals with UA were less likely to attempt to correct their errors compared to individuals who were aware of their apraxia. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that action knowledge (how tool actions look and feel) serves a key role in error detection and awareness of apraxia and may contribute to the difficulties with everyday tasks experienced by many people with apraxia.

papers.title: High-resolution temporal profiling reveals synchronized dynamics of the mouse gut microbiome
papers.abstract: Background The gut microbiome undergoes diurnal oscillations entrained by host circadian rhythms and feeding behavior, and disruption of these oscillations has been linked to metabolic dysfunction. However, the temporal organization of microbial activity within these oscillatory cycles remains poorly understood, largely because conventional sampling approaches lack the temporal resolution needed to resolve rapid microbial dynamics. Results To address this gap, we developed a fully automated fecal collection system that enables continuous sampling from individual mice at minute- to hour-scale resolution without manual intervention. Using this platform, we collected fecal samples at hourly intervals over 14 consecutive days from individually housed mice. To reconstruct genome- and function-level trajectories from these data, we developed a cost-effective method (GORIN) that combines full-length 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing with long-read metagenomic references. Applying a newly developed phase-analytic method (NPPD) to determine the instantaneous phase of each genome and functional gene, we found that the gut microbiota is organized into two phase-coherent groups corresponding to the light and dark phases of the host circadian cycle. These two groups differed in gene content, suggesting distinct carbohydrate utilization strategies, with the light-phase community enriched in mucosal glycan-degrading enzymes, whereas the dark-phase community was enriched in carbon storage metabolism and motility-related functions. Within each phase, microbial taxa and functional genes displayed reproducible temporal succession across individual mice. Perturbations, including cage transfer and antibiotic treatment transiently disrupted phase synchronization, as measured by the phase order parameter, followed by gradual recovery of phase coherence. Conclusions These findings reveal reproducible phase-synchronized temporal organization in the mouse gut microbiome, with community-level phase relationships that can be quantified and tracked over time and following perturbation. The automated sampling platform, genome-resolved profiling framework, and phase-analytic metrics introduced here provide a scalable strategy for characterizing community-level temporal dynamics in host-associated microbial ecosystems, with potential applications for understanding how disruption of microbial temporal organization contributes to dysbiosis.

papers.title: Toward defining loss functions in neuroscience: an XOR-based neuronal mechanism for local learning
papers.abstract: Of the three components often used to map deep learning onto neuroscience (architecture, learning rule and loss function), the biological counterpart of the loss is the least understood. For binary signals, the mismatch between an externally evoked response and its internally generated reconstruction is the XOR function, and its two asymmetric components, undershoot and overshoot, form a signed error that also indicates the direction of the required change. In a companion study, an eight-neuron, Dale-compliant signed-XOR motif, a six-neuron XOR comparator with two feedback neurons of opposite identity, was found in several connectomes and shown in spiking simulations to compute this signed error. Here we ask whether this signed error can serve as an effective learning signal. We use the logical function of one comparator per output unit as the only error signal of a binary autoencoder, with fixed random sign feedback to the hidden layer. Without backpropagation, a fully connected autoencoder trained for five epochs on binarized MNIST reaches 97.7% bit-wise and 94.8% balanced reconstruction accuracy (five seeds), and a convolutional variant with 533 parameters reaches 96.3% and 89.2%; without the sign of the error, learning collapses. Controls show that performance is carried by the comparator-driven decoder: a suitably initialised fixed random encoder reconstructs digits about as well or better, encoder learning improves digit readout mainly in narrow hidden layers, and a gradient-trained reference reaches 99.3% and 97.3% balanced accuracy. The signed error thus suffices for the synapses it reaches directly; credit assignment to earlier layers remains open.

papers.title: TMEM106B mediates ACE2-independent replication of the SARS-CoV-2 S-E484D variant in airway-derived cell models
papers.abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to cause significant respiratory disease, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although ACE2 is the primary receptor for viral entry, previous studies have identified a naturally occurring, ACE2-independent entry pathway that depends on cell surface heparan sulfates and the E484D substitution within the receptor-binding domain of Spike (S). In this study, we expand the panel of airway-derived cell lines that support ACE2-independent, S-E484D-dependent entry and identify the host lysosomal transmembrane protein TMEM106B as the alternative receptor for infection. Specifically, we show that knockout of TMEM106B completely abolishes infection by SARS-CoV-2 SE484D in NCI-H522 and NCI-H661 cells. Ectopic expression of the luminal C-terminal domain (CTD) of TMEM106B-either alone or redirected to the plasma membrane - is sufficient to enable viral entry largely independent of cell surface heparan sulfates in non-permissive cells. We show that S-E484D is required for TMEM106B utilization, whereas other Variants of Concern substitutions at S-E484 are unable to mediate entry. Fc-TMEM106B-CTD fusion protein binds to a chimeric VSV-SARS-CoV-2 SE484D with a higher affinity than WT virus and blocks infection by SARS-CoV-2 SE484D, supporting a direct interaction between S-E484D and TMEM106B-CTD. Serial passaging experiments with VSV-SARS-CoV-2 SE484D identify a V951A mutation within the heptad repeat 1 region that enhances viral spread and fusogenicity in the ACE2-independent cell models. Together, these findings demonstrate that TMEM106B is a key mediator of a naturally occurring ACE2-independent pathway in multiple airway-derived cell lines and suggest that variation in the S protein can expand receptor usage by SARS-CoV-2.

papers.title: iPSC modeling of pulmonary arterial hypertension to uncover pathomechanisms and unrecognized modes of action of sotatercept
papers.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a potentially fatal disease characterized by obliterative remodeling of distal pulmonary arteries, commonly associated with bone morphogenetic receptor type 2 (BMPR2) gene mutations. In patients with PAH, sotatercept, an activin signaling inhibitor, improves hemodynamics and outcomes, but clinical responses vary ranging from rapid improvements within weeks to no clinical benefit, suggesting additional mechanisms beyond its anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects. Using patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived smooth muscle cells (iSMCs) with BMPR2 extracellular- or kinase-domain mutations, we reproduced Activin A-driven PAH traits, including hyperproliferation, reduced apoptosis, enhanced contraction and excessive matrix production. We identified smooth muscle cell-to-myofibroblast transition as a previously unknown contributor to pulmonary vascular remodeling and demonstrated its inhibition by sotatercept. Beyond its established effects, sotatercept rapidly reduced contractility, collagen-integrin mechanotransduction and TGFbeta receptor expression, disrupting a pathological positive feedback loop, reflected by lower levels of circulating TGFbeta1 in patients on sotatercept. Taken together, our patient-derived iSMC platform links mutation-dependent mechanisms of pulmonary vascular remodeling to variable drug responsiveness and reveals previously unrecognized, potentially rapid-acting modes of sotatercept in PAH.

papers.title: Impact of ecotourism on the diversity of bacteria, archaea, and fungi in the freshwater stream of the Agua Azul Waterfalls in southeastern Mexico
papers.abstract: Natural freshwater streams harbor diverse microbial communities that support ecosystem functioning. Due to their great biodiversity and geomorphological characteristics, these ecosystems are often very attractive ecotourism destinations, which makes them highly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbances. The Agua Azul Waterfalls (Cascadas de Agua Azul, in Spanish), a major ecotourist destination located in Indigenous territories of southeastern Mexico (Chiapas, Mexico), offer a unique setting to investigate how sustained human activity influences microbial diversity and quality of water and sediments, as well as the role of local management in conserving biodiversity. To determine the ecological sensitivity of this freshwater stream to tourism pressure, we sampled sites spanning gradients of ecotourist activity and performed an integrated analysis of the physicochemical properties, elemental composition and microbial community composition (bacteria, archaea and fungi) of water and sediment samples. Areas associated with ecotourism activities showed notable changes in physicochemical parameters and microbial community composition, indicating localized human-induced impacts on this ecosystem. Although no significant differences were observed between zones, the detection of anaerobic methanogenic archaea and ammonia-oxidizing archaea in shallow sediments suggests that oxygen availability, methanogenesis (both acetoclastic and hydrogenotrophic), and nitrogen metabolism may play important roles in shaping the functioning of this ecosystem. Our findings highlight the potential of microbial diversity in combination with physicochemical parameters as a tool to detect early stages of human impacts on freshwater ecosystems and establish a basis for future monitoring and conservation efforts.

papers.title: Variation of Human Transfer RNA Demand and Supply
papers.abstract: Codons function as translation units in open-reading-frames of genes to encode for proteins. Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) connect every codon to its cognate amino acid. The genetic code defines the correspondence between codons and amino acids, yet whether individuals share a common quantitative relationship between tRNA supply and codon demand remains incompletely understood. Here, we established Marathon-tRNA-sequencing combined with matched mRNA-sequencing to reproducibly quantify tRNA and mRNA abundance from blood cells of ten healthy donors. We apply a precision-biology approach quantitatively integrating transcriptomic codon- and corresponding tRNA abundance across all 61 sense codons to compute the relative tRNA supply per codon. Thereby, we discover that relative tRNA supply varied approximately 1000-fold across codons, with broadly consistent patterns of highly and lowly supplied codons across donors. The extent of interindividual variability differed between codons and was highest for ACG (threonine). Relative tRNA supply also differed among synonymous codons, and genomic preferences did not consistently identify the codons with the highest relative supply. In summary, our findings reveal that pronounced inter-codon heterogeneity in relative tRNA supply constitutes a broadly conserved feature of human blood cells, with codon-specific degrees of interindividual variation. By distinguishing shared codon-specific patterns from human variation, this study establishes a reference for investigating codon-dependent gene regulation and synonymous sequence variation.

papers.title: Identification of PUFA interaction site on ASIC3 suggests a complex regulatory mechanism
papers.abstract: Inflammatory mediators including polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) potentiate ASIC3 by altering channel gating, yet the molecular basis for their interactions remains poorly defined. Using all-atom MD simulations and electrophysiology, we show that DHA accumulates around ASIC3 through interactions with a membrane-facing electropositive region along the outer leaflet of TM1. In the open state, a more buried binding site for the lipid is exposed that allows the carboxylate head group to bind a critical arginine along with nearby polar residues. Mutation of this site eliminates the DHA-mediated slowing of channel desensitization and also modestly reduces the effect PUFAs have on the proton sensitivity of channel activation. The same mutations do not prevent regulation by other lipid classes like N-acyl amino acids or lysophosphatidyl choline. Our results provide the first detailed description of a PUFA binding site on ASICs, offering new insights into lipid modulation and potential strategies for developing novel treatments for inflammatory pain.

papers.title: In vivo imaging of autophagy dynamics in the intact mammalian brain using a fluorescence lifetime-based sensor
papers.abstract: Autophagy regulates neuronal development, plasticity, and metabolism, yet our ability to monitor its spatial and temporal organization within intact mammalian neural circuits remains limited. We developed an imaging approach combining a pH-sensitive fluorescence lifetime readout with independent morphological labeling to quantify autophagic vesicle state, abundance, and trafficking in vivo. Following pharmacological, genetic, and ultrastructural validations, we resolved compartment-specific autophagy levels across somata, dendrites, and axons of layer 2/3 cortical excitatory neurons in the intact mouse brain. We uncovered distinct patterns of dendritic autophagy in vivo, revealing faster autophagic vesicle trafficking in distal than proximal dendrites, that were preferentially sensitive to sensory experience. Using a newly generated transgenic mouse line, we found distinct cell-type-specific basal autophagy in excitatory neurons, interneurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. These findings reveal the spatial, cell-type-specific, and activity-dependent organization of autophagy in the brain and establish a framework for investigating its regulation during development, plasticity, and disease.

papers.title: Knockdown of the long non-coding RNA DNAAF3-AS1 activates the p53 pathway and remodels the H3K36me3 landscape
papers.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.

papers.title: Interactions of Sleep and Repetitive Behavior in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Autism, and Intellectual Disability
papers.abstract: Objective: Sleep problems and restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) feature in neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disabilities (ID). It is unclear whether their interaction differs between conditions, and whether symptom dimensions might capture differences better than diagnostic categories. Method: In a preregistered cross-sectional analysis of the Healthy Brain Network community sample enriched for neurodevelopmental conditions (n = 2,394, 5-21 years), linear regression modeled parent-reported sleep disturbance and RRBs by diagnostic category and symptom dimensions (autistic traits, ADHD traits, IQ). Results: All symptom dimensions predicted sleep disturbance (p < .001), whereas only ADHD consistently predicted greater sleep disturbance (d = .35, 95% CI [.24, .47]) among diagnostic categories relative to typical development. All diagnostic categories and symptom dimensions were associated with RRB severity. Sleep disturbance and RRBs were associated in the entire sample (beta = .30, p < .001). Sleep disturbance predicted RRBs at all levels of autistic and ADHD traits, but most strongly with high autistic and low ADHD traits (beta = .16) and least strongly when both were high (beta = .13). Dimensional measures explained more variance than diagnoses for sleep disturbance (R square = .14 vs .03) and RRBs (R square = .38 vs .21), and provided better model fits in all comparisons. Conclusion: Autistic and ADHD traits shaped the relationship between sleep disturbance and RRBs, whereas diagnoses did not. Neurodevelopmental symptom assessments might be more informative than diagnoses to manage sleep and RRBs, though the cross-sectional design and parent report limit inference.

papers.title: Three-dimensional T1 mapping demonstrates the transfer of oxygen into cerebrospinal fluid during hyperoxia
papers.abstract: Background: This study optimised a non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging technique to investigate the transfer of oxygen into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) across the whole brain of healthy subjects. Methods: A shortening of the T1 (longitudinal relaxation time) of CSF was induced by 100% hyperoxia and measured using a 3D SPACE sequence at 3T in 29 subjects, thereby demonstrating the diffusion of oxygen from blood to CSF. T1 mapping was performed at high resolution (0.9-mm isotropic, taking approximately 16 minutes) to capture anatomical details of the CSF spaces and was also repeated more rapidly at a lower resolution (3-mm isotropic, taking approximately 3.5 minutes) to capture the temporal dynamics of T1 changes. Results: Significant region-dependent reductions in T1 were observed, indicating increased oxygen concentration in CSF. These occurred most prominently and rapidly in the cortical subarachnoid space and basilar cisterns, stabilising between 7 and 10 minutes after initiating hyperoxia, suggesting that oxygen diffusion primarily occurs via pial arteries and arteries at the base of the skull, both of which are in proximity to CSF-filled spaces. Over a timescale of 16 minutes, smaller T1 changes, only observed on the high-resolution T1 maps, occurred in the posterior lateral ventricles, where the choroid plexus is found, and the cisterna magna, possibly because of mixing effects with the adjacent basilar cisterns. Conclusions: This study provides insights into the structure of CSF and dynamics of blood-CSF oxygen exchange, including their regional dependence. Moreover, the methodology presented here could, in the future, offer a valuable tool for characterising the passive diffusion of oxygen across cerebral blood vessel walls (i.e., their oxygen permeability), thereby providing a potential marker of cerebrovascular integrity.

papers.title: Dynamic brain states during encoding and their post-encoding reinstatement predict episodic memory in children
papers.abstract: Episodic memory, the ability to rapidly learn and explicitly remember past events and experiences, plays a critical role in children's academic learning and knowledge acquisition. The formation of lasting memories relies on the brain's ability to dynamically organize its activity. How these neural configurations unfold moment-by-moment across encoding and offline phases remains poorly understood. To probe these dynamics, we applied a novel Bayesian Switching Dynamic Systems approach, a hidden Markov model with automatic state detection, to fMRI data from children performing scene encoding followed by an offline post-encoding rest. We identified four distinct brain states during encoding with unique activation modes between visual, medial temporal lobe, and frontoparietal and default mode network nodes. An 'active-encoding' state with integrated visual-hippocampal and frontoparietal activity dominated encoding and predicted individual memory performance, while an inactive state negatively predicted performance. State transition dynamics revealed that flexible shifts into the active-encoding state enhanced memory formation, whereas transitions toward inactive states impaired it, demonstrating that memory success depends on dynamic neural flexibility. Critically, encoding states spontaneously reemerged during post-encoding rest. A 'default-mode' state characterized by enhanced default mode network activity showed sustained maintenance during rest and robustly predicted memory outcomes, an effect specific to post-encoding, not pre-encoding rest. These findings establish that episodic memory emerges from coordinated brain state sequences bridging online encoding with offline consolidation, providing a computational framework for how moment-to-moment neural dynamics support memory formation in children.

papers.title: Calibrated Variant Effect Prediction at the Residue Level Using Conditional Score Distributions
papers.abstract: Effective clinical use of variant effect prediction (VEP) requires models that are both accurate and well-calibrated. Calibration refers to a model's ability to produce meaningful and reliable probability estimates. Benchmarking 30 VEPs, we show that while models appear well-calibrated on average, they remain markedly miscalibrated within specific variant subgroups. We propose VEP calibration at the residue level and introduce a calibration approach based on differential score mapping per variant subgroup. When calibration targets are chosen appropriately, our calibration approach can also improve model discrimination. Leveraging these insights, we develop RaCoon (Residue-aware Calibration of Conditional Distributions), implemented on ESM1b, which provides multicalibrated and interpretable predictions. RaCoon introduces Gaussian mixture models-based sampling fitted on model score distribution which substantially reduces labeled-data requirements for calibration. The method maintains low calibration error across variant subgroups and datasets while also improving AUROC on multiple benchmarks. Our calibration strategy is readily transferable to other VEPs.

papers.title: Transgenerational plasticity reflects local adaptation, but is not always advantageous for fitness
papers.abstract: Transgenerational plasticity (TGP) could contribute to phenotypic differences as much as allelic variation and within-generation plasticity. Here we use northern and southern populations of Mimulus cardinalis collected prior to and following a severe drought and grew plants in a multi-factorial experiment across three generations to tease apart allelic, TGP, parental effects, and plasticity. Where grand-offspring are likely to experience similar stressors as grandparents, TGP is often considered advantageous; our results show no such advantage. Instead, we find a TGP pattern analogous to local adaptation. Regardless of current environment, grand-offspring exhibit increased fitness when grandparents were exposed to environments that matched historical conditions and reduced fitness when exposed to foreign environments. We also find the evolutionary loss of TGP; prior to drought, northern flowering time and southern pollen viability were significantly affected by grandparent treatment but following four years of drought, grandparent treatment no longer affected these reproductive traits. Lastly, we find that TGP can have a greater effect on fitness than allelic change, parental environment, and within-generation plasticity. Our results indicate an additional way that phenotypes arise, sheds light on the potential for how rapid evolution might occur, and has significant implications for how we design evolutionary ecology experiments.

papers.title: Proneural lineage identity is the primary determinant of embryonic synchrony patterns in the developing hindbrain
papers.abstract: Does the stem cell origin impact on how daughter neurons acquire functional characteristics? Here, we uncovered that progenitor identity, defined by proneural gene expression, hardwires the functional mode (synchrony vs. asynchrony) of a neuron. Multimodal cell lineage reconstruction combining intersectional lineage tracing, newly developed computational tools, and genetic knockouts revealed that different progenitors produced functionally distinct neuronal subtypes in the zebrafish hindbrain. Dynamics of neuronal production suggest that progenitor competence changes over time. Whereas neurog1-expressing progenitors contributed to both glutamatergic and GABAergic lineages at early embryonic stages, later, other progenitor pools also assumed this role. Whole-hindbrain 3D atlases, in which we combined calcium imaging to monitor spontaneous neuronal activity with genetic perturbations and progenitor origin, unveiled that the emergence of neuronal activity patterns was presaged by their progenitor identity. This suggests a link between cell ontogeny and neuronal activity in the zebrafish hindbrain, and more fundamentally how the embryonic progenitor identity controls the emergence of neuronal diversity in glutamatergic and GABAergic neuronal populations.

papers.title: Contextual encoding of states and indices for episodic memories make goal-directed action selection flexible, transparent, and efficient
papers.abstract: When we want to solve a problem, our brain helps us by recalling related experiences. Furthermore, it can selectively recall only those experiences that fit especially well to the current context and contingencies. In addition, it provides explanations for chosen actions in terms of prior experiences. We show that experimental data on underlying neural codes of the brain, in particular contextual encoding of states and index cells for episodic memories, enable us to port essential aspects of the problem solving strategy of the brain into a simple algorithm. It only requires local online learning in shallow neural networks with low resolution of synaptic weights in order to explore a new environment, and it supports low-latency decision making. Hence it is especially suited for implementation in edge devices. Surprisingly, the performance of this light-weight algorithm on a standard benchmark task, navigation in Markov Decision Processes, is competitive with that of commonly used but computationally more demanding, less flexible, and less transparent reinforcement learning approaches.

papers.title: Uterine ERBB3 signaling is critical to cultivate stromal environment for functional gland branching
papers.abstract: Preimplantation uterine gland differentiation, involving glandular branching, is a prerequisite for secretion of leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), thereby establishing uterine receptivity to embryo implantation. This differentiation process is disrupted by the absence of FOXA2, a transcription factor specifically present in uterine glands. It remains unclear whether preimplantation glandular differentiation is regulated exclusively by gland-intrinsic mechanisms or is influenced by the surrounding microenvironment through mesenchymal-epithelial interactions. We show here that uterine deletion of Erbb3 leads to impaired gland branching and FOXA2 expression, as well as reduced female fertility. In contrast, females with uterine epithelial-specific deletion of Erbb3 show normal fertility, suggesting a critical role of stromal ERBB3 signaling. A transcriptomic profiling of day 3 stromal cells identified Igf1 as a candidate paracrine factor mediating the stromal-epithelial interaction. Thus, the uterine deletion of Igf1r leads to a reduced gland branching phenotype similar to that observed in Erbb3d/d uteri. These results demonstrate that ERBB3 regulates glandular branching and embryo implantation via the ERBB3-IGF1-IGF1R signaling pathway.

papers.title: Self-Supervised AI Reveals a Hidden Landscape of Prognostic Spatial Patterns in Multiplex Immunofluorescence Images
papers.abstract: Modern spatial proteomic methods, such as multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging, offer a data-rich view of spatial biology in intact tissues. However, interpreting its complexity is a major bottleneck, limiting its potential for biological discovery and clinical translation. Current computational methods often rely on segmentation-based approaches that discard crucial morphological information and are limited to testing pre-defined hypotheses. Here, we introduce a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that enables hypothesis-agnostic, context-aware discovery of biomarkers directly from mIF images. Our approach extracts rich feature representations that capture holistic architectural patterns, which integrate cellular morphology, marker interactions, and microenvironmental context without human supervision. Applying this framework to over 7,000 mIF tissue images from over 1,800 patients in two distinct cancer types, we demonstrate superior prognostic performance over conventional segmentation analyses. The method autonomously identified previously unknown and potentially clinically actionable biological patterns. In lung adenocarcinoma, these include a Ki67-mediated immune evasion phenotype, a subcellular pattern of GLB1 expression which aligns with low-grade EGFR-driven tumours, and distinct modes of tumour-immune interaction in PD-L1+ patients. We also find a regulatory T-cell-mediated immunosupressive environment promoting tumour budding in colorectal carcinoma. Our work establishes SSL as a powerful, scalable, and unbiased platform to decode tissue ecosystems while being fully explainable without pre-defined hypotheses. This paradigm shift transforms high-plex imaging from a hypothesis-testing tool into a hypothesis-generating engine that can accelerate the discovery of next-generation spatial biomarkers.

papers.title: EEG decodability of facial expressions and their stereoscopic depth cues in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: Face perception typically occurs in three-dimensional space, where stereoscopic depth cues enrich the perception of facial features. Yet, most neurophysiological research on face processing relies on two-dimensional displays, potentially overlooking the role of stereoscopic depth information. Here, we combine immersive virtual reality (VR), electroencephalography (EEG), and eye tracking to examine the neural representation of faces under controlled manipulations of stereoscopic depth. Thirty-four participants viewed computer-generated faces with neutral, happy, angry, and surprised expressions in frontal view under monoscopic and stereoscopic viewing conditions. Using time-resolved multivariate decoding, we show that EEG signals in immersive VR conditions can reliably differentiate facial expressions. Stereoscopic depth cues elicited a distinct and decodable neural signature, confirming the sensitivity of our approach to depth-related processing. Yet, expression decoding remained robust across depth conditions, indicating that under controlled frontal viewing, the neural representation of behaviorally distinguishable facial expressions is invariant to binocular depth cues. Eye tracking showed that expression-related gaze patterns contained comparable information but did not account for neural representations, while depth information was absent in gaze patterns--consistent with dissociable representational processes. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of EEG-based neural decoding in fully immersive VR as a tool for investigating face perception in naturalistic settings and provide new evidence for the stability of expression representations across depth variations in three-dimensional viewing conditions.

papers.title: Wetting and localization of chromatin condensates by surface-enriched proteins
papers.abstract: We put forward a novel mechanism for the positioning of chromatin within the cell nucleus that does not rely on polymer adsorption to the nuclear lamina. Using a field-theoretic model of a chromatin condensate formed through polymer--protein co-condensation, we show that surface enrichment of chromatin-binding proteins can localize the condensate at the nuclear lamina even when chromatin itself is repelled from the surface. The competition between the tendency of the protein component to wet the surface and the conformational restrictions of the polymer near the impenetrable boundary produces a nonmonotonic chromatin density profile with a maximum at a finite distance from the lamina, consistent with live-cell experiments [Sci. Adv. \textbf{7}, eabf6251 (2021)]. We further demonstrate that a non-binding protein competing for surface association can regulate the position of the condensate, providing an alternative pathway by which compositional changes of the lamina can induce chromatin repositioning. A phase diagram of the surface-localization transition reveals how surface affinity, protein availability, and polymer--protein interaction strength control the switch between peripheral and central chromatin configurations. This wetting-based mechanism contrasts with direct polymer adsorption and provides a general framework for understanding how multicomponent condensates interact with responsive biological surfaces.

papers.title: Mantpy: a framework for extracellular matrix analysis in spatial proteomics
papers.abstract: Spatial proteomics technologies now profile cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM) together in situ. Yet analysis tools remain cell-centric, despite the ECM playing an essential role in health and disease. Here we present Mantpy, a framework that represents the ECM, and its interface with cells, as spatial graphs. Mantpy builds ECM graphs directly from matrix markers and links them with cell graphs for joint cell-ECM analysis, supporting graph statistics, explainable graph deep learning and visualisation. Mantpy extends from a single ECM marker to multiplexed cell-ECM panels. It recovers layered tissue architecture in the intestine from collagen IV alone, quantifies infection-associated ECM remodelling in mouse liver, and relates cells to the surrounding matrix in mouse lung, where cellular context recovers synthetically corrupted matrix labels. Released with ECM-inclusive datasets and interoperating with the scverse ecosystem and pytorch geometric.

papers.title: A Transcriptionally Distinct Intermediate Activation State Precedes Langerhans Cell Migration from the Epidermis
papers.abstract: Langerhans cells (LC) are antigen-presenting cells that form dense epidermal networks for immune surveillance. Upon antigen uptake, LCs are activated and subsequently orchestrate immune responses by migrating into the lymphatic system. However, the regulation of transcriptional programs during activation and the behavior of LCs in vivo during this transition remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study combines single-cell transcriptomic analysis with intravital imaging to reconstruct the activation trajectory of epidermal LCs. In particular, the study generates a high-resolution single-cell transcriptomic dataset comprising over 22,000 high-quality epidermal LCs under both homeostatic and injury conditions.
