Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results. A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline (B[SE]=0.067[0.033], p=.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment (B[SE]=0.056[0.033], p=.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap x age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence (B[SE]=-0.007[0.003], p=.033). Conclusions. These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk.

papers.title: Enhancing working memories using repetitive TMS
papers.abstract: Working memory, the ability to retain and manipulate information no longer present in the environment, is fundamental for goal-directed behavior (Baddeley, 2012; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; D'Esposito, 2007; D'Esposito & Postle, 2015). Alpha oscillations (~8-12 Hz) have two apparently contradictory roles in working memory. Alpha activity gates irrelevant information through inhibition, a role causally supported by rhythmic transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of parietal cortex at alpha frequency when a retrospective cue renders a memory item irrelevant (Bonnefond & Jensen, 2012; Riddle et al., 2020). Yet alpha activity also tracks the content of memory and binds the features of memorized objects during maintenance (Foster et al., 2016; Pagnotta et al., 2026). Whether alpha oscillations causally support the fidelity of memory representations during maintenance is untested. Here, 24 participants received short trains of repetitive TMS (rTMS) at theta (6 Hz) or alpha frequency (10 Hz), or in an arrhythmic control pattern, during the second half of the delay of a color working memory task, over the left posterior inferior frontal sulcus or the left intraparietal sulcus. A mixture model separated memory precision from swap errors and guesses. Alpha stimulation of the intraparietal sulcus specifically increased memory precision, whereas rhythmic stimulation of either site reduced response error, guesses and swaps irrespective of frequency. These results provide causal evidence that alpha oscillations support the fidelity of working memory representations during maintenance, and show that rhythmic stimulation at the appropriate frequency, site and time can enhance human working memory.

papers.title: Technology solutions for immune loci: integrated high-resolution KIR genotyping reveals allelic, structural, and KIR-HLA diversity across 24 human populations
papers.abstract: High-resolution genotyping of killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) genes remains challenging because of extensive sequence homology, copy-number variation, and complex haplotype structures. Although KIR allelic variation influences receptor expression and function, routine typing has largely been limited to gene presence or absence. Here, we evaluated an integrated short-read sequencing system combining a four-reaction, two-stage multiplex PCR assay (ScisGo-KIR-v3), centralized cloud-based copy-aware allele analysis, and interactive genotype review. The system was applied to 2,298 individuals representing 24 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project, with matched high-resolution HLA class I genotypes. Independent validation against complete, phased PacBio KIR sequences from 48 samples demonstrated 98.6% automated copy-number concordance and 92.8% combined copy-number and allele concordance across 768 gene-sample comparisons. Following desktop review, all evaluated assignments were concordant with the reference sequences. In a separate comparison of four computational genotyping methods involving 311 shared samples, the automated Scisco pipeline showed the lowest overall mismatch with the four-method consensus (1.62%). Population analyses identified substantial allele diversity and distinct centromeric and telomeric haplotype-motif distributions. Although exact haplotype pairs were frequently ambiguous, structural assignments became increasingly resolvable at the motif level, and motif backgrounds exhibited characteristic allele compositions. Paired KIR and HLA analysis revealed inherited receptor-ligand configurations concealed by gene-content typing. Among 1,401 KIR3DL1/HLA-B Bw4 co-carriers, 57 lacked an allele annotated for ordinary surface expression, while 457 of 1,175 KIR2DS4 co-carriers of six specified HLA-C allotypes carried only truncated receptor forms. Allele-specific KIR2DL1 and KIR2DS5 classifications further distinguished receptor properties and published ligand-binding annotations that varied among populations. Although potential receptor-ligand repertoire composition differed across populations, analyses did not establish preferential KIR-HLA genetic association after accounting for population structure and multiple testing. Together, these findings demonstrate that integrated short-read KIR genotyping can provide scalable, high-resolution allele and copy-number information while explicitly retaining uncertainty in inferred haplotype structures. Compatibility with established HLA laboratory workflows provides a practical foundation for incorporating allele-resolved KIR analysis into immunogenetic research and future clinical investigations.

papers.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates
papers.abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

papers.title: Cerebral Organization in the trilobite Yunnanocephalus yunnanensis
papers.abstract: The clade Trilobita is recognized for its extraordinary morphological diversifications amidst a highly constrained body plan. This raises the question of whether trilobite nervous systems were conservative or comparably diverse. However, despite the identification of thousands of trilobite species and increasing evidence for neural preservation in other Paleozoic euarthropods, the recognition of a fossilized trilobite brain has remained elusive. Here we describe the identification of a trilobite brain and its spatially constrained position within its cranidium. An unusually preserved specimen of the lower Cambrian trilobite Yunnanocephalus yunnanensis reveals a bilaterally organized organ connected to its lateral eyes. Comparisons to the brain of a trilobitomorph xandarellid support the interpretation of this organ as a modest cerebrum comprising prosocerebral, protocerebral, and deutocerebral domains, an organization typifying the euarthropod cerebral ground pattern. These findings suggest that the cerebrum of Yunnanocephalus could have supported the multimodal sensory processing and behavioral repertoires of trilobites, while retaining the deep evolutionary conservation of brain organization across euarthropod lineages

papers.title: Autonomous sampling and eDNA metabarcoding for offshore biodiversity monitoring: a pilot study around an FPSO in the Southwestern Atlantic
authors: do Amaral, D. L. A. S.
papers.abstract: Characterizing biodiversity around offshore infrastructure is necessary to assess possible influences of industrial activities on marine communities and distinguish persistent ecological change from short-term variability. Combining environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding with autonomous sampling offers a way to expand biological, spatial and temporal coverage while reducing dependence on crewed field operations. We evaluated this approach around a floating production, storage and offloading unit (FPSO) in the Santos Basin, Brazil, to establish an initial biodiversity reference and inform subsequent monitoring. A third-generation Environmental Sample Processor integrated into the W Tupan II uncrewed surface vessel enabled autonomous water sampling at coastal sites, transit locations and the FPSO area, yielding 64 biological samples. We used mitochondrial 12S and 16S metabarcoding to assess taxonomic diversity, sampling completeness and spatial and short-term temporal variation. Around the FPSO, 47 samples from 21 points detected 34 species with 12S and 28 with 16S, representing 74.3% and 65.4% of the respective estimated species richness. Local analyses showed weak radial differentiation across 300-1,500 m around the FPSO, with no near-far taxonomic indicators remaining significant after multiple-testing corrections. Samples collected at the same point approximately 1-2 h apart were almost as dissimilar as samples from different points, whereas technical replicates of post-extraction processing closely matched their source DNA profiles. Taxon turnover accounted for approximately 73% and 80% of temporal Jaccard dissimilarity for 12S and 16S, respectively. Regional analyses recovered a coastal-offshore compositional contrast, with geography and sampling date jointly represented. This pilot supports autonomous eDNA sampling as an operational approach to offshore biodiversity monitoring. The findings favour repeated sampling across campaigns to distinguish transient detections from recurrent patterns and persistent compositional changes.

papers.title: Additive and dominance gene effects described by a logistic function in concentration-limited metabolic pathways at steady state out of equilibrium
papers.abstract: Abstract Additive (a) and dominance (d) gene effects are key to phenotype manifestation. We investigated the relationship between these effects and gene-encoded enzyme rates in an n-step linear metabolic pathway with mass limitation at stationary state out of equilibrium, where internal flux depended on internal enzyme concentrations (Ei, i=1 to n) and external flux on input/output enzyme/transporter concentrations (Ee). Using coupled reversible Michaelis-Menten (MM) equations for Ei rates and irreverisble MM for Ee rates we found that stationary-state metabolite concentration (Si) was a logistic function of Ei. Its inflection point (S0i, E0i) depended on the total mass of the system ({Sigma} Si) and on Ee saturation, shifting from negative to positive values as reaction kinetics transitioned from first to mixed or zero order. Moreover, {Sigma} Si and Ee saturation explained negative, partial, and complete dominance in this metabolic system, provided phenotypic value of trait T is linearly dependent on Si at certain sink. The system was unstable when approaching closure (Ee=0). In this condition, asymptotic Smax equaled equilibrium concentration, being equilibrium displacement the driving force of flux. In pathways with n>1 reaction steps there was a change of regime in early reactions when increments in En passed E0n. This change of regime led to peaks raising at some Si previous to Sn and Sn+1 that were modeled by adding a Gaussian component to the logistic equation. Therefore, if T is determined by some of these Si, overdominance and dominance reversals may be explained. We obtained a good fit when applied this equation to Ei and Si data obtained from silicon-cell models developed with specific kinetic equations and experimentally determined kinetic parameters. In addition, we applied this framework to experimental data on amylose accumulation in starch granules catalyzed by granule-bound starch synthase I, and found that the logistic function fitted data from six plant species. This framework may contribute a partial explanation of the non-linearity between genotype and phenotype from the metabolic standpoint, which may be useful in the future for plant or animal breeding technologies.

papers.title: Dissociable episodic memory performance and subjective experience across the aphantasia imagery spectrum
papers.abstract: Mental imagery is often assumed to support episodic memory, yet whether this relationship depends on conscious access to imagery, and how reduced imagery differs from total aphantasia, remains unclear. The present study compared objective episodic memory performance, subjective trial-by-trial vividness, confidence, and response times in people reporting normal imagery, reduced imagery, or total aphantasia, across younger and older age groups. Participants completed an incidental-encoding episodic memory task requiring identification of visual or spatial changes in targets within scenes, alongside trial-by-trial vividness and confidence ratings. Across the full imagery spectrum, trial-level fluctuations in vividness were related to memory performance, whereas trait-level and averaged vividness measures were not. Moreover, reduced imagery and total aphantasia showed dissociable patterns of episodic memory performance and subjective experience. In the reduced-imagery group, vividness was a stronger predictor of accuracy and response times, vividness judgements were slower, and confidence was lower, suggesting greater metacognitive uncertainty when imagery is weak and inconsistent. Controls outperformed reduced and aphantasic groups on visual but not spatial changes, and both groups responded more slowly than controls; confidence did not differ between control and aphantasic groups. Age-related memory decline was observed in the control and reduced groups but not in the aphantasic group. Exit questionnaire data highlighted limited awareness of aphantasia among typical imagers and a persistent belief among aphantasic participants that their memory was inferior. Together, these findings show that reduced imagery should be distinguished from total aphantasia rather than treating both as a single population, and that trial-level fluctuations in vividness reveal relationships with episodic memory that trait-level and averaged measures do not capture.

papers.title: Neuroscience in Conversation: Tracking Scientific Change Through an Open Seminar Archive
papers.abstract: Scientific talks capture how researchers frame questions, debate ideas, and communicate emerging methods, providing a complementary record of scientific change to the published literature. We investigated whether an open neuroscience seminar archive could reveal shifting scientific attention and contain predictive information about subsequent discourse. We analysed 470 English-language transcripts from the Clinical Neuroanatomy Seminars YouTube channel, spanning 2010-2026 and approximately 2.6 million words, using longitudinal vocabulary analysis, unsupervised topic clustering, conceptual comparisons, and rolling temporal forecasting. The archive captured sustained discussion of language, white matter anatomy, connectivity, clinical neuroscience, and neurobiological mechanisms, alongside changes in their relative prominence. Network-related terminology became more prominent than localisation-related terminology, references to individual variability and computational approaches increased, and open science practices became more visible in scientific discussion. Beyond retrospective description, a regression model predicted keyword frequencies one and two years ahead with approximately 12% and 17% lower mean absolute error, respectively, than a persistence baseline. This modest gain is better explained by smoothing of year-to-year fluctuations than by genuine prediction: terms showing the strongest recent growth tended to fall back rather than continue rising. These findings suggest that spoken scientific discourse shows clear longitudinal change but offers limited evidence of information about subsequent shifts in attention. Interpretation remains grounded in the archive curated scope and changing content composition. By making nearly two decades of freely accessible neuroimaging education amenable to systematic analysis, this study connects open educational practice with the study of science itself. Open seminar archives can serve as reusable research resources, preserving the conversations through which scientific communities develop and revise their ideas.

papers.title: Daylight exposure improves sleep and subsequent sleepiness
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: The causal effects of daylight exposure on sleep remain poorly understood, particularly under real-world conditions. This study aimed to address this gap by examining the effects of an afternoon daylight intervention on subsequent sleep. Methods: Ten healthy participants (4 males; 19 to 28 years) completed two randomized 3-h afternoon outdoor walks under high-intensity light (HIL; clear goggles) or attenuated light (AL; neutral-density-filtered goggles; ~10 photopic lux) conditions. Light exposure was centered around the estimated crossover between the phase-advancing and phase-delaying portions of the light phase-response curve, individually determined from baseline dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). Subsequent nocturnal sleep was assessed using at-home polysomnography (PSG), and subjective sleepiness and sleep quality were assessed using the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and Groningen Sleep Quality Scale, respectively. Differences between conditions and across time were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Results: There were no significant differences between conditions in DLMO timing or the phase angle between DLMO and sleep onset, indicating that the light manipulation did not produce a detectable shift in circadian phase. Sleep duration and self-reported sleep quality were also unchanged. However, nighttime delta power accumulated more rapidly following HIL exposure, accompanied by greater NREM sleep and reduced wakefulness after sleep onset (all p < 0.01). Participants were also significantly less sleepy upon awakening following HIL compared with AL exposure (p < 0.05). Conclusions: High-intensity natural daylight exposure may promote greater sleep intensity and reduce sleepiness upon awakening. These findings highlight a potential role for daytime light exposure in modulating subsequent sleep physiology and next-morning sleepiness, independent of changes in circadian phase.

papers.title: Dimensionality Reduction for Cyclic Compositional Data
papers.abstract: The cyclic nature of many biological systems is frequently reflected in periodic gene expression patterns. Standard dimensionality reductions can reveal such variation but do not link a sample's position on a cycle to an ordering of the molecular features that define it. We introduce clrcycle, which applies a centered log-ratio transformation, learns a cyclic feature ordering by maximizing variance captured by the first Fourier mode, and projects samples onto the corresponding cosine and sine coordinates. The resulting two-dimensional geometry assigns each sample a phase and a radius measuring the magnitude of its projection onto the learned Fourier circle. Across a mouse circadian atlas, clrcycle recovers known temporal organization and reveals tissue-specific differences in rhythmic timing. In FUCCI-profiled single cells, clrcycle represents independently measured cell-cycle phase in two-dimensional coordinates more reliably than conventional two-dimensional embeddings. In human endometrium, a circular coordinate learned from 250 highly variable genes recovers menstrual-stage organization and can stage unseen endometrial biopsies. Together, these results establish clrcycle as powerful, explicitly circular dimensionality reduction technique to quantify high-dimensional cyclic variation across biological cycles.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.

papers.title: Genome-Wide Transcriptomics Uncovers a Lung-to-Aorta Inflammatory Program Driving Influenza-Induced Atherosclerosis Exacerbation
papers.abstract: Influenza infection increases cardiovascular risk in individuals with pre-existing atherosclerosis, yet the genome-wide transcriptional basis of this association remains undefined. We performed bulk RNA sequencing of aorta and lung tissues from high-fat diet-fed Apoe-/- mice infected with influenza A/PR/8/34 versus PBS-treated controls at day 15 post-infection, identifying 6,828 differentially expressed genes across both tissues (5,694 in the lung and 1,134 in the aorta; adjusted p < 0.05). In the lung, influenza sustained a CXCR3-driven chemokine storm, comprehensive Th1, Th17, and exhaustion T-cell activation programs, coordinated monocyte recruitment through Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl8, and Ccl12, a broad acute phase response including Saa3 and A2m, alveolar identity collapse through loss of Nkx2-1 and surfactant proteins, and broad metabolic dysregulation involving suppression of fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial function, and circadian metabolic regulators. In the aorta, influenza drove macrophage and DAMP activation through Trem1, Fpr2, and S100a8, cytotoxic T-cell engagement, smooth muscle cell dedifferentiation through Myocd loss, convergent bioenergetic failure, and an ectopic lung-identity gene signature representing a previously undescribed cross-organ communication mechanism. Circadian clock and Hippo/YAP pathway suppression were shared across both tissues, identifying systemic vulnerabilities connecting pulmonary infection to vascular structural compromise. Consistent with the in vivo findings, influenza-infected Apoe-/- bone marrow-derived macrophages exhibited inflammasome activation, DAMP amplification, M1 polarization, and suppression of prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory resolution. Together these findings define a lung-to-aorta inflammatory and metabolic axis driving atherosclerotic plaque destabilization during the post-infection recovery period and identify CCR2/CXCR3 antagonism, NLRP3 inhibition, and YAP pathway activation as candidate therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Bird-assisted sampling of air temperature reveals three-dimensional cooling effects of urban vegetation
papers.abstract: Air temperature in cities is highly variable horizontally and vertically, reflecting the complexity of the urban landscape. Yet, studies of urban temperature still depend largely on ground-based meteorological stations and satellite-derived surface temperature products, both of which provide limited information on near-surface air conditions and vertical structure. We tested a bio-assisted monitoring approach to characterise fine-scale three-dimensional patterns of summer air temperature in the city of Rome, Italy, using homing pigeons (Columba livia) equipped with lightweight GPS loggers air-temperature sensors. Flight data collected during summer sampling campaigns between 2023 and 2025 revealed pronounced spatial, vertical, and temporal variability in air temperature over the urban area. Modelling results showed that vegetation had a measurable cooling influence within the lower urban atmosphere with grass cover and wooded patches were both associated with lower air temperatures. Thermal contrasts between land-cover types were the strongest at low altitudes and during morning hours, when air above artificial surfaces was up to approximately 5 {degrees}C warmer than above vegetated areas. We also observed a buffering effect associated with green areas: air temperature, particularly near wooded vegetation, remained relatively stable up to approximately 300 m from the patch edge before increasing by as much as 3 {degrees}C. These findings suggest that animal-borne sensing can complement conventional monitoring by capturing air temperature variability across urban landscapes and heights, while also helping to identify when and where urban vegetation most effectively mitigates heat exposure. This approach offers new opportunities to support climate-resilient urban planning and targeted heat mitigation strategies.

papers.title: BenchMHC: a reproducible framework for peptide-MHC presentation prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting which peptides an MHC molecule presents is the first step in neoantigen and epitope discovery pipelines. Most published predictors are released for inference only, and each is trained on a different dataset, so the effect of a new method cannot be separated from the effect of its training data. We present BenchMHC, an open framework that reproduces, retrains and evaluates pMHC presentation models on public data only, and that records every implementation decision made in a reproduction. Our NetMHCpan-4.1 reproduction reaches 0.794 per-allele Mean Top-K against 0.790 for the official webserver, and 0.0025 Median FRANK against 0.0022. It scores 280,000 peptide/allele pairs in 27 s, about 350 times faster than the original binary. We then examine the training data. In the public NetMHCpan-4.1 eluted-ligand sets, 86 to 99% of hits are found in the human proteome, against about 12% of their decoys, so a model can separate hits from decoys using this difference rather than features related to MHC binding. Redrawing the decoys within the source protein of each hit and matching their cysteine status, with no other change, raises per-allele Mean Top-K on the regenerated v2.0.0 evaluation set from 0.734 to 0.755, and increases Median FRANK on CD8 epitopes from 0.0025 to 0.0053. The same change improves one evaluation set and degrades the other. Code (Apache-2.0) and model checkpoints (CC BY-NC-4.0): https://github.com/instadeepai/BenchMHC-public.

papers.title: Scalp EEG detects motor sequence replay signatures during wakeful rest
papers.abstract: Brief wakeful rest may support motor-memory processing through replay of recently practiced neural sequences, but human motor replay has been demonstrated mainly with invasive recordings or magnetoencephalography. Here we tested whether ordered motor-sequence replay can be detected from scalp EEG across wakeful rest during motor skill learning. During rest, participants received no cue, regular or accelerated auditory targeted-memory reactivation (TMR), or randomized tones. Neural states re-emerged in the practiced sequence order, revealing forward replay across conditions. Accelerated TMR enhanced total learning; within this condition, stronger forward replay showed the clearest exploratory relationship with micro-offline gains, while forward and reverse replay also covaried with gains across the cohort. The apparent replay timescale shifted systematically with decoder temporal resolution, showing that measured timing reflects both neural dynamics and the observation model. These findings support scalp EEG as a scalable approach for studying ordered motor-sequence reactivation during wakeful rest.

papers.title: Asking the Data: Conversational Interrogation of LC-MS/MS Proteomics Data Sets with an LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Proteomics workflows are designed to answer predefined questions, leaving analytical problems that emerge after first results difficult to investigate without additional bioinformatics work. We introduce data set interrogation, a conversational framework in which a researcher uses a large language model (LLM) agent to translate emerging questions into executable tests, check the answers against controls, and keep the code, inputs, and decisions in a dated record. Applied retrospectively to four LC-MS/MS data sets, the framework exposed problems that changed the interpretation of three in-house studies: a search database lacking one of two symbionts, a swapped pair of tandem mass tag (TMT) channels, statistics inflated by non-host proteins, and false deamidation assignments caused by selection of the 13C isotope peak as monoisotopic; the same question asked of every data set revealed failed or partial cysteine alkylation in all three. A public TMT data set was reanalyzed from raw files in 24 min, a feasibility measure without a human comparison; among spectra identified by both workflows, 99.2% received the same peptide assignment as in Proteome Discoverer, and protein fold changes correlated (r = 0.93). In seeded tests, a purpose built channel assignment check detected all 216 between strain channel swaps and none of 90 within-strain swaps. The framework couples natural language interaction with executable analyses, explicit controls, and traceable decisions, enabling researchers to investigate questions not anticipated by the original pipeline. These results establish feasibility in a limited retrospective setting with one researcher; broader evaluation across users, models, and data sets is required to determine general performance.

papers.title: Best Practices for Pre-Processing Large-Scale ATAC-Seq Data: Why Epidemiological Studies Demand Greater Stringency
papers.abstract: Assay for transposase accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) and related techniques provide critical insight into the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate gene expression in health and disease. Accurate identification of biologically meaningful chromatin accessibility signals remains an underexplored analytical challenge. Advances in sequencing technologies have increased both the magnitude and complexity of ATAC-seq datasets, leading to demand for scalable, reproducible and robust computational analysis frameworks. Peak calling, which identifies regions of chromatin accessibility, is a critical step that underpins all downstream quantitative analyses. However, there is a lack of consensus regarding the optimal peak calling strategy. Here, we present a novel bioinformatics pipeline PIPPA (Pipeline for Integrative Peak calling in Population-scale ATAC-seq), for quality control and peak set curation of large-scale ATAC-seq datasets. Using two independent cell-type sorted ATAC-seq datasets, we show that peak calling performance is dataset-dependent and that no single significance threshold performs optimally across all scenarios. We provide practical recommendations for parameters to generate high-confidence chromatin accessibility profiles. Our peak calling approach is applicable for other genome wide epigenomic assays such as ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag. By standardising this process, the PIPPA pipeline enhances epidemiological studies focused in identifying epigenetic dysregulation associated with development and disease.

papers.title: Stimulation strategy matters: A B-cell focused single-cell transcriptomic study on in vitro stimulated immune cells
papers.abstract: Distinct in vitro B-cell stimulation strategies, defined by stimulation condition and incubation duration, have been described in diverse studies. Often, these approaches are considered interchangeable due to comparable flow-cytometric outputs concerning fluorescence intensities and B-cell subset distributions. However, whether these phenotypic similarities also reflect comparable underlying transcriptional states have not been systematically evaluated yet. In this study, we provide an unbiased comparison of B-cell activation strategies on healthy individuals, resulting in a single-cell transcriptomic atlas (4 donors; ~2,029 cells per sample; 81,160 cells in total with 56.3% annotated as B cells). Two T-cell independent stimulators targeting toll-like receptors (ODN2006 and IFN-{gamma}/R-848), were assessed next to two T-cell dependent stimulators (anti-CD40 and anti-CD3/CD28 antibodies), all incubated for eight and 30 hours. Observed overlap for differential abundance, differential gene expression and cell-cell interactions could directly be linked to T-cell (in)dependent working mechanism. Strategy-specific results uncovered time-point specific transcriptional changes, revealed the largest set of differentially expressed genes for IFN-{gamma}/R-848 and ODN2006, and showed that IFN-{gamma}/R-848 and anti-CD3/CD28 induced the majority of the cell-cell interactions. Ultimately, our reference atlas emphasizes the importance and facilitates the rational selection of optimal B-cell stimulation strategies, particularly for studies aiming to interrogate B-cell dysregulation in immune-mediated diseases.

papers.title: ProtCell: a foundation model for single-cell proteomics
papers.abstract: Single-cell proteomics provides a direct functional readout of cellular states, but targeted assays measure limited and non-identical protein panels, fragmenting information across experiments. Here, we present ProtCell, a foundation model developed using approximately 380 million cells from 98 datasets for pretraining and evaluation. ProtCell combines protein-identity and continuous-abundance embeddings in a transformer encoder and learns cell- and protein-level representations through masked abundance modeling. ProtCell first connects fragmented profiles through transferable annotation and batch correction while preserving biological organization. It then extends limited profiles through abundance reconstruction and inference of an unmeasured cytotoxic protein program enriched in natural killer cells and memory CD8$^+$ T cells. The learned protein dependencies further guide the selection of compact panels that retain information for profile reconstruction and biological classification. ProtCell thus provides a framework for connecting fragmented proteomic profiles, extending information beyond measured panels and guiding more informative measurements.

papers.title: What do navigating animals see? Reconstructing the visual histories of desert ants
papers.abstract: To understand how brains translate sensory input into behavioural outputs requires a fuller account of the sensory experience of individual animals in their natural settings. Previously we developed a visual rendering software capable of reconstructing the information that insect's compound eyes perceive (Millward et al, 2022). In this work, we extend this software pipeline to integrate data from animal tracking, habitat mapping, and compound eye modelling methods. The result is a new type of dataset that documents the natural foraging behaviour of desert ants (a model species for the study of animal navigation) within their natural habitat, combined with simulation tools to accurately reconstruct the visual experience of each forager as they learned to navigate their surroundings. This addresses a long-held need to create realistic training input for brain models complimented with verification tests in the same real ecologically relevant scenarios.

papers.title: MPFIL: Multi-Level Protein Feature Integration for Predicting Mutation-Induced Protein-Protein Binding Affinity Changes
papers.abstract: Predicting mutation-induced changes in protein protein binding affinity ({triangleup}{triangleup}G) is challenging because mutations can affect both local residue environments and the structural organization of protein complexes. Existing approaches often rely on handcrafted physicochemical, energetic, or evolutionary features, which introduce additional computational costs and require domain-specific knowledge. In this work, we propose MPFIL, a multi-level protein feature integration framework for predicting mutation-induced protein-protein binding affin ity changes. MPFIL integrates structural and sequential infor mation to characterize mutation effects from complementary perspectives. Its structural feature extraction module captures mutation-induced structural changes and differential information between wild-type and mutant complexes, while sequence feature extraction modules model local residue context and long-range dependencies. The resulting features are integrated for {triangleup}{triangleup}G prediction. We evaluate MPFIL on three benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate competitive and consistent performance across different protein complex settings, while ablation studies verify the contribution of the structural and sequential features. These results support the effectiveness of multi-level protein feature integration for modeling mutation induced changes in protein-protein binding affinity.

papers.title: Taxon-in-context reveals ecological individuality in the human gut microbiome
papers.abstract: Ecological theory holds that a microbe's role depends on its surrounding community. Yet abundance profiles and fixed ecological groupings leave its individual context implicit. We introduce taxon-in-context, a reproducible representation of each microbe's context within an individual's microbiome. Across 7,700 metagenomes, we show that common gut species occupy different contexts in different people. This flexibility peaked in early life and declined through adulthood, a pattern reproduced in a larger genus-level compendium. For selected species, context within each person's microbiome revealed age associations beyond species abundance and the person's context mixture. In an independent longitudinal urinary tract infection cohort, microbes switched contexts within individuals. Taxon-in-context enabled recurrence prediction where an abundance-based model performed near chance. Taxon-in-context and these findings expose a measurable, dynamic and individualized layer of microbiome organization, providing a basis for investigating why the same microbe or intervention may have different biological consequences across people.

papers.title: CATFISHR: integration of transcriptome and inferred CNV profiles for comprehensive malignant cell identification
papers.abstract: Malignant cell identification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) remains challenging because transcriptomic cell typing, somatic variant detection and inferred copy-number approaches each have modality-specific limitations. Rare or ambiguous malignant populations are especially vulnerable to misclassification or exclusion, despite their relevance to treatment resistance, minimal residual disease, and metastasis. We developed CATFISHR, a semi-automated workflow that integrates RNA-expression similarity, inferred copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and consensus cell typing to classify malignant cells relative to high-confidence references. CATFISHR was evaluated across eight cohorts, including seven scRNA-seq datasets spanning multiple carcinomas and melanoma subtypes, and one 10x Visium spatial transcriptomics sample. Compared with available benchmarks or ground truths, CATFISHR achieved balanced accuracy > 0.85 in six of eight cohorts and F1 score > 0.80 in six of eight cohorts. Cells uniquely identified by CATFISHR as malignant ("Hidden" cells) were present in every dataset and were not consistently explained by standard quality-control metrics. In several cohorts, Hidden cells were transcriptionally closer to benchmark malignant than non-malignant compartments; in Visium data, sampled Hidden spots contained histologist-confirmed morphologically malignant cells. CATFISHR reduces missed malignant calls while preserving rare, transitional and benchmark-discordant populations for downstream investigation.

papers.title: Metric-driven Pre-acquisition Diagnostics for Automated Microscopy Ultraviolet Surface Excitation (MUSE)
papers.abstract: Background Automated microscopy enables large-scale tiled imaging but remains sensitive to variations in alignment, illumination, focus, and sample coverage that may only be detected after acquisition. We present an adaptive pre-acquisition quality-control framework for microscopy ultraviolet surface excitation (MUSE) that uses sparse scout imaging and tile-level metrics to guide acquisition and selective rescanning. Methods The framework quantifies brightness, dynamic range, focus, tissue fraction, and exposure error across the field of view. For example, in a representative 10 x 10 acquisition (100 tiles, 20-megapixel imagery), the mean p99 brightness was 0.525 (CV 10.4%), the mean dynamic range was 0.331, the median focus score was 0.0333, and the median tissue fraction was 0.943. Furthermore, applying a conservative exposure-error threshold (|error| > 0.25) identified 25% of tiles as rescan candidates. Results These results show that compact tile-level metrics can be converted into actionable quality gates, enabling early detection of local acquisition errors and targeted rescanning to improve mosaic consistency while minimizing unnecessary acquisition.

papers.title: Astatine-211 injury induces an immunostimulatory melanoma-cell state and promotes systemic antitumor immunity
papers.abstract: Targeted alpha therapy is generally evaluated by absorbed dose and direct tumor-cell killing, but whether alpha-particle-injured tumor cells can induce systemic antitumor immunity remains poorly defined. We investigated the immunogenic consequences of astatine-211 (211At) injury in a prophylactic melanoma vaccination-challenge model. B16F10 cells were exposed ex vivo to 211At, etoposide, or ultraviolet irradiation under conditions that reduced viable-cell counts at 24 hours to approximately 40% of untreated controls. Injured cells were administered subcutaneously to syngeneic C57BL/6J mice before intravenous challenge with viable B16F10 cells. Vaccination with cells exposed to 1 MBq/mL 211At suppressed pulmonary metastasis, reduced regulatory T-cell proportions, and elicited tumor-reactive interferon-{gamma} responses and antibodies. Transcriptomic profiling revealed enrichment of type I interferon, inflammatory, and chemokine-related signatures, together with suppression of cell-cycle, translation, and metabolic programs. At the cellular level, 211At injury was accompanied by {gamma}H2AX accumulation, G2/M arrest, increased reactive oxygen species and cytosolic double-stranded DNA, and senescence-like changes. These features arose without consistent increases in classical damage-associated molecular patterns or prominent induction of senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors at 1 MBq/mL. In vivo pharmacologic inhibition of stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling attenuated the antimetastatic effect of vaccination. Together, these findings demonstrate that 211At injury can generate an immunostimulatory tumor-cell state characterized by DNA damage and altered inflammatory signaling. STING contributes to the resulting immune protection, highlighting immunogenic tumor-cell conversion as a consideration in the design of targeted alpha therapies.

papers.title: An ITK - SLP-76 Y173 Axis Regulates TCR Signal Persistence and Thymic Development
papers.abstract: The TCR-induced tyrosine kinase cascade results in ITK-mediated phosphorylation of at least two substrates: PLC-{gamma}1 Y783, an essential mediator of TCR signaling, and SLP-76 Y173. We previously provided evidence that SLP-76 Y173 supports proximal TCR and Fc{varepsilon}RI signaling; but its role in thymocyte development was never explored. Here we demonstrate that SLP-76 Y173 was required for TCR/CD28-induced degradation of I{kappa}B; moreover, both ITK and SLP-76 Y173 were required for persistent TCR-induced phosphorylation of PLC-{gamma}1, ERK and p38. To explore whether SLP-76 Y173 may mediate ITK-dependent events in vivo, we replaced SLP 76 Y173 with phenylalanine in a mouse model. Like ITK-deficient thymocytes, SLP-76 Y173F thymocytes exhibited reduced thymic cellularity, reduced CD4/CD8 ratios, and reduced surface expression of CD5. In ex vivo-stimulated thymocytes, mutation of SLP-76 Y173 or inhibition of ITK reduced the persistence of TCR-induced calcium flux; moreover, TCR-induced phosphorylation of ERK and p38 depended on SLP-76 Y173. Like ITK-deficient thymi, SLP-76 Y173F thymocytes exhibited decreased production of CD4- iNKT1 thymocytes, coupled with increased production of innate-like CD4+ and CD8+ SP thymocytes. Our results provide strong evidence that the ITK substrate site, SLP-76 Y173, promotes TCR signal persistence that is required to mediate the thymic developmental effects of ITK.

papers.title: Data-driven frame-by-frame analysis of surface swimming and terrestrial walking in the coastal beetle Phaleria atriceps
papers.abstract: Background. Inter-leg coordination of insects changes depending on environmental conditions. Although locomotor changes between terrestrial and aquatic environments have been examined in various insects, relatively little is known about coastal insects living at the boundary between these environments. We therefore compared the inter-leg coordination during terrestrial walking with that during surface swimming in the coastal beetle Phaleria atriceps. Methods. Surface swimming was recorded in 17 individuals and terrestrial walking in 10 individuals using high-speed video at 1,000 frames/s. The six leg tips and anterior and posterior body landmarks were tracked frame-by-frame using DeepLabCut, and leg movements were quantified in a body-centered coordinate system. Leg movement periods were estimated from sinusoidal fits to longitudinal leg-tip trajectories. Inter-leg phase relationships were calculated for all 15 leg pairs and integrated to reconstruct a representative six-leg phase organization for each locomotor mode. Results. Leg movement periods were significantly longer during surface swimming than during terrestrial walking for all six legs. During walking, the six-leg phase relationship closely matched an alternating tripod pattern, with a left foreleg (L1), a right middle leg (R2), and a left hind leg (L3) forming one phase group and a right foreleg (R1), a left middle leg (L2), and a right hind leg (R3) forming the opposing group. The same broad grouping was observed in the six-leg phase relationship during surface swimming, although significant differences in relative phase were detected for L1-L2, L1-R2, and R1-R2. Conclusions. Phaleria atriceps exhibited six-leg phase relationships broadly consistent with an alternating tripod pattern during both terrestrial walking and surface swimming, whereas leg movement periods and certain inter-leg phase relationships differed between the two locomotor modes. These findings provide a quantitative description of the similarities and differences in inter-leg coordination between terrestrial walking and surface swimming in a coastal beetle. Further mechanical and comparative studies will be needed to clarify the functional and evolutionary significance of these findings.

papers.title: Manifolds for the neural representation of 3D spatial experience
papers.abstract: The precision with which animals navigate and interact with objects depends in part on how their brains represent position and orientation in three dimensions. A central challenge is to explain within a common framework how neural systems ranging from insects to primates represent three-dimensional (3D) pose. Here we develop a framework based on the hypothesis that neural representations of pose lie on manifolds derived from the Special Euclidean Group, SE(3), which describes the full space of rigid-body positions and orientations in three dimensions. The framework shows how movement constraints, object geometry, and visual features jointly determine the topology of the resulting pose manifold, yielding a taxonomy that guides experimental tests. We apply the framework to derive low-dimensional manifolds for neural representations of 3D object orientation in macaque parietal cortex and head direction in the limbic systems of fruit bats, mice, and monkeys. This analysis also guides the construction of neuronal tuning functions that respect the topology determined by experimental conditions. Together, these results provide a common approach for linking the geometry of 3D pose to neural coding across species and brain systems.

papers.title: Fine-tuning an intracellular allosteric pocket programs GPCR signaling bias
papers.abstract: Biased signaling of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) offers a route for precise therapeutics with fewer adverse effects. Intracellular allosteric ligands can impose such bias, yet how subtle chemical changes within these pockets reshape receptor-transducer coupling and downstream signaling remains unclear. Here, we systematically fine-tuned the intracellular allosteric pocket of neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) through chemical modification of the {beta}-arrestin-biased ligand SBI-553. Minor changes to the ligand scaffold altered transducer-coupling preferences, generating distinct profiles of G-protein and {beta}-arrestin signaling. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of NTSR1-{beta}-arrestin2 complexes bound to designed allosteric probes revealed ligand-dependent remodeling of the intracellular cavity that reshapes the receptor-effector interface. Alanine scanning identified transducer-sensitive residues within and beyond the immediate ligand-contact region. In mice, SBI-553 and N065 produced distinct physiological profiles, with N065 improving survival in a lethal endotoxemia model. Finally, phosphoproteomic profiling revealed partially overlapping but distinct downstream signaling profiles among the three modulators. Together, these findings establish the intracellular allosteric pocket as a tunable determinant of transducer coupling and show that closely related modulators can generate distinct signaling and physiological profiles.

papers.title: A minimal model of a forest after neutral theory
papers.abstract: Community ecology seeks the mechanisms underlying biodiversity, and simplified models can reveal them. Neutral ecology exemplifies this approach, but it doesn't distinguish species, limiting its capability for forecasting and prediction. We address this by developing a predictive, minimal model for forest dynamics. We show in a neotropical forest plot that environmental variation couples to the community as a single common effect on all species' growth rates. Life history acts on that variation, forecasting species' gains and losses a decade ahead. Finally, immigration, coupled to competition and life history, allows us to predict long-run species abundances. Simple rules thus govern the dynamics of this forest: competition, immigration, and the effect of the environment on growth. Beyond that, species are set apart by their life histories alone.

papers.title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
papers.abstract: Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. However, how familiarity alters the coordination of neural representations across distributed brain networks remains unclear. Rhythmic neural activity provides a potential mechanism for coordinating information across sensory and higher-order brain regions in the light of previous experience. Here, we thus investigated whether familiarity alters the coordination of brain rhythms during naturalistic viewing. Participants who were either familiar or unfamiliar with the television series Game of Thrones viewed clips from the series while EEG or fMRI was recorded. We calculated the intersubject correlations of neural activity across EEG frequency bands and related this rhythmic activity to fMRI BOLD responses. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

papers.title: Computational markers of rhythmic timing in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: Sensorimotor synchronization requires the nervous system to predict upcoming events while continuously correcting the timing of ongoing actions. Parkinson's disease (PD) is associated with impaired temporal processing, but it remains unclear which cognitive-computational mechanisms underlie rhythmic timing deficits. Here, we applied the Adaptation and Anticipation Model (ADAM) to synchronized finger-tapping data from participants with PD and controls across four steady tempi. After data screening, analyzes included 35 participants with PD and 28 controls. PD was associated with reduced synchronization accuracy and stability, reflected in larger absolute asynchronies and higher variability of asynchronies. ADAM parameter estimates indicated lower phase correction (coupling strength) and higher central timekeeper noise in the PD group, whereas period correction (tempo matching) and peripheral motor noise showed no robust group differences. Across participants, timekeeper noise predicted synchronization accuracy. Phase correction, timekeeper noise, and motor noise predicted synchronization stability, but their associations differed between groups: phase correction was more closely associated with stability in PD, whereas timekeeper and motor noise were more closely associated with stability in controls. These findings suggest that sensorimotor synchronization deficits in PD reflect reduced use of recent timing errors to guide upcoming movements and less precise internal timekeeping. Error correction and timekeeper noise thus emerge as candidate computational markers of altered rhythmic timing in PD, with potential relevance for understanding individual differences in responses to rhythmic auditory cueing.

papers.title: Disease-associated NK-cell state remodeling reveals transcriptional profiles predictive of clinical phenotypes
papers.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells adapt their cellular states to diverse tissue and inflammatory environments, yet how this plasticity manifests across pathological contexts and relates to patient-level disease phenotypes remains poorly defined. Here we established the Human NK-cell Atlas (HNKA) from over 1 million NK cells, including samples from 1,632 donors spanning 50 diseases. Within a shared NK-cell state architecture, analyses of state abundance and matched-reference exceedance distinguished disease-biased redistribution from transcriptional displacement. Fine-grained analyses localized disease-associated remodeling to specific NK-cell states, including CD56dim NK ISG15 in infection and autoimmunity and CD56bright NK ITM2C in tumors. These patterns were accompanied by recurrent interferon responses and state-specific regulatory activity. Cytokine perturbations recapitulated key transcriptional features of disease-associated NK-cell states. We developed NKceiver, a model based on state-specific NK-cell expression profiles for patient-level prediction. It distinguished 18 diseases and predicted COVID-19 severity and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, with predictive performance retained in unseen patients and studies. Collectively, our results reveal that disease-associated remodeling within the diverse NK-cell state repertoire resolved by HNKA is biologically interpretable and clinically informative, supporting disease discrimination and prediction of clinical phenotypes.

papers.title: A Cell-Autonomous Cold Sensor Promotes Lipolysis Through Phase Separation
papers.abstract: Temperature is a fundamental determinant of mammalian metabolism. The canonical cold-adaptation pathway involves cold sensing by peripheral sensory neurons, which activate sympathetic outflow, {beta}-adrenergic signaling, and lipolysis in adipose tissue. In contrast, we report here a cell-intrinsic mechanism by which physiologically relevant cooling temperatures (27-31 oC) enhance lipolysis in subcutaneous adipose tissue. Mechanistically, cooling drives liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of perilipin 1 (PLIN1), the dominant lipid droplet coat protein, promoting its condensation and the local recruitment of PKA to the droplet surface. This spatial reorganization selectively amplified PKA-mediated perilipin 1 phosphorylation, CGI-58 release, and ATGL-dependent lipolysis. The process depends on the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of perilipin1, where four aromatic residues, conserved in endotherms but not in ectotherms, are required for cooling-induced LLPS and lipolysis in vivo. Notably, targeted delivery of an LLPS-competent perilipin 1 variant to the inguinal adipose tissue of mice enhanced local lipolysis and reduced depot mass. Together, these findings uncover a cell-intrinsic thermosensitive mechanism that can tune lipolytic responsiveness, offering a possible strategy for targeted depot-selective fat reduction.

papers.title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
papers.abstract: Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.

papers.title: A splenic reservoir of pro-angiogenic neutrophils supports blood flow recovery after peripheral tissue ischemia
papers.abstract: Background: Neutrophils accumulate at sites of ischemic injury, where a distinct subset characterized by CD49d+CXCR4hiVEGFR1hi expression promotes angiogenesis and contributes to blood flow recovery. This study investigated the function, origin, and recruitment mechanisms of these pro-angiogenic neutrophils (PANs) in a murine model of hindlimb ischemia and explored whether a corresponding population responds to acute ischemia in humans. Methods: Using spectral flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry, PANs and classical neutrophils were characterized in ischemic gastrocnemius muscle following hindlimb ischemia in mice. Blood flow recovery was assessed by laser speckle flowmetry. To determine the origin and mobilization mechanisms of PANs, splenectomy, chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA), and surgical splenic denervation were performed. Translational studies examined blood samples collected during elective abdominal aortic aneurysm repair to assess PAN mobilization following acute lower limb ischemia induced by aortic cross-clamping. Results: PANs rapidly accumulated in ischemic muscle through a CD49d-dependent mechanism, and blockade of CD49d impaired blood flow recovery. During homeostasis, PANs were maintained within a splenic reservoir and were rapidly released into circulation following ischemia. Splenectomy and disruption of splenic sympathetic signaling significantly reduced PAN recruitment to ischemic tissue and impaired functional recovery. Mobilization was driven by ischemia-induced sympathetic activation, which decreased CXCL12 levels in the splenic red pulp, disrupting CXCR4-mediated PAN retention. In humans, a phenotypically similar PAN population was identified in peripheral blood, which increased rapidly following lower limb ischemia during aortic cross-clamping. The speed of this response is consistent with release from an extramedullary reservoir, although its anatomical source remains unknown. Conclusion: These findings identify the spleen as a reservoir of pro-angiogenic neutrophils in mice and reveal a neuroimmune mechanism regulating their mobilization and recruitment after ischemic injury. The rapid appearance of PAN in human circulation after acute ischemia suggests that comparable extramedullary neutrophil reservoirs may also exist in humans.

papers.title: Studies on a luminescent antimicrobial metal complex reveal a method to directly image pathogenic bacterial infection in a living organism using optical microscopy
papers.abstract: Methods to render Galleria Mellonella larvae transparent allowing three-dimensional viewing of larvae through orthodox light microscopy techniques are reported. To explore this models capability, we exploited the imaging properties of a metal complex antimicrobial to probe its therapeutic action against a pathogenic Acetinobacter baumannii infection. To illustrate the general utility of this method, we have also used the commercial fluorescent dye, Alexafluor-488, to image bacteria within live larvae.

papers.title: Lysosomal adaptation to extracellular acidity compromises CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity
papers.abstract: Extracellular acidosis is a hallmark of aggressive tumors and suppresses cytotoxic-T lymphocyte (CTL)-mediated killing, but how sustained acid exposure reshapes T cell cytotoxicity is poorly understood. Here we show that chronic acidosis drives lysosomal remodeling in human CD8+ T cells, converting the lysosome into a proton sink whose adaptation ultimately impairs killing by depleting the intracellular granzyme B reservoir through constitutive vesicle release. Quantitative proteomics of CD8+ T cells cultured at pH 6.5 identified lysosomes as the dominant target of acid-driven remodeling: CTLs upregulated the V1 sector of the vacuolar H+-ATPase and hyper-acidified the lysosomal lumen. The remodeled compartment accumulated lysosomal membrane proteins (LAMP1, LAMP2, CD63, CD68) post-transcriptionally, acquired higher cathepsin abundance and increased proteolytic activity. Chronic acidity also enlarged endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lysosomal Ca2+ stores without altering cytosolic Ca2+, and drives constitutive, Ca2+-dependent release of LAMP1+ lysosome-derived vesicles, which drains the intracellular reservoir of granzyme B, contributing to reduced CTL activity. These findings establish lysosomal adaptation as a cost of surviving extracellular acidosis and identify lysosomal hydrolase activity as a possible target for improving CTL function in the acidic tumor environment.

papers.title: Targeting PRMT5 Across Cancers and AI-Driven Discovery of Candidate Compounds
papers.abstract: Protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) is a promising anticancer target, yet existing inhibitors shown limited clinical efficacy. Here, we paired multi-omics pan-cancer profiling with a machine learning virtual screening pipeline. Bioinformatics analyses with TIMER3, GEPIA2, UALCAN/CPTAC, the Human Protein Atlas, cBioPortal, STRING and Enrichr revealed widespread of PRMT5 mRNA expression, protein abundance, survival, genetic alteration, immune infiltration and co-expression networks with tumor-specific prognostic impact in GBM, LGG and KIRC. A deep neural network screened about 1.5 million PubChem compounds and deep neural network reached a ROC-AUC = 0.9857 and prioritized three candidates, CID 44345182, CID 2794188 and CID 44345334. Subsequent molecular docking against PRMT5 (PDB ID: 4X61), ADMET filtering and toxicity prediction, and 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations identified CID 44345182 as the potential hit, similar the docking scores of -9.8 compared with -9.2 kcal/mol for the reference ligand in binding affinity and trajectory stability. These findings clarify the context-dependent roles of PRMT5 and further experiment validations are needed to establish CID 44345182 as a promising candidate.

papers.title: Chromosome-level Atlantic switchgrass assemblies reveal a supernumerary B-Chromosome with transcriptional and evolutionary impacts
papers.abstract: Supernumerary B-Chromosomes are extra genetic elements that frequently deviate from Mendelian inheritance to ensure their own survival. Their evolutionary origins and biological impacts within natural plant populations remain largely unexplored. Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a model for studies of local adaptation, but reliance on a single reference genome has limited the detection of lineage-specific genomic content. We generated chromosome-level genome assemblies from the diverged Atlantic switchgrass subpopulation and discovered a previously undetected genomic element: a ~34 Mb supernumerary B-Chromosome, validated by Hi-C contact mapping and long-read depth, which indicates two to four B copies per nucleus. The B-Chromosome has a bipartite architecture including a gene-rich, single-copy proximal region (~8 Mb) and a repeat-rich, gene-poor distal region (~27 Mb) dominated by LTR/Ty3 (Gypsy) elements and punctuated by Mutator TIR peaks. High-resolution mapping reveals a highly rearranged chimera of fragments from multiple autosomes, biased toward the N-subgenome. Intact LTR retrotransposons on the B-Chromosome are younger than those on the A-Chromosomes, especially in its distal region, consistent with a B-Chromosome that arose and expanded within the Atlantic lineage. Population screening and phylogenetic analysis indicate that the B-Chromosome is largely restricted to the Atlantic subpopulation and likely has a single origin. In a typical family, 70% of open-pollinated progeny of B-positive maternal plants were B-positive, with substantial variation among families. Finally, B-Chromosome presence is associated with expression differences in A-Chromosome genes that differ between genetic backgrounds. Together, our results show how accessory chromosomes contribute to the evolutionary and genomic diversity of natural plant populations.

papers.title: Timed binary WNT activity is sufficient to model the early human neural axis
papers.abstract: The vertebrate nervous system develops into functionally distinct domains along the body axis[1]. Developmental studies implicate multiple signaling pathways in coordinating this process, but the order of specification events, sufficiency of individual signals, and molecular basis of competency remain unclear [2,3], leaving the field without a unified model of neuraxis patterning. Enteric nervous system (ENS) and midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) progenitors have reached clinical and preclinical testing [4-11], yet neither is produced at full purity, and yields vary markedly across human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) lines, reflecting incomplete control of axial identity. Here we use single-cell genetic fate mapping to demonstrate that hPSCs can commit to anterior or posterior cranial fate within the first 24 hours of differentiation, before neural induction. Building on this finding, we show that the duration of a single saturating WNT pulse is sufficient to specify three 'first-order' domains: anterior cranial (0 h), posterior cranial (24 h) and trunk (48 h), each pre-neural and competent for CNS, neural crest and epidermal lineages. Nested 'second-order' domains are specified within first-order domains in response to WNT, FGF, and retinoic acid. Mechanistically, an anterior gene regulatory network repressing WNT targets is irreversibly shut down during the transition to posterior identities. Applying this binary WNT patterning logic, we generate mDA neurons and ENS progenitors robustly across hPSC lines and establish an assembloid model combining first-order progenitors to produce all major regions of the nervous system.

papers.title: Host genetics structure Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages and their co-variation in sympatric fire coral species
papers.abstract: Host genetic and environmental filtering are key determinants of microbiome assembly, yet their relative influence across multiple symbiotic compartments remains poorly understood. In coral holobionts, studies typically focus on either algal or bacterial symbionts and rarely account for host genetic variation below the species level. Here, we combined host microsatellite genotyping with ITS2 and 16S rRNA metabarcoding to investigate the drivers of Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages in three sympatric fire coral species (Millepora cf. exaesa, M. tenera, and M. cf. platyphylla) across three adjacent but environmentally contrasting reef habitats on Reunion Island. Both symbiont assemblages were structured by host identity and habitat, although host genetics consistently outweighed environmental effects on the microbiome composition. At the subspecies level, host genotypes explained up to 54% of the variation in Symbiodiniaceae assemblages compared to 20% for the prokaryotes. Symbiodiniaceae communities were dominated by Symbiodinium A16 and A3 radiations, while showing marked specificity across species and habitats. All Millepora species consistently associated with the Spirochaetaceae, Kiloniellaceae and Desulfobacteraceae bacterial families across all habitats, suggesting evolutionarily maintained core associations. Integrative analysis further demonstrated genotype-specific co-variation between algal and bacterial symbionts, with some genotypes maintaining stable and co-varying symbionts across clones, while others exhibited more flexible assemblages. Together, our results indicate that sympatric fire coral acquire symbionts from locally available pools through host genotype-dependent filtering. This study highlights host genotype as a major determinant of coral holobiont assembly, shaping the composition and co-variation of both Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages.

papers.title: Mitigating Permittivity-Charge Cross-Sensitivity in Biomolecular Sensing: Electrostatic Decoupling and Feedforward Biasing in an Asymmetric Dual-Gate a-IGZO FET
papers.abstract: Permittivity-based biomolecular identification is inherently ambiguous in real-world sensing environments because analyte charge also influences the measured electrical response. Different combinations of charge and permittivity can produce similar electrical responses, so a change in the measured response cannot be uniquely attributed to permittivity. This work combines electrostatic decoupling through device engineering with charge-conditioned feedforward biasing to mitigate this cross-sensitivity and recover both analyte properties through direct drain-current readings from a single transistor. We provide a proof of concept through technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulations of an asymmetric dual-gate, dual-nanogap amorphous indium-gallium-zinc oxide (a-IGZO) transistor. Gate-insulator dielectric engineering and nanogap optimization establish complementary drain-current responses, with the bottom gate predominantly sensing analyte charge and the top gate predominantly sensing permittivity. Feedforward biasing further suppresses residual charge interference in the top-gate response. First, the bottom-gate drain current provides an estimate of analyte charge. This estimate and a preliminary top-gate current reading are used to select the voltage for the final top-gate measurement. The drain current measured at that voltage then determines permittivity. Three sequential current readings thus provide permittivity-based biomolecular identification without prior knowledge of analyte charge, alongside complementary charge measurement. Mean charge and permittivity extraction errors remain below 1.8% and 0.6%, respectively, across the calibration and independent test datasets.

papers.title: Goal directed closed-loop training of network bursts in cortical cultures produces improved performance and error correction over days
papers.abstract: Dissociated neural cultures are living systems with no evolutionary history in their current form, which makes them a testbed for asking what goals neural tissue can learn to pursue once it is removed from its evolved body. It remains unclear which features of network activity such a culture can be trained to control, and whether that training is retained from one day to the next. We built an open-source closed-loop platform, the Holistic Agential Learning platform (HAL), that detects a network burst on a high-density microelectrode array, estimates its spatial origin in real time, and applies a minimal reinforcement rule. Here, a burst that originates off the goal side triggers global random stimulation that persists until the next burst. Over days of training, rat cortical cultures (n=10) increased the fraction of bursts that initiated on the goal side. This gain accrued between sessions, with little change within a session, a consolidation-like pattern that we interpret as a statement about timescale while the mechanism remains untested. The burst origin moved toward the goal side, while the burst peak and the repertoire of propagation directions were preserved. Trained cultures also recovered from incorrect states more reliably over days, while the rate at which they entered those states was unchanged, and this recovery effect was the most robust difference from unstimulated controls (n=6). Cultures that began on either side of chance converged to a similar level of performance. Damaged cultures (n=6) with comparable burst statistics showed neither the across-day gain nor the consolidation-like pattern. Training reweighted the activity patterns each culture already had, and we saw no new ones, which we read as a simple form of niche construction in which the tissue keeps a trace of its history that biases what it does next. These results identify burst initiation and error recovery as trainable variables in a novel living system, and they support training the tissue rather than engineering the machine.

papers.title: Brain FACTs: A same-section workflow for Fiber Architecture, Cytoarchitecture and cell Types in large-scale brain sections
papers.abstract: Understanding the human brain's multiscale organization requires linking cells, connections and architecture, yet conventional methods are incompatible within a single specimen, and inter-individual variability confounds cross-brain comparisons. Multiple-label immunohistochemistry for different cell types has been applied in interleaved sections but remains challenging within a single large human brain section and, has never been combined on the same tissue with 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) for three-dimensional fiber architecture. Here we introduce a sequential multimodal workflow integrating 3D-PLI, multiplex chromogenic immunohistochemistry and Nissl staining on the same large human brain section, preserving each technique's quality and specificity. The method was validated on vervet monkey and Wistar rat sections. The resulting paired high-resolution images eliminate inter-subject variability and enable direct micron-scale mapping of fiber tracts relative to molecularly defined cell types, yielding previously inaccessible insights such as molecular identification of white-matter components, refined cortical layering and cytoarchitectural disambiguation.

papers.title: Delayed bleaching-induced coral mortality limits reef recovery after a marine heatwave
papers.abstract: Coral reefs worldwide are increasingly exposed to marine heatwaves, which cause recurrent coral bleaching and mass mortality events. While the immediate impact of bleaching has been extensively studied, the longer-term consequences and recovery trajectories remain poorly understood. By integrating two long-term monitoring datasets, we quantified how fine-scale variation in heat stress exposure shaped post-bleaching trajectories. We examined patterns of coral mortality and recovery across 13 sites in Mo'orea (French Polynesia) after the most severe marine heatwave recorded on the island in 2019. The maximum accumulated heat stress (AHSmax) varied between sites (from 5.76 to 6.26 {degrees}C weeks), allowing the assessment of heat stress-related mortality between coral genera. Pocillopora mortality increased with AHSmax, and mean coral cover collapsed from 35% to 17% within one year. Acropora experienced consistently high mortality rates across all sites (median: 84%), reducing mean cover from 5% to 1%. Six years of tracking individual Pocillopora colonies revealed strong size-dependent bleaching responses.
