Although prior research has shown that political ideology can shape shared neural responses to sociopolitical content, less is known about how individual differences in national identity ideology are associated with inter-individual similarity in neural dynamics during naturalistic viewing, particularly in sociopolitical contexts where national identity is highly salient in public discourse. We examined Greater Chinese ideology, one dimension of national identity ideology, in relation to positive engagement and neural dynamics during viewing of the same pro-China video across two samples in Taiwan. In Study 1 (N = 52), higher Greater Chinese ideology was associated with greater positive engagement. In Study 2 (N = 60), participants underwent fMRI while viewing the same video. Intersubject representational similarity analysis showed that greater similarity in participants' Greater Chinese ideology item-response profiles was associated with greater similarity in neural dynamics in regions associated with the frontoparietal control, salience, and default mode networks. Notably, the within-versus-between neural similarity effect was stronger among participants with relatively lower Greater Chinese ideology scores than among those with relatively higher scores. These findings link Greater Chinese ideology to positive engagement and similarity in neural dynamics during viewing of this pro-China video. Further research is needed to determine whether similar associations can be observed across other dimensions of national identity ideology and different political narratives.

papers.title: Role of leg campaniform sensilla proprioceptive feedback in Drosophila melanogaster adaptive walking
papers.abstract: With the newly uncovered access to a genetic line labeling all campaniform sensilla in Drosophila melanogaster and the many insights gathered from larger insects, we analyzed the distribution and patterning of this class of proprioceptors throughout the fly nervous system and studied CS function in motor control. We demonstrate via two-photon calcium imaging microscopy that campaniform sensilla activation induces activity in many leg muscles, showing that these proprioceptive stimuli can influence motor neuron activity. We then dissected how the lack of these proprioceptive stimuli influence walking behavior, leg kinematics, and interleg coordination in freely-walking flies using transient optogenetic inhibition and video tracking with high spatiotemporal resolution. We show that campaniform sensilla inhibition robustly affects Drosophila melanogasters ability to reach their typical walking speeds. Detailed analysis of leg kinematic suggests that shorter stance amplitudes characterized by their long-lasting duration were behind the speed deficits. Dissecting this phenotype also revealed the inability to maintain coordinated interleg stepping patterns as well as postural control in absence of proprioceptive force and load feedback.

papers.title: Characterization of Fetal Cortical Development Using Spectral Analysis of Gyrification (SPANGY)
papers.abstract: The prenatal period of human brain development is critical for mental health and cognition across the entire lifespan. During this period, the cortex undergoes a dramatic transformation from a smooth lissencephalic surface into an elaborately folded structure, a process whose precise characterization is essential for understanding neurodevelopmental trajectories. This study represents the first application of Spectral Analysis of Gyrification (SPANGY) to a large multi-centric fetal brain MRI dataset (635 subjects, 20-38 weeks gestational age). SPANGY characterizes geometric variations on a surface based on the wavelength of folds, hence, providing a quantitative local description of gyrification at the individual level. Using rigorous normative modeling (GAMLSS) and statistical harmonization (ComBat-GAM), we established age-specific reference trajectories for multi-scale gyrification features (spectral frequency bands). We provide the first ever quantification of the temporally-ordered emergence of cortical folding in successive waves during the entire second half of pregnancy: the earliest-emerging low frequency, deep fissures are progressively superseded by the accelerating expansion of higher frequency folds. The normative curves provide the first step in taking prenatal neurodevelopmental assessment from qualitative inspection into a rigorous statistical inference, creating an objective reference against which deviations from healthy brain growth could be caught earlier.

papers.title: Neuronal stop-codon readthrough is associated with ribosome pausing and appends lineage-restricted extensions that can alter protein localization in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Stop-codon readthrough (RT) diversifies proteomes and is particularly prominent in neurons. However, the regulatory logic that specifies neuronal RT and the structural and cellular consequences of the resulting C-terminal protein extensions remain poorly understood. Here we leverage neuron-specific ribosome profiling datasets in Drosophila to construct an in vivo atlas of 163 neuronal RT transcripts. Sequence-based modeling distinguished RT from non-RT transcripts and highlighted an extended post-stop region enriched for stable predicted RNA structures. Beyond these cis-associated features, ribosome-footprint analysis revealed pronounced stop-codon pausing on RT transcripts, accompanied by upstream periodic peaks consistent with ribosome queuing. At the protein level, neuronal RT appended polypeptides enriched in polar residues and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Evolutionary comparisons suggested that most analyzed extensions show shallower phylogenetic conservation than their associated conventional proteins, whereas in two genes a stop-codon appears to have been gained within ancestral coding sequences. Finally, an in vivo dual-color reporter showed that RT of the RNA-binding protein Bru3 alters localization from the nucleus to cytoplasmic granules. Together, our results suggest that neuronal RT is associated with structured post-stop RNA regions that reshape termination dynamics and produce lineage-restricted, IDR-rich C-terminal protein extensions with distinct subcellular localization.

papers.title: A foldable respiratory siphon enables near-surface locomotion through asymmetric rowing in Helophilus larvae
papers.abstract: Specialized animal structures often perform multiple functions, yet how their structural adaptations support distinct behaviors remains poorly understood. Eristaline hoverfly larvae, commonly known as rat-tailed maggots, possess exceptionally elongated and extensible posterior respiratory siphons that allow them to breathe while submerged. Here, we investigated the structural basis of siphon extension and its potential locomotor function in Helophilus virgatus larvae. Fluorescence labeling showed that siphon elongation involves the unfolding of previously concealed structures, while phalloidin staining revealed an extensive array of transversely oriented muscle fibers within the siphon. Behavioral observations further revealed a previously undescribed mode of horizontal locomotion just beneath the air water interface, involving asymmetric rowing movements of the posterior siphon. Kinematic analyses showed that most forward body displacements occurred during the backward stroke, which was associated with increased siphon straightness, whereas the forward stroke produced little net forward displacement. These findings reveal structural features underlying siphon extensibility and demonstrate that a specialized respiratory organ also contributes to locomotion, highlighting the multifunctionality of specialized body structures in aquatic environments.

papers.title: False discovery rate control enables trustworthy deep-learning-based de novo peptide sequencing
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based de novo peptide sequencing identifies peptides beyond predefined databases, but confidence thresholds do not consistently indicate false discovery rates (FDRs). We develop Counterpart Calibration Theory (CCT), which uses counterpart counts to estimate incorrect target predictions and defines conditions for conservative FDR estimation and threshold selection. We implement CCT in {pi}-NovoQC at the peptide-spectrum match and peptide levels, integrating it with {pi}-xNovo sequencing models, protein inference and quantification. Evaluations across sequencing models and datasets examine FDR estimation and correct-identification retention. Isotope-labelled data provide complementary evidence for identifications recovered from database-unidentified spectra. In the Deep Human Proteome dataset, the workflow recovers low-abundance peptide evidence that extends protein-group inference and quantification. These results support the incorporation of de novo identifications into proteomic analyses at specified FDR thresholds.

papers.title: A GPX4 phosphorylation switch by FGFR1 guards against ferroptosis
papers.abstract: Ferroptosis is driven by lipid peroxidation, yet the mechanisms by which cells rapidly adjust their sensitivity to ferroptosis in response to extracellular cues remain elusive. We identify a direct phosphorylation switch controlling the activity of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), the core ferroptosis regulator4. The receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) FGFR1 directly binds and phosphorylates GPX4 at Tyr180/Tyr196 in a kinase-dependent manner, requiring FGFR1 Tyr730 as a docking site. This phosphorylation enhances GPX4's catalytic activity and suppresses ferroptosis. In cardiac ischemia/reperfusion injury, the FGFR1-GPX4 axis is suppressed, and a selective FGFR1 agonist (FGF-1DeltaNT) reactivates it to protect against ferroptosis-mediated damage. Critically, a phosphorylation-deficient GPX4 knock-in mouse exhibits hypersensitivity to injury and is non-responsive to this agonist, demonstrating that GPX4 phosphorylation is essential. Our findings reveal a rapid mechanism for regulating ferroptosis via GPX4 tyrosine phosphorylation, directly linking RTK signaling to ferroptosis, and offering new strategies for treating ischemic- and other ferroptosis-associated diseases.

papers.title: Phylogenetic coherence in microbiome composition across environmental gradients
papers.abstract: Global surveys of microbial communities across biomes have shown that environmental variables such as depth and pH are strong determinants of community composition. However, we do not understand how the traits of individual taxa, and their evolutionary conservation, conspire to give rise to these patterns. Exploiting large-scale surveys of top soil and marine microbiomes, we use canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to concurrently infer directions of environmental variation and the associated compositional changes. We find that the primary canonical direction, capturing the dominant environmental gradient, exhibits a strong phylogenetic signal: individual species' responses to environmental shifts along this direction are similar among taxa with shared evolutionary history. In contrast, secondary canonical directions show weak or no phylogenetic structure. Together, these results suggest a two-scale view of microbial community assembly. Deeply evolutionarily conserved traits govern community reorganization along the main environmental driver of community composition. Additional environmentally driven changes in community composition then reflect traits that are more evolutionarily labile.

papers.title: Hepatic urea cycle suppression drives brown fat thermogenesis to counter obesity and liver disease
papers.abstract: The hepatic urea cycle is consistently suppressed in liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but whether loss of individual enzymes contributes to disease progression remains unknown. We investigated the role of urea cycle enzyme argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1) in diet- and carcinogen-induced liver disease using hepatocyte-specific deletion of Ass1 in mice. Complete loss of hepatic Ass1 is lethal, but a high-fat diet extends lifespan. Unexpectedly, animals with approximately 85% loss of hepatic Ass1 are markedly protected from diet-induced obesity, liver steatosis, fibrosis, and HCC. Hyperammonemia induced by hepatic Ass1 loss activates brown adipose tissue fatty acid oxidation, driving thermogenesis and increasing energy expenditure. Importantly, targeting Ass1 after obesity onset promotes weight loss and reverses liver steatosis. These findings implicate hepatic ASS1 as a critical regulator of systemic lipid metabolism with therapeutic potential against obesity, liver disease, and HCC.

papers.title: Mesoscale Functional Reorganization of Cortical Networks After Cortical Spreading Depression
papers.abstract: Background: Resting-state functional imaging is increasingly used to understand how cortical networks modulate and respond to pain. Awake imaging with a minimally invasive approach is key to observe the natural state of the brain. As migraine with aura, a common headache disorder, can be experimentally modeled by cortical spreading depressions (CSD) in rodents, it is essential to understand the impact of CSD on functional connectivity and network topology to find imaging cues of trigeminovascular activation and headache. Methods: We used awake widefield intrinsic optical-signal imaging (IOSI) on optically cleared windows to non-invasively characterize the impact of CSDs on bihemispheric resting-state static and dynamic functional connectivity patterns and network topology. A subset of mice was chronically treated with amitriptyline to examine the effect of susceptibility to CSD on connectivity. After baseline imaging, CSD was triggered optogenetically and confirmed by laser speckle contrast imaging. A group of mice received intraperitoneal naproxen after CSD to suppress headache. IOSI was repeated at 30 minutes, 60 minutes, 4 hours, and 24 hours after CSD. The mouse grimace scale was scored at each time point for behavioral headache documentation. Results: We observed time-dependent changes in resting-state functional connectivity that were reversed by naproxen. Amitriptyline, a prophylactic migraine medication, decreased susceptibility to CSD and modified resting-state functional connectivity differently than controls. Network analysis with graph-theoretical methods revealed barrel and retrosplenial cortices as potential key players in trigeminal pain processing after CSD. Dynamic functional connectivity analysis demonstrated functional connectivity states, with fractional occupancy and mean dwell time of these states showing distinct CSD and pain-modulated states. A support vector machine was utilized to predict CSD-mediated dynamic connectivity changes in controls. Conclusion: Our results bring insight into potentially headache-associated changes in resting-state cortical functional connectivity after CSD and how this functional reorganization is influenced by acute and chronic medications for migraine.

papers.title: Curated neurodegeneration axis signals are sensitive to cell composition and analytic choices: an adversarial re-analysis of a transcriptomic scoring pipeline
papers.abstract: Background: Curated gene-set ("axis") scores are widely used to summarise disease biology in postmortem brain transcriptomes. In bulk tissue such scores can also change with cell-type composition, with broad transcriptome shifts in diseased tissue, or with analysis choices made after the results were seen. We tested these explanations on our own published pipeline, NeuroFate, whose preprint reported an Alzheimer's disease (AD) "neuronal vulnerability" axis and a Parkinson's disease (PD) "divergent" synuclein-mitochondrial axis. Results: A code audit found that the AD discovery axis averaged Sst, Pvalb and Lamp5 interneuron cell-type proportions together with its gene-expression features; that 90 endpoint x axis tests were run before the endpoints were locked; that axes were defined from the cohorts later cited as discovery evidence; and that the PD-divergent label came from an axis-specific rule defined after the result. Their contribution to the AD association could not be quantified because the donor-level data were not archived. In GSE7621 (16 PD, 9 controls) the synuclein-mitochondrial association reproduced (exact p = 0.0011) but depended on the scoring method (exact p from 0.001 to 0.057; with per-gene standardisation no axis reached Benjamini-Hochberg significance), lay at the 2.4th percentile of 10,000 expression-matched random probe sets (two-sided p = 0.06), and was attenuated by 76% (95% interval 26% to >100%) after adjustment for a dopaminergic-marker expression proxy (PD coefficient -1.13 to -0.27 SD). A small laser-captured cohort (GSE20141; 10 PD, 8 controls) was inconclusive: no axis reached p < 0.05, and the synuclein-mitochondrial effect had the same sign. In 1,000 simulated cohorts, a naive test called a purely composition-driven gene set significant in 82% of cohorts, whereas the proposed battery classified it as composition-independent in 5% while recovering a planted within-cell effect in 98% (moderate effect) and 50% (weak effect) of cohorts. Conclusions: The original axis associations do not establish composition-independent disease programs; their interpretation is sensitive to feature construction, scoring and adjustment for cell composition. Curated axis scores in bulk brain tissue should be reported with competitive null distributions, composition adjustment, exact small-sample inference, and endpoints and scoring fixed before analysis. We provide code for these checks.

papers.title: The epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor family network in cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure
papers.abstract: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) network comprises 4 receptors (EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4) and multiple ligands (EGFR-Ls; for example, AREG/EGF/TGFA that bind to EGFR, EREG/HBEGF that bind to EGFR/ERBB3, and NRG1 that binds to ERBB3/4). NRG1 and ERBB2/ERBB4 are cardioprotective, whilst other EGFR-Ls are implicated in cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. We sought to understand the importance of this network in human heart failure and development of cardiac hypertrophy. By mining data from the Human Protein Atlas, we established that the EGFR family and EGFR-Ls are expressed in different cardiac cells. Furthermore, EGFR-L mRNAs were modulated in failing vs non-failing human hearts implicating them in end-stage disease. In rat cardiomyocytes, EGFR-Ls all activated extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1/2 (ERK1/2) and Akt. However, NRG1 preferentially activated Akt whereas AREG/EREG/HBEGF/TGFA preferentially activated ERK1/2. EGF and NRG1 differentially regulated early gene expression with the response to NRG1 having a greater requirement for ERBB2. To determine if the network is involved in developing cardiac hypertrophy, mice were treated with angiotensin II (AngII) without/with afatinib (to inhibit all EGFR family members). Expression of EGFR-L mRNAs was modulated by AngII over 3-7d. At 7d, echocardiography and segmental strain analysis identified greater cardiac dysfunction in hearts from mice treated with afatinib/AngII compared with AngII alone, associated with inhibition of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and enhanced cardiac fibrosis. In conclusion, the EGFR network plays an important role in cardiomyocyte and cardiac hypertrophy and is dysregulated in human failing hearts. Further insight into the network may enable identification of novel therapies for cardiac disorders.

papers.title: Inferring fluctuating interaction probabilities in ecological networks across environmental change
papers.abstract: Knowledge of species' interactions unlocks our understanding of how ecological communities respond to climate change or habitat loss, explaining their resilience and robustness. Such knowledge requires inferring the presence, sign, and per capita strength of species interactions, as well as species' intrinsic growth rates. While various studies have attempted to infer these parameters in isolation, none has successfully inferred them simultaneously. Here, we solve this grand challenge using an integrative approach combining ecological mechanistic models and statistical inference to simultaneously infer these parameters across time, capturing environmental change. We validate our approach on synthetic data in constant and changing environments with both abrupt and gradual changes. Applying our method to a manipulated microcosm experiment demonstrates its ability to infer environmental change in empirical data. Finally, its application to a mesocosm experiment recovers the expectations from biological knowledge and unveils network rewiring due to unplanned environmental change. Our approach goes one step further in bridging the gap between mechanistic models and empirical ecology. It advances the understanding of ecological networks and their dynamics, thereby helping to validate existing hypotheses, spark new theories, and guide ecological management and conservation.

papers.title: Consistent crown phenology, not functional traits, predicts whether tropical trees can be mapped from imaging spectroscopy
papers.abstract: - Airborne imaging spectroscopy can identify tree species in hyperdiverse tropical forests, but accuracy varies greatly among species. We asked which ecological and evolutionary attributes make a tropical tree species spectrally separable. - In moist tropical forest in French Guiana, we fitted the learning curve of accuracy against the number of labelled crowns for 169 species, then tested six hypothesised determinants on 45 species rarefied to ten crowns, at species, species-pair and crown scales. - Dispersed sampling and larger crowns increased accuracy, and liana infestation more than halved the odds of correct identification. Phenological regularity, how closely conspecific crowns share one leaf cycle, in step or not, was the strongest species-level correlate and survived every multivariate analysis. It did not act by making conspecifics uniform on the acquisition date: regular species were spectrally more distinct from other species, and within species the crowns that best followed the species' leaf cycle were classified correctly. Congeners reduced accuracy; leaf and bark traits did not predict separability. - Separability depends on the consistency of a species' signal, how faithfully its crowns express a shared leaf cycle, how widely it is sampled and how free its crowns are from contamination, rather than on its measured functional traits.

papers.title: Building computational benchmarks: an Omnibenchmark reimplementation of a single-cell preprocessing pipeline evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: In the past few years, we have seen a veritable surge in single-cell (e.g., RNA-sequencing) techniques and datasets, enabling increasingly detailed characterization of cellular heterogeneity across tissues and conditions. This surge in single-cell techniques has been complemented by a large number of analysis frameworks and pipelines, and a large parameter space and researcher degrees of freedom to use them. Many neutral benchmarks have been presented for various computational tasks, but most make design decisions that render them incompatible with each other, e.g., through the use of different datasets, metrics, or parameter sets. Results: We showcase Omnibenchmark, a recently developed framework to build reproducible, extensible, and standardized method comparisons for an arms-length benchmark that evaluates five single-cell RNA sequencing pipelines, spanning filtering, normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, on three datasets. The framework facilitates the broad investigation of pipelines used in single-cell data analysis while highlighting how the process of building benchmarks can be streamlined and unified. This standardization enables benchmarks to be extended in several directions, including broader parameter sweeps, comparisons across software versions and architectures, isolation of pipeline steps, and integration of additional pipelines, datasets, and metrics. As an example, our harmonization of pipelines highlighted that tools implement the (clustering) resolution parameter differently. Conclusions: Omnibenchmark provides a reproducible, extensible, and standardized approach for benchmarking. By unifying the process of benchmark construction, it can facilitate more consistent method comparisons and provides a foundation for broader, more flexible, and more sustainable benchmarking efforts.

papers.title: Generative augmentation recovers prognostic disease signatures from underpowered transcriptomic datasets
papers.abstract: Identifying reliable gene-expression signatures from small transcriptomic datasets remains challenging. We present GeneLift, a framework that augments underpowered datasets using Gaussian mixture modelling in an analytically invertible latent space, retains genes reproducibly recovered across augmentations, and dates each against the literature using EvidenceClock, a Bayesian PubMed co-occurrence score, as antecedent, subsequent or unreported. Across 52 microarray and RNA-seq datasets spanning breast cancer, ovarian cancer, diabetes, sepsis and tuberculosis, GeneLift recovered candidate genes missed by standard differential expression analysis in all five diseases, including 326 in breast cancer and 976 in ovarian cancer. These candidates carried disease-specific literature support, including genes reported up to 18 years later such as the survival-associated ARL4D, and stratified overall survival in independent cohorts: TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC (log-rank P=6e-21 and 1e-42) and TCGA high-grade serous ovarian cancer (P=1e-37). In benchmarking, Gaussian mixture modelling outperformed more computationally intensive transformer-based generative adversarial networks. Together, GeneLift and EvidenceClock provide an efficient, reproducible framework for recovering prognostically informative signatures from underpowered transcriptomic studies.

papers.title: DiffDriver Detects Context-Associated Selection of Cancer Driver Genes
papers.abstract: Positive selection of somatic mutations is a driving force for cancer progression. Growing evidence shows that the emergence of a driver mutation in a tumor sample depends on individual-specific contexts, for example environmental exposures or the germline genetic background. Mutations in a driver gene could potentially bring different growth advantages in different contexts, resulting in differential selection of genes in varying contexts. Identifying which contexts modulate selection strength provides critical insights into the selection forces driving tumorigenesis. However, due to the sparsity of somatic mutations and heterogeneous background mutational process across positions and individuals, identification of differential selection has limited power with current statistical tools and is prone to false positives. To address this, we developed a powerful statistical method, DiffDriver, that identifies associations between contexts and selection strength of a driver gene across individuals. DiffDriver accounted for variations of mutation rates across bases and individuals, while taking advantage of functional information of sequences to improve power. In simulations, DiffDriver reduced false positives and boosted power compared to current methods. Multiple individual-level factors created significant heterogeneity in the strength of selection acting on driver genes: 24.3% of driver genes showed differential selection in at least one of the clinical traits studied, and 8.2% of genes had differential selection in different tumor immune subtypes. These results provide insights into the context-associated forces driving cancer evolution.

papers.title: scTGCL: A Transformer-Based Graph Contrastive Learning Approach for Efficiently Clustering Single-Cell RNA-seq Data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables characterization of cellular heterogeneity at unprecedented resolution. However, accurate clustering of scRNA-seq data remains challenging due to high dimensionality, dropout-induced sparsity, and technical noise. Existing contrastive learning methods usually create augmented views by perturbing gene expression values, so the uncertainty in cell-cell relationships caused by dropout events is not properly modeled. Results: We propose scTGCL, a novel Transformer-based graph contrastive learning framework that learns robust and discriminative cell representations directly from gene expression data. scTGCL employs multi-head self-attention to adaptively construct weighted cell-cell graphs and a Transformer encoder to generate cell embeddings from them, capturing diverse biological relationships. For contrastive augmentation, we apply feature-level gene masking together with attention masking that randomly drops edges of the learned attention matrices, enabling the model to withstand dropout events and technical noise. A symmetric contrastive loss maximizes agreement between original and augmented representations, while joint optimization with reconstruction and imputation losses preserves biological interpretability. Extensive experiments on twenty real and simulated scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that scTGCL achieves the highest average performance among nine state-of-the-art baseline methods in clustering accuracy, normalized mutual information, and adjusted Rand index, while also achieving superior imputation performance and substantially lower runtime on large-scale datasets. Furthermore, biological analysis confirms that the learned clusters align with known cell types and yield biologically interpretable pathway enrichment, validating the utility of scTGCL for downstream cell annotation and marker gene discovery. Availability and Implementation: The source code and test data are freely available at GitHub (https://github.com/ShoaibAbdullahKhan/scTGCL)

papers.title: A New Information Theoretic Approach Shows that Mixture Models Outperform Partition Models for Phylogenetic Analyses of Amino Acid Data
papers.abstract: Partition and mixture models are widely employed in Maximum Likelihood phylogenetic analyses of large genomic datasets. Comparing the fit of the two types of models has been challenging, because standard information-theoretic approaches cannot be applied. Mixture models are increasingly popular for the analysis of amino acid datasets and can lead to different conclusions compared to partition models. This raises an important question - which type of model tends to perform better? Susko et al. (2026) recently introduced the marginal Akaike information criterion (mAIC), which allows mixture models and partition models to be directly compared for the first time. Here, we use the mAIC and a range of other approaches to compare the fit of mixture and partition models across a diverse set of empirical amino acid datasets. We show that the mAIC favours mixture models in all the datasets we examined. This has important implications for interpreting empirical analyses and suggests that continued development of mixture models is an important avenue for future research.

papers.title: pamiR: INVESTIGATING PLANT CELLS ONE ORGANELLE AT A TIME
papers.abstract: Plant cell biochemistry is highly compartmentalized. Hence, forward genetic screening in an organelle-specific manner holds great potential to reveal novel loci controlling cell physiology. However, conventional forward genetics is a) limited by functional redundancy that can mask phenotypes in plant gene families and b) lacks organelle specificity. Here, we present the plastid-focused artificial microRNA (pamiR) resource designed to silence individual nuclear genes or co-targetable gene-family subsets encoding the organelle's proteome. The library contains 2,285 artificial microRNAs directed against 2,202 genes selected from a plastid-enriched, proteomics-supported target set. The constructs are expressed by a constitutive UBQ10 promoter in a binary vector carrying the FAST seed-fluorescence marker, allowing transformant selection before germination. Two proof-of-concept screens, one using photosynthetic phenotyping and one using paclobutrazol, a gibberellin biosynthesis inhibitor, recovered lines with phenotypes previously associated with simultaneous perturbation of multiple members of redundant plastid gene families such as light-harvesting complex b1 (LHCB1), K+ efflux antiporter (KEA), and 9-cis-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase (NCED). We experimentally confirmed specific target depletion for selected candidates, including paralogue-resolved LHCB1 depletion by mass spectrometry, and provide predicted off-target annotations for all 2,285 guides. Untargeted LHCB family members remained unchanged, and across the proteins included in the proteome-wide differential-abundance analysis, no additional significantly decreased protein was detected. KEA1 immunoreactive signal also fell below the immunoblot detection limit in pamiRkea1/2 and an independent KEA1/KEA2 amiRNA line. Together, these data establish pamiR as a plastid-specific screening resource and provide a framework for prioritizing and independently validating candidate phenotypes.

papers.title: Dual reinforcement-learning network modules for modeling decision-making with multiple strategies
papers.abstract: Animals and humans use multiple behavioral strategies to perform tasks. However, neural implementations of multiple strategies remain elusive, as some studies propose distinct pathways, while others observe overlapping brain regions associated with strategies. We propose a hybrid deep reinforcement learning (H-DRL) method, in which one network model implements model-free and inference-based behaviors through synaptic plasticity and recurrent activity. H-DRL uses a single updating rule and switches the strategy according to task demands without an explicit arbitrator. H-DRL reproduced mixed strategies of humans in a two-step task. In the mouse perceptual decision-making task, H-DRL adapted the recurrent dynamics with rich learning when the task condition required inference-based behavior, while adopting model-free behavior with lazy learning for a simple condition. The activity of H-DRL units showed condition-dependent maintenance of previous events, consistent with orbitofrontal cortical activity in mice. Our model provides a unified view that one cortical network automatically determines strategies in use depending on task conditions.

papers.title: Horizontal transfer of an antimicrobial peptide across insects
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are key defence molecules of the innate immune system. Understanding the origins of AMPs can help to explain how immune systems acquire novelty and vary in their defence capacities. However, AMPs evolve rapidly, and so the origins of similar AMPs across organisms is often unclear. Furthermore, false negatives due to low search sensitivity are common and can hinder confident annotations about true absences. As a result, understanding whether similar AMP genes found in diverse organisms represent ancestral molecules or evolutionary novelties has been challenging. Here, we present evidence of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of the antifungal peptide gene Drosomycin across insects. We show that in Diptera, the presence of Drosomycin is restricted to the Drosophila Melanogaster species group and additionally the distant relative Drosophila busckii. We go on to recover Drosomycin genes in cockroaches (Blattodea), mantises (Mantodea), katydids (Orthoptera), beetles (Coleoptera), parasitic wasps (Hymenoptera), and a recently acquired and pseudogenized Drosomycin locus in Liposcelis booklice (Psocodea), but not other insects. Explaining this diversity through shared ancestry requires at least 60 independent loss events, or just nine HGT events. Previous studies have suggested that similar AMPs found across divergent species reflect conservation from a common ancestor, or due to their small size, that they arose via convergent evolution. Our findings suggest horizontal gene transfer can be responsible for the presence of some AMP genes scattered across the tree of life. By presenting a mechanism through which immune systems can acquire novelty, our study also suggests a possible explanation for certain lineage-specific defence competencies against infectious disease. While loss of AMP genes is well-documented, here we suggest gain of AMPs can occur just as suddenly.

papers.title: Decoding the physicochemical basis of taxonomy preferences in protein design models
papers.abstract: Recent improvements in machine-learning protein design have enabled models to generate more promising candidate sequences than can be experimentally tested, placing increasing reliance on scores whose determinants remain poorly understood. Here, we profile 14 models grouped by scoring context to disentangle taxonomic and biophysical contributions. Controlling for protein family and measured biophysical properties removes 91 to 93% of apparent species-level variation in backbone-conditioned scores, compared with only 15 to 29% in sequence-only likelihoods. Species rankings also diverge: backbone-conditioned models favour archaeal and thermophilic proteins, whereas sequence-only models favour eukaryotic proteins. Backbone-conditioned scores instead reflect compactness, packing and charge, with these biases propagating into redesigned sequences. Further training ProteinMPNN on extremophile secretomes alters designed surface chemistry with minimal structural cost but largely preserves species rankings. Together, these findings show how scoring context and training data shape what protein design models favour, with implications for which sequences are generated and prioritised for experimental testing.

papers.title: PhaseICA: Resolving Individual-Specific Macroscale Brain Propagations
papers.abstract: Understanding complex dynamics from spatiotemporal signals requires robust tools capable of decoding reoccurring patterns. Traditional ICA methods often overlook the spatially non-stationarity nature of brain activity across both the frequency and spatial domains. We propose a novel data-driven approach, named PhaseICA, designed to extract reoccurring spatiotemporal patterns, referred to as brain waves. Unlike conventional ICA methods that focus solely on amplitude, PhaseICA incorporates phase information directly into the component estimation, preserving the nonstationary property that real-valued ICA methods typically discard. The method performs spatial independence optimization in the complex domain by minimizing a complex entropy bound over the eigenvectors of Hilbert-transformed signals. The proposed method captures spatial propagation across brain regions with interpretable and compact representations, offering a promising foundation for decoding brain dynamic systems and revealing the temporal relationship of regions.

papers.title: TAFFISH: shell-native command-level reproducibility for bioinformatics
papers.abstract: Bioinformatics analyses often rely on shell commands and small shell scripts whose executable context is difficult to preserve, inspect and reuse. TAFFISH addresses this gap by packaging command-line tool calls and lightweight shell flows as installable, versioned and inspectable executable units. Through a curated public Hub, TAFFISH indexes command interfaces, execution backends, platform constraints, release metadata and smoke-test/validation records. Together, these components provide a command-level reproducibility layer that works directly in ordinary shells and can also be invoked from existing workflow systems.

papers.title: Estimating population range distributions from animal tracking data
papers.abstract: Quantifying the space requirements of a population is a fundamental problem in spatial ecology, particularly as it relates to the identification of important utilization areas and the designation of protected areas for conservation and wildlife management. Traditionally, population space use estimation techniques scale up from the individual to the population level by aggregating individual animal tracks and then using a single pooled distribution estimator like minimum convex polygons (MCP) or kernel density estimation (KDE). These techniques fail to account for the high levels of temporal autocorrelation in modern tracking datasets, and estimates are often sensitive to the number of individuals sampled. We introduce a new population kernel density estimator (PKDE) that accounts for temporal autocorrelation in tracking data, propagates uncertainty from the individual to the population level, accounts for inter-individual variation when scaling up to the population level, and is not highly sensitive to the number of individuals tracked. Through a combination of simulated data and empirical GPS tracking datasets from three species: (a) grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis); (b) lowland tapir (Tapirus terrestris); and (c) bobcat (Lynx rufus), we demonstrate that PKDE produces minimally biased estimates of population-level space use compared to conventional methods like MCP and KDE. The use of conventional estimators can lead to substantial underestimation of population space usage, making them unsuitable for area-based conservation planning. The statistically efficient PKDE estimator provides relatively unbiased estimates of space use with fewer individuals sampled. This method has been made available as a function in the ctmm R package.

papers.title: KLinterSel: Assessing Spatial Concordance among Selective Sweep Detection Methods, with an Application to the common cockle (Cerastoderma edule)
papers.abstract: Detecting signals of natural selection, including selective sweeps, in genomic data often involves applying several methods in parallel. Regions identified by multiple approaches are usually considered strong candidates, as agreement among methods is often taken as supporting evidence. However, the extent to which such overlaps exceed random expectations is rarely evaluated formally. When genomic elements are not independent, coincident candidate sites may arise from the underlying structure of the data rather than from genuine methodological concordance. To address this problem, we introduce two complementary statistical tests designed to evaluate whether the observed overlap among candidate sites detected by different methods exceeds what would be expected by chance. The first is a fast parametric test based on a sequentially conditioned hypergeometric framework that evaluates k-way intersections among candidate sets across genomic windows. The second relies on Monte Carlo simulations and compares the observed inter-method distance profiles with those expected under random association, taking into account the empirical distribution of SNPs along the genome. By capturing different aspects of concordance, these approaches allow agreement among methods to be assessed across multiple spatial scales. Both tests are implemented in the program KLinterSel, which also identifies clusters of candidate sites detected by different selection-detection methods within a user-defined distance threshold. We illustrate its application using candidate loci associated with resistance of the common cockle (Cerastoderma edule) to the parasite Marteilia cochillia. The software is written in Python and is available on GitHub together with documentation and precompiled executables for major operating systems.

papers.title: Lymphatic dissemination is a major route of systemic invasion by diverse extracellular bacteria in soft tissue infection
papers.abstract: Extracellular bacterial pathogens cause substantial global mortality, yet how they disseminate from peripheral tissues into the bloodstream remains poorly understood. Systemic infection is typically attributed to direct vascular invasion, with draining lymph nodes considered terminal sites of containment. Here, using a murine soft-tissue infection model, we show that onward lymphatic dissemination from a distant tissue site through sequential draining lymph nodes is a major route of systemic invasion across diverse extracellular bacterial pathogens. Clinical isolates of Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Streptococcus agalactiae spread from local draining lymph nodes to downstream lymph nodes and systemic organs. Non-draining lymph nodes, exposed to the same systemic circulation as downstream draining lymph nodes, contained markedly fewer bacteria even during bacteraemia, indicating lymphatic rather than haematogenous spread. Staphylococcus aureus was a notable exception, remaining largely restricted to local draining nodes with limited systemic spread. Deletion of the S. agalactiae capsular polysaccharide significantly reduced lymphatic and systemic spread without significantly reducing bacterial burden at the infection site, showing that capsule can promote lymphatic dissemination independently of local bacterial burden. In contrast, digestion of the secreted exopolysaccharide of P. aeruginosa did not alter dissemination, distinguishing the impact of surface-attached capsule from secreted exopolysaccharide. These findings establish lymphatic dissemination through sequential lymph nodes as a major invasion route across key extracellular bacterial pathogens, with important implications for systemic disease and immunity.

papers.title: Rare mutations implicate CGE interneurons as a vulnerable axis of cognitive deficits across psychiatric disorders
papers.abstract: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia (SCZ) share genetic risk factors, including rare high penetrance single nucleotide variants and copy number variants (CNVs), and exhibit both overlapping and distinct clinical phenotypes. Cognitive deficits and intellectual disability-critical predictors of long-term outcomes-are common to both conditions. To investigate shared and disorder-specific neurobiological impact of highly penetrant rare mutations in ASD and SCZ, we analyzed human single-nucleus whole-brain sequencing data to identify strongly affected brain cell types. Our analysis revealed Caudal Ganglionic Eminence (CGE)-derived GABAergic interneurons as a critical nexus for cognitive deficits across these disorders. Notably, genes within 22q11.2 deletions, known to confer a high risk of SCZ, ASD, and cognitive impairment, showed a strong expression bias toward vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing cells (VIP+) among CGE subtypes. To explore VIP+ GABAergic interneuron perturbations in the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome in vivo, we examined their activity in the Df(16)A+/- mouse model during a spatial navigation task and observed reduced activity along with altered responses to random rewards. At the population level, VIP+ interneurons exhibited impaired spatial encoding and diminished subtype-specific activity suggesting deficient disinhibition in CA1 microcircuits in the hippocampus, a region essential for learning and memory. Overall, these results demonstrate the crucial role of CGE-derived interneurons in mediating cognitive processes that are disrupted across a range of psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: Optimisation of single-nuclei isolation and RNA sequencing of parasitic nematodes
papers.abstract: Single-cell/nuclei transcriptomics has revolutionised our understanding of cell, tissue, and organismal biology in humans and model organisms across health and disease. However, for non-model species, reassessment and refinement of conventional methods is needed to address novel technical and biological challenges. Here, we evaluate three established nuclei isolation protocols and, building on these experiences, develop an optimised protocol for single-nuclei isolation of parasitic nematodes (SNIP). SNIP recovered 1.7- to 4.1-fold more nuclei than the three established protocols, and 3.2-fold more RNA per nucleus than the best-performing of these. We validated SNIP across macroscopic and microscopic life stages and both sexes of two phylogenetically distinct gastrointestinal nematodes, Haemonchus contortus and Trichuris muris, and used it to generate single-nuclei RNA-seq data revealing sex- and stage-specific gene expression and putative tissue-specific expression in both species. By enabling flexibility with frozen samples and consistent recovery across diverse parasitic nematode life stages, SNIP provides a practical foundation for building cell and nuclei atlases in other non-model species, toward advancing understanding from fundamental biology to infection and disease.

papers.title: Drinking-Water 4,4'-Methylenedianiline Establishes a Longitudinally Tractable Mouse Model of Cholestatic Liver Injury
papers.abstract: Longitudinal studies of liver injury require models that can be maintained with simple administration, low procedure-related stress, and acceptable survival. Drinking-water thioacetamide (TAA-DW) is useful for this purpose, but it mainly produces centrilobular hepatocellular injury. Few drinking-water models are available for cholestatic liver injury. Here, we tested whether 4,4-methylenedianiline (MDA), a known bile-duct-damaging hepatotoxicant, can be used to build a practical drinking-water model of cholestatic liver injury in mice. Male C57BL/6JJcl mice received MDA in drinking water for up to 28 days. A route- and administration-schedule-matched TAA-DW model was used as a reference. Drinking-water MDA (MDA-DW) caused sustained ALT elevation without observed mortality under the tested regimen. Compared with TAA-DW, MDA-DW produced stronger cholestatic biochemical features, including increased ALP, TBIL, and TCHO. Histology showed bile duct hyperplasia with degeneration, periportal/peribiliary fibrosis, and scattered focal hepatocellular necrosis. Whole-slide image analysis supported the distinct lesion distribution between MDA-DW and TAA-DW. Early time-resolved multimodal profiling showed model-specific responses: MDA-DW showed ALT elevation around Days 2-3, increased CD8-positive T cells on Day 8, and enrichment of fibrinolysis-related gene sets, whereas TAA-DW showed a sharp early injury peak and transient eosinophil increase. Impact Statement: This study expands the range of drinking-water liver injury models by providing a low-mortality MDA-DW model with cholestatic liver injury. The model offers a simple platform for time-resolved studies of liver injury progression, tissue remodeling, and model-specific inflammatory responses.

papers.title: Longitudinal Imaging in a Mouse Model of Focal Cortical Dysplasia Reveals Lesion Expansion and Loss of Pre-Discharge Neuronal Recruitment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective: Focal cortical dysplasia type II (FCD II) is a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy, yet how its lesional circuits behave and change over time in vivo has not been directly observed. Methods: We used a mouse model of FCD II carrying the patient-derived gain-of-function mTORp.L2427P variant introduced by in utero electroporation. Through a chronic cranial window over the lesion, we performed repeated in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of identified dysmorphic neurons, pyramidal cells, and VIP interneurons at defined time points, combined with video-EEG monitoring, to determine seizure status and relate cellular activity to interictal discharges. Results: The lesion was not static in adulthood. Dysplastic cortex expanded progressively. This expansion occurred without the tenascin R/C accumulation reported in human FCD II, and was partly explained by continued somatic growth of dysmorphic neurons. Dysmorphic neurons were generally hypoactive; in seizing mice, both dysmorphic and pyramidal cell activity progressively declined, whereas VIP interneuron activity increased slightly in non-seizing animals. In non-seizing lesional cortex, neurons were reliably recruited immediately before interictal discharges. By late disease stages, pre-discharge recruitment had weakened to the point that lesional layer 2/3 neurons were no more active before discharges than expected by chance. Significance: These findings recast FCD II as a lesion that continues to remodel structurally and functionally throughout adulthood, and does so most markedly in animals with seizures. Growth, a cell-type-specific shift in spontaneous activity, and a progressive loss of the lesion's temporal lead over interictal discharges together suggest that FCD II is a dynamically evolving lesion whose relationship to epileptiform activity changes over time. If the lesion progressively loses its generative role, the window in which removing it can arrest the disease is finite, consistent with clinical evidence favoring earlier surgery.

papers.title: Sex-dependent Aβ RA-Low threshold mechanoreceptors alteration in diabetic conditions
papers.abstract: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is a major complication of diabetes that profoundly affects quality of life, yet its cellular mechanisms remain poorly defined. Neuropathic pain and sensory loss in DPN are thought to arise from progressive alterations in peripheral nerves usually described as a glove-stocking distribution, but the specific contribution of sensory neuron subtypes has received little attention. Here, we focused on A{beta} rapidly adapting low-threshold mechanoreceptors (A{beta} RA-LTMRs), a large-diameter sensory neuron subtype best known for mediating touch and vibratory sensation. Using an intersectional genetic approach, we generated AdvillinCre; MafAFlpO; Ai65 mice, allowing us to selectively label MafA-expressing sensory neuronal populations, which we identified as A{beta} RA-LTMRs. We provide the first detailed characterization of how diet-induced type 2 diabetes alters A{beta} RA-LTMRs. After 16 weeks of high-fat diet (HFD), we observed striking sex-dependent effects. Male mice developed impaired glucose tolerance, mechanical hypoalgesia, and thermal hyperalgesia, which correlated with a decrease of A{beta} RA-LTMR central projections in the dorsal horn. By contrast, female mice showed no changes in either their glycemic status or their sensory sensitivity. These findings demonstrate that A{beta} RA-LTMRs are vulnerable to early diabetes-induced alterations in a sex-dependent manner and highlight distinct peripheral versus central mechanisms contributing to sensory dysfunction.

papers.title: Replacing H2O with D2O in cryo-EM reduces radiation damage in biological samples
papers.abstract: Radiation damage limits the resolution achievable in electron microscopy of biological specimens. Hydrogen is the most abundant atom in these specimens, and its low mass maximizes the recoil energy it receives from incident electrons, making it the atom most readily lost under the beam. Substitution of hydrogen by deuterium halves this recoil energy and makes the bonds involved slightly harder to break, yet its protective effect on vitrified protein crystals has not been tested. Using cryogenic electron diffraction at 200 kV, we show that hen egg-white lysozyme crystals grown directly in D2O withstand a dose 1.7 times higher than crystals grown in H2O before their Bragg intensity at 10-7[A] falls to 1/e (13.2 {+/-} 1.0 against 7.7 {+/-} 0.4 e-/[A]2), with every D2O-grown crystal outlasting every H2O-grown crystal. The protection is achieved with deuteration confined mainly to the solvent and the exchangeable hydrogens at the protein surface, which form the hydrogen bonds that hold the crystal lattice together. The protein itself need not be deuterated by expression in deuterated media. Direct crystallization in D2O involves only a single substitution in the mother liquor and offers an accessible strategy to extend the usable dose in electron diffraction of protein crystals.

papers.title: A Pilot Study Investigating the Impact of Oral Probiotic Supplementation on the Vaginal Microbiota and Aspects of Well-being
papers.abstract: This double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled pilot study investigated the effects of a six-strain probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus crispatus CUL40 and L. gasseri CUL09 on vaginal microbiota composition and well-being in 40 women with recurrent vaginal discomfort. Participants received either the probiotic (20 billion colony-forming units/day) or placebo for 20 days. Vaginal samples collected at baseline, midpoint and endpoint were analysed using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, microbial culture and species- and strain-specific quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Vaginal symptoms and broader well-being were recorded daily. At endpoint, vaginal detection of CUL40 and CUL09 was significantly higher in the probiotic group, with neither strain detected in the placebo group. Viable L. crispatus CUL40 was recovered from vaginal cultures, whereas viable CUL09 was not recovered. L. gasseri relative abundance was significantly higher in the probiotic group at midpoint and endpoint, while Gardnerella counts were significantly lower at endpoint. Probiotic supplementation significantly influenced beta diversity over time between groups, although community state types remained broadly stable. During the second half of the intervention, rates of vaginal itchiness, burning sensation and anxiousness were significantly lower in the probiotic group. Bloating was also less frequent throughout the intervention. These findings demonstrate increased vaginal detection of orally administered probiotic strains, including recovery of viable CUL40, alongside changes in vaginal microbiota composition and reduced vaginal discomfort. Larger studies are warranted to confirm these exploratory findings and establish longer-term effects. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07364383).

papers.title: Rapid femtosecond laser trenching accelerates cryo-electron tomography lamella workflows
papers.abstract: Transmission electron microscopy requires electron-transparent specimens, typically below 200 nm thick. For cellular and tissue samples this is typically achieved by focused ion-beam (FIB) thinning to form lamellae. Milling times scale with specimen thickness, and high-pressure-frozen specimens more than 10 m thick can take up to 2 hours per lamella. We present a pre-processing approach in which bulk material is removed by ultrashort-pulse laser ablation prior to milling, rapidly generating large trenches in vitrified grids under cryogenic conditions and leaving material to be finished by conventional milling to yield electron-transparent lamellae. Laser ablation completes in seconds (4 seconds per pattern), compared with minutes to tens of minutes for FIB trench milling, and introduces negligible damage to the final lamellae. By replacing the most time-intensive, contamination-sensitive bulk-removal steps with seconds-long laser trenching, this open-source approach reduces time-to-lamellae, increasing throughput and preserves compatibility with standard cryo-FIB/SEM polishing and cryo-ET data-collection pipelines.

papers.title: Decoding the Physical Mechanisms of Protein-Small Molecule Association by Multiscale Kinetic Monte-Carlo Simulations
papers.abstract: Protein-small molecule association involves multiple recognition stages governed by distinct physical interactions, yet resolving their kinetic contributions remains computationally challenging. Here, we develop a multiscale Monte Carlo framework that combines an atomistic, conformationally flexible ligand with a coarse-grained protein binding pocket and an atomistic steric envelope. Association is decomposed into three stages: molecular encounter, pocket entry, and productive binding. We evaluate the framework using ten protein-ligand complexes representing nine distinct targets, with experimentally derived association rates spanning nearly four orders of magnitude. Simulated pocket-entry rates exhibit the strongest correspondence with experimental kinetics (Pearson r = 0.617; Spearman {rho} = 0.758), whereas productive-binding rates show closer agreement in absolute magnitude. Systematic perturbations of electrostatic interactions, hydrophobic attraction, hydrogen bonding, and ligand torsional flexibility reveal stage-dependent sensitivities. Initial encounter is comparatively insensitive to these perturbations, while hydrophobic attraction and conformational flexibility influence pocket entry. Productive binding exhibits additional sensitivity to local interactions, with excessive hydrogen-bond strengthening potentially hindering native-pose formation. Probability-derived kinetic-stage barriers and normalized mechanism descriptors further reveal heterogeneous recognition behavior across protein targets. Together, this framework provides a computationally efficient and interpretable approach for investigating protein-ligand association pathways and their physical determinants across diverse molecular systems.

papers.title: Host brain infection induces RNAi epimutation in Mucor circinelloides and enhances blood-brain barrier invasion
papers.abstract: Mucorales fungi cause mucormycosis, a rapidly progressive invasive fungal disease with high mortality, particularly in immunocompromised patients and in severe disseminated infections. Central nervous system involvement is among the most devastating manifestations of mucormycosis, yet the mechanisms that enable Mucorales to adapt to the brain environment remain poorly understood. In Mucor species, RNA interference (RNAi) can generate reversible heritable epimutations that silence specific genes without altering DNA sequence, providing a transient and reversible mechanism for antifungal drug resistance. Here, we show that host brain infection induces RNAi-dependent silencing of endogenous fungal loci that promote central nervous system adaptation. Small RNA sequencing of Mucor circinelloides recovered from infected mouse organs identified seven brain epimutation loci, named bepA to bepG, that accumulated small RNAs preferentially after brain infection. Among these, bepA encodes a conserved mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)-like serine/threonine kinase related to cell wall integrity signaling. Deletion of the bepA gene confers resistance to the calcineurin inhibitors FK506 and cyclosporin A, allowing hyphal growth under conditions that impair calcineurin-dependent morphogenesis. BepA modulates FK506-induced MAPK signaling and controls a transcriptional program enriched in cell-wall remodeling genes. To model fungal central nervous system entry by a filamentous fungal pathogen, we established a human blood-brain barrier transwell platform that quantifies Mucor migration across brain endothelial monolayers. This model revealed that bepA mutation enhances fungal migration across brain endothelial monolayers without detectable changes in electrical barrier resistance. These findings identify brain-induced RNAi epimutation as a mechanism of organ-specific fungal adaptation and reveal reversible silencing of a MAPK-like kinase as a route to enhanced central nervous system invasion.

papers.title: Uncoupling of STING Accumulation and Activation upon Chromosome-Derived Extrachromosomal Circular DNA Formation
papers.abstract: The innate immune system maintains cellular homeostasis by recognizing cytosolic nucleic acids. While the cGAS-STING pathway is well characterized in detecting non-self-DNA, its response to self-DNA originating from the host nucleus remains unclear. Extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA), a form of self-DNA often enriched in cancer, has been implicated in immune modulation, yet its ability to activate cGAS-STING remains unresolved. Here, we developed a Cre-loxP-based eccDNA reporter system, where Cre-mediated eccDNA formation triggers expression of the fluorescent protein mCitrine, enabling time-resolved, single-cell analysis of chromosome-derived eccDNA dynamics and STING activation. Using an mRuby3-STING reporter, we found that low-dose plasmid transfection induced STING activation, as evidenced by modest STING accumulation and downstream cytokine induction. Cells carrying chromosome-derived cytosolic eccDNA also showed a modest, cGAS-dependent accumulation of STING. However, this accumulation was uncoupled from detectable STING-Ser366 phosphorylation or induction of downstream cytokines. These findings indicate that chromosome-derived eccDNA does not drive detectable STING signaling under the conditions tested, and that STING accumulation and its activation are mechanistically separable steps. This work provides a foundation for understanding the immunological roles of eccDNA in genome instability and cancer.

papers.title: Hsp10 Targets the C-Terminus of α-Synuclein to Inhibit Secondary Nucleation and Remodel Labile Fibrils
papers.abstract: Aggregation of a-synuclein is a central pathological feature of Parkinsons disease and related synucleinopathies. The co-chaperonin Hsp10, a component of the Hsp60/Hsp10 chaperonin system, has recently been proposed to possess independent chaperone activity and has been found to co-localize with a-synuclein aggregates in diseased brains, suggesting a role in regulating a-synuclein assembly. Here, we combine solution NMR spectroscopy, cryo-electron microscopy, and kinetic analyses to define a multistage mechanism by which Hsp10 modulates a-synuclein aggregation. Hsp10 transiently interacts with monomeric a-synuclein, with residues on the inner surface and top-loop regions of Hsp10 primarily engaging the acidic C-terminal region of a-synuclein. Hsp10 exerts a concentration-dependent, biphasic effect on aggregation, accelerating fibrillization at substoichiometric concentrations while inhibiting de novo aggregation at higher concentrations through suppression of secondary nucleation. Furthermore, Hsp10 decorates fibril surfaces through interactions with the exposed a-synuclein C-terminus, thereby limiting secondary nucleation. Hsp10 also promotes the disaggregation of thermodynamically labile fibrillar fragments. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for Hsp10-mediated regulation of a-synuclein assembly and expand the functional landscape of Hsp10 beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial protein folding.

papers.title: Large-scale integrated single-cell analysis reveals molecular subtypes and microenvironmental remodeling in cutaneous T cell lymphoma
papers.abstract: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL) comprises a clinically and molecularly heterogeneous group of skin-homing non-Hodgkin lymphomas for which robust biomarkers remain limited. Prior single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have provided important insights into CTCL biology, but many of these prior studies have been limited by small sample sizes and focused on niche questions of interest. Additionally, many studies have suffered from pseudoreplication, resulting in inflated test statistics and reduced external validity. Here, we assembled and integrated scRNA-seq data spanning 244 unique samples and 132 patients across CTCL, healthy control (HC), and benign inflammatory dermatoses (BID) conditions, generating the most diverse atlas of CTCL to date. Following identification of malignant cell populations and heterogeneous, within-sample gene expression alterations, we applied pseudobulk aggregation and robust linear mixed-effects modeling to nominate recurrent changes across this highly heterogeneous patient cohort. Interrogation of the skin microenvironment identified significant compositional and cell type-specific expression changes in CTCL lesions as compared to control lesions and across clinical stages of disease. Finally, we used unbiased clustering to identify stable, molecularly defined subtypes of disease that were predictive of outcome in an independent dataset. Together, this study provides a rigorous analysis of the most diverse scRNA-seq dataset of CTCL ever compiled, nominating specific alterations in cell type composition and gene expression across malignant cell and microenvironmental populations with significant clinical implications.

papers.title: Histological morphometric correlates of MRI-defined cortical thinning in temporal lobe epilepsy
papers.abstract: Large-scale MRI studies have consistently demonstrated progressive and age-accelerated neocortical thinning in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). These findings are frequently interpreted as evidence of cumulative neurodegeneration. However, the histopathological substrates underlying MRI-confirmed cortical thinning in epilepsy remain poorly defined. In particular, it is unknown whether cortical thinning reflects irreversible neuronal loss or potentially reversible epilepsy-related network alterations in cortical microstructure. We analysed the resected middle temporal gyrus from 117 individuals undergoing surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy, including cases with (n= 74) or without hippocampal sclerosis (HS) and 12 cases with additional temporal lobe sclerosis (TLS, or Focal Cortical Dysplasia IIIa), defined by a distinct pattern of cytoarchitectural reorganisation and gliosis involving superficial layers. All cases were stratified by the presence or absence of pre-operative MRI-defined cortical thinning of the middle temporal gyrus, quantified using CAT12 relative to healthy controls. On NeuN-immuno-labelled sections using automated image analysis we assessed neuronal spatial distributions relative to their size and packing density; relative cortical layer thickness and sulcal-gyral cytoarchitectural variation were also quantified. MRI-defined cortical thinning was not associated with diffuse neuronal loss. Instead, thinning correlated with increased neuronal density and altered cell-size spatial organisation in superficial and deep layers, particularly in right temporal lobe epilepsy cases with HS. There was limited evidence of layer-specific laminar thinning, being confined to layer VI in the right TLE/HS group only. Of note, TLS cases did not show either cortical thinning on MRI or laminar thinning on histology compared to cases without TLS but altered neuronal densities and composition that was not confined to the superficial cortex. MRI cortical thinning was also characterised by attenuation of normal sulcal/gyral cytoarchitectural variations suggesting disruption of cortical architectural gradients. In contrast, cases with HS but without MRI cortical thinning demonstrated loss of the expected inter-hemispheric cytoarchitectural asymmetry, indicating a distinct pathological process dissociated from thinning. Clinical-pathological correlations were lateralised, including age of onset, further supporting distinct mechanisms contributing to MRI cortical thinning between left and right TLE. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MRI-defined cortical thinning in epilepsy reflects progressive neuronal degeneration. Rather than laminar neuronal loss and atrophy, thinning was associated with altered neuronal packing and cell-size distributions between layers. This points towards altered neuropil volumes, including myelin content and dendritic remodelling, in turn suggesting potentially reversible dynamic seizure- or network-related processes.

papers.title: Conserved Brain-Associated CD8+ T Cell Programs and Their Regulation by the Brain Microenvironment
papers.abstract: CD8+ T cells are increasingly recognized as components of the healthy brain, yet whether their specialized functional characteristics are conserved across species and how the brain microenvironment regulates their effector programs remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized brain-associated CD8+ T cells in the common marmoset and investigated their regulation by brain-derived signals. Flow cytometric analysis revealed a substantial population of CD8+ T cells in the healthy marmoset brain parenchyma that exhibited high IFN-{gamma} competence but minimal granzyme B (GzmB) expression, resembling the functional phenotype previously identified in mice. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of mouse and marmoset CD8+ T cells revealed tissue-associated transcriptional heterogeneity and distinct differentiation- and effector-associated programs. To investigate how the brain microenvironment shapes these characteristics, we exposed activated mouse CD8+ T cells to brain lysate and performed targeted CRISPR interference screening of 107 cell-surface receptor genes coupled with single-cell RNA sequencing. Brain lysate selectively reduced Gzmb and Ifng expression while increasing Tnf and Xcl1, indicating differential regulation of cytotoxic and inflammatory effector programs. Receptor perturbations revealed heterogeneous transcriptional responses and identified candidate pathways potentially involved in sensing brain-derived signals. Together, these findings identify shared functional characteristics of brain-associated CD8+ T cells across rodents and nonhuman primates and establish a framework for understanding how the neural microenvironment shapes adaptive immune function.

papers.title: Genomic and oceanographic evidence of reef connectivity across the western and central Indian Ocean
papers.abstract: Connectivity among coral populations, via larval dispersal, is one of the key mechanisms supporting reef recovery after climate-driven bleaching events. This study examines reef connectivity of remote atolls of the understudied central and western Indian Ocean seascape, focusing on a key reef-building species, Acropora aff. tenuis. Using genomic data from ultra-conserved elements alongside particle-tracking simulations, we investigate patterns of population structure and gene flow, and the influence of ocean currents. Results show asymmetrical connectivity: strong gene flow occurs within the Chagos Archipelago and between Chagos and the Inner Seychelles, highlighting their importance as regional larval sources. In contrast, the Outer Seychelles mainly functions as a larval sink, and IIes Glorieuses appears to be the least connected. Whilst population structure suggests a partially permeable dispersal barrier between the Inner and Outer Seychelles. Differences between genetic patterns and simulated ocean-driven dispersal suggest that ocean currents are not the only important driver of connectivity patterns. Additional factors, such as stepping-stone dispersal among atolls, fine-scale oceanographic processes, and species biology likely play important roles. Overall, we find widespread genomic connectivity across this seascape, which has positive implications for reef resilience, though future resilience will depend on frequency and severity of future bleaching events.

papers.title: Sensitivity of stochastic growth rate and lifetime reproductive output to kin effects: A nonlinear feedback model
papers.abstract: Humans exhibit a coevolutionary relationship between the trajectory of social evolution and senescence. A focal individual's kinship network is a function of his/her life history, while that network in turn shapes the focal individual's life history through kin effects on reproduction, generating a dynamic, nonlinear feedback loop across the population. Assessing directional selection on kin effects, therefore, requires explicitly modelling the feedback between the kinship network and life history. Here, we develop such a framework and apply it to examine selection pressures on the cooperative behaviour of closely related kin, including mothers, grandmothers, and older sisters. We hypothesise that the negative association of grandmothers, mothers, and older sisters (>10 years) with child mortality are under positive selection because increasing the absolute values of these kin effects would increase the stochastic growth rate. Furthermore, we hypothesise that the positive association of older sisters with child mortality is subject to negative selection, as increasing this effect would reduce the stochastic growth rate. We estimate kin-specific slope coefficients for child mortality using a Bayesian hierarchical model and solve a system of nonlinear equations linking kinship structure and survival to account for the nonlinear feedback between kinship and child survival. Thereafter, we compute stochastic sensitivities of both the stochastic growth rate and the mean lifetime reproductive output to these slope coefficients. Consistent with our hypotheses, all slope coefficients for kin presence on child mortality are negatively sensitive to both fitness metrics. We discuss the applications of our framework to examine the coevolution of social behaviours and senescence in age-structured populations.

papers.title: Multimodal functional characterization of the LDLR noncoding landscape
papers.abstract: The expression level of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) gene is a critical determinant of circulating low-density lipoprotein concentrations and the corresponding risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. While the importance of sterol response elements in LDLR transcriptional regulation has been firmly established, the functional contribution of other potential cis-regulatory elements (CREs) remains poorly understood. In this study, we developed and applied a variety of high throughput functional genomic tools to systematically interrogate the noncoding space at the LDLR locus. These included saturation CRISPR nuclease, CRISPR activation, and CRISPR inhibition screening as well as a massively parallel reporter assay. With each approach, we observed robust discrimination of control sequences and significant effects for other regions with a previously unrecognized influence on LDLR expression. The CREs identified by each modality were overlapping but distinct, both in relation to each other and to those regions predicted to harbor CRE activity. Collectively, our findings clarify the functional landscape of the LDLR locus and highlight the complementary nature of different functional genomic approaches to CRE identification.

papers.title: Anti-GABAB receptor autoimmunity causes cognitive decline by presynaptic pathology
papers.abstract: The GABAB receptor is a central regulator of neuronal transmission and excitability by pre- and postsynaptic mechanisms. Its dysfunction causes severe neurological disease, but the underlying pathomechanisms remain elusive. Here, we exploit a distinct CNS autoimmune disorder in which patients develop specific autoantibodies against GABAB receptors causing autoimmune encephalitis with severe memory dysfunction and epilepsy. We demonstrate that human autoantibodies target the sushi-domains of the GABAB receptor B1a subunit and the B2 subunit and interfere with presynaptic signaling. This specific presynaptic pathology results from exclusive functional antagonism of the B1a subunit and disrupts short- and long-term synaptic plasticity, abnormally amplifies hippocampal network oscillations and coupling in vivo, and ultimately impairs memory consolidation. Our results demonstrate that autoimmune presynaptic pathomechanisms alone are sufficient to interfere with memory processing, thus defining a causal link between molecular GABAB receptor disturbance, synaptic pathology, circuit dysfunction, and dementia distinct from classical neurodegenerative processes.

papers.title: Novel extracellular, extra-embryonic and intercellular γ-tubulin assemblies in mouse oocytes and preimplantation embryos
